# Preface of the Editor.

## Honored Reader,

No doubt the reasons for my silence until now regarding all the polemical writings <note>original: "Streit-Schrifften." These were the harsh theological pamphlets common in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> published against me since the year 1702 are not unknown; for they are clearly visible both in the preface to the *Supplements to the Church History* <note>original: "Supplementa der K. Hist." referring to Arnold's landmark *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie*.</note> as well as in the *Tract on Deviations and Temptations* <note>original: "Tract. von Abwegen und Versuchungen."</note> Book II, Chapter 1, Section 38 and following, as well as in the Appendix on page 609. Upon these stated grounds, I have been very well content to rest for these past seven years, and I have not needed to concern myself with the mockery that some have directed at this intention of mine; just as I have never regretted it to this hour, nor can I ever regret it.

(2.) Since then, however—as it was mentioned in the *Deviations* on page 610 that the refutation of the opponents would follow at the right time—it has pleased the Most High, who holds all things in His hand, to interrupt my purpose for a time through several friends. This happened partly through their Christianly-offered and actually-performed collaboration, and partly through the thorough presentation of many important motives as to why I ought to publish a summary defense <note>original: "Summarische Verantwortung." A formal account or legalistic response.</note>. The most prominent among these are: (1) my own limitation, which I had added in the cited writings, and even before that in the *Final Representation* <note>original: "Endlichen Vorstellung."</note> Chapter IV, Section 4—namely, that defensive writings are permissible where God’s honor and His pure truth require it, and where one can hope it will lead to good.

(3.) The second motivation was the ever-accumulating debts <note>Arnold uses "debts" (Schulden) metaphorically to mean the moral transgressions or errors of his critics.</note> of some critics <note>original: "Censorum."</note> (I speak, however, only of some), who, using the excuse <note>original: "evasion."</note> that their accusations would remain unanswered, exceeded their bounds in an increasingly irresponsible manner. To this came a third reason: namely, their vain glory, as if I now regretted the testimony I had given and that it was already completely nullified; and conversely, as if all their contradictions were irrefutable. The fourth cause was the noticeable damage done both to the known truths themselves and to many well-meaning souls. For a reader who is not fully experienced in historical matters <note>original: "in Historicis."</note> and other subjects, nor practiced in the mystery of godliness <note>original: "Gottseligkeit," a core Pietist term for practical, inward holiness.</note>, may be led astray by intricate and often very cunningly made counter-arguments, or perhaps even moved to participate in the same sins.

(4.) These and other spiritual causes, of which I name only the most important here, have finally forced a different resolution from me. The others, however, which I specified in a private letter published by Mr. Joachim Lange, rest mostly on external circumstances which have prevented me from making any apology <note>original: "Apologie," meaning a formal defense or explanation of one's position.</note> until now

<summary>Gottfried Arnold explains why he is breaking his seven-year silence to defend his work, citing the need to protect the truth and prevent readers from being misled by his critics' "cunning" arguments.</summary>
<keywords>Gottfried Arnold, preface, polemics, Church History, Joachim Lange, defense of faith, Pietism, theological controversy</keywords>

permitted to happen: these include my frequent changes and constant new professional duties / through new and different vocations <note>original: "Vocationes," referring to official appointments to church or academic positions</note>; the little knowledge I had of such polemical writings / their mostly obvious wretchedness, and other such things. <margin>(See the *Sincere Reports* <note>original: "Aufricht. Nachrichten," a contemporary journal</note> Volume VII, Order 2, pages 48, 49.)</margin>

(5.) But I say with truth / that such a resolution <note>original: "Resolucion," referring to his decision to finally respond to his critics</note> was forced upon me / specifically by the aforementioned internal and external causes. For how heavily one approaches such a conflict afterward / when one has actually enjoyed pure blessing, salvation, and peace in patient silence / no one believes this / except he who sows and reaps the fruit of righteousness in peace. Furthermore, all the harsh accusations against my soul have certainly not harmed me / but have been more useful / than one believes according to human reason. I have been especially preserved by grace from many powerful temptations under this frequent shame / with which the world covers me / and have been all the more richly comforted / for which God be praised / who prepares a table / and lets goodness and mercy follow everywhere. For which reason I might well have remained silent regarding the accusations / if I were permitted to observe my own benefit more than that of my neighbor.

(6.) Since, however, a summary response has now been required; people will be all the less angry about it / the more everything in these apologies <note>original: "Apologien," formal written defenses of one's conduct or beliefs</note> clearly aims toward improvement and peace. If someone is concerned only with the pure truth / he will not be opposed to the fact / that such truth, along with my innocence and sincere opinion, comes more clearly to light / and thus he will not continue in contradiction / nor make his bonds harder. My blameless explanations will also, hopefully, remove much anger / and the ill-conceived notions that many have harbored against me. But if someone does not have the mind of Christ within him / but rather a desire to quarrel further / then I, along with all the peace-loving, will be satisfied with God's grace and truth / and the peace / which Christ leaves and gives to His own / cannot be diminished or taken away / once I have laid out my well-meaning mind toward all people / even toward enemies.

(7.) But let whatever will happen following these defenses / according to God’s permission: it will nonetheless be recognized from them / whether people have proceeded according to the truth in the published reports concerning me. And so that I may briefly show this here only in those points / which concern my humble person / and thus cannot be noticed by anyone else: the readers have been quite wrongly informed of these matters in many hostile writings. From which one might recognize / what trust is to be placed in such contradictions regarding long-past matters / since they merit no approval regarding present things involving people who are still living.

(8.) I do not wish to mention here the enthusiasm <note>original: "Enthusiasmo," a 17-century term for religious fanaticism or claiming direct private revelation</note> and libertinism <note>original: "Libertinismo," the belief that one is free from moral laws</note> so often thrown at me and burdened upon me, because the opposite is as clear as the sun even from my recent writings and official duties: but I only wish to mention other circumstances of my life. The cited *Innocent Reports* <note>original: "Unsch. Nachrichten," a prominent Lutheran theological journal</note> state in the year 1701, page 95, in my biography / as if I / after I had studied at Wittenberg / had supported myself in Frankfurt am Mayn by correcting books. This report would indeed signify nothing extraordinary / since many an honest student supports himself with such work. However, the gentlemen authors themselves reveal their false intention / why they have invented such circumstances. Namely, they draw this conclusion: It is no wonder / that such a person might have read a great deal / because in his former laborious way of life he necessarily

<column-break/>

already acquired a great deal of reading <note>original: "Lection," referring to the breadth of his scholarly reading</note>, as Mr. Scharff says in the writing against Mr. Lange on page 92.

(9.) But both the narrative and the conclusion drawn from it are without the slightest foundation. For until my thirtieth year, I never went out of Saxony / my fatherland / nor have I in all my life come to Frankfurt am Mayn / and have never seen it with my eyes / let alone that I should have supported myself therein / regardless of the fact that a while later, in the year 1697, I lived in office at the University of Giessen / and thus near it. Likewise, in my entire life, I have never corrected a single sheet from a foreign author, least of all have I needed to support myself with such work / and consequently have acquired nothing in my reading through that; but everyone sees / where such disparaging accounts and conclusions are aimed.

(10) Of other such self-invented reports I do not wish to say much / such as when these authors in the year 1702, page 1109, claim / that the *History of Spiritual Kinship* <note>original: "Historia Cognationis spiritualis"</note> was formerly published in a shorter form under the title *On the Naming of Brothers and Sisters* <note>original: "de fratrum & sororum appellatione"</note>. The book was indeed reprinted and the title slightly changed / but not the text itself / much less made shorter under such a title. They also there, on page 1111, oppose this book to my other minor writings / and seek to confound me / as if that book was published first after the *Church History*: though that one had already been printed several years before / and had likely been written 16 years ago.

(11.) But I gladly pass over these and other lesser circumstances / even though the gentlemen authors exaggerate the slightest trivialities in my affairs as falsehoods <note>original: "Falsa"</note> / and search them out for that purpose. Much more dubious, however, are other reports in various pieces / for example, in the preface of Mr. Dr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian, a staunch defender of Lutheran orthodoxy</note> over his *Further Proofs*, it says from another's report: I had at that time (1702) gone with my father-in-law to Allstädt / which some wished to consider fatal. Now, I had indeed lived for three and a half years in the Princely Castle there / and also publicly brought to light what I taught there. But my Mr. Father-in-law did not visit me there until the year 1705 / and then only for a single day / after he had been called to the provostship in Stolpe / and had previously been an inspector for 2 years; other than that, he never set foot there / much less did he go there with me upon my arrival. Likewise, in my time at the Princely Court there, nothing fatal or restless occurred / but everything remained quiet / as even those of a contrary mind must testify. Yes, the faithful God and Father has helped me to give a better testimony in word and deed / against all ill-intentioned reports / which would gladly describe me as another Thomas Müntzer <note>A radical reformer and leader in the German Peasants' War, often used as a shorthand for a dangerous rebel</note> (as according to the report it is said to have happened recently in a Wittenberg disputation) / precisely at the place where this rebel lived. To Him alone be the praise for this!

(12.) I have hesitations about spending time presenting more such reports / especially since they gradually disappear of their own accord and are in fact annihilated. But I do not deny this / that all such encounters have, through the grace of the Lord, given me great joy / to remain faithful to Him and His truth; because I have seen / with what weapons the battle against me was fought. And when would one ever be finished with all those accusations / that are poured out against me? New ones are presented to me almost daily, both orally and in writing / through which the enemy seeks to make me weary. Yes, as I have heard / even an atheist / whom I once faithfully warned and sought [to help] / has recently attacked me with a violent defamatory writing. But I do not consider myself worthy of the shame,

# Preface

kingdom/ of which the Savior has now deemed me worthy for over 10 years; instead, I only wish to stand firm in him until the end / and to confess him constantly before men, so that his threat in Matthew 10:32 <note>Matthew 10:33 actually contains the threat: "But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven."</note> may not strike me.

(13.) With this and no other intention have I undertaken my work until now / and at that time also the Church History / and I am aware of no malice or intentional guile therein; rather, according to my understanding at that time (in which we must indeed always become more perfect), I aimed thereby at my neighbor's best. Along with this, many errors and oversights may certainly have mingled in / especially a displeasure regarding the common misery <note>Arnold refers to the perceived spiritual decay of the established church</note> / which then might very easily hinder one—especially in younger years—from acting in all things as gently, wisely, and inoffensively as the pure mind of Christ always requires. I have never denied this of myself / nor am I now in denial of it / and I have very gladly accepted all well-intentioned, friendly reminders / as I can assure with truth / after I had publicly asked for them. And if those / who wished to remind me of something / had done so with a gentle spirit / sincerely without twisting my words and other such evil ways / then this dispute would have turned out to be for nothing but improvement. However, I have not deserved such anger and fury from men. Most have attacked me quite un-Christianly as the worst enemy; others have indeed testified to their <term>zeal</term> <note>original: "Eifer," often used in this era to describe a biting, self-righteous religious fervor</note> / either generally and publicly or also secretly / but never wished or were able to show thoroughly <term>specifically</term> <note>original: "in specie"</note> / wherein I had actually erred. In this way, the truth has suffered much damage / the ignorant have been more and more confounded / and I myself have let most of it pass over me in patience. But following the example of true Christians, I have found it to be the first and best thing / to refute all the slanders by deed / namely, how I remain in teaching and life with the medicinal words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with the doctrine of godliness. Thus, following those previous defenses, these explanations regarding my faith and conduct now follow before the whole world. Thereby, certainly, confused souls shall be advised / and my conscience shall also be saved in this regard. The fruit and all else I leave to the Lord / who will also know how to maintain / what is His; all other things must come to nothing / no matter how long they rise up against Him and His truth. I would also deny the faith / if I did not hope in Him alone in all things / and sought to become strong through being still / since He has until now so faithfully and wisely ordered everything and turned it for the best. As easy as it appears to others / to write as a Christian <term>by authority</term> <note>original: "pro Autoritate"</note>: <term>I make this or that man the leader of the Fanatics</term> <note>original: "hunc vel illu facio principium Fanaticorum"; the term "Fanatic" was a common slur for Pietists and radicals who emphasized inner experience over church dogma</note>: so easily can a Christian endure such heretic-making / and bring it to nothing by his deeds.

(14.) But so that I may finally report the most necessary things regarding the occasion / arrangement, and writing style of these Apologies; I have had to recognize no less of Divine Providence herein / how faithfully it watches over the aggrieved truth. Several <term>critiques</term> <note>original: "Animadversiones"</note> regarding some adverse writings were already delivered to me a few years ago / which I laid aside / until gradually more and more such observations were contributed / and I was thus relieved of the labor. These I have finally revised in some spare hours with little effort / corrected in several places / and / as far as possible / brought into a uniform writing style and order / so that the varying style and method might not become burdensome to the reader. Where it was otherwise necessary / I have also added my <term>sincere attestations</term> <note>original: "sincere Contestationes"</note> and counter-reports / regarding the points known to me /

<meta>catchword: been/</meta>

---

been/ added. And this ensures / that my otherwise usual writing style is to be seen here and there / although some pieces entirely elaborated by others remained unchanged / and the difference otherwise shows itself well.

(15.) The mildness of a modest, friendly answer used throughout here—responding to the highly unfriendly and partly un-Christian conduct of the gentlemen opponents—arises from no despondency regarding the eternal truth / but rather from that Christian duty / which the gentlemen contradictors have for the most part lost sight of. My wish and prayer before God has gone mostly toward this / that matters might be treated impartially / but mildly without counter-scolding / reviling, and mocking; considering / that it is not my cause / but the cause of truth. God knows / how much I hate every false way and error / but also how heartily and wisely the right Divine means against them are to be sought and used / where one wishes to maintain truth. For this reason, the reader will also find some passages here / wherein the <term>doubts</term> <note>original: "Dubiis"</note> of some censors are yielded to in a certain measure / which I also gladly leave standing out of love for the truth. Not to mention / that the good explanations of my teaching and practice will leave no appearance of shaming me even to those / who are most heatedly inflamed against me: Unless / they wished to use no fairness at all; in which case one would certainly have to leave such people to God and be at peace.

(16.) But regarding the fact that these writings are only now coming to light / I can report the following. Divine faithfulness has so ordered it / that the most important accusations against me should be laid low rather and more powerfully through deed and reality itself / than through words. The truth-loving reader will be able to notice here / how no vice and horror of atheism / sorcery / rebellion / and similar crimes / can be thought of / of which I have not been accused. All this could indeed not be refuted more powerfully / than through a conduct constantly maintained in public church offices. Whatever might still remain through the devil's lies / that will fall away in due time / for anyone who can only have patience. In the meantime, ask those / who have heard me in so many places / and have seen my conduct; they will indeed have to testify / that I am being wronged. And since many, given my silence, have become ever more daring / to confidently revile and accuse / in the opinion / that no cock (as they say) would crow about it <note>A German idiom meaning "no one will care" or "no one will call them out"</note>: So their injustice now lies all the more clearly in the light of day / and is sufficiently refuted. Thus some are only now beginning / to attack me / after most of my works have already been out for over 10 years: Therefore a proper answer still comes out timely enough / and little or nothing is neglected thereby: Although this printing was also hindered and delayed for a time against my will. However, should anyone think / that enough has not yet been done for him or others hereby / such can always follow in the future according to God's will / where it seems necessary / provided it is intended and reminded of in a Christian and sincere manner.

(17.) He who does not exactly know the entire <term>mystery of lawlessness</term> <note>original: "mysterium iniquitatis," a biblical term from 2 Thessalonians 2:7, here referring to the perceived corruption within the church hierarchy</note> / and at the same time does not have a sufficiently deep insight into the church affairs of all times / he may perhaps still retain all sorts of scruples / as if too much were happening to one or the other / or also too little. However, the truth has always had the fewest supporters / and many (especially during persecutions) have remained standing as if from afar. But its lovers have nevertheless not turned away from it / but defended it unto death / and

and God has fought for them. May those of good heart and those who are weak simply not allow themselves to be led astray by every wind of human rumor, but instead look upon the cause of Jesus Christ, which consists in repentance and faith. And even if no one at all stood by the truth any longer—which, praise God! is not yet the case—the Lord would still know how to protect and carry out His own work; this should bind us all the more powerfully to yield nothing of it, so that the God of love and peace may be and remain with us.

(18.) Furthermore, since I cannot learn specifically <note>original: "in specie"</note> from those with whom I have conferred regarding this matter—whether in writing or in person—exactly what the perceived shortcomings <note>original: "Desiderata"</note> of the Church History consist of, but rather they all only refer to the general outcry and the claims of others; I therefore wish to once more earnestly request all lovers of the truth that is in Christ to show Christian love, not so much to me as to so many other souls. Please be so kind as to communicate to me, without grievance, what particular scruples regarding these or my other works might still remain with you after reading these reflections. I sincerely promise to accept such reminders <note>original: "Monita"</note> appropriately and to use them for the common good. However, should anyone have neither the time nor the desire for such an act of love—to speak thus to one's neighbor—it would undoubtedly be more beneficial for his own soul not to burden himself and others with further judgment or suspicion. Moreover, I hope no one will misuse the typographical errors (which will likely occur even in my absence, as has happened before) as substantive defects for further opposition. May the faithful God prevent these and all other sins! Written in Perleberg, March 2, 1709.

->**G. Arnold.**<-

# Summary Preliminary Report.
## Regarding the Objections Made Against G. Arnold’s Writings.

All accusations against these writings speak of either false doctrines or false reports.

I. The false doctrines of which the author is accused are so thoroughly debunked in these responses that the purity of the Gospel will sufficiently justify itself, provided one is willing to read the following defenses without prejudice.

For such doctrines must either touch upon the articles of faith <note>original: "Dogmata fidei"</note>, or the practice of a Christian life and conduct.

As for the former, the author’s innocence is once again brought into the light of day by this entire treatise. Even where he seems, here and there, to have judged this or that heretic too mildly, it is nevertheless shown here from other passages <note>original: "Locis"</note> that he himself did not subscribe to those errors or advocate for them. This is because elsewhere he has declared himself clearly and with orthodoxy, and has even utterly detested <note>original: "detestiret"</note> the heresies themselves. The kind reader will find this to be true for his own peace of mind when investigating the most ghastly heresies—such as Arianism, Socinianism, Pelagianism <note>These were major theological movements often labeled as heresies: Arianism denied the full divinity of Christ; Socinianism was an early form of Unitarianism; Pelagianism argued that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace.</note>, and the like. He will see that the author can neither love nor harbor such errors, because he so clearly abominates and rejects <note>original: "respuiret"</note> them.

Regarding what follows concerning the practice of Christianity itself—wherein some have tried to charge him with enthusiasm, fanaticism, or libertinism <note>In this era, "Enthusiasm" and "Fanaticism" were insults for those claiming direct inspiration from God outside church structures; "Libertinism" implied a rejection of moral law.</note>—all such claims fall away of their own accord. This is evident through his constant and long-standing conduct, not only in his private life (in which even his enemies will find nothing evil), but also through the important official duties entrusted to him, with which those enormities...

He specifically distances himself from classic heresies like Arianism and Pelagianism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold’s "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" against its critics. The previous page ended with Arnold requesting specific corrections from his readers; here, he addresses the general accusations of "falsification" and "errors" that have been leveled against his work by contemporary theologians.</meta>

# Summary Preliminary Report.

<meta>catchword: num.</meta>

...cannot in the least bit hold up or persist. And thus our author will remain orthodox <note>literally "right-believing"</note>, not only before God and His truth, but also among his congregation, his fellow laborers in churches and schools, and among all true Christians standing in faith and love—even if the world refuses to recognize him as such, for the world knows neither the Father nor His true children (John 17:25).

The reported false reports are alleged (according to the claims) to consist partly of falsifications and partly of errors.

II. Regarding the errors, the following should be observed in general <note>original: "in genere"</note>, as is plainly demonstrated <note>original: "ad oculum demonstriret"</note> for each specific charge:

(1.) Our opponents call even the slightest and clearest clerical and printing errors either "historical errors" or even "intentional falsifications." This is as clear as day to see from Part IV of these reflections, No. 64, § 2; from Part V, § 89, 111, and 113; and from Part II, No. 70, § 6 and 13.

Now, the *Church History* was copied by various persons before printing and was printed over 30 miles away from the author; thus, with so many names, numbers, and unfamiliar matters, many clerical and printing errors crept in. Therefore, it is unfair to blame an author for the errors of printers or even secretaries <note>original: "Amanuensium"</note>, or to present them as falsifications. Writers have protested against such injustice at all times, and our theologians call it "looking for a knot in a bulrush" <note>original Latin: "nodum in scirpo quærere," an idiom meaning to look for difficulties where there are none</note>, as Dr. Thummius, among others, says in his *Examination of Menzer’s Defense*. Similar protests against this are also produced here from the most recent authors in No. 70 of Part II, § 6.

(2.) Meanwhile, the author of the *Church History* has not denied actual errors, as can be seen in the cited location <note>original: "l. c."</note> § 2, 3, and 4.

(3.) Such errors, however, do not prejudice an extensive historical book so much that any author can or should be completely exempt from them. If this had been considered in the previous disputes—oh, how much useless quarreling and writing would have been avoided!

III. Regarding the imputed falsifications, the reader will find the following summary report truly grounded <note>original: "reipsa fundiret"</note> in the cited passages of these reflections.

(1.) The accusers frequently and quite obviously and noticeably distort and falsify both the words and opinions of the author of the *Church History*. All of Part I is full of such examples, as is Part V from § 16 to 58, as well as § 95, 110, 107, and 115, all of which are unnecessary to specify. A curious reader may look them up for himself and will be amazed. The same is found in Part II, such as No. 6, § 6; No. 11, § 1; No. 12, § 5; No. 19, § 7; No. 20, § 3; No. 24, § 12; No. 27, § 3; No. 29, § 5; No. 42, § 6; No. 36, § 9; No. 37, § 5. In Part IV, No. 34, § 4; No. 65, § 4; No. 84, § 5; No. 103, § 2.

<column-break/>

No. 110, § 2; No. 112, § 2; No. 114, § 7; No. 121, § 4; No. 125, § 3 and 17; No. 134; No. 135, § 4; No. 140, § 2; No. 145, § 9; No. 162 and following.

(2.) They have also, in part, not quoted Arnold’s words accurately and unchanged, but in such a way that sometimes the meaning <note>original: "Sensus"</note>, or at least the phrasing, sounds quite different from what he intended to show. See Part II, No. 70, § 17 and No. 95, § 2, as well as regarding other authors in No. 65.

(3.) Some often mock the author as if he had abbreviated, yet they clearly do the same themselves, as Part III, No. 20, § 7; No. 23, § 3; No. 24, § 15; No. 29, § 5, and all of Part I demonstrate. Indeed, they even defend such abbreviating themselves as a permissible thing. See the *Innocent News* <note>original: "Unsch. Nachrichten," a leading theological journal of the time</note> of the year 1706 in the Preface, and compare it, if you please, with Mr. P. Langius’s *Antibarbarum*, specifically in the *Epistle to the Theologians* <note>original: "Epistola ad Theologos"</note> page 13, whose words in this passage <note>original: "in hoc passu"</note> are very thoughtful and profound: <note>The following is translated from Latin and Greek</note> "It should be well noted that the mind of an author cannot always be conveyed in his own words; for in their connection <term>συνάψειᾳ</term> <note>coherence or sequence</note> the sequence and logic are sometimes such that, if torn from the body of the discourse, they should be placed not merely literally <term>κατὰ ῥητὸν</term> <note>word-for-word</note>, but according to the intended meaning <term>κατὰ διάνοιαν</term> <note>according to the thought</note>, seeking to express the sense."

(4.) Even if the passages <note>original: "Loca"</note> of the authors are perfectly correct in the *Church History*, some still unfairly, and out of a truly morose and fault-finding stubbornness, demand the addition of words that do not belong to the matter, just so they have something to carp about. See Part III, No. 12, § 6 and Part IV, No. 71, § 5.

(5) Sometimes, some did not even possess the authors or the editions that the author of the *Church History* used, and yet they wanted to pass judgment on them. Regarding this, see Part IV, No. 26 and 134, and Mr. Carolus’s *Innocence of the People of Württemberg* <note>original: "Wirtend. Unschuld"</note> itself, pages 66, 439, 443, 459, 466.

(6.) Indeed, what is most surprising is that many cry out against Mr. Arnold as a falsifier regarding books that such a critic has never known, seen, or read in his life, but instead manifestly confuses them with other books, of which a very notable example will be found in Part III, No. 20, § 1 and following. One becomes so blinded when trying to make others out to be falsifiers!

(7) Furthermore, they have no hesitation in rejecting our most respected theologians themselves when they notice the weight of their testimonies, even though they must admit they are unfalsified. This is what Mr. Carolus specifically did with Dr. Chytraeus, Dr. Bidenbach, Dr. Kirchner, Dr. Homberger, Dr. Tettelbach, and others, according to Part IV, No. 92, § 2; No. 124, 111, and 109.

(8.) They also contradict our church teachers on very important points of doctrine which were maintained by them against the Papacy, as will be recognized from Part IV, No. 29 and Part V, No. 94 and 99.

(9.) No less, they label people as heretics who are nonetheless recorded among us Protestants as witnesses of the truth. See Part II, No. 34 and 56.

(10.) From time to time, they clearly allege that the author uses spurious passages from writers <note>original: "supposititia Loca Scriptorum"</note> which have been rejected even by our own antiquarians and theologians: as demonstrated, among others, by numbers 98 and 108 in Part V.

(11.) Things that are written in those books in clear, plain words, they negate—as if the words were not even there—and label them a "falsehood" against the obvious evidence of one's own eyes. Examples are found in Part IV, numbers 111 and 113; in Part V, numbers 88, 103, 104, 105, 112; and in Part II, numbers 17, 63, 64, 98, § 1.

(12.) Or they also pretend that the matter itself is not found in the cited author, when evidently not just one author, but several, are cited; thus, what is not in one is nevertheless clearly to be found in the others, as shown among others by number 98 in Part II, § 2.

(13.) Even when it is said that Mr. Arnold <note>referred to as "Herr A." in the text</note> takes more from the writers than is actually in them, the critics do the very same thing themselves <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, which an example in Part II, number 17, § 3, illustrates.

(14.) Likewise, the most important passage and the "nerve" <note>the core strength</note> of the proof has been omitted by the plaintiffs, from which one could have seen the innocence of the defendant. See the same place, number 62.

(15.) Sometimes Mr. Arnold’s meaning and presentation are not understood accurately enough, or not taken in their full context <note>original: "Connexion"</note>; all of which the plaintiffs would call a "falsification" if Mr. Arnold had done it. See Part II, number 70, § 8, 9; numbers 58, 61, 66, 68, and 95.

(16.) Not infrequently, they have completely reversed the "state of the question" <note>original: "Statum Quæstionis," the core issue being debated</note> and, in their own conception, formed it according to their prejudices so that it fits neither the intent of the cited authors <note>original: "Menti Auctorum allegatorum"</note> nor the reporter’s meaning. Plenty of examples are found in Parts III and IV, especially in the former, number 28, § 7; number 30, § 8; number 24, § 6, etc.

(17.) They also often confuse completely different things <note>original: "divertissima"</note> in order to make their contradictions seem plausible. See Part IV, number 17, § 5; number 29, § 30, 31; number 37, § 5; in Part V, page 89, and others of this kind.

(18.) Explanations and applications that are well-founded both in the facts themselves and in the consensus of authors are called "falsifications." See Part II, number 55. Indeed, even the best logical conclusions, which are quite common among our historians, are rejected and misinterpreted. Examples of such historical deductions are before everyone's eyes in all history books; some regarding church matters are in the *Magdeburg Centuries* <note>a famous 16th-century Lutheran church history</note>, Century XII, page 845; in the *History of the Church of Gotha*, Book II, chapter 4, section 4, § 8, and elsewhere. They go so far as to partially deny the very principles and sources of true history.

(19.) But where someone complains about the omission of another's words, a visual inspection <note>original: "oculari inspectione"</note> reveals that it could not possibly have happened by design or through deceit <note>original: "studio oder dolose"</note>. This is because such words (sometimes bypassed unintentionally) actually argue even more strongly for the presentation made than the remaining words do. See, among others, Part III, number 24, § 9; Part IV, number 50, § 5; number 93, § 2; number 102, § 2; number 121, § 7.

<column-break/>

(20.) In no few places, the author of the *Church History* himself—especially when quoting well-known writers—has candidly and in express words <note>original: "expressis verbis"</note> indicated that he wished to excerpt only a few passages for the sake of brevity <note>original: "Prolixität"</note>. In those cases, he certainly could not have committed, nor did he wish to commit, any deceit <note>original: "Dolum"</note>, by virtue of the foundation cited above in § 3 from Mr. Lang. And yet, it is held against him, as can be found among other places in number 35 of Part III, § 12.

(21.) Critics have also been over-hasty in their censoring by repeatedly failing to consider which subjects or other circumstances are being discussed, or whether the author of the *Church History* presupposes a certain matter as already known and settled, or has already demonstrated it in the preceding text; upon which he could then all the more certainly accept and apply the cited passages. A notable example is in number 70 of Part II, § 16, and elsewhere.

(22.) Likewise, they have not thoughtfully reflected on what comes before and after <note>original: "antecedentia und consequentia"</note>, as is proper according to the laws of interpretation <note>original: "secundùm leges hermeneuticas"</note>. Instead, they presented the words of the *Church History* out of context, simply so that they must appear paradoxical and impertinent. The reader will encounter this specifically in Part III, number 2, § 2; number 12, § 8; number 34, § 15.

(23.) Furthermore, when in the *Church History*—for the sake of avoiding tedious length—only the sense and content of a passage are presented, and therefore such a passage is not expressed internally with other words as is otherwise usual with the foreign words of authors: then one or another critic has seized upon <note>original: "arripiret"</note> this quite common method (which happens all day long and is expressly founded in the rules of interpretation) and misused it to impute a "falsehood" that the author never thought of. This is despite the fact that in the matter itself <note>original: "in re ipsa"</note> and in the meaning, nothing was changed, added, or taken away. If one takes the trouble to look in Part III, number 12, § 5; likewise number 5, § 8; number 33, § 6; and in Part II, number 70, § 13, one will become aware of such forced accusations <note>original: "Zundfügigungen"</note>.

(24.) Finally, some opponents have made quite improper demands of the author of the *Church History*: For example, that he should not have cited our theologians, should not have agreed with them against the Papacy, or should not have confused political figures with presbyters <note>original: "Presbigern," likely church elders</note>, and such things. Also, that he should not say exactly what our own historians admit. See Part III, number 12, § 6, and elsewhere. So much for the imputed falsifications.

IV. Alongside these observations, it should further be noted generally <note>original: "generaliter"</note> that the opposing gentlemen—due to lack of time and other reasons, primarily out of vexation and anger—have not thoughtfully and dispassionately read through, examined, and judged the book itself in its full sequence and connection. Instead, they have done so largely and primarily from and according to the index <note>original: "Register"</note>. Indeed, they even refer to it so openly in express words, to say nothing of the places where they do not let it be known. See Mr. Carl of Württemberg's *Innocence* <note>original: "Unsch."</note>, pages 24, 25, 394, etc.; Mr. Dr. Cyprian's *Preliminary Report*, § 18, twice; and the *Remarks*, page 68; Mr. M. Scharff against Mr. Lang, page 101, and others.

Having previously addressed specific accusations of "falsification," the author now moves to a broader defense against critics who judge the book solely by its index or who exhibit personal and regional biases in their critiques.</meta>

### Summary

Now, it is well known that indices are generally made by others and therefore should not be strictly attributed to the authors themselves. For the *Church History* <note>original: "K. Hist.," referring to Arnold’s *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie*</note>, someone else also projected and for the most part completed the index <note>original: "Registr."</note>. Out of a certain zeal, this person did not record the positive testimonies regarding Lutheranism (which nonetheless appear in the book and are repeated here) as diligently as he recorded the complaints. Some have once again greatly abused this for their own purposes, accusing the author of the book based on the index. However, among people who look at the actual facts and reasonably weigh the connection <note>the overall context</note> of the book itself, such a preposterous way of proceeding <note>original: "præposterus procedendi modus"</note> finds no entry and carries no weight. For who would want, for example, to defame the late Mr. Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the "Father of Pietism"</note> as if he had asserted the following propositions absolutely and universally, which nevertheless stand without any limitation in the index of his *Theological Considerations*? There it says under the letter A: **Atheism of Lutheran theologians**; letter C: **The clergy's self-interest in the struggle against the Pietists**; further: **Consistories** <note>administrative bodies of the church</note> **are quite wretched nowadays**. Letter E: **Exegesis of Scripture is not properly practiced in either lower or high schools**. Letter G: **The so-called clergy set themselves most strongly against good and true Christianity**; further: **Resistance to the good from universities**. Letter P: **Among politicians there are more good people than among theologians**. Letter S: **Theological study is neglected in schools and universities**. Letter V: **The corruption of our church is almost incurable, and indeed in all estates**, and so forth. These examples, which are right at hand for me, show how unfairly one concludes from the index of a book about the book itself, since the former, for the sake of brevity, is usually set down without the (even most necessary) limitations. Indeed, what is more, do you not find, dear reader, in almost all indices such propositions that seem offensive at first glance <note>original: "prima fronte"</note> because of their universality, yet are not so in the book itself with regard to the whole context <note>original: "quoad totum contextum"</note>? To give a common example: in the index of the Altenburg volumes <note>a famous 17th-century edition of Luther's works</note> of Luther, there are many harsh expressions against academies in general, such as Chapter X, page 962b: **Youth are corrupted in high schools; high schools contribute most to the suppression of faith, are gates of hell, Molochites** <note>worshippers of the idol Moloch; here meaning those who sacrifice children to false learning</note> **within them**, and so forth. In the text itself, Luther also often speaks quite harshly without any restriction, and yet no one has held it against him, except those who wished to interpret him wrongly and did not want to grasp his meaning.

To the rest of the conduct of such opponents belongs the fact that some (1.) have displayed their own inconsistency <term>ἀνισογενίαν<gloss>original Greek: inequality or inconsistency of nature</gloss></term> in their censures, as is very noticeably shown, among other places, in Part III, number 20, and in Part IV, number 137.

(2.) Many have also presented their false principles in factual matters <note>original: "in realibus"</note>, which are refuted—especially in Part I and at the beginning of Part IV—by our own historians and theologians.

(3.) Various people have promised proper modesty on the title pages of their polemical writings; but in reality, they have allowed themselves to be carried away by partisanship and violent passions into scolding, mocking, and persecuting, filling the pages with slanderous invectives, exaggerations, oratorical excesses, analogies <note>original: "Similibus"</note>, irrelevant matters <note>original: "Allotriis"</note>, and unnecessary citations <note>original: "Allegatis"</note>. This superfluous behavior is best met with short and well-grounded answers.

<column-break/>

<header>Preface.</header>

(4) Some expose their partisanship even more through a morose and overly-sensitive defense of their local matters <note>original: "rerum Patriarum," or matters of their own fatherland/region</note>, whereby they often despise and diminish other nations and their teachers—more than they could or would ever impute to the *Church History*. Thus, Mr. Carolus <note>likely referring to a specific critic like Andreas Adam Hochstetter, who used the pseudonym Carolus</note> especially defends his Württemberg theologians, some of whom are related to him by blood, as he admits; and in contrast, he rejects the Saxon, Hessian, and several others—even the late Johann Arnd, Chytraeus, etc.—insofar as these might stand in the light of the fame of his own people. Greater partisanship cannot easily be committed: yet one wishes to punish others for it at the same time!

(5.) How often is it found in the comparison of the disputed passages here that they have sought out only such passages from the *Church History* which are set down somewhat mildly or even favorably toward this or that rejected person by other authors? In contrast, however, they pass over all preceding or following passages <note>original: "Loca"</note> through which those favorable-sounding words are weakened <note>original: "enervirt"</note>, limited, or, according to the circumstances of the matter, entirely annulled. On the other hand, they exaggerate the necessary observations that are there concerning one or another church teacher and their failings, but remain silent about all the added praise and good confession of them, which, as it were, swallows up or at least diminishes and limits the former, by virtue of an impartial report <note>original: "Relation"</note> in which evil and good are presented according to the state and condition of the people <note>original: "pro statu & condicione hominum"</note>. One can find enough examples of this by following the index here in the histories of the heretics and also of the church teachers. It is, however, especially clear and bright from the history of Luther and what has been criticized therein; for all the master censors—except for the Court Councilor Pfanner—passed over the praise that stands quite extensively in the *Church History* and only urged and scolded the other observations. Regardless of the fact that, in such a partisan manner, one would also have to reject the highly famous and beloved Mr. von Seckendorff <note>Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff, author of a major history of Lutheranism</note>. For he writes expressly in the Epilogue of his *History of Lutheranism*, page 699: <quote>I have not been silent about the flaws <note>original Latin: "Naros," literally "noses" or "sneers," here meaning blemishes</note> in the opinions and customs of Luther and his followers; I have long known they were men, and I found no others after diligent consideration of what they wrote and did; but nonetheless, I judged that what they taught according to the guidance of divine truth stood on a firm footing <note>original: "firmo stare talo," literally "stands on a firm heel"</note>.</quote>

(6) If the testimonies of the ancients <note>original: "Testimonia veterum"</note> strike them too strongly, so that they cannot deny them, they seek either to make them out to be false or even to annul the credibility of the manuscripts <note>original: "fidem manuscriptorum"</note>, against all custom among scholars. If, however, everyone wanted to reject such writings that did not please him, then finally no published book could be trusted, since they were all first printed from written codices. And who will grant belief to the *Innocent News* <note>original: "Unsch. Nachr.," a conservative Lutheran periodical</note> and other such books according to this principle, since they have published so many intercepted private letters against law and right <note>original: "contra jus & fas"</note>? They do not consider that it is impossible for one to invent such particulars—indeed, such highly specific details—that harmonize so intimately with the printed histories and the entire state of the times, as one finds in the *Church History*, especially from the manuscript letters of theologians. Many, for example, wanted to deny the history of the personal physician Dr. Ratzenberger <note>Matthäus Ratzenberger, whose biography of Luther was controversial</note>, and yet it was afterwards published by others and found to be correct. Thus it will happen with many other writings bit by bit.

### Summary Preliminary Report.

V.

<meta>catchword: Remem-</meta>

As for the specific small treatises considered here, the so-called **Innocent News** <note>original: "Unschuldige Nachrichten," the first major German-language theological review journal, known for defending Lutheran Orthodoxy against Pietism</note> rightfully stand at the forefront. Mr. Dr. Hecht explicitly calls these "Judgments" <note>original: "Judicia"</note> or "Opinions and Censures" (*Philoc.* p. 183), though they themselves claim not to have intended them as such. These reviews have produced contradictions against almost all of the author's writings, partly from others and partly from themselves. Their primary author is Mr. Dr. Löscher the younger <note>Valentin Ernst Löscher (1673–1749), a leading Orthodox Lutheran theologian</note>, as Mr. Scharff admits in his writing against Mr. Lange on page 50, where he also calls him the President <note>original: "Præsidem," meaning the presiding head or editor</note> on page 210. It is well enough known how many famous authors have been compelled to remind these "News" of their errors, as seen in so many thorough arguments <note>original: "Deductionibus"</note> by Mr. Dr. Rechenberg, Mr. Dr. Breithaupt, Mr. Prof. Francke <note>August Hermann Francke, a central figure in Pietism</note>, Mr. Dr. Acussen, Mr. Dr. Petersen, Mr. Senior Müller, Mr. J. E. Kessler, Mr. Freylinghausen, and among political figures, Mr. Court Councilor Pfanner, as well as among medical doctors, Mr. Dr. Richter, and likewise so many anonymous authors, such as in the *Judgment on the Old and New*, the *Literary Observations* <note>original: "Observationum Litterariarum"</note>, and so forth.

Specifically, Director Lange in Berlin has clearly shown the errors and inaccuracies of these "News" in his *Sincere News* <note>original: "Aufrichtigen Nachricht"</note>, particularly in the first volume of the preface and on page 3; in the third volume on pages 1, 62, 70, 114; in the fourth on page 112; and in the sixth on pages 21 and 107. He discovers other things therein no less in Volume II on pages 4, 58, 82, and elsewhere, here and there with great emphasis, against which they have been unable to produce anything substantial. What sins they have committed particularly against Mr. Arnold’s writings is to be noted here in the first part in every line. Thus, when the honorable authors see from these considerations how the passages they challenged have been found, explained, and rescued quite differently than reported against them, it is expected of them—out of fairness—that they will fulfill their own request, which Mr. Dr. Löscher made to others, for the sake of their peace of conscience. It appears in the *Evangelical Tithes* <note>original: "Evangel. Zehenden"</note>, and from there in Mr. Lange, Vol. VI, page 135, as follows:

> "Let us see to it that in all disputes we notice this: to yield nothing regarding the matter itself; but, when it is sufficiently protected and the words are tolerable, even if they do not express everything with the greatest accuracy, we should not strive further."

If this is done by them, many useless words of censure and disputation will be left aside, and time will be applied more salutarily.

The second part of these considerations deals with Mr. Dr. Cyprian’s <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1723), a staunch defender of Lutheranism against Arnold’s history</note> recent writings against the *Church History*. The author of the *Sincere Remarks on the Church History* <note>original: "K. H."</note> has already clearly noted his harsh conduct on pages 349, 377, 383, 412, and 423. The source of such unmixed mockery and vehemence—which the author himself did not deny on page 243—may have been suspicion and agitation over a so-called lampoon <note>original: "Pasquills," a type of anonymous satirical attack</note>, which was also mixed into the matter itself (See here No. X, § 3). This was despite the fact that the accused party, in the *Supplements* <note>original: "Supplementis"</note> (Preface, page B 3), publicly offered to provide a legal defense and in the meantime took it upon his conscience. Out of this intense commotion, the dear man often hurried too much in his judging and did not rightly or deliberately perceive the true sense of the person he chose as his opponent. In the old, heated dispute of the friend who

c

wrote the reminder at that time, our peaceful purpose does not permit us to interfere. Our goal is only to consider the factual matters <note>original: "Realia"</note> that have since been brought forth by Mr. Dr. Cyprian against the *Church History*, and to do all this in Christian modesty <note>original: "Chriſtlicher Modesté"</note>, free from such angry and mocking mental agitation—which, in the end, must and will be regretted. If Mr. Dr. Cyprian (of whose change <note>a promotion or change in status</note> we have only just heard, and who thus will not take offense at his previous title in this second part) has since made use of a thousand writings (according to his own explanation), the fruit of this will hopefully show itself in Christian gentleness and impartial love. This is especially so since the entire practice of the accused author, alongside this mild remonstrance, bears living witness that Mr. Arnold <note>original: "Hr. A."</note> has acted with ill will toward neither a single person nor the Church.

In the third part, all the personal matters <note>original: "Perſonalia"</note> that an anonymous author mixed in at great length <note>original: "prolixiſſimè"</note> have been bypassed for the sake of edification. This is because the person about whom and through whom the question was raised <note>original: "Quæſtio movirt"</note> has since passed away, and moreover, one was dealing only with an unnamed author. Thus, reflection was made only on the matters themselves brought against the *Church History*, and hopefully not a single passage will remain to which a corrective measure has not been applied.

The fourth part has become somewhat more extensive because it contains many serious questions. We have gladly spared the author (who has now also passed away) out of love, considering further that he may not have been better informed about the matter or about Arnold’s person. Alongside this, we have also gladly and willingly left the worthy land of Württemberg <note>original: "Wirtenberger Land"</note> with its traditional fame in this quite mild counter-proof, as its state <note>original: "Status," referring to its official political/ecclesiastical position</note> does not take part in such particular disputes. Nevertheless, that land also had to suffer enough judgments because of the recent Stuttgart Bible, as well as because of the New Testament of the late Mr. Dr. Hedinger, and because of Mr. Dr. Reuchlin. (See *Innocent News*, Year 1705, pp. 432 and 600; also Year 1707, p. 595.)

The fifth part contains various shorter answers to newer writings in which the author's matters were perhaps attacked, particularly the *Preliminary Notions* <note>original: "Prænotionum"</note> and the *Journals* <note>original: "Ephemeridum"</note>, as far as the latter were published at that time. It is certainly hoped that the unfairness of such incitements <note>original: "Zundthizungen"</note> will shine so clearly before the eyes of every honest <note>original: "cordaten," meaning hearty or judicious</note> reader that further presentations will not be necessary—unless in time it should please the Most High that the remaining objections or new interspersions should be further addressed, especially where these might be presented with Christian moderation. For no lover of the truth will withdraw from investigating it in such a peaceful manner without weight reasons; for truth is not obscured or harmed <note>original: "lædirt"</note> by this, but is instead always further clarified <note>original: "illuſtrirt"</note>. But alas, this manner is not found in the writings of the opponents, except perhaps what was recently offered by Mr. Dr. Leyser, among others.

### Summary Preliminary Report.

...might have written quite mildly. However, his writing became known quite late, and for that reason, it had to be saved for a future opportunity.

And so, this time, the entire matter is left to God and to Time, with the certain confidence that what has been done here was required by both love for one's neighbor and by the truth. For this reason, everything has been written with fitting modesty, without anger or heat, without a desire for slander, counter-scolding, or malice, according to the Apostolic command: *Let all things among you be done for edification* <note>original: "Lasset alles zur Besserung unter euch geschehen," a reference to 1 Corinthians 14:26</note>. Some pleasant and wholesome matters have been partly further explained and defended, and partly thoroughly proven. May God grant it for good edification! Thus, one can well assure that this book is not so much to be called a polemical treatise <note>original: "Streit-Schrifft"</note> as it is a quite peaceful contemplation of historical-theological truths, pursuing peace in the truth.

### Historical-Theological
# Observations
### Part One:
#### Concerning the so-called
## Old and New,
#### And specifically, first regarding the so-called
## Proof,
#### which was reviewed there in the year 1702, page 58 and following.

This writing was immediately answered in general at that time, in the very same year 1701, by Mr. Arnold through the **Final Presentation** <note>original: "Endliche Vorstellung," a specific defensive work by Gottfried Arnold</note> (printed in quarto <note>a book size where the sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note> in Frankfurt by Thomas Fritschen). And here, as with the other writings of the author <note>original: "Concipiente," referring to the person drafting or composing the text</note>, his sense and purpose are brought to light: namely, that he indeed repeats the writings of the opponents with great praise and exaggeration, but passes over the resulting defenses in silence. Regarding those accusations which he repeated from the writing already and immediately answered, they are the following; which shall also be examined more broadly below in Part III.

### The 1st Charge:

That Arnold presumed to slander and touch upon the honorable reputation of a certain Theologian. p. 58.

### Answer:

(1.) Mr. Arnold did not write the cited "Postscript" <note>original: "Nacherinnerung"</note> in which the Theologian is said to have been attacked, as the Mr. Composer <note>The author of the critique against Arnold</note> could have seen from the Presentation <note>Referring to Arnold's *Vorstellung*, a preliminary defense of his work</note>.

(2.) In that same "Remembrance," the opposite is actually stated, namely: That one gladly respects D. V.'s <note>Likely Dr. Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff or another contemporary critic</note> age and does not wish to take away his hard-earned merits. However, what was mentioned in general regarding the misery of many teachers was done according to the clear eternal truth, in consensus with daily experience, and without any application to specific persons; thus, it cannot be called a defamation of honor.

(3.) In contrast, the Honorable Dr. V. in his writing called the author of the Remembrance a "reborn Pietist," and other such things.

(4.) Arnold himself declared in the *Presentation*, p. 28, that he did not mean to touch upon Dr. V.'s person or office in the slightest; and on p. 37, that one rightly honors a gray-haired, experienced man according to his merit, even if one does not like to see such authority abused. However, because the aforementioned theologian has since passed away, it is not necessary to stir the matter further.

### The 2nd Charge:

That he spoke in favor of all heretics and fanatics <note>original: "Schwärmern," often translated as 'enthusiasts' or 'fanatics' in a religious context</note>, and even atheists. p. 58.

### Answer:

(1.) Anyone can find the clear opposite proven, first in general, in the *Presentation*, Chapter III, §. 6, 7 and following, p. 30, and even more extensively in the *Sincere Remarks* <note>original: "aufrichtigen Anmerkungen"</note> attached to the *Supplements*, Chapter II, p. 345 and following, from which the reader may find satisfaction.

(2.) In particular, it is proven that Mr. Arnold rejected Simon <note>Simon Magus, often cited as the first heretic</note> (see *Presentation*, p. 31; *Supplements*, p. 2, regarding which Arnold's clear confession also appears here immediately at the 5th Charge, as well as further below in Part III, no. 19). Furthermore, he rejected the Gnostics (*Presentation*, p. 32; *Supplements*, p. 49; *Additions to the Church History*, p. 2), the Manichaeans (*Supplements*, p. 60), the Donatists (*Remembrance*, p. 67; *Explanation*, p. 17; *Supplements*, pp. 116, 388), the Arians, Noetians, Sabellians, etc. (*Remembrance*, p. 84; *Supplements*, p. 109), and the other heretics of ancient times;

<column-break/>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>Part I. No. 2. On the so-called "Old and New." 3</header>

to say nothing of the more recent ones, the citations for which can be found in the *Supplements*.

(3.) It is one thing to show—as our own theologians and historians have done, such as Dr. Kortholt, Dr. Ittig, and even Colberg himself (who casts doubt on the fable of the Gnostics) and others—based on clear evidence, how biased circumstances were reported regarding many "erroneous" people, or how they were treated unfairly in certain matters, or how they were perhaps excused by some. It is quite another thing to justify and approve of the heretics themselves and their errors or excesses. The former was done by Mr. Arnold following the example of proven writers, as is apparent. The Mr. Composer himself does not entirely reject this, as he calls it "tolerable as a singularity" <note>An unusual but acceptable instance</note> when an author approves of the defense of the Ophites, Ebionites, and other heretics. *Year 1707, p. 524.* But in this other way <note>the way of justifying heresy</note>, he has not spoken for a single one, let alone *all* heretics or atheists. Thus, this accusation remains once and for all unprovable and fundamentally false, through which people have sought to make a work—well-intentioned in itself—hateful to the ignorant. One may also read his last Remonstration on this in the appendix of the *Treatise on Deviations* <note>original: "Tractats von den Abwegen"</note>, §. 10 and following, p. 602 and following.

(4.) In that very same year when the *Church History* was published, the moderate theologian Calvör reasoned in the *Preface to the Rifts of Zion* <note>original: "Præf. ad Fissuras Sionis"</note>, page 6, thus: *Not even the more sensible of the Romans <note>referring to Roman Catholics</note>, those who do not have a pumpkin for a heart <note>a Latin idiom for being foolish or heartless</note>, deny how unreliably historical matters have sometimes been handled, both by them and by others, and even by the older writers themselves. Whatever the case may be, I cannot be brought to believe that everything written about the extreme rages and delusions of the ancient heretics is true and genuine; rather, [I believe] it was partly hatred and rivalries, partly credulity—which too often carelessly embraces a lying rumor as history—and partly ignorance, which has sometimes attributed such foul dreams to others. -- I add that the first heretics, as they are called (Syrians or Egyptians using either the Hebrew or Syriac language). Thus, the Greek and Latin Fathers, mostly being ignorant of Oriental languages, could with difficulty penetrate into the genuine meaning of their adversaries, etc.* And a diligent reader will indeed encounter such remarks here and there among our own Gentlemen Theologians. But who has ever interpreted them as poorly as is now being done?

(5.) Regarding the atheists in particular, it is (a) to be seen from the *Church History* that Mr. Arnold, along with all true believers, has an utter abhorrence for all types of atheism, whether it be called "gross" or "subtle," as it cannot be otherwise where even a tiny spark of divine light remains in a

can maintain the upper hand in a soul: much less where one has received the true divine knowledge through grace. He [Arnold] has also cited very sorrowful complaints from the Lutherans themselves regarding the atheism that has crept into our church, as in Book XVI, Chapter 13, Section 7; also in Chapter 16, Section 3; and in Book XVII, Chapter 16, Sections 4 and 6.

(6.) Furthermore ($\beta$), he has also cited such complaints from our fellow Lutherans, stating that the evil suspicion of atheism against innocent people is a grave sin and—in the words of Morhof <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a German writer and scholar</note>—nothing is more gruesome than such a calumny <note>slander</note>, yet—according to Dr. Weber's observation—nothing is easier to commit, in Book XVII, Chapter 16, Section 1. Likewise, he notes that many "theological atheists" are found among preachers, based on the complaints of Spizelius, Kortholt, Francisci, and Scriver. Sections 4 and 5.

(7.) Thirdly ($\gamma$), he has earnestly abhorred such things and all other types of atheism, revealing once again his blameless Christian opinion. For instance, in Section 7, after recounting French atheism, he concludes: **The misery of the supposed religion (of the Papists) is sufficiently visible from this, namely, because so many of the clergy there are also atheists.** And in Section 16, he observes that the Polish nobleman Liszyński was not helped in his soul by his over-hasty execution. Likewise, in Section 17, he reminds us of the Wittenberg atheist, noting that he listened more to perverted reason and false scholarship than to the simple Word of God. In Section 18, he thinks of those who perhaps fall into despair through their contempt for God. He also cites and recommends books written against atheism, such as those by Undereycken, Großgebauer, and *Lassenius*, which contain many thought-provoking circumstances; also Burnet's *The Despairing Atheist*, and so forth—not to mention what H.A. <note>Hottfried Arnold</note> has otherwise testified quite earnestly against atheism in his other writings.

(8.) If he now, fourthly ($\delta$), presents one or two doubts regarding some people who were accused of atheism within Popery <note>Catholicism</note>, questioning whether they were actually and properly atheists; he does not thereby excuse real atheists, much less all atheists, and least of all atheism itself, which is and remains a work of Satan. Rather, he merely performs the duty of an honest historian <note>original: "Historici"</note> who must distinguish the true from the false, and the certain from the doubtful in questions of fact <note>original: "quæstionibus facti"</note>.

(9.) A clear proof of this can be seen below in the 87th Accusation regarding the history of Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher executed for atheism</note>, as to whether H.A. had cause to doubt the credibility <note>original: "Fidem"</note> of those Popish writers on this point <note>original: "in hoc puncto"</note>, since they are those to whom...

### The 3rd Charge:
->That he intended to slander all teachers of the ancient and current churches. page 58.<-

### Answer:

(1.) Such a claim is once again tangibly refuted in the *Presentation* <note>Arnold's *Vorstellung*, his preliminary defense</note>, Chapter III, Sections 11, 12, 13, and following, pages 32 and 33, and in the *Supplements*, pages 7, 56, and 105.

(2.) On the contrary, it is sufficiently proven there how highly and dearly H.A. always holds the true teachers of the Church, even if he, along with Protestant theologians in general, would not make idols of them.

(3.) In particular, his high esteem has been demonstrated among the Church Fathers <note>original: "Patribus"</note> toward Irenaeus and Augustine (*Presentation* p. 33, *Supplement* p. 118), toward Athanasius (*Supplement* p. 105), Jerome (*Supplement* p. 118), and all other upright and blameless teachers of the ancient Church.

(4.) To repeat it here briefly: he writes very good praises of Irenaeus, which can be read in the following 5th Charge. He speaks of Clement in the most respectful way in Book 1, Chapter 2, Section 1; as well as of Ignatius, Polycarp, and other early teachers. Furthermore, of Athenagoras, it is stated in Book II, Chapter 2, Section 1, that he wrote a beautiful defense; and of Dionysius of Corinth, an excellent teacher. Regarding Justin Martyr in Section 2: one finds in him a fine taste of the initial purity and gravity <note>original: "Gravität"</note>. Of Ignatius in Section 3: he was a disciple of the Apostles and a very excellent Christian. He also speaks of Polycarp’s pure faith, magnificent gifts, and good reputation, and generally in Section 6, of the simplicity of the teachers of that time.

(5.) From the 3rd century, H.A. praises Cyprian in Book III, Chapter 3, Section 9, as a light among the martyrs and leaders because of his gifts, diligence, vigilance, and love. He also praises Tertullian in Sections 7 and 8; Gregory of Neocaesarea in Section 14; Minucius Felix in Section 16; Origen and others in Book IV, Chapter 4, Section 2; Ambrose in Section 4; Hilary in Section 7; Cyril of Jerusalem, and so forth with the following, as much as is consistent with the truth. To repeat all of this would take too long: for he could not and should not have overlooked the flaws <note>original: "Nævos"</note> of the later writers <note>original: "sequiorum Scriptorum"</note> any more than any other Protestant historian.

(6.) Among the more recent writers, his [Arnold's] reverence toward Luther is evident in the 16th Book of the *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics* <note>original: "K. H. C. V." referring to Arnold's *Unparteiische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie*</note>, Sections 17, 18, and 19; and from the *Life of Luther* in his work *The Life of the Believers* <note>original: "Leben der Gläubigen"</note> pages 404 to 536 (which the honorable Drafter <note>original: "H. Concip." referring to the accuser or author of the opposing brief</note> himself recognizes as being very well written on page 383). Likewise, it is seen in the *Representation* <note>original: "Vorstell."</note> page 10, *Supplement* pages 133 and 451; indeed, even from the confession of the Court Councilor Pfanner and others, who noted in Mr. Arnold an all-too-great love for Luther. Likewise, from the Drafter's own confession on page 277, that Mr. Arnold frequently praises Luther and holds the beginning of the Reformation in high regard. One may also see here, especially in the second part, the accusation where Arnold's own words appear.

(7.) Regarding other upright teachers, one see’s Mr. Arnold's love in his testimonials of the blessed Arnd <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), a central figure in Lutheran pietism</note>, in Book XVII, Chapter 6, Section 3 and following, and in the *Life of the Believers* page 536. He also speaks of other most famous theologians here and there, such as Varenius, Tarnovius, Müller, Gerhard, and many more. Not to mention what is praised at length from the 16th century in Book XVI, Chapter 9, regarding so many Lutheran teachers such as Myconius, Mathesius, Weller, Hausmann, and others; and thereafter regarding Dr. Meisner, J. V. Andreæ, Dorsch, Walther, Tarnovius, Saubert, Egard, Mengering, Meyfart, Kesler, Glassius, Lutkemann, Quistorp, Schupp, Scriver, and so many others in Book XVII, Chapter 5, Section 10 and following.

(8.) From this, let a reasonable person draw their own conclusion: whether Mr. Arnold slanders all teachers of the Christian Church, or whether he has not also praised the best according to their merit? Indeed, in all his books, and especially in the *Description* <note>original: "Abbildung"</note>, he continually cites and makes use of them. To be sure, for the sake of truth, he could not and should not remain silent regarding certain deficiencies in the practice of the Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to the Lutheran Church</note> churches, following the example of other Protestant writers.

(9.) This accusation remains, once again, a palpable untruth that can never be proven. For if a historical account—or rather, a repeating of old documents concerning the misery of one teacher or another—were to be called slander, then all such confessions and judgments made by our own theologians about other Lutheran teachers would have to be the same. Yet our theologians did not take these from other authors, as Mr. Arnold did, but stated them of their own accord according to the truth.

(10.) And to illustrate this with only two examples: what judgment could be sharper, or sound harsher in the ears of those who do not wish to see the Church Fathers criticized, than when the blessed Luther declared the most beloved Fathers to be in error, specifically in the dispute against heretics? He writes <note>original: "schreibet:"</note>:

<meta>catchword: writes:</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>Part I, No. 4, regarding the so-called Old and New.</header>

writes: (Volume III, Jena Latin edition, folio 123 a.) <note>original: "Idem est cernere in summis Theologis..."</note> *The same is to be seen in the greatest theologians, such as Augustine, Bernard, and those older than them, Cyprian, Tertullian, and the like. When they treat Scripture in public, they treat it candidly and purely. But when questions are proposed, they rarely stay on the path without taking something away from Scripture, attributing it to the cause or the person, and twisting the words. Look at them in this, where Jerome writes against Jovinian, Augustine against the Manichaeans, Bernard against free will, and you will see that I speak the truth. To such an extent has no saint stripped off all flesh, or worn away its passions.* One may read further on this in his *Table Talk*, Chapter 30, Section 11. This is the first example regarding the Church Fathers, whom Luther does not declare free of having stepped off the path in disputation, having taken something from Scripture, having attributed things to the cause or person, or having twisted God's word. But the blessed man [Luther] by no means slandered the ancient teachers because of this; he only spoke the truth, which sometimes sounds harsh to delicate and idolatrous ears.

(11.) Regarding more recent teachers, a single example may suffice: when the beloved Rostock theologian Dr. Affelmann writes as follows concerning Dr. L. Osiander, the enemy of Arnd: *He has written most wickedly, schismatically, most falsely, proudly, and impiously* <note>original: "pessime, schismatice, mendacissime, superbe, impie"</note>; *he posits absurd and weak conclusions, indeed even the crime of falsehood; he long ago renounced candor, modesty, and pious doctrine,* etc. A Lutheran theologian writes this of another; and yet another theologian at Wittenberg repeated this from him, namely Dr. Mich. Walther Jr. in his disputation *On the Fellowship of the Divine Nature* <note>original: "de Θείας κοινωνίᾳ Φύσεως" — a reference to 2 Peter 1:4</note>, page 15. Because of this, however, neither of the two became a slanderer of Lutheran teachers, much less the blessed Mr. Varenius, who publicly proved the very same abominations regarding Osiander. More regarding the Fathers can be found below in Number 21.

### The 4th Accusation.

-> He is said to have shamefully disparaged the Evangelical Church to the Papists. p. 58. <-

### Answer:

(1.) Through all centuries, he has uncovered the abominations of the Papacy with the greatest earnestness and zeal, and has particularly demonstrated the necessity of the Reformation in great detail, so much so that Dr. Veiel himself observes that Arnold sang the "praises" of the Papacy <note>Arnold's defender is likely being ironic here, or suggesting that Arnold's harshness toward his own church was misinterpreted by his critic, Dr. Veiel, as being favorable to Catholicism</note>.

(2.) According to his own recognition, he is more convinced of the Anti-Christianity of the Roman Church than to write anything to please them.
