<header>Historical-Theological Observations, Part I, No. 5</header>
<meta>catchword: will be</meta>

(3.) While he certainly had to impartially reveal the state of our churches, he never did so to please the Papists <note>A common early modern term for Roman Catholics</note> or to support their cause, something for which an Evangelical Christian must have an utter abhorrence.

(4.) Furthermore, he never directed his descriptions of the flaws within the Evangelical <note>Protestant, specifically Lutheran</note> churches to a single Papist, much less defamed the church to such people—whom he mostly described as fallen and blinded. Least of all did he do so in a shameful manner; indeed, he did so no more than those authors of our own church from whom he drew his documentation.

(5.) Even assuming that some Papists might misuse this book against our church—as the preacher of controversies in Strasbourg is said to have done according to Dr. B.'s report—such misuse is of as little harm as the **misuse** that the Papists practice with Holy Scripture or with the writings of Luther and other theologians. These authors are not guilty of the misuse, and the *History of the Church* is just as little to be blamed, despite those who wish to denigrate it for that reason.

(6.) This, then, is a crystal-clear defamation, against which Mr. Arnold <note>H. A. refers to Hieronymus or Gottfried Arnold</note> rightly employs the answer that **Mr. Lange** <note>Joachim Lange (1670–1744), a prominent Pietist theologian</note> gave to similar accusations in the fifth part of his *Sincere Report*, page 97: "I do not attach a stain of shame to our church through the testimony of truth; rather, I endeavor, as much as I am able, to remove from her that most hideous blemish which has been attached to her by pseudo-orthodoxy." More on this can be seen in Part III, No. 9.

### The 5th Accusation.

->That he protected Simon Magus, the Gnostics, and others, while insulting Irenaeus and other teachers. page 59.<-

### Answer:

(1.) In general, this was already found to be completely false above in number 2.

(2.) Specifically regarding Simon the Sorcerer <note>Simon Magus, a figure from the New Testament often cited as the first heretic</note>, it is written in the *History of the Church*, Book I, Chapter 4, Section 4, that Satan awakened Simon. This man bewitched the people; likewise: during his life he did not concern himself with God, whom he also insolently blasphemed and scorned. In the *Recognitions of Clement*, which Mr. Arnold edited in German, such testimonies and refutations against the malice and heresies of Simon Magus can be read in abundance. This

<column-break/>

<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>Part I, Nos. 5 & 6 concerning the so-called Old and New.</header>
<sig>B</sig>
<meta>catchword: share</meta>

will certainly never be called "protecting Simon as a **heretic**" by any reasonable person.

(3.) To be sure, some fables regarding this Simon were investigated by using other writers, but again with the sufficient consensus of Protestant writers, many of whom must at least consider Simon's dispute with Peter in Rome to be fictional, insofar as they maintain that Peter was never in Rome. However, such investigation of these fables never occurred with the intention of justifying this godless person or his doctrine and practice in the least, but only to distinguish **true history** from the false according to the law of history <note>original: "ex lege historiæ"</note>. The same is true regarding the other heresies, about which our own theologians and philologists reported many differing accounts long before Mr. Arnold.

(4.) Regarding Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Church Father</note>, he wrote in the *History of the Church*, Book II, Chapter 2, Section 2, that he was a listener of Polycarp (the apostolic man) and a martyr, and that his books could be used for much information; and in Chapter 4, Section 60, he wrote that Irenaeus did not approve of the insolence of the Roman Bishop, but rather opposed him. On the other hand, it is noted in Chapter 5, Section 5, in agreement with Protestant theologians, that Irenaeus elevated the authority of the Roman See too much. Almost all Protestant church histories remind us of such things; however, this does not mean they insult this teacher, or other Fathers, by recounting their faults <note>original: "nævorum," meaning blemishes or errors</note>.

(5.) Thus, this also remains a mere and entirely unauthorized imposition in the eyes of all sensible people, and will be further examined below in Part III, No. 19.

### The 6th Accusation.

->That he wishes to completely abolish external worship and the churches. page 59.<-

### Answer:

(1.) How necessary and beneficial Mr. Arnold considers worship can be clearly found by the reader in his *Explanation*, pages 17, 18, 21, 33, and 43; and in the *Supplements*, pages 8, 52, and 130; but primarily in *The Deviant Paths of the Pious* in the second chapter of the second book.

(2.) His own consistent attendance at public worship, as well as his instruction of others to do the same according to the Scriptures, proves his manifest and blameless conduct to date. Accordingly, both his own testimonies and the slanders of his adversaries must be judged

### The 7th Charge.

->That he wishes to completely abolish the preaching office <note>the ministry</note>. p. 60.<-

### Answer:

(1.) This calumny <note>slander</note> is put to shame by his actual calling, in which he has stood by God’s grace as a preacher and overseer of several congregations and their teachers for eight years, dating from the time of this very dispute: so that no further answer is required.

(2.) Let the Honorable Author <note>original: "Concip." – referring to the opponent who drafted the charges</note> consider and apply to his own untruth his own reminder, which he set down in Volume III, page 132: **It is to be wished that such people, before they criticize anything, would pay close attention and not look at the matter superficially or according to their prejudices; then they would not so easily accuse their neighbor or think the worst of his work.**

### The 8th Charge.

->His *Church History* is a harmful work, a *hæreticissima hæresiologia* <note>original Latin: "most heretical study of heresy"</note>, a mystery of malice. p. 60.<-

### Answer:

This will be discussed below, when we come to the Honorable Author's review, or rather his vilification, of this book.

### The 9th Charge.

->He has translated the *Fragmentum Theodoti* <note>An excerpt from the writings of Theodotus, an early Gnostic teacher</note> so very poorly, committed over 100 errors in it, and did not understand the Greek words. page 60.<-

### Answer:

(1.) In the *Final Representation*, Chapter V, page 43, it has already been shown that H. A. did not make this translation, but someone else entirely—as the self-appointed Censor <note>The critic of Arnold's work</note> himself even suspected. Therefore, no ignorance of Greek <note>original: "in Græcis"</note> can be attributed to him. The Honorable Author should have noted this and retracted the false claim if he had intended to review the work sincerely.

(2.) The Censor himself calls the Greek fragment a very dark,

<meta>catchword: dark/</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>11</page-num>
<header>Part I, No. 9. On the so-called Old and New.</header>
<sig>B 2</sig>

dark, and Dr. B. calls it an unintelligible writing <note>original Latin: "scriptum"</note>, in the *Proof*, page 38.

(3.) The Censor himself was doubtful and uncertain in his own translation, and often had to guess and conjecture, even asking the reader's pardon for it, as he very often writes: presumably, perhaps, as I believe, it can be understood both ways, by all appearances, it could be, *ni fallor* <note>original Latin: "if I am not mistaken"</note>, etc. pp. 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 25, 27. Indeed, on page 25 he confesses: he did not know what it was.

(4.) The author [the Censor] himself presumed to create *varias lectiones* <note>original Latin: "variant readings"</note> in difficult passages according to his own opinion. On the other hand, he mocks H. A. if the latter perhaps read <term>σέβας</term> <note>sebas: awe or reverence</note> for <term>σεβὰ</term>, <term>προσνέχειν</term> <note>prosnechein: to apply oneself to</note> for <term>προσήνειν</term>, and so forth.

(5.) He [the Censor] did not everywhere understand good German, but used his own dialect instead of the Upper Saxon and famously pure idiom.

(6.) In that same *Representation*, page 47, it is proven how one should not immediately conclude an ignorance of the language from one or two errors in a translation (especially of obscure writings), unless one also wishes to charge the most distinguished critics—even Luther himself—with such blame.

(7.) In particular, on page 30 and following, it is further shown through undeniable evidence, citing Greek writers, how the Censor's critiques are frequently unfounded and contrary to the *genium linguæ* <note>original Latin: "the spirit/nature of the language"</note>.

(8.) But as for what the Author repeats separately—as if the translator did not know what <term>ἔξοδος</term> <note>exodos: departure/exodus</note>, <term>ἥττων</term> <note>hetton: lesser/inferior</note>, <term>εὐώνυμος</term> <note>euonymos: of good name/left-hand side</note> and the like meant—he would surely never convince even a schoolboy who can open his lexicon. Such ignorance is not to be suspected in any person with even the slightest experience.

(9.) The Censor himself does not dare to charge H. A. with this. Nor can he with any justification, as sufficient evidence <note>original Latin: "specimina"</note> is publicly available showing how well-versed he is in this branch of study <note>original Latin: "in hoc studiorum genere"</note>.

(10.) If, however, the Honorable Author in the *Reports* still seems to aim this at H. A., then he himself afterwards in the year 1702, page 1109, acknowledged something quite different regarding Arnold's book *De Cognatione Spirituali* <note>original Latin: "On Spiritual Kinship"</note>, in which very many passages from the rarest and most difficult Greek of every age—especially the Scholiasts—are often cited *verbotenus* <note>original Latin: "word for word"</note>.

11. And thus this false conclusion falls away entirely—namely, that the authors were not properly versed, or that such incorrect translations were laid as a foundation. For in this specific case, this *Fragmentum Theodoti* was not laid as a foundation for the history, but was included only so that the doctrine of the Valentinians <note>A prominent Gnostic sect from the 2nd century</note> might be seen somewhat more precisely therein.

### From the Judgment against the *Church History*. p. 95.

In this unchristian and entirely unprovable—indeed, truly confused—judgment, the following accusations are contained:

#### The 10th Charge.

->The *Church History* is such a highly dangerous book, designed so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led astray by it. pag. 95.<- <note>This is a reference to the warning in Matthew 24:24 regarding false prophets.</note>

#### Answer:

(1.) The drafter <note>original: "H. Concip.", referring to the opponent who drafted the legal or theological charges</note> himself, along with others of his kind who oppose us, accuses the book of such crude and obvious malice that, if things were as he pretends, not even reasonable people—let alone the elect—could be led astray by it; he thus misuses the words of Christ.

(2.) The purpose of the Author is well known to God and to all impartial people: that he aims not at deception, but at the true recognition of the common misery—which the drafter himself admits—and the improvement that should follow from it.

(3.) This accusation of "leading astray" is so common that even Christ himself, as the Master of the House, along with his Apostles, was counted among the deceivers by the Scribes and Pharisees; therefore, his followers should not be surprised by it.

(4.) However, when these followers, as servants of God, warn others against deception, it is not done with such crafty conclusions as the drafter uses here (as seen in the following proof), but with the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, and according to the truth.

(5.) In the fourth part of the *Church History*, p. 845, §. 4. and 5., Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> had written: "This imperfect work may have its use, which is then left to God. Meanwhile, it is my heartfelt wish that no one should suffer the slightest loss, hindrance, waste of time, or other unintended effects from it. Just as I do not wish to discourage anyone from using this book, I also cannot specifically advise anyone to do so: since I have become certain through experience how easily natural curiosity, inquisitiveness, boastfulness, self-love, and similar shameful natural forces can mingle with

reading such things." The drafter twists this well-founded and highly necessary sincere admonition to suit his own purpose, wishing to persuade the reader that the author wants his book to remain unread and considers it useless. Arnold warns against the *misuse* of the book, but the Censor warns against the proper use, which is in itself innocent. Arnold addresses the false intentions of the reader; the drafter addresses the work itself. Could these opposing gentlemen reveal the mindset of their hearts any more clearly? Many have wondered at this perverse way of proceeding.

(6.) Such a perverse wish and the conclusion aimed at it have not been fulfilled; instead, they themselves still complain that this book is being read, regardless of the author's own reminder.

(7.) The divine prophecy from Matthew 24:24 is applied here quite absurdly; for that passage speaks of signs and wonders by which even the elect, if possible, might be led astray. Here, however, there are neither signs nor wonders, but a presentation of historical truths, about which some are so concerned that they fear it will exert its power over the elect—which is why there has been so much shouting against it for these ten years.

(8.) Ah, may God grant me a death pure from these cares that kill me, and fortify me with a pure life within myself, in His desires, forgetful of all futility," etc. <note>original Latin: "Abhorrebat tot Voluminum..."</note>

What reasonable person has ever drawn such absurd conclusions from this as are found here? Will this Censor and his helpers not finally...

...wish that his censures would no longer be read by anyone, because he has acted so entirely against all reason?

### The 11th Charge.

Let Mr. Arnold <note>original: "H. A.", Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the author of the controversial *Impartial History*</note> convince his conscience that a love for paradoxes <note>In this context, "paradoxes" refers to unconventional or heterodox doctrines that contradict established church teaching.</note> and for doctrines rejected by the whole world, a contempt for everything he has learned, immeasurable self-love, and a suspicious mind prevail within him. p. 96.

### Answer:

(1.) The Drafter <note>original: "H. Conc.", referring to the opponent who drafted the legal or theological charges against Arnold</note> speaks of the "dominion" of such pernicious sins, and thus of a great degree of them: but because such things cannot coexist with faith and love, and thus with true repentance, he does Mr. Arnold too much wrong here. However, since this comes from someone who lacks the spirit of discernment, it is borne gladly, and better understanding is wished for him.

(2.) That Mr. Arnold does not convict his conscience of such prevailing abominations—against which saving grace warns and chastens him—of this his conscience itself bears witness to him, and indeed in the Holy Spirit with all joyfulness, yet through the pure mercy of God.

(3.) He leaves it, however, to the Drafter to examine more closely from what suspicious, self-loving mind these unspiritual pronouncements against Mr. Arnold have flowed; and he wishes him the necessary light of grace, which he has hitherto fled and rejected, for such an important work as his conversion. That Arnold rejects nothing of what he has learned requires no proof.

### The 12th Charge.

Mr. Arnold's intent is to show the image of corrupt Christianity, or to instill in every reader the conception that there is no other Christian Church than that which abolishes external worship, sermons, and sacraments. p. 96.

### Answer:

(1.) The first part is true: namely, that the *Church History* <note>original: "K. H.", shorthand for *Kirchen-Historie*</note> was intended to show the decline alongside the initial purity.

(2.) But it is false when this purpose is conflated with the other by the Drafter, or presented as one and the same—namely, to instill in the reader the idea that this is the Christian Church: that which abolishes worship and sermons.

(3.) For if it were the same thing to show the decline and to abolish everything, then all those who complain about corrupt Christianity—of whom...

<column-break/>

<page-num>15</page-num>
<header>Part I, Nos. 12, 13. Concerning the so-called Old and New.</header>

...nearly all honest theologians and historians have left behind similar accounts, would have to be burdened with such slander, as has indeed happened to many in fact.

(4.) Where has the Drafter ever read a single letter in Mr. Arnold’s writings of such talk, that the Christian Church is that which abolishes such things? Can one not say here with Paul regarding all descriptions of the common corruption: "What? Do we nullify the law (external order, doctrine, and discipline)? No, we uphold it." <note>A reference to Romans 3:31: "Do we then nullify the law by this faith? Not at all! Rather, we uphold the law." Arnold argues that criticizing the corruption of the church is not the same as wanting to destroy its structure.</note>

(5.) Not only do Mr. Arnold's words testify irrefutably to the contrary, as shown above in number 6 from his clear confessions, but also his constant practice to date, as he himself, being a preacher, helps conduct external worship.

(6.) Even granted that one point or another regarding the abolition of the <term>opus operatum</term> <note>Latin: "the work performed." A theological concept often criticized by Protestants, referring to the idea that sacraments are effective automatically by the mere act of performing them, regardless of the faith of the recipient.</note> and other such soul-harming abuses in worship appears in Mr. Arnold's writings, this can never be applied to the matter itself and its proper use without sinful distortion.

(7.) Such wicked accusations against the "witnesses of truth" from all ages are well known, and every person must willingly take this upon themselves as a suffering if they wish to testify to the general corruption.

(8.) Thus, the Drafter will never be able to verify this sentence from the *Church History*: "This is a Christian Church which abolishes everything external." For by that very act, a congregation would cease to be Christian or a true Church if it wished to throw away all external aids, which even the Quakers <note>A radical Christian group known for their rejection of formal ministry and outward sacraments; Arnold argues that even they maintain some form of community and order.</note> and others do not do.

### The 13th Charge.

He teaches that there is no other Christian Church than that which harbors the most dangerous heretical errors. p. 96.

### Answer:

(1.) Here again, various deceptions are hidden: namely, as if the *Church History* taught, firstly, that the heretics are the true Church; secondly, that no other is the true Church but the heretical one; and finally, that these must be not just common, but the most dangerous heresies.

(2.) This accusation is so shameless that it requires no refutation, but rather a great shaming, which the Holy God...

God wants to and will work within the conscience of the Drafter <note>original: "Concipienten", the person who drafted the legal or theological accusations against Arnold</note> himself; whether it happens sooner or later.

### The 14th Charge:
->He says that the outward worship and orthodoxy of all religions are of the devil. p. 96.<-

### Answer:
(1.) Upon first appearance, the Mr. Drafter did not know how to express this blasphemy severely enough to scare the readers away from the *History of the Church*. However, there is once again craftiness and sophistry behind it.

(2.) For "outward worship" and "orthodoxy" mean either only the common corruption and the abuses that have broken in—both in the practice of church service and in the crept-in un-Christian opinions that induce a false sense of security—or they mean the inherently innocent and necessary doctrine and practice itself, as much of it as may still remain under the state of decline.

(3.) The Mr. Drafter must necessarily mean the latter, for he speaks without condition or restriction regarding the abuses; nor does he wish to recognize any decline in doctrine. Therefore, his accusation is godless when he attributes such gruesome blasphemies to Mr. Arnold, as if he had accused all worship and doctrine itself—even where both are right and good—as being devilish. From this, God has faithfully preserved him and will preserve him eternally.

witnesses before Mr. Arnold have already confessed and confirmed with their blood that such deviations are not from Him who is holy, but from the spirit of the world, which does its work in the children of unbelief.

(5.) (2.) In truth, he has neither gathered a church of his own nor even a sect. Instead, he has publicly demonstrated his abhorrence of all partisanship and sectarianism and has confirmed this through his public office.

(6.) His accusers have never fundamentally proven that Mr. Arnold calls all the named people "witnesses of the truth" without distinction. Instead, they simply state it flatly to deceive the readers and make the danger appear quite great.

(7.) Even if a historian were to quote a few words from one or another erroneous or rejected person as a testimony of the common misery, no sensible person could or would immediately defame him by claiming he belonged to the church of such erroneous people himself.

(8.) The repetition of one or another testimony spoken according to the truth does not suddenly make a reporter a participant in or bound to the entire heresy. Otherwise, no theologian or historian would ever have been allowed to fetch testimonies of truth from the Papacy <note>original: "Testimonia veritatis ex Papatu"</note> or the ancient Christians from Heathenism <note>original: "ex Ethnicismo"</note>. It would be a blasphemous conclusion to say: the first Christians drew upon the heathens as witnesses (following Paul’s example in Acts 17:28), and our theologians draw upon the Papists; therefore, they belong to the church of the heathens or the Papists.

->He excuses and praises most heretics, indeed all atheists. Page 97.<-

### Answer:
(1.) This same untruth was already refuted in the 2nd Charge, where-

to this further accusation is added: that Mr. Arnold not only excuses the heretics but also praises them. In the accusation, these two are treated as one and the same, yet they are very different and quite distinct from one another. He who excuses a defendant does not immediately praise him; rather, he only removes one or another accusation from him.

(2.) To what extent and with what precautions <note>original: "Cautelen"</note> Mr. Arnold excuses some who have been accused of error—following the example of our own historians—has already been shown above, and indeed throughout all these observations, according to the truth. But that he should praise a single "heretic" properly so-called, or even all atheists, is a malicious imposition. It is, in fact, the highest degree of slander—as Morhof <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a polymath and historian</note> calls it—which no one can ever verify. It is much worse, and a higher degree of malice, to praise all atheists than to be an atheist oneself. ### The 18th Charge:
->He makes Julian into a highly virtuous man who was plagued by the Christians. Page 97.<-

### Answer:
(1.) In Book IV, Chapter 1, Paragraph 17, Mr. Arnold expressly protested that he did not wish to excuse Julian’s <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor who tried to roll back Christianity</note> person or his <note>Note: "NB." stands for "nota bene," or "take note"</note> unbelief. (2.) Where, then, does it speak of a "highly virtuous man"? Is an unbelieving, pagan, abominable person virtuous? Or can there be true virtue in the midst of unbelief? Mr. Arnold believes, with all true Christians, that pagan virtues are far from being true virtues before God. Moreover, Julian had few or none of the kind of virtues that one otherwise reads about in other pagans.

(4.) More on this can be found in the *Supplements*, page 62.

### The 19th Charge:
### That he makes Emperor Wenceslaus into a fundamentally pious Christian.
page 92.

#### Answer:

(1.) Even if Mr. Arnold <note>original: "H. A."</note> had described this Emperor as not being so wicked and bad, he would have caused no offense to any upright Protestant, nor acted against the truth. This is because histories clearly state that he stood by Jan Hus against the Papists, according to the testimony of Dubravius <note>Jan Dubravius (1486–1553), a Bohemian historian</note> and Theobaldus <note>Zacharias Theobald (1584–1627), author of a history of the Hussite wars</note>; which even Dr. Kortholt <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian</note>, among others, considers praiseworthy in him, *Ecclesiastical History, 14th Century, Section 3, page 595*. <note>original: "quo solo nomine laudem promeruit" — by which name alone he earned praise</note>.

(2.) Nevertheless, Mr. Arnold writes very cautiously in Book XIV, Chapter 1, Section 4: "I will never excuse the vices themselves that are attributed to him." And in Section 6: "Granted that some [of his vices] were true, he has suffered enough for them." There, he examines the most prominent accounts of him and, based on the confessions of irreproachable writers, casts doubt on several of them.

(3.) All of this demonstrates quite palpably that Mr. Arnold never made him out to be a good ruler, let alone a fundamentally pious Christian. Rather, this exaggeration and hyperbole from the Commission <note>original: "Conc.", likely the theological faculty opposing Arnold</note> is, like the previous one, a formula and figure of the usual "fashionable" style of preaching, where many often call evil good and good evil, light darkness and darkness light, and do so with great exaggerations and hyperboles.

### The 20th Charge:
### That he rightly excuses the loathsome blasphemer Adelgreiff.
page 97.

#### Answer:

(1.) It is one thing to excuse or justify a blasphemer in his wickedness and insofar as he blasphemes God; it is quite another thing to wish for a blinded man that he might have been

<column-break/>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>Part I, Nos. 20. 21. N. regarding the so-called Old and New.</header>
<sig>C 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: So</meta>

rightly guided with more gentleness, patience, wisdom, and power, or that his improvement had been waited for, rather than his being executed immediately in his blindness before he had enough time to convert or even come to his healthy senses. The reader will find that the former, and not the latter, is what was done by Mr. Arnold regarding this history. Thus, the opponent accuses him here in vain, and tries to persuade people without cause that Mr. Arnold colludes with the worst blasphemers. Indeed, the opponent blasphemes that which flowed from Christian love for the conversion of such people—may the Lord grant him to recognize this and not hold it against him!

(2.) Mr. Arnold writes of this man <note>Johann Albrecht Adelgreiff, executed in 1636 for claiming to be God's representative</note> in Part III, Chapter 4, Section 60, that he held himself to be a divine person out of an erroneous delusion, and that he should have been brought back to what is right with gentleness, or his change should have been expected with patience. He further regrets, in Section 62, that they tried to convert him through torture, as Hartknochius <note>Christoph Hartknoch (1644–1687), a historian and educator</note> admits. From Franckenberg’s judgment <note>Abraham von Franckenberg (1593–1652), a mystic and biographer of Jacob Böhme</note>, Section 64 also notes that this man was "trapped in his own nature" and did not know himself what he was imagining, etc. In short: Mr. Arnold did not excuse the man's delusions and blasphemies, but only desired <note>original: "desideriret"</note> the long-suffering and patience of his judges and the preachers, as all the words there prove. And who would even want to excuse such foolish pretenses of the poor man? Can it even be suspected of someone who still has his five senses?

### The 21th Charge:
### He slanders the Church Fathers and almost all Evangelical teachers. p. 98. Also Mr. M. Scharff against Mr. Langen. p. 97.

#### Answer:

(1.) Above, it was said that Mr. Arnold slanders *all* teachers; here it says *almost all*. Thus, the testimony agrees nowhere.

(2.) It was clearly demonstrated above in the 3rd Charge that Mr. Arnold slanders no upright teacher, let alone all or almost all, but rather honors, loves, and praises them—even if he was not permitted to remain silent about their human faults in his history. Thus, this untruth also falls away.

(3.) When the late Luther was accused by the Papists (who elevate the Church Fathers <note>original: "Patres"</note> all too high) of speaking shamefully of them—for example, saying that Jerome had devastated the whole Gospel, deserved hell more than heaven, and was a heretic; that Basil was of no use; that Cyprian was a weak theologian, and such things...

### The 22nd Charge:

->He slanders the Emperors Constantine the Great, Theodosius, and Charlemagne. page 98.<-

### Answer:

(1.) This has already been answered in detail, specifically regarding *Constantine the Great* <note>original: "Constant. M."</note> in the *Supplements, pages 61, 63*, and especially extensively on *pages 66–105*, against which deduction no one has since been able to bring forward anything significant.

(2.) Regarding *Theodosius*, the general warnings <note>original: "Monita"</note> made there must be observed; namely, how a historian certainly has the right and justification to investigate the truth even regarding such persons and not to remain silent about their vices; however, this is by no means the same as slandering. Mr. Arnold <note>original: "H. A."</note> has also shown much that is praiseworthy about *Theodosius* in Book IV, Chapter 2, Section 23: how even the pagans praised his wealth; likewise in Chapter 3, Section 9, that he abolished many pagan abominations, and so on.

(3.) The same is all the more certain regarding *Charlemagne* <note>original: "Carolo M."</note>, as he lived in the very midst of the Papacy. Nevertheless, Mr. Arnold has impartially acknowledged of him that, as a witness to the truth, he reformed the clergy, maintained many truths, checked the malice of the clergy in many ways, and made many good arrangements; and according to his understanding, he earnestly took up the improvement of the church and held strictly to good discipline, etc. Book IX, Chapter 1, Section 3. On the other hand, for the sake of the truth, he

<meta>catchword: sake</meta>

<header>Part I, Nos. 23. 24. N. on the so-called Old and New.</header>

sake <note>original: "willen"</note> could not remain silent about those things regarding *Charlemagne* which our own theologians and historians, indeed even the oldest writers, found lacking <note>original: "desideriren"</note> in him. But just as little as these writers slandered him, so little can the same be said of Mr. Arnold.

### The 23rd Charge:

->He slanders the Prince-Electors of Saxony who lived at the beginning of the Reformation; likewise: He reviles his native sovereign lords. page 98.<-

### Answer:

(1.) If Mr. Arnold had falsely and without basis written evil things about such persons, he would indeed have slandered them and would be punishable.

(2.) However, only certain human failings of such lords—especially Elector John Frederick <note>John Frederick I (1503–1554), a key patron of Luther</note>—have been recounted impartially from clear documents; but never were they themselves slandered in the least in their high persons, much less was their magisterial authority attacked.

(3.) Furthermore, such accounts are taken from domestic authors <note>original: "domestiquen Autoribus"</note> who for the most part lived at that same time and were children of the Saxon land, or at least subjects, or indeed even *Ministers* of the same. Had they not left behind such histories, Mr. Arnold would not have known them nor been able to recount them.

(4.) If these authors committed no slander against their native and presiding lords in whose own lands they lived, then the repetition of it can even less be called such, as has already been shown in the *Supplements, page 136*.

(5.) Within the last 10 years in Saxony itself, so many complaints about the falling away to the Papacy and other offenses have been printed, yet no one has wanted to or been able to consider them slanders.

### The 24th Charge:

->He wishes to make holy angels out of Müntzer and the Anabaptists in the IVth Part. page 98.<-

### Answer:

(1.) The drafter of the charge <note>original: "H. (2.) But that Mr. Arnold does not make "holy angels" out of these very people (which is again merely a rhetorical figure), but rather according to the truth...

->**The 25th Charge:**<-

->**He concludes that one should abandon offices and everything else and start a different Christianity. page 98.**<-

->**Answer:**<-

(1.) In the conclusion of the *Church History* <note>original: "K. H.", referring to the "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie"</note>, Mr. Arnold had spoken according to his insight at the time concerning the obstacles to true self-denial and the following of Jesus Christ. He spoke from a sincere heart and made a brief confession as to why he, for his own person, deemed this necessary.

(2.) However, with this, he does not suggest with a single word **that others should abandon their offices and everything;** for that would indeed be acting unwisely and indiscreetly—wanting to force his own paths and particular divine leadings upon others.

(3.) Much less does he wish to see **a "different Christianity" started** than that which Jesus Christ and his Apostles left behind for us through word and deed. He has also sought no other

### Answer:

(1.) This accusation, along with the previous one at the end of page 98 <note>original: "p. 98. in fine"</note>, is set down so presumptuously out of a perverse zeal, yet it is not proven with even a shadow of a reason. If one were to attempt to prove it, however, the clear impossibility of doing so would be easily seen.

(2.) The intention is to make this book hated by the readers, as if those who are typically branded as heretics—the very ones often called rogues and thieves—were presented as honest, and conversely, as if honest patriots were turned into thieves.

(3.) To say that everything concerning the heretics has been interpreted in the best possible light is a double untruth: namely (a) that *everything*, and not just a little or a fair amount, but indeed (b) was interpreted in the *best* light.

(4.) For it is proven by all the numerous passages in which the dangerous errors of those rightly called heretics are recounted and rejected, that not only was everything *not* interpreted well, but nothing inherently evil was interpreted even slightly well, let alone in the best light. Regarding Simon <note>Simon Magus, often considered the first heretic in Christian history</note>, the Gnostics, the Manichaeans, the Donatists, the Arians, and others, it has already been shown above in the 2nd and 5th accusations that the errors of these people were properly punished.

(5.) However, so that such gruesome claims might be put to shame here by even a single example, it is expressly written of the <term>Münster Anabaptists</term> <note>A radical sect that took over the city of Münster in 1534, leading to a violent siege</note> in the place cited above in the 15th accusation: That they held gruesome errors and gross misconduct. Regarding the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, it states clearly in Book IV, Chapter 8, § 1: they showed themselves to be anything but faithful in such cruel persecution and blasphemy (namely, against Christ). And in § 18: on their side, Christian duty was set aside; they had brought forth mere opinions and shallow questions instead of active Christianity. Again in § 21: Reason was put to shame among the Arians and brought about nothing but discord. The confused dealings that occurred among their sects are impossible to describe—along with many more such rebukes against them.

(6.) Let someone now conclude from this and say, along with the drafter of these charges <note>original: "H. Concip.", referring to the person who drafted the list of accusations against Arnold</note>, that everything was interpreted in the heretics' favor. The reader sees from these few points that no further proof is needed against such unfounded accusations; rather, it shows that these accusers are accustomed to interpreting not just some things, but *everything* about their neighbor in the worst possible way, just as they have been—

### The 28th Accusation:

He claims regarding the great disagreement <note>original: "Dissensu"</note> between the Valentinians and Anabaptists that they all run upon the same foundation; on the other hand, he forces the slightest disputes upon the teachers of our Church as major divisions <note>original: "Capital-Dissensus"</note>. Page 99.

### Answer:

(1.) Concerning the first part of the accusation, I cannot find at this time where the disagreement <note>original: "Dissensus"</note> of the Valentinians <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic sect</note> and Anabaptists is touched upon; the passage <note>original: "Locus"</note> is also not cited by the drafter of the charges.

(2.) Even assuming it were written in the *Church History* that they ran upon the same foundation, this is by no means written in a biased or false manner, and much less is it prejudicial to the Evangelical Church, because both of these sects are held to be erroneous; thus, whether they disagree or agree <note>original: "Dissensus oder Consensus"</note> neither harms nor benefits the Truth itself.

(3.) One also cannot see how this could have served to excuse one sect or the other, since according to common principles, one person in error cannot justify another through their agreement.

(4.) The second part of the charge is again framed so deceptively out of emotional bias and must be properly investigated. That not only minor but also very great disputes often arose within the Lutheran Church is evident from history and can in no way be denied. Both types necessarily had to be described in the *Church History*, which all sensible people recognize and admit, because it is a primary component of history itself.

(5.) Now the question is whether Mr. Arnold <note>original: "H. A."</note> not only describes the slightest disputes but also "trumpets them up," and specifically as major divisions <note>original: "Capital-Dissensus"</note>. The drafter of the charges says so, but proves it with not a single word or the citation of a single passage. How then can one believe him?

(6.) The contrary, however, shall be clearly evident from the direction of the places where these matters are handled. In Chapter 30 of Book XVI, where the internal and minor disputes of the Lutherans are treated specifically <note>original: "ex Professo"</note>, these modest words stand at the beginning of that history in § 10: "We wish to briefly touch upon a few more particular disputes which did not exactly result in a public schism, but nevertheless caused one or another problemat—"

### The 29th Accusation.

He passes over the odious <note>repulsive or hateful</note> matters of the Fanatics <note>original: "Fanaticorum"; a term used then for radical reformers who claimed direct divine inspiration</note> in silence; e.g., Menno Simons’ dispute with David Joris <note>Meno Simonis (1496–1561) was a leader of the Anabaptists; David Joris (1501–1556) was a more radical mystic</note>, Breckling's controversy with Kuhlmann, the Quakers' recent schism <note>original: "Schisma"</note>, p. 99.

#### Answer:

(1.) This untruth could be refuted generally by all those passages in which the odious matters of such people are clearly uncovered, as the visual evidence in the description of every sect shows.

(2.) But to stay only with the cited examples, let one judge from the following words whether (α) the *Mennonites’* <note>original: "Menisten"</note> odious matters, and (β) *Menno’s* dispute with *Joris* were passed over in silence?

(3.) In general, it is expressly stated in Book XVI, Chapter 21, §. 33, that many offensive and punishable things occurred among the Anabaptists <note>original: "Widertäuffer"</note>, and that there were many hypocrites even among them. Furthermore, in the same place: The new Anabaptists themselves admitted their divisions. And in Book XVII, Chapter 12, §. 31, their other recent divisions and separations are further recounted, and it is then impartially concluded: From these and other of their affairs, one concludes a great stubbornness, self-complacency, and Pharisaism, as can easily happen in sectarian matters. Are stubbornness, self-complacency, and Pharisaism then not "odious" things, and were they passed over in silence in the *Church History* <note>Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie"</note>? Let the conscience of the Accuser <note>original: "H. Concip." – referring to the drafter of the charges</note> now answer to that, and let all reasonable readers decide for themselves.

(4.) Furthermore, concerning Menno and his followers in particular, it is stated in Book XVI, Chapter 21, §. 38, that a great division arose—

<column-break/>

<page-num>29</page-num>
<header>Part I, No. 29. 30. regarding the so-called Old and New.</header>
<sig>D 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: covery</meta>

arose among them, and that their adversaries took great occasion from this to judge them poorly, and the guilty parties themselves publicly discovered their own foundation (namely, how miserable it was.) In Number 39, they are called a sect, and it is further acknowledged that Menno was all too harsh and legalistic, and that his people practiced a Pharisaic rather than a living Christianity. Following this, it is expressly stated: David *Joris* also wrote sharply to him and wanted to show how much he still lacked in true divine knowledge. And finally, it is recounted: *Menno’s* followers had exalted him too much: and lastly, it is impartially concluded: Just as in general the sectarian factions <note>original: "Rotten"</note> have established nothing good, and for that reason were rejected by Paul. How will the Accuser now demonstrate that Mr. A. <note>Arnold</note> concealed the odious matters of these people? He is certainly bound to retract this false accusation along with all the previous ones.

(5.) Concerning the other named disputes of *Breckling* and the *Quakers*, these primarily fall, according to their actual outbreak, in the time after the year 1688, which is the cutoff date <note>original: "Terminus"</note> of the *Church History*, and therefore it was neither necessary nor possible to touch upon them, especially as the documents <note>original: "Documentis"</note> were also lacking. Nonetheless, the recent schisms among the Quakers are described in detail in Numbers 59 and following of Chapter 20 in Book XVII. And one can otherwise see from all other descriptions of the sects that not even the slightest dispute was concealed with intent; at the very least, no impartial person will attribute it to malice.

(6.) As for *Breckling* <note>Friedrich Breckling (1629–1711), a mystic and critic of the Lutheran church</note>, the Accuser unchristianly places him among the Fanatics, which Mr. Lange has irrefutably proven in Part III of the *Sincere Reports*, p. 7, and in Part IV, p. 96; consequently, this complaint also falls away, as if Mr. A. had not recounted the dispute of the Fanatics.

### The 30th Accusation:

That he published entire records <note>original: "Acta"</note> which serve to wound the Protestant Church, and applied everything in the most embittered <note>original: "vergalleste" – literally "most gall-filled"</note> way to our church state. p. 99.

#### Answer:

(1.) That some records were published is true; but with what intentions is best known to GOD—namely, solely for greater insight into the misery of many unenlightened teachers and leaders, and not for the wounding—

### The 32nd Accusation.

->He shames G. Major <note>Georg Major (1502–1574), a Lutheran theologian involved in controversies regarding the necessity of good works</note>, insofar as he held with the Protestant Church/ but praises him/ insofar as he held singular new opinions. p. 99.<-

### Answer:

(1.) Both are a deliberate untruth/ as can be seen from the following passages of the Church History <note>original: "K. H." abbreviated for Kirchen-Historie</note>. In Book XVI. Ch. 27. and thus in the very same chapter where Major's new opinions are recounted/ §. 2 states: This Major was a disciple of Luther <note>original: "Lutheri Discipel"</note>, and had been very dear to him / who also greatly praised his faithfulness. Here Major is not shamed/ insofar and as long as he held with the Protestant Church/ but praised.

(2.) Conversely, it is recounted immediately thereafter from a Chief Physician of Electoral Saxony / that Major supposedly brought forth his opinion later at the persuasion of a counselor/ to flatter the Papists <note>Catholics</note> all the more. Here Major is not praised at all insofar as he held his new opinion/ and where he is perhaps excused or his opinion is softened <note>original: "emollire," from Latin</note>, all this occurs with the words of Lutheran theologians themselves and based on the nature and circumstances of such a dispute. And so the reader will also find this history throughout to be impartial and according to the truth/ but especially clearly recognize/ that Major, with Luther, gave many good reminders against false delusional faith and the abuse of the Gospel.

(3.) Thus, where the Mr. Accuser <note>original: "H. A."</note> claims Major was shamed / cannot be seen: for what is written several times in the preceding Chapter 26 regarding Major's opinion on the Interim <note><term>Interim</term>: The Augsburg Interim (1548), a temporary religious law ordered by Emperor Charles V following his defeat of the Protestant League</note>, therein he was entirely at one with the most renowned theologians / such as Eber, Menius, Pfeffinger, and Melanchthon, as can be seen there in §. 5. and 7. But what is shown in Chapter 3 from undeniable documents/ therein the Mr. Author <note>H. A.</note> could not act against the truth / but for it.

### The 35th Charge:

His most prominent dogmas <note>established church doctrines</note> are supposedly: Sunday, all festivals, churches, confession, Holy Communion, weddings <note>original: "Copulationes"</note>, and funerals should be abolished. p. 100.

#### Answer:

(2.) Although he has written boldly <note>original: "cordate"</note> in some parts of his writings about the *abuse* of certain church customs for the sake of greed and the like, he has nowhere rejected the truly God-pleasing *use* of them. Even his adversaries can produce no trace of proof for such a claim.

(3.) When it is specifically recounted concerning the first Christians in Book 1, Chapter 2, § 7, that they did not have such things, this is, firstly, certain from their practice according to the circumstances of that time; and the opponents would have to prove otherwise. Secondly, the conclusion is drawn in vain from such a report as to whether today—when circumstances and constitutions are entirely different—nothing of the sort is permitted or may be maintained under Divine patience.

(4.) By thus baselessly attributing to him the total abolition of such things, they seek nothing other than to bring the ignorant into a zeal and loathing against him and his testimonies. GOD knows best how far He will let them succeed or not.

### The 38th Charge:
->There are traditions outside of God's Word that must be followed. p. 100.<-

#### Answer:
(1.) H. A. writes quite clearly in Book I, Chapter 2, § 7, in the margin: **the first Christians had their spiritual exercises without human-made ordinances.** And in Book III, Chapter 5, § 1, also Book IV, Chapter 5, § 1, he shows the origin of traditions during the period of decline / just as in Book VI, Chapter 2, § 6, he shows how they were finally **placed alongside the Bible** during the extreme apostasy. Furthermore, in Book II, Chapter 5, § 5, he laments / that as early as the 2nd Century <note>original: "II. Seculo"</note> the traditions of the ancestors were made into a rule.

(2.) When, therefore, with such a pure Evangelical mind, he rejects human traditions but mentions those traditions in a historical manner which the Holy Apostles of Jesus Christ themselves mention—such as 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 3:6—and which the very first teachers mentioned: then in this he is also at one with our theologians / who certainly admit / that there were certain traditions <note>original: "Traditiones"</note> in the **Early Church** which stem from the Apostles / and perhaps concern Christian morals, customs, and orders. A different question is / whether we still have such things today / which no one would say / except a Papist. Of these, the old Lutheran theologian Sarcerius <note>Erasmus Sarcerius (1501–1559), a prominent Lutheran reformer</note> says among other things in his book *On Discipline*, page 134: a) **There are several Apostolic ordinances beyond these [written ones] which they did not leave to the churches in writing. And there are two kinds: Some true and some false. == These we must gather together from the books of the Fathers, and so forth.** Compare Isaac Casaubon <note>A renowned scholar of the late Renaissance</note> *Dedication to the Exercises* <note>original: "Dedic. Exercit."</note> p. b. 4. & Exercise 1. num. 38. p. 89. and following; likewise: Hülsemann in *Against Bellarmine* <note>original: "Anti-Bellarmino"</note> cited in Quenstedt's *System* <note>original: "Syst. P. I. p. 116"</note>.

(3.) The Apostles could certainly point their listeners to such oral teachings and traditions at that time / because they spoke nothing else orally than what was contained in their writings. That, on the contrary, after that time and especially under the Papacy, no supposed oral traditions of the Apostles are to be trusted / is well known among the Protestants by our theologians / of whom Dr. Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian</note> is particularly worth reading /

When Mr. Drafter therefore alleges / that H. A. holds with Stiefel / he could easily commit no greater audacity / since the complete contrary shines forth from all these lines.

(4.) To the third / that H. A. believes in a deification / let the truth-loving reader look up what H. A. himself has extensively presented against this error in his *Treatise on Deviations* in Book I, Chapter 12, § 23 to 39, with the agreement of old and new theologians / where he well distinguishes the right use of this expression <note>Theosis or union with God</note> from the abuse and mere imagination of the ancients / and describes this abuse as a **spiritual pride and dangerous error**. With this, Varenius’s *Consideration against Rockius* page 105 and following may also be compared / and especially Mr. Professor Francke’s <note>August Hermann Francke, a leader of Pietism</note> last defense against Dr. Meyer / who had also accused him of such things / that every Pietist was God / from page 283 to 308. Mr. Drafter will hopefully notice and repent of his injustice from this.

### The 45th Charge:
->That he speaks so faithfully in favor of Magic. p. 101.<-

### Answer:

(1.) The Author of the charges will surely also recognize and admit a good and healthy understanding of Magic, as ancient and modern Christian authors do, of whom a great number could be cited. "The word magic," <note>original: "Magiæ vox"</note> said Voëtius <note>Gysbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian known for his strict orthodoxy</note> among others in Part II, *Select Disputations* page 539, "was first accepted in a good sense. — it signifies a wise man skilled in divine and human matters." <note>original: "primo in bonam partem accepta. -- significat sapientem rerum Divinarum & humanarum peritum."</note>

(2.) Now, the Author of the charges speaks without proper distinction; but because his intention is to accuse the *Church History*, he will naturally understand magic to be an evil and devilish art, and thus present H. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> as a "magus" <note>A sorcerer or magician</note> or wizard, or at the very least wish to make him suspect of it.

(3.) Such a capital crime <note>original: "Capital-Crimine"</note> would also require a formal and thorough proof; yet once again, not a word of it is to be found here.

(4.) He will likely want to guess it from the excerpts <note>original: "Excerptis"</note> concerning magic that appear in Part IV, page 159 and following. However, he could have clearly seen in that very place that the author excerpted there condemns false magic as devilish sorcery, warns against it, and clearly describes its types—namely "Cacosophia" <note>False wisdom or malicious magic</note> and "Cacodaemonia" <note>The worship of evil spirits or demons</note>—and also carefully distinguishes them from the true kind.

(5.) These excerpts stand there plainly in the words of the authors, and H. A. has not added a single syllable of his own; consequently, he has spoken in favor of sorcery as little as other writers who excerpt such passages from rare authors. Therefore, the Author of the charges must also recognize his slander in this matter.

### The 46th Charge:
->That he leaves no atheist without an excuse. p. 101.<-

### Answer:

This has already been found otherwise above in the 2nd Charge, and is to be considered further in Part III, No. 17, and in Part IV, No. 143; likewise in Part V, sections 17 to 28.

### The 47th Charge:
->Satan's intent is, α.) to introduce total Skepticism through the *Church History*, and to lead everyone astray. p. 101.<-

### Answer:

(1.) H. A. has nothing to do with Satan. He knows in whom he believes, and who governs him in his writing. Let the Author of the charges take care that he does not blindly attribute the workings of the Good Spirit to Satan, and thus commit a grievous offense against it; especially since he speaks dubiously, saying "it may well be," <note>original: "es möge wol seyn"</note> whereas as a theologian he should not base such important and dangerous accusations on mere conjectures.

(2.) Since the Author of the charges and others attribute a unique religion of his own making to H. A., they themselves liberate him from the suspicion of Skepticism. For whoever starts a religion of his own is no skeptic; much less does he introduce Skepticism to others, but rather he points to certain opinions and principles which he holds to be religion.

(3.) But that H. A. is nevertheless no skeptic—even though he has not started his own religion—nor wishes to lead others to it or make everyone go astray, is proven by his conduct in doctrine and life to this very day, to the shame of his accusers. They can always hear of this from his fellow workers and listeners in churches and schools if they wish. Meanwhile, let one read what the late Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism," who was Arnold's mentor</note> answered on this point to a similar accusation against "Spenerian Skepticism" by Dr. Pfeiffer; thus one will soon emerge from such doubts.

### The 48th Charge:
->(β.) To love Arianism, Manichaeism, and other most harmful errors. p. 101.<-

### Answer:

Had the accuser known of worse heresies <note>original: "Ketzereyen"</note> to name, he would have done so. But even this very wicked slander <note>original: "Verleumdung"</note> has already been uncovered above in the 32nd and 33rd Charges.

### The 49th Charge:

(γ.) To make the pure, zealous teachers—who urge true godliness—seem suspicious by placing them in the midst of the greatest fanatics, rebels, atheists, and singularists <note>non-conformists or those holding peculiar, isolated views</note>. p. 101.

->Answer:<-

(1.) Fleshly and perverse zealots and offensive teachers are indeed exposed here and there according to the truth; however, Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the Pietist historian being defended</note> has always held pure, zealous teachers who push for true godliness in high regard, and he has had to endure much specifically in their defense.

(2.) Never has he sought to make them suspicious, nor has Satan sought to do so through him—as the Author of the charges <note>original: "H. Conc." (Herr Concipient), the opponent drafting the accusations</note> blasphemously claims—because such teachers are far too dear and precious to him.

(3.) If he is said to have placed some among the greatest fanatics, rebels, or even atheists, then: a) the question is whether such people were actually fanatical, rebellious, and atheistic in fact, or whether they were merely denounced as such by others, as is still the practice today. b) The Holy Spirit gives Mr. A. testimony in his conscience that even if some were truly such evil people (which is not admitted), he nevertheless never placed righteous teachers among such people for the purpose of making them suspicious. Thus, the Author of the charges describes him in vain and in a malicious manner as the worst of scoundrels, who supposedly mixed the best men of God among rebels and atheists with intent. Experience—alas!—teaches us that so many pure, zealous teachers have been made suspicious by the gentlemen of Wittenberg <note>the center of Lutheran Orthodoxy, often at odds with Arnold's Pietism</note> and others, and placed among fanatics and singularists. The most recent examples involving Mr. Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the "Father of Pietism"</note> and others are still fresh in memory, and the 5th Part here will show more of this.

### The 50th Charge:

(δ.) To throw all good church and civil order <note>original: "Policen-Ordnung" refers to the regulation of public life and governance</note> into a single heap <note>i.e., to overthrow or disregard all established order</note>. p. 102.

->Answer:<-

This slander has already been put to shame several times above with words, and even more so by deeds.

### The 51st Charge.

(ε.) To include magic, rebellion, and other terrible wickednesses in his draft <note>his writings</note> as if they could easily coexist with the Spirit of God. page 102.

> May God have mercy on us and shortly tread Satan under our feet as an accuser! Amen! <note>A paraphrase of Romans 16:20</note>

### The 54th Charge.
That he teaches that experienced Christians are entirely free from external church affairs. p. 265.

#### Answer:
(1.) His words there are well-limited and restricted in Chapter V. §. 15. p. 26. The ancient teachers describe experienced Christians, as living temples, as being indeed <note>original: "NB." (Nota Bene/Note Well)</note> **free from external church affairs so far as they have attained the purpose of these things, though they do not abolish other intentions for them; namely that those who do not need them <note>original: "NB."</note> nevertheless use one thing or another out of Christian discretion and love for peace according to the freedom of their conscience under Divine patience,** as he explains on p. 22, and hereafter proves from Luther.

(2.) The Drafter <note>original: "Concip." – the person drafting the charges against Arnold</note> diligently, but very maliciously, leaves out this highly necessary limitation so that it sounds all the more horrific in the ears of the ignorant; suggesting that Mr. Arnold does not want experienced Christians in the church, and so forth, which was nonetheless not his meaning, as is evident from his confessions found above in No. 6 and in Part II, No. 3, 5, and 26.

(3.) For the rest, it should be known that Mr. Arnold published this explanation by order and with the approval of the Royal Commission of that time, which was also at peace with this, his blameless and well-limited declaration on this point <note>original: "in hoc puncto"</note>.

### The 55th Charge:
Arnold teaches that Luther finally lost the power of the Gospel noticeably and erred greatly. p. 265.

#### Answer:
(1.) He has nowhere spoken with such exaggeration as to say that Luther "erred greatly"; rather, he first testified with great modesty in general: It would be better if one were not forced to rebuke such things, Chapter VI. §. 3.

(2.) Concerning the matter itself, however, he said nothing further than this: **At the end, in a state of contradiction <note>original: "in statu contradictionis"</note>, he sometimes cast into doubt or even contradicted what he had taught against Papist things.** In this regard, it is cited as an example how he rejected the Epistle of James <note>Luther famously called the Epistle of James an "epistle of straw" because it seemed to contradict his doctrine of justification by faith alone</note>.

### The 56th Charge.
Arnold’s chief opinion is that a true believer does not desire to go to public worship or into the churches; he does it only for the sake of peace. p. 266.

#### Answer:
(1.) These captious and craftily presented propositions do not appear in the entire writing currently under consideration, and they provide an example of how not at all upright the Messrs. Drafters are in reviewing and excerpting other people's books, and how much they sin there with the mutilation and corruption of meaning and expression.

(2.) Mr. Arnold’s entire presentation there is primarily directed toward this—and this is therefore his chief opinion—that external worship is most necessary for the ignorant and weak, and that, conversely, those who have more practiced senses nevertheless also come to it out of love for God and their neighbors. But in no way does he say: a believer does not even desire to go there; least of all, that he does it only for the sake of peace <note>original: "Ruhe" - can mean rest, quiet, or public peace</note>.

(3.) When he says on p. 19: Although a living temple does not strictly have need or even a desire to go to church, he still goes in: He speaks—as he clearly explains himself there (especially §. 8. p. 23)—of the commonly corrupted style of worship, when the preachers speak only of useless things, or even scold and revile and such like; after which kind of sermons certainly no sensible person will desire to go, nor should it be taken ill if someone does not desire them. However, regarding truly Divine teachings, that is not the question there, as every Christian must desire those.

### The 66th Charge:

(2.) ### The 67th Charge:

That he places all the <term>Papists</term> <note>original: "Päbstler", a derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> at the top, and counts so very few pure <term>Evangelical</term> <note>Protestant/Lutheran</note> teachers, but by contrast so many erroneous people among his saints. p. 384.

### Answer:

(1.) In the ordering, chronology was mostly observed; therefore, one had to begin with those persons living before and around Luther’s time, who certainly lived within the Papacy, but who were also not at one with its main errors, and thus are not to be called Papists through and through.

(2.) If the Drafter now wishes to abuse this innocent order—as he does with other such circumstances—for the sake of slander, as if Mr. A. had placed them at the top to despise others, let him do so at his own peril. (3.) It was not enough that the Drafter spoke of erroneous and suspicious people; he should have also clearly proven in detail for the readers' information who such people were.

(4.) It is also mocking and malicious when he calls them "Mr. A.’s saints," as if Mr. A. were first making these people saints or canonizing them, when they were already known and beloved for their teaching and life for more than 100 or 200 years before him.

#### The 69th Charge:
That Divine Wisdom, as the glorifying power of the Holy Trinity, would not be a mystery in itself, since even the pagans recognized such power. p. 368.

#### Answer:
(1.) Thus the Drafter <note>the author of the charges</note> speaks and concludes about the matter, thereby demonstrating his ignorance of the Kingdom of God—indeed, his own heterodoxy <note>unorthodox belief</note>—by teaching of the pagans **that they recognized such clarifying power of the Holy Trinity**, which no true Christian, let alone a theologian, will grant him or overlook. Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> himself protested against pagan concepts in the preface at § 11 and 12; yet the Censor falls upon it anyway and says **the pagans had recognized the glorifying power of the Holy Trinity**:

<meta>catchword: recognized:</meta>

<column-break/>

recognized: One cannot understand or rescue his words in any way other than what has been indicated; rather, he has entangled himself while trying to brand others as heretics. But how will he ever prove it?

(2.) The description, however, which Mr. A. has set down is in accordance with Scripture, as in the Book of Wisdom VII, 25 <note>a book of the Apocrypha</note>, it states that she is the breath of the Divine power, etc., of which there are more passages <note>original Latin: "Loca"</note> in the said book.

(3.) But so that one may quickly emerge from all scruples <note>doubts</note> over such a presentation, it is important to know that Mr. A., along with all true theologians, understands by Divine Wisdom nothing else or more than the eternal Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, the Wisdom of the Father (as he himself has cited so many testimonies of Scripture and Antiquity in Chapter IV, § 10 and following, p. 32, 33); and specifically, in so far as this eternal Wisdom grants itself to be known and enjoyed by the faithful in a hidden manner, yet one described in Holy Scripture.

#### The 70th Charge:
He teaches that Wisdom is a particular Divine Being which has its own characteristics. p. 368.

#### Answer:
(1.) If Mr. A.’s words are kept in their proper context and not cited in such a mutilated way, the reader can clearly see the blameless and scriptural meaning. Thus He says in the mentioned place, p. 35, § 3: **The Spirit of Jesus and the Spirit of Wisdom are not two distinct spirits, but a single spirit and an inseparable essence.** And § 5: **Wisdom is a particular Divine Being, which is indeed in itself—Note well—one with the eternal Godhead, and never works or creates anything without or outside of the same, yet nevertheless makes itself known under its own Divine character.**

(2.) Here it clearly states that Wisdom is one and an inseparable essence with the eternal Godhead and especially with the Son of God, and that she nevertheless makes herself known under her own *character* <note>distinctive mark or expression</note>. Thus, it is primarily speaking of the communication or illumination as a work that flows out upon the creatures, wherein a certain *character* is attributed to Wisdom—namely, for the sake of human weakness.

(3.) But as far as the name *character* is concerned, no one should take offense at it who has heard it applied to Christ in Holy Scripture itself.

### The 71st Charge:
->That she <note>Wisdom/Sophia</note> is distinct from the Trinity; so that one could almost make a fourth person of the Godhead out of it. p. 368.<-

### Answer:
(1.) The words of Mr. A. are once again mangled and torn out of context, and thus presented perversely. On p. 49 § 10, he had cited the words of Augustine (a beloved Church Father) from Book XII of the *Confessions*, Chapter 15, § 2. 4. and further from his *Meditations*, Chapter 19, § 2. In those passages, Augustine calls *Wisdom* the mind of our pure mother, the City of God, which is the "creature of all creatures" <note>original Latin: "creatura creaturarum"</note> and the Bride of God, being a pure mind that is most intimately one with God.

(2.) Here Mr. A. paraphrases Augustine’s discourse: namely, how Wisdom—insofar as Augustine calls her the Heavenly Jerusalem, or rather the mind of the same—is something distinct from the highly blessed Trinity, and yet (Note Well!) is a being united with the Trinity and exceedingly glorious, as the New Jerusalem. There, following Augustine, the Heavenly Jerusalem and its mind are well distinguished, just as he calls it Wisdom, or as John calls it in Revelation 21:23, the lamp—namely, Wisdom. Of this Heavenly Jerusalem, Mr. A. now says it is something distinct from the Holy Trinity, and yet also one with it. He could hardly have spoken more clearly, yet also more cautiously and with better distinction, regarding such a deep mystery from Augustine. But whoever cannot grasp it should also beware of rejecting and slandering it.

### The 73rd Charge.

In the aforementioned Chapter IV, § 10 and following, it is proven from Scripture and Antiquity <note>The writings of the early Church Fathers</note> that Wisdom is Christ and His Spirit. Should he perhaps have first spent a long time critiquing <note>original: "criticiren"</note> or discoursing philosophically <note>original: "philosophice"</note> upon it before showing its use? If so, he would indeed have departed from God's Word. But here the Compiler clearly contradicts himself: he says Mr. A. leaves the Word, and yet admits he treats it applicatively. He will never be able to prove that applying Scripture is the same as abandoning it. God have mercy on such wretched theology and exegesis! <note>original: "Exegeſeos" - Greek: of exegesis</note>

One should also see the **passages of the Fathers** <note>original: "loca Patrum" — writings of the early Church leaders</note> regarding this necessary practice in Mr. Arnold’s *Treatise on the Deviations*, Book 2, Chapter 9, § 15 and following, pages 37, 38.
(3.) In this derangement of his senses, he also accused the late Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jacob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism"</note> of an inexcusable error regarding this same truth of inwardness in *the year 1706, p. 104*, for which he had to be thoroughly rebuked by Mr. Lange in *Volume VI, p. 16*.

For Mr. Arnold does not understand the "innermost" as a special, immediate light or the like, as the Compiler may imagine; rather, he simply means the entire internal state of the soul as it stands before GOD, which one must examine in repentance, but not to learn something new or different from it than what is in the Holy Scripture.
(5.) This is also shown by his words cited by Dr. Löscher <note>original: "H. D. L." — Valentin Ernst Löscher, a prominent Orthodox Lutheran critic of Pietism</note> himself on page 421: "One should learn to pay attention to one’s heart, <insert>Note Well:</insert> what is going on inside it." How many thousands of times have the **practical theologians**,

**Arndt**, **Müller**, **Geier**, and others spoken in this way? Yes, the Compiler must finally be compelled by the truth on *page 412* to confess that it is highly necessary to go into one’s heart to teach oneself. And yet he adds: but that one would want to learn *from* one's heart is perverse. Of course it is perverse; but Mr. Arnold has not used such perverse words, nor has he rejected the external Word of God.

### The 80th Charge:

(1.) How could he have forgotten the Means of Grace, and indeed "entirely," when he himself preached this at the time and later had it printed? That is surely also a Means, namely the preaching of the **Gospel**. How poorly one is deceived by his complaint!
(2.) That Mr. Arnold called the Means of Grace "a noise" cannot be true, for he would then have had to call his own speech at that time such and reject it. Therefore, by "noise," he meant the hindrances to conversion—the disorder and distraction of the heart—which do not allow a person to become sober in the face of their own ruin. The Compiler might well notice this in himself, if he had not so lost and unsettled himself in so much **censoring** and judging of others (over whom he is not appointed) that it may be difficult for him to get out again and come to that Divine rest in his soul, which one nonetheless wishes for him.

(2.) He has also presented the sense of the ancient Church extensively regarding both the right use and the abuse of such phrases, and pointed out the errors therein, in his *Depiction of Internal Christianity*, Book 1, Chapter 1, whereby all these false accusations fall away.

### The 82nd Charge:
That he teaches that the Divine is already within man. p. 421.

->Answer:<-

(1.) This statement does not appear by a single letter in the cited places, nor anywhere else; rather, it is once again concocted by the Compiler <note>original: "Hn. Concip." — the person drafting the charges against Arnold</note>, and indeed without proper qualification.

(2.) For either the Compiler (whose words these are, and not Mr. Arnold's) understands by "the Divine" that which remains of the **Image of God** <note>The theological concept that humans were created in God’s likeness, which was damaged but not entirely destroyed by the Fall.</note>, as even our own theologians recognize; if so, everyone allows him this point. (See below the passages of our teachers in the appendix of this first part, § 36 and 48, and here at No. 135).

(3.) But if he understands by this the entire Image of God, or some other Divine life, essence, or light that is supposed to be in man before his rebirth; then such a thing remains false regarding the fallen, unregenerate man, who "has not the Spirit," according to the Epistle of Jude, verse 19, and will be maintained by no true Christian. Thus, the Compiler ought to recognize his own error here.

### The 83rd Charge.
The "Spark of God" is said to be the Christ within us, which is set in opposition to the Christ outside of us. p. 421.

->Answer:<-

(1.) The Compiler shall never be able to deduce these false propositions from Mr. Arnold’s book; on these two pages that are cited, he has not mentioned the "Christ in us" with a single word, as if He were in man before conversion.

(2.) Rather, Mr. Arnold proves there on page 18 quite earnestly that man, even <note>original: "NB." — nota bene, or "mark well"</note> before his conversion, feels a secret longing for **tranquility of soul** (as the heathens do too), and that this arises from the feeling of the eternal Spirit in man and his Divine Spark: yet the natural man cannot help himself, but wanders ever further. Thereupon he shows how God comes to man in His Son: Jesus approaches the soul first. p. 19.

(3.) Here the Compiler should see whether he has not done Mr. Arnold an injustice by attributing this error to him. Does he not clearly say: "Jesus approaches the soul first"? Does he then establish a "Christ in the unconverted" as the Spark of God? But in just this way, he also distorted the innocent words of the otherwise so-

(4.) And with what will he prove that Mr. Arnold opposes "Christ in us" to "Christ outside of us"? Does he not everywhere confess and praise the one Christ, the Son of God and of Mary, as He wishes to be both in us and outside of us? ### The 84th Charge.

->Answer:<-

(1.) The Censor <note>original: "H. Censor" — likely referring to the same opponent as "The Compiler"</note> has again omitted what could destroy his accusation; thus he commits another unchristian act. For Mr. Arnold says on page 13: "Now Christ comes <note>original: "NB." — note well</note> **also** in secret and invisibly in the spirit to each soul in particular, to actually accomplish the work of eternal redemption within it."

(2.) This sounds entirely scriptural. For the word **also** indicates that Mr. Arnold had previously spoken of the external, first advent <note>The birth and earthly life of Jesus</note>. The phrase **in the spirit** shows how he now speaks of the spiritual or inward advent, which the Compiler must surely admit. By the "accomplishing of redemption," it is shown how Christ indeed accomplished everything on the Cross and "found and brought about an eternal redemption," but must now make it available to us, **apply** <note>A theological term for how the benefits of Christ's death are personally realized by a believer through the Holy Spirit.</note> it, and thus complete it or actually carry it out in each individual through faith.

(3.) But whoever looks at these mangled words would have to conclude that Mr. Arnold denies the first visible advent of Christ in the flesh and the external redemption. And this is exactly what the Censor intends; but he thereby incriminates himself ever further, and makes his bonds—alas!—harder than he may yet recognize.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold against theological charges.
