68 Historical-Theological Observations Part I. Nos. 85. 86.

even that which stands in the Scriptures with clear expression, and to which he himself directs others, as "Jewish dreams" <note>A common derogatory term in 17th-century polemics used to dismiss mystical or millenarian ideas as non-Christian fantasies.</note> according to his own reason: for he twists the words of the Holy Spirit, which are innocent in themselves, into a Jewish sense, only so that he might have something to accuse.

(2.) It was already reminded and stipulated above at the 81st accusation that God is not the **matter of the creatures**, and consequently that they are not something Divine or true **Sephiroth** <note>In Jewish Kabbalah, the Sephiroth are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself. Here, the author clarifies that Arnold does not believe creatures are literal "emanations" of God's essence.</note> but remain true creatures, infinitely distinct from the Creator.

(3.) Therefore, when it is said of the creatures by the Fathers <note>The early Church Fathers, such as Augustine or Origen.</note> and other proven teachers: **God has flowed out into them**: this is certainly not meant as an essential outflow—as if God had applied His own essence directly to the creatures and given it to them. No; Mr. Arnold, along with all sound teachers, is far from such a crude concept, and the Honorable Compiler <note>original: "H. Concip." — the person drafting the charges against Arnold</note> truly sins greatly against such an innocent expression of Scripture by wishing to stain it with such an error.

(4.) Rather, the discussion is only about the **outflow of the power of God** as the cause or *efficient cause* <note>original: "causæ efficientis"</note> in creation; that God, according to His power and creative effect, has flowed into the creatures. And indeed, nothing is more common in philosophy, especially among the Scholastics <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note>, than for them to describe an "influence" or "inflow" of God into the created beings, which is fundamentally the same as an "outflow," whether it be for creation or preservation.

(5.) All of this was thoroughly discussed in the previously cited place in the **Representation of Inner Christianity** <note>Arnold’s influential work, *Abbildung des innern Christenthums*.</note> and with the agreement of the Church teachers, so that there is no need for further dispute, but rather for a salutary use of and obedience to such truth.

(6.) Furthermore, this error was long ago attributed to the late Arnd <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), a famous devotional writer whose work paved the way for Pietism.</note> by the Osiandrians <note>Followers of Andreas Osiander, often involved in disputes over the nature of justification.</note>, against whom Varenius rescued him using this very distinction between the Essence and the Cause: Part II, p. 309. And yet, such accusations are brought forward anew: just as Mr. Freylingshausen in Vol. III, page 664, and many others on page 805, must also suffer them.

### The 86th Charge:

->It is said to be a Kabbalistic wish: **Form us all, O Lord == all in all.**<-

### Answer:

(1.) It is pitiable and at the same time terrible when these speeches, which are founded

<column-break/>

almost word-for-word in Holy Scripture and in the usage of the Church, must nevertheless be called "Kabbalistic," and when natural reason deviates so far even from the letter of the Scripture (as with the ancient Jews) that it will no longer even tolerate Biblical expressions!

(2.) The first words: 
> **Form us all just as You recognized us before the world;** 
are clearly the very thing that stands in Romans 8:29: **For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.** And Ephesians 1:4, 5, and 6: **He chose us through Christ before the foundation of the world was laid, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. And he predestined us for adoption to himself through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace, by which he has made us accepted in the Beloved.**

are likewise founded in Romans 11:36. Indeed, one constantly sings them in the Doxologies <note>Short hymns of praise to God, such as the "Glory Be."</note>: **As it was in the beginning == unto eternity.** Clement of Rome <note>An early Christian bishop (1st century AD) and one of the Apostolic Fathers.</note> also used this very expression, as is well known.

(4.) The final words are once again not from Mr. Arnold, but from Paul in Romans 11:36: **From him, and through him, and in him are all things.**

(5.) Upon this clear proof, one might cry out with better right than the Compiler has done: Oh, dear Christians, let us remain with the revealed Word of God! Yes, may God grant him and all such critics that they earnestly begin to rightly understand God’s Word through the Holy Spirit and accept it in faith, as it truly is God’s Word: then they will no longer try to master the Spirit of God in His pronouncements, nor accuse Him of Kabbalistic, magical, or other speeches!

(6.) It is thus evident that Mr. Arnold has followed the clear rule of Holy Scripture and has in no way started a "Kabbalistic, Magical, Hermetic, and Platonic Christianity," to which his conscience—praise God!—gives him enough testimony, as do all sensible readers who wish to believe and live simply according to the Scripture.

Likewise, [he must prove] that the proceedings in France against so many thousands of **Evangelicals** <note>Protestants.</note>, who were burned as atheists and heretics, are right and good.

# 74 Historical-Theological Observations. Part I. No. 88. 89.

### From the Censorship of the *Mystical History*.

#### The 88th Charge:
The Author’s intention is that Mystical Theology alone is the true theology, and therefore it alone should be practiced. p. 592.

#### Response:
(1.) What **Mr. Arnold** repeats in this booklet from the Church Fathers regarding the abuse of theology and mere academic knowledge will likely not have pleased the Mr. Censor; however, because he could not contradict it as clear truth, he seeks to do so in another way—notwithstanding that Dr. Loescher <note>likely Valentin Ernst Löscher, a prominent orthodox Lutheran critic of Pietism</note> himself has elsewhere given an even better confession on this matter, as cited in this very booklet.

(2.) In particular, it is contrary to proud reason when one proves from God’s Word that theology does not consist in mere knowledge—indeed, that such knowledge is far from being true theology, and that a wicked and hypocritical person is far from being a theologian.

(3.) This charge, however—namely that **Mr. Arnold** considers Mystical Theology alone to be the true theology—is answered and refuted by the Honorable Compiler himself, where he states that **Mr. Arnold** admits there is also a *Catechetical Theology* <note>The basic, instructional study of Christian doctrine</note> outside of Mysticism.

(4.) And **Mr. Arnold** indicated this even earlier, if only one had wished to see it without a spirit of fault-finding, where he observes in §. 3. p. 2. that among the Church Fathers, **Christian doctrine in general, and especially the doctrine of the Triune God and of Jesus Christ and His divine nature**, is called Theology; indeed, the entire Holy Scripture was called Theology by the ancients (§. 5). Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian</note> is called a "Theologian" for this very reason. Now, it is well known that the doctrine of the Holy Trinity and of Christ's divinity is, regarding its theoretical foundations, practiced more in Catechetical, Exegetical, and Polemic <note>Theology focused on defending the faith against opposing views</note> Theology than in Mystical Theology. Thus, **Mr. Arnold** did not view Mystical Theology as the *only* true theology, but only as the most noble and best part of theology. Much less does he wish that it alone should be practiced, which is also evidenced by his other writings, especially the *Portrait of the First Christians*.

(4.) It is also not unknown that our theologians, when faced with new controversies, have also invented many new *technical terms* <note>original: "Terminos"</note> in order to untangle the matter more skillfully. In this regard, the *fertile genius* <note>original: "felix ingenium"</note> of Dr. Dannhauer <note>Johann Konrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian and teacher of Spener</note> is especially popular with many, as his writings are full of new inventions and expressions. Whatever is held to be free in *Polemical* and *Thetic Theology* <note>Polemical theology deals with refuting errors, while Thetic theology deals with stating positive doctrines</note>, provided it is *conforming to the use of the Word of God* <note>original: "quoad usum V. ### The 92nd Charge:
A. supposedly holds it to be an imperfection (p. 80) that one uses any *Method* <note>A systematic way of teaching or organizing thought</note> in Mystical Theology. p. 598.

->Response:<-

(1.) This is yet another mutilation of words: For in Chapter VI, §. 1, it does not speak of a *Method* in general and without condition, but of a certain, limited, humanly prescribed or devised <insert>Note Well</insert> and artificial order or method, to which they were not accustomed to bind themselves so <insert>Note Well</insert> anxiously and *absolutely*.

(2.) Here the *meaning* <note>original: "Sensus"</note> comes out quite differently than the Compiler craftily presents it. The discussion is not about free and necessary ways of teaching and good order (no one will reject those; indeed, even the Mystics themselves, including Mr. A., observe a good order and method).

(3.) Rather, the discussion is only about artificial *methods*, specifically insofar as these are required *absolutely* and anxiously. Sensible people no longer like to endure such things even in the homiletic and moral styles of speaking <note>referring to preaching and ethics</note>, let alone in the Mystical. But because the Mr. Compiler still wishes to propagate the artificial method with his *dispositions* <note>structured outlines for sermons or treatises</note>, which often turn out anxious and forced enough, this sentence was contrary to him; thus, he had to present it in a mutilated and falsified way so that he would have something to accuse, and so that his "art" would not suffer any loss.

### The 93rd Charge:
A. calls it a most precious truth (p. 42) the teaching of the pagan philosophers that the soul is a "little piece of God." p. 598.

79

Part I. No. 93. 94. 95. regarding the so-called Old and New.

->Response:<-

(1.) Had the Mr. Compiler known a more offensive expression, he would have gladly used it to frighten the ignorant reader and create a loathing for the book. But where does this phrase actually appear in that place: "The soul is a little piece of God"? Not a single syllable of the whole matter stands there, let alone a letter of those words. Mr. A. has never made use of such an expression elsewhere, either.

(2.) And even if Mr. A. repeated with Paul from *Aratus's Phenomena* <note>A Greek didactic poem quoted by St. Paul in the New Testament</note> that we are "of His offspring" (Acts 17:28, 29), what would he be saying in a scripturally pure sense other than what our theologians, following the Church Fathers, have long since acknowledged? Just as Michael Neander <note>A 16th-century educator and theologian</note> quoted from Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German mystic</note>, and later Johann Arndt <note>Author of "True Christianity," a key influence on Pietism</note> in Varenius’s *Defense* (p. 309, Part II), repeated these sayings (which are still far from appearing in Mr. A.’s writing) and defended them as correct:

> The soul flowed out from God.
> The origin of the soul is God.
> In man there is something that compares to God, so that man can become capable of the highest Good.
> The soul came purely from God.

(3.) Had Neander, Arndius, and Varenius (the latter of whom was also highly esteemed by Hülsemann <note>Johann Hülsemann (1602–1661), a strict Lutheran theologian</note>) lived in our time, they would likewise have been burdened with such false conclusions, as if they called the soul a "little piece of God"—just as Osiander did against Arndt. However, the perversion of such innocent teachings is now all too obvious, and the accuser's own conscience strikes them, showing that they are in the wrong. (See below, No. 157 and 164.)

Historical-Theological Observations. Part I. No. 95. 96.

->Response:<-

(1.) This is yet another mutilation of words and a slander drawn from it. Mr. A. relates in that place the dispute of Luther against Eck over Tauler’s <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a famous German mystic whose writings influenced Martin Luther.</note> writings; he shows how the Catholics themselves had refuted Eck, and concludes from this: **the disputing parties were thus fundamentally at one.** In what way and to what extent they were at one (namely, before and around the beginning of the Reformation, of which he speaks), he explains immediately as follows: When such a separation had once occurred, and the parties were established, the *judgments* <note>original: "Judicia"</note> of each side—Note Well—regarding *Mystical Theology* <note>original: "Mystica Theologia"</note> remained fundamentally unanimous and entirely favorable.

(2.) There, Mr. A. nowhere says with a single word that Papists and Protestants were at one in the whole of religion and its—Note Well—foundation, which is indeed not true: rather, he speaks only *specifically* <note>original: "in specie"</note> of *Mystical Theology*, saying that the parties were at one in their *judgments* regarding its foundation, and he verifies this from the whole of history.

(3.) Now, the Mr. Compiler <note>The author of the critique Arnold is answering.</note> himself previously admitted that Mr. A. recognizes other *species* of *theology* besides the *Mystical*, such as Catechetical, etc. Thus, he could have easily seen that when Arnold describes the unity of religions regarding the *Mystical*, he does not, on the other hand, deny their disunity in *Theoretical Theology*, as it indeed cannot be denied. Does the Compiler then see his very unchristian distortion once again? May God grant him improvement!

(4.) He himself admits in that same place that Mr. A. elsewhere condemned the *sacred dominion* <note>original: "Dominatum sacrum"; referring to the hierarchical power structure of the Catholic Church.</note> in the Papacy as the greatest of abominations. From this, he should have looked more closely at Mr. A.’s words, if he had not preferred to *search for a knot in a bulrush* <note>original: "nodum in scirpo"; a Latin idiom meaning to look for a difficulty where there is none.</note>, according to his habit, and desired to waste his own and others' time.

(5.) Thus, his own conclusion and wish are highly necessary for himself: Oh, that such people would learn to think and speak more soberly of spiritual things, and better take to heart the punishment for offensive words (especially slander and false testimony) which the Lord has threatened!

and spiritual insight without God’s Word, in which he was deeply enough involved and has misled others. p. 642.

->Response:<-

(1) Mr. A. has never claimed revelations outside and without God’s Word regarding his life and conduct, much less appealed to them, and least of all wanted to know or do anything without God’s Word; therefore, he consequently could not have recognized the "poor certainty" of revelations.

(2) What is said of the discipline of wisdom and God’s governance from the Scriptures must be allowed to stand by those who still accept the letter of the Scripture, and they must not criticize it. The Mr. Compiler himself wishes in Volume III, p. 16, that heavenly wisdom would grant Mr. A. something to recognize: Mr. A. has sought nothing more or less in his actions and omissions.

(3.) But what *special* and immediate revelations are necessary here regarding whether one should marry or not? Do we not have both options, with certain *conditions*, clearly enough in the Scripture, so that only the Spirit of wisdom and truth needs to apply <note>original: "appliciren"</note> them to each believer's state and show what is good or evil, advisable at one time and not at another?

(4.) Thus, if God does not yet recognize marriage as beneficial for someone, He can make the words of Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:1, 7, 8, 27 so living and powerful to the heart that such a person may not only proceed in that same certainty for as long as it is good for him, but may even be fully persuaded <note>original: "persuadirt"</note> that he would remain so for life. On the other hand, God can also later make the opposite clear and certain to him at the right time from that very same chapter or other scriptural passages, so that in such assurance he again joyfully bears the judgments of the ignorant, because he knows whom he has believed. The world knows nothing of such Divine ways—the world that marries and is given in marriage, and enters such a state without sufficient testing of the Divine will, like the heathens who despise God: from this come such unwise judgments.

->Response:<-

(1.) Previously, on page 646, the Censors admitted that everything said in this writing about marriage that conforms to God's Word can already be found frequently in the writings of Evangelical teachers. And afterwards, on page 649, they noted that much that is praiseworthy and good is to be found in this little book, for which they thanked Divine Providence.

(2.) In particular, on page 629, they confess: **we gladly sign off on the sighs over the corrupt marriages of many Christians.** Thus, they admit that the state of marriage, at least among the ungodly, exists only under the mere patience of God.

(3.) But that the marriage of the converted also stands under God's tolerance is clear from 1 Corinthians 7, where the state of marriage is said to be established because of fornication, and indeed without restriction to the pious or the wicked. Indeed, they themselves essentially confess the same when they are accustomed to repeating from Psalm 51 without distinction: **They were conceived in sin, and for the most part seen to and born in it.** Now, in whatever state sinful conceptions and births occur, that state stands merely under Divine long-suffering—that is, in that state, God bears the impure with patience. Mr. A. intended to indicate this and nothing else, and thus he set down no incorrect proposition in stating that **marriage is a monument of the Fall:** unless the Censors wish to claim that marriage after the Fall is the same as it was before it; which they cannot do, nor, hopefully, would they want to.

(4.) For our theologians also confess this regarding the use of marriage, such as Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> in *Theological Commonplaces* <note>original: "LL. Theol." abbreviated for "Loci Loci Theologici"</note> Volume 7, page 648: *After the Fall, the leprosy of lust and the vice of depraved desire were mixed into the work of procreation: — Likewise, the leprosy of sin has seated itself deep within the members dedicated to procreation. — Therefore, pious spouses acknowledge both: namely, that the heat and flames of desire adhering to the holy work of procreation arose from sin; and yet, nonetheless, that disorder <note>original: "ἀταξίαν" (ataxian), meaning a lack of order or a state of confusion</note> which was added through the Fall is covered by the honesty and holiness of marriage... although it is no longer as pure and clean as it was before the Fall,* 1 Corinthians 7:6. Likewise, Dr. Arnold Mengering <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran superintendent and author of devotional works.</note> in *Information for the Catechetical Conscience*, Chapter 10, page 799: **God-fearing and conscientious spouses should recognize and repent of such disorder <note>original: "ἀταξίαν"</note>, and call upon God for forgiveness for all impure acts and thoughts: likewise, they should beg God's pardon for all such clinging stains.** Indeed, he even calls the use of marriage there a **practiced unchastity—namely, by reason of the disorder <note>original: "ἀταξίας"</note>.** Luther confesses this very often, especially in his Commentary on Genesis.

<meta>catchword: Genesis.</meta>

<column-break/>

Genesis. And thus the old theologians did not consider marriage to be absolutely holy for this reason, as people today praise all marriages without distinction: claiming they have "entered into the holy state of matrimony," whether the individuals <note>original: "Subjecta"</note> within it are faithful and holy or not. Rather, they well recognized and lamented the adhering corruption. One may confer here the defense of Court Councilor Stryck <note>Samuel Stryck (1640–1710), a famous jurist who wrote on marriage law.</note> against Dr. Meyer, page 47 and following, as well as his dissertation *On the Remnants of the Sacrament in Matrimonial Causes*, page 92 and following.

(5.) Whoever still has scruples about this, or wishes to hear more, can read the remarks attached to such a booklet, as well as the *Portrayal of First Christianity* in Book 6, Chapter 1.

(6.) Meanwhile, this remark is by no means to be interpreted as if there were nothing good left in the state of marriage after the Fall. For the order itself, which comes from that very patience and condescension of God, and God's purpose in it, is glorious and good. So also the marriage of the pious is good through faith, but God tolerates the adhering corruption, and thus also the marriage itself.

(7.) From this truth—namely, insofar as marriage stands under the Fall—flowed the confessions in the book *Of Divine Wisdom*, which the Censor has vainly set in opposition to the subsequent ones. Especially since in the former, he expressly speaks of fleshly unions; whereas regarding the true marriage of a believer, entirely different testimonies are to be found in the *Book of Marriage*, Chapters 9 and 11. Thus, human reason cannot reconcile what the Holy Spirit nevertheless harmonizes in Holy Scripture.

->The 98th Charge.<-

His speeches do not agree with the dialect of the Holy Spirit.

->Response:<-

(1.) Whether the Mr. Compiler <note>The critic/author of the charges against Arnold.</note> knows the dialect of the Holy Spirit in its right sense, understanding, and power, those with practiced senses have long since seen from his judgments.

It seems to me that if a writer were to write ever so earnestly against a vice that is already common, it should be pleasing to a preacher; he should not look long at the words or start a dispute over them, but rather thank God that testimony is being born everywhere against wickedness.

### The 99th Charge.
#### The naturalistic <note>In this context, "naturalism" is a theological accusation that a person relies only on human nature and reason while rejecting divine revelation and organized religious structures.</note> inclination toward the abolition of all religions and outward worship sits deep within Mr. A. p. 650.

### Answer:

(1.) From the answers to the 6th, 26th, and 99th charges, and the words of Arnold cited there, Dr. L. could have already been sufficiently convinced that Mr. A. is never inclined to abolish a single religion, let alone all of them, or outward worship; rather, it is and remains an unchristian calumny <note>A false and malicious statement meant to damage someone's reputation.</note> against him.

(2.) Every natural man might seek "Naturalism" in his own bosom, as was reminded above in point number 2.

(3.) The proof offered is supposedly this: Mr. A. writes on page 11 of the "great Babylonian Whore" <note>A common term in the Reformation and among Pietists, derived from the Book of Revelation, used to describe a corrupt or worldly institutional church.</note> who charms all nations under the name of religion and godliness, etc. Now, Mr. A. is dealing there with spiritual harlotry, and consequently with that which occurs within the church. Here the Censor might have sincerely examined himself to see who, with his unchristian censures, still belongs to the Babylonian Whore and the fallen clergy (so that honest teachers are not lumped in with them), who lead people away from God Himself and toward men, sects, certain times, places, persons, and toward the letter and mere words. If his conscience were free of this before God, he would rejoice that the abuse of things that are good in themselves is rejected here as spiritual harlotry: for the right use is certainly not intended here, even if the Censor would like to interpret it that way.

(4.) Should these words still sound too harsh to someone, let them maturely consider that the very same words were used more than 100 years ago by Mr. A.’s countryman, a Lutheran Court Preacher to the Elector of Saxony—namely Paulus Jenisius in his *Admonition to the Senate and People of Annaberg*, 1604, p. 64. For there he specifies all imaginable sins and abominations according to the Ten Commandments, and proves

# From the Censure of the Supplements to the Church History, Year 1703.

## The 103rd Charge:

A. also advised everyone to make outward use of the Lord’s Supper <note>Holy Communion or the Eucharist.</note>. page 159.

->Answer:<-

(1.) While this is indeed approved by the Drafter <note>The person who composed the official charges against Arnold.</note>, it is nevertheless contrary to the Author’s intention and is not accurately expressed. For Mr. A. does not write there so unconditionally that he advises *everyone* to take the Lord’s Supper; otherwise, he would also have to advise the godless, the unrepentant, or the unworthy to do so. He would also be approving the lightheartedness of those secure preachers who allow everyone to participate without examination or reminder—indeed, who drive and force people to it for the sake of profit; which would certainly be against the mind of Christ and Paul.

(2.) Rather, he writes as follows: **"The best thing might be that everyone, while maintaining the right outward observance of the Lord’s Supper, should earnestly strive for the inward [meaning]."** The meaning is: whoever goes to it should <margin>(α)</margin> observe it correctly and <margin>(β)</margin> thereby strive for the **inward** or for the power of the sacrament. This is certainly far removed from the presentation given by the Censors.

## The 104th Charge.

A. confesses that what he wrote regarding the excessive treatment of heretics was mostly done based on conjecture.

->Answer:<-

His words do not actually indicate as much as the Drafter would like to extract from them for his own wishes. Rather, Mr. A. says only this:

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>Part I. No. 105. 106. regarding the so-called Old and New.</header>

Mr. A. page 7: **"I could not have depicted the heretics more truthfully, as I showed—alongside their errors now and then, and indeed mostly conjecturally without a presumptuous decision—where they might have suffered too much from others."** <note>Arnold argues he was being cautious and non-judgmental rather than admitting he made things up.</note>

## The 105th Charge:

A. considers confession to be something useful. page 159.

->Answer:<-

(1.) He considers confession to be useful there only insofar as, according to the *Augsburg Confession* <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, 1530.</note>, people are examined, heard, instructed, and the matter is handled wisely and godly in all things.

(2.) On the other hand, he has proven in the *Church History* from the own words of Luther and others of his followers that for those who are practiced and well-tested Christians, it is neither useful nor necessary, and was left as a matter of freedom by Luther himself. See the 12th Chapter of the 16th Book, paragraphs 10, 11, and 12, namely because it is a human tradition <note>A practice established by people rather than commanded by God in scripture.</note> and is subject to many abuses. See also paragraphs 13 and 14 of the same; also Chapter 20, paragraph 17; Chapter 21, paragraph 20; and in the 17th Book, Chapter 13, paragraph 44; Chapter 17, paragraph 32; Chapter 19, paragraph 48.

(3.) But he has nowhere said that it is useful in general and without such conditions, much less by reason of the "confession penny" <note>A customary fee or tip paid to the pastor at the time of private confession, which Arnold and other reformers often criticized as simony or bribery.</note> or otherwise in the manner customary in most places. For in the case of an unwise and ungodly use without examination and distinction of people, it is highly harmful and ruinous to souls. The Censors themselves confess in the year 1705, page 724, that many abuses of confession have been discovered until now, and many a secure and all-too-sleepy preacher has been awakened in this regard. *Item:* it should be accepted with thanks if someone could be rid of this most heavy priestly burden, etc.

A. now confesses on page 133 that he should have said that there were still many Protestant teachers whose reading could stir the mind a little toward heavenly goods. page 159.

->Answer:<-

Scioppius <note>Caspar Scioppius (1576–1649), a controversial scholar and convert to Catholicism known for his sharp polemics.</note> had written this, and Mr. A. had only cited <note>original: *allegirt*</note> him; on the other hand, Mr. A. had already acknowledged all the good in many Protestant teachers, such as Luther, Arndt, Matthesius, Weller, Meisner, Gerhard, Tarnow, Varenious, Meyfart, Mengering, Glassius, and many others. ### The 107th Charge.

A. <note>Arnold</note> previously wished to know nothing of any single heretic regarding their doctrine and opinions. page 160.

### Answer:

(1.) This is the old, unprovable accusation which could be refuted immediately from the remarks placed before the *Church History* <note>Arnold’s famous *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (Impartial History of the Church and Heretics)</note>, where Mr. A. expressly says in Point I. §. 1. concerning the first centuries: **Some perverse people were avoided by the upright teachers as heretical, and indeed without limitation as to whether they were heretics in doctrine or life.**
(2.) How he *specifically* <note>original: *in specie*</note> protests against the Arian and Socinian <note>Arianism and Socinianism were theological movements that challenged traditional views on the Trinity and the divinity of Christ; they were widely considered heresies.</note> errors in the preface itself, and points them out in the history itself, lies plain as day before everyone's eyes. It remains, therefore, a dishonest imputation that Mr. A. wished to know of no single heretic in doctrine.

### The 108th Charge:

He previously rejected all orthodoxy and dogmatic propositions as useless. page 160.

### Answer:

(1.) That "orthodoxy" is to be viewed in different ways, and has become a mockery through great abuse, was recently reminded by Mr. Lange <note>Joachim Lange, a prominent Pietist theologian and ally of Arnold</note>; he thereby proved to the Mr. Drafter <note>the opponent who composed the charges</note> how he could never demand that a true Christian agree in all things with the kind of orthodoxy that the Mr. Drafter defends, but rather that such "orthodoxy" harbors many errors, such as Pelagianism <note>The belief that human nature is not corrupted by original sin and can choose good without special divine grace—a major point of contention in Protestant theology.</note> and the like. And these, Mr. A. also considers useless according to the Word of God.
(2.) On the other hand, regarding the true, Divine, unadulterated doctrine of the Gospel, he still holds to what he also confessed in the *Supplements*. Indeed, even in the *Church History*, he has **carefully distinguished the abuse of orthodoxy from the doctrine itself**, as when he sets this modest limitation in the 15th Chapter of the 16th Book, §. 5., specifically regarding Luther’s sentence: "O glory, glory, how great a harm you are!" <note>original: "O δóξα, δóξα, quam magna es noxa!" mixing Greek and Latin.</note>: **Orthodoxy is harmful, namely (Note Well) when it is used for quarreling and pride.** Whereby he indicates:

<column-break/>

89 Part I. No. 109. 110. N. regarding the so-called Old and New. 89

The orthodoxy is not harmful if it is not so abused. What more irreproachable confession could one demand?

### The 109th Charge:

It is suspicious that on page 4 it is written of the Holy Scripture that it only belongs to beginners, and is an "outflow" of God. page 162.

### Answer:

(1.) Mr. A. sets down there quite deliberately: **That the Holy Scripture is indeed (Note Well) unavoidably necessary and wholesome,** (Note Well) especially and primarily for beginning Christians.
(2.) Here it does not say it belongs *only* to beginners, as the Mr. Drafter craftily patches onto it, but (a) it is (Note Well) **unavoidably necessary** and (b) **wholesome**, (c) **but especially and primarily for beginning Christians, namely thereafter also for the experienced.** For it is concluded there thus: **Which is not at all a disparagement of the Holy Scripture, but rather highly-praiseworthy, that the power and wisdom of God is placed therein to (Note Well) lead believers always further, because it can never be exhausted nor fully fathomed.**
(3.) The other point is just as twisted. For it stands thus: **The meaning is not to do the slightest harm to the respect of the holy Word of God: which (namely the respect of the Word) in turn takes nothing away from the honor of God in enlightened souls, but in righteous order and degrees gladly yields to the highest Author as an outflow.**
(4.) There, the "respect of the Divine Word," or its authority and Divine power, is called an "outflow" <note>an emanation or manifestation</note> of God, but not the Word itself; and even if the Word were so called, what would the Mr. Drafter wish to make suspicious about it?

### The 110th Charge:

A. refers the reader on page 58 to a libelous pamphlet. page 162.

At the time when Mr. A. wrote this, these *Monthly Conversations* <note>original: *Monatliche Unterredungen*, a journal by Thomasian that was controversial for its time.</note> were not yet forbidden, as happened later: and this cited point was in itself quite clear and indeed explained in German, although in a provocative manner that one might not like. The Mr. Drafter, however, should consider on the other hand how many countless times Dr. Schelwig <note>Samuel Schelwig, a strict Lutheran orthodox opponent of the Pietists</note>, books, and others have referred to the "mischief" <note>Unfug</note> condemned in Saxony in the most important matters...

### The 117th Accusation:
->He concludes that sanctification in this life must reach perfection. p. 487.<-

### Answer:
(1.) They wish to prove this from page 751, where after a description of perfect righteousness and truth, it is said: **"Let no one consider this impossible."**

(2.) Mr. Arnold follows the clear words of Paul in Ephesians 4:22 and following, upon which he is preaching, and shows that the "new man" must be put on in righteousness and the holiness of truth. He argues that this is not impossible, and warns against blaspheming and denying this truth.

(3.) But he nowhere specifies with a single word whether or when it is possible in this life. Instead, he only exhorts that one should begin step-by-step. He in no way defines perfection itself, much less does he urge that it must be perfectly achieved. Nor does he engage in a war of words over such a matter, which is intended to be practiced rather than disputed. Therefore, the Mr. Censor unfairly calls Arnold's words "horrible formulas" <note>original Latin: "horrendas Formulas"</note> in his unchristian demand to Dr. Breithaupt on page 58. This is no doubt because they seem terrifying to the "Old Adam" <note>The sinful, unregenerate nature of man</note>, who prefers theses like the one the Censors set against Dr. Breithaupt on page 51: "The terms 'perfection' etc. are to be used with reluctance regarding those who are renewed." <note>original Latin: "ægre voces Vollkommenheit &c. de renovatis usurpandas"</note>

(4.) However, the Mr. Censor and those like-minded would act much more safely for their own souls if they did not set themselves up as judges over perfection, but first performed true repentance and began to receive God's kingdom as little children. Then, through experience according to the Scriptures, they would be able to make a sound judgment about it.

### Answer:
(1.) The Author <note>original: "Hr. Concip."</note> pretends that Mr. Arnold is speaking here of the natural man before conversion, and therefore claims it could lead to Naturalism and Fanaticism, poisoning everything good. Whether this...

Whether this follows *in and of itself* <note>original Latin: "per se"</note> and properly from the thesis as understood by unconverted and natural men, I will not investigate at this time.

(2.) For, on the contrary, it can be seen from Mr. Arnold’s clear words that he is speaking of this **little spark** in a converted soul, insofar as it is awakened and strengthened by grace. ### The 119th Accusation:

(1.) In the ears of an unenlightened person, everything sounds dangerous that does not accord with his reason and prejudices. He is therefore accustomed to sin only through suspicion or "evil mistrust"—which the Censor himself admits to there—forgetting his own rule in Volume III, page 132.

(2.) He is terrified by the clear repetitions of the words of Paul from Romans 11:36 as if they were the **Silence** <note>original Greek: "Sige," a term used by the Valentinian Gnostics to describe a primordial emanation of God.</note> of the Valentinians, and so forth.

We wish for the Mr. Censor that he would turn his zeal against himself and against those who do not recognize and praise God as they ought.

### The 120th Accusation:

The author should have remembered his own words used on page 664. Page 489.

### Answer:

The best and most necessary part has once again been left out by the Mr. Censor, because it would have struck him himself. For this is how Mr. Arnold’s words, which were cited by him, actually hang together after he spoke of the contempt for simplicity on page 664: **"Indeed, one would rather form oneself into all human commandments and teachings, or seek high and grand-sounding words or things; the simple expressions of God concerning his dear Son are too lowly for the proud mind."** Yes, indeed, to the proud mind mentioned above, the simple expressions of God concerning His dear Son and the clear words of Scripture regarding Christ and his **Restoration** <note>original: "Wiederbringung" - the 'restoration of all things' (Apocatastasis), a Pietist hope that all creation would return to God.</note> were too lowly—even dangerous!

### The 121st Accusation.

Arnold sets down the words quite uncertainly, which the Spirit of God never does. Page 489.

### Answer:

(1.) To an untrained mind, the words of truth seem uncertain; indeed, the Scripture itself is a sealed book to the unspiritual, but the truth itself is not to blame for that.

(2.) When the words seem uncertain to the Drafter <note>original: "Concip."</note>, the fault is usually his own haste, as he only picks out and twists one or another passage <note>original Latin: "Locum"</note>, rather than maturely pondering the whole context, much less the true meaning of the writer—of which so many clear proofs have appeared so far.

(3.) An example of "uncertain words" is said to be when Mr. Arnold says on page 267: **"The external Lord's Supper may also be a beneficial exercise."** The uncertainty arises for the Drafter once again from the aforementioned cause: namely, because he did not look at the connection. It says there: **"Let us not only think of the mere external Lord's Supper, which (namely the merely external one) may also be a beneficial exercise, NB. where it is handled rightly."**

(4.) What is "uncertain" about this, when one says: The **NB. merely external** Lord's Supper may be beneficial where it is handled rightly; and conversely: where the merely external is not handled rightly, it may well be unbeneficial? Are these not clear and—

### The 122. Accusation:

Ah yes, within us / in the middle of man lies the seed of all evil. In the understanding and will are abysses of horror from Satan. (2.) Who can conclude from this / that the Devil is nothing but ourselves? Such wretched wars of words are stirred up even against the most well-known presentation! These are no "extremes," nor words pushed "all too high" / but the necessity of the matter requires them / and one could show this with many parallel passages <note>original Latin: "Parallel-Locis"</note> from other preachers / if it were worth the effort.

### The 124. Accusation.

Thus, this too is not only tolerable in Mr. A. / but also conformable and gemäß <note>meaning: "consistent with"</note> to the wholesome doctrine.

### The 125. Accusation:

On p. 353, he presents Baptism as an external image. p. 490.

### Answer:

(1.) He does not say that Baptism itself is merely an image / and an external one at that / but rather writes in that place: The <term>Savior</term> <note>original: "Heyland"</note> named the water in Baptism externally as an image / namely as an image of the spiritual water, John 4:14. This is a completely different presentation / than the one Mr. Author of the Accusation <note>original: "Hr. Concip."</note> has formulated according to his ill intent.

(2.) For water is indeed not the entirety of Baptism / much less the spiritual essence itself / and Baptism is not merely "plain water," according to Luther’s own expression.

(3.) Now, if Mr. A. calls only the water / and not the whole of Baptism / an image / he then agrees with the clear pronouncement of the Teachers / who accept the external water as a <term>Type</term> <note>a "Typus" or "Type" is a symbolic prefigurement, often something in the physical world representing a spiritual reality</note>, a **Symbol**, and an image of the spiritual water.

(4.) Thus, for example, among the Ancients, **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note> speaks in Oration 40, p. 641: Baptism consists of water and Spirit; the former is visible and bodily / the latter is an invisible and spiritual manner. **"The one is typical/symbolic"** <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν τυπικῶς"</note>, the former is a prefigurement or **Type**, the latter (the Spirit), as the True One, also cleanses the depths (namely of the heart.) And **Basil the Great** in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 15: the water presents the image of death (**"contains the image of death"**) <note>original Greek: "τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ θανάτου περιέχει"</note>. Likewise among the Latin Fathers, **Eucherius** in *Book of Spiritual Formulas*, Chapter 4: **"Water also indicates baptism"**, where he cites this very place explained by Mr. A., John 5. Also: **Paschasius** in Book II *Against the Macedonians*, chapter 5: **"Through water is celebrated the imitation of the tomb, through the Holy Spirit is bestowed the truth of life."** To say nothing of others.

(5.) Among our theologians, **Dorschaeus** writes in *Theology of Zechariah*, Part I, Chapter 7, § 116, p. 140: **"That water is indicative of the fountain of the Holy Spirit"**, citing John 4:14 and 6:37. Which **expressions** <note>original: "Expressiones"</note> indicate just as much / that the water is an image. And if the Fathers, especially **Augustine**, call the **Sacraments** themselves **"visible signs of divine things"** (Book on *Instruction of the Unlearned*, chapter 26 & elsewhere) / and our theologians also admit / that the **Sacraments** in a certain sense can be called **Signs**, marks, and images; as can be seen in **Gerhard**, *Book on the Sacraments*, § 9, Vol. IV, p. 123 and others; so one will much more be permitted to describe the visible part of them / and thus also the water / in an innocent sense: **"That which was to be demonstrated"** <note>original Latin: "Id quod erat demonstrandum," a common logical conclusion</note>.

### The 126. Accusation:

**Jacob Böhme’s** <note>A famous German Christian mystic (1575–1624) whose unorthodox vocabulary often drew criticism</note> turns of phrase occur in this book almost as frequently as Biblical turns of phrase. p. 490.

It can also be quickly **judged** <note>original: "dijudicirt"</note> by visual inspection / for which I add only one or another page / and appeal to the conscience of a sensible reader / whether all these following turns of phrase are not Biblical and blameless. You poor and miserable / you weary and sick sheep among the mixed multitude / see: your Shepherd and Healer is near! You timid and faint-hearted / He is gracious and kind to you! You struggling and oppressed / your victory and salvation comes! Behold, His reward is before Him / and His recompense with Him! He comes and will help you / yes, He will actually redeem you. Receive then this word of promise even today / so you may escape His word of threat. For two kinds of words or sayings go out of this King’s mouth: A word of love and mercy / and then a word of wrath and justice. Whoever has not believed and followed the sweet word of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelii"</note> here / to him the King will say at the time of judgment / be it here or there: Depart from me, you cursed! I never knew you / and so forth. One of these two / the soul must...

However unpleasant the reproof of the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "H. Who then can show this most certainly and shame the conscience thereby / but the Spirit of Wisdom / who searches the depths and discovers everything fundamentally / and knows the thoughts of men? Therefore / it is his first office and work in us / that he rebukes sin / and represents it to the conscience as it is / in its ugliness and shame / also making the person anxious and afraid / holding before him the righteous judgment <note>original: "Buße," which here likely refers to the penalty or reckoning required by God</note> of **GOD** / and thus placing him into a true change of mind. This he does / as soon as he comes or knocks at the soul / which without him would otherwise likely wander astray eternally / and cover up its nakedness. We cannot dispense with such holy reproofs even further in and after true conversion / as long as sin or a worldly mind remains / and as long as evil is to be discovered and cast off in daily repentance. For how quickly can even a soul / which was initially faithfully humbled / become lukewarm again and fall into self-love / so that it does not even notice its failings / evil habits / and trickeries? Oh / how good then is the chastisement of the Almighty / and with what thanks is it to be accepted / even if it reproves and sweeps ever so sharply!

(4.) Finally / the conclusion for the 24th Sunday after Trinity reads as follows:

> If anyone wishes in all earnestness to come to **GOD** / and have his salvation rightly founded / he may indeed diligently and unwaveringly turn and hold to **God's** love and mercy / so that it alone may rule and manage him unhindered. For where this eternal grace becomes powerful in a person / there it makes him not only upright and faithful / but also powerful and victorious. Whereas otherwise / with slavish fear / one remains only false and hypocritical. Now / this very Mother-Love <note>This "Mother-Love" of God is a recurring theme in Pietist and mystical literature, emphasizing God's nurturing nature.</note> of **GOD** has also awakened and convicted many / indeed most among us / through the grace of the Spirit. For such and all other souls / nothing is now more necessary / than that they constantly take new strength from this very grace from the Fatherly heart of **GOD** for the breakthrough into the new life of **JESUS**. For / beloved! it truly requires a mighty earnestness / and a proper tearing-through and penetrating into the new birth / out of the false foundation of corrupted nature / so that one would rather let everything go for the sake of the prize / otherwise it always remains a mixed existence / and one mostly limps on both sides <note>A biblical idiom referring to indecision or divided loyalty, as in 1 Kings 18:21.</note>. There / power is needed / and indeed divine, invincible power for such a divine birth. It is also very near to everyone in their mouth and heart / whoever will only use it. For it is that very eternal love of the Father / **JESUS Christ** himself / who not only awakens the person to life and begets / but also gives birth / and brings forth into the light of life.

(5.) So far these excerpts from the book itself. Now let an impartial reader conclude from this / whether **Jacob Boehme's** <note>A famous German Christian mystic (1575–1624) whose complex terminology was often criticized by orthodox theologians.</note> ways of speaking occur here almost as frequently as the Biblical ones. I am certain / no one will be able to maintain this with any consistency of truth regarding a single page of this entire book.

(6.) But perhaps it might conversely occur to some / how nonetheless from today's "artful sermons" <note>Arnold is critiquing the overly rhetorical, academic sermons of his orthodox rivals.</note> it is / alas! all too clear / that therein the ways of speaking of either worldly orators / and poets / or also those of the Scholastics <note>original: "Scholasticorum"; referring to medieval and post-Reformation academic theologians who used strict logic and terminology</note> and the like occur almost as frequently as the Biblical ones; which yet by the world and its lovers is not esteemed suspicious at all / but rather praiseworthy. More has been reported on this above in No. 99.

It can never provide any edification / that A. [Arnold] in citing the passages of the New Testament does not use Luther's / but his own translation. p. 490.

<page-num>106</page-num>
<header>Historical-Theological Observations. Part I. 127. N.</header>

->Answer:<-

(1.) **Luther’s Text** <note>original: "Lutheri Text"</note> has by no means been set aside; rather, it is fully expressed at all times before every sermon, and thus has been thoroughly maintained.

(2.) However, regarding the fact that in the treatment of the text, the cited **scriptural passages** <note>original: "loca Scripturæ"</note> are mostly quoted according to the **original text** <note>The Hebrew and Greek originals rather than the German translation.</note>, the **Author** had his reasons, which he indicated in the preface, paragraph 8, as follows:

(3.) No sensible person should take offense at this, considering it is the same thing whether one first gives the common version and then repeats how it sounds more precisely in the **original text** (as happens in almost all other sermons), or whether one immediately uses the latter for the sake of brevity and to avoid wearying the listeners. For in all other respects, I hold **Luther’s Bible** in high esteem and value; I am also far from despising or criticizing the work of others, but merely make use of that freedom which every preacher has to investigate the **original text**.

(4.) The specific occasion for this **practice** <note>original: "Instituto"</note> was actually this: some listeners gave the **Author** to understand that the verses sometimes brought forth from the **original text** had great emphasis and blessing in their hearts, adding the request that the text might always be presented in this way. Accordingly, based on such experience, there is no doubt whether this **method of presentation** <note>original: "modus proponendi"</note> provides edification, especially since it also makes the minds of the listeners more attentive to the matter itself.

(5.) It is also not a thing without precedent. The late **Dr. Lütkemann** <note>Joachim Lütkemann (1608–1655), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> very often took the **original text** into consideration in his book of epistles and defended himself against common criticism (in the **Dedication of the 1st Edition, Anno 1652**): I do not hide the fact that in several places I have looked not so much at the common German text as at the original language of the Holy Spirit—which a kind-hearted Christian should **NB.** <note>Latin "nota bene," meaning "note well."</note> not interpret poorly—since my intention in these sermons has been to explain the text thoroughly according to the purpose of the **Holy Spirit**, as much as **GOD** has granted me grace, etc.

(6.) To be sure, the **accuser** <note>original: "Hr. Concip." (the one who drafted the charges).</note> opines that this often happens without the slightest cause, but of this "often" he cites no other example than this single one from **Revelation 12** <note>original: "Apoc. XII."</note> where it says "the old serpent" <note>Luther's version</note> and he writes "the serpent, the ancient one." Yet even this example does not prove it was done without cause, especially since the emphasis of the **article** <note>The specific grammar of the Greek text.</note> repeated for the second time in the **original text**—

## From the Year 1705.

### The 130th Accusation:

Such a mystery (of **subtle Manichaeism** <note>A dualistic heresy that Pietists were often accused of, suggesting they believed in two opposing divine powers or viewed physical matter as inherently evil.</note>) is to be seen with more clarity from the visionary books of Dr. Spener, Dr. Petersen, and especially from the two new Manichaeans, A. and Dippel. p. 603.

### Answer:

(1.) These are actually the words of an anonymous person whose considerations, or rather harsh blasphemies against the new **Stuttgart Bible**, the Messrs. Censors have incorporated into their reports here, thus making themselves partakers of such sins.

(2.) Since this author—who could easily be guessed—not only slanders the blessed Arnd’s **Biblical Guide** <note>Johann Arndt's *Informatorium Biblicum*</note> and accuses him of Manichaeism and pagan errors, while also praising Dr. Schelwig’s "Instruction" (which was thoroughly refuted by Mr. P. Schützen) against it on page 602, but also harshly attacks Dr. Spener and other well-known teachers: it is therefore obvious "what spirit's child" he is <note>A German idiom meaning one's true character or alignment is revealed.</note>, and his slander requires no laborious refutation.

(3.) For this reason, it will be enough to mention only so much here: that **specifically** <note>original: "in specie"</note> Mr. A. is (1.) linked with **Democritus** <note>A pseudonym for Johann Konrad Dippel (1673–1734), a radical pietist and alchemist.</note> contrary to the Censors' own proof and confession, as we heard above in Number 23 from their own mouths. (2.) That A. stays far away from the accused "subtle Manichaeism," and his confessions stand directly opposed to the errors of the Manichaeans, as is—God be praised!—obvious to all truth-loving people. (3.) That it is pure malice from this author when he calls A. a Manichaean and his books "visionary": which blasphemies are returned to him just as they were cast out without proof. Just as he will one day have to give an account for rashly accusing the mentioned Stuttgart Bible of so many heresies, namely **Donatist**, **Enthusiast**, and others. Among men, Mr. Lange has already thoroughly punished this in the **Sincere Report** <note>Joachim Lange's *Aufrichtige Nachricht*</note>, Volume V, page 74 and following.

### The 134th Accusation:
->He is said to write better now regarding other matters that were previously disputed by him and his kind. p. 169.<-

### Response:

(1.) The common invention <note>A rhetorical device or tactic.</note> of our Censor is this, as we have often observed: that he occasionally, whenever it seems good to him, pretends that this or that author has now improved himself and now teaches differently than before. By this, they seek to rightly shame honest people, as if they had previously taught erroneously and were now recanting such heresies, or had perhaps even been convinced by the refutations of such Censors.

(2.) But what is it in which Mr. A. is supposed to be writing "better" here than before? Two points are specified. The first is: He, A., introduces the satisfaction of Christ <note>original: "Gnugthuung Christi." This refers to the theological doctrine that Christ’s suffering and death satisfied God's justice on behalf of humanity.</note> as a Divine truth on page 77; the other is: that on page 67 he confesses that Christ is also a mystery outside of us.

(3.) Regarding the first point (1), one should notice above all this sophistical mode of presentation, where the Mr. Drafter <note>original: "Hr. Concip." referring to the author of the accusations.</note> groups the Author together with others and says: A. and "his kind" had made these things matters of dispute. His conscience told the Mr. Drafter that A. had always written clearly and Evangelically concerning the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ. However, so that he could still pin an error on him, he does not speak of him alone, but also of "his kind." But who are these "his kind"? Why have they not been named? Why have the passages <note>original: "loca"</note> not been specified in which Mr. A. supposedly denied or rejected the satisfaction of Christ? Is it then sufficient or responsible to accuse only so indirectly and confusedly, and to group the accused with others whom he does not know or with whom he does not agree?

(4.) The Mr. Drafter has misused and excerpted so many passages from A.'s previous writings; why then did he not also pay attention to how clearly the Author taught on this matter previously, just as in this Postil <note>A book of sermons or scriptural commentaries.</note>. Here, in the passage approved by the Censor himself on page 77, it says: **For once, I gladly confess with the entire Christian Church that Christ, in His life, suffering, and death, earned and prepared salvation for us, to which the entire Scripture bears witness. But Scripture witnesses just as much to how such earned grace must be made beneficial to every soul, without which the earning of it helps nothing.**

(5.) This—

Therefore, your efforts are lost, and the more pious you wish to become outside of Christ, the deeper you will fall into your misery. For there is no <term>value</term> <note>original: "utis." ### Die 138. Anklage:

One also cannot see how the words on p. 193 could be explained without offense. p. 171.

### Antwort:

(1) The words are as follows in their full context. Such (namely, for the sake of love to become all things to all men) Christ Himself did. For since He well knew that the Temple would soon be destroyed, He nevertheless went in and used everything therein for the spreading of the truth. As if we already see that the current unreasonable services of God and human traditions <term>human traditions</term> <note>original: "Menschensatzungen"; religious rules created by humans rather than commanded by God.</note> will not always endure, we can still, out of love for the truth and to pull some still out of the fire, subject ourselves to such things for a while, in patience and faith, yet without fear of man and hypocrisy.

(2) All this is shown from Paul’s example in 1 Corinthians 9:20, 21, 10:33, Acts 21, and so forth. Herein, for a lover of the pure truth who has eyes to see, there is nothing offensive; it can all be explained very well.

<header>Part I. 138. N. on the so-called Old and New. 119</header>

(3) One also does not want to hope that the Lord Censor will find offensive what is written there regarding **unreasonable services of God** and **human traditions**. How heartily one wished it did not have to be said! If that is a reasonable service of God when true Christians give their bodies to God as a holy, living, and well-pleasing sacrifice, according to Romans 12:1, then the opposite is certainly an unreasonable or unintelligent service.

(4) Now go through the customary inherited ways, ceremonies, and practices in many church services, and test with an enlightened eye of understanding what among them is commanded by God in His word, or what is devised by men and kept from Popery <note>original: "Pabstthum"; a polemical term for the practices of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. Likewise, what happens in a divine sense with the sacrifice of the heart and the whole person, or what does not; and what is thus holy, living, and well-pleasing to God. Thus one will be surprised that the Lord Censor can still consider such testimonies offensive, or doubt that it is said they could not always endure.

<margin>St. Paul here calls all sacrifices, works, and worship unreasonable if they—**NB.**—happen without faith and the knowledge of God.</margin>
(5) If such an expression sounds too harsh to him, it is precisely the same one that follows naturally from the interpretations of our theologians and from their comparison with common practice. Luther glosses over Romans 12:1 in the margin thus: The Weimar Bible explains it likewise no differently: A reasonable service of God is that which proceeds from a heart enlightened and inhabited by the Holy Spirit, and—**NB.**—does not consist in external Levitical ceremonies <note>refers to the formal rituals of the Old Testament law</note>, but is performed in spirit and in truth. With which also Dr. Aegidius Hunnius agrees in his commentary on this passage, where he requires for it an understanding reformed and enlightened by the Holy Spirit <note>original Latin: "Intellectum per Spiritum S. reformatum & illuminatum"</note>.

(6) If one now looks at today’s church services in many places among most so-called Christians (we are not speaking of all), then according to such a rule of the Word of God, he will not deny that there are enough unreasonable services of God everywhere. Much consists, alas! in a wretched *opus operatum* <term>opus operatum</term> <note>A Latin theological term meaning "a work performed"; it refers to the belief that a religious ritual is effective simply by doing it, regardless of the faith of the participant.</note>, of which the Apology of the Augsburg Confession <note>The "Apology A.C." is a foundational document of Lutheranism.</note> rightly says: Article 12, p. 256. The reasonable service of God is not only contrasted with the Levitical, but also with that service in which it is imagined to be offered through the work performed <note>original Latin: "in quo fingitur ex opere operato offerri"</note>.

### The 139th Charge:

Regarding the Word of God, he writes on p. 273 that it is a seed that must touch each and every heart; God has also revealed it to the heathens. p. 171.

### Answer:

(1) The correct connection of the words is this: God leaves nothing undone, and spares no effort, no *Note Well* <note>original: "NB." for *nota bene*</note> means, no seed nor powers of His love, to make the field fruitful. == It is certainly a universal seed that must touch each and every heart (namely, according to God’s intention and general purpose) for the world is called the field, and He thus announces Himself to everyone through the drawing and knocking of the Holy Spirit. God has indeed also revealed to the heathens that which can be known of Him. <note>original Greek: "το γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ" (*to gnoston tou Theou*)</note>. It is manifest in them, as Paul says in Romans 1:19; therefore no one is to be excused, which would otherwise be the case if the seed did not affect all people.

(2) Here the Author speaks quite clearly in the very same sense that Paul expressed regarding the natural knowledge of God in the heathens, which indeed happened through a certain kind of writing of the law into the hearts and the revelation of God, as is witnessed in that same place in Romans 1:19 and 2:15. Our theologians very gladly recognize this and call it a revelation of nature <note>original: "revelationem naturæ"</note>, as can be seen in Balduin's Commentary on Romans, Chapter 1, p. 80; indeed, a divine writing <note>original: "divinam γραφὴν"</note> which is intimately connected with the knowledge of the law <note>original: "γνωστῷ νόμου"</note>, as Quenstedt says in *Theol. Did.* Vol. I. p. 252.

(3) If the Lord Drafter <note>The critic or accuser who drafted the charges against Arnold.</note> says that a seed is nevertheless named here that must touch all hearts, then here too Mr. A. [the Author] speaks in accordance with Scripture and with our theologians. For thus Dr. Dannhauer calls natural knowledge a universal calling <note>original: "vocationem universalem"</note> dispensed within man *Note Well* through the seeds of innate knowledge <note>original: "per semina notitiæ innatæ"</note>, whereby he refers to Romans 1:19-20, in *Hodosophia Phænom.* IX. p. 865. And Gerhard observes very well that in Scripture, the law is also understood under the term "seed": the law, however, is not only externally revealed and repeated, but also written into the hearts. See *Homil. Evang.* Part I. homily 1. in *Sexages.* p. 385.

(4) If the reader would now take the trouble to look up the entire context in the Postil <note>A book of sermons or scriptural commentaries.</note>, he would find that in these cited words, guidance was primarily given according to the teaching of Luther, how

He also expressed himself correctly on this in his *Apologetic Repetition*, chapter 6. Scripture a **living-word** <note>original: "Lebewort"</note> and not let it remain merely a **reading-word** <note>original: "Lesewort"</note>, as Varenius repeats in his *Considerations on the Admonition of Rostius*, page 34. ### The 141st Charge:

Likewise, the expression is dangerous: "There lie within man such powers of the soul through which he can grasp everything. These are dead and suppressed through sin. The Word awakens the dead power so that the person begins to use grace in a way that is blessed and good." (page 171).

->Answer:<-

(1.) These altered words actually read as follows on page 1048: "There lie within man such powers of the soul through which he can perceive, grasp, and let into himself everything that is outside of him. These are dead and closed or suppressed through sin and separation from God, just as the powers of hearing are hindered and dead in a physically deaf person. Now, when the Word of the Almighty cries out to and calls upon such a deaf soul again, and the soul does not stubbornly resist Him, then this Word of Life penetrates into such a mind and awakens the dead power, so that the person begins to perceive God’s counsel again and lets it become powerful within him; and thus uses grace in a way that is blessed and good for him. See, then your will shall be awakened and renewed. — Thereby your inward ear of the spirit is opened, etc."

(2.) Had these words been presented in their entirety, every reader could have recognized their pure Evangelical meaning. For what is more consistent with the Gospel and the teachings of Luther than that man is by nature dead in sins, including in the powers of his soul (with which he could grasp everything before the Fall); furthermore, that he cannot awaken himself, but that God calls him through His Word, and if he does not resist, God awakens him and makes him able to hear?

(3.) What does the critic find to blame in this? This: that it is spoken of as if the spiritual powers were not gifted and— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the argument on the next page.</note>

### The 142nd Accusation.

->Regarding Holy Baptism and its power, he speaks several times with ambiguity on pages 751 and 752. p. 171.<-

### Answer:

(1.) On the first page, 751, baptism is not mentioned by a single word, but only rebirth, and what an important work it is. How then can baptism be spoken of ambiguously there, since nothing of baptism is mentioned at all?

(2.) On the following page, the author first begins in the middle of it to speak about the words **"out of water and Spirit"** <note>A reference to John 3:5.</note>; he derives the **institution of water** from the first creation, when the Spirit hovered over the waters, and applies it thus without any ambiguity:

(3.) **"And for this purpose"** (for making alive unto Divine life) **"he has ordained baptism in water"**, so that the desire of faith might grasp it, and allow itself to be baptized and permeated with the love of God through the Holy Spirit, who—*Note Well* <note>original: "NB."</note>—is in and with the water, as one who shall be a sign of the spiritual seal to new life, by virtue of faith, which believes and trusts such a word of God in the water. Out of this water of grace, united with God’s word, we should now allow ourselves to be born anew, etc.

(4.) Here the author speaks mostly with Luther’s own words, and indeed concerning the power of baptism; there is surely nothing ambiguous, and everyone will understand it who is eager to experience the matter itself in his soul—namely, the fruit of baptism. But if the Mr. Drafter <note>original: "Hr. Concip.", referring to the author of the accusations.</note> has brought a suspicious and thus ambiguous sense to the reading of this book, contrary to the author’s intention, then no one else is to blame for it.

### The 150th Accusation.

That B. P. Karl allegedly confessed before a certain Consistory <note>A church court or administrative council.</note> that he gathered the *Collectanea* <note>original: "Collectanea," meaning a collection of source materials or notes.</note> for the book *Luther before Lutheranism* <term>Luthero ante Lutheranismum</term>, while the well-known G. A. organized these materials, added the questions, and prepared it for printing. p. 632.

### Answer:

(1.) Not a single word of this entire claim is true, as Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold.</note> has publicly testified with a clear conscience. The falsehoods betray themselves by the fact that the author of this fake report does not name himself in such a significant accusation, nor does he name the alleged Consistory before which Mr. Karl is said to have made this statement, as is repeated in the year 1707 on page 539. And Mr. A. is certain that this man is being falsely slandered here, and that such words never left his mouth—as if A. had helped prepare this writing. Such is the extent to which the accusers deal in falsehoods.

(2.) And how well do the testimonies agree? The unnamed author of the preface to the Royal Danish Edict against private meetings claims that Mr. A. produced the *Extract* of this *Luther before Lutheranism* printed in Copenhagen, thus blaming the book itself on someone else. But these others attribute the book itself to him.

(3.) It is not at all Mr. A.’s custom to publish things without providing his name, the year, and the publisher; he is not ashamed of the truth, and has suffered so much for it that he has no reason to act in a hidden manner. However, he did not write so much as a line of this book, nor of its *Extract*; he also does not agree with its contents in every respect and therefore has nothing to do with it; his style is even less in agreement with it. In short: it remains a false accusation.

### From the Censure regarding "True Christianity," Old Testament. <note>Refers to a critique of Johann Arndt’s famous work "True Christianity."</note>

### The 154th Accusation:

> Oh, that he would everywhere keep himself strictly and purely to the instruction of sound doctrine; then one could look upon the good that he often presents with complete joy. p. 499.

### Answer:

(1.) The good in such writings shines everywhere before the eyes and into the conscience of Mr. C. <note>Likely referring to a specific critic, possibly Carpzov.</note>, so that he is forced to confess various things here.
(2.) However, since the author is already hated by him for the sake of the witnessed truth, the critic seeks to extract all sorts of things from this book to frighten the reader away. He presents this in the manner of hypocrisy with a "wish," the better to cover his own falsity.
(3.) He claims that the "weeds" are still growing quite strongly. And indeed, they grow strongly enough in such hearts that plague themselves with the invention of foreign errors and wish to forcibly extract them from innocent writings. We shall listen to his accusation properly and weigh it briefly.

### The 155th Accusation:

> He writes more than too fanatically, p. 9, concerning the way to God: You need only let the little spark <term>Füncklein</term> <note>The "spark of the soul" is a mystical concept referring to a remnant of divine light within a person.</note> that lies under the ashes in you be blown into a flame by the Holy Spirit; then you are advised and helped. p. 500.

### Answer:

(1.) Above, at number 139, it was shown how Dannhauer <note>Johann Conrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> describes the *universal calling* <note>original: "Vocationem universalem"</note> as occurring also *through the seeds of innate knowledge* <note>original: "per semina innatæ notitiæ"</note>. Furthermore, in number 135, how Balduin <note>Friedrich Balduin (1575–1627), another orthodox Lutheran professor.</note> calls these *little fires* <note>original: "Igniculos"</note> or little sparks, and Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), the most influential Lutheran scholastic theologian of the 17th century.</note> calls it a *pedagogy for the restoration of the divine image* <note>original: "Pædagogiam ad instaurationem Imaginis divi-"</note>

<header>Part I. 155. 156. Note. Concerning the so-called Old and New.</header>

*image* <note>original: "næ," completing "divinæ" from the previous page.</note>, as do Johann Arndt and others, who show how man should allow himself to be guided by all of this toward his conversion.
(2.) With these theologians—Dannhauer, Gerhard, Balduin, and Arndt—Mr. A. <note>The author, likely Gottfried Arnold.</note> speaks clearly here and admonishes that the natural man should allow the "little spark" of divine knowledge within him to be blown into flame, specifically by the Holy Spirit, so that it may lead him to supernatural knowledge; thus he will be helped.
(3.) That this is the harmless meaning of the author is proven by these words which immediately follow: *Only look upon the good intention of your good creation, and what you were in Adam; without doubt, you will receive a desire to gradually regain that same glory.* Here he shows that the *remnants of the divine image* <note>original: "Reliquiæ imaginis divinæ"</note> should become a guide back to the complete image of God, as Gerhard says.
(4.) Now, if these theologians have written thus, and indeed *in these very terms* <note>original: "in Terminis"</note>, why then should it be interpreted as "fanatical" when another person explains it clearly? And why is one so hasty—or rather, so incautious and bold—to immediately reject everything as fanatical as soon as one catches sight of the name of the "little spark"? Will such rash censures not one day be regretted too late?

### The 156th Accusation:

> He asserts on p. 11 that the virtues from which the image of God consisted had comprised the entire essence of the Godhead. p. 500.

### Answer:

(1.) Without being mutilated, the words read as follows: *Furthermore, he (Paul, in Colossians 3:12) names such divine virtues which we should put on again according to the image of God, which certainly contain and prove the entire essence and life of the Godhead, such as heartfelt love, mercy or innermost stirrings, kindness, and gentleness.* For, **Note Well**, God is love itself and does not merely have such external attributes as one might think in a human way according to reason.
(2.) Everyone sees from this that the author is reflecting on the love which is required for the image of God according to Colossians 3. Now, because God Himself is love (according to 1 John), and nothing is in God that is not God Himself (according to the well-known rule of the theologians), one can say with all right: the divine virtues that we are to put on according to His image are the life and essence of the Godhead.

(3.) For we are to "put on Jesus Christ," Romans 13:14; and He is the "true God," 1 John 5:20. And thus we become "partakers of the divine nature" and the "childship of God," according to 2 Peter 1:4. Adam was also a partaker of this before he sinned. What, then, is blameworthy here? Do not our own teachers also speak this way in part?

(4.) The blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a highly influential Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note> aims precisely at Divine Love when describing the Image of God, when he writes in his *Commonplaces on the Image of God* <note>original: "Loco de Imag. DEI"</note> §. 37. p. 97.
