And in §. 10, he observes that some placed the *formal* aspect or the *relation* of the Divine Image in the "grace-filled indwelling of God and in the richest communication of the highest goods," for which he cites *Johann Arndt's* 2nd Chapter in the 1st Book of *True Christianity* <note>original: "vom W. Chr." (Vom Wahren Christentum)</note>, whom he calls his "friend to be honored in a father's stead." Indeed, in his *Gospel Sermons* <note>original: "Homiliis Evang."</note> p. 148, he teaches regarding Christ from John 1 that He, as the self-subsistent Word, was the life of humans before the Fall; He gave them not only natural life, but also spiritual life.

(5.) If each and every Divine attribute shone forth in Adam, and Christ was his life, then they must also have been *in* him—not indeed "through a transfusion of the divine essence" <note>original Latin: "per divinæ essentiæ transfusionem"</note>, nor "through the conversion of human nature into the divine" <note>original Latin: "per naturæ humanæ in divinam Conversionem"</note>, but through an innermost union and communication of God; just as this same Gerhard distinguishes well in his *Harmony of the Gospels* <note>original: "Harmon. Evang."</note> Vol. III. cap. 176. p. 1323, alongside our other theologians.

(6.) That this union and indwelling of God is also to be understood according to His essence is a settled matter, specifically from that same cited passage of Peter, from which, among others, <term>Hülsemann</term> <note>Johann Hülsemann (1602–1661), a Lutheran theologian known for his strict orthodoxy.</note> in his *Breviary* cap. 14. th. 2. Suppl. clearly states: The <term>κοινωνία θείας φύσεως</term> <note>original Greek: koinōnia theias physeōs; "participation/communion in the divine nature"</note> signifies here the "grace-filled indwelling (Note Well!) of the Divine Essence in us," and the power received from it to strive for divine innocence and purity. And <term>Calovius</term> <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading representative of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> in his *System* Vol. X. art. qu. 1. r. concludes from this: Those with whom God so unites Himself that He makes them partakers of His nature must be connected with Him not only according to His effects and gifts, but also according to the union and connection of His Divine Essence.

So, if man in the rebirth after the Fall has the entire divine essence and life dwelling within him: how much more so before the Fall? And thus H. A. <note>Refers to Johann Arndt.</note> has spoken in agreement with our theologians, and indeed with the *Formula of Concord* itself, which maintains this in Articles 3 and 8.

### The 157th Accusation:

> That man is supposedly excluded from God, p. 5, 8; that he is supposed to have something of God in him, p. 8; that his soul is supposed to be a breath from God, p. 500.

### Answer:

(1.) The last point on p. 7 is expressed from the text of Genesis 2: "God breathed into his nose a living breath." The speaking of God brought into man the living, rational spirit, or "breath from God." This is further proven there from Acts 17:28-29, Ecclesiastes 12:7, Luke 1:38, Hebrews 12:9, Leviticus 32:18, and is moreover illustrated by the testimonies of the Church Fathers: Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory the Great, etc.

(2.) However, it is also carefully limited there on p. 8, stating that the human spirit is not God Himself, but only an "outflow" and a "fruit" of God—a breath or *flatus* <note>Latin for "breath" or "blowing."</note>, according to Augustine and Eucherius.

(3.) Furthermore, this practical use is drawn from it: because the immortal essence in man sighs again for God, for it "has something of God in itself" that cannot die, one should therefore bind oneself more closely to God, etc.

(4.) The first expression on p. 5 reads as follows in its proper context: "Why do we then delay to turn ourselves back into this Good, from which we flowed, and to seek again the first right and access to such goods?"

(5.) Whoever still doubts this entirely innocent presentation should read through the entire 1st Chapter of the 1st Book of the *Depiction of Inner Christianity* <note>Refers to Arndt’s work.</note>; there he will recognize the complete harmony of ancient and modern teachers with the Scripture in this matter, and will willingly let go of the untimely objections which have already been addressed above in Numbers 81, 85, and 119.

(1.) Regarding faith, these are among the clear words of the accused author <note>Referring to Johann Arndt (1555–1621), author of *True Christianity*.</note> in this very same censured book; at the 17th Proverb on page 261, he asks: What is Abraham’s faith actually? Just as on page 364, this faith, this seizing of God's grace in Christ, is imputed to such a soul as that righteousness which counts before God, etc. Thus, he describes faith as a seizing of the grace and righteousness of Christ, just as all Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to the Lutheran tradition.</note> teachers do.

Does a believer not trust the Lord Jesus with all his power? Has Luther sung of it wrongly? Does he not find it necessary to yield and sink oneself into Jesus? If he says yes, then he cannot interpret it as heresy for Mr. A. [Arndt] when he teaches it to others and practices it himself.

### The 160th Accusation:

(1) In homiletic writings <note>writings intended for sermons or spiritual edification rather than academic debate.</note>, one must not turn an author's

his manners of speaking into pure propositions, as if he intended to present and throw out nothing but theological theses for the sake of disputation. (4) What is there to criticize in this? The Church Fathers speak even more deeply and "questionably" to Reason on this matter, as can be seen in the *Illustration of Inward Christianity* in the 2nd Chapter of the 1st Book.

### The 167th Accusation.

Thus he asserts regarding our church on page 1115 that it stands in perverted zeal / that no one should be directed to it / that it should not be called a true church / indeed not even a church. p. 502.

### Answer.

(1.) Here too, the Mr. Accuser <note>original: "Hr. Conc."</note> has dealt very unscrupulously with the author’s words. If the reader compares the following context with the poor excerpts of the Mr. Accuser / his malicious intention and the author’s innocence will be clearly recognized.
(2.) The title is: **Of the Invisible Community of the Saints.** <note>In Lutheran theology, the "invisible church" refers to the true body of believers known only to God, as opposed to the "visible church" or the earthly institution.</note> There it is shown on p. 1114 how every party claims to be the only true church / and thus the discussion is not actually about ours / but about all those who condemn others and consider themselves alone to be the best.

Do you not see that you too, like other sects, stand in perverted zeal / which **NB.** <note>Latin "nota bene," meaning "take special note."</note> cannot be present in the true church.
(4.) The reason is this: For the head of the true church, Christ, does not act so: namely, that He would stand in perverted zeal. Furthermore, it says: You complain constantly about the miserable state of the church / which you nevertheless think you are building. Why then **NB.** do you call this a church / (namely, this miserable state or corruption) which you yourself do not consider as such / except only for the sake of the name and appearance of a religion.

### The 168th Accusation.

(4.) It is further proven according to the Scripture: "For that Christ died / even the devils know. But what does it help / if one does not die to one's corruption in the death of Christ? Can one's knowledge redeem him from the heavy fall?"
(5.) How do you then comfort yourself now, o vain man / in your knowledge...

And thus, I certainly do not wish to contest the authority of the Scripture—which I acknowledged in §. 40 was indeed very great—but I only wish to show that the first Christians, especially in the first two centuries, did not have such a closed Canon <note>The "Canon" refers to the official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture.</note> as we have today, but rather that they tested everything well, and what they found to be pure, they accepted as Divine.

(12) To make my meaning even clearer and to protect it against all malicious interpretations <note>original Latin: "sinistras interpretationes"</note>, I will illustrate this with the books that were formerly regarded as Apocrypha <note>The author is referring to the "Antilegomena," books of the New Testament whose inclusion in the Bible was once disputed.</note>, such as the Epistles to the Hebrews, James, Jude, John, etc. For because people doubted the authors of these letters, and consequently also their <term>Divine Inspiration (Theopneustia)</term>, it is evident from this that there was not yet such a closed Canon at that time, and that one had to test whether they were genuine or not. Indeed, even to this day, the prefaces of Mr. Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the central figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> to the Epistles to the Hebrews and James testify that he rejected the authority of these Epistles, or at least called them into doubt. One also finds elsewhere in Luther's writings very harsh expressions regarding the presentation of James in his letter, even calling the holy Apostle James a fool. Now, however, it is held as a settled matter that the said Epistles were written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Why is this done now, and why does one not agree with the opinion of Mr. Luther? It must certainly come from the fact that these Epistles have been better tested and the Apostolic spirit recognized within them.

(13) Therefore, Dr. Johann Olearius <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian and author of "Exemplary Art of Prayer" (Beth-Kunst).</note> also writes of this matter in his *Exemplary Art of Prayer* on page 1005: "What the Papists reproach us with concerning Luther's prefaces to these books is meant in no other way than hypothetically <note>original Latin: "hypothetice"</note>, with a certain condition: if these Epistles were truly contrary to the other indubitable books of Holy Scripture, they could not be regarded as God’s Word; for His Word is truth without any contradiction or adverse incorrectness." But now that all such doubt has been thoroughly removed—as can be seen from the Nuremberg Ernestine Bible <note>A famous 17th-century study Bible promoted by Duke Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha.</note>—no one has cause to reproach a conditional opinion of our Church as if it were unconditional. He knows no other way to excuse it, and thus expressly testifies that all doubt which Luther had regarding these Epistles has been thoroughly removed.

of 1 John 4:1: "Test the spirits, whether they are of God." They judged spiritual matters spiritually (1 Corinthians 2:13). The discussion is only about those books written by God's inspiration, and of those it is said that the first Christians accepted and used them after they had tested them and recognized the Divine element. But they never recognized Petronius’s lewd farces as Divine.

(26) To the passages in Romans 11:36 and 1 Corinthians 8:6, the Mr. Opponent <note>original: "Herr Contradicent," the author's term for the person arguing against him.</note> answers that these verses refer to spiritual gifts, which certainly come from God. However, he proves this with nothing more than his own claim: that the circumstances show it must be understood this way. Yet the Apostle speaks quite generally, and particularly in 1 Corinthians 8:6, he opposes the true, living God to pagan idols precisely because the idols are not the creators of Heaven and Earth, whereas the true invisible God is the one "from whom are all things," etc. Therefore, other commentators—whom he cannot suspect of heresy—also explain these dictates as referring to Creation. For example, the well-known Dr. Nikolaus Selneccerus <note>A primary author of the Lutheran Formula of Concord.</note> in his *Full Commentary on all the Epistles of Paul*, adds this gloss to the words of 1 Corinthians 8:6, "From whom are all things": **as the eternal cause and origin** <note>original Latin: "tanquam causa & origine æterna &c."</note>; likewise, **from whom**—note this—**all creatures were founded through the Son by the power of the Holy Spirit** <note>original Latin: "ex quo NB. omnes Creaturæ per filium virtute Spiritus S. sunt conditæ"</note>; in this, he also cites the passage in Romans 11:36 as a parallel.

(27) The blessed Mr. Luther did indeed render the little word *ek* <note>The Greek preposition ἐκ, meaning "out of" or "from."</note> as **from** <note>original: "von"</note> (though in other places like Romans 9:21, 10:17, and 11:6, he rightly used **out of** <note>original: "aus"</note>). It would have been better, however, if it had been translated as **out of** here as well as in other places. Had he translated the *ek* in Galatians 4:4 as **out of**, the emphasis of the Apostolic meaning would be even clearer in German: namely, that Christ was not just born **of** Mary (as some ancient heretics are said to have claimed—that Christ passed through Mary only like water through a pipe, and was thus born *of* her) but was born **out of** Mary, that is, out of her human seed. For this reason, He is also called the "seed of the woman" in Genesis 4. Likewise, it would better match Moses' report of the creation of Eve if Luther had written in 1 Corinthians 11:12 according to the Greek: "As the woman is **out of** the man"; for in Genesis 2:21 it says explicitly that God took a rib **out of** Adam’s body and built the woman from it.

(28) In the same way, the passages in Romans 11:36 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 are translated better as **out of** than as **from**. A learned man excuses Mr. Luther for this, saying: "The good man was troubled by it and thought that if one said 'out of Him,' it would seem as

<column-break/>

<page-num>165</page-num>

if God were a material substance. **For matter is that out of which a thing is.** <note>original Latin: "Nam materia est, ex qua res est."</note> God would have to be an external cause; for according to metaphysics, an efficient cause is an external cause." Thus, they think one should not use the little word **out of** at all. But I say: One should stick with the word *ex* or **out of**. What does that signify? It serves to confirm to people that their philosophy is worthless and entirely false when it claims that an efficient cause <term>efficient cause (the primary source of change or rest; the 'maker' of a thing)</term> must always be an external cause, and that the "source out of which a thing comes" must always be physical matter. For I can rightly say that a thought is made **out of** my head, and yet neither brain nor skull became part of the thought.

(29) The explanation of the passage in Hebrews 11:3, found in the year 1702 on page 538 (to which I am referred), is not against me insofar as the author himself writes: that which we now see came not from things that appear, but rather from things that appear quite contrary. For I readily admit that it seems very contrary to human reason when one teaches, according to God's Word, that all things have arisen out of God. Dr. Johannes Cluverus, a distinguished Danish theologian, paraphrases this cited passage in his *Orthotomia Apostolica* (which Dr. Calovius praises highly in a preceding preface, p. 502) as follows: **That such faith (namely, the evidence of things not seen) is also evident from the past: For we have not seen God working all these things, and yet we believe that all things were founded out of—note—invisible things that appear nowhere.** <note>original Latin: "Talem esse fidem (nempe ἔlegchon blepomenōn) constat etiam è præteritis: Neque enim vidimus DEum universa hæc operantem, & credimus tamen ex NB. invisibilibus & nusquam apparentibus omnia esse condita."</note> Just as this learned man proves with what precedes that "not out of things which appear" is the same as "out of invisible and non-apparent things," so this truth is strengthened: namely, that visible things have come from invisible things.

(30) Concerning the passage in Hebrews 2:11, the Mr. Opponent writes that by "**the One**," God is not meant, but rather Adam. However, the previously mentioned Dr. Cluverus glosses it himself on page 458, saying: **He who sanctifies (Christ) and those who are sanctified (purified from uncleanness) are all from the one (God the Creator, etc.).** <note>original Latin: "Qui sanctificavit (Christus) & quæ sanctificantur, (ab immunditia purgantur) ex uno omnes (DEO Creatore &c.)"</note> And thus he understands "**the One**" not as Adam, but as God Himself. So I am not alone in taking the cited dictate to refer to God, but have the authority of a completely orthodox Lutheran teacher before me. I leave the rest unanswered because this truth has already been sufficiently rescued, and I wish to avoid all long-windedness—especially since the Mr. Opponent himself skipped several other passages I cited as proof without any refutation.

(31) I therefore conclude this short apology and confess with all my heart that I believe, with Dietericus in his *Catechism* (p. 284), that God created all things **out of nothing, that is, out of no pre-existing matter at all.** <note>original Latin: "ex nihilo, id est, ex nulla omnino præexistente materia"</note>

# Second Appendix to Part I.

## Counter-Report to the Unfounded Accusations,
### with which the authors of the so-called *Innocent News* seek to cast suspicion upon the *Theological Councils and Responses* of an anonymous person, which Mr. Arnold brought to light in the year 1705.

The gentleman authors of the *News* <note>Referring to the "Unschuldige Nachrichten," a prominent orthodox Lutheran journal that criticized Pietism.</note> reviewed the *Godly Theological Councils and Responses* as the first new item in the tenth order of 1704, page 601. They excerpted bits from the beginning and end, through which they intended to prove that more than enough "weeds" <note>A common metaphor for heresy or false doctrine.</note> had crept in. For this reason, they strongly warn against this book. However, an impartial reader will recognize from the following deduction that they were led by pure prejudice and were prevented from observing the sincerity of a "good interpreter" <note>original Latin: "boni interpretis"</note>; instead, they assigned the very worst

<column-break/>

<page-num>167</page-num>
<header>Part I, Appendix II, regarding the Theological Councils and Responses of an Anonymous Author, etc.</header>

meaning to every expression unfamiliar to them, from which such an unjust judgment over the *Councils* arose.

(2) Initially, it is certainly dubious that they exert such effort to blacken this book and describe it in the most dangerous terms, even though they themselves must praise it on page 602, saying that it urges zealous and inward life-improvement and the power of Jesus in sanctification. Had they been willing to recognize the words they cited—from which errors were supposedly identified—within their context and according to the author's true meaning through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, they would have to confess that the *Councils* were only so offensive and seemed erroneous to them because the author did not write in the common scholastic manner and did not use the expressions, definitions, and distinctions typically used among scholars.

(3) Now, however, the authors themselves suspect on page 602 that it is evident from the work that the person from whom these *Councils* originate—as an instrument of God—is of the female sex; indeed, they think it corresponds quite closely with the writings of Johanna Eleonora Petersen <note>A famous female Pietist writer and theologian.</note>. Although they did not hit upon the actual facts or the specific person with this guess, they still should have reasonably considered—since they believed the book had not a male author but a female author <note>original German: "Autorin"</note> whom they themselves call the "originator" on page 608—that, according to their own principles, a woman should be shown some leniency if she perhaps uses this or that seemingly misshapen phrase not arranged with precision <gloss>Greek: kat’ akribeian</gloss>. One is obligated not to interpret everything in the worst way according to one's preconceived school-opinions, but rather in the best way, especially since other clear testimonies of the author's pure foundation of faith appear in this book, and the censors themselves must praise her for urging inward life-improvement and the power of Jesus in sanctification.

(4) How can the atonement <note>original German: "Gnugthuung," referring to the doctrine of satisfaction/atonement.</note> and the precious merit of Christ be more clearly confessed than when it says in the *Councils*, page 376: "Jesus gladly takes the sins of all people upon Himself, so that sin is forgiven"; and page 533: "Christ seeks that which is lost again and heals the wounded; Christ always restores and binds up, and does not mock the frail." Likewise, page 346: "The Godhead manifests itself in human salvation, and the Father’s heart is pure mercy; whoever sinks into it is healed and blessed. — You stream of glory—"

(5) Even more such proofs of **Orthodoxy** <note>original: "Orthodoxiæ"</note> in the **foundation of faith** <note>original: "fundamento fidei"</note> could be cited if required. Would it not have been better and more Christian if the gentlemen Censors had passed over the passages they found offensive in these **Advisories** <note>original: "Consiliis"</note> and instead cited such clear confessions, from which even the simplest person could grasp the author's true meaning and be edified? True love for one's neighbor requires that everything in a teaching which can be interpreted without force should be turned for the best, and nothing should be explained poorly that can admit a good and scriptural meaning. Wise theologians experienced in Divine mysteries have done this with **Tauler**, **Kempis**, **Arndt**, and the like <note>referring to Johannes Tauler, Thomas à Kempis, and Johann Arndt—mystical and devotional writers popular in Pietist circles</note> when they encountered certain ways of speaking that seemed obscure or strange to reason. # 170 Counter-Report to the Unfounded Accusations, Part 1, Appendix II / Part 1, Appendix II on the Anonymous Theological Councils and Responses, etc. 171

Ecclesiastes 7:28 <note>Original citation: "Pred. VII, 29." The author is quoting the verse "I have not found a woman among all these."</note>. *I have not found a woman among them all*: This does not refer to a female person, but to an effeminate, lamenting person / rather than one with **manly courage**. But such people are rare. There are those who are "women" and not men / namely, even if they are of the male sex. Just as Luther here understands the word "woman" to mean a "womanly mind," it is not entirely wrong to view it this way elsewhere. The author also does not exclude the biological sex / insofar as it exists in its corruption without a true rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit / therefore, on page 343, he warns strongly against the "serpent in the natural woman" / and explicitly writes: **Let everyone take care / that he is not captured by womanly cunning and teaching or even love / and led astray into mixed, frivolous dealings.** For such "women" should rightly remain silent in all spiritual matters / as long as they have not recognized and cast out the serpent within them. Thus, the author does not wish to introduce the **Quaker** custom / which allows women to preach in the public congregation / but he only wishes to show proud men / that they should not boast of their mere sex / and thereby believe they are exempt from the Apostolic command.

(10) But that Paul imposes silence upon women not simply **on account of their sex** <note>original: "respectu sexus"</note>, but rather **on account of the vices** <note>original: "respectu vitiorum"</note> to which this sex is especially prone / and that this commandment therefore also applies to male persons / who possess such **vices** <note>original: "Vitia"</note> / no divinely enlightened person would deny. For the Holy Spirit commands or forbids nothing in Holy Scripture without an important cause and intention for this or that benefit or harm that follows. Since those / who may be men by sex / but are womanly in the nature of their minds / that is / talkative / soft / fickle / lightheaded / wavering / inquisitive / cunning, and self-complacent / thereby make themselves unfit / to teach others with profit / it is certainly not wrong / if one applies the Apostle's prohibition to them as well. (11) Experience indeed testifies, especially in these days given the great corrupted state of Christianity / that many men / even teachers and preachers themselves, possess such **vices** <note>original: "Vitia"</note> / which the Apostle punished in the young widows of his time. 1 Timothy 5:11–13. ## Counter-Report on the Unfounded Imputations, Part I, Appendix I.

The author of the *Counsels* <note>Referring to the *Theological Counsels* (Theologische Consilia), likely by Gottfried Arnold.</note> does not deny that this passage deals with the birth of our Savior. However, that it can also be applied in a **mystical sense** <note>original: "Sensu mystico"</note> to the spiritual birth of Jesus within us is evident from the single small word **unto us** <note>Hebrew: לנו (*lanu*)</note>, that is, for our benefit and salvation. But if we are to truly partake in such benefit and salvation, then Jesus must also be born spiritually in us. He must indeed take shape within us (Galatians 4:19), so that we can say: "Christ lives in us" (Galatians 2:20), or: "Christ is our life" (Philippians 1:21). Concerning these Pauline words, the late Arndt <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), a highly influential German Lutheran theologian whose work *True Christianity* laid the groundwork for Pietism.</note> writes in his *True Christianity*, Book 1, Chapter 12: "Blessed is the person who can say from the heart: 'Christ is my life,' not only after this life, but even now; while you still live here, Christ must be your life, that is, he must live in you. --- The more you die to the world, the more Christ lives in you." Indeed, this man of God teaches in the same work, throughout the entire sixth chapter, how the Word of God must demonstrate its power and become alive in a person through faith.

(19) Everything that the Scripture teaches externally, he says, must happen within a person through Christ in spirit and faith. ---
> What is the New Testament according to the letter other than an external testimony that everything must happen within a person through faith? For the entire New Testament must be completely within us, and it forces its way there because the kingdom of God is within us (Luke 17:21). For just as Christ was physically conceived and born of Mary through the Holy Spirit in faith, so must he be spiritually conceived and born in me, etc. Just as Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading theologian of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> says in his *Meditation 51*: **"Christ must be conceived, born, and live in you."** <note>original Latin: "Christum in te oportet concipi, nasci, vivere."</note>

(20) This can also serve to answer what the *Reports* (p. 684) reject as erroneous in the *Counsels* (p. 56, 57). It is not at all a "terrible thing"—though the *Reports* present it as such—when the author calls the tormenting and killing of our **old man** <note>The "old man" refers to the sinful, unregenerate human nature.</note> the "death of Jesus." In this, the author means nothing other than what Paul calls "the dying of the Lord Jesus," which we are to carry in or on our body, so that his life may also be made manifest in our body (2 Corinthians 4:10). There, Paul uses the word **putting to death** <note>original Greek: νέκρωσιν (*nekrōsin*)</note>, which he also uses to describe the barren and "deadened" body of Sarah (Romans 4:19). This is to show that the "dying" or the "death of Jesus" is understood as nothing other than the weakening and eradication of sin, which happens through Jesus within us. For since we cannot die to sin without Christ's grace, power, or cooperation—which is nevertheless required of us (Romans 6:2, 1 Peter 2:24)—through such an expression, everything is 
<meta>catchword: JESUS</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>175</page-num>
<header>Part I, Appendix II, regarding the Counsels and Theological Responses of an Anonymous Author, etc.</header>

rightly attributed to the Lord **JESUS**, and all honor is given to him. In this sense, one can certainly say that Christ's dying occurs in us when we die to sin. And from such a death or "dying of Jesus" in us, Christ must certainly swallow up the old life as the new life in us, as the author states. That is: when we have died to sin with Jesus in the aforementioned manner, the body of sin is destroyed, and we then no longer live, but Christ lives in us. But because we cannot die to sin within ourselves with Jesus if we oppose his holy workings through a **willful or stubborn resistance**, the "dying" is indeed attributed to us **to the extent that we are open to his inspirations** <note>original Latin: "eatenus, quatenus ejus instinctibus vacamus"</note>. It is said in Holy Scripture that we die with Christ (2 Timothy 2:11), are planted with him in a death like his, and are buried with him (Romans 6:4, 5); that we become like him in his death through the fellowship of his sufferings (Philippians 3:10), and have died with Christ to the regulations of the world (Colossians 2:20). We cannot, however—as already mentioned—die in this way by our own strength if Christ does not drive and strengthen us to do so. Therefore, it is nothing but a vain **dispute over words** <note>original Greek: λογομαχια (*logomachia*)</note> when the *Reports* try to make the phrasing regarding the "process of Christ in us" suspicious, as Mr. Lange <note>Joachim Lange (1670–1744), a prominent Pietist theologian at Halle.</note> has also shown in the fourth part of his *Sincere Reports* (p. 88 ff.).

(21) Regarding the words quoted by the *Reports* from the *Counsels* (p. 6): "I, the eternal birth, bear myself anew in my Son in you through the power of my Spirit"—I believe that this contains more than one **typographical error** <note>original Latin: "Sphalma Typographicum"</note>. Indeed, the *Counsels* do not lack such printing errors which can cause misunderstanding. I believe the manuscript originally read: "I bear my Son in you through the eternal birth by the power of my Spirit," which indicates nothing other than the revelation of the Son of God from the Father within us (Galatians 1:16; cf. 4:6). Nevertheless, the words "I bear myself in my Son" can have a good meaning **through a fair interpretation** <note>original Latin: "per interpretationis æquitatem"</note>, especially if one considers that Christ is the image of the Father's essence (Hebrews 1:3). For because the Father begets a Son who is of the same essence, power, and glory as himself, it can be said of the Father that he begets himself in his Son—that is, he **expresses** and allows his own essence and attributes to shine forth in the Son. For this reason, the Son is called **the radiance of his glory** <note>original Greek: απαυγασμα της doxης αυτου (*apaugasma tēs doxēs autou*)</note> (Hebrews 1:3).

To say that he should be killed through Christ, they understand as nothing other than **being fleshly minded** <note>original Greek: φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός (*phronēma tēs sarkos*)</note> *Romans 8:6.* And this must certainly be weakened and killed, because it is an enmity against God. (23) The words spoken in the name of God in the *Counsels* <note>original: *Consiliis*</note> *p. 16*: "Many know something of me in the Word, but this is far from knowing me as I am," deal with the great difference between the **literal** and the **spiritual** or **living knowledge** of God. Concerning this, **Gerhardus** <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading theologian of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> says in *Commonplaces on Free Will, p. 412*: "One is the knowledge of the letter, another of the Spirit. Hypocrites mixed among the reborn in the Church understand the article of the Trinity, of the incarnation of the Word, etc. But that knowledge is so constituted that it consists of the letter rather than the spirit." <note>original Latin: *Alia est notitia literæ, alia Spiritus. Just as **Georg Möbius** <note>Georg Möbius (1616–1697), a Lutheran theologian and professor at Leipzig.</note> cites this passage in his *Theologia Canon, under Canon 36. p. 145.* which says: "Words of knowledge simultaneously denote the affection of the heart." <note>original Latin: *Verba notitiæ simul denotant affectum cordis.*</note> From which he finally concludes: "To know the Word denotes not speculative knowledge, but practical or living and effective knowledge, in which movements of the soul follow sensory cognition." <note>original Latin: *Verbum nosse non notitiam speculativam, sed practicam sive vivam & efficacem notat, in qua cognitionem sensualem motus animi sequuntur.*</note> Likewise, the famous Wittenberg teacher **Dr. Calovius** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a champion of Lutheran Orthodoxy against syncretism and Pietism.</note> in his *Synopsis of Controversies p. 66. §. 13.* asserts this thesis against the Socinians: "True and salvific understanding of Scripture cannot be had without the special and internal illumination of the Holy Spirit." <note>original Latin: *Vera & salutaris Scripturæ intelligentia non potest haberi sine speciali & interna Spiritus S. illuminatione.*</note> Therefore, he concedes to the Pharisees and scribes the literal, but not the living and salvific knowledge of God, when he writes of them in *Exegetical Augsburg Confession Art. 5. c. 3. §. 9.*: "These surely frequently read the Sacred Scriptures (Acts 15:21), they were professedly Doctors of the law and Masters of the Scriptures (Matthew 2:4; Romans 2:19; 1 Timothy 1:17). Yet they are pronounced blind by Christ, and leaders of the blind (Matthew 15:14). Note: because they did not understand the divine oracles spiritually." <note>original Latin: *Hi sane frequenter legebant S. S... Cæci tamen a Christo pronunciantur... quod oracula divina spiritualiter haud intelligerent.*</note>

(24) Now I come to those words in the *Reports* <note>original: *Nachrichten*, likely referring to a critical publication or newsletter of the time.</note> *p. 605.* which are called truly terrifying. However, that they are not terrifying, but rather truly comforting, joyful, and entirely scriptural words, is evidenced not only by the heading: *Transformation of Mourning into Joy p. 309.* but also by the content itself. This content presents nothing other than the state of a soul in which God's righteousness and zeal manifest or powerfully show themselves against all defilements of the flesh and the spirit, to bring the soul to the denial of all ungodly nature. After the soul has become obedient in faith, it is refreshed again through the pouring out of the sweet love of God and gladdened with the pure delight of the spirit. For this is precisely what the author means with the words: "The spirit finally perceives that darkness is as the light, yes, that darkness is a cause of the light." Since he understands no other darkness than the **darkness of mourning** <note>original: *Trauer-Finsterniß*</note>, which is caused by the withdrawal of the Sun of Grace in the soul, as the entire context clearly shows. Such darkness is described in Holy Scripture, as the Jews experienced it there, *Psalm 107:10, 14.* and David himself, *Psalm 143:3.* Who could also thank God for the redemption from such darkness and say to God: "You make my darkness light." *Psalm 18:29.* Item: "Unto the upright there arises light in the darkness." *Psalm 112:4.*

(25) Such darkness or sorrow certainly comes primarily from the Father, as the first person of the Holy Trinity. For when a person is to be truly converted to God, first the Father's righteous wrath over sin manifests through the Law in that person. Therefore, the Lord Jesus himself says: "No one can come to me except the Father draw him," *John 6:44.* Which drawing certainly does not happen without anxiety and the darkness of mourning (as David often calls it), for he scourges every son whom he receives, and if we endure chastening, he offers himself to us as to children, *Hebrews 12:6-7.* He reveals and brings forth his Son in us, *Galatians 1:16.* Whereby the previous darkness is transformed into a bright, joyful light; for Jesus, the Son of Love, is primarily presented in Holy Scripture under the image of a light, *John 1:9; 3:19; 8:12.* Where then is the "abominable depth" that the authors of the *Reports* claim to have found here?

# Part II.

## Consisting of clear answers to Director Cyprian’s accusations, and specifically first to his second preface regarding the general observations. <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745) was a leading Lutheran theologian and a fierce opponent of Pietism and Arnold’s "History of the Church and Heretics."</note>

### The 1st Accusation:

Arnold is a man who, under the appearance of promoting the fear of God, falsifies the Christian religion or even overthrows it entirely.

### Answer:

(1) In these and the following accusations, there is no proof whatsoever: such highly important points would certainly require proof, and one could therefore quite rightly leave them unanswered; however, the following serves as a brief reply.

(2) That Mr. A. [Arnold] has sincerely intended some promotion of the fear of God with his small amount of work before **GOD**, his conscience still bears witness to him at this hour; and although he does not wish to boast of it, he is also sufficiently convinced from the outside that such work in the **Lord** has not been in vain.

(3) But whether all of this was merely "appearance" is a matter of conscience, of which the Searcher of Hearts <note>A common Pietist term for God, emphasizing His knowledge of internal sincerity over external ritual.</note> alone must judge; and even more so, whether he has thereby sought to falsify the Christian religion or to overthrow it. Until this hour, it is manifest that he has not falsified the true Christian religion, but rather, according to his small measure, has sought to maintain it for himself and to recommend it to others: since he well knows in whom he believes. All his oral and written work is aimed toward that, in which he also serves the high ordinance of the Christian religion.

(4) Because this accusation, as mentioned, stands here purely without the slightest proof, there is nothing further to answer, especially since similar points have already occurred above in Part I, No. 26 and 99.

### The 2nd Accusation:

He robs the Holy Scripture of its power and divine privilege.

### Answer:

(1) Against this, let the reader consider Mr. A.'s confession and explanation...

## The 3rd Accusation.
### He blasphemes the Sacraments.

->Answer:<-

(1) Although, once again, no proof is provided here—which is nonetheless indispensable in such important matters—the following declarations can clearly demonstrate the opposite. Namely, regarding Baptism, Mr. A. <note>Referring to the author, Gottfried Arnold.</note> sincerely confesses in the *Supplements*, page 52, that he is indeed at one with the theologians that children are by no means to be deprived of Baptism; and he himself, during such an act, when it is performed with earnest prayer, has perceived no small blessing through the presence of the Holy Trinity.

(2) Thus, Mr. A. neither could nor would blaspheme Baptism by what he reported historically from antiquity concerning the Baptism of adults. For he well distinguished the *question of fact* <note>original: "quæstionem facti"</note> from the *question of law* <note>original: "quæstione juris"</note>, and has explained himself in the aforementioned manner in a Christian and blameless way.

(3) Indeed, his further accounts of Baptism sufficiently show that he never blasphemed Baptism in its use established according to the mind of Christ, but rather honored and held it in high esteem; rather, he only criticized the *mechanical ritual* <note>original: "opus operatum"; a theological term referring to the belief that a sacrament works automatically by the mere outward act, regardless of the faith of the recipient or minister.</note> and other abuses. In Book 11, Chapter 3, § 10, he writes: That in the 11th century, Baptism was still conducted somewhat reasonably, without the delusion of the *mechanical ritual*, and so forth. Conversely, he laments the abuses that crept in through all centuries.

(4) Now, whoever laments and describes the abuse of a matter is precisely seeking thereby to uphold the matter itself with its proper use; and consequently, he will never blaspheme it. No Christian would blaspheme Baptism in itself; how then could Mr. A. be accused of such blasphemies?

(5) The same is to be understood with proper distinction regarding the Lord's Supper.
<meta>catchword: know.</meta>

<column-break/>

Mr. A. often praises the simple and pure use of it according to Christ’s institution, especially among the first Christians, and how they did not admit the ungodly to it; regarding this, the entire last chapter in the Second Book of the *Portrait* <note>Referring to Arnold's "Portrait of the First Christians" (Abbildung der ersten Christen).</note>, along with so many passages in the *Church History*, can sufficiently satisfy a reader.

(6) On the other hand, he reports so many various abuses of it during the decline and afterwards under the Papacy itself through all the centuries: and he especially notes in Book 16, Chapter 12, § 4, how at the beginning of the Reformation, the Lord's Supper was celebrated so simply and purely by some congregations.

(7) Thus, nothing remains in which Mr. A. could have blasphemed the Lord’s Supper. For what was objected long ago regarding the coercion or strict binding to the *Lord's Supper*, one has already been able to find explained in the response to Dr. Hannekenius <note>Philipp Ludwig Hanneken, a Lutheran theologian and critic of Arnold.</note> § 21, as well as in the *Remembrance*. See also the *Supplements* page 6, where he describes his intention: namely, to contrast the primarily free and mysterious—indeed truly Divine—use of the table of the **LORD** with the ensuing abuse and especially with the coercion. And Mr. Director Cyprian himself confesses in this very preface of his: The devil persuades his servants that it is *Pietism* <note>original: "Pietisterey"; a derogatory term used by critics to label the movement for inward spiritual renewal as heretical or fanatic.</note> when one declares the worship service performed out of mere habit, as well as the impenitent use of the Lord’s Supper, to be insufficient or rather highly harmful; and he calls this a precious truth. Mr. A. has testified to this very same thing.

(8) From this, the conclusion follows: Mr. A. does not blaspheme the Lord’s Supper, because he distinguishes the abuse from the right use, and has never rejected the matter itself, but has always retained it, and still retains it.

### The 5th Accusation:
->He says that the external church system is of no use.<-

### Answer:

(1) To what extent Mr. A., along with others of our writers, has described and rejected the abuse and decay of the external church system, has already been very clearly demonstrated from his own words above in Part I, Nos. 6, 12, 35, and 39. Mr. Cyprian himself calls the testimony against the abuse, or against the divine service performed out of mere habit without benefit or improvement of the heart, a **precious truth** which the Devil makes hateful to his beloved ones, as if it were heretical. Thus, in this matter, he is at one with Mr. A. and wrongly accuses him of something more.

(2) But that the external church system in and of itself, and in its beneficial Christian use, should be of no use, Mr. A. has said nowhere; rather, he has earnestly proven the opposite with words and deeds until this hour, by virtue of his words cited in the thought-of place and his daily practice.

(3) Indeed, even in the *Explanation*, Mr. Dr. C. clearly saw the opposite, where Mr. A. expressly wrote in Part II, Chapter 5, §. 5: **No sensible and modest Christian will entirely reject the church system in itself.** == But it were to be wished,

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

<page-num>207</page-num>

that the poor people also got something good in their hearts in the church, etc. Here Mr. A. says with undeniable words that the church system is certainly useful: which is answer enough for such persons who are concerned only with truth and justice in every matter.

### The 6th Accusation:
->He says that for the foundation of salvation in the Christian church,<-
->the knowledge of the Holy Trinity and the divinity of Christ is not<-
->required, but that one can be saved without this.<-

### Answer:

**Praise God!** that even this evil accusation, which also stands there without proof, is completely annihilated by so many undeniable testimonies cited above in Part I, Nos. 41, 71, and 173: according to which the reader is to recognize and judge Mr. A.

### The 7th Accusation:
->A. is a Pietist and a whitewashed tomb, because in his writings<-
->he poured out all such filth against the Word of God and the blessed<-
->knowledge of JESUS Christ.<-

### Answer:

(1) Here, alas! the corruption of the natural heart manifests itself all too clearly through such name-calling and scolding.

(2) Of the filth with which Mr. Cyprian wished to besmirch Mr. A. and his good reputation, nothing has been found in his writings by virtue of the answers given so far; and every man would certainly have to answer for it if he called the testimonies of truth "filth." One has hardly sinned against one's neighbor in this way, and one will be unable to justify these unchristian labels of "Pietist" <note>At this time, "Pietist" was often used as a derogatory label by the Lutheran Orthodoxy against those who emphasized internal spiritual life over formal dogma.</note> and the like before either Divine or human courts according to the rule of Christ (to which one appeals oneself, and which one wishes to be observed by others).

### The 8th Accusation:
->His students do no better.<-

### Answer:

(1) That he has no students, much less a following <note>original: "Anhang"; meaning a sect or a party of supporters.</note>, as Mr. Dr. Cyprian believes or intends, was proven as clear as day above in Part I, No. 63: thus Mr. Cyprian here speaks according to his own will.

(2) If one believes that those persons who perhaps wrote something before Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a Pietist historian whose "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" caused great controversy by treating "heretics" with sympathy.</note>, or might still write, were his students, such people might perhaps be too old for that, or might even have to protect themselves against such a concept. ### The 9th Accusation:

He has described the Christian Church in his History only according to its blemishes and defects, in order to inflame everyone to hatred against it.

### Answer:

(1) If someone reads this who does not know the true basis of the matter, they may well form a strange concept of the *Church History*. However, it has already been demonstrated in the *Reminders* Chapter 10, page 62 and following, that Mr. A. has also faithfully presented the good he found in the History regarding our church <note>The Lutheran Church.</note>, particularly concerning the work of the Reformation and the praise of Luther; the first simple way of divine service, the Lord's Supper, the beautiful hymns of Luther and his friends, and the like, of which entire accounts stand in the *Church History*.

(2) Therefore, he has described it not only according to its defects, but also according to its good: and consequently, he sought no hatred therein. For his conscience testifies to him—and no one will or can take this joy from him—that he did not intend this, but merely the recognition of historical truth.

(3) And how should Mr. A. have sought to inflame everyone to hatred against our church, since he himself has always remained unceasingly within it, taught, and by God's grace served everyone?

(4) But so that the reader may have at least some samples of how faithfully Mr. A. has written of Luther's cause and religion, only a little of it shall be excerpted from the *Church History*: then it will be clear as day that Mr. A. has acknowledged the good and the foundation of Christianity in no other religion as much as he praises and proves it in ours.

(5) In Volume XVI, Chapter 3, § 3, Mr. A. defends Luther against the accusations that he had advised against war for political reasons, and proves from Luther's own words that he founded his teaching on the essence of Christianity and the Gospel: likewise, that he condemned those evil affects of those who had a desire for weapons under the pretext of the Gospel. It is also observed there how Luther followed the clear will of God at that time,

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>209</page-num>
<header>Part II, No. 9. Accusations of Director Cyprian.</header>

and foretold all the unfortunate dealings, just as they actually followed afterward. And in § 5, Mr. A. says it could be that the dear man <note>Luther.</note> was over-deafened by the secular jurists and, through some intervening weaknesses, was led away from his previous pure mind, to which he had previously faithfully adhered when he was abandoned by everyone. And of the Lutheran theologians, he states in § 6: The good people had to suffer not only this after it had happened, but even much greater things.

(6) In the entire 5th Chapter of this book, the work of the Reformation is praised and defended in all circumstances. In No. 1 and following, much is written of the misery before Luther; in No. 7, of the hope and joy over the Reformation: In No. 11, this is written in detail regarding Luther’s teaching: Meanwhile, the blessed Luther retains the priority in this, that he publicly did the most, and first encouraged and led many others. — Among our writers, a direct inspiration, impulse, or divine reminder is particularly attributed to him, which is elaborated upon there. Furthermore, in § 17 it says: One finds an excellent image of a true Evangelical Christian and teacher in him in the first years, and according to the first foundation of Christian doctrine, in which he was full of power, and truly powerfully governed and used by God as a precious instrument of His grace: (which is explained from Seckendorff <note>Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff (1626–1692), author of a famous defense of Lutheranism.</note>.) First, it is manifest that God gifted him through His Spirit with a most precious knowledge of His true Gospel, which he was also able to present in a quite magnificent and penetrating way. — All the more was this divine gift to be highly esteemed in Luther, and all the more blessing and breakthrough did it give in the beginning. — One need only read his first writings, with what power and emphasis he exalts and praises Christ. Item <note>original: "Item" (Latin for "likewise").</note> § 18. So he also always pressed powerfully at that time for true sanctification, and showed the distinction thereof.

(7) Regarding Luther's life, Mr. A. testifies there as follows: He himself was also blameless in his life, so that even his enemies knew of nothing truthful to reproach him with, though they slandered and lied about him enough. (To which the confession of Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous humanist who famously disagreed with Luther but respected his character.</note> is added.) Furthermore, it is written of his many temptations, of his zealous, constant, and powerful prayer, and righteous exercises and struggles, of his humility, discipline <note>original: "Zuche," likely a misprint for "Zucht" (discipline/modesty).</note>, and lowly manner, modesty, etc.

# Clear Answers to Part II, No. 9.

(8) Furthermore, his **courage**, **heroic nature**, and how they were sanctified through Grace are praised with many examples; [as are] his **heroic faith** and his singular expressions and speeches, in which few could equal him. Likewise [noted are] his **openness** and **unfeigned integrity**, **patience** in the face of disgrace and insult, great and earnest **contentment**, contempt for earthly things, modesty, gentleness, and so on. Whereupon, following the truth, the subsequent changes are also noted, and finally, in section 33, it is lamented and shown that his good writings have remained so unknown and without use.

(9) Next to the praise of Luther’s person, the *Reformation* itself is further described in a laudatory manner in Chapter 6. For there it stands in section 1 how Luther used good and wholesome means for it, and taught the beginnings of Christianity, and how it was a matter of great earnestness for him to awaken the true fruits of the Gospel. It is said that a great movement and change of hearts arose in countless people, and among many, the "first love" <note>A biblical reference to the early, fervent faith of a believer or church, as in Revelation 2:4.</note> was still present.

(10) In the second number, it is shown how several of the first teachers immediately pressed for a change of life, how the people became visibly pious through this, and how scandals and vices were abolished. And particularly, a very beautiful description of the first purity is repeated from Biblicanus <note>Theobald Billicanus (c. 1493–1554), a German reformer.</note>. Along with this, in section 3 and following, the obstacles to the Reformation are specified, while also recounting the first visitations <note>original: "Visitationes"; official inspections of parishes to ensure proper doctrine and conduct</note> in Saxony and elsewhere one after another; just as in the following 7th Chapter, the Reformations throughout Germany and other parts of Europe <note>original: "Europæ"</note> [are described].

(11) In the 8th Chapter, the false accusations of the Papists <note>A common, though often derogatory, term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics.</note> against Luther are refuted, and conversely, the malice and vices of his enemies are shown. Attached to this, one finds a narrative of the cruel persecutions and the praise of the martyrs who suffered for the sake of the Gospel. In the 9th Chapter, however, the method of teaching after the Reformation is shown, namely how Luther truly demonstrated the beginning and foundation of true righteousness and salvation, and how people gradually departed from it. Especially many Lutheran teachers are praised and described there, such as Matthesius, Weller, Hausmann, Myconius, and others. In the 10th Chapter, the best schools of the Lutherans are sought out one after another, along with the deficiencies that followed them.

(12) In the 11th Chapter, the method of teaching and divine service is discussed; in sections 1 and 2, [it describes] how Luther especially began the catechism instruction <note>original: "Catechisation"</note> initially with great

<column-break/>

# Part II, No. 9, 10. Accusations of Director Cyprian. 211

zeal, gave all sorts of proposals for improvement, and made good arrangements through his diligence, so that the youth at that time understood more of God’s Word than many a Doctor in the Papacy. Indeed, [it shows] how he let nothing be lacking in himself for the instruction of the youth, and how his zeal provoked very many to diligence in this matter, and how such earnestness gradually grew cold, both in teaching and in divine service. Whereupon also, particularly in section 33 and following, the Lutheran hymns are recounted and praised, of which Luther says in his section 33: "It was a great and precious blessing from God for the instruction and encouragement of the weak." God gave him the songs with great power, concerning which the confessions of Scultetus <note>Abraham Scultetus (1566–1624), a German professor and theologian.</note> and others stand in section 35.

(13) These and many other upright confessions can convince <note>original: "convinciren"</note> anyone who doubts it that Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> described our church not only according to its defects, but also quite clearly according to its good qualities and virtues, especially those which it truly possessed at first. And even if, finally, the deep corruption of the church had been presented alone (which nonetheless did not happen), no more would have happened than what was witnessed of the Jewish people in Isaiah 1:5–6: *The whole head is sick, the whole heart is faint; from the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it, but only wounds and bruises, etc.*

### The 10th Accusation:

-> No clod-hopper, no boy who tends swine, could defend himself in a more fleshly, untamed, and tasteless manner with insults and abuse than Mr. A. and his Christian friends. <-
<note>The term "clod-hopper" (original: "Rasenwälzer") refers to a crude, unrefined, or uneducated person.</note>

### Answer:

(1) What was answered at that time by Mr. A. himself to the very harsh and dangerous accusations of Director Cyprian <note>original: "Hn. D. C."</note> with appropriate earnestness and the foundation of truth is clear as day in his *Explanation*: where not a single scolding word, branding of heresy, or the like—let alone tasteless abuse and insults—can be pointed out; much less the manner of clod-hoppers or swineherd-boys, as such things should happen to no one. Even if, in response to such a bitter treatment (which Director Cyprian almost admits himself, by posing the case that he might have hurt Arnold, and not exactly denying it), one or another expression escaped the author which should have been more Christian and gentle, he will gladly seek to improve such things, especially since such improvement does no harm to the matter itself.

(2) Regarding the attached reminder from a friend, however, it is not denied that it could have been more moderate in its manner of presentation; the Author <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> himself sincerely recognized this later after a private representation was made. But he also regretted that he had been provoked into it by the so-unjust outbursts of his opponent. If it were still at hand, he would have expressed himself <note>original: "expectoriret," from the Latin for clearing one's breast or speaking one's mind</note> sufficiently and publicly about it.

(3) But when Mr. D. C. <note>Director Cyprian</note> without proper distinction also mingles Mr. A. among the authors of a so-called <term>Pasquill</term> <note>A "Pasquill" or pasquinade is a satirical lampoon or libelous pamphlet intended to publicly shame someone.</note>, he sins too harshly against his neighbor. Mr. A. immediately, publicly, and quite clearly demonstrated his innocence in this matter in the Presentation Chapter 1, Section 1, and following, and in the Preface to the *Supplements* in the Post-Script, and further offered to prove it before any proper legal judgment. Moreover, he is in complete agreement with Mr. D. C. that one should not make libels against one's brother; likewise, that such things do not spring from a soul governed by the Holy Spirit. But he should also consider before God whether his own "Preliminary Report" was composed according to the Rule of Christ, as he demands of others.

(4) If, after some time—when the first heat of anger might have subsided—he were to consider his first expressions and accusations against Mr. A. with a quiet mind and impartially before God, he would see in all truth (if he were willing to know himself) that he did not allow the gentle and humble spirit of Jesus Christ to govern him at that time. Instead, he uttered mostly worse and more dangerous things in that "Preliminary Report" against his neighbor than many a libel or defamatory writing contains. However, just as Mr. A. forgave him long ago and has proven his patience through suffering and silence until now, so it is hoped that the resentment in Mr. D. C. has also softened, and that he has allowed more room in his heart for true love, which thinks no evil.

### The 11th Accusation:
#### From the short Preliminary Report on A.’s Religion.

Since the so-called "Preliminary Report on A.’s Religion" has long since collapsed of its own accord—inasmuch as Mr. A. remains, as before, a member and preacher in the Lutheran religion—the formal refutation of the Report regarding personal matters <note>original: "quoad personalia"</note> would be superfluous and in vain. Therefore, only the specific articles upon which the entire report rests shall be examined one after another. For if these are found to be incorrect, the report built upon them cannot stand; which, in any case, is not orderly

composed or—as it should be in such an important matter—thoroughly drafted, as one always falls from one thing to another and nowhere presents a binding demonstration.

### The 12th Accusation: p. 7.

> He has, through his *K. H.* <note>The "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" or "History of the Church and Heretics."</note>, given cause for Christ to be shown the door, and has dragged His necessary knowledge through the mud under the name of <term>brain-formulas</term> <note>Arnold used the term "Hirn-Formeln" to criticize those who held to intellectual dogmas without experiencing a living, spiritual faith.</note>, and indeed has turned the entire Christian religion into nothing but a mockery and a laughingstock.

#### Answer:

(1) If all these horrors that Mr. Cypr. <note>Cyprian</note> names here (for they truly are horrors) had not appeared earlier, and even more frequently and horribly, than after the publication of this book, then one would have to believe this terrible accusation. But since the opposite is known from all histories, the book remains free from such an accusation.

(2) That Mr. A., in his writings and also in the *K. H.*, promoted the living knowledge of Jesus Christ most of all and most zealously—indeed, wishing to know nothing but Jesus Christ, and never showing Christ the door (as such a precious Savior, whom God has graciously allowed the Author to know)—this, anyone can see and conclude from almost every passage. No one will believe the opposite unless they have not looked into his books or read them with a Christian heart.

(3) And oh, that the Lord Jesus were not shown the door in His gentleness by all such very harsh contradictions, and that He were not so branded as a heretic, reviled, and persecuted in His true members! Therefore, it is rightly said: they think they are doing God a service because they know neither Jesus nor His Father in a living and powerful way (or in any way other than literally).

(4) Mr. A. has also nowhere dragged the necessary knowledge of Jesus Christ through the mud under the name of "brain-formulas," but knows well how to distinguish the former from the latter. Indeed, he has suffered the most for this until now: for distinguishing human statutes from Divine truths, and for commending the pure knowledge of Jesus Christ from the Scriptures to all people instead of human commandments and teachings.

(5) Finally, that no mockery was made of the Christian religion, nor any cause given to others to do so, was proven above in this part under Number 1.

### The 13th Accusation: p. 8.

He has defended almost every heresy.

### Answer:

Dr. Bebel <note>original: "D. Beiel," referring to Balthasar Bebel, a Lutheran theologian</note> wrote formerly that Mr. A. had spoken in favor of all heretics; Mr. Cyprian, however, puts it somewhat more modestly and cautiously, saying he defends almost all heresies: the former speaks only of the heretics and persons, the latter of the heresies themselves. That neither is actually the case has been strengthened—praise God!—above in Part I, Numbers 2, 13, 17, 27, 104, 107, and 148, as well as in other writings cited there; and the distinction has been shown between certain historical remarks on the stories of heretics and the defense of manifest errors. In particular, the passage by Luther <note>original: "Locus Lutheri"</note> in the 13th number of the first part is quite notable, wherein it is observed that the Fathers <note>original: "Patres," the early Church Fathers</note> in the struggle against Arius, Manichaeus, and the like, twisted the Scriptures and did not remain on the right path, etc. <note>Arnold's point is that even Martin Luther admitted the early Church's "Orthodox" defenders sometimes used poor arguments against heretics like Arius.</note>

### The 14th Accusation:

->A. and his friends have the foulest knowledge of God, and they receive the most detestable heretics as brothers in Christ.<-

### Answer:

(1) If Mr. A. were to receive a single (in deed and truth) detestable—let alone the most detestable—heretic as a brother in Christ, then he would indeed have the foulest knowledge of God. Although this expression <note>"foulest knowledge"</note> is not even customary in the Church, but rather flowed from a heated and over-hasty mind, as they did not know how to express it excessively enough.

(2) But since it was shown so very clearly above in Part I, Numbers 2, 13, 17, 27, 104, and 107, that Mr. A. neither receives anyone actually so-called a heretic, nor much less considers them a brother in Christ: thus everyone sees the precipitancy of this judgment. And truly, he who would wish to attribute a foul—let alone the foulest—knowledge of God to Mr. A. based on his testimonies would have to be blinded.

(3) Many hundreds, even thousands of readers and listeners give the Author a different testimony, and know that the pure and good Spirit of God has governed and still governs him in his writings, which serve for edification and purification. This testimony will not be taken from him by human and indeed perverse judgment. But every one among us all has to see to it that he does not rail against as "foulness and filth" that which has been drawn from a pure source. And this should be taken to heart all the more, the more one rejects the knowledge itself, and not just the person.

### The 15th Accusation: p. 8.

->He goes about everywhere intending (a) to make the love for true religion, and the regulations established for its preservation, appear abominable and to describe them as such.<-

### Answer:

(1) Mr. A. does not deny that he has wished to make abominable the abuse, the mere knowledge without deed and power, the coercion of conscience in spiritual things, and other such manifest excesses, as are practiced under the name of religion by Papists <note>A term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics</note> and others.

(2) But the right love for true religion ordained by God, and the Christian regulations established for its preservation according to the Gospel, he holds at all times high and dear, as is known to the living God and his authorities <note>original: "Obrigkeit"</note>; never, however, has he wished or been able to make such things abominable to anyone, as dear as his salvation and the common welfare have been to him. But alas! that one had not, on the other hand, sought to make one's innocent neighbor abominable and hated through precisely such accusations! See the *Upright Remarks*, Chapter IV, page 450 and following.

### The 16th Accusation: p. 9.

->(b) That he presented the most important religious disputes as trifles—<-

### Answer:

(1) Because this is a general accusation without specific proof, it also requires no specific answer. Mr. A. has noted and rejected the actual and important errors with great earnestness in his writings. God indeed knows his heart; his listeners and others, who indeed know well what religion is, also give him the testimony of how far removed he is from all unsound doctrines which are contrary to the pattern of the salutary Apostolic teaching.

(2) Whatever Dr. C. <note>Cyprian</note> will specifically cite as proof from such points shall be answered quite clearly and thoroughly, as the evidence will show.

### The 17th Accusation: p. 9.

->It is false that at the Council of the Apostles <note>The Council of Jerusalem described in Acts 15</note> one did not ask so much what one should think, speak, and claim—as what one should do and leave undone.<-

<header>Clear Answers to Vol. II, Nos. 17, 18.</header>

->Answer:<-

(1) Firstly, Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a Pietist historian famous for his "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics."</note> speaks deliberately; it was not so much "opinions" that were being questioned: and thus he does not exclude speeches and opinions, but rather includes them; as it is indeed written in Acts 15:24, that the Apostles had examined this speech.

(2) However, he proves from this very history that the question was primarily about *practice*, or about "doing and refraining," which the clear history provides, in that the decision <note>The "Decisum" or Apostolic Decree from the Council of Jerusalem.</note> also aimed primarily at certain practical matters.

(3) By no means, however, did Mr. A. intend to disparage the efforts for pure doctrine; rather, he only wished to show how one should not rest in mere theory without practice. Therefore, his conclusion cited there from Part I, p. 45 remains correct, which Dr. Zierold, Director Lange, and others have hitherto demonstrated in detail.

### The 18th Accusation: p. 9.

He calls the doctrine of the Nicolaitans <note>An early Christian sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, accused by early Church Fathers of promoting licentiousness.</note> a "war of words," and thus makes the Holy Spirit a "word-warrior."

->Answer:<-

(1) I ask that Mr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a leading opponent of Pietism.</note> reflect more carefully, whether he has not also here overextended himself out of fierce zeal and concluded from Mr. A.'s words—according to his own prejudices—what he should not have concluded, nor ever could. What creature would want to take such damnation upon himself and make the Holy Spirit himself a "word-warrior," whether it be done directly or indirectly? And what has Mr. A. lamented more than the wars of words, which—alas!—still have no end? Has not the Holy Spirit himself condemned these in 1 Timothy 6:4? Who then would attribute such things to Him without blasphemy?

(2) Mr. A.'s words in the cited Vol. I, Book 4, Chapter 14, § 14 read as follows: It is notable that not so much their propositions and <note>original: "NB." for "nota bene" or "Note Well"</note> **wars of words** are mentioned, as their *works*, which one <note>original: "NB."</note> should *hate*: Inasmuch as God in His judgment does not look upon the former so much as the latter; for which reason He (namely, the Holy Spirit) does not command one to dispute with them for a long time, but only to hate their works. Thereupon Mr. A. recounts their works, namely fornication, etc. Here, the summary stands in the margin: <margin>regarding their godlessness.</margin>

(3) Here let the reader judge whether Mr. A. attributed the "wars of words" to the Nicolaitans or to the Holy Spirit, and whether he has blas-

<header>Vol. II, Nos. 18, 19. Accusations of Director Cyprian.</header>

phemously made the Holy Spirit a word-warrior? He will recognize and admit, along with all reasonable readers, that it is one thing to call the doctrine of the Nicolaitans themselves "wars of words," or rather to say that the Holy Spirit does not mention their wars of words (which are Mr. A.'s clear words); and quite another to accuse the Holy Spirit of being a word-warrior or of having started a war of words. Mr. A. indeed confesses the godlessness of the Nicolaitans; he also does not deny their doctrines, that they possessed such; but he only shows from the clear expression of Scripture, which speaks of their works, that one must look primarily at the life, and not solely or merely at the doctrine; and he has thus indicated an entirely blameless sense in this matter: of which more shall be brought forward below in the 55th accusation.

Similar examples are notorious regarding Dr. Balthasar Meisner, Johann Arndt, and other theologians.

### The 20th Accusation: p. 10.

> He makes the disputes with the <term>Socinians</term> <note>A non-trinitarian sect that denied the full divinity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> so insignificant that one should almost consider them a metaphysical war of words. ->Answer:<-

(1) Regarding the ancient <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius who believed Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, the orthodox and honest Salvianus once judged thus in Book V of *On the Governance of God*, pages 162, 163: They were *heretics, but not knowingly; among us, he says, they are heretics, but among themselves they are not. <note>original: "Hæretici ergo ſunt, ſed non ſcientes. Denique apud nos ſunt hæretici, apud ſe non ſunt."</note> --- Therefore they err, but they err with a good heart, not out of hatred, but out of a love for God, believing they honor and love the Lord. Although they do not have the right faith, they nevertheless consider this to be the perfect love of God. How they are to be punished for this very error of false opinion on the day of judgment, no one can know except the Judge. In the meantime, God grants them patience, as I believe, because He sees that even if they do not believe correctly, they nonetheless err with a pious affection; especially since He knows that they do those things which they do not know, while our people neglect what they believe; and through this, those [the heretics] sin through the fault of their teachers, while ours sin through their own; those are ignorant, ours are knowing; those do what they think is right, ours do what they know to be perverse, etc.* <note>Arnold is using this long quote from the 5th-century writer Salvian to show that even "orthodox" fathers recognized that some heretics were sincere in their search for God.</note> In the event that someone should make this confession in our times, he would certainly be suspected of a secret <term>collusion</term> <note>A secret cooperation or conspiracy.</note> with such erring people. And how many would want to prove their zeal against it! Now, however, since *Mr. A.* has publicly demonstrated his disagreement with the Arians in the manner indicated, one should fairly interpret his words as Christianly as one interprets those of Salvianus, which are set down according to general love, rather than according to the angry, partisan sense of the natural man, and which harmonize quite well with *Mr. A.'s* words.

(2) The proof of this important accusation is now said to be this: because *Mr. A.* writes that they [the Arians/Socinians] had mostly stumbled over the <term>Scholastic Terms</term> <note>Technical philosophical language used in academic theology, which Arnold felt obscured the simple truth of the Bible.</note> and desired rather to speak with the Scripture.

(3) From the very first preface of the <term>History of the Church and Heretics</term> <note>Arnold’s most famous work, the "Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie."</note>, Dr. Cyprian could have immediately seen how earnestly *Mr. A.* had testified against the Arian and Socinian errors. (2) Mr. Arnold speaks in the cited passage in Book I, Chapter 5, Section 8, regarding the very first Christians or the immediate disciples of Christ and his Apostles, who thus knew nothing of the disputes that followed later. (4) Now the question arises: Whether such people, who want to measure the Godhead according to reason and philosophy with technical terms, are Catholic Christians (in the proper sense of that word), or whether it was not much more the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine, often criticized by later reformers for over-complicating faith.</note> with their shallow questions and word-wars? (5) For our own theologians also do not approve of the hair-splitting philosophical questions of the Scholastics, for example: <note>original: "An Filius DEI procedat è Patris intellectu, Spiritus S. è voluntate?"</note> *Whether the Son of GOD proceeds from the Father's intellect, and the Holy Spirit from the will?* and more of the like, which clearly conflict with the divine simplicity and purity of true faith. And the above words are certainly aimed primarily at these, speaking quite clearly of philosophical whims and technical terms. Just as <term>Erasmus</term> <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance humanist.</note> clearly confesses in the Preface to <term>Hilarius</term> <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers.</note>: <note>original: "Doctrina Christi, quæ prius nesciebat λογομαχίαν, cœpit à Philosophiæ præsidiis dependere. Item : ad sophisticas contentiones articulorum myriades proruperunt."</note> *The doctrine of Christ, which previously knew no word-battling <note>original: "λογομαχίαν" (logomachia)</note>, began to depend on the supports of philosophy. Also: myriads of articles broke out into sophisticated contentions.*
