## The 26th Accusation: p. 13.

->He allegedly clears the Arians of all heresy.<-

### Answer:

(1) That this is false can be judged from Mr. Arnold's own words in Book IV, Chapter 8. In the history of the <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> itself, he says in Section 18 regarding both the Arians and their opponents: Both parties had deviated from the first simplicity of faith and had brought forth mere opinions, empty propositions, technical terms, and shallow questions instead of active Christianity. And in Section 20: No community could truthfully boast of holy and pure doctrine—therefore they also walked in nothing but uncertainty and error. Again, in Section 21: Reason with all its inventions in divine things was put to shame among the Arians; likewise: they were slaves of reason. Indeed, in Book VII, Chapter 2, Section 5, Mr. Arnold explicitly and seriously calls them heretics, etc.

(2) Instead of Mr. Arnold clearing the Arians of heresy—and of *all* heresy, and doing so *openly*—he expressly and seriously accuses them of errors, mere opinions, empty propositions, slavery to reason, heresies, and the like; as he also testifies very seriously in the first preface of the *K. H.* <note>The *Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (History of the Church and Heretics), Arnold's most famous work.</note> against the errors of the Arians and <term>Socinians</term> <note>A non-trinitarian sect that denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note>. Where then does this claim of the accuser remain? May GOD forgive him for this as well!

(3) However, why Mr. Arnold also had to impartially touch upon the faults of the Orthodox in this history, and in what manner the most important points against the Arians emerged from his history, can be seen in the *Supplements*, pages 110 and 111.

He defames the three main Creeds because they present the Trinity. Page 14.

### Answer:

(1) From the previous counter-proof and from many other extensive confessions, it is clear that Mr. Arnold believes in and worships the Holy Trinity; thus, he cannot possibly defame the three <term>Creeds</term> <note>The Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds, referred to by the Latin "Symbola."</note> for that reason.

(2) He defames or slanders them as little as other historians who perhaps call into question their authors or other circumstances—for example, whether the Apostles' Creed was made by the Apostles, and the Athanasian by <term>Athanasius</term>.

(3) Mr. Arnold also had no reason to defame such <term>Creeds</term> because this precious teaching of the Holy Trinity was not first established in these <term>Creeds</term>, but is written so deeply by the Holy Spirit into his heart that he also joyfully bears such evil accusations over it, and knows in whom he believes. Let another see to it whom he perhaps defames and slanders in Christ's members, whom he does not recognize!

(4) What Dr. C. <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian, the "Director" and Arnold's chief critic.</note> judges regarding the book called *<term>Sophia</term>* <note>Referring to Arnold's "Göttliche Sophia" or "Divine Wisdom," a central concept in his mystical theology.</note> has been thoroughly examined above in Vol. I, Numbers 69 to 75.

(5) That Mr. Arnold did not deceitfully omit the most powerful testimonies of Christ's divinity, as he is accused, has been demonstrated thus far, especially in Number 28.

(2) Mr. A. <note>Referring to Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a German Pietist historian.</note> certainly regards the **Scripture** as **God’s** Word, by which everyone must examine themselves to see if they avoid the evil suspicions and other sins against their neighbor forbidden therein. But whoever does not believe this may well take or explain the words of even the most innocent writer differently, and thereby only sin all the more, despite all appeals to Scripture.

(4) Thus, there is no need here for violent contradiction or scolding over such a holy matter; rather, we all only need to practice the teaching of **Jesus** Christ ever more from Christ’s word, and to demonstrate more love and gentleness even in such disagreements according to this rule: which the **Lord Jesus** grant to us all!

(5) Meanwhile, let Mr. D. C. <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a Lutheran orthodox theologian and Arnold's primary critic.</note> be assured that Mr. A. has never grown weary of the Bible, but certainly has of all those other human books, and most of all of those that defend their supposed pure doctrine with nothing but pride, violence, and worldly cleverness. He also does not test the Scripture according to his imagination, but only wishes that everyone might first recognize their own imagination, where it appears most plausible and righteous, and wishes to fall upon its neighbor by twisting his innocent words.

### Answer:

### The 32nd Accusation:

# The 33rd Accusation:
->That he does not speak the truth / in saying that the first Christians held the Lord's Supper daily during their meals.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) This was proven long ago in the second book of the *Portrait of the First Christians*, <note>Gottfried Arnold's seminal work, *Abbildung der ersten Christen* (1696).</note> in Chapter 15, § 10 and following; that evidence will carry more weight than a mere contradiction without any proof.

(2) And although no one would suggest that absolutely every single Christian held Communion at every single meal, it is sufficient that daily Communion was maintained in the Church for a long time. Mr. Cave himself—whom Mr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), the primary Lutheran critic of Arnold.</note> would surely accept—proves this thoroughly, as can be read in German in his *Primitive Christianity*, page 354, where he cites Cyprian, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine on this matter. He specifically notes that this remained for some time as a sign of the early Christians' devotion and fear of God. One could also produce many other Church Fathers who testify to this, as well as modern historians like Spanheim, Leidecker, and others, if it were necessary in such an obvious matter. Others, especially Catholic writers, are included in the appendix to Molinos's booklet. <note>Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696), a Spanish mystic whose "Quietist" teachings were influential and controversial.</note>

(3) Our own theologians also partially approve of this; for example, Stephanus Prætorius, who comes to mind just now, writes in his *Book of the Lamb of God*, page 580: "We read that the first Christians, who were so fiery and wished to burn with zeal for Christianity, took the Lord's Supper every day after hearing the Word." --- It is said: *as often as* <note>original: "quotiescunque"</note>, yes, even daily, one should use the Sacrament, and so forth.

(4) Since Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714).</note> praises daily Communion as something good, he certainly does not despise or reject this institution of Christ. Rather, his other words must be understood as referring to the harmful abuses, coercion, and other creeping disorders that conflict with the original purity of the practice.

(5) Mr. A. wrote so extensively about the main purpose of the Holy Supper in the aforementioned 15th chapter that his pure intentions can be clearly seen. And when he regards it as idolatrous and superstitious if one uses it like a **panacea** <note>original: "Panaceam"; a cure-all or universal remedy.</note>, he certainly means the abuse of the **work performed** <note>original: "Operis operati"; the theological idea that a sacrament is effective simply by being performed, regardless of the recipient's faith.</note>, where people imagine that the external act helps with everything, and that no further struggle

<column-break/>

or other exercises of faith are required; which terrible error is, alas, common and has even been noted by Mr. Dr. Cyprian himself.

(6) And when Mr. A. complains that idolatry and **Capernaism** <note>original: "Capernaismus"; a term derived from John 6, referring to a "fleshly" or literalistic misunderstanding of eating Christ's body, as the people of Capernaum did.</note> prevail among the Orthodox, while Mr. Dr. Cyprian **objects** <note>original: "excipirt"</note> that such people are not truly orthodox, Arnold certainly only meant those who lack a better understanding and do not demonstrate a holy life of love. Therefore, he does not write about *all* the Orthodox, but only about "as many as it happens among," that is, the many who merely call themselves such. May God grant that such a life of love be better recognized in the future and no longer be hindered by such violent zeal!

# The 34th Accusation:
->That he wants our churches torn down. p. 22.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) That Mr. A. never testified against the **churches themselves**, but only against their abuse, could have been seen in abundance throughout his *Clarification*, especially on pages 17, 18, 21, 33, and 43, where his innocence in this regard is demonstrated. To say nothing of what was later noted in the *Supplements*, page 8, regarding how he never rejects such things **absolutely** <note>original: "absolute"</note> or in practice, outside of the historical context.

(2) As proof, it is cited that Mr. A. calls the words of **Peter of Bruys** <note>A 12th-century French reformer who rejected the physical church building and the veneration of the cross.</note> regarding the tearing down of churches a "glorious testimony" in Book XII, Chapter 5, § 11. However, first of all, that passage speaks purely of the Papal abuse, extravagance, and pomp of the churches, which was so detestable in those wretched times that many witnesses of the truth, in their zeal, considered it better that such churches did not exist at all than that such abominations be practiced within them. In this matter, however, he had to suffer the same judgment as Arnold, just as Stephen experienced in *Acts of the Apostles VII, 54 and following.*

(3) Furthermore, this accusation against Mr. A. is invalid because other Protestants have also regarded these testimonies of **Peter** as good, and held him to be a pious man. For it says, among other places, in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, Book XV, page 561: "Peter and Henry were not unlearned men, nor (Note Well) alien to piety. Since with a certain keen judgment they recognized the superstitions in temples built with greatest expense beyond all necessity: they criticized certain false opinions and some abuses." <note>original Latin: "Fuerunt Petrus & Henricus homines non indocti, neque NB. à pietate alieni. Quum sagaci quodam judicio cognoscerent superstitiones in templis præter omnem necessitatem maximis sumtibus ædificandis: falsas opiniones & abusus non nullos taxarunt."</note> And afterwards, the author explains this very testimony quite appropriately on page 562, Number 7.

### The 37th Accusation:

> He shames and slanders all the Creeds <note>term: Symbola (Creeds). These are the formal statements of faith adopted by various church bodies, such as the Nicene or Augsburg Confessions.</note> that are held in the Empire, whether they be called the Nicene, Athanasian, Tridentine, Dortian, or Augustan, and especially the binding commitment made upon them. p. 23.

->Answer:<-

(1) Because Mr. Dr. C. <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a staunch Lutheran Orthodox opponent of Arnold.</note> mixes everything together here and places the most contrary Creeds side-by-side, forming a single general accusation from them, one must answer with proper distinction.

(2) Many might wonder why he, as a Lutheran, complains or accuses Mr. A. of shaming and slandering the Tridentine Creed <note>The "Symbolum Tridentinum," the statement of faith from the Roman Catholic Council of Trent.</note>; since so many famous theologians from our own and the Reformed Church have so laboriously and earnestly demonstrated its horrors and wickedness. He can surely never accuse them of having "shamed" the so-called Tridentine Creed, even though they have testified a thousand times more against it than was done in the *K. H.* <note>Arnold’s "Unparteyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (Impartial History of the Church and Heretics).</note>.

(3) Furthermore, Mr. Dr. C. has elsewhere accused the author of flattering the Reformed, writing of them with great devotion, etc. But here, he claims the author has shamed their Creed of Dort <note>The "Symbolum Dortrectanum," the confession of the Reformed Synod of Dordrecht (1618–1619).</note>. Let everyone judge for themselves, without much prompting, whether these are impartial judgments, and whether there has not been an attempt to make the author hated by both Catholics and the Reformed? Conscience itself will give the verdict on whether one has fought purely for God’s honor when one tries to present the discovery of so many errors and practices in the Tridentine Creed as mere "slanders."

(4) Regarding the Creeds chosen by our own people <note>The Lutheran confessions, such as the Augsburg Confession (Augustanum).</note>, the author considers them very valuable and good insofar as they agree with God's Word. However, insofar as they are not the immediate Word of God given by the Holy Spirit,
<meta>catchword: given</meta>

<column-break/>

given, but originate from men, he—at that time acting as a historian—necessarily had to recount the human circumstances that occurred during the establishment of such Creeds. He particularly had to point out, following Vossius <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar who used historical criticism to examine the origins of the creeds.</note> and many other scholars, that the so-called Apostles' and Athanasian Creeds do not actually have the Apostles or Athanasius as their authors.

(5) But as for the claim that he shamed and slandered the Creeds—and indeed all of them—Mr. Dr. C. provides no proof, and thus Mr. A. remains free from such an unproven charge. The reader can see the opposite, for example regarding the Nicene Creed, in the *Supplements* page 106 and following.

### The 38th Accusation:

234 Clear Answers to Vol. II, Nos. 39, 40.

### Answer:

(1) What Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the radical Pietist historian being defended here.</note> has made known and lamented regarding this, he did not do with his own words, but rather from the clear complaints of Lutheran teachers, of whom he cites a great many in that place.

(2) However, he speaks deliberately regarding the **action** or **act** <note>original: "Actu"</note> and thus regarding the circumstances or celebration of the Lord’s Supper, and not regarding the Lord’s Supper itself. He considers the sacrament in itself to be good and unobjectionable, since Christ Himself instituted it. But regarding the action, or the **manner** <note>original: "Modo"</note> and **act**, as it is commonly celebrated, he says nothing more than what Lutheran teachers have long since said.

(3) Thus, a preacher from Lübeck, Lubertus, says in the booklet *Regarding the Ban*, Chapter 8, § 4, page 74, without exception: "With the external Lord’s Supper, among the great multitude, it is nothing but shadow-boxing." <note>The German "Spiegelfechten" implies a sham or a hollow, deceptive performance.</note> Brunnemannus, the famous jurist, <note>Johann Brunnemann (1608–1672), a prominent legal scholar.</note> says in *Ecclesiastical Law*, page 139, that the sacrament is "shamefully prostituted." Egardus writes in *Princely Right*, p. 38, that it is "pure hypocrisy and flattery." ### The 40th Accusation:

He calls our church a "corrupt heap," shaming and slandering it so that all the Jesuits together could not make it worse, etc. p. 23.

### Answer:

Mr. A. has never lamented the common corruption in any other way than with the words of our own teachers themselves; he has also said no more—in fact, much less—than those said long before him. And if one considers in the fear of God what actually constitutes "shaming and slandering" according to the sense of the Holy Spirit, and whether this can be said of a well-meaning Christian historian, then one will not so easily attack the witnesses of truth with such accusations (who speak for the sake of improvement, and not, like the Jesuits, for the destruction of the community).

### The 45th Accusation:

**A. <note>Arnold</note> defames our Church so cruelly that one could hardly defame the Turkish <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire or Islam, often used in this period as a benchmark for "infidelity."</note> one more; therefore, he is partisan. p. 97.**

On the other hand, it is obvious that Dr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a prominent orthodox Lutheran theologian and critic of Arnold.</note> has judged more from the index, as was shown in the preface regarding this matter.

(2) Therefore, this accusation is too harsh and excessive. α) That he defamed the Church: For defaming and exposing corruption for the sake of improvement based on the Church's own confessions are as different as heaven and earth. β) That one could hardly do the same to the Turkish one. And what do the books of Fritsch, Lubbertus, and others concerning the "Christianity and Lutheranism shamed by Turks and Heathens" aim at, if not such salutary testimonies? One does not defame a community whose improvement one faithfully seeks.

(3) GOD knows with what heartache and mercy all such presentations were made, and how Dr. Cyprian read them in a completely different sense than they were written. One may read further on this in Arnold’s *Explanation* p. 39 and the *Representation* p. 24 and following. He <note>Cyprian</note> shows himself far too partisan in his judgments, and thus it is impossible for him to judge whether such testimonies are partisan or not: since it does not depend on partisan decrees.

### The 46th Accusation:

### The 48th Accusation:
->That he had almost nothing good to say of those who hold the Symbolic Books <note>original: "Libros Symbolicos"—referring to the official confessional documents of the Lutheran Church, such as the Book of Concord</note>; but of their adversaries, he wrote almost nothing bad. p.<-

### Answer:
(1) In his first writing, Dr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a staunch defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy</note> placed this in the summaries of Chapter VII, Section 3: "A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> has not written a single word in favor of our Church." Here, however, after he found the opposite to be true, he limited his statement, saying: "almost nothing good was written."

(2) It has already been demonstrated many times how much good and laudable material Mr. Arnold has recorded regarding Luther's teachings and his true followers, and how much evil, by contrast, he noted regarding other parties in accordance with the truth. To repeat all such passages would be superfluous; anyone can find them for themselves, as they have already been noted above in Number 9 and in Volume I, Number 3.

---

### The 49th Accusation.
->When Arnold tells the history of the Arminians <note>A theological movement following Jacobus Arminius that disagreed with Calvinist views on predestination</note>, he suggests they had "troubled no water" <note>An idiom meaning they were entirely innocent or did no harm</note>.<-

### Answer:
(1) In that very history, in the 8th Chapter of the 17th Book, Section 5, it is shown how the agreement of the Arminians with our Church regarding the point of the election of grace <note>The doctrine of predestination</note> was well received by Calovius, Tarnovius, and others. Meanwhile, in the same place (Section 15), the excessive curiosity in divine matters <note>original: "curiosität in divinis"</note> of Conrad Vorstius, an Arminian, was rebuked, and in Section 26, the decline of their initial fervor was noted among all of them.

(2) Concerning Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, one of the most prominent Arminians, Mr. Arnold candidly confesses this in Volume IV, Section 3, Number 7, page 482: His sharp reason, led astray by political intentions, moved him to attribute or concede more to the Papacy than might be proper or even healthy according to the pure sense of the Gospel. Thus, the deviations of these people are likewise noted—how they troubled the pure water of Christian doctrine—and from this, Mr. Arnold's partiality cannot be proven.

### Answer:
(1) That Mr. Arnold neither accepts the Socinians himself, nor accepts those who treat them as brothers, Dr. Cyprian could well have seen from the first preface of the *History of the Church* <note>Arnold's "Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie"</note>, Section 54. For there, the author publicly and in the strongest terms protests against anyone drawing an adverse conclusion or approving of the objectionable teachings of the Arminians and Socinians themselves. And again: therefore the author can never have fellowship with any rationalizer <note>original: "Vernünffteling"—Arnold's derogatory term for those who used human reason to challenge divine mysteries, specifically Socinians</note>, but instead commends such blind and poor souls to the eternal light. More can be recognized from the preface to Alixius's treatise on the judgment of the Jewish Church concerning the Holy Trinity.

(2) Regarding the Anabaptists, the same was clearly substantiated above in the 23rd Accusation of Volume I: how he recorded their errors. Not to mention what is noted below in Number 60 from Capito and Beza, how these men, with good distinction, were not ashamed to call the erring ones "dearest brothers" in a certain sense, which Mr. Arnold never did in his entire life. Thus, this mocking accusation remains powerless.

(2) β) Nor is there any lack of other testimonies from Lutherans that Peucer was <term>treated</term> <note>original: "tractiret"</note> too harshly (for that is the only question here, not his doctrine). (3) Furthermore, γ) that Peucer supposedly wanted to write his history out of self-love, or actually did so, would be very difficult to prove. (6) Yes, our late Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation</note> likewise acknowledges this "short and well" in the first part of the *Church Postil* <note>original: "Kirchen-Postill," a collection of sermons for the church year</note> on the first Sunday of Advent, p. 88. Where life is not good, it is nonetheless strange for one to preach rightly; he must always preach against himself, which he rarely does without a <note>NB: Latin *nota bene*, "note well"</note> addition and secondary doctrine. Now, if this is the true confession of our teachers—that evil works are the ground, beginning, and purpose of evil doctrine, indeed that all heresies have arisen from preceding godlessness—then in the opposition against heretics, one must not reflect so much or primarily and first upon their doctrine as upon their works. Just as one must turn away a harmful river not so much and primarily by hindering its course, but by plugging the source itself. This is what A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> intended to say here.

(7) Above all, others also specifically agree in the interpretation of this scriptural passage, that the works of these heretics are primarily targeted. Among the ancients, these are the words of Primatius <note>A 6th-century North African bishop and commentator</note> (whose commentary on the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> was already recommended by Cassiodorus) concerning the 15th verse on the doctrine of Balaam, p. m. 292: "These two are the principal things for whose enjoyment hypocrites contend: eating and fornicating, just as the Lord says: Inside you are full of greed, incontinence, and all iniquity." <note>original: "Hæc duo sunt principalia, quibus fruendis hypocritæ militant, edere & fornicari, sicut Dominus dicit: Intus estis rapina & incontinentia & omni iniquitate pleni"</note> Since he considers the works to be the most prominent thing in the doctrine of Balaam and all hypocrites, into which their doctrine ultimately resolves. Andreas of Caesarea <note>A 6th-century Greek bishop</note> observes in his commentary on this passage, Chapter III, how souls are seduced from one evil deed to another. Balaam seduced Israel through harlotry to idolatry, as an image of Satan, whom he calls "mystical Balaam" <note>original: "βαλὰαμ μυσικὸν"</note>, which he thereafter applies in the same sense to the sectarians. Thereupon he paraphrases Chapter VI, verses 24 and 25, thus: (from the version of Peltanus) "I will not demand from you (the simpler ones) a battle of words, but only a faithful keeping of the doctrine you have received, until I finally take you from here to myself." <note>original: "non exigam à vobis (simplicioribus) pugnam verborum, sed fidam tantùm doctrinæ, quam accepistis, custodiam, donec tandem vos hinc ad me assumsero"</note>

(8.) Among our own interpreters, Dr. Johannes Winkelmann describes this heresy in his commentary on the Apocalypse, p. 60: "that they abused the deed of Nicolas to establish carnal license, and committed fornication impudently and profusely." <note>original: "quod facto Nicolai abusi sint ad licentiam carnis stabiliendam, & impudenter effusèque fornicati sint"</note> He cites Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Church Father</note> from Book I, Chapter 27. This author, however, first says of the Nicolaitans: "They live without discretion;" <note>original: "Indiscretè vivunt"</note> only after describing their life does he describe their doctrine: "Teaching that there is no difference in committing adultery and eating things sacrificed to idols." <note>original: "Docentes in moechando & idolothyto comedendo nullam esse differentiam"</note> Kromayer, in his commentary on this passage, p. 68, likewise writes that this "doctrine of Balaam" and heresy consisted in this: "that just as he [Balaam], when he was forbidden to speak evil, by clever counsel enticed the Israelites to physical and spiritual fornication—that is, idolatry—through the Moabites: so they held harlotry, otherwise most common among the nations, and the eating of idol-sacrifices as indifferent <meta>catchword: things</meta>

things, and thus contaminated themselves and others with physical and spiritual fornication." <note>original: "ut hic Israelitas, cum prohibitus fuisset male dicere, callido consilio ad fornicationem corporalem & spiritualem h. e. idololatriam per Moabitas pellexit: ita illi scortationem aliàs inter gentes usitatissimam & esum idolothytarum pro rebus indifferentibus habebant, & sic fornicatione corporali & spirituali se & alios contaminabant"</note> All this he thereafter collectively calls "error" and "mistakes" <note>original: "errorem" and "errata"</note>, and draws from it on p. 61 this "inference" <note>original: "porisma"</note>: "Scandals in faith and life must be confronted, etc." <note>original: "Scandalis in fide & vita occurrendum esse, &c."</note>

(9.) Most ancients also aim at this in their description of this heresy: that Nicolaus <note>Nicolas the Deacon, traditionally (though perhaps inaccurately) associated with the Nicolaitans</note> supposedly wanted to make his wife common property, and therefore devised this tenet, in which others followed him with their "practice." <note>original: "praxi"</note>

Furthermore, A. <note>Arnold</note> has nowhere denied that the Nicolaitans' heresy did not also consist in doctrine, nor has he presented it as a mere "strife of words" <note>original: "Wort-Gezäncke"</note>, as we saw above in number 18. Rather, following the guidance of the aforementioned teachers, he only observed that the Revelation primarily rebukes their works as the evil source of their false doctrine.

### The 56th Accusation.

->He ascribes to the liking of heretics—even people still living—that which they expressly deny. p. 102.<-

### Answer.

(1.) As an example, the history of **Arnold of Brescia** <note>A 12th-century Italian reformer who called for the church to renounce property and political power.</note> is cited, whom **Dr. Cyprian** calls a heretic; yet this is improper and entirely contrary to the mindset and custom of Protestants. And one may well recall here from **Dannhauer’s *Theological Confessions*, Part II, Vol. 1, p. 237: For they cannot be ascribed to this faction, except through a persistent injustice, those champions of a trembling liberty, the witnesses of truth.** <note>original: "Neque enim ad hanc factionem adscribi, nisi per protervam injuriam possunt Thrasybuli, libertatis tremefactæ vindices, veritatis testes."</note> For these do not call him a heretic, but a witness of the truth, as he is expressly included in **Flacius’s *Catalog of Witnesses***, <note>A famous 1556 work by Matthias Flacius Illyricus listing historical figures who opposed the Papacy before the Reformation.</note> **Book XIV, p. 482.** Indeed, **Mr. Schilter** himself counts him in the cited place, point 8, among those **Reformers who began to examine the new dogmas and institutions of the Roman Popes**, and says: **he began to criticize the dogmas and customs of the Roman Church and all the clergy, and to reclaim the Imperial Majesty stolen from the Kings, and to assert Liberty.** <note>original Latin: "eum cœpisse dogmata & mores Ecclesiæ Romanæ & omnis Cleri taxare, Majestatemque Imperatoriam Regibus ereptam vindicare, Libertatemq; asserere."</note>

(2) Almost all Protestant **Historians** do the same: such as **Micrælius** in *Church History*, **Book III, chapter 30**, who calls him **a spirited man** <note>original: "virum animosum"</note> or praises the assertion of Roman liberty against the Pope; also in **chapter 22, p. 161**, he counts the **Arnoldists** among the **witnesses of truth**; likewise the **Gotha *Church History*, Book II, chapter 4, p. 607**, and **Osiander** in his *Epitome*, **Vol. II, Century XII, Book chapter 7, p. 266, etc.** **Joachim Hesterberg**, in his work on the *Waldensian Church* approved by **Dannhauer**, **article 2, § 18**, described three kinds of **Arnolds** who were persecuted by the Papists, among whom this **Brixiensis** <note>Arnold of Brescia</note> is called by **Baronius** the **Patriarch and Prince of Political Heretics.** <note>original: "Hereticorum Politicorum Patriarcha & Princeps"</note> But he concludes quite rightly in **§ 19**: **Though different in other matters, these Arnolds agree in this: that they condemned both the vices and the arrogated supremacy** <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴν" — hyperochen</note> **of the Roman Church**; <note>original: "In aliis diversi, in hoc tamen Arnoldi hi conveniunt, quod Romanæ... manæ Ecclesiæ & vitia & arrogatam ὑπεροχὴν damnarunt"</note> and many others.

(3.) Protestant writers generally count such persons among the witnesses of the truth who have shown zeal against the Papacy in certain matters, even if they are not considered entirely correct in other points. The whole **Catalog of Flacius** demonstrates this; and so that one may see an example from the **more recent ones**, the **U.-Reports** <note>Likely the *Unschuldige Nachrichten*, a contemporary theological journal.</note> write of **Johannes Wessel**, that he had his faults, loved **Plato** too much, and often behaved quite **singularly** (which is now called a particular heresy): nevertheless, it is acknowledged that he may well be counted among the **Witnesses of the truth** <note>original: "Testes veritatis"</note>. **Year 1707, p. 214.** Thus **Arnold** was not actually a heretic, and **Mr. Cyprian** has himself presented the history incorrectly here, and conceded far too much to the Pope against the witnesses of the truth. But he called him a heretic so that it would appear as if the histories of the heretics had been falsified.

(4.) Since **Arnold** thus has the **favor of the cause** <note>original: "favorem causæ" — a legal term meaning the benefit of the doubt or a favorable standing</note> among the Protestants, **Gottfried Arnold** writes this not to please him as a heretic, but as a **witness of the truth**; consequently, **Arnold of Brescia’s** discourse can, as far as possible, be **vindicated** <note>original: "salviret"</note>. And when **Gottfried Arnold** cites **Mr. Schilter in defense of Arnold**, he certainly did not **weigh** <note>original: "ponderiret"</note> his own words so precisely, and has already sincerely admitted such an oversight in his **supplement, p. 126.** For **Mr. Schilter** certainly does not say that the proposition is correct and a precious truth: **that clergy who possess temporal goods cannot be saved.** <note>original: "non posse salvari possessores Clericos bonorum temporalium."</note>

(5.) Meanwhile, such an oversight is not immediately a falsification. For **Gottfried Arnold** indeed found enough in **Schilter** to show that **Arnold** undoubtedly spoke with the Savior: *It is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.* **Mr. Schilter also excuses** him there as best he can, including in this **question of the property of the clergy**, and says: **he criticized rightly, he urged most rightly, etc.** Thus, he will never agree with **Mr. Cyprian** that **Arnold** was a heretic or taught heresy, as he explained and justified Arnold's words quite **judiciously** and **conveniently** alongside other Protestants; regarding the proposition attributed to him about the damnation of clergy with property, however, he shows **tacitly** that it was falsely attributed to him by his enemies.

(6.) It is therefore only an oversight (which is indeed possible among such innumerable **citations** <note>original: "locis"</note> and has never been denied by **Gottfried Arnold**) that it was written of this proposition that **Mr. Schilter** had approved it. However, **Gottfried Arnold** has not in the least falsified **Schilter’s** words, nor could he have, because he did not cite them **word for word** <note>original: "verbotenus"</note>. And so, whoever [labels] such an oversight of an author among so many **distractions** (which)...

(7.) But if every incorrect conclusion drawn from an author were to be immediately called a falsification, then certainly the conclusions found thus far would often have to be called such—especially when, in such a question regarding a witness of the truth in No. 34, the words of **Arnold** <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical pietist historian who wrote a famous history of the church and its "heretics."</note> were clearly violated and a false consequence was attributed to him. ### The 57th Accusation.
#### He shamelessly falsifies the words of Sulpitius Severus: p. 103.
### Answer.

(1.) This accusation is said to consist of Mr. Arnold translating the word <term>restless</term> <note>original: "inquies"</note> with the word <term>active</term> <note>original: "actif"</note>. Now, the word <term>active</term> is well known to be a <term>neutral term</term> <note>original: "μέσον" (mesón) — a word that can be used in either a positive or negative sense.</note>, and can indicate either a <term>vicious</term> restlessness or a liveliness of the spirit. Dr. Cyprian arbitrarily interprets Mr. Arnold's words as if he had said: **Priscillian** <note>A 4th-century bishop in Spain who was the first person in the history of Christianity to be executed for heresy.</note> was "nimble" according to the testimony of **Sulpitius** <note>Sulpitius Severus (c. 363–c. 425), an early Christian chronicler known for his biography of Saint Martin.</note>. However, Mr. Arnold does not only say this, but he expresses even more with the word <term>active</term>, and does not exclude the restless meaning, but includes it. Consequently, he has not falsified Sulpitius, but translated him in such a way that the author's meaning is expressed fully and not in a mutilated fashion.

(2.) The other falsification is said to be that Mr. Arnold translated <term>nature/intellect</term> <note>original: "ingenium"</note> as **disposition** <note>original: "Gemüth"</note>. Now, he has already gladly admitted in the **Supplement, page 116**, that **an excellent intellect** <note>original: "ingenium optimum"</note> could be called a "good head." However, it is not immediately a falsification if one takes it to mean the sense or disposition, as even the best authors have used this word in that way, as is known from **Terence** <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright.</note> and others. The general understanding of this word usually refers to the entire nature and character of a person, and only specifically refers later to the nimbleness and teachability of the head. In translating, one always prefers the former over the latter sense, as long as the text does not clearly show otherwise. Whether Sulpitius attributed no good disposition to Priscillian is entirely uncertain from his words; for he gives him the testimony of **moderation and frugality**, and as for what he thinks of magical arts, he does not dare to assert it as fact, but speaks only by conjecture or hearsay: One

<column-break/>

251 To Dr. Cyprian's Accusations. Vol. II, Nos. 57. 58.

believes it, or as Dr. Cyprian himself expresses it: he was under suspicion.

(3.) Meanwhile, one should consider whether Dr. Cyprian himself has not expressed Sulpitius's words too **excessively**, and against his meaning, when he says Sulpitius claims Priscillian was the most dissolute man. That is found nowhere in Sulpitius, neither in word nor in sense; rather, it says he was not greedy and was very frugal in his habits. To be vain and puffed up by knowledge of worldly things is a long way from being the "most dissolute man." For how many scholars are of such a nature, who are not therefore necessarily dissolute, and least of all the *most* dissolute, nor do they wish to be? Had Mr. Arnold said this from the text, it would have to be called a falsification. From this, one can see how easily **preconceived opinions** <note>original: "præconceptæ opiniones"</note> can cause a writer to rush into judging others, potentially committing the very same fault of which they wish to convict others.

### The 58th Accusation.
#### He falsifies the words of King James. p. 104.
### Answer.

(1.) It is claimed he should have specified which **Presbyterians** the King was speaking of: namely, those few who made up the **Family of Love** <note>original: "Familiam amoris" — a mystical religious sect founded in the 16th century.</note>. However, the King himself limits his **proposition** so that he is not speaking only and solely of this "family," but only **principally** <note>original: "præcipue"</note> and primarily; thus, he did not entirely exclude the others.

(2.) Are the King's words supposedly violently falsified if Mr. Arnold writes that the King speaks of the Presbyterians: **"Anyone who denied even the smallest bit of their chatter, they called a heathen"**? Now, this is exactly what the King says in the words cited by Dr. Cyprian: **"All others, who will not swear to their fantasies, they denote as profane."** <note>original: "Cæteros omnes, qui in eorum phantasmata jurare nolint, pro profanis denotant."</note> It is claimed to be false that "even the smallest bit" was added; yet the King himself immediately complains thereafter that they **"excited no less tragedies over any small matters of ecclesiastical policy"** <note>original: "non minores tragoedias in quibusvis Ecclesiasticæ politiæ minutiis excitirten"</note>; by which he clearly indicates that they would not even tolerate it if small details (<term>Minutiae</term>) were denied against them. Mr. Arnold focused on these words in his summary repetition of the complaints, as he was bound to, because the King attributes great stubbornness and pride to them therein, and thus he is not guilty of the slightest falsification.

(3.) The remaining words after the last sentence correspond entirely with the Latin text of **James**, where Mr. Arnold gave the words: **"Christian Princes are not even to be commended to God in prayers"** <note>original: "Christiani Principes ne quidem precibus Deo commendandi sunt"</note>. One

...should not pray for Christian authority. To this, he attached the second clause—for the sake of brevity, as if in a summary repetition—namely: "but rather resist them." To be sure, it could have been stated more accurately: "it is not forbidden for us to take up arms against them." That this King <note>Likely referring to a historical figure in the context of the Thirty Years' War or the Bohemian Revolt.</note> was otherwise still stuck in many a superstition, and that not all his words are to be believed without distinction, has been demonstrated among others by Dr. Beemann on the **point** <note>original: "puncto"</note> of the water ordeal in his *Dissertation on the Judgments of God*, Chapter IV, Section 5. As for what Mr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian and Arnold's critic.</note> throws in there regarding pasquils <note>A pasquil is a satirical protest or lampoon, often posted in a public place.</note>, he would have had not the slightest cause before God and men for it, if he had wanted to recognize Mr. Arnold's innocence in this matter. ## The 59th Accusation.
->He does the Bohemians an injustice.<-

### Answer.

(1.) It is said to be a falsification when Mr. Arnold writes of the Bohemians: they had said that Electoral Saxony <note>One of the most powerful Protestant states in the Holy Roman Empire, whose relationship with other Protestant groups was often tense.</note> was persecuting the Reformed. For in the *European Theater* <note>original: "Theatro Europæo" — a massive 17th-century chronicle of European history.</note> it only says: Electoral Saxony was vehement against the Reformed, therefore they would have to endure a persecution.

(2.) But let every sensible reader judge whether this—in a summary account where one does not repeat everything word-for-word—is not fundamentally the same thing: when someone is "vehement against" the Reformed, and when he "persecutes" them? One will, of course, distinguish **between the will and the act of persecuting** <note>original: "inter voluntatem & actum perſequendi"</note>; however, it is well known from history that in Electoral Saxony at that time, not only was the will there, but it also broke out into action. And for that very reason, the Bohemians concluded they would have to endure persecution. They would never have blamed such a potentate for this if they had not experienced examples of it, which simply cannot be denied. Thus, no injustice has been done to the Bohemians in this matter. Especially since (as already mentioned) their **arguments** <note>original: "rationes"</note> are not cited according to their exact words or **word-for-word** <note>original: "verbotenus"</note>, but are only reported as a summary.

## The 60th Accusation.
->He shares with the Anabaptists the rejection of infant baptism and church assemblies.<-

### Answer.

But how wrongly Mr. Arnold is burdened with this is clear and as plain as day from the above Nos. 3, 5, 32,

## The 61st Accusation.
->He speaks on their behalf with completely terrifying falsifications of the authors.<-

### Answer.

(1.) Above all, in the following **defenses** <note>original: "Apologien"</note>, it is earnestly **affirmed** <note>original: "conteſtirt" — to formally state or bear witness.</note> that one remains free from the Anabaptist <note>The "Wiedertäuffer" or Anabaptists were radical reformers who practiced adult baptism and were often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> errors and only deals **in the terms of a just defense** <note>original: "in terminis juſtæ defenſionis"</note> regarding some **questions of fact** <note>original: "quæſtionibus facti"</note>, and thus has nothing to do with the doctrine itself here.

(2.) The first example is said to be: Arnold says people complained about them because they wanted to prove their case with nothing but scriptural passages; therefore, they were considered unworthy of an answer. Now, granted that it was done with bare scriptural passages, the **sense** <note>original: "Senſus"</note> remains correct: that they had cited nothing but verses and nothing else. And this is also contained in the words cited from Ottius <note>Johann Heinrich Ott (1617–1682), a Swiss historian and theologian.</note>, where it says: **"because they were bare citations of scripture, they were not accepted as a response."** <note>original: "quia nudæ ſcripturæ allegationes erant, haut pro reſponſo ſuſceptum fuit."</note> And before this, on the very same page 277, it says: The Anabaptists had actually said: **"Because the holy opinion is contained in his letters and in other writings."** <note>original: "Quia ſententia S, in ſuis literis & in aliis ſcriptis continetur."</note>

(3.) Here it can be seen that: α) they wanted to prove their case only with bare scriptural passages, namely without proper **logical derivation** <note>original: "Deduction"</note>; β) that this was not accepted as an answer; and γ) that consequently they were held to be unworthy of an answer. For what one does not consider an answer, one also deems not worth an answer. Thus, calling this a "terrifying distortion" is in vain.

(4.) For Mr. Arnold does not say that the Anabaptists could have proven everything with scripture, or actually did prove it—which would certainly be false—but only that they *wanted* or *attempted* to, and indeed with bare scriptural passages, which is clearly stated in Ottius. Indeed, it is not only Ottius who says this, but the old Lutheran theologian Johannes Brentius <note>Johannes Brentius (1499–1570), a prominent reformer in the region of Württemberg.</note> mentions this **expressly** <note>original: "expreſſè"</note> in the opinion he gave regarding the Anabaptists, as recorded by Dr. Bidenbach in *Decade IV, Counsel 1, page 186*: The Anabaptist business is a hidden error, **Note well** <note>original: "NB"</note>, supported with the verses of scripture. Mr. Arnold indicated exactly this, which Brentius acknowledges: namely, that these people referred to the Holy Scriptures

### The 62nd Accusation.

-> He writes to them for their benefit. p. 107. <-

### Answer.

(1.) The proof is this: he says that Hornbeckius <note>Johannes Hoornbeek (1617–1666), a Dutch Reformed theologian and author of "Summa Controversiarum."</note> reminds us that the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wiedertäuffer" — a radical Reformation group known for rejecting infant baptism and emphasizing the separation of church and state.</note> did not so much oppose the doctrine of the Orthodox with another or a new one, as they simply did not correctly grasp or understand the latter.

(2.) This is said never to have entered Hornbeckius's mind. However, Mr. Cyprian has rushed ahead and not read Hornbeckius in the full context, but merely stumbled upon this single passage. Arnold, on the other hand, has weighed the context very precisely and therefore provided a sufficiently thorough report of it, and in this, he had reason to praise Hornbeckius's modesty.

(3.) For if one looks at Hornbeckius’s words, to which he explicitly directs the reader with the words: *Loquimur de quinque famosis supra nominatis;* <note>original: "We are speaking of the five famous [points] named above."</note> it becomes obvious that he is speaking not of some, but of all Anabaptists, and indeed of their common doctrine. For he says on page 358: *Apud nos vulgo noti sunt cum quinque articulis,* <note>original: "Among us they are commonly known for five articles."</note> namely concerning **a.)** infant baptism <note>original: "pædobaptiſmo"</note>, **b.)** rebaptism <note>original: "anabaptiſmo"</note>, **c.)** Christ's incarnation <note>original: "Christi incarnatione"</note>, **d.)** the oath <note>original: "juramento"</note>, and **e.)** the civil magistrate <note>original: "Magiſtratu"</note>. Thus, no doubt remains that he speaks, by his own indication, of each and every Anabaptist—just as he also writes on page 363 without the exception of any teachers.

(4.) Secondly, they wish to say that Hornbeck does not speak of their doctrine, the opposite of which can now be grasped with one's hands from his own words, and can be recognized even more clearly from the following. For in that place, page 362, it is written expressly and generally concerning the errors without any limitation or restriction to the error regarding the incarnation of Christ: *Benignus semper judicarunt Docti de Adversariorum erroribus;* <note>original: "Learned men have always judged the errors of their adversaries with kindness." This sentiment is contrasted with the "unkind judgments" Arnold's critics often displayed.</note> (which judgment should be well noted against the unkind verdicts regarding friends, for which Arnold has been most suspected.) After this, he goes specifically **α)** to the error regarding the oath and the magistrate; *præsertim illis, qui circa juramenti usum & officium Magistratus omnes fere ex magna distinguendi imperitia orti videntur.* <note>original: "especially those [errors] which, concerning the use of the oath and the office of the magistrate, seem almost all to have arisen from a great lack of skill in making distinctions."</note>

(5.) Afterward, he naturally also comes to the piece belonging among the five points—the doctrine of the incarnation—of which he says: *quia hic bene distinguere nequiverunt, illorum error de negata Christi ex Maria incarnatione ortum habet.* <note>original: "Because they were unable to distinguish well here, their error regarding the denial of Christ’s incarnation from Mary took its rise." This refers to the Anabaptist "Celestial Flesh" doctrine, which argued Christ brought his body from heaven rather than taking substance from Mary.</note> — And yet, he immediately falls back upon infant baptism and concludes from this (namely, because they cannot well distinguish the office from the benefit <note>original: "officium a beneficio"</note> and in general): *Hinc tamen est, quod considerantes nonnulli mitius de illis judicent.* <note>original: "Yet from this it follows that some, considering [this], judge them more mildly."</note> To which he immediately adds: *Gravissimus autem istorum (namely, the five errors) est de Christi incarnatione error.* <note>original: "The most serious of these, however, is the error concerning the incarnation of Christ."</note>

(6.) All these preceding, highly necessary points are omitted in this accusation, and one falls merely upon these words cited out of context (upon which, however, Arnold generally reflects), which are not sufficient to see into Hornbeckius’s mind. For Hornbeckius had previously and sincerely noted the steady, kind, and gentle judgments of the learned regarding the Anabaptists' errors; he had also not contradicted them, but specifically maintained them for the reason that these people did not know how to distinguish well. To this he now adds, in the words cited by Mr. Cyprian, that they also did not grasp or understand the true thesis, which Mr. Cyprian also admits.

(7.) And although he speaks conditionally, but in the present tense: *si thesin contrariam haud tenent;* <note>original: "if they do not hold the opposite thesis;"</note> he nevertheless says immediately afterward: *Hodie corpus Christi in Mariæ utero formatum, quamvis non ex ejus substantia, asserunt.* <note>original: "Today they assert that the body of Christ was formed in Mary’s womb, though not of her substance."</note> And further on page 364, he cites Capito’s <note>Wolfgang Capito (1478–1541), a Reformer in Strasbourg known for his irenic/peaceable approach.</note> words: *quosdam inter Anabaptistas esse bonos, veros servos Dei, Christi martyres & clarissimos fratres nostros,* <note>original: "that some among the Anabaptists are good, true servants of God, martyrs of Christ, and our most illustrious brothers,"</note> along with the commentary of Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), successor to John Calvin.</note>: *quis miretur Capitonem illos distinxisse?* <note>original: "Who would wonder that Capito distinguished them?"</note> Likewise, Erasmus’s judgment: *quosdam ex Anabaptistis esse commiseratione dignos.* <note>original: "that some of the Anabaptists are worthy of pity."</note> And upon this, he concludes from their Martyrology: "we know of no one occurring there who suffered for an error in this positive article, but rather in a negative one, while he suspended his judgment regarding this matter and did not explain it." Since he spoke conditionally above, he confesses here that none of their martyrs maintained anything positive in this case, and consequently, he removes his own condition from these people themselves and acts very courageously therein. This is exactly what Arnold wanted to indicate in the contested passage, in that he did not set down this note from all Reformed teachers, but only this: namely, how the Anabaptists did not correctly grasp the Reformed doctrine but suspended their judgment.

(8.) Accordingly, Arnold has neither monstrously tortured this writer, nor wished to torture him, but has indicated even much less than—

Hornbeckius <note>Johannes Hoornbeek (1617–1666), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> wrote with moderation against these people in that same passage. And so, Mr. Cyprian is assured that everything was considered in a Christian manner / but also that in the correct connection, it was not found as he claimed. ## The 63rd Accusation.
That he has undertaken a similar falsification for their benefit.

### Answer.
(1.) This is said to consist of the following: H. A. writes in Book XVI, Chapter 21, § 17, that the adversaries of the Anabaptists were very worried and anxious for right, consistent grounds against re-baptism / and urgently asked one another for the communication of the same. This report resolves into two particular propositions: namely a) that these people were worried about the refutation of re-baptism / and b) that they asked one another for the communication of the grounds against re-baptism. For each proposition, H. A. alleges a correct and undeniable example.

(2.) Here, Mr. Cyprian is asked / not to rush / as may have happened before in zeal / but to consider the following well and calmly. For certainly H. A. has proceeded here very thoroughly and deliberately / if only Mr. Cyprian had also taken the consequence into account / which he has passed over <note>original: "präterirt," from the Latin *praeteritio*</note> either in haste or with diligence; although out of love, one does not want to blame him for the latter as much as he has done against H. A. Regarding this report, H. A. cites not only one example / as Mr. Dr. C. claims / but indeed two / immediately following one another. The first he cites is how the refuters of the Anabaptists were sometimes concerned / that these people might seize upon something from their books for their own use: *Let no one believe,* <note>original: "Nemo credat"</note> says Mycronius <note>Martin Mikron (1523–1559), a Dutch Reformed theologian who worked in London and East Friesland.</note>, *what boasts they would breathe out, and that they would even now promise themselves victory among everyone.* Indeed, he confesses / if their cause were burdened by the prejudice of Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Reformed theologian.</note>, it would be all the more difficult to stop their adversaries' mouths / precisely because they were *most cunning men* <note>original: "homines astutissimi"</note>. He also asks

<column-break/>

Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), the successor to Zwingli in Zurich.</note> for the sake of Christ's name / that Musculus keep his opinion quiet / so that Menno <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561), the leader from whom the Mennonites take their name.</note> does not misuse his authority against them. For Musculus had already published his opinion on generation <note>original: "de generatione"</note> in his commentary on Genesis 17 / whose words the Anabaptists had cited for themselves. This Mycronius regretted, and confessed / *that many brothers and ministers of the Word were anxious along with him in this cause.* <note>original: "multos fratres & verbi ministros in hac causa secum esse anxios."</note>

(3.) From this letter it is as clear as day / that the refuters of such people were often anxious and worried / that they, as "shattered heads," <note>original: "zerschlagene Köpffe" — a derogatory term for fanatics or those with broken logic.</note> might claim a victory on one occasion or another. And H. A. wanted to prove this much from the first example / and has proved it clearly enough.

(4.) On the other hand, he cited the other example from that same Ottius <note>Johann Baptist Ott (1661–1744), author of the "Annales Anabaptistici."</note> immediately following it / namely what concerns infant baptism <note>original: "Kindertauffe"</note> in particular; of this he writes: Another confesses / that he indeed did not want to fall silent at their objections / and yet could not speak skillfully enough against them / because he well knew / how little provision <note>original: "Vorrath"</note> he had in this matter. This is taken from Fabricius's clear words there on page 128: *It was far more bitter to me, that while I did not wish to fall silent before the common people embracing the most foul errors of Anabaptism in crowds, I was nevertheless unable to speak aptly. For I am not ignorant of how meager my provisions are. Therefore, since I could not cure this evil, I finally went to Frankfurt with a sad heart, etc.* <note>original: "Longe mihi fuit acerbius, quod idiotis turmatim Catabaptismum teterrimos errores amplectentibus obmutescere nolens, apte tamen loqui non potuerim. Non enim sum ignarus, quam mihi sit curta suppellex. Quare cum malo huic mederi non possem, mæsto tandem animo Francofurtum me contuli, &c."</note>

(5.) That all the words are now brightly and clearly proven and deduced from the cited words / everyone will see obviously. For that infant baptism is the subject, especially in the last example / cannot be doubted / because it is the most prominent and chief doctrine of this sect. And accordingly, H. A. remains innocent of such falsifications / he has not falsified Micronius's words at all / much less abominably / and thus has not written un-Christianly or partially / least of all protected these people in a way that would benefit the Turks <note>A common rhetorical comparison of the time, suggesting that defending heretics was as dangerous as aiding the Ottoman Empire.</note>; but has cited and reported as an honest historian. Also, no one would have needed to be astonished by it / if everything had been exactly weighed according to the connection without passions and with a gentle, quiet heart / so that one does not dig pits for others / and might fall into them oneself.

<header>Clear Answer to II. Part 64. 65. N.</header>

Cyprian therefore wrote: If one must protect the Anabaptists <note>original: "Anabaptiſten"; a radical wing of the Reformation often persecuted for their belief in adult baptism and separation of church and state.</note> in such a way, then one could no less come to the aid of the Turks, and would hardly need so much falsification. However, the root of this over-hasty accusation is clearly revealed from the preceding.

(2.) But he wishes to prove this current charge from the fact that H. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold, the author being defended.</note> takes the promise of the Dutch Anabaptists as a completed deed. It is said to stand again in *Ottio* <note>referring to Johannes Heinrich Ottius (1617–1682) and his work *Annales Anabaptistici*.</note>, he writes, which is false. For it does not say that they did it, but that they promised to do it.

(3.) However, he has once again precipitated his judgment all too much (for I would rather express it thus *most gently* <note>original: "molliſſimè"</note>, and leave the rest—whether it happened by intent—to his own conscience). As is his habit, Dr. Cyprian <note>original: "H. D. C."</note> looked at only a single sentence of the cited page, even though on that very same 166th page of *Ottius* it is explicitly stated—and was even noted in the margin by H. A. during his work—how Prince William <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange (1533–1584), leader of the Dutch Revolt.</note> attested in clear words in a letter that several Anabaptist households had served him in various military campaigns. From this experience, this same Prince also assured the Lords of Middelburg <note>A city in the Netherlands.</note> that they had requested to bear all taxes in honesty alongside others. And that this offer was indeed fulfilled is shown by the testimonies of the famous jurist Huber <note>Ulrik Huber (1636–1694), a Dutch lawyer and professor.</note> and others cited there; as anyone who has been to Holland can also attest.

(4.) Dr. Cyprian was indeed offended by the first Amsterdam riot, and H. A. himself raised the objection in the following 23rd section regarding the affairs of Müntzer and Münster <note>referring to the violent radicalism of Thomas Müntzer and the Münster Rebellion of 1534, which many mainstream Lutherans used to label all Anabaptists as dangerous rebels.</note> (which he himself recognizes elsewhere as diabolical); however, sensible historians (who are produced here under number 103) gladly distinguish between the first confused times of this sect and the following times, when they became somewhat more sober and modest. And the cited *testimonies* <note>original: "teſtimonia"</note> apply to these later times.

(5.) Hopefully, Dr. Cyprian will also see this accusation more clearly and liberate his conscience from it, as from a grave insult to his neighbor before God's holy eyes.

### The 65th Accusation.
->That he, for the sake of the Quakers, twists the words of Mr. Croese.<-
->p. 110.<-

### Answer.
(1.) This is said to consist of H. A. taking the words of Croese <note>Gerard Croese (1642–1710), author of *Historia Quakeriana*.</note> to apply to all Quakers,

---

<page-num>259</page-num>
<header>I. Part 65. 66. N. Mr. Doctor Cyprian's Accusations.</header>

when he only says: *there were among them* <note>original Latin: "eſſe inter eos"</note>, that is, there were such people among them.

(2.) Here it is to be known in general that Croese gave a good testimony to the Quakers in many matters—so much so that he was even counted among them, or at least among their favorites, by some authors, as is well known; even though the Quakers themselves attacked him over his history, as evidenced by the so-called Philaletha’s or Kohlhans’s *Clarifications of the Quaker History* <note>original Latin/German: "Philalethæ oder Kohlhanſens *Dilucidationes in Hiſtoriam Quakerianam*"; refering to a critique of Croese's book.</note>, which was published in Amsterdam in 1696.

(3.) Now this historian writes of the English Quakers (of whom the vast majority—and according to the report over 60,000—are in London alone) at the cited place, page 42: *Nothing else could be detected by opinion or suspicion than that there were among them those who led a life consistent with their words.* <note>original Latin: "Neque aliud opinione aut ſuſpicione poterat deprehendi, quam eſſe in eos, qui vitam ducerent conſimilem verbis."</note> H. A. is said to have twisted these words when he concludes from them: that the Quakers' lives match their words.

(4.) But Dr. Cyprian has undoubtedly seen from the whole history, especially from § 57, how H. A. recounted not only the faults but also specifically the riots of several Quakers. From this it is further obvious that when he otherwise refers to Quakers, he does not mean such notorious evildoers, but the rest of the group, as is customary among historians. And thus one gladly agrees with Mr. Cyprian that Croese is not speaking of the rebellious Quakers. So too, H. A. does not speak of each and every Quaker; for Croese does not say that either, but only speaks in general of such people. And Croese himself, immediately following, speaks without any distinction or restriction: *Such gentleness and mildness in dealings with men, such moderation in society, such serenity of countenance... there shone among them especially love and care in those things pertaining to religion, and an inspection of how each person conducted themselves in them, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Tanta in commerciis cum hominibus manſuetudo, lenitas, in ſodalitiis moderatio, in vultu ſerenitas, — eminebat inter eos maxime amor & cura cum in iis rebus, quæ pertinent ad religionem, inſpectio, quemadmodum quiſque ſeſe in iis gereret, &c."</note> all of which, along with what follows (which Dr. Cyprian does not attend to), are nothing but general testimonies of their conduct. And finally, on that very same page, he concludes quite clearly regarding all Quakers and all their behavior at that time: *Thus they all took care so that in everything they might express not the form of some new church, but the image and simplicity of manners of those ancient and first Christians, as well as their gravity and virtue.* <note>original Latin: "Ita id operam dabant omnes, ut in omnibus non novæ alicujus Eccleſiæ formam, at illorum priſtinorum primorumque Chriſtianorum imaginem & morum ſimplicitatem, ſed tamen & gravitatem virtutemque exprimerent."</note> Dr. Cyprian has once again skipped over this, and therefore exerted himself in vain to attribute "twists" to the author.

<header>Clear Answer to II. Part 66. 67. N.</header>
<meta>catchword: irato (angry)</meta>

one has cited this in Switzerland as the reason why the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wiedertäuffer"; a radical Reformation group known for rebaptizing adults and refusing to take oaths or bear arms.</note> were to be driven out: that they presumed to present their scruples after the sermon.

->Answer.<-

(1.) This is said to be proven incorrect from Ottius <note>Johannes Heinrich Ottius (1617–1682), a Swiss historian and theologian.</note>. However, these are the words found in his work, p. 225, after the reasons were cited why excommunication was not to be introduced in Zurich, because the Anabaptists demanded three other points besides this ban, among which the third was: The Baptists—especially the well-read ones and those who imagine much of themselves—want to have the freedom to speak in the church, as Hans Landis <note>A Swiss Anabaptist leader and martyr, executed in 1614; he was one of the last to be put to death for his faith in Zurich.</note> insisted; they will not be satisfied, after hearing the sermon, to seek out the preacher privately, either alone or with someone else, regarding doubtful matters.

(2.) Here Mr. Cyprian says that the idea of "driving out" occurred to no one in this context. However, H. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> had in mind Ottius’s entire connection or sequence of accounts, which this passage eventually follows. Now, not only on almost every page beforehand, but also specifically on p. 222, it is told of several people who were banished from the country. And in these very words, one is named Hans Landis, who insisted on such questions for the preachers: the same man, for these and other reasons—such as that he baptized, performed marriages, and would not vacate the land—was even beheaded <note>original: "decollirt"; from the Latin *decollare*, to behead.</note>, as it stands on p. 220. Thus, it is also easy to imagine that the preachers did not endure the contradictions of such people for very long, and instead insisted on their removal. Especially since they also expelled such Anabaptists who lived quietly for themselves without tumult, as seen on p. 231 and in more examples elsewhere. Therefore, A. has fabricated nothing, but found everything together in good connection, one after another, in Ottius.

### The 67th Accusation.

That he, in order to present a thing as "cruel," omits some words.

->Answer.<-

(1.) These words are: *at a clearly adverse time* <note>original Latin: "tempore plane adverso"</note>. Regarding these, it is first to be noted how Mr. Cyprian himself interpreted and applied them incorrectly and against the author’s meaning—indeed, against the context. For thus it stands sequentially in Ottius p. 289 (Basel Edition 1672, quarto, which H. A. used): the Anabaptists had begun to emphasize to others: <term>they had begun to emphasize that, at a clearly adverse time, wars were sent as a punishment by an</term> <note>original Latin: "inculcare occœperant, tempore plane adverso bella poena loco mitti ab"</note>

---

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header>II. Part 67. 68. N. Accusations of Dr. Cyprian.</header>
<sig>Kk 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: vor- (pre-)</meta>

angry Deity <note>original Latin: "irato Numine"</note>. Here stands a comma, and thus the following words also belong to the following sense, and the sense is obviously this: by virtue of the clear distinction: This was the Anabaptists' claim: that the angry God sent the war as punishment at such a contrary or miserable time.

(2.) On the other hand, Mr. Cyprian interprets these last words quite differently, as if they belonged to the verb "to emphasize" <note>original: "inculcare"</note>, as if the Anabaptists had contradicted at such an "inconvenient" time. However, this cannot be the case: when one considers that α) the distinction points exactly to the contrary; β) and the word *adversus* <note>Latin for "against" or "hostile"</note> regarding time never means "inconvenient" or "uncomfortable" among good authors (whom the author of the epistle, as his fine style shows, intended to follow), but always means "adverse," "unfortunate," as when they write *res adversæ* (misfortune), *tempestas* (stormy weather), *valetudo* (poor health), *fortuna adversa* (unlucky fortune), *casus adversi* (adverse events), and so forth.

(3.) Now, because this circumstance—namely, that times of war are unfortunate times—does nothing for the matter here, and H. A. anyway did not translate such passages word-for-word <note>original: "verbotenus"</note>, but only wanted to allege the most noteworthy sense: he did not consider such words necessary, or perhaps (as easily happens) let them pass by; but not out of a "malice" to represent the words as "cruel," as it is improperly interpreted.

(4.) That the epistle itself was written to the authorities, H. A. has nowhere said: but he did say that the accusers of the Anabaptists had complained to the authorities: upon which they also reported this in this epistle, or as H. A. says: "it was said." For who would doubt that they would also bring this important point to the authorities, since they did not omit it in a letter to foreigners?

(5.) Mr. Cyprian also cites the last words, *by the laws of the fatherland* <note>original Latin: "patriis legibus"</note>, differently than they stand in the text: for there it stands: *by the most ancient laws of the fatherland* <note>original Latin: "antiquissimis patriæ legibus"</note>, and he can see from this how easily he himself can fail in such citations <note>original: "allegationibus"</note> and repetitions, yet such a thing should not immediately be made out to be "wickedness" or "falsification."

->Answer.<-

(1.) Here it is again to be noted that H. A. did not translate Croese’s words word-for-word; for otherwise he would have had to translate from word to word thus: He was a man who was excellent or magnificent, as much because of his...

...both because of his excellent nobility and his great desire for knowledge and science: Instead, he merely <term>expressed the sense</term> <note>original: "sensum exprimiret"</note>, which was sufficient for the matter. Even Mr. Cyprian himself did not consider such an extremely precise translation necessary, but simply said: **Excellent in his great desire for science:** and thus he distorted <term>Croese</term> <note>Gerardus Croese (1642–1710), a Dutch historian who wrote about the Quakers and Helmont.</note> just as little as Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> did.

(2.) If one wishes to say that science and the desire for science are not the same thing, that is certainly true in itself; however, in the <term>application</term> to this learned and experienced man, they are one and the same. This is because he possessed not only the desire into his old age, but also the science itself to a high degree. Thus, one can rightfully attribute both to him, which <term>Croese</term> nowhere denies nor wishes to deny. Indeed, Mr. Cyprian himself admits he had good knowledge in part, and thus not merely a bare desire for it.

(3.) It is also alleged to be false that <term>Croese</term> wrote that Helmont had learned the <term>transmigration of souls</term> <note>original: "revolutionem animarum"</note> from a Countess. But his words clearly show <term>Croese's</term> claim that Helmont, during <term>discussions</term> based on <term>Plato</term>, fell into this opinion simultaneously with her: <note>original: "Cum eadem sæpe ac multum de placito illo Platonico disserreret, cum illa huc deveniebat, ut ambo in eandem opinionem inciderent." — Since he often and at length discussed that Platonic tenet with her, he reached the point where both fell into the same opinion.</note> However, the author of the *Dilucidations* <note>Referring to the "Dilucidationes" or "Clarifications," likely a contemporary defense of Helmont's views.</note> proves that Helmont held this <term>opinion</term> many years earlier, as is cited there; and thus <term>Croese</term> has nonetheless <term>reported</term> this incorrectly, as Mr. A. noted.

(4.) As for what is further written there regarding the laughing at the **Witnesses of the Truth** and the like, one may rightly pass over it. Mr. A. never presented Helmont as a witness of the truth, much less of his own truth. If one were to view all the persons whom Mr. A. had to describe historically as "witnesses of the truth," or as if Mr. A. had presented them as such, one would be greatly mistaken and clearly do him an injustice. Everyone is free to form their own judgment regarding Mr. A.'s books; but the author is also free to decide what he should think of such judgments in turn.

### The 69th Accusation.

-> **As unbelieving as A. is when one says something good about our church, so gullible is he when one attacks and scolds it. p. 96.** <-

### Answer.

(1.) In this <term>summary</term> of Section 16, Mr. A. is accused on two points: a.) that A. believes nothing good of our church.

The clear and undeniable opposite of this was shown to anyone willing to read back in the 9th Accusation of this Second Part, and the 3rd Accusation of the First Part. For good measure, Mr. Cyprian is <term>specifically</term> assured that Mr. A. does not merely believe much good of our church (insofar as it still follows God's Word), as if it were not visible and clear, but he actually sees it; and he does so while he himself teaches within it and, through God's grace, helps to build and improve it.

(2.) The second point of the complaint is that A. is gullible when our church is attacked and reviled. This harsh, summary accusation is <term>explained</term> on page 113, where Mr. Cyprian "Christianly admonishes" A. not to accept all complaints against our church as if they fell down from heaven.

(3.) A Christian is duty-bound and willing to gladly accept Christian admonitions. However, it is well known that one who admonishes must first prove such things in himself as a true Christian if they are to bear fruit in his neighbor. Mr. Dr. C. <note>Dr. Cyprian</note> has certainly published the most dangerous capital accusations against Mr. A., and many have accepted them as true out of ignorance or prejudice. But the groundlessness of these has, thank God, been brought to light until now. Thus, let him in turn now be Christianly admonished and requested that he no longer undertake such things against his neighbor, but let the previous transgressions be enough for the sake of his own conscience's peace!

(4.) On the other hand, Mr. A. likewise assures that he demonstrates all Christian and due love toward our church and all its members, and thus also toward Mr. Cyprian. But he has also never accepted all complaints against it as if they fell from heaven—that is, as divine <term>oracles</term> or infallible <term>pronouncements</term> <note>original: "effata"</note>. Rather, his conscience bears him witness that he has an abhorrence for all <term>excessive</term> complaints, and even more so for scolding and attacking, and that he has truly viewed all the complaints of others that he perhaps published as being for improvement and not for destruction. And since God has blessed these for the good of many, he can rightfully rest in such a blessing; the insults, however, he bears as a Christian, and has now received other work and cares from God.

(5.) <term>Specifically</term>, it is now written of Breckling <note>Friedrich Breckling (1629–1711), a controversial mystic and critic of the Lutheran church whom Arnold often cited.</note> that he is a "good, simple man," by which his testimony is called into doubt. But that this man is not simply "simple" or foolish, but rather had a deep insight into the decay [of the church] before Mr. A. and others were even born, and also sealed his testimonies with disgrace and other sufferings—that has recently...

Mr. Director Lange of Berlin, an impartial witness in Part II of his *Sincere Reports* <note>Joachim Lange (1670–1744) was a Pietist theologian and supporter of Arnold.</note>, page 29 and following, and in Part III, page 3 and following, and in Part IV, page 96 and following.

Regarding his <term>Catalog</term> <note>Arnold included a "Catalogus Testium Veritatis" or "Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth," a list of people throughout history who he believed held to the true faith despite being labeled heretics by the institutional church.</note>, Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> inserted it faithfully as he received it. And although it remains certain enough that many true <term>witnesses of the truth</term> <note>original: "testes veritatis"</note> are described therein, and many other good specific reports of church matters appear in it, Mr. A. himself has modestly admitted that such a Catalog requires a more thorough execution.
