### The 70th Accusation.

->Answer.<-

(1.) Mr. Cyprian himself writes of this in general as follows: page 120. **As far as errors are concerned, we all know well that humans are subject to them from time to time; therefore, it should not be held against anyone if he sometimes errs, especially in <term>historical matters</term> <note>original: "Historicis"</note>.**

(2.) Now, Mr. A. himself—immediately upon the publication of the *Church and Heretic History* <note>Arnold's most famous work, the "Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie."</note> and several times thereafter—explicitly and sincerely requested that people kindly point out the errors that occur in such an extensive work, and he would be ready to faithfully correct them. He has often repeated such requests and declarations: in the dedication of *The Way to God*, in the *Explanation* chapter II § 16, in the *Presentation* chapter IV § 5, and elsewhere.

(3.) He has also incorporated all those reminders sent to him privately into the *Supplements*, and through the very writing just mentioned, he has further publicly demonstrated that he is no more ashamed than other <term>writers</term> <note>original: "Scribenten"</note> to confess his committed errors. On the contrary, it is also evident how many have sought—either without any basis or in a hostile manner and with unchristian intention—to accuse him not only of vain errors but of gross ignorance, malice, heresies, and other evil things.

(4.) But because the truth is dearer to the Author than his own honor or anything else in the world—which has also become apparent through so many harsh and underserved persecutions and insults directed against him—it was out of such love for the truth that he eventually became indifferent as to how the truth might be discovered in history, or how the errors might be noted. Therefore, such obser-

<column-break/>

<page-num>265</page-num>
<header>Part I, No. 70. Regarding Director Cyprian's Accusations.</header>

vations are not without use, and it matters little who writes the truth, as long as it is done sincerely and thoroughly.

(5) It is true that Mr. Dr. C. <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1723), a prominent Lutheran orthodox critic of Arnold.</note> did not present some of these points very modestly or with much love, but sometimes exaggerated them without necessity or reason; for instance, when he writes of misprinted or misplaced numbers and the like, calling it "grievous." Nevertheless, he himself had to note over 10 lines of printing errors in his own recent writing of 5 sheets; this is common to all books and sometimes even more frequent, especially when a book must first be copied, as happened with the *Church History* <note>Arnold's *Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie*</note> while the <term>author was absent</term> <note>original: "absente autore"</note>.

(6) And so that this might not be seen as a mere excuse, I will cite two of the latest adversaries of Mr. A. with their own confessions, who recognize that accusations based on clerical or printing errors are insufficient. Thus Mr. M. Scharff writes in the *Innocent Reports* <note>original: "Unschuldige Nachrichten," the leading orthodox Lutheran theological journal of the time</note> against Mr. Lange on page 82, regarding the work *Democritus's Scourging of Popery* <note>original: "Papismo vapulante Democriti"</note>, which they had cited but not with the correct location: **Once again, the digits were merely miswritten by a single page, and page 328 was mistaken for 320.** And on page 83, he writes against Mr. Lange: **Although he now seeks to make our <term>citations</term> <note>original: "Citata"</note> suspicious in general and cannot say where any fraud or malice lies: yet the kind reader is informed for his own good that it is nothing more than a mistake partly in writing and partly in printing, where one related digit was swapped for another: which one can forgive the authors as a misfortune to which all books in the world are subject.** Likewise Mr. Bücher in his *Zierold* <term>in this matter</term> <note>original Greek: "en touto"</note>, preface § 7: **I pass over the printing errors in the citations of scriptural passages, for which we cannot be held responsible since the writings were printed in our absence. And yet such errors are punished as severely as if we had intentionally attributed false teachings to the cited author for which we could provide no proof from their writings. Therefore all our citations must be suspicious.** What these people demand from their own censors, one must no less grant to another author, especially in a work of such great length.

(7) Meanwhile, one could demonstrate from Mr. A.'s <term>manuscript</term> <note>original: "MSto" / Manuscripto</note> that many such printing errors were identified as actual historical errors; the author already protested against this in the first preface, § 17. However, he is still always willing to accept friendly reminders without opposition.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold against the criticisms of the Lutheran theologian Ernst Salomon Cyprian. The previous section addressed accusations of general inaccuracy; here, the text moves into specific defenses against claims of chronological errors, factual mistakes, and plagiarism.</meta>

<page-num>266</page-num>
<header>German Answers to Volume II, Number 70.</header>
<meta>catchword: Mr. A.</meta>

However, Mr. Cyprian <note>Ernst Salomon Cyprian (1673–1745) was a prominent defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy and a fierce critic of Arnold’s Pietist views.</note> will surely not object if one or two things remain to be addressed regarding the errors he pointed out.

(8) The year given for the Imperial Edict of Restitution <note>A decree issued by Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II in 1629 during the Thirty Years' War, attempting to restore the religious and territorial situations established by the Peace of Augsburg.</note> as 1628 is obviously a misprint—namely, an 8 instead of a 9—and should read 1629, which can easily be found in any common chronicle or table. Yet Mr. Cyprian remarks that this is "far worse" (page 122). Similarly, regarding the reign of **Henry the Fowler** <note>original: "Henrici Aucupis"; Henry I (c. 876–936), the first King of the Ottonian Dynasty of Germany.</note>, the text has 16 instead of 17, which is a simple transposition. On page 124, the meaning is not that **Curcellæus** <note>Étienne de Courcelles (1586–1659), a Remonstrant theologian.</note> entered office in the year 1634; rather, the passage speaks of **Episcopius** <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643), a Dutch theologian who helped systematize Arminianism.</note>, who came to Amsterdam in 1634 and died in 1643, after which Curcellæus <term>succeeded him in the same year</term> <note>original: "eodem anno succedirt"</note>. Thus, there is no contradiction or error here. Likewise, it is no mistake that Dr. Andreæ wrote "godlessly" about **Flacius** <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a strict Lutheran reformer.</note> after his death (page 125), for it is once again a printer’s error where 1573 stands for 1575, which <term>date</term> <note>original: "datum"</note> can also be found in Andreæ’s letter in Fecht (page 519). Therefore, there is no contradiction; in fact, Mr. Carolus himself recognized this as a misprint in his *Innocence of Württemberg* (page 201). Even Mr. Cyprian himself rightly says on page 128 that such things are not worth the effort.

(9) However, something regarding <term>factual matters</term> <note>original: "realibus"</note> must be mentioned. For example, on page 122, Mr. Cyprian calls it an error to say that the Jesuits and others of the Roman persuasion incited the Emperor against the [Protestant] Electors, citing **Scioppius’s *Bugle Call*** <note>original: "Scioppii Classicum"; Caspar Schoppe (Scioppius) wrote "Classicum Belli Sacri" (A Bugle Call to Holy War) in 1619, urging Catholic princes to take up arms.</note> as proof, as this book was supposedly published before the Bohemian coronation. Here, Mr. A.'s <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> meaning was misunderstood. He does not say that the Papists incited the Emperor only after the Battle of Prague <note>The Battle of White Mountain (1620), a major Catholic victory in the Thirty Years' War.</note>, or that Scioppius only did so then; for such <term>public writings</term> <note>original: "publica scripta"</note>, not to mention private reminders to great lords, were issued constantly. Rather, he only indicates in general how diligently they had <term>instigated</term> the Emperor even before then. Notably, Scioppius published his *Bugle Call* shortly after the **Defenestration of Prague** <note>original: "Pragiſchen Fenſterauswerffen"; the 1618 event where Protestant nobles threw Catholic officials out of a window, sparking the Thirty Years' War.</note>, and thus precisely <term>at the right time</term> <note>original: "in tempore"</note> to achieve his purpose.

Yet Mr. A. did not cite only Avila, but also two <term>passages</term> <note>original: "loca"</note> from **Hortleder** <note>Friedrich Hortleder (1579–1640), a historian who compiled documents on the Schmalkaldic War.</note>, as well as a <term>manuscript account</term> <note>original: "Relationem MStam"</note> concerning Johann Friedrich. Among these three <term>authors</term> <note>original: "Autoribus"</note>, each touches upon certain unique circumstances that do not appear in the others. Thus, while this detail is not in Avila, it is indeed in the <term>manuscript</term> <note>original: "MSto"</note> cited alongside it, which can be read word-for-word in Volume IV of the *History of the Church and Heretics* <note>Arnold's own magnum opus, the "Unparteyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie."</note>, page 91. [The author] used [the source] and saw therein how many years each part contained; however, in the citation, a number or something else could easily be set incorrectly.

(14) But as for the specific accusation that he cites incorrectly in order to make the reader weary of looking things up: Mr. Arnold <note>original: "H. A."; referring to the author, Gottfried Arnold.</note> declares in all seriousness before the living God that he considers such malice—which Mr. Cyprian almost suspects of him—to be un-Christian, and that he never had such an intention, nor ever would. Rather, the main reason why in some paragraphs, especially in the *history of the Middle Ages* <note>original: "historia medii ævi"</note>, the *passages* <note>original: "loca"</note> in the authors are sometimes not specified, is this: the manuscript was copied at another location, where the copyist, *without consulting the author* <note>original: "inconsulto autore"</note>, began to write the *cited passages* <note>original: "allegata"</note> outside the text on a separate volume, and sometimes *out of carelessness* <note>original: "ex incuria"</note> omitted the *passages* (as can still be shown from the manuscript at this hour). This could not easily be corrected later during printing, as the author was some 30 miles away. This is the true cause; and the author is wronged when one suspects him of such evil trickery in this matter. From this same oversight, it happened that in one instance regarding **Gregory the Great** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), a central figure in medieval church history.</note>, the epistle *to Boniface* <note>original: "ad Bonifacium"</note> was cited without the number.

(15) Regarding the words about **Karlstadt** <note>Andreas Rudolph Bodenstein von Karlstadt (1486–1541), a radical reformer who was initially a colleague of Luther but later broke with him.</note> from Chapter 19 of Book XVI, § 11: Mr. Cyprian claims this is a version of Luther’s words that is far too harsh. However, it is evident that this was not meant as a forbidden <unclear>word</unclear>, but only indicated in a general *sense* <note>original: "sensu"</note> what happened with Karlstadt's writings—namely, a prohibition and *suppression*. In substance and in the matter itself, it was the same whether the writing had already been published or not. Indeed, a *suppression* before publication would be harsher than if it had happened after, because in the latter case some *copies* <note>original: "Exemplaria"</note> would have reached the people’s hands, which was not possible through the former.

(16) Likewise, it is hardly an exaggeration or forced interpretation to conclude from the words of Gregory the Great (*Book IX, Epistle 71*) that on the feast days of martyrs, the pagans gorged and drank in the green huts near their temples. This should surprise no one if one considers: **a)** that they were pagans; **b)** that they were allowed to slaughter cattle and hold banquets just as they did at their idol festivals; and especially **c)** that the Christians themselves in the preceding 4th *century* <note>original: "Seculo"</note> practiced similar luxury and debauchery on their feast days, as **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), Archbishop of Constantinople, known for his eloquent preaching and critiques of Christian moral laxity.</note> expressly lamented in *Sermon 8 on the Resurrection* <note>original: "Serm. 8. de Resurr."</note>.

(17) In the final note on page 128, Dr. Cyprian has again not accurately reviewed or repeated Mr. Arnold's words, even though he demands this from Mr. Arnold.

He says Arnold writes that Luther still always considered Karlstadt to be an **Anabaptist** <note>original: "Wiedertäuffer"; a radical Reformation movement often persecuted by both Catholics and mainstream Protestants for their belief in adult baptism and separation of church and state.</note>. ### The 71st Accusation:
Arnold presents the history of the **Quakers** <note>A Christian movement (the Religious Society of Friends) founded in 17th-century England; at the time, they were often viewed as dangerous radicals.</note> in a biased manner.

### Answer:

(1) Regarding this, the history of **Nayler** <note>James Nayler (1618–1660), a prominent early Quaker leader who was famously punished for blasphemy after re-enacting Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.</note> is cited. Mr. Arnold described it in Book XVII, Chapter 20, § 57, and reminded the reader at the very beginning that it gave great cause to describe the Quakers as rebels. Mr. Cyprian thinks it should have been done more extensively; however, Mr. Arnold named those *authors* (such as **Lassenius**, the *Brood of Fanatical Spirits* <note>original: "Schwarmgeister-Brut"; likely a reference to polemical works against radical sects.</note>, **Berckenthal**, **Cræsius’s** German version, etc.) who also deal with it at length in the German language. Since the chapter had already become too large, he presented the history in summary, yet in such a way that the actual circumstances were observed and not suppressed. Furthermore, he included **Nayler's** own confession of his fall in its entirety, so that everyone could see it was a gruesome sin, idolatry, and blasphemy, which Nayler himself had to condemn afterward.

(2) When it is recounted from **Cræsius** <note>Gerard Croese (1642–1710), author of a well-known early history of the Quakers.</note> that the Quakers generally rejected Nayler's cause, he does not say that each and every one did so, but rather "commonly," "mostly," "almost universally," or "many or the greater part here and there." The word "insgemein" [commonly] in German is often used for *indiscriminately, mostly, for the most part* <note>original: "promiscue, plerumque, ut plurimum"</note>, and it occurs very often in this sense in the author's writing style. On the other hand, Mr. Cyprian understood the word as *categorically* <note>original: "generatim"</note>, and under such persuasion attributed a falsification to Mr. Arnold.

(3) That these people performed such detestation [of Nayler's act] earnestly can be seen in part from their own writings, among which Mr. Arnold [cites] **William Ames** <note>An early Quaker preacher who was active in the Netherlands and Germany.</note>...

# The 72nd Accusation:
## That he conceals the failings of the Quakers. (p. 4).
### Answer:

(1) That this claim is by no means consistent with the truth can be seen immediately in the following § 8, Number [X] of this chapter, where it states in the margin: *The Quakers' known failings*, and in the text they are all specified. These failings (namely, their erring) have indeed been recognized and pointed out by the newer Quakers, specifically when they reduced or omitted the all too harsh, contrary, and incomprehensible expressions of the first Quakers. Whereupon are specifically named: **stubbornness, pride, self-complacency, assumed infallibility, Pharisaic appearance, and external holiness**, insofar as they are elevated without the true ground of faith, etc. These are indeed enough failings that Mr. Arnold points out, and which he, as well as other Evangelical writers, has detected in the Quakers.

(2) Furthermore, Mr. D. C. <note>Director Cyprian</note> says that he [Arnold] did not even observe that Mr. Arnold cast doubt on the accounts of the Quakers' hardships. However, if Mr. Arnold had cast doubt on the *passages* <note>original Latin: "loca"</note> of Croese or other authors he cited regarding this, it would likewise have been held against him. Moreover, with such recent history, for which correct documents are still available everywhere, he had no reason to do so. In contrast, in the old stories of the martyrs, not only he, but a large number of learned people long before him, had cause to cast many things into doubt because of so many obscure traces of them; and such a thing was held against no one, but rather one now seeks even among the Catholics a

### The 74th Accusation:

> That he picks out, to the *advantage* of heretics, primarily those sentences in the presentation of their doctrine which he considers to be testimonies of truth, and skips over the most cruel ones.

### Answer:

(1) An example is said to be in Book XVII, Chapter 9, in the account of the opinions in England from the year 1640 to 46. There, Mr. A. immediately noted in § 11 that for the sake of brevity he would only cite the most remarkable ones, because these 180 often quite long sentences would take up too much space in a work that had grown unexpectedly large (since the publisher originally only wanted to print a single quarto volume). Nevertheless, he filled over 7 columns and almost an entire sheet with them.

(2) Dr. Cyprian wishes to assert this evil intention of Mr. A., claiming he picked out those doctrines which he and his brothers held to be the truth, etc. However, no one will act so un-Christianly as to attribute to him these and similar sentences—that he might hold them even as *tolerable*, let alone as truth: **That Scripture cannot be called the Word of GOD; that it is a dead letter; that it deserves no greater belief than all human writings; that Scripture cannot reveal GOD; that it is a pure allegory**, and other such false teachings, all of which are *specified* in the Church History at the cited place.

(3) What is said there about "brothers" belongs to the evil suspicion harbored against one's innocent neighbor; for he has neither sought nor had such a following or sectarian brothers, but has always earnestly testified against all such factions.

(4) Therefore, it has also been cried out in vain: **That it would hinder the propagation of his Universal Syncretism if one were plagued with such doctrines even now.** That Mr. A. sought no such *Universal Syncretism* <note>The attempt to unify all different religious sects and confessions into one.</note> is also manifest to all the world *after the fact* <note>original: "ex post facto"</note>, since he has lived, taught, and written blamelessly as a quiet subject and Evangelical <note>Lutheran</note> preacher in our church since the time of this dispute, and has intended nothing less than a *syncretism*, let alone a universal one. May GOD forgive the accuser this injustice as well!

The wretched man writes in the 16th chapter of the 17th book that the complaints about the atheism that has broken out in Germany primarily concern Lutheranism.

### Answer:

(1) That Mr. A. has shown how atheism exists among all religions and in all countries can be seen directly from the summaries of that very chapter, where §. 7 states: **France is full of atheists;** §. 6 **Italy is the origin and the sinkhole of the same; England likewise, and Holland is a cesspool of atheists <note>original: "sentina Atheistarum"</note>.**

(2) Thus, he in no way justifies other religions or excludes them from this abomination: for the misery is indeed great enough everywhere! In particular, however, as a German writing of Germany and as a Lutheran writing of the Lutheran provinces, he repeats the complaints of <term>Kortholt</term> <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian</note>, <term>Francisci</term> <note>Erasmus Francisci (1627–1694), a polymath and writer</note>, <term>Spizelius</term> <note>Theophilus Spizelius (1639–1691), a theologian and historian of learning</note>, <term>Großgebauer</term> <note>Theophilus Großgebauer (1627–1661), a Lutheran reformer</note>, <term>Scriver</term> <note>Christian Scriver (1629–1693), a popular devotional writer</note>, and <term>Pfeiffer</term> <note>August Pfeiffer (1640–1698), an Orthodox Lutheran polemicist</note>. But nowhere does he say that the majority of atheists in Germany profess our religion.

(3) But what can one say when <term>Dannhauerus</term> <note>Johann Konrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran theologian</note> calls the atheistic religion "the most universal and greatest" <note>original: "Catholicisiman, maximam"</note> and the "great religion" in Volume 1 of his *Theological Conscience*, Part H, Section 2, page 506? He truly did not mean the other parties alone, but also complained about the atheists within our own religion.

## The 76th Accusation:

He writes: "The following (opinions) are more questionable and consequential than others": that is (according to Dr. C.’s interpretation) the following suit me and my brothers well, or can at least be easily tolerated.

### Answer:

(1) This has already been answered in Number 74: namely, that one should not burden one's neighbor with such suspicion and a false understanding of his words. It has also been shown through examples that those

theses which Mr. A. repeats are just as intolerable, and even less appealing to Mr. A. He also knows of no such "brothers," God be praised!—as we have seen in Number 74.

(2) Mr. Cyprian further asks: why did Mr. A. omit the 11th and 12th articles: that God is the cause of sin? The answer is: because he had already excerpted similar blasphemous teachings where it says: **No one is damned because of sin,** but because God willed it so. ## The 77th Accusation:

He excuses the heretics in a very ridiculous manner.

### Answer:

(1) This allegedly happened because he added an explanation to the thesis—"He would be a blessed man who had never placed his trust in the crucified Christ"—namely: "outside of such true communion with him." To this, Mr. Cyprian asks very mockingly: "How does the prophet know that this was the meaning?"

(2) Here, one might have asked him in return (though without mockery): how does he know that in the words preceding Number 76, this was Arnold's meaning? However, one prefers to pass over this and speak with proper seriousness about such an important matter.

(3) It is well known that our best theologians require, in addition to faith in Christ, true communion with him (or that he dwells in our hearts through faith). Without this, faith and trust in him are vain and a human delusion that the depths of the heart never experience; as the blessed <term>Lutherus</term> <note>Martin Luther</note> in the preface to the Epistle to the Romans and elsewhere, as well as <term>Arnd</term> <note>Johann Arndt</note>, <term>Spener</term> <note>Philipp Jakob Spener</note>, and others explain at length. And what is more common and necessary in upright preaching than to urge this against the great complacency and the abuse of the Gospel?

(4) Now, Mr. A. had remarked generally about these theses in §. 24 that it is evident that people—whose characters were varied—had caught these and those words confusedly, arranged them as they pleased, increased them, or mutilated them. This may well have happened with these sentences: namely, that some were speaking against the hypocritical faith of "mouth-Christians" <note>those who offer only lip service</note>, noting that while they seemed to trust in Christ or hope for great things from him, they did not want to have true communion with him or let Christ dwell and rule within them through faith.

### The 79th Accusation:

### Answer:

In what way this is supposed to be proven cannot be seen. Thus, no partiality is seen.

### The 80th Accusation:

->In order to excuse them, he presents their propositions much too mildly.<-

### Answer:

(1) Namely, in the cited place of Book XVII, Chapter 9, §. 30, Mr. A. recounts from <term>Hornbeek</term> that the <term>Brownists</term> <note>an English separatist group</note> fought against the reading of pagan books in schools. (2) <term>Reggius's</term> account is also quite clearly repeated according to the <term>sense</term>; even that which Dr. C. seems to <term>find lacking</term>, namely regarding the eradication of all books and liberal arts. For Mr. A. writes there in §. 31 (which, however, Mr. Cyprian passes over): *They wanted to burn the pagan writers; they recognized no commonplaces or systems, no commentaries, no polemics or controversial writings—indeed, generally no books at all—as good, except for the Bible.* Thus, everything has been correctly reported according to the <term>sense</term>.

### The 83rd Accusation:

->He tells the story of Chancellor Crell from a <term>writing confiscated</term> by the Empire and presents it as credible.<-

#### Answer:

(1) Mr. A. presented this story from proven and mostly Saxon <term>authors</term>, such as **Weccius, Heidenreich, Ziegler, Alberti, Schmid, Blum,** as well as **Carolus, Hartnaccius, Lundorpius, Osiander, etc.** and thus not solely or even mostly from the <term>confiscated writing</term>, as the accusation seems to suggest.

(2) In doing so, he only <term>cited</term> the **Counter-Report of Crell's friends** on a few points, as is customary in <term>questions of fact</term> to use the <term>writings</term> that have been published <term>for and against</term> <note>original: "pro und contra"</note> the matter. But he never knew or saw that this writing had been <term>confiscated</term> by the Emperor. Rather, he himself saw in Dresden for four years that this <term>confiscated</term> little book was very often sold without hesitation in public <term>auctions</term>, and even at the market; he could therefore conclude nothing less than that it was <term>confiscated</term>, or that it was impermissible to <term>cite</term> something from it. And how many <term>confiscated authors</term> are used in <term>historical works</term>, and even cited as rare and <term>curious</term>?

(3) Regarding the <term>questioned</term> point, however—namely, whether the **judgment was spoken by the Emperor—Mr. A. did not deny this (since the Imperial Edict was issued against it) but expressly recounted that the judgment was obtained in Prague.** However, he mentioned in passing <note>original: "obiter"</note> from the Counter-Report that **Crell had spoken against it, saying it was not according to the case files and that he had not been heard enough;** for which reason he also sent in a clarification. In this, Mr. A. only <term>reports what was reported</term> <note>original: "relata referirt"</note> and adds no <term>opinion</term> of his own to it, much less made himself a party to such contradictions. Indeed, he impartially recounted in Section 37 that the friends of <term>Dr. Philipp Nicolai Crell</term> refuted <term>Pierius's Examination</term>.

->**The 87th Accusation:**<-

->He recounts the disputes between Strauch and Calixtus against his better knowledge in a very disparaging way.<-

->**Answer:**<-

(1) Everyone knowledgeable of the matter must admit that in the <term>Syncretistic Controversy</term> <note>A 17th-century theological dispute within Lutheranism about seeking common ground with other Christian denominations.</note> scandalous things happened both for and against the participants. And Mr. M. The wretched monuments of those polemical writings still lie before everyone's eyes, showing how the theologians treated each other in offensive and unchristian ways; so that it cannot be called into doubt.

(2) Nevertheless, Mr. Arnold is said to have treated <term>Calixtus</term> <note>Georg Calixtus, a professor at Helmstedt who advocated for religious peace.</note> in an unchristian manner by historically reporting Dr. Strauch's clear words about him and adding nothing more. Mr. Arnold would also gladly let the actions of such persons rest; but because Mr. Cyprian accuses the author of shameful partiality and charges him as if he had written simply and against his better knowledge that Calixtus, according to Dr. Strauch's claim, had been in brothels: Therefore, let the reader check the Church History himself: there he will find nothing more than this: The former (Strauch) had written of the young Calixtus: "It would be no wonder if the suppressed Lutherans could not be found in the drinking houses and brothels of the French and Italians."

(3) Now, Dr. Strauch later explained himself regarding these words: but Mr. Cyprian himself doubts whether this explanation has any basis: he will also see it very differently, namely because the words speak all too clearly of <term>wine taverns</term> <note>original: "tabernis vinariis"</note> and <term>brothels</term> <note>original: "fornicibus"</note>. And if Mr. Arnold had immediately added this forced <term>explanation</term> <note>original: "Explication"</note>, which, to his recollection, had not occurred to him at the time; it might also have been interpreted poorly against him, as if he wanted to show no mercy to these theologians by citing such wretched explanations.

II. Part 87. 88. N. Mr. Director Cyprian's Accusations. 283

(4) Furthermore, one does not take it ill of Mr. Cyprian that he <term>venerates</term> <note>original: "venerirt"</note> the younger Calixtus as his teacher: On the other hand, because Mr. Arnold had no connection in this case with Calixtus, he cannot be blamed for seeing it differently; Mr. Cyprian, however, only mentions the <term>Quakers</term> and <term>Weigelians</term> <note>Followers of Valentin Weigel, an early mystic; both groups were often viewed as heretical by the orthodox.</note> as the author's friends out of mockery, and he may see how he accounts for that himself.

->**The 88th Accusation:**<-

->Arnold undeservedly accuses Dr. Beyer of lying.<-

->**Answer:**<-

(1) First, Mr. Cyprian asserts that the history of <term>Weigel</term> <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and mystic whose works were published posthumously.</note> is completely distorted. The reader, however, will find that the distorted reports of this man were instead thoroughly investigated and corrected, and indeed from unimpeachable writers. (See below in Part IV, n. 162. seqq.)

(2) This is said to be an example of distortion: Schelhammer, in his refutation of Weigel's *Postils* <note>A collection of sermons or commentaries on scripture.</note>, had only conjectured that Weigel might have read <term>Hermes</term>, <term>Paracelsus</term>, the <term>Sibyls</term>, and <term>Dionysius</term> in his father's library: then the opponents of Weigel lied by adding that Weigel lay over these books day and night.

(3) To this, it is kindly answered: (α) that Schelhammer speaks only conjecturally not only here, but also in other indicated points, is clearly to be seen from his words; and among other things, where he also suspects or rather feigns that the theologians of Wittenberg and Leipzig would have surely examined him and deposed him as a fanatic and deceiver—which, however, did not happen and is a well-known fiction.

(4) Thus, (β) only the question remains whether the following writers propagated such conjectures about Weigel. Concerning this, Mr. Arnold cites not only Dr. Beyer, Colberg, and Hornbeck, but many others. None among these, however, proves in the slightest that Weigel took his ideas from <term>Paracelsus</term>, <term>Schwenkfeld</term>, or <term>Lautensack</term>, but they only surmise it and do not know it for certain. ### The 89. Accusation:

->**A. deceives and forges: he has falsified Böhme’s history without any forehead or shame.** <note>The German idiom "ohne Stirn und Scham" means to do something utterly shamelessly.</note><-

B.) etiam vocatus Dresdam, ubi coram Doctoribus Hoe, Meisner, Balduin, Gerhard, Lyser & duobus Professoribus Matheseos doctrina suæ examen subiit."</note> For this reason, however, Dr. Kortholt does not deceive or forge at all, and thus neither does Mr. Arnold.

(2) Firstly, to prove such a harsh accusation, it is produced that: Mr. Arnold wishes to prove Jacob Böhme’s examination from such authors who are either his friends or his enemies.

(3) In this regard, Mr. Cyprian first rejects Hegetitium and Matthæi as friends of the <term>Boehmists</term> <note>Followers of Jacob Böhme’s mystical philosophy.</note>; the former of whom lived shortly after Böhme’s time. (Regarding the insult "Boehmists," one can read Mr. Lange’s reports in Volume V, page 34, and see how false it is.) Furthermore, he rejects the late Dr. <term>Spener</term> <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism," who emphasized personal devotion over rigid dogma.</note>, who discussed this whole matter in detail in *The Freedom of Believers*, page 102 and following, and who showed himself here neither as an enemy (which his Christian moderation never permitted) nor as a friend, since he never approved of Jacob Böhme, but rather found much wanting, as is clear from his aforementioned treatise.

(4) Now, one should reasonably not so directly reject such a man—whose sincerity and wisdom Mr. Cyprian otherwise estimates himself—especially since he was not only at that time, when he wrote this, the Chief Court Preacher and Church Councilor in Dresden, and thus at the place in question <note>original: "in loco quæstionis"</note>, but he also expressly testified against Calovius’ *Against Böhme* <note>original: "Anti-Boehmum"</note> that the alleged testimony of Baron Friesen against this examination was not there; Calovius

### The 93rd Accusation:

->He is said to have falsified the documents of the most prominent Böhmians <note>followers of the mystic Jacob Böhme</note> to favor the Böhmians.<-

### Answer:

(1) It is claimed there is no honest *intention* <note>original: "Intention"</note> here because Mr. A. [Arnold] reported from Franckenberg <note>Abraham von Franckenberg (1593–1652), Böhme’s friend and biographer</note>: *Jacob Böhme wrote everything down in his manuscripts cleanly and without copying.* This is said to be (a) poor evidence because Franckenberg, a Böhmain, says it: (β) it is also said to be falsified because the word **Everything** is supposedly an addition.

(2) However, (a.) Franckenberg’s testimony can very well be sufficient proof, because he was an eyewitness <note>original Greek: "testis αὐτόπτης"</note>, and otherwise has a good testimony of honesty in his writings and his entire conduct, so that even his enemies can say nothing bad about him. Indeed, Prof. Kranz in Breslau praises him (even though he accuses him of Böhmiansim) as follows: *He is altogether a pious man, which we cannot deny* <note>original Latin: "Pius omnino, quod negare non possumus"</note>, as found in the author of the Refutation by Dr. Buddeus, p. 63. (b.) The word **Everything** is not actually an addition, but it is contained in the overall sense <note>original: "Sensu"</note>, when it says: **In the writings, not a single little word was seen to be changed or crossed out;** Now, where not even a single little word is changed, everything is indeed clean. One also sees clearly from Mr. A.'s context that he did not excerpt the words exactly, but only the sense briefly, since it was only after these words that he marked the following as the author’s own words *in the margin*; the worthy reader may please look it up for himself. Thus, his intention as well as the expression was honest.

(3) For (c.) it is claimed that it was written more falsely and partially than even by J. B.'s most heated *apologists* <note>defenders</note>, when Mr. A. says that Hegenitius <note>Gottfried Hegenitius, an author who wrote about his travels and encounters</note> wrote that J. B. answered the theologians in Dresden so gently and modestly. Not a word of all this is said to be in Hegenitius’s letter; they claim the fraud cannot be excused.

(4) Here there would certainly be great cause to convict Mr. Cyprian of fraud; however, I would rather view it as a mistake. For Mr. Cyprian has once again been very overhasty with his judgments of falsehood, de-

### The 95th Accusation.

[Arnold] leaves out what Croese adds to it: "hac ætate juvenili," in his young years.* But one should look at Arnold’s version to see if he omitted these words, where he states: *Croese assures us that he showed remarkable piety and modesty in his youth.* Here the words stand in plain letters. Truly, Mr. Cyprian would not like it if someone tried to refute him and, in doing so, brought such unprovable and false charges against him. What exaggerations and mockeries would then follow? He should consider here what he would say if he were treated for such falsifications in the same way he has encountered H. A.: and he should

[...of our] churches / that it seems / he begrudges them hellish fire as gladly / as any worldly hardship. Many would stand on the right hand [of God] whom A. [Arnold] painted blacker than the Devil, and so forth.

#### Answer:

(1) Mr. Dr. Cyprian will not be able to deny / if he reads these embittered accusations once more with even the slightest awe before God / that his heated zeal misled him into such excessive expressions <note>original: "excessive Expressiones"</note>. One could with all right and according to appearances / and with the approval of every dispassionate reader / turn this back upon him / considering how he must have been minded during this writing of his. But what would it use or build? God grant him grace / to look deeply into the state of his own soul / and then to fight earnestly against the fury of nature / which must commonly be called a zeal for religion / so that he might instead put on more love toward his neighbor / whom he has looked upon with an evil eye / in repentance through faith!

(2) He nevertheless swears by a great oath that this is truly so of Mr. A. / that he begrudges our teachers hellish fire and all hardship. Nevertheless, the conscience of the so harshly and wickedly accused Mr. A. gives him this testimony in the Holy Spirit now and at all times / that he does not begrudge even temporal plagues / let alone hellish fire / to a single poor creature of God / whom Christ has purchased with His blood. Indeed, has he not been most vehemently branded a heretic by Mr. Cyprian for this very reason / because he only wished or hoped / that in the end all things might be restored? <note>This refers to the doctrine of "Apocatastasis" or universal restoration, which Arnold was often accused of holding—making the charge that he "wished hell" on people particularly ironic.</note> Thus the emotions / in which the author was attacked and such important matters were treated / are plain to see; yet in such a state it is not possible / to remain fit for the proper investigation of truth.

#### The 97th Accusation:

### The 98th Accusation:

->That he has erred yet again.<-

### Answer:

(1) First, Mr. Cyprian says it is an error that Michael Maier <note>original: "Michael Meyer," a famous alchemist and physician</note> published the *Silence after the Clamors* <note>original: "Silentium post clamores"</note> without a name. To be sure, it is stated of the first edition that it was indeed published without a name, and only under the letters R. M. F. Furthermore, it is stated of the second edition: that it also came out soon in the year 1617 in German with the title. Mr. Dr. Cyprian has only seen this second edition, and thus thought there was only one; however, both were known to Mr. Arnold, as he possessed a great collection <note>original: "Apparatum"</note> of such writings. Thus, it is not Arnold, but Mr. Cyprian who has erred.
(2) The other error is said to be that Arnold tried to force the number of the three students <note>original: "Studioforum"</note> out of Piccart. However, no force was needed; for he did not cite Piccart alone in the 13th Chapter of the 17th Book, Section 12, but also the original letters <note>original: "Epistolas autographas"</note> of Hæpner and Schræder, two well-known theologians, in which the number is named.
(3) It is true that Mr. Arnold first calls Soner a student, but afterward he corrects himself and calls him, in Section 15, a Professor of Physics and Medicine. But in such circumstances, one error or another is quite possible in a work of such great extent.

## The 101st Accusation:
->That everything is true which *Sandius* <note>Christopher Sand (1644–1680), a historian of the Socinians</note> prattles about the Socinians.<-

### Answer:
(1) That Mr. A. used *Sandius's* reports in the history of the Socinians <note>A non-trinitarian sect that emphasized reason in interpreting Scripture</note> is true, and he found it necessary because other historians have done so as well, since otherwise one has few detailed reports of this sect, and most of their records have been suppressed.

(2) But as for the claim that he should hold all of *Sandius's* "prattle" to be true, the opposite is clearly recognizable from his first General Protest against the Socinians as Rationalists <note>original: "Vernünfftlinge," a derogatory term for those who put reason above revelation</note> in the preface to the *History of the Church and Heretics*. This is the mark of one who does not wish to burden his neighbor without true cause. He has not only read *Spanheim’s* judgment against *Sandius*, but also that of many other learned people. He also knows what *Gardiner*, *Bull*, and especially Mr. Dr. *Majus* at Giessen have written thoroughly against him.

(3) But he specifically cited the very Christian and gentle judgment of the famous theologian and philologist at Leiden, *Stephen le Moyne*, regarding this poor erring man in the 13th Chapter of the 17th Book, page 26. This is particularly remarkable among others because this theologian confesses,

confesses, and remembers with such a joyful conscience (in the *Prolegomena to Various Sacred Matters* <note>original: "Prolegomenis ad Varia Sacra"</note> page 34, line *) that he vindicated and maintained the cause of the Son of **God** against this learned and diligent enemy. He notes that *Sandius* himself, had he lived, would not have been unwilling to approve of his humanity and his manner of disputing, which was not at all coarse or boorish <note>original: "Methodum non ἀγροῖκον" (a non-rustic method)</note>. We also have the most recent examples <note>original: "exempla recentissima"</note> of Mr. Dr. *Spener* and Mr. Dr. *Antonius* <note>Leaders of the Pietist movement</note> before our eyes, who certainly remained owing nothing to the Socinian errors. Such a friendly manner of disputing is still to be wished for in many others, so that more fruit and blessing might be seen from polemical writings than is often the case. However, when one breaks out immediately into such slanders without true cause, as is to be seen soon in the following number, then it is not exactly a method that is not uncouth <note>original: "methodus non ἀγροῖκος"</note>, much less a Christian one <note>original: "χριστιανικὴ"</note> or one that characterizes Christianity <note>original: "χαρακτηρίζουσα τὸν χριστιανισμόν"</note>, as *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom, an Early Church Father</note> speaks of Christian love in the 31st Homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews.

## The 102nd Accusation:
->All who know the matter must laugh at such folly.<-

### Answer:
(1) Firstly, this is said in justification: Mr. A. spends so many pages on the defense of the Anabaptists <note>Radical reformers who rejected infant baptism</note>, but barely touches upon their horrors at Münster in 19 lines.

(2) However, the pages are not merely spent on or full of excuses, but rather with the narrative of circumstances and histories in sequence, as many of them as could not well be passed over. In this regard, Mr. A. himself complained right at the beginning in the 16th Book, Chapter 21, Section 1, about the vastness and confusion of this history, of which so many large books exist.

(3) Thus, Director *Cypr.* has viewed the entire history as a mere and professedly <note>original: "ex professo"</note> presented excuse. This is, however, quite different, especially as Mr. A.’s confessions against these people could already be seen in the 60th and following accusations. And whatever testimonies he cited regarding the little good that was still among them (as there is likely no sect so evil that it does not still have something good), these are mostly confessions of their own refuters, which were invented by no one. Therefore, it is not forbidden to repeat them in a history; indeed, they are just as necessary as the opposing views.

(4) On the other hand, he [Arnold] has also described the abominations of those of Münster on page 17 as much as was required for the knowledge of the matter: and who would not abhor them, since they are indeed quite inhuman? He expressly relates there in §. 15: They had alleged many prophecies and other things; that John <note>John of Leiden (1509–1536), the self-proclaimed "King of Zion" during the Münster Rebellion</note> had sought dominion in every way and otherwise all freedom of the flesh, and among other things had committed many abominations with unchastity, murder, and cruelty; had made himself king and allowed himself to be turned away from his conceived imagination by no means. Furthermore, he says in §. 16: one finds very many signs of the terrible confusion of these wretched people: each one strove to be the most prominent, and committed much violence and many murders against one another: for which reason **GOD** also gave them into the hands of their enemies: Likewise, this tragedy came to a wretched end. Similarly in Chapter 21, §. 5: they had shown themselves so insolent and un-Christian in the riot, etc.

(5) Here, of course, many specifics of their abominations could have been brought forward: However, the authors are also sufficiently indicated therein, from whom everyone can read it for himself, especially since such descriptions are found in abundance in almost all German history books (particularly in *Sleidanus* <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), the most influential historian of the Reformation</note>, which can even be seen in German in citizens' houses, and from which all the others have taken it).

(6) It is indeed judged from this that A. speaks quite "tenderly": that John *shall have* <note>the German "sol" implies "is said to have"</note> committed many abominations; just as if one did not even know it for certain yet. However, the fact that Mr. A. does not write tenderly of this man is well proven by his words just cited. But while he <term>expresses</term> <note>original: "exprimmirt"</note> the history once through such language, he in no way denies the facts.

(7) For he speaks, moreover, throughout the entire narrative certainly as of an indisputable history. But here he speaks only relatively and from the mind of others. As it is not unusual in histories that even with the most certain facts, one who repeats them from others, and not as an <term>eyewitness</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐτόπτης" (autoptes)</note>, is accustomed to say: It is said (namely, from the report of this or that person) that this and that happened: for that reason one does not cast the fact into doubt, but rather lets it rest on another’s credit; as one could bring forward many examples of this, if it were necessary. Meanwhile, it would be easy to show that not every single circumstance, as they are commonly found concerning those of Münster, actually occurred in truth: but time must be turned to something more necessary.

For the rest, one gladly allows Director Cyprian his laughter; but perhaps the weeping or mourning over such over-hasty judgments against his brother—that one has scolded a fool without cause—also has its time, according to Solomon's saying <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 3:4, "a time to weep, and a time to laugh"</note>, upon which the authors of the *Innocent Reports* <note>original: "Unschuld. Nachrichten," a leading orthodox Lutheran journal of the time</note> knew how to strongly invoke themselves in a similar case in the year 1706, p. 642.

### The 103rd Accusation.

A. wishes to persuade us that the remaining Anabaptists separated themselves from those of Münster, especially Menno <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561), the leader of the peaceful Anabaptists from whom Mennonites take their name</note>.

### Answer:

(1) Precisely this has already been persuaded to us by the Protestant historians themselves, before and until A. began to write about it, and Mr. A. has clearly proven such from the confessions of their opponents. For thus writes the Dutch theologian cited by him, Melchior Leydecker, in his notes on Hornius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Period III, Article 37, p. 342, regarding Menno: *He differed from those of Münster, and disapproved of polygamy; he also wrote against the blasphemies of John of Leiden, who had sold himself as King; yet he acknowledged the Münsterites as his brothers, though not approving of their disturbances.* <note>original Latin: "Diffensit a Monasteriensibus, atque Polygamiam improbabat..."</note> In this, he cites Brandt’s *History of the Reformation*, Part I, page 139.

(2) Yes, *Hornius* himself testifies there that much: that the following Anabaptists began to take up more peaceful counsels, *especially under the authorship of Menno, who, while retaining most of their dogmas, taught that they must abstain from weapons.* <note>original Latin: "pacatiora consilia... autore inprimis Mennone..."</note> This confession of Menno against the Münster riot can be read in his book about Christ the true King.

(3) Joh. Henricus Ottius, who wrote expressly against them, notes this of them in the Preface on the *Kinds of Anabaptists*, page C. 3: *Just as the first Anabaptists erred in excess in the exercise of magistracy, or regarding a worldly kingdom, even if not called to it: so the modern ones [err] in deficiency, with all power plainly trampled and cast away; they detest the deed of the former, although they are their parents and progenitors, along with polygamy and enthusiasm.* <note>original Latin: "Quemadmodum primi Anabaptistae peccarunt in excessu..."</note>

(4) Indeed, among our own theologians, Dr. Melchior Nicolai, Provost at Stuttgart, confesses very clearly in his *Refutation of Anabaptism*, and thus precisely during the controversy against these people, in Chapter V, p. 254: It may well be that the satanic spirit of lies has not yet gone through the whole Anabaptist swarm and infected them with the above-mentioned abominations of those of Münster, indeed that

(6) Among the most recent authors, Dr. Buddeus <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a leading Lutheran philosopher and theologian</note> in his *Dissertation on the Reconciliation of the Christian Religion and the State*, Chapter VI, §. 2, p. 130, observed this: "On account of either the dogmas or the deeds of the followers of Müntzer and the Münsterites, the rest are by no means to be blamed, since they clearly profess themselves to be very far removed from them." <note>original: "Ob Munzerianorum & Monasteriensium aut dogmata aut facta reliqui neutiquam sunt culpandi, quippe qui ab illis longissimè se adesse disertè profitentur."</note> And he strengthens this from so many old and new documents which indeed cannot be denied, all of which support the report in the Church History. Compare also the same Dr. Buddeus in *The Blameless Defense of Moderation*, p. 12 and following.

(7) Against these unanimous testimonies of our teachers and those of the Reformed, Dr. Cyprian now objects that the Anabaptists nevertheless all called one another brothers. However, the aforementioned Leydeckerus has himself admitted in the cited words that these people still call each other brothers, even if they do not agree on certain questionable points, such as this one [the rebellion] alongside <term>Enthusiasm</term> <note>The belief in direct, private revelations from the Holy Spirit over scripture</note> and polygamy. Indeed, what is more, Capito <note>Wolfgang Capito (1478–1541), a Reformer of Strasbourg</note> called several Anabaptists his "dearest brothers" in his words cited above at the 60th exhibit, yet he remained a Protestant and stayed separate from the Münsterites.

(8) He says further β) that these Münsterites were only abandoned by the others after their misfortune. This may indeed be true, as there were also many Münster-minded people in the Amsterdam uprising. However, it is even clearer from their public protests that they were not only deterred by the evil outcome, but also by the godless and rebellious teaching itself.

(9) He also cites γ) Menno’s <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561), the leader of the peaceful Anabaptists from whom the Mennonites take their name</note> *Foundation Book*, where the author supposedly calls the Münsterites his brothers and calls their uprising only a "small sin" for which **GOD** would nevertheless be merciful to them. In this, it is 

<column-break/>

<page-num>301</page-num>
<header>Vol. II. TH. 103. N. Accusations of Director Cyprian.</header>

however, to be noted that the authors he cites clearly show how Menno and Obbe Philips <note>An early Anabaptist leader who, like Menno, turned away from the violence of the radical movement</note> did not agree with them on this point. For Hornbekius <note>Johannes Hoornbeeck (1617–1666), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note> repeats these words of Philips on page 353: that his soul was terrified and saddened by the Münster and Amsterdam affairs; likewise over the false missions, prophecies, visions, dreams, revelations, and the unspeakable spiritual pride of the same, etc. Also, Menno's words: that it is not fitting for others to follow them in that which they have sinned and erred <note>original: "gedoold" - a Dutch term for straying or erring</note> against the **LORD**, etc.

(10) Ottius likewise, who also cites Menno's words on page 97, nevertheless notes that Menno’s book was directed "against the greatest blasphemies of John of Leiden" <note>original: "contra maximas blasphemias Johannis Leydensis"</note> and that on page 934, he wipes away all kinds of calumnies, especially as if they [the Mennonites] had descended from the Münsterites. And on page 74, he admits of Menno: "Although not in all things, yet in many he agreed with the Münsterites," <note>original: "Licet non in omnibus, tamen in multis Monasterianis consensit"</note> and adds that "it is doubtful whether or not Menno had a part with these people." <note>original: "dubium, annon Menno partem habuerit cum hisce"</note> From all this, an impartial reader will be able to decide the matter for himself and at the same time see the truth of this entire contradiction.

# The Third Part.

## On an Anonymous person’s so-called Presentation of many intentional falsifications committed by G. A. <note>G. A. refers to the author, Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714).</note> against ancient and modern writers, and his offensive defense of Heretics and Atheists.

### The 1st Accusation:

He often speaks very contemptuously and insultingly of high, even highest authorities without lawful cause. p. 20.

->Answer:<-

(1) The reasons why those *personal matters* <note>original: "Personalia"</note> which the Mr. Anonymous brings forward concerning the deceased Mr. Dr. Veiel <note>Elias Veiel (1635–1706), a Lutheran theologian and critic of Arnold.</note> are passed over here have already been sufficiently reported above in the preface. The intention here is only to briefly but thoroughly illuminate those *substantive matters* <note>original: "Realia"</note> or objections which have been brought against the *I. H.* <note>Arnold’s "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" (Unparteiische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie).</note>

(2) Regarding this first imputation, an impartial reader will have already encountered enough sincere proof above in Part 1, Num. 33, that Mr. Arnold does not hold even the slightest lower authority in contempt, let alone the high or highest. Indeed, he has constantly proven by his deeds, and has received testimony from all his *superiors* <note>original: "Superioribus"</note> to this day, that he is subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether it be to the king as supreme, or to the governors as his envoys, according to 1 Peter 2:13–14.

(3) The proof for the *contrary* <note>original: "contrairen"</note> imputation, however, rests on the words which the Anonymous person misuses from the *I. H.* (Vol. II, Book 3, Ch. 5, § 12), where the Emperor Theodosius II is called a hypocrite because he titled Cyril "the Most Holy." <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444), a powerful bishop known for his central role in the Council of Ephesus.</note> But who does not see that this does not insult high authority at all, but only *expresses* <note>original: "exprimiret"</note> the historical truth concerning an Emperor who died more than 1,000 years ago, as it clearly lies before us *from the facts* <note>original: "ex factis"</note> themselves? Even a child can recognize Cyril's unholiness from what we will encounter regarding him below in Num. 24. §. 4. And what do other *historians* <note>original: "Historici"</note> not criticize in this same Emperor—that he banished his wife and had the innocent Paulinus executed on mere suspicion—and yet they have not insulted the authorities because of it? Indeed, what do countless writers not *judge* <note>original: "judiciren"</note> concerning the vices of other Emperors? How vehemently they rail against Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363), who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note>, who was nevertheless
<meta>catchword: as</meta>

---

<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>Part III. 1. 2. N. on old and new writers and defense of H. and A. 303</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

also ordained by God as an authority? Should they therefore commit the *crime of treason* <note>original: "Crimen læsæ Majestatis," referring to the legal concept of injured majesty or treason against the crown.</note>? No rational person would say so. It is also known from church histories that teachers complained *specifically* <note>original: "in specie"</note> about this Emperor Theodosius II, that he was all too negligent and *indulgent* <note>original: "indulgent"</note> in punishments and *executions* <note>original: "Executionen"</note>. Such and other *vices* <note>original: "Vitia"</note> are *reported* <note>original: "referirt"</note> daily in histories regarding the highest heads of state, and no one interprets it as an insult to authority (unless they have the un-Christian intention of slandering their neighbor).

### The 2nd Accusation:

He falsifies Ottius. p. 22. <note>Johann Heinrich Ott (1617–1682), a Swiss theologian and author of a history of the Anabaptists.</note>

->Answer:<-

(1) This is said to have occurred in the 16th Book of the *I. H.* at the 14th Chapter, § 21. There it says: The Anabaptists were severely pressured because they considered drinking feasts and other such banquets to be wrong.

(2) Here Anonymous *requires* <note>original: "desideriret"</note> it to be said that the Anabaptists were severely pressured for this reason, because Ottius, *in the place cited* <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> p. 91, only tells of a *colloquy* <note>original: "Colloquio," a formal theological discussion.</note> of Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a prominent Protestant reformer.</note> with these people. However, not the slightest thing is falsified here; rather, the matter was *reported* <note>original: "referirt"</note> according to its *sequence* <note>original: "Suite"</note> as it stands in Ottius. For Mr. Arnold *reflected* <note>original: "reflectirt"</note> upon the whole *connection* <note>original: "Connexion"</note> of the author, and upon the *precedents* and *consequences* <note>original: "Antecedentia und Consequentia"</note>, as was certainly proper.

(3) Now, it stands in Ottius previously—and indeed from the Cassel records themselves—how *in the same year* <note>original: "eodem anno"</note> 1536, when this *colloquy* took place, the *responses of the theologians* <note>original: "Theologorum Responsa"</note> to punish the Anabaptists with the sword were repeated, and the Landgrave himself was *resolved* <note>original: "resolvirt"</note> to resist this sect through *inquisition* <note>original: "Inquisition," meaning a judicial inquiry.</note>, imprisonment, and legal severity (p. 86 and 89). Following that, this *colloquy* is related, and finally on page 93 it is mentioned how several imprisoned Anabaptists requested the same from the Prince.

(4) From all these obvious circumstances, it is to be concluded with truth that also on account of such matters as drinking feasts and similar *questions* <note>original: "Quæstionibus"</note>, these imprisoned people were severely pressured; especially since even now these and other such things are usually very urgently *defended*, as can be seen further in Part IV, Num. 124.

### The 3rd Accusation:

He considers the Imperial Coronation Banquet to be an Epicurean feast. p. 22.

->Answer:<-

(1) The full answer to this reproach was provided in Part IV, Num. 124; what the Anonymous critic scatters in particular consists of the following:

(2) He says on page 23 that Mr. A. <note>Arnold</note> speaks quite shamefully of the royal coronation ceremonies of that time. However, he does not speak shamefully, but rather truthfully and earnestly according to the rule of Christ's teaching. Nor does he carp at the ceremonies or the meal itself, but rather at the overly lustful praise that *Crusius* <note>Martin Crusius (1526–1607), a humanist historian known for his detailed accounts of public festivities.</note> expressed regarding it.

(3) The Anonymous critic says that at the coronation of Solomon, they ate and drank with great joy (1 Kings 1:39–40). It says there, however—which the Anonymous critic omits—that it happened "before the Lord," in His fear, and as if before His face.

(4) Furthermore, he says: Mr. A. did not act as an impartial historian when he so vehemently condemned this meal, since the Emperor *Ferdinand* was never drunk from wine, etc. But A. has nowhere spoken of the person of this Emperor or his son, but only of the strange fame that *Crusius* attributes to this meal, and of the well-known German custom of which the Anonymous himself must present the confession of *Camerarius* <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a scholar and associate of Melanchthon.</note> below on page 136, § 7: "the greatest drinking contests were then fought in the courts." <note>original: "poculorum certamina maximè tunc in aulis certabantur."</note> That is to say, they boozed at the court banquets. Since such a large banquet does not occur without excess and the abuse of God's gifts, it should be mourned and sighed over rather than praised or excused, even though *Crusius* calls it "delightful things" <note>original: "delectabilia"</note> and "such great glory" <note>original: "tantam gloriam"</note>, and therefore concludes thoughtfully: "It pains me so much that time could not and cannot be halted in its joy. For if this were possible, how many splendid banquets, how sweet the music, how lovely the dances would continually remain!" <note>original: "Tantum dolet mihi, tempus in lætitia non potuisse nec posse ſisti. Si enim hoc fieri poſſet, quot splendida convivia, quàm suavis muſica, quàm amabiles choreæ continenter manerent!"</note>

(5) The judgment of this is left to the Christian-minded reader, as is the question of whether Mr. A. speaks well of no one but the wicked, and ill of the good, as the Anonymous concludes. Let one judge whether these words of *Crusius* are good or evil, whether the excuse of the Anonymous is Christian or not, and whether A.'s thoughts on it are right or wrong: for here it is purely a matter of the truth, and not of the prestige of the person.

## The 4th Accusation:
He protests [his innocence], even when he has evil in mind. p. 26.

<meta>catchword: Ant-</meta>

->Answer:<-

(1) The Anonymous critic takes an example from *Luther’s* history, in which Mr. A. first protests (in Vol. 16, Ch. 5, § 21) but later cannot tolerate it when people compare *Luther* with *Elijah*, *John*, and *Paul*.

(2) As for the protestation, anyone who reads it in the cited place without prejudice will recognize that the author was serious, and that (as he says) he did not want to blacken this magnificent instrument <note>referring to Luther</note> or agree with the malicious slanderers in the Papacy.

(3) But the evil that the author is supposed to have had in mind is by no means evil if one wishes to follow the rule of the Gospel. For should it be evil when an Evangelical Christian desires moderation regarding these and similar excessive expressions; which are cited there in the *K. H.* <note>Arnold’s "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" (Unparteiische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie).</note> § 22 from *Eobanus Hessus* <note>Helius Eobanus Hessus (1488–1540), a celebrated Latin poet of the Reformation.</note> (whose drunkenness the Anonymous himself must admit below on p. 136)?
> "Forgive me, but the eloquence of great Paul
> Scarcely moved gasping men toward holy teachings
> As much as the words of the apostolic Luther moved them."
<note>original: "Vix ita, da veniam magni facundia Pauli / Movit anhelantes dogmata ſancta viros, / Sicut Apoſtolici moverunt verba Lutheri."</note>

(4) Here too much is indeed said—namely, that *Paul* could hardly move people as much as *Luther*. It is surely permitted among Evangelicals to observe this *modestly* <note>original: "modeste"</note>, and it is nothing evil, but impartial and good; especially since above in Part I, Num. 3, the praises of *Luther* from the *K. H.* show how worthy and dear he is to the author.

## The 5th Accusation:
He accuses *Luther* of some errors and falsifies *Mathesius*. p. 26. <note>Johannes Mathesius (1504–1565), a student and biographer of Luther.</note>

->Answer:<-

(1) Why Mr. A., along with all Evangelical Christians, must not make an idol out of any man and must write the truth about *Luther* himself, he has proven himself in the mentioned place. Moreover, this was touched upon somewhat above in Part I, Num. 55, but it is also evident enough from God's Word.

(2) Based on this foundation, and following the proper words of praise for *Luther*, he has now quite modestly noted in the cited place § 25: That in many important points it was human for him (*Luther*) to err, as is evident from his writings; which from his—

(3) Now, in this matter Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> speaks with our theologians, who have indeed always acknowledged that these non-<term>specified judgments</term> <note>original: "specificirte Judicia"; refers to vague or unsupported opinions</note> are by no means justifiable. And do not many still <term>object</term> <note>original: "excipiren"</note> to Luther’s early writings whenever this or that point does not suit them? They <term>establish</term> <note>original: "statuiren"</note> <term>by the very fact</term> <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> that Luther, being a man, erred; indeed, they clearly acknowledge this even regarding the "Papist" opinions that still clung to him. Proof <term>in a manifest matter</term> <note>original: "in re Manifesta"; a matter that is self-evident</note> is unnecessary.

(4) Regarding the <term>imputed</term> <note>original: "imputirte"; alleged or blamed</note> falsification of Matthesius <note>Johannes Matthesius (1504–1565), a student and biographer of Luther</note>, the following should be observed. This <term>disciple</term> <note>original: "Discipulus"</note> of the late Luther recounted in his 6th Sermon on Luther, page 57, how some people, whom he calls <term>enthusiasts</term> <note>original: "Schwärmer"; a derogatory term used by Luther and his followers for radical reformers like the Anabaptists</note>, judged Dr. Luther: they said he had indeed begun in the Spirit and won several battles and skirmishes against the Pope; but now, because he had ordered the rebels to be struck dead <note>A reference to the Peasants' War of 1524–1525, where Luther sided with the nobility</note>, the Spirit had departed from him, just as it departed from Saul.

(5) These <term>formal points</term> <note>original: "Formalia"</note> are all repeated in the *Kirchen-Historie* <note>Church History</note> in the place cited. And yet Matthesius is said to be falsified: (1) because it is not stated that these people were "enthusiasts" and enemies of Luther; (2) because it says "many," when it was supposedly only one person.

(6) Regarding the first point: in this <term>passage</term> <note>original: "Loco"</note> of the *Kirchen-Historie* (§ 25 and following), there appear sequentially not only this <term>judgment</term> <note>original: "Judicium"</note> of his enemies, but also many other confessions from Luther’s friends, as well as many examples of his subsequent weaker state. In particular, this <term>sentiment</term> agrees with them in certain parts, though every reader can see for themselves that it is too harsh and thus not the judgment of a friend, as a friend would never compare Luther to Saul’s spirit-less condition.

(7) However, if the name "enthusiast" <note>original: "Schwärmer"</note> is not included in the *Kirchen-Historie*, it was not done out of any malice to <term>confuse</term> <note>original: "confundiren"</note> the reader so they would not know if friends or enemies said it—since, as indicated, the judgment itself already showed something hostile to everyone—but rather because this slur is not found to be consistent with the Gospel or inoffensive, and such weakness of the dear elders could well be passed over.

(8) Regarding the second point, it should be considered that although Matthesius <term>reports</term> <note>original: "referirt"</note> the words of only a single person (for many could certainly not speak at once), he nevertheless explicitly mentions three of them, and before that speaks quite <term>indefinitely</term> in the <term>plural</term> of many who were all united in these and other points. Thus, the author could write of "many" with total truth and has consequently falsified nothing in this matter either.

### The 6th Accusation:

->That he falsely accuses the theologians through a malicious <term>citation</term> <note>original: "Allegation"</note> of the *Wittenberg Councils* <note>original: "Conciliorum Wittebergensium"; a collection of legal and theological opinions from the Wittenberg faculty</note> page 29.<-

### Answer:

(1) After the <term>Anonymous critic</term> <note>original: "Anonymus"</note> on page 28 could not deny what Mr. Court-Councilor Pfanner had written—namely, that he knew of no point of accusation against the Lutherans that should be <term>removed</term> <note>original: "expungiren"</note>, and that there were thus (as the Anonymous critic <term>paraphrases</term> and admits) teachers and listeners among the Lutherans who were stained with this or that vice, and that therefore such points of accusation cannot be denied—he also does not wish to deny in § 6 that there were some among the Lutheran theologians who changed their <term>offices</term> <note>original: "Officia"</note> for the sake of higher positions of honor.

(2) However, he seeks (1) to <term>retort</term> <note>original: "retorquiren"</note> that there are similar people among the promoters of piety, though he brings forward no example of it.

(3) Secondly, he claims the passage in the *Kirchen-Historie* is false, unjust, and even godless, where the changing of offices out of ambition is discussed in Book 16, Chapter 15, § 2, and an example from the *Wittenberg Councils* Volume 11, page 52, is cited. There, the question is <term>framed</term> whether a <term>transfer</term> <note>original: "Translation"</note> of a <term>Superintendent</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative official in the Lutheran church</note> from one church to another—while still retaining his <term>oversight</term> <note>original: "Inspektion"</note>—can be accepted with a good conscience and without injury to his honor?

(4) The answer of the theologians to this is, among other things: Although a <term>relocation</term> <note>original: "Translocation"</note> is undertaken for the gentleman, he is nevertheless not expelled from his churches, over which he carries spiritual <term>oversight</term> and the superior care of souls as <term>Superintendent</term>, much less driven out of that city and church; rather, he remains in his <term>supreme dignity</term> <note>original: "suprema Dignitate"</note>. — And thus we do not see how he could be harmed in his honor and worth by this, etc.

(5) These <term>expressions</term> <note>original: "Expressiones"</note> aim at temporal honor and highest dignity, as well as at the avoidance of worldly disgrace and contempt. Now, if one <term>compares</term> <note>original: "conferirt"</note> such things with the teaching of Christ and his Apostles—who placed such great blessedness in disgrace and being ill-spoken of, and were content with bad rumors and shame, indeed, did not heed them but rather rejoiced over them—then it is nothing wrong, much less false or godless, if the <term>contrary</term> <note>original: "Contrarium"</note> is noted in the *Kirchen-Historie*.

have been repeated in Part II, Number 9. No Papist, no Reformed, or Socinian would ever have done so as <term>heartily</term> <note>original: "cordat"</note> and urgently. Whether the Author is a Lutheran for these or other reasons, however, does not depend on the <term>judgment</term> <note>original: "Judicium"</note> of any private and biased judge: time and experience best unravel such raised doubts.

### The 9th Accusation:

The <term>Church History</term> <note>Arnold’s *Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (K.H.)</note> makes people into Papists because it rejects <term>Polemical Theology</term> <note>The branch of theology focused on defending a specific doctrine and attacking opposing views</note>. Page 33.

### Answer:

(1) Dr. Veiel, whom the Anonymous Critic defends here, confessed in his writing against the *Church History* that Mr. Arnold had "sung the praises of the Roman clergy." Yet the Roman clergy, along with the entire Papacy, is actually portrayed in the *Church History* so extensively according to its false foundations that one must wonder how anyone could fall into such an absurd <term>slander</term> <note>original: "Blame"</note>.

(2) The Anonymous Critic wants to show an easy and plausible way using Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the father of Pietism</note>. Namely, that Mr. Arnold describes theological disputes as "useless school-chatter," and specifically (in Book 16, Chapter 9, Section 11) calls Polemical Theology a "word-war."

(3) We must first check whether this is actually the case. In the cited place, Section 11, the text initially speaks of the "addiction to disputing" and shows how faithfully Luther, Weller, and others warned against it; thereafter, it shows how others judged those controversial writings. Furthermore, Camerarius’s complaint is produced: that people have already looked more at what might be approved through much disputing than at what kind of life they led. Yet disputing is only <term>Note Well</term> <note>original: "NB." or "nota bene"</note> good—especially that which is <term>Note Well</term> conducted regarding religion, office, and virtue—when one concludes something not only with <term>Note Well</term> words, but also proves it with harmonious works. Finally, it concludes with Chyræus’s words from his epistle in Fecht, page 753: "He is tired of such chatter; theology does not consist of words, just as the forest is not made of wood."

(4) The reader may now judge for himself whether the entire relation does not aim at the obvious excess and abuse of theological disputes, rather than at the moderate use, consistent with the teachings of Christ and the Apostles, to rebuke those who contradict. Indeed, the author names <term>word-wars</term> <note>original Greek: "λογομαχιας" (logomachias)</note> through his critique of Polemical Theology, of which Paul speaks in 1 Timothy.

->### The 10th Accusation.<-

->### Answer.<-

(1) Firstly, the Anonymous Critic admits that Arnold (A.) cites some passages <note>original: "Loca"</note> from good **Lutherans**. These are purely Lutheran teachers, not a single one of whom is objectionable by reason <note>original: "Ratione"</note> of their subject matter.

(6) The Anonymous Critic lists 8 examples of this. While a Papist writer repeats this from him, it is confirmed by actual practice <note>original: "Praxi"</note>. Here it is (1) acknowledged that **Surius** is a Papist; (2) that he has it from **Wigand** [a Lutheran]; and (3) that practice confirms it further. Our writers very often cite Papists with such cautions. And as for **Comenius**, this man still well deserves credibility in history <note>original: "fidem in historia"</note>, as **Dr. Buddeus** and others have recently shown.
