### The 11th Charge:

He supposedly wants to prove the accusation of atheism among teachers using the works of Lassenius and Spizelius <note>Johannes Lassenius (1630–1692) and Theophilus Spizelius (1639–1691) were prominent Lutheran theologians who criticized the moral decay of their time</note>, but without sufficient grounds. p. 36.

### Answer:

(1) The presentation in the *Church History* (K. H.) in Book 17, Chapter 16, § 4, speaks (1.) expressly of **many** among the preachers—not of **all**, as the Anonymous Critic indefinitely alleges, once again taking upon himself the very thing he wishes to convict others of.

(2) He speaks using almost the same expressions as the cited theologians, especially Lassenius, from his book *On the Secrets of Atheists*, which deals throughout with such matters.

(3) The Anonymous Critic also admits that Lassenius described "Atheistic Statists" <note>term: Statisten (Statists); here referring to worldly or politically-minded individuals who prioritize the state or their own status over true piety</note> in general, as they are to be found in **all** estates, noting that they may be **spiritual or worldly**. He only refuses to admit that Lassenius applied this to the teaching estate <note>the clergy</note>.

(4) However, he further (4.) concedes and posits that Lassenius reflects on one case or another in which an innocent man was driven out under the pretext of being a "heretic" or a "Quaker" based on the testimony of **worldly-minded clergy**. One should only not conclude from this that such things happened often or too much.

(5) If one did not know of so many complaints from our theologians—that the "Weigelian" <note>Followers of the mystic Valentin Weigel, often viewed as heretics by the orthodox church</note> influence had become so common (of which documents appear above in Part II, No. 19, and below in Part IV, No. 136 and 162)—and likewise that people so readily turn honest folk into "Quakers" (as Pastor Winckler of Hamburg deduced in his *Unjustly Quaker-ized Lutheran*), one would willingly agree with the Anonymous Critic's postulate. However, experience confirms even more that Lassenius wrote correctly when he says on page 197:

(6) "It is a proven method to seize upon **religion**, and say: 'That fellow has no true religion; he is contrary to our fathers' **divine service**; he uses suspicious **speech** in his writings; he seeks to lead the people astray **under the appearance of right** <note>original Latin: "sub specie recti"</note>. Beneath the smooth words he gives out, he has hidden a secret poison of heresy. What does it matter? This single word will soon bear fruit. --- He is a **Quaker**; do you not hear how he punishes people for their vices, even to the point of attacking the authorities and preachers? And that is exactly what true Quakerism is.' If one demands still more proof, it will be a small thing for a 'Statist' to twist such a fellow's words—"

### The 12th Charge:

He allegedly falsifies and mutilates Spizelius's words of complaint regarding atheism. p. 37.

### Answer:

(1) The words in the *Church History* (K. H.) in the cited place read as follows: (1.) it is said of all estates in general that such atheism consists primarily in **practice**, since all godless people in **all** estates wish in their hearts, and in fact live, as if there were no **GOD**.

(2) Following this, (2.) the complaint of Lassenius from his *Political-Atheistic Secrets* <note>original Latin: "Arcanis Politico-Atheist."</note> No. XI, p. 196 is produced, which the Anonymous Critic himself admitted here in No. 11, § 4, also applies to preachers or worldly-minded clergy.

(3) Regarding this complaint, it says (3.) that Spizelius repeats the same; whereupon the words of both these authors are cited relatively. In what, then, is this scandalous falsification supposed to consist?

(4) The Anonymous Critic says: in the fact that Spizelius did not mention preachers with a single word, as Arnold (H. A.) nonetheless posits. However, he refutes himself by producing Spizelius's Latin words from the *Epistle on Uprooting Atheism* <note>original Latin: "Epistola de Ath. eradica."</note> p. 11, where it expressly stands: these people (**Practical Atheists**) <note>original Latin: "Athei Practici"</note> **inculcated religion to the laity, and held none themselves.**

(5) Now the question arises: are those who are opposed to the laity, or at least distinguished from them, **Clergy** <note>original Latin: "Clerici"</note> or not? Are those who inculcate or present religion preachers or politicians? Everyone must confess: they are **preachers**. How then can it be said that Spizelius does not mention preachers with a single word, when he mentions them with many words? And how then has Mr. Arnold (H. A.) falsified his words or committed an obvious falsehood? He spoke first of all estates in general with these two authors, and afterwards specifically of many preachers.

(6) This is therefore once again a notable example of how wickedly the *Church History* (K. H.) is accused and charged with falsehoods. It is the same with the alleged "mutilation." It had been noted before the citation of Spizelius that he repeats Lassenius's complaint. Then the words, as Spizelius sets them down from Lassenius and has them printed in different type, were presented; these go only as far as they can be read in the *Church History*. (10) Just as little follows from Mr. A.'s *judgment* <note>original: "Judicio"</note> what *Anonymus* thinks / namely that the **Manichaean heresy is of slight consideration.** Whoever considers the errors *imputed* to the Manichaeans / will judge quite differently / and Mr. A. has clearly *explained* <note>original: "explicirt"</note> himself on this in the cited *Supplements* / where he mentions the horrors of the heavy accusations against the subsequent Manichaeans.

(11) Should everyone / however / who calls something of the history of such people into doubt / immediately be called a defender of heretics / then I ask / what one would want to say about the following words of the late *Luther* / when he writes thus on the 17th Chapter of the 5th Book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> Vol. III. Jena Latin edition, folio 123:

> “It is
> to be seen in the greatest theologians / such as are Augustine, Bernard /
> and the older ones / Cyprian, Tertullian and the like / who when they
> handle the Scripture openly / they handle it uprightly and purely: but
> as soon as questions of dispute arise / they seldom remain in the right
> path / so that they do not withdraw something from Scripture / and attribute it to the person or
> matter / and thus twist the word of God.”

Look only at this / when they write against *Arius* / when *Jerome* writes against *Jovinian* / **Augustine against (Note Well) the Manichaeans,** *Bernard* against free will / so you will see / that I speak the truth. Mr. A. has not said nearly as much / as *Luther* expresses against *Augustine* / that *Augustine* did not remain in the right path against the Manichaeans / twisted God’s word / etc. and yet *Luther* did not *favor* <note>original: "favorisirt"</note> the Manichaeans / but only freely revealed his thoughts on the *conduct* <note>original: "Conduite"</note> of the parties / as should indeed be proper among Christians.

## The 14th Accusation.

->*That he defends the Arian heresy by rejecting the Council of Nicaea. p. 46.*<-
<note>Arianism was a 4th-century belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal or of the same substance as God the Father. The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) was called to resolve this conflict and ended by condemning Arius as a heretic.</note>

## Answer:

(1) It is superfluous to once again deflect this so-often repeated blame, since it has already been thoroughly addressed multiple times, such as in the *Supplements* <note>original: "Supplementis"</note> p. 109 and following, and here in Part I, No. 41, 71, and 173; in Part II, n. 6, 20, 25, 26, and 27; and in Part IV, n. 159. We have also just heard in § 11, No. 13 from **Luther**, what he found lacking in the Church Fathers during the struggle against **Arius**; yet for that reason, he is no Arian, nor does he defend such heresy.

(2) Therefore, Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> has with all joy called Arianism a heresy in Book VII of the *Church and Heretic History* <note>original: "K. H." (Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie)</note> Chapter 2, § 5, and described the Arians as "slaves of reason" in Book V, Chapter 8, § 21; likewise, in the preface to Dr. Allix's judgment of the Jewish Church against the **Unitarians** <note>Those who reject the doctrine of the Trinity</note>, he clearly displayed his earnest abhorrence of it.

(3) Much less does he defend the Arians by rejecting the **Council of Nicaea**. For it is one thing that he (1.) has observed, along with Luther and all Protestants, how no council has ever occurred among all of them where the Holy Spirit ruled perfectly (from the Altenburg edition of Luther's works, Volume IV, folio 112). (2.) He set aside the doctrine itself for a time (in Book IV, Chapter 7, § 6); and (3.) he noted the "excesses" of the members. It is quite another thing to suggest he rejected the Council itself and its doctrine. Concerning the latter, he declared himself more boldly in the *Supplements*, p. 107: the doctrine maintained there, together with the **Nicene Creed** <note>original: "Nicænischen Symbolo"</note>, remains in its proper value, and therefore he by no means rejects it.

(4) The Anonymous critic wants to deduce the opposite from these words in Book IV, Chapter 7, § 13, where it supposedly says that this Council, as it consisted of such members, was not founded in the right true faith, and thus could not truly be called **Orthodox** <note>original: "Orthodox"</note>. However, this does not target the main doctrine of the deity of Christ, but rather—as the entire context shows—the secondary points concerning the prohibition of marriage for church ministers, the rebaptism of the **Samosatenians** <note>Followers of Paul of Samosata, who held a non-trinitarian view of Christ</note>, and the like. Our own theologians consider these secondary points to be erroneous, even though they were decided upon at Councils. Thus, indeed, the members of the Council were not founded in the right true faith insofar as these specific points were concerned.

(5) More on this is shown specifically <note>original: "in specie"</note> there, and Mr. A. is not at all opposed to the judgment of Dr. **Spener** <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the leading figure of Lutheran Pietism</note>: namely, that these bishops proved themselves Christian in that they yielded to **Paphnutius** <note>A 4th-century bishop who argued against mandatory celibacy for clergy at Nicaea</note> on the point of the marriage prohibition. Since Dr. Spener by no means claims that they had not previously erred in this, or that they had shown themselves blameless in other points at all times—for example, in their letters of complaint against one another which they presented to **Constantine**, in the disputes with the philosopher, in the violent assertions of doctrine, and so forth.

(6) Therefore, when the Anonymous critic finally on p. 47 calls Mr. A. a **Crypto-Arian** <note>A secret or hidden follower of Arianism</note> and suggests one could say he should not be tolerated in the Roman Empire at all, everyone can see the unfair imposition and the attempted persecution.

## The 15th Accusation:

->*That he denies that the Holy Spirit is true God and an actual person. p. 47.*<-

## Antwort:

(1) First, I ask the impartial reader to note carefully with me that Mr. A., in the history of the conflict over the deity of the Holy Spirit, explicitly <note>original: "expressè"</note> called the **Macedonians** <note>A 4th-century group, also called Pneumatomachi, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit</note> unbelievers in Book IV of the *Church and Heretic History*, Chapter 8, § 23. And afterward in § 32, he rebukes these people for not being obedient to the Holy Spirit, nor letting themselves be led by Him into all truth.

(2) Moreover, in the *Supplements*, p. 114, § 32, he wrote uprightly: the knowledge of the deity of the Holy Spirit and the supreme power flowing from it certainly belongs to the divine walk and life. Likewise: He is certainly at one with those teachers who have testified against this grave error concerning the deity of the Holy Spirit, and indeed in the power of this very Spirit of God. With these, he repeats from the bottom of his heart that the Holy Spirit is certainly true God (Acts 5, etc.), where he then also specifically repeats **Cassian’s** words against the error of **Macedonius**, and on p. 115 conforms himself to **Athanasius** <note>The 4th-century bishop of Alexandria and chief defender of Trinitarianism</note>.

(3) The Anonymous critic now cites in his accusation, first of all, Dr. Spener's passages on the deity of the Holy Spirit against the **Socinians** <note>A rationalist sect that denied the Trinity and the deity of Christ</note>. Mr. A. is also in agreement with him and other Evangelical teachers in this matter. However, how the Anonymous critic was minded toward Dr. Spener can be recognized below from No. 31, § 9.

(4) Besides this, he says that Arnold is quite concerned for the Macedon—

As also on p. 115: "According to the mind and counsel of this Divine Spirit, mere **theory** and literal knowledge without true obedience is poorly approved."

### The 16th Accusation.

->He slanders the **Orthodox** <note>The established leaders of the early Church</note>, and specifically **Athanasius**, and speaks blasphemously of the doctrine of the **Holy Spirit**. p. 49. 50.<-

### Answer:

(1) The first point of the complaint concerns the **Orthodox** in general and **Athanasius** <note>A 4th-century bishop of Alexandria known for defending the Trinity</note> in particular. Here it must be well considered that in the works of the **Church Fathers** <note>original: "Patribus"</note> and especially in Athanasius, regarding the most important doctrines of faith, certain <term>words of Scripture <note>original Latin: "dicta Scripturæ"</note></term> are very often cited as proof which sometimes not only fail to prove the point, but occasionally even prove the opposite. Those who have reviewed the <term>blemishes of the Fathers <note>original Latin: "Patrum nævos"</note></term>, such as Daillé, Rivet, Scultetus, and others, know enough examples to present. I do not say this to insult the Fathers or to cast doubt on the divinity of the Holy Spirit, of which—praise be to GOD!—I am divinely convinced. Rather, the matter is quite well known to scholars who have read the Fathers even a little, and it could be documented through many passages if it did not seem superfluous.

(2) **Mr. Arnold** <note>original: "Hr. A."</note> had also sufficiently noted this; therefore, he spoke quite harshly at that time based on such knowledge (especially for sensitive and superstitious readers), yet not without foundation. Namely, Athanasius answered a **Macedonian** <note>A follower of the sect that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit</note> who made an objection against worship based on 1 Chronicles 1:24 <note>Likely 1 Chronicles 29:20 in modern numbering</note>, expressly saying: <term>“For this reason especially we say the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped” <note>original Greek: "διὰ τοῦτο μάλιστα λέγομεν προσκυνητὸν τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα"</note></term>; and he deduces this worship of the Holy Spirit as follows: the prophet Nathan would not have worshiped David if he had recognized him as a mere man. But Nathan had been taught that David was the Lord’s Anointed and anointed with the holy oil, therefore he worshiped him because of the effect of the Holy Spirit in the holy oil. (*Dialogue I against the Macedonians, Vol. II, Works, p. 264.*)

(3) One finds even more such arguments there and in the works of others,

Now, someone who observes the insufficient scriptural proofs of the Fathers in a history does not immediately slander them, as the **Anonymous writer** says, but rather speaks as he finds and recognizes the truth to be.

## The 17th Accusation:
**That he clears Vaninus of Atheism and defends him as much as possible. p. 52.**

->Answer:<-

(1) This entire matter has been sufficiently discussed in Part I, Number 84, as well as regarding atheists in general in Numbers 17, 46, and 87; therefore, at this point, we only have to reflect on the specific objections.

(2) First, the Anonymous accuser repeats the history of the matter from Book XVI, Chapter 16, Section 8 at length, and forms several questions upon it: "Whether Mr. Arnold only described the unjust trial of the <term>Papists <note>A term used by Protestants of this era to refer to Roman Catholics.</note></term> against <term>Vaninus <note>Lucilio (or Giulio Cesare) Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher executed for atheism and blasphemy.</note></term>? And whether he did not much more protect, excuse, and even to some extent recommend Vaninus himself and his writings?"

(3) The answer to this is to be given from so many of the author's confessions: that he acknowledges, praises, and worships the true, triune, eternal Godhead through the Divine Word by the power and grace of the Holy Spirit. That he is therefore neither an atheist himself nor a defender of atheists, much less a recommender of such books. Specifically, that out of many 
<meta>catchword: many</meta>

<page-num>325</page-num>
<header>Part III. 17. No. on old and new Writers and Defenders. § 8. and A. 325</header>

many important motives, he called into question the trial of the Papists against such notorious people, as demonstrated in Part I at the cited place. All of this can be left to the judgment of scholars just as easily as the Anonymous accuser has done.

(4) This accuser further charges the author with bypassing the words of <term>Morhof <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a prominent German scholar and historian of literature.</note></term>, in which he (Book I, *Polyhistor*, p. 75) attributes a poison of atheism to Vanini's *Dialogues*, and only mentioning the other words where he calls his ***Amphitheatrum*** <term>sufficiently sound <note>original Latin: "satis sanum"</note></term>.

(5) Now, let an impartial reader weigh the whole matter for themselves. In the contested passage (Section 9 of Book 16), the discussion was solely and exclusively about Vanini’s *Amphitheatrum*, for the sake of which he was burned. For it stands in the *History of the Church* at the cited place: "the primary cause for his cruel execution was taken from his book, the title of which is: *Amphitheatrum*, etc." Now, those who have read the book itself confess that his *Amphitheatrum* is <term>sufficiently sound <note>original Latin: "satis sanum"</note></term>, or written with enough understanding.

(6) Since the question here was only about that specific book over which the author was burned, the Anonymous accuser demands against all fairness that all the preceding words of Morhof, which deal with another book—namely the *Physico-Magico*, or the *Dialogues on the Admirable Secrets of Nature*—should have been added; especially since they did not belong at all to this point regarding the occasion of his death. Furthermore, authors distinguish strictly between these two books. See Weber’s *Judgment on Atheists*, p. 52, 53.

(7) From this, one may judge impartially whether this well-founded account by Mr. Arnold is a mutilation, a terrible deed, or a godless practice. No one, except one who demands more willfully and morosely from an author than is rightfully possible just to have a case against him, will be able or willing to agree with these biased judgments.

(8) The objection that Vaninus highly praised the **Jesuits** in the preface of the *Amphitheatrum*, and thus could not have been persecuted by them out of envy, is easily dismissed. One must consider that Vaninus flatters the Roman clergy even more with words elsewhere, and yet later in <term>reality <note>original Latin: "re ipsa"</note></term> goes against their principles. Therefore, they did not care for the former but suppressed the latter all the more eagerly. And if this had happened in a <term>lawful manner <note>original Latin: "legitimo modo"</note></term> and not in the Papist way through fire and sword, no one would have disapproved of it. For everyone is bound in a Christian manner to check atheistic matters.

<header>326 Response to an Anonymous Presentation of many Falsifications by G. A. Part III. No. 18.</header>

### The 18th Accusation:

That he <note>Gottfried Arnold</note> treats Spinoza far more gently than he does the Orthodox, defends him, and clears him of atheism. p. 56.

### Answer:

(1) Although the Anonymous author immediately admits that Mr. Arnold occasionally criticizes <note>original: "taxire"</note> Spinoza somewhat (though he portrays this as lukewarm and cold), he nonetheless seeks to strengthen this accusation against all evidence. However, Mr. Arnold does not merely criticize "something" about Spinoza, but rather everything, when he observes right before his history (in the 17th Book, 16th Chapter, § 36) that such people (like Cherbury, Spinoza, etc.) did not know the true way to God. He notes they hindered the light—which gladly wishes to enlighten all people—through disobedience and self-will, or even through shame and sin; hence they fell further into doubt regarding the truth of the Christian religion and staggered from one blindness into another. He states that their misery is to be attributed to the humans' own wantonness <note>original: "Muthwillen"</note>. This is subsequently applied to Spinoza.

(2) Although, I say, all of this was clearly to be read in the *Church History* <note>Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (1699), a landmark work that treated heretics with more sympathy than was common at the time.</note>, and particularly in § 37 concerning Spinoza—that he followed his sharp reason ever further and devoted himself purely to speculation—and indeed in § 38—that his deceitful heart and reason led him to all sorts of opinions, whereby the entire matter of Spinoza is declared as evil—the Anonymous author still pretends that Mr. Arnold only criticizes "something," and does so in a lukewarm and indifferent manner. Let the reader judge for themselves according to the truth!

(3) The charges are now as follows: First, the Anonymous author criticizes the citation of Kortholt <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian who wrote against Spinoza and other perceived atheists.</note> from his treatise *On the Three Great Impostors* <note>original: "de 3. Impost." refers to "De tribus impostoribus magnis," a book identifying Herbert of Cherbury, Thomas Hobbes, and Baruch Spinoza as the three great deceivers.</note>, where it is supposedly written that Spinoza does not deny God's existence with express words, for the Anonymous author claims nothing of this sort can be found there. To this, it serves to note that through a printing error, page 169 was placed instead of 166. On this leaf, Kortholt reviews some of Spinoza's seemingly plausible speeches and then asks: "Who would charge him with atheism, and indeed of that coarser kind by which the existence of God itself is denied?" <note>original: "Quis Atheismi eum postulet, & quidem craſſioris illius, quo ipſa Dei exiſtentia negatur?"</note>. He further reminds us that such concealments are merely a fraud; and on the other cited page 171, he writes of the author of the Preface: "He confesses that to deny the existence of God is a horrific crime" <note>original: "Dei negare exiſtentiam horrendum facinus eſſe fatetur"</note>, and of Spinoza himself: "He leaves no stone unturned so that he might be believed to acknowledge God" <note>original: "Omnem movet lapidem, ut Deum agnoſcere credatur."</note>.

(4) These observations certainly provide enough evidence that Spinoza did not write expressly and openly in his

---

<page-num>327</page-num>
<header>Part III. No. 18 on old and new writers and defense of the K. and A. 327</header>

writings: "There is no God." However, they do not deny that he did so in a cunning manner, as Mr. Arnold himself acknowledged above in § 1, saying Spinoza fell into doubt over religion and from one blindness into another. And thus, he has never defended this man as an atheist, but only observed what others have observed: namely, that he did not deny God's existence with coarse, clear words. Least of all has he defended him against the Divine Majesty—from which may God wish to preserve all people, just as He has (God be praised!) also preserved Mr. Arnold, even though He has allowed such evil slander to be cast upon him.

(5) And since it has now been proven here—just as above in Part I, Numbers 2, 17, 46, 87, and also in Part IV, Number 143—that one circumstance or another regarding such notorious people was investigated in the *Church History*, but never were they or their atheism defended: it is therefore a sign of excessive zeal when the Anonymous author finally asserts that the *Church History* is a godless and highly harmful book. No less so when he ill-reports the reader by saying Mr. Arnold speaks so mildly, modestly, and advantageously for the atheists, naturalists, and deists.

(6) For is it truly "mild" or "advantageous" to speak of them as is repeated here from § 1 and 4: that such people have hindered the true light through sin and shame, fallen into all blindness, and must attribute their misery to their own wantonness? And so forth. More can be seen in the aforementioned places regarding how seriously Mr. Arnold has written against the naturalists and others, even if he did not precisely cast about with nothing but curses and maledictions—which serve no one who seeks only the improvement of his neighbor and not his destruction.

(7) How can the Anonymous author further say that, given the aforementioned serious and thorough testimony against Spinoza, curious people would gain a desire to read his works? Especially since Spinoza is expressly accused of disobedience, self-will, misery, shame, sin, blindness, and the like. Or how can one use the "maxims of excuse" employed by Mr. Arnold to overturn the greater part of the accusations against the Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to the Lutheran or Protestant theologians.</note> theologians, as the Anonymous author claims? This can never happen without the greatest violence to the text, as anyone can easily see. For these serious judgments against Spinoza warn curious people not to let themselves be caught and ruined by such "snares of Satan" as that man was.

->The 19th Accusation:<-

->He defends Simon Magus, and treats Irenaeus as a forger of lies. p. 62.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) From the words of the Church History <note>original: "K. H.", referring to Arnold’s *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics*</note> which can be found above in No. 5 of Part I, everyone can judge how earnestly the author detested Simon’s <note>Simon Magus, a 1st-century figure described in Acts 8 as a sorcerer who tried to buy spiritual power; traditionally considered the "father of all heresies."</note> affairs.

(2) Anonymus <note>The unnamed critic attacking Arnold’s work.</note> objects that the discussion is not about Simon’s malice and godlessness in his deeds and works, but about his godless doctrines; he claims Mr. Arnold <note>original: "Hr. A."</note> seeks to absolve him of these. But this too is false. For (1) he everywhere presupposes that a pure doctrine cannot possibly remain alongside a godless life. Since Mr. Arnold attributes a godless life to Simon, he has thereby also attributed a godless doctrine to him.

(3) Secondly (2), let the reader judge from the following words of Mr. Arnold whether he defends Simon according to his doctrine. In Book IV, Chapter 4, § 4, it stands: **Satan has awakened this Simon; although some do not even wish to recognize him as such (namely, as a heretic) because he only acted like a Christian until his baptism, and his heart was never upright before GOD, Acts VIII, 20. And in § 7, Arnold writes: He blasphemed and scorned GOD impiously.** That is surely a rejection of Simon’s doctrine, which is also to be found in the entire 8th section.

(4) Thirdly (3), even in those words of the Church History where some reports <note>original: "Relationes"</note> of distant authors are called into doubt, nothing is found from which one could conclude that Simon was defended or absolved in his doctrine. For Mr. Arnold bases himself primarily on the Acts of the Apostles and says: **It is certain (from Acts VIII, 10) that the people said of him publicly: this man is the power of GOD. For he had truly bewitched the poor people, etc.** These are indeed godless doctrines which are recounted in the Scriptures.

(5) Now, when he additionally (4) writes: **He is blamed for the following abominable doctrines, although mostly on the faith and credit <note>original: "Treu und Glauben"</note> of those who lived long after him and seldom truly agree;** then everyone sees that he (a) recognizes the doctrines as abominable; (b) but questions whether Simon taught all of them, because the authors lived a very long time—some several hundred years—afterward, and in the oldest and earliest writings nothing more is to be found than what stands in the Acts of the Apostles—

stands. (c) That the authors also do not harmonize in everything; all of which is well known to the learned.

(6) Anonymus refers to the following words: **one could see from this that everyone, according to their own whims, blamed such people for the most terrible things of which they likely never thought.** However, he himself commits here what he has so often wanted to reproach Mr. Arnold for, and mutilates the same words by omitting what was most necessary. For in the Church History it stands as is now repeated. But Anonymus leaves out the restrictive and conjectural particle <note>Arnold likely used words like "perhaps" or "it seems," which the critic removed to make the statement sound absolute.</note> and thereby makes it a categorical proposition: **Everyone blamed the heretics for the most terrible things of which they never thought.** Mr. Arnold spoke only by way of conjecture and did not entirely deny that such terrible things were taught by them: but Anonymus wants to blind the reader by making it seem as if Arnold had said absolutely that they had not even once, or not at all, thought of such things.

(7) Thus, one deals very poorly with the Church History in these accusations. Irenæum?"</note> Also p. 244: *That is of the same sort <note>original: "Ejusdem furfuris est illud," literally "of the same bran."</note>;* and on p. 257 he calls his narrative a *fiction* <note>original: "Commentum"</note> etc. Scultetus <note>Abraham Scultetus (1566–1624), a German professor of theology.</note> reviews in *The Marrow of the Fathers* <note>original: "Medulla Patrum"</note> Part I, Book III, chapter 8, Irenaeus's *dangerous opinions, inconsistent doctrines, and improper phrases* <note>original: "periculosas opiniones, inconstantes doctrinas und incommodiores phrases"</note> and says *that he built so much straw upon the foundation of doctrine* <note>original: "eum fundamento doctrinæ tot stipulas superstruxisse"</note>; indeed, on p. 96 he calls a certain passage *dangerous and intolerable* <note>original: "periculosum & intolerandum"</note>; and on p. 97 he specifies such *errors of his, that to have reviewed them is to have refuted them* <note>original: "errores von ihm/ quos recensuisse sit refutasse"</note> etc. The same is done by the Magdeburg Centuriators <note>A group of 16th-century Lutheran scholars who wrote a massive history of the church.</note> in Century II, chapter 10, p. 227, where it is also reasoned in chapter 6, p. 113, *that he is often negligent and improper in his speech.* <note>original: "eum sæpe in dicendo negligentem esse & improprium."</note>

(9) Despite these examples which Mr. Arnold had before him, he nonetheless did not treat Irenaeus as badly as Anonymus thinks. Inasmuch as he does not entirely deny that Simon never thought of such terrible things; but only leaves it in doubt, because one otherwise finds more such unfounded reports of heretics, and Irenaeus lived so long after Si-

## The 20th Accusation:

->He falsely cites Colbergius, Kortholtus, and Thomasium. p. 64.<-

### Answer:

(1) If one had the desire to exaggerate an adversary's unfounded accusations, as he himself does, there would be enough material here for it. Mr. Arnold had also cited these historians of ours in the *Church History* <note>original: "K. H.", Arnold's *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics*</note> Book II, Vol. 4, Ch. § 24 and following, in the history of the <term>Gnostics</term> <note>Early Christian groups often labeled as heretics for their belief in secret "gnosis" or knowledge.</note>, and among them (1) <term>Colbergius</term> <note>Ehregott Daniel Colberg (1659–1698), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, specifically his treatise *On the Origin and Progress of Heresies* <note>original: "de origine & Progressu Hæresium"</note> Chapter II, § 1, where he brings forward all sorts of doubts regarding the common opinion about the Gnostics.

(2) The Anonymous critic did not possess this book, nor had he even seen it; instead, he took it to be Colberg’s <term>Platonic Christianity</term> <note>A different book by Colberg titled *Das Platonisch-Hermetische Christenthum*.</note>, looked up Chapter II, § 1 in that volume, and because he found nothing there regarding this matter, he found it a pleasant discovery to once again convict Mr. Arnold of a "falsification." Therefore, he very hastily placed this slander twice—in the summaries and later in the margin: *Arnold falsely cites Colbergius.* And in the text it says: *It is a shameless untruth,* whereby he inserts the entire page from *Platonic Christianity* and consumes paper, time, and everything with it.

(3) Now, it is well known to those who have even a little <term>knowledge of books</term> <note>original: "notitiam librorum"</note> that Colbergius published the aforementioned treatise in the year 1694, which is

vastly different from *Platonic Christianity*. For the latter was already released in the year 1690. The former is in Latin, the latter in German; the former in quarto, the latter in octavo <note>These refer to the physical size of the books.</note>; the former printed at Schneeberg (*Nivemontii*, as it says on the title page), the latter at Leipzig. The Anonymous critic confuses these two entirely different books and bases the alleged falsification and "shameless untruth" upon such a poor confusion. Whether it happened by design, out of ignorance, or out of over-hasty zeal, GOD may know: I would rather believe the latter as the most lenient option. The confusion and false citation are, at the very least, as clear as day.

(4) Here one might well ask: who has committed a falsification or shameless untruth: Arnold or the Anonymous critic? For the former did not falsify the slightest thing in this matter, just as little as in <term>Kortholtus</term> <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note>, whose "falsification" the accuser imputes to Mr. Arnold; yet Arnold only suggestively posits that the sect might well (or presumably) be a fiction.

(5) Since the Anonymous critic himself admits as much: Kortholt opines (in the book *On the Christian Life* <note>original: "de Vita Christ."</note> Chapter IV, p. 116 seqq.) based on various reasons, that the <term>abominable feasts</term> <note>original: "nefandæ epulæ"; referring to ritual crimes often attributed to heretics, such as cannibalism or orgies.</note> of the Gnostics may well be a fiction. If Arnold had written this, it would have to be said that he "defends the heretics" and "takes them under his protection." The late man <note>referring to Kortholt, who had died by the time of this writing.</note> also strengthened this with irrefutable arguments there in the entire 9th chapter from pages 94 to 151, and also referred to the <term>consensus of Bosius</term> and J. Thomasius; and he especially considered such a question and its ventilation to be entirely blameless historically (contrary to the Anonymous critic). But whether he also calls into doubt the existence of such Gnostics themselves can be seen, among other places, from these words of his in § 8, p. 110: **Justinus and others provide a clear sign <note>original Latin: "non obscurum faciunt indicium..."</note> that they knew absolutely nothing about heretics of their time who had committed such a crime.** And in the entire chapter, he urges this argument: that the Christians would not have kept silent about it against their accusers if such people had existed upon whom they could have cast the blame for such deeds. Thus, Arnold falsifies nothing here, but speaks suggestively that they might well be a fiction—namely, such a sect—and regarding the "feasts," he only cites Kortholt’s point that Epiphanius brought forward such accusations.

(6) Regarding the third author whom Mr. Arnold is said to have misled, Kortholtus clearly testifies in the same place (p. 115) that Jacob Thomasius <note>A famous philosopher and jurist.</note> had passed a favorable judgment on this matter and its arguments in his *Schediasma*, p. 34. And this is also found in this book, § 38, page 65 (Halle edition, 1699), where he writes: **Kortholt surpasses Heraldus in the quantity and elaboration of his arguments, and**

H.", Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie"</note> shows. For this reason, the Anonymous critic's remaining objections do not apply to Mr. Arnold, as he only speaks of a sect and questions its existence along with other authors, while not defending the teachings themselves with a single word. And if he questioned the reliability of Epiphanius <note>original: "Epiphanii fidem"</note> in this matter, he did so following the example of Dr. Kortholt and other historians of ours; more on this in the following number.

# The 21st Accusation:
-> That he defended the Gnostics and unfairly criticized Epiphanius. <-
-> page 66. <-

# Answer:

(1) Beyond what was reminded regarding this grievance in the previous number, the following will serve for better information. Mr. Arnold observes in Book II, Chapter 4, § 26, some contradiction from Epiphanius’s *Against Heresies* <note>original: "Hær. 24. N. 5."</note>, as he accuses the Gnostics of pride and of boasting about their knowledge, but at the same time complains that they kept their affairs so secret and would not willingly let anything be known.

(2) Both of these stand clearly in Epiphanius, as the Anonymous critic himself cites. Only, he wishes to see no contradiction in it, and leaves the judgment
<meta>catchword: judgment</meta>

---

<page-num>333</page-num>
<header>Part III. No. 21. on old and new writers and defense of R. and A. 333</header>

judgment to the learned. I also do the same gladly, as anyone may well see that one cannot with good reason say of someone who does not let his affairs be known and keeps them secret, that he makes a great boast of his knowledge.

(3) Now, whoever doubts such a statement with good reason does not immediately defend such a person, much less their doctrine or errors; nor does he unfairly criticize the one who says it if he cannot immediately "make it rhyme" <note>idiom: make it make sense/harmonize</note> (as Mr. Arnold says here). Rather, he only puts his *doubts* <note>original: "Dubia"</note> on display and gives the reader something to consider.

(4) Regarding the other passage of Epiphanius (*Hær. 40. N. 1.*), what the Anonymous critic interjects is even more questionable. Mr. Arnold observes (1) in the cited location that Epiphanius accuses the Gnostics of pride. The Anonymous critic says on the contrary (p. 68. § 9.) that Epiphanius does not mention the pride of the Gnostics with a single word. Nonetheless, the former writes expressly in *Hær. 24. N. 5.* that Basilius (a Gnostic) said they alone were humans, and the others were only dogs and pigs. Now, whoever accuses someone of these words also accuses them *by that very fact* <note>original: "eo ipso"</note> of pride, self-exaltation, and contempt for other people.

(5) Afterward, the Anonymous critic says it is false that the signs of the accusations against this Gnostic were because he lived in solitude and renounced all his own; specifically, the true cause of the judgment against the Gnostic consisted in the fact that he harbored and spread the heresy of the Gnostics.

(6) But if one looks at Epiphanius's own words, the opposite will be evident. The Anonymous critic himself cites them as follows regarding Eutactus, a Gnostic: "For this old man, the clothing was at first of a horrible roughness, and affected for pretense" <note>original: "Huic seni vestitus erat initio asperitate ipsa horribilis, & ad simulationem affectatus"</note> (how many hermits are described this way in the *Lives of the Desert Fathers*?). About this, Epiphanius judges thus: 
> While he was clothed outwardly in sheep’s skin, he was inwardly a most rapacious and hidden wolf. Indeed, he seemed to be a hermit living in a cave. He drew many to himself who had renounced all their fortunes. He distributed whatever he had to the needy and gave alms daily, etc. <note>original: "Cum extrinsecus ovis pelle esset indutus, lupus erat intus rapacissimus & occultus. Anachoreta quippe esse videbatur in spelunca degens. Qui quidem plerosque abdicatis fortunis omnibus ad se pertraxit. Idem quidquid habebat, in egenos distribuere ac quotidie stipem erogare &c."</note>
Here one clearly sees that he views these things as suspicious and hypocritical, calling them into question.

(7) Thereupon he breaks loose with the other charges: that he had given himself over to all sorts of heresies from youth (although none are specified), was afterward brought before Bishop Aerius and convicted of the Gnostics' heresy, and was deposed from the priesthood, and (note well) driven out, whereupon Epiphanius himself excommunicated him or placed him under the ban, and he was cursed by all

and had been condemned. Now, anyone who knows **Epiphanius’s** vehemence and harsh disposition toward those in error will be well able to judge what is to be held of this his account, in that he does not bring to light a single opinion for which it would have been so necessary to banish, curse, and condemn him, since he led a solitary, quiet life, as **Epiphanius** himself reports.

(8) But so that no one takes offense if **Epiphanius’s** authority is called into doubt, let one hear how **Chemnitz** <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a preeminent Lutheran theologian</note> reasons about him in the *Examination of the Council of Trent, Part IV, page 218*: "Epiphanius neither correctly recounts nor refutes the Montanists' laws concerning fasting, but attributes this opinion to them" <note>original: "Epiphanius nec rectè recitat, nec refutat Montanistarum leges de jejuniis, sed affingit ipsis hanc opinionem."</note>. Whereby he observes that **Epiphanius** himself posits that which he reproaches in other **Montanists** <note>A 2nd-century prophetic Christian movement often accused of legalism regarding fasting</note>. Further on page 221, he writes: "That description of Montanus’s error concerning fasting, which Epiphanius attributes to Montanus, is false... he attributes and assigns something to him which Montanus expressly denies. But that which Montanus truly felt, and which the ancient Church condemned in him, Epiphanius praises and approves as true... And this certainly is not good faith; for Epiphanius ought to have described the history of the ancient Church—what it had condemned in Montanus—in good faith, not substituted his own opinions" <note>original Latin: "Falsam esse illam descriptionem... Et hac certè non est bona fides, debuisset enim Epiphanius veteris Ecclesiæ historiam... non suas opiniones substituere."</note>. Finally, he concludes for our warning thus: "And this must be diligently observed, so that we may know how much we ought to attribute to such writers; and the following will show how much those have harmed the Church who have not described the judgments of the ancient or primitive Church in good faith, but have twisted them toward their own preconceived opinions" <note>original Latin: "Et hoc diligenter observandum est, ut sciamus, quantum hujusmodi Scriptoribus tribuere debeamus..."</note>. What can more powerfully overturn **Epiphanius’s** credibility than this well-conceived judgment of **Chemnitz**, who also observed exactly this in general in his *Oration on the Reading of the Fathers*, as did **Osiander** and others. Not to mention that even in the Papacy <note>Refers to the Roman Catholic Church</note> no such idol is made of him as is now done among us. **Rivet** confesses of **Petavius** in the *Book on the Authority of the Fathers, page 60*, that he often harshly chastised him <note>original: "quod eum sæpe duriter castiget"</note>. The histories also show what quarrels he started against **Chrysostom** and that his mind was full of passions.

### The 25th Charge:

He defends **Pelagius** <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418) was a monk and theologian whose views on human nature and free will were condemned as heresy by the early Church</note> and treats his opponents as godless heresy-makers. p. 76.

### Answer:

(1) Before we examine this reproach, the author's meaning should first be understood from his own declaration, which in the *Supplementa* <note>Additional notes or volumes Arnold published to clarify his history</note> p. 119, reads as follows: Everything reported therein (in the *R. H.*) <note>Referring to the *Radicale Historie* or Arnold’s main history</note> for and against the heresy of Pelagius does not speak in the slightest word in favor of those errors regarding the power of **free will** and the belittling of **natural corruption** <note>Original: *natürlichen Verderbens*, a reference to the concept of Original Sin, which Pelagius was accused of denying</note>, which are in themselves reprehensible and harmful, as they all flow from pagan principles. Upon this, he repeats the judgments of **Augustine**, **Fulgentius**, **Prosper**, and others, and conforms himself to them.

(2) Furthermore, he reminds us on p. 120 that whatever is noted regarding the occasion of this conflict, as well as the inadequate method of the refuters and other circumstances "by the liberty and right of History" <note>original: *libertate & jure Historiæ*</note>, can and shall never prejudice the Divine Truth itself. Whoever well considers these declarations will be able to view and decide upon the raised contradictions of the **Anonymous Critic** all the more impartially, especially if one compares how blamelessly Mr. Arnold has expressed himself regarding **Augustine** and other Fathers who had to deal with the **Pelagians**. In the *Presentation* p. 33 and in the *Supplementa* p. 118, the specific objections will appear in the following numbers: Here everyone already sees *in general* so much: that Mr. Arnold seriously abhors **Pelagianism** and never intends to favor it.

### The 26th Charge:

He falsely cites **Chemnitius** <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a preeminent second-generation Lutheran theologian</note>. p. 77.

### Answer:

(1) Regarding the person of **Pelagius**, Mr. Arnold had observed in Volume 5, Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 1, that he must have been in earnest, and that he hit upon his main teaching out of great zeal against the hypocritical nature of the Christians of that time, etc., as the theologians themselves confessed. Here **Chemnitius** is cited, and his "Section on Free Will" <note>original: *Locus de Lib. Art.*, referring to Chemnitz's "Loci Theologici"</note>, where in the printing the specific citation was omitted, namely Chapter 8.

(2) This theologian <note>Chemnitius</note> reasons about it thus: He [Pelagius] had this opportunity to stir up such a conflict: (1.) He wanted to sharply refute the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that Augustine once belonged to; Pelagius felt they gave humans an excuse to sin by blaming an evil nature</note>; (2.) ### The 27th Charge:

### Answer:

(1) The "glossing over" is supposed to be this, as it stands in the cited place, Sections 1 and 2: The **Orthodox** had interpreted this as a great heresy in Pelagius, that he—from Christ's clear words in Matthew 19:23 and Mark 10:24—said: A rich man, if he keeps his wealth and does not renounce it, cannot enter the Kingdom of God. Along with this, **Hilary's** inquiry and **Augustine's** answer are cited.

(2) Here the **Anonymous Critic** exaggerates against Mr. Arnold, claiming he cited these Fathers incorrectly; however, the untruth of this will clearly show itself. When Mr. Arnold cites **Hilary's** Letter 88, he does so merely because it was an inquiry to **Augustine** concerning this question, in which nothing was yet conceded, but which was only connected to the following response, and thus had to be cited with it. With what appearance of truth can the accuser then pretend that he is in the least a falsifier?

(3) Much less has this happened with **Augustine**; the **Anonymous Critic** cites a passage from the following Letter 89 and wants to prove that therein, the speech against the **Pelagians** is quite mild. ### Answer:

And regarding what concerns *polemical forms* <note>original: "specie Polemica"</note> / we have seen above in Number 9 / that such things are not at all rejected in their good and truly innocent use / but rather that, following Luther, the human elements mixed into them must be viewed with impartial eyes.

(5) Now we come to the alleged false report concerning Luther. For from this one sees indeed *by a sound and natural consequence* <note>original: "per bonam & pronam consequentiam"</note> that Luther did not consider polemical matters necessary or even healthy for everyone. Mr. Arnold had immediately before cited a *passage* <note>original: "Locum"</note> from the letters of this very Chytraeus, page 236 / in which he complained / how our universities were full of disputes / and that he had learned this through great suffering. To this, the above observation *by the same author* <note>original: "ejusdem Auctoris"</note> was not ill-suited / wherein a certain limit is set to those disputes.

(7) The second untruth is supposed to be / that Luther thought little or nothing of polemical writings / and that Chytraeus judged thus. But who said this / or where does it stand in this passage of the *History of the Church and Heretics*? Nothing further is indicated / than that Luther, by omitting the sects in the Small Catechism, indicated / what he thought of polemical writings / namely that such things are not necessary or useful for all people / but not / that he thought little or nothing of them / the opposite of which is clear from his many polemical writings. And who would deny that? For one can certainly consider a matter not necessary or useful for certain persons / and yet think more than little or nothing of it. Does one not see clearly / that the Anonymous author wants to antagonize the reader / in order to bring a charge of untruth against Mr. Arnold?

(8) So it is also with the third untruth / as if Chytraeus had reported / that Luther intended to show, by omitting the names of the sects, what he thought of polemical writings. The Anonymous author is himself doubtful / whether this might not be true / as he concludes: "Which neither Luther nor Chytraeus may have thought of," nevertheless he presents it as an untruth.

### The 33rd Accusation:
->That he uses shady tactics and falsifies Hutter’s words, page 93.<-

### Answer:
(1) The Anonymous Author says the "tactic" is this: "Everything must serve to the advantage of the **heretics**, but to the disadvantage of the **Orthodox**. If the Orthodox write sharply against the heretics, he represents it as slander and blasphemy, and mockingly titles it 'Theological Gentleness'; but if they proceed with them moderately and mildly, he either omits it or twists their words completely so that it appears as if they themselves considered such errors to be trivial."

(2) Among these many parts of the accusation, each of which is grave enough, the Anonymous Author has sought to substantiate none but the last: he produces one example of this from Book 16, Chapter 30, § 4, which we must weigh against the accusation.

(3) In that place, Dr. Huber’s <note>Samuel Huber (1547–1624), a theologian who argued for universal election—that God chose all people for salvation—which led to fierce conflict with strict Lutherans.</note> first published confession regarding the **universal election of grace** is reviewed, and afterward this judgment of Dr. Hutter <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a cornerstone of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> is added, from the *Letters to Marbach*, page 757. <margin>(a)</margin> **His opinion is certainly better than his expression; and whoever cannot distinguish between the love, the calling, and the election of God will immediately agree with Huber’s opinion, recognize his condemnation as unjust, and burden the Meissen churches and teachers with a heavy prejudice, as many have already done.**

(4) Here, Mr. Arnold indeed faithfully reports that only those (according to Hutter’s warning) would agree with Huber who could make no distinction, and that such people burdened the teachers with a heavy prejudice. In what way does the Anonymous Author now wish to verify his accusation from this—namely, that Mr. Arnold twisted the mild words of the Orthodox against the heretics to make it seem as if they held such errors in low regard? He says (a) Mr. Arnold omitted part of Hutter's words. However, he has omitted nothing that actually belongs to the matter itself; the Anonymous Author has also not specified such omissions.

(5) Furthermore, he says (b) Arnold falsified them by pretending Hutter had written that whoever cannot distinguish between love, etc., would immediately agree with Hutter’s opinion—whereas Hutter’s own words only said that at the time, the imprudent and inexperienced, by simply accepting Huber’s confession, had agreed with his opinion.

would agree <note>original: "ne/ werde"</note>: whereas Hutter’s own words only said that the imprudent and inexperienced, by simply accepting Huber’s confession, had agreed with his opinion.

The latter says: *Most would follow Huber’s opinion with their feet, as they say*; <note>original Latin: "Plerique in Huberi sententiam pedibus, quod ajunt, concedant." <meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold against the "Anonymous" critic. It specifically addresses the 34th accusation concerning Johann Wigand, a prominent Lutheran theologian, and his conduct toward both fellow clergy and the Anabaptists. The text examines whether Arnold was fair in attributing "temporal motives" (political or economic gain) to Wigand’s calls for religious persecution.</meta>

<page-num>358 / 359</page-num>
<header>358 Response to Anon. Presentation of many Falsifications by G. A. Part III, No. 34 / Part III, No. 34 of Old and New Scribes and Defenders of the Church and Antiquity 359</header>

(3) Furthermore, on page 479, one may read: It did not stop with the removal <note>The Latin term *remotio* refers here to being dismissed from a church or academic office.</note> of Heshusius; rather, Dr. Wigand <note>Johann Wigand (1523–1587), a strict Lutheran theologian and Bishop of Pomesania.</note> played the same game with those who took Heshusius’s side. — He tried to force the preachers in Königsberg to his side by power. — The Council confronted him about his unchristian behavior. — But because Dr. Wigand noticed that he still had not achieved his purpose with his dismissals, but had instead brought upon himself the unspeakable hatred of many people, especially foreign theologians, he published several small treatises, etc. Finally, it is said that Heshusius <note>Tilemann Heshusius (1527–1559), another leading Lutheran who often clashed with colleagues over doctrine.</note> had been his benefactor and promoter.

(4) A Lutheran historian recounts all of this about Wigand according to the truth. If this historian committed no offense against God or men by writing this, then the Anonymous critic cannot rightly write of Mr. Arnold: (p. 98) *That he has grossly sinned against God and Wigand* by observing that Wigand caused persecution against the Anabaptists <note>A radical wing of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and was often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note>, and indeed through temporal motives.

(5) However, the Anonymous critic says this matter here concerns the heretics, namely the Anabaptists, about whom Arnold writes in Book XVI, Chapter 21, § 27. But let us take up the points of complaint one by one: a) He urges the gloss <note>An explanatory note or commentary.</note> in which Arnold says someone had quite rightly concluded from Wigand's words that Wigand had only spurred on the government to such severity for the sake of their temporal benefit. This "someone" was Ottius, who in his *Annals of the Anabaptists* (page 171) mentions Wigand's book on Anabaptism and says that in the dedication, he argues: "The magistracy, out of respect for its own temporal benefits, ought not to tolerate incurable and blasphemous Anabaptists." <note>Original Latin: "Magiſtratum commodorum ſuorum temporalium reſpectu Anabaptiſtas inſanabiles & blaſphemos tolerare non debere."</note>

(6) Here let the reader judge whether this so-called gloss does not follow from this: Ottius had quite rightly concluded from Wigand's words that the latter was spurring on the government, and indeed only for the sake of temporal benefit. For whoever argues—and indeed with such vehemence as Wigand's words show—that the government should not tolerate certain people for the sake of temporal benefit, is indeed spurring them on to such severity. The Anonymous critic has not indicated with a single word the contrary, or how any other conclusion follows.

(7) Further, b) he says Ottius testifies to the exact contrary in these Latin words just cited. The "contrary," according to the natural sense, would have to be this: Wigand did *not* spur on the government to severity only for the sake of temporal benefit. Now, let an impartial reader try to see if he can take this meaning from Ottius's words without doing them violence. For the entire proposition is divided into these

<column-break/>

these two parts: 1) The government should not tolerate the Anabaptists, and 2) for this reason, namely, because of its temporal benefit.

(8) This very clear understanding, which strikes the reader's eye immediately, is also confirmed by Wigand’s own words when he writes in his book under the 6th Reason, after having described them in the preceding ones as "incurable and blasphemous," etc., and having said in the 6th that they rejected the government: "And to such people, who treat pious magistrates with such great ignominy, and being armed, refuse to go forth to keep watch together with other citizens, shall Christian magistrates grant shelter, provide defense, and offer sustenance? What kind of justice is this, what kind of equity?" <note>Original Latin: "Et talibus, qui tantâ ignominiâ Magiſtratus pios afficiunt, & armati nolunt ſimul ad excubias prodire cum aliis civibus, Magiſtratus Chriſtiani tecta concedent, defenſionem exhibebunt, victum præbebunt? Quænam hæc eſt juſtitia, quæ æquitas?"</note> And in the 9th Reason: "Because the blessing of God is undoubtedly driven away from those places where such impenitent and blasphemous men dwell among true Christians. It is most truly said: 'The blessing of the Lord makes one rich.' (Proverbs 10). The antithesis is thus simultaneously clear: 'The curse of the Lord makes one poor.' ... Therefore, he who wishes to be rich with the blessing of the Lord must not only love the uncorrupted voice of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, but also with true and burning zeal hate, curse, flee, and remove those things which openly fight against the doctrine of God, etc." <note>Original Latin: "Quia benedictio Dei ſine omni dubitatione in iis locis pellitur, ubi tam impœnitentes & blaſphemi homines inter verè Chriſtianos confederunt, Verisſimè dictum eſt, Benedictio Domini divites facit. Prov. 10. Antithesis igitur ſimul patet: Maledictio Domini pauperes facit. --- Qui igitur cum benedictione Domini velit eſſe dives, eum neceſſe eſt non tantum amare incorruptam Evangelii J. C. vocem, ſed etiam vero & ardenti zelo odiſſe, execrari, fugere, removere, quæ palam cum doctrina Dei pugnant, &c."</note>

(9) If one looks at Mr. Arnold’s report without partiality, one can easily see that his argument was this: Wigand wanted to persuade the government to such persecution by suggesting they should only, or at least primarily, consider their temporal convenience and the damage resulting from the opposite. Indeed, he [Arnold] explained himself this way in § 29, where he concludes from Wigand that worldly people are moved to such bloody judgments only by temporal advantage and fear of harm.

(10) But that he also, on the other hand, did not omit the preceding spiritual motives that Wigand cited—as the Anonymous critic claims—is clearly shown by these words which he alleged from Wigand: "Should you patiently protect and carry in your protection such terrible enemies of holy baptism, and the defilers, indeed blasphemers, of the Holy Trinity who reborn you in baptism? Will you not look upon such important matters? Where is the zeal for the honor of God? Where is the zeal for the house of God?"

(11) Mr. Arnold would not even have needed to include these and the other spiritual motives, because the discussion there was only about the persecutions that had occurred for the sake of temporal intentions. But since he included those as well, one can complain about him even less, as if he had left out something necessary or maliciously distorted the text, as the Anonymous critic accuses him. For with what appearance of truth can he pretend that...

### The 37th Charge.

->That he misused the Marbach Letters. p. 109.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) As an example, Anonymous cites a *passage* from the second part of the *Church History, Book VI, Chapter 20, Section 22*, the *summary* of which he presents thus: Arnold relates that Schwenckfeld <note>Caspar Schwenckfeld (1489–1561) was a Protestant reformer who disagreed with Luther and was often persecuted as a sectarian.</note> accused the Schmalkaldic theologians of condemning him by their own hand and without the involvement of the Estates <note>The "Estates" (Stände) refers to the political authorities and ruling ranks of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>.

<meta>catchword: (2) This</meta>

---

<page-num>365</page-num>
<header>Part III, No. 37, 38. Response to old and new writers and defense of Church and Arnold. 365</header>

(2) This *grievance* of Schwenckfeld’s appears clearly in the letter of Martin Frecht produced by Mr. Arnold (*Marbach Letters, page 37*), who writes thus: *The boastful Thraso* (this is what he calls Schwenckfeld) <note>Thraso is a character from Roman comedy representing a "braggart soldier"; here used as a derogatory nickname.</note> *then blurted out that this condemnation was made only by the priests, and not likewise by the Lutheran magistrates.* <note>original Latin: "Glorioſus etiam Thraſo (...) tum effutiebat, hanc condemnationem tantum à Pfaſſis, non item a Magiſtratibus Lutheranis eſſe factam."</note>

(3) Anonymous now considers this a calumny and injury to Schwenckfeld—that he said the theologians had condemned him without the involvement of the Estates—and accuses the author of the *Church History* of promoting this injury as much as he was able, and thus making himself a participant in it by omitting the last and *immediately* following words.

(4) Had Mr. Arnold presented this complaint of Schwenckfeld’s *absolutely*, Anonymous might have a semblance of a reason to complain. However, he lacks this because he writes merely *relatively*: S. *objects* that the decision was not made by the protesting Estates. For this does not deny that the Estates *approved* the decision of the theologians—which Frechtus alone asserts (*that all counsels were strongly approved by the legates*) <note>original Latin: "à Legatis omnia conſilia valde eſße probata"</note>—but only that it was *made* by the Estates.

(5) Anonymous deliberately confuses these two things by giving the words this sense: that S. was condemned without the involvement of the Estates. Yet there is a great difference between making a decision oneself and merely *approving* it. Frechtus says the latter of the Estates in the letter, but not the former. And thus, Mr. Arnold here remained faithful to the *text* of the letter, but Anonymous has changed the meaning so that he could formulate a charge against Arnold, as if he had made himself a participant in an injury and accused others in a godless manner, etc.

it stands <note>Referring to Arnold's *History of the Church and Heretics*</note> how far in the Church History <term>raisonniret</term> <note>reasoned or argued</note> has been done regarding these people, based on and with several writers.

(3) In addition, in the specific passage under attack, a distinction is made; namely, regarding those who were different from the insurrectionists <note>The violent Anabaptists of the Münster Rebellion (1534–1535)</note>. Such a distinction is likewise further observed in Part II, Number 102, and is clearly to be found in the original authors.

(4) Now, when it says here of such people that they were described by their enemies as showing an "external holiness": 1.) the insurrectionists are thereby excluded, and 2.) the others are attributed only an external holiness, and thus only an appearance. This is also what Sleidanus <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a historian of the Reformation</note> says: they maintained a spiritual appearance. The marginal note, however, was added by someone else, and it is self-evident that an external or "apparent" piety is meant; this is therefore no untruth, but is contained within Sleidanus. Likewise, in Volume XVI of the *Church History*, Chapter 21, Section 39, a "Pharisaic Christianity" is attributed to the Mennonites <note>original: "Menisten"</note>, which is the passage that explains this marginal note here.

(5) It is further claimed that the words of Scultetus <note>Abraham Scultetus (1566–1624), a German Reformed theologian</note> were falsified, specifically a) in that these words: *vitæ integritatem præ se ferebant* <note>Latin: "they displayed an integrity of life"</note> were translated far too mildly; namely, that "they demonstrated an innocent life." However, unless one refuses to accept common usage, one need only look up Cellarius's Lexicon <note>Christopher Cellarius (1638–1707), a famous lexicographer</note> to find that *præ se ferre* has this good meaning alone: namely, to have no shame of something, to confess it publicly, and to demonstrate it.

(6) Anonymous most strongly urges point b) that Mr. Arnold called the *justitiam operum* <note>Latin: "righteousness of works"</note>—as it is practiced by the Papists <note>A common early modern term for Roman Catholics</note>—a "godly, active Christianity." However, he expressly translated these Latin words as "righteousness of works," and only added his own concept in parentheses, stating that it should perhaps be called an "active Christianity." The fact that the parenthesis marks were omitted in the printing and the words were not printed in a smaller typeface <note>original: "typo"</note> is not the fault of the author, who was over 30 miles away at the time. Thus, he suffers the accusation of insertion and falsification by Anonymous innocently. Anyone who has seen the author's other writings knows well how earnestly he testifies everywhere against self-righteousness through works. He certainly did not wish to gloss over this error here, as Anonymous claims.

(7) Finally, it is said to be a "partisan gloss" when, following Scultetus's observation of the "righteousness of works," it is remarked:
> "A true Christian
> "could easily find how far this judgment reaches, and how far the complaint
> "thereby applies to their earnest admonition to godliness."

It had
<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<page-num>367</page-num>
<header>Part III, No. 38, 39. On old and new writers and defense of Arnold, 367</header>

but Mr. Arnold had seen from so many documents that among these people (excepting those from Münster), many may have meant well and sought to live according to the Word of God. Because they then admonished others to do the same, this was interpreted as a "holiness of works," as the writings still show.

(8) Based on these circumstances, he added this observation here; though Anonymous may call it partisan, it is founded on the harmony of history. Meanwhile, it never contradicts the eternal foundation of Paul in Romans 10:3 <note>"For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness..."</note>, which Mr. Arnold emphasizes in all his writings. And if these notorious people wanted to assert Papist works-righteousness anywhere, he would not approve of it at all. He only had doubts at that time regarding Scultetus's words: that this author calls them *sic integros vitæ, frugales in victu, parcos in sermone* <note>Latin: "thus upright in life, frugal in diet, sparing in speech"</note> and the like, and yet simultaneously attributes a "righteousness of works" to them. It must surely be permitted to investigate this without being called partisan, and to discover no "scruples" <note>moral doubts or hesitations</note>, especially in historical circumstances.

(9) How partisan, on the other hand, Anonymous writes when he claims a) that Arnold denied purity in doctrine and life to the Evangelical theologians <note>Lutherans</note> and, contrary to justice and fairness, attributed it to the Anabaptists; and indeed b) specifically to those who called infant baptism a "dog-bath" <note>original: "Hunds-Bad," a derogatory term used by radical reformers to suggest the water was useless or profane</note>.

First, it cannot be proven from Scultetus that he is speaking here on page 265 of the same Laurentius of whom he recounted those words on page 263; for he mentions nothing of the kind regarding anyone else. Secondly, he attributed nothing further to them than what Scultetus himself admitted of them, or what follows by logical consequence <note>original: "per bonam consequentiam"</note> from such an admission.

...also showed his profane mind through an offensive simile <note>A comparison or parable</note> of the shoemaker and shoemaker's apprentice, but should desist from the case of the unjustly dismissed Deacon <note>The "Diaconus" was an assistant minister in the Lutheran church hierarchy</note>.

b) That he claims the greatest cause for the accusation against the Pastor was presumably because he ousted the Deacon from office.

c) That he reports he does not know why the Pastor dismissed the Deacon.

(2) Regarding the first point, it serves to note that all the specified assistance consists in a historical doubt <note>original: "historischen Dubio"</note> as to whether the Pastor could truly have been convicted of such reported heresies—such as those recounted in the *Church History*: that the (so-called) Calvinists agree entirely with the Lutherans in the three main articles; that they are at one with us in the topic of Justification <note>original: "loco de Justificatione"</note>; that the dispute was only over a minor matter, namely the Holy Supper <note>original: "de Coena Sacra"</note>; that they received the body of Christ with faith because He could not be present everywhere; that a Lutheran might well partake of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Coenam Domini"</note> among the Calvinists, and so forth. Or whether the Deacon perhaps fabricated such assertions <note>original: "Asserta"</note> about him—as is indeed not uncommon—and accused him because he had ousted him from office. "Anonymous" assumes as infallible that the Pastor defended erroneous doctrines. But whoever knows how things go in such affairs will not be able to believe it immediately, even if it stands in the *Theological Opinions* <note>original: "Consiliis Theol."; these were formal legal and religious judgments issued by university faculties</note>. Regarding the parable of the shoemaker and shoemaker's apprentice, the defendant's counter-response by right belonged there as well; the authors would have acted more laudably then if they had observed the principle that **the other side must also be heard** <note>original: "audiatur & altera pars"</note> and had first questioned the Pastor orally or in writing as to whether he admitted to all points or not.

(3) Regarding the second: it is evident from the Response <note>original: "Responso"</note> itself how the dismissed Deacon accused the Pastor of heresies both before and after the dismissal, to which it is also answered in the Response that such things are not in accordance with the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church</note>. And Mr. Arnold speaks of this accusation, which occurred after the dismissal, but not of the first, as his words sufficiently show.

(4) Thirdly, Mr. Arnold could very well say he does not know why the Deacon was dismissed; since he had before him only the one-sided testimony of one party, namely the Deacon, but found cause to desire the counter-report of the other, because such contradictory theses <note>original: "contradictoriæ theses"</note> (which are generally called Calvinist in the Response, regardless of the fact that Arians, Anabaptists, and Papists are also blessed therein) are attributed to him, about which the Pastor should rightly have been questioned first.

(5) In short, he could not fully believe those things reported in the Response, because it also stands doubtfully <note>original: "dubie"</note> in the *Wittenberg Theological Opinions*, Part I, page 476: "The Pastor is said to be the author of the assertions; he is said to have taught; he is said to have persecuted the Deacon." If someone wants to take all this as known, let him not immediately impute a partisan abuse to someone else who brings his doubts <note>original: "Dubia"</note> to light about it, or cannot believe that the person in the Response can be declared a Calvinist who considers Arians, Papists, and others to be blessed if they only read the Bible. Especially as the Reformed gentlemen <note>The Calvinist church was officially known as the "Reformed" church</note> have protested very strongly against such a description.

### The 41st Charge:

(2) Here the conclusion sounds different than the first accusation. For at first it was said Arnold had committed malice and sloppiness: but here

When, for example, that Rector in Moravia, Persisterius, in the midst of Popish <note>A contemporary Protestant term for Roman Catholic</note> authorities—and to the vexation and mockery of the Jesuits—performed a comedy of Susanna in German rhymes with his schoolboys and may have mocked them therein, also dressing up many Pickelherings in Jesuit hats that had nothing but fools' bells hanging from the corners.

(5) Now the reader may easily judge from a comparison of both accounts what sort of "malice" lies in Mr. Arnold’s version—whether everything is not stated clearly enough in the author's words, and whether he did not intend to present the great imprudence and levity of these people. In Catholic lands, they dangerously provoked their own enemies, the Jesuits, to the detriment of the local Sovereign. Should they not have much rather followed the advice of Luther and other theologians who teach that one should not scold or mock so boldly among the Papists? This can be seen in Matthew in *Syracuse*, chapter 27, page 8; Baldwin’s *Cases of Conscience*, Book IV, chapter 5; Dannhauer’s *Theological Conscience*, Volume I, Part II, page 925, and others.

(6) To be sure, the Anonymous writer wants to interpret it as malice that Mr. Arnold writes at the end: The Papists and the authorities became so embittered over this that they banished all Lutherans shortly thereafter. He concludes: Arnold thereby showed his pleasure over the persecution of the Protestants <note>original: "Evangelischen"</note>.

(7) However, not a single syllable of such "pleasure" is to be seen;
