<page-break/>

<page-num>371</page-num>
<header>Part III, No. 41. On Anatomy and New Writers and Defense of the Righteous and Arnold.</header>

rather, Mr. Arnold observes, disapproves, and regrets that these people brought persecution upon their own heads through such foolish and even offensive dealings.

(8) And how can such people be called truly "Evangelical" who 1) arrange such excessive and unedifying buffoonery <note>original: "Gauckeleyen"</note> in the school; 2) dress up so many young boys as Pickelherings, and through foolish talk <note>original: "Narrentheidinge"</note> pervert and offend their tender hearts; and 3) do this indeed with the garments of those who were held in high regard by the local Sovereign? Even if it was not done to insult them, the authorities could still interpret it as such. Did Christ command even the slightest bit of this in His Gospel? Did He not rather earnestly forbid it all through true self-denial, love of enemies, and prudence among the wolves <note>The OCR "Abössen" is likely a corruption of "Wölfen" (wolves) or "Bösen" (evil ones), referencing Matthew 10:16</note>, etc.?

(9) Just as the account of such dealings is not "malice," neither is it "shoddy work" <note>original: "Sudeley"</note>, which is anyway an obscure and unusual term in our Upper Saxony. If the Anonymous writer wants to call it "shoddy work" because Mr. Arnold attributes to the Rector what Homberger actually reports of the Cantor: one can easily see that it would have been impossible for this comedy to take place without the Rector's knowledge and will, even if he later excused himself when danger arose—just as the Sovereign also demanded an accounting from him. However, resentment over this clear matter has moved the Anonymous writer to pass such judgments, since he had nothing to object against the matter itself <note>original Latin: "rem ipsam"</note>.

(10) But should the Anonymous writer have considered such droll plays with Pickelherings and indecencies to be permissible and harmless for the poor, innocent youth—as one must conclude from his resentment toward this truthful account—then one should well take to heart what wise theologians <note>original Latin: "cordate Theologi"</note> in our Church have always judged about this according to God's Word. They cite, among others, the following reasons <note>original: "Rationes"</note>: 1) All shameful words and foolish talk are forbidden to Christians (Ephesians 5:4; 1 Thessalonians 5:22). 2) Fornication and impurity shall not even be named among them (Ephesians 5:3; Colossians 3:8). 3) The exchange of men's and women's clothing is an abomination to the Lord (Deuteronomy 22:5). 4) Such things cannot possibly be done in faith, and are therefore sin (Romans 14:23). 5) Much less can they be done in the name of Jesus or to His honor (1 Corinthians 10:31; Colossians 3:17). 6) Evil company and the portrayal of vices corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33). 7) For the sake of our neighbor, we are bound to avoid even the appearance of evil, not to mention for the sake of the youth.

# The 42nd Accusation:
### Another example is his account of Eobanus Hessus, page 136. <note>Helius Eobanus Hessus (1488–1540) was a famous German Latin poet of the Renaissance.</note>

# Response:

(1) As for me, I would gladly pass over this passage in silence, as it is just as much a hateful matter <note>original Latin: "res odiosa"</note> as the previous one. But since the ill-will of the Anonymous writer once again accuses this undeniable account of a double crime—namely, malice and shoddy work <note>original: "Sudeley"</note>—it must be recapitulated against my will so that the reader can form a sound judgment.

(2) Joachim Camerarius <note>A famous classical scholar and friend of Melanchthon</note>, in his *Life of Eobanus Hessus*, writes of the well-known poet among other things:
> He thought that even in drinking contests, he should not be defeated by another... And he achieved this as well, so that no one wanted to contend with Eobanus for the prize in that category. But in a short time, the excessive fullness severely afflicted his youthful body and weakened his strength considerably. <note>original Latin: "Putavit se etiam inter poculorum certamina... non vinci ab altero oportere... Atque est ille hoc quoque consecutus, ut de palma in isto genere cum Eobano contendere vellet nemo. Sed brevi tempore repletione nimia juvenile corpus graviter afflixit, & vires nonnihil enervavit."</note>

(3) Thereupon he relates at length what Mr. Arnold summarized briefly in Book 16, Chapter 14, Section 21: Another famous drunkard had come and set before him a large wooden vessel <note>The text notes: "it should be called a vessel (Gefäß) and not a cask (Faß), as it was a misprint"</note> of Danzig beer, thrown a ring into it, and said: if he drank this all down, he should have the ring. Whereupon Hessus drank the vessel dry and turned it over. <note>original Latin: "evacuat bibendo, & cum everteret, sicut mos fert compotantium," meaning "he emptied it by drinking, and turned it over, as is the custom of drinking companions."</note>

(4) Everyone who is a lover of Christian moderation and, conversely, an enemy of the vaunted "German Gluttony" <note>Völlerey</note> as a mortal sin, will disapprove of this deed and the immoderate lifestyle of this poet, who nevertheless boasted so much of the Gospel and of Luther himself in his verses. Nor should anyone easily suspect that any person, let alone a—

---

Part III, No. 42. Response to old and new writers and defenders of the Church and Arnold. 373

—teacher would disapprove of such true accounts of the foolishness and gluttony of certain men of letters. However, the Anonymous writer calls it "malice" and "shoddy work," and even a "dishonorable injustice."

(5) Since, however, he finds no appearance of fault in the matter itself for his insults, he says that Mr. Arnold dishonorably wrongs the honest historian <note>Camerarius</note> when he says that he [Camerarius] wrote of this drinking contest among his [Hessus's] "praises" <note>original: "Lob-Sprüche"</note> and could not approve of it for shame. It is almost a waste of precious time, yet this briefly serves as a response.

(6) The Anonymous writer here falsifies Mr. Arnold’s words in a very cunning way, thinking no one would notice. For he does not keep the expression and construction of the words as found in the *History of the Church and Heretics* <note>Arnold's primary work</note>, but twists them into a completely false sense. For it is one thing to say Camerarius wrote something *among* his [Hessus's] praises <note>Arnold used the Ablative case here: "unter seinen Lob-Sprüchen"</note>, and quite another to say he wrote it *as* one of his praises <note>The Accusative case: "unter seine Lob-Sprüche"</note>. The former only implies that Camerarius, while praising Hessus or writing his eulogies, also included this fact, regardless of whether he actually praised it or offered it as a point of merit. The latter, however, means he explicitly set it down as an actual point of praise among the others. As small as this difference seems, it is significant.

(7) Now the question is: did Mr. Arnold say the first or the last? I answer and prove it was the first: a) from the clear words of the *History of the Church and Heretics*, where it can plainly be read: "Camerarius writes this *among* his [Hessus's] praises"; and the Anonymous writer repeats them as such himself, but then immediately twists them in the 12th line and changes the Ablative into the Accusative. b) From Mr. Arnold’s own qualification, where he notes: Camerarius did not wish to approve of it, and could not for shame—namely, even though he otherwise praises him. c) From the fact that Mr. Arnold elsewhere writes of Camerarius quite honorably, as this learned and moderate man well deserves. d) From Camerarius's own protestations, which he uses in this very history, revealing his displeasure:
> One thing I fear: even if the matter does not please me, and I have often been indignant in my soul, that this evil also seized Eobanus, etc. <note>original Latin: "Unum vereor: & si mihi res non placet, & saepe indignatus fui animo meo, hoc etiam malum corripuisse Eobanum &c."</note>

(8) I leave this to the reader to consider, who will now recognize how the "falsifications" alleged by the Anonymous writer on the title page and in the margin—

# Part IV.
## Consisting of the response to the so-called *Württemberg Innocence* by Mr. Andreas David Caroli, Superintendent at Kirchheim.

### The 1st Accusation:
That Mr. Arnold is stuck in preconceived false **principal-opinions**. <note>The term "principal-opinions" refers to core theological assumptions or foundational beliefs.</note> page 8.

### Answer:
These are not actually specified, much less proven or refuted; yet the author intends to remedy them through seven remarks—or rather contrary **principal-opinions**—which he undoubtedly wants to set against those others. We shall now briefly examine these to see how far they reach.

## The I. Presupposition is:

-> Even those could be pure teachers, and be heard with benefit, who commit heavy sins. <-

(1) Two things are said here: namely, that ungodly teachers or willfully heavy sinners can teach α) purely and β) usefully or salvifically. This is intended to be proven through several similes, as is commonly the case when a lack of true Divine grounds leads one to take refuge in such *limping similes* <note>original: "similibus claudicantibus." This refers to analogies that do not quite fit the situation or "fall short" of the logic required.</note>. For there is no clear Divine proof to be found in Holy Scripture that an ungodly teacher can present all his teaching purely and salvifically; rather, the manifest opposite is found in Matthew 15:14 and Luke 6:39: namely, that if a blind man leads another, they both fall into the ditch. Indeed, that an ungodly person teaches nothing right because it does not come from GOD, according to Sirach 15:9 <note>Sirach 15:9: "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner, for it was not sent him of the Lord."</note>, and that therefore GOD does not want one who hates discipline to take His covenant into his mouth, Psalm 50:16, etc.

(2) However, if this matter had not been debated <note>original: "ventilirt"</note> by so many for so long and the opposite maintained, it could be done here in detail. One remains safest with Christ’s clear statement, which no reason can criticize: namely, that no blind man can show the way to another,

---

IV. Part 1. No. 1. Preface. Mr. Andreas David Caroli etc. 377

and consequently can teach neither purely nor usefully. That a coarse sinner or ungodly teacher is blind to the Kingdom of GOD, and as a natural man does not himself understand the things of the Spirit of GOD, will hopefully be denied by no one against Holy Scripture and daily experience. For further evidence, one should consult the very latest *Program* of Mr. Dr. Johann Olearius, Senior in Leipzig, *on the danger of new Hypotheses, regarding the true illumination of ungodly Doctors* <note>original: "de periculo novarum Hypothesium, de vera impiorum Doctorum illuminatione." This refers to a contemporary academic debate on whether unregenerate men could possess spiritual insight.</note>; then one will hopefully see things with quite different eyes.

(3) The words cited from Mr. Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the leading figure of Lutheran Pietism.</note> do not say everything that Mr. Caroli says—namely, that an evil teacher teaches purely and usefully: rather, they only say that the Word does not have its power from the preacher, which no Evangelical Christian will contradict. Meanwhile, Dr. Spener does not say that the power cannot be hindered or even suppressed by an evil preacher: as, among others, **Gerhard** acknowledges in *Topics on the Ministry, number 275* <note>original: "Gerhardus Loc. de Minist. num. 275," referring to the "Loci Theologici" of Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a giant of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note>, and as experience also daily shows the listeners. Therefore, Dr. Spener’s short words must be explained from his more detailed deduction, which is found in his *General Theology* <note>original: "Allgemeinen Gottesgelehrtheit."</note> page 255 and following. There, he does not wish to say that such a teacher can teach nothing good at all: or that what he repeats from Scripture (namely, unadulterated) cannot have its power: nevertheless, he maintains on page 257 (citing our own theologians) that such a person is not fit to perform everything in the instruction of others that **edification** <note>The term "edification" (Erbauung) was a central goal for Pietists, meaning the building up of the soul in actual faith and practice, rather than just intellectual learning.</note> requires. One reason, among others, is this: because such a person must necessarily distort the best and most necessary grounds of Christianity—concerning repentance and the power of faith, for which he has no desire—and pull them toward a fleshly, security-inducing sense, so that he is not punished by his own listeners.

(4) And since the blessed Dr. Spener is cited here—whom he also calls "the dear Dr. Spener" below on page 122—Mr. Caroli could have found his confession on this question better and more closely from his other passages in the *Theological Reflections* <note>original: "Theologischen Bedencken," a famous collection of Spener's responses to spiritual and ecclesiastical questions.</note>, which Mr. Caroli also alleges below on page 44. There, in Part III, page 416, he very earnestly grants this sentence in its healthy sense: That GOD’s Word, when handled by the dead <note>In this context, "the dead" refers to those who are "spiritually dead" or lack a living, personal faith.</note>, is without effect; and he refers to his *General Theology*, where it is fully deduced, especially on page 255. He also holds in Part I, page 409, that the corruption arising through evil preachers is a piece of Divine judgment and a further means of it; and this is specifically because through such preachers, security and coldness are fostered.

### The III. Presupposition is:

->The Lutheran Church has never approved the sins of its teachers. page 10.<-

(1) Here it is first to be noted / that Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the radical Pietist historian whose work "A." refers to here.</note> has nowhere attributed to the entire Lutheran Church / that it approves the sins of its teachers. (2) He pretends / that Arnold has used these testimonies with violent abuse: but the evidence here will show the contrary. Yes, he even demands on page 17 / that one should not deify the Church Fathers <note>The authoritative theologians of the early Christian church.</note>; and thus can let such things be all the less opposed to him by newer teachers.

(6) Just as certainly as these teachers are forgiven for their incorrect doctrines and deeds, even if one does not call them good or praise them for them; so certainly can one also forgive the Lutheran teachers and not deal with them shamefully, even if one cites and expresses the matter itself according to the law of history <note>original: *ex lege historiæ*</note> as it actually was. Meanwhile, this does not indicate such a great innocence when one must nonetheless confess inexcusable things and only pretend to seek forgiveness and excuse.

That the Lutheran Church also has its great flaws,

but that this does not come from her teachers alone, and therefore one should not complain about all of them. p. 17.

(1) Two different questions are mixed together here which should be well distinguished. For it is one thing whether the flaws come from the teachers alone; it is another whether they come from all teachers, or from each and every teacher. Neither of these will Mr. Arnold or any impartial person affirm absolutely. Mr. Arnold himself specified so many pious Lutheran teachers who complained about the flaws and consequently were not to blame for them.

(2) But there is still a third option <note>original: *Tertium*</note> remaining: namely, that the flaws come partly from most of the teachers, and partly primarily and first of all from them. This is what each and every righteous teacher has themselves lamented at all times, of which sufficient examples <note>original: *Specimina*</note> could follow, if the matter were not already, alas, actually clear!

(3) I will not mention the almost countless confessions of so many martyrs and witnesses of the truth under the Papacy, which are repeated in the *Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth* <note>original: *Catalogo Testium Veritatis*, a famous work by Matthias Flacius Illyricus listing people who opposed the Papacy before the Reformation.</note>, in Wolfius’s *Memorable Events* <note>Johannes Wolfius (1537–1600), author of *Lectionum memorabilium et reconditarum centenarii XVI*.</note>, and others, partly also in the *Church History*; where, for example, entire chapters stand in the works of Nicolaus de Clemangis <note>A 15th-century French theologian known for criticizing clerical corruption.</note> and others regarding how the priests were to blame for all the misery in the world. Regarding this, Luther also addressed them so heartfully in the preface to his Small Catechism: *You are the ones to whom, perhaps alone, that calamity of the Christian religion is owed; ... yours is that fault.* <note>original: "Vos estis, quibus vel solis illa religionis Christianæ calamitas debetur; --- vestra ea est culpa."</note> Rather, for the sake of brevity, we want to hear from some Lutheran theologians. Selneccerus <note>Nikolaus Selnecker (1530–1592), a primary author of the Formula of Concord.</note> confesses regarding the 71st Psalm, p. 137: That evil preachers are more harmful than heretics. A false teacher who holds the right doctrine but does not live according to it gives much offense; he is a hypocrite, or a secure, reckless person who does more damage than an open heretic whom one can guard against.

<meta>This page continues a rebuttal against Andreas David Caroli’s defense of the Lutheran clergy. The author is arguing that the primary cause of spiritual decay in a nation is the corruption of its ministers, citing Pietist leaders like Spener and historical figures like Chrysostom to support the claim that "fruitless" preaching is often the fault of the preacher, not just the congregation.</meta>

# Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence, Part IV, Section I, No. 7. Preface.

others mention this in the *Watchman’s Voice* <note>original: *Wächter-Stimme*</note>, Chapter 6, pages 84–85: When the estate of the church ministers becomes corrupt, the most noble members of the church perish. Beneath the heavens, there is nothing more excellent than the Office of the Holy Spirit; but when it is corrupted by pride, greed <note>original: *Geit*, an archaic form of *Geiz*</note>, or false doctrine and the like, nothing is more harmful. This contains a nation's greatest misfortune. How often did the blessed Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the influential founder of Pietism who called for individual renewal and spiritual reform within Lutheranism.</note> uncover this fountain of all misery? For example, in his *Pious Desires* <note>original: *Piis Desideriis* (1675), Spener's most famous work outlining the need for church reform.</note> on page 10, he confessed: "We cannot deny that most of the corruption breaks out among the congregation from our two upper estates <note>The "upper estates" refers to the nobility and the clergy.</note>." In doing so, he cites the words of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an early Church Father known for his eloquent preaching and his critiques of the clergy.</note> from Varenius <note>August Varenius (1620–1684), a Lutheran theologian.</note> in the place cited <note>original: *l. c.* (loco citato)</note>, stating that the rot of a tree comes from the root, and the rot of a people comes from the priesthood. Indeed, in the third part of his *Theological Reflections* <note>original: *Theol. Bedenck.*</note>, page 561, he also observes from experience that reform is primarily hindered by such people. And there are many more such complaints which are still found to be true daily in practice <note>original: *Praxi*</note>.

(5) Now that this truth is clear from such irreproachable testimonies—and alas! even clearer from experience—Mr. Caroli’s proof must be examined briefly. He proves it with the parable of a house-father and ruler who bears no guilt for the disorder. And yet, he immediately admits that this is often the case, or it applies only to some extent, or not at all. He also says that teachers are sometimes innocent, thereby admitting that they are sometimes—indeed often, as he said above—not innocent. He must now undoubtedly admit this specifically <note>original: *in specie*</note> regarding his own fatherland; consequently <note>original: *consequenter*</note>, the *Württemberg Innocence* <note>The book being refuted, which defended the local clergy from charges of corruption.</note> cannot possibly stand as correct in all matters, as much as one might wish it for them.

(6) He further presents the case <note>original: *Caſum*</note> where a teacher might do his part honestly, and yet success does not follow. For this, he cites the words of Mr. von Seckendorff <note>Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff (1626–1692), a prominent Lutheran statesman and historian.</note> from *The Christian State* <note>original: *Chriſten-Staat*</note>, page 557, saying that even the most edifying and zealous preachers of repentance <term>preachers of repentance: *Buß-Prediger*, ministers who focused on the necessity of internal conversion and sorrow for sin.</term> nevertheless accomplish little. However, the idea that no fruit follows a pure and divine presentation of the Word contradicts God's clear promise in Isaiah 55:10 and following. Conversely, that this lack of fruit—when it occurs—is a certain sign that God's Word was not preached as it should be, God says clearly again in Jeremiah 23:22: **"But if they had stood in my counsel, and had caused my people to hear my words, then they should have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings."**

(7) But if often the most zealous preachers of repentance accomplish little,
<meta>that</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>Part IV, Section I, No. 7. Preface. Mr. Andreas David Caroli, etc.</header>
that should not lead us to the delusion that it is not also the fault of the preachers. Rather, one should learn from this that the doctrine shows its fruit in proportion to how it is conducted. If a teacher preaches the word of the Gospel entirely without any mixture of human things, he will also find true Evangelical fruits and have "living letters" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:2, suggesting the transformed lives of the congregation are the proof of a minister's success.</note> of his office. If he preaches only legally or zealously, and not purely according to the Gospel of truth regarding Jesus Christ (as Mr. von Seckendorff seems to suggest), he will indeed experience little fruit, and what he finds will not be the right kind.

(8) Again, Mr. Caroli says: Success is not in the teacher's power. On the contrary, however, it *is* in his power to hinder the Word, either through an impure and mangled presentation and application, or through a bad example. And if it is not in his power, then he likely does not seek or pray for such power from God, who would gladly give it to him; thus, such a person is once again left without excuse. It is a different matter, however, when a righteous teacher in a state of spiritual trial <note>original: *Anfechtung*, referring to a period of doubt or intense spiritual struggle.</note> cannot see any fruits, even though they are actually there; regarding this, Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the radical Pietist historian whose work sparked this debate.</note> has observed much in his *The Shape of an Evangelical Teacher* <note>original: *Geſtalt eines Evangeliſchen Lehrers*</note>, Chapter 16, § 22 and following.

(9) The example of Jeremiah is not at all fitting here and proves less than nothing. For the question here is not whether the people also share the guilt for the corruption—which indeed no one denies—but rather whether the *most* guilt lies with the teachers. It is obvious that in Jeremiah's time, the people had already been so corrupted and misled by the teachers *before* his time that they were now entirely hardened and close to the outbreak of Divine judgments, which Jeremiah himself lived to see. There, Jeremiah was certainly not at fault, and yet he still found one or two souls in whom his word bore fruit, as is known from his history. Just as Mr. Caroli confesses of Ezekiel, that he nevertheless made a few obedient. On the other hand, [Jeremiah] expressly referred in the aforementioned passage (Chapter 23:22) to the fact that where God's Word was truly preached, the people would also be converted. And when Mr. Caroli places the blame on the people, one gladly agrees with him, provided that the entire blame is not cast upon them alone.

(10) For Mr. Caroli himself speaks so harshly of evil preachers that such expressions might well be held against Mr. Arnold if he were to use them. He says there on page 19: **The evil preachers were given to the people by God in His wrath**, and the Lutheran Church has, if such reprehensible teachers exist within it, such...

Dogs and evil workers / world- and belly-priests <note>Terms derived from Philippians 3:2 and Romans 16:18, often used by reformers to describe clergy more interested in worldly status and physical comfort than spiritual duties.</note> are present; one is rightfully entitled to complain about them to the highest degree. ### From the Preface of the Anonymous Publisher.

#### The 2nd Accusation:

He allegedly does not just help one or another type of sect and heresy, but rather takes up the defense of all of them, ancient and modern alike, without distinction and with great skill.

#### Answer:

(1) Before we turn to the book itself, there are various things to remind the reader regarding its title, especially when the rulers of the Duchy of Württemberg are mentioned as if they were attacked in the *Church History*, when in fact only one was mentioned: namely, Duke Ulrich. <note>Duke Ulrich of Württemberg (1487–1550), who introduced the Reformation to his lands but had a tumultuous and often violent reign.</note> However, for the sake of brevity, we will pass over this and answer the main complaints themselves.

(2) This first general accusation, however, has already been addressed in the previous answers with such clear distinction that impartial readers need only look there. They will see the grounds quite clearly regarding if and how far Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the Pietist historian whose "Unbiased Church and Heretic History" argued that "heretics" were often truer Christians than the institutional clergy.</note> reported on the heretics: namely, in Part I, Nos. 2, 13, 17, 27, 104, and 107; in Part II, Nos. 13 and 43; and in Part III, No. 32.

(3) It is also clear by comparison <note>original: *ex collatione*</note> that Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus (1658–1707), a Lutheran theologian who wrote the "Württemberg Innocence" to defend the state church against Arnold's criticisms.</note> has partly drawn and repeated his accusations from those authors who were already answered in Parts II and III; therefore, those answers apply here as well.

#### The 3rd Accusation:

He allegedly coats the holy and most-wholesome Reformation of our church with a thousand insulting stains everywhere, as much as he is able.

#### Answer:

(1) Regarding how respectfully and laudably Mr. A. described Luther’s Reformation in all its circumstances, one need only take the trouble to look at the answer to the 9th Accusation above in Part II.

(2) Whether and how far he had to historically <note>original: *historice*</note> note the subsequent decline and other failings of some teachers has already been examined in the previous Part I, Nos. 3, 21, 49, and 106.

### From the Preparation.

#### The 4th Accusation:

He allegedly makes the entire Church of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530.</note> endure the most gruesome predicates, and he leaves nothing back with which he thinks he can cause it pain. p. 6.

#### Answer:

(1) Before the author comes to these specific <note>original: *special*-Anklagen</note> accusations, he rambles at great length about the persecutions and the poor treatment of those who confess the pure Gospel—how they are scolded, persecuted, slandered, etc. Although Mr. A. might have much to say about such treatment from his own experience—how he has been dealt with regarding his testimony about the abuse of the Gospel and its unhappy fruits—it is nonetheless more necessary at this time and place to go to the matter itself and answer the reproaches against him. Anyone who wishes to read the latest on the treatment of the witnesses of the truth <note>original: *testium veritatis*</note> can look at the introduction to the *Vindication* <note>original: *Ehren-Rettung*</note> by Counselor Brenneysen. <note>Enno Rudolph Brenneysen (1669–1734), a jurist and official who defended Pietists and advocates of religious tolerance.</note>

(2) Mr. Carolus undoubtedly calls the Lutheran church the "Church of the Augsburg Confession," and by this he understands either those souls who, according to Luther's testimony, believe the Gospel and walk worthily within it, or only such teachers who indeed boast of the Gospel but deny its power. Mr. A. certainly never sought to cause pain to the former; for he holds such people in high and dear esteem, knowing that what is done to them as members of Christ is done to the Lord himself. Likewise, such true Evangelical Christians cannot and will not take the testimonies of general decline as a cause of pain; rather, they rejoice in the truth even in this, and do not take it as poorly as so many have done until now.

(3) If, however, Mr. Carolus understands "the Church" to mean those teachers who have indeed fought much over the letter of Scripture and over philosophy mixed into theology, but who [lack] the mystery of faith in the power...

[one who] preserves [the truth] for himself and others with a pure conscience: thus, their misery has indeed had to be uncovered. However, Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the Pietist historian being defended here.</note> never sought to intentionally cause them pain, but only to improve them and others, or to remedy <note>original: "remediren"</note> the damage caused thereby, as much as was in his power.

### The 5th Accusation:

He is said to be particularly harsh toward the overseers and teachers of the Church, begrudging them anything that could or should serve to preserve their good and blessed memory. p. 6.

### Answer:

(1) It has been demonstrated above from his own clear confessions that Mr. Arnold grants the upright Evangelical-Lutheran teachers much—indeed, all—honor and good memory. He has highly praised many from the 16th century, such as Luther, Weller, and Mathesius <note>Hieronymus Weller and Johannes Mathesius were prominent early Lutheran theologians and associates of Martin Luther.</note>, as well as many from the 17th century. See Part I, the 3rd Accusation, § 6.

(2) Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus (1658–1707), a Lutheran orthodox theologian and critic of Arnold.</note> himself must later admit this to some extent on page 7, when he says: "If he does report something laudable about them, he either seeks an advantage in it, or he casts doubt on the already known matter, etc." Now, anyone who reports something laudable about someone certainly grants them that credit. The "evil suspicion" that is interspersed here cannot hold weight against such honest confessions as those we find regarding Luther in the *Church History*, which are quite exceptional.

(3) The remaining specific complaints <note>original: "special-Klagen"</note> attached to this on page 7 will be dismantled as we proceed through the investigation of the examples; although most of this has already appeared above.

### The 6th Accusation:

He is allegedly under the delusion that whoever wishes to be a true Christian must separate themselves from the Lutheran Church, just as from all sects. p. 7.

### Answer:

(1) How powerfully this slander—which Mr. Carolus merely repeats after others—has been refuted by both word and deed can be seen in Part I, No. 26, and can still be recognized daily from Mr. Arnold's conduct.

(2) Since the author <note>Carolus</note> makes this the primary basis for his following accusations, and yet it completely collapses and has been proven null before the whole world—given that Mr. Arnold still constantly confesses to and remains with our Lutheran Church—one will simultaneously find all the contradictions built upon it

<column-break/>

<page-num>391</page-num>
<header>Part IV, Nos. 6, 7. Mr. Andreas David Carolus, etc.</header>

to be powerless and void, as the progress of this work shall demonstrate.

(3) It is equally malicious when it is written, without the slightest proof, as if Mr. Arnold handles the doctrine very poorly in many respects, and that his conceptual framework consists of the most dangerous errors. The opposite has been shown one after another in the above deductions <note>original: "Deductionibus"</note>; and who would believe such charges without a binding demonstration <note>original: "Demonstration"</note>? Indeed, it takes more than a mere accusation to declare someone erroneous.

### The 7th Accusation:

Regarding Arnold's procedure, one must remember that which the author of the *Bibliotheca universalis* dared to do against Augustine.

### Answer:

(1) This procedure is described in Poiret's <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystic and philosopher.</note> book *On Erudition* <note>original: "de Eruditione"</note>, page 482, stating that the author intended to recognize and describe nothing good in Augustine, but only pure evil. Mr. Carolus suggests Mr. Arnold has proceeded in the same way with Lutheran teachers, because he says: *the application fits quite accurately in the case of many an accused theologian.*

(2) But let it be noted here impartially: a) that it is highly unjust to compare the author <note>Arnold</note> to a pure satirist <note>original: "Satyrico"</note> and mocker, or even a Socinian <note>original: "Socinianer" — followers of a non-trinitarian doctrine often viewed as the most extreme of heretics by the orthodox.</note> (as that other author is considered), while wanting to compare all Lutheran teachers (among whom, by Mr. Carolus's own admission, many were wicked) to Augustine. To stay on this subject: Mr. Arnold has certainly and sincerely praised Augustine’s conversion, honest confessions, and merits <note>original: "Meriten"</note>. He has never mocked such workings of the grace of the Holy Spirit as that other author did, as can be seen in the *Church History*. And thus, one gladly accepts Poiret's judgment <note>original: "Judicium"</note> of Augustine and every teacher like him.

(3) In the meantime, however, one should consider even more maturely which and how many teachers of our church could truly and without flattery be compared to Augustine. Specifically, on this point that Poiret primarily cites in defense of Augustine: namely, a true, thorough conversion of the heart, and the resulting confession of previous blindness and other deviations. One gladly hopes for the best from everyone, but one also knows that, next to Luther’s thorough conversion from Pharisaism <note>original: "Pharisäismo" — here meaning a reliance on outward religious laws rather than internal faith.</note> to Evangelical Christianity, not every single person has experienced the path of thorough repentance and thus powerfully recommended it to others as Augustine did.

(4) Finally, regarding what Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the Pietist historian whose "Church and Heretic History" caused significant controversy for its sympathetic portrayal of "heretics."</note> complained of in his general remarks on page 25, and which is cited by Mr. Carolus: namely, how people often seek to harm innocent men through evil interpretations and the twisting of their words, or how they are falsely quoted, mutilated, or added to—alas! he has had to suffer enough of this until this very hour. And though Mr. Carolus believes it has been shown to Arnold's face how he himself has played such a game, any impartial person can well recognize the injustice of his opponents from the previous and further defense, and distinguish light from darkness.

### The 8th Accusation:

->He sought to justify his wicked work with a worthless self-persuasion. p. 22.<-

### Answer:

(1) In the preface to his *Church History* § 32, Mr. Arnold had answered the objection that one should not uncover the shame of the ancients to their disgrace. To this he had replied: 
> "a) Holy Scripture itself and all historians nevertheless recount such faults; b) not all the ancients are to be compared to Noah; and c) the mocking, malicious laughter of Ham <note>In the biblical book of Genesis, Ham mocked his father Noah's nakedness, whereas his brothers covered him; this was often used as a metaphor for whether a historian should expose or hide the failings of Church Fathers.</note> is far different from a righteous, compassionate, and cautionary narrative, etc."

(2) Against these answers, Mr. Carolus objects: a) that Scripture had special motives which no historian can have. However, the motives are unquestionably and consistently the punishment and suppression of evil, and the praise and spreading of good (no one can name any closer or better motives), and these another person can and must also have. For Mr. Arnold still keeps this testimony in his conscience before the living GOD through His grace: that he has had and still has these two main motives for his purpose in all his work. No human contradictions shall take this certainty and joy from him.

(3) When our own theologians debate <note>original: "ventiliren"</note> this question—whether the <term>shame of Noah</term> <note>original Latin: "pudenda Noæ." This refers to the biblical account of Noah's drunkenness and nakedness.</note> should always be covered—they distinguish between mere weaknesses and those things that are <term>deliberate</term> <note>original Latin: "proæretica"</note>, scandalous, publicly harmful, contrary to the glory of the Divine, or required by a judge for discovery. Indeed, they say this should be done not with an intent to mock, but—take note!—with an intent to correct and warn. To this end, they cite the examples of Jacob uncovering the shame of Laban, David uncovering Saul, and Paul uncovering Peter. Whoever wishes can find all of this in Dannhauer <note>Johann Conrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note>, in *College on the Decalogue*, disputation XI, question 1, page 654. There, Rivet's answer to this reproach of Mr. Carolus is also cited

->Arnold appeals in vain to all historians.<-

(1) Nevertheless, Mr. Carolus himself admits that through their pens, many faults of our ancestors have been discovered, p. 23. He then scolds him as an advocate for separatists or free-thinking eccentrics—indeed, for all fanatics and enemies of the clergy.

Who these might have been, he specifies with no example, and thus one cannot answer further, because specific proof is lacking.

(4) One also gladly leaves the judgment to GOD alone, as Mr. Carolus does. In the meantime, however, strong evidence might unfortunately still exist to doubt whether any Lutheran has ever denied that it is possible, in a divine walk through God's grace, to come as far as Noah. For alas! in these last years, especially in the struggle against Mr. Dr. Spener, Mr. Francke <note>Philipp Jakob Spener and August Hermann Francke, the founding fathers of Lutheran Pietism.</note>, and others, this truth...

### The 10th Accusation.
->He engages in mocking, scornful laughter. p. 23.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) First of all, Mr. Carolus accepts Mr. Arnold’s **warning narratives** as being justified by the circumstances, and thus acknowledges that such things are indeed to be found in the **Church History** <note>Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (Church and Heretic History), a landmark Pietist work.</note>. However, he seeks to verify this specific accusation from three passages. The first *) is contained in Part II, Chapter 16, § 3, where a letter from Sulcerus <note>Simon Sulcer (1508–1585), a Swiss reformer.</note> is cited with these words: "The reason for this (namely, for the affected preference) was to be found among many, that they immediately let their hair grow as they hurried toward the preaching office, so that they might have a prestigious appearance and look truly venerable, just as someone advised a certain young candidate." In this context, Sulcerus’s letter is cited from Fecht's *Supplement to Church History* <note>original: "Supplem. H. E." (Supplementum Historiae Ecclesiasticae)</note> p. 400, where he writes: "I also advised them that, because they professed to be candidates of Holy Theology, they should grow their hair and wear clothing appropriate to that profession." <note>original: "Monui etiam ipfos, ut, quia S. Theol. Candidatos ſe profitebantur, comam alant, & veſtitu utantur eam professionem decente."</note>

(2) Sulcerus wrote this in the year 1571, when preachers no longer wore their hair short in simplicity, as Luther and the ancients had done, but let it grow long. Why they changed it is easy to imagine. Mr. Arnold notes this here, which is certainly not forbidden to a **Historian**: and although he speaks of the "venerable appearance," every reader can see that he is not engaging in mocking, scornful laughter; otherwise, the words would have to sound quite different.

(3) The second **) example is said to be from Hunnius’s College <note>Likely referring to the school of Aegidius Hunnius, a staunch Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note>, which was already discussed above in Part II, No. 51. However, Mr. Arnold does not engage in the slightest mockery there, but expresses in precise terms the condition that was set there—namely, regarding those **theologians burning with zeal**. How else could he have reported the matter? If such passages in the **Church History** had not been read with a preoccupied mind in order to find some fault in the author, the words would have been found entirely innocent.

(4) The third γ) example is cited regarding **Dr. Krakewitz** <note>David Krakewitz (1582–1634), a Lutheran theologian and general superintendent in Pomerania.</note>, which Arnold is said to have cited four times. Now, I will not repeat these here, lest I also be accused of doing so out of mockery. The account appears twice in the history itself as an event that

is indeed strange and bad enough—that a **Doctor of Theology** was treated in such a way. But that the entry in the **Index** is also counted toward this, simply so that the number four can be reached, is something no one will hold against the accuser: for **Indexes** are not made into **realities** <note>meaning: the index is not the primary substance or evidence of the work</note>; they only point to the text and thus signify nothing on their own. Furthermore, the **Index** was not prepared by Mr. Arnold himself.

(5) And yet, it can be clearly seen in the context itself, namely in Book XVII, Chapter 1, § 22, that this deed is mentioned primarily as an example of the cruelty perpetrated by the Imperial forces in Pomerania at that time, as the marginal note explicitly states. And oh, that it might not have to be said how duty is exceeded in such zeal! Then there would be no need for complaints about the description of such things later.

### The 11th Accusation.
->He shows his passion for slander everywhere. p. 24.<-

->Answer:<-

(1) That Mr. Arnold does not **slander** in his reports, but describes histories as they occurred, has been explained many times here in the first three parts. And even if the accusers insist on such "slander," the author’s conscience and every dispassionate reader absolve him of it.

(2) Mr. Carolus thinks he can deduce this from the **Index**, specifically from the **titles: Lutheran, Clergy,** and **Orthodox**. Now, if those **titles** were not **verified** in the history itself, but were simply placed there without foundation or the testimony of capable **writers**, they might rightly be called slanders. But as it is, such **reports** are nothing but the words of other—and mostly **domestic authors** <note>writers from within the same tradition or era</note>—which no one can deny, and which are still, alas, confirmed daily by experience! How then can this be called a passion for slander before **GOD** or the world?

(3) Regarding the **Index**, information can be found above in the preface as to how it proves nothing against the author *in this matter* <note>original: "in hoc passu"</note>. Mr. Arnold would later have liked to see it arranged more cautiously by its compiler, because the good things contained in the history regarding our Church were mentioned too briefly in the **Index**. Therefore, those who wish to refute a book should not perversely start with the **Index**, but look at the text itself; thus, much useless strife would be avoided.

## The 12th Accusation:
->He only treats the name "Orthodox" with mockery. p. 24.<-

### Answer:
(1) This reproach has already been irreproachably addressed in Part I, Numbers 59 and 108. It was specifically shown how Mr. Arnold, in his *Church History*, <note>Gottfried Arnold’s "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie," a famous and controversial work of the time.</note> carefully distinguished the abuse of "orthodoxy" from its proper use, and how he holds the latter, alongside Divine doctrine itself, in high and worthy regard. For the rest, it is common nowadays that those who find themselves affected by his critiques immediately complain about mockery of orthodoxy. This was also the case with Court Councilor Pfanner in the *Innocent News* <note>original: "Unschuld. Nachrichten," a leading Lutheran theological journal of the era.</note> where he was similarly accused in the year 1707, p. 180.

(2) From these clear arguments <note>original: "Remonstrationibus"</note>, the slanderous conclusion of Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus, the primary critic Arnold is answering.</note> falls away of its own accord—specifically where he calls Mr. Arnold a "Ham" who invents a "nakedness" for many a "Noah." <note>A biblical reference to Ham, who saw his father Noah’s nakedness and was cursed; Carolus is accusing Arnold of shaming the "fathers" of the Church.</note> Oh, if only there had always been many "Noahs" among the crowd of Christendom! How gladly would Mr. Arnold, and anyone else who longs and works for general improvement, have covered their nakedness or faults!

Yet Mr. Carolus confidently repeats such harsh accusations from other adversaries of the *Church History*, to the significant detriment of the truth and his ignorant neighbor!

(2) He further accuses: It was not possible for Arnold to show as much sincerity to the teachers as Calvin showed to Luther. Now, let everyone read the repeated speeches of praise for Luther—as the head of all Lutheran teachers—found in Part II under the 9th Accusation; likewise, his life in the *Life of the Faithful*. <note>Another work by Arnold.</note> One will then be able to grasp the untruth of this accusation with one's own hands. ->The 16th Accusation:<-
### He smears Duke Ulrich, saying whatever he thinks serves to totally destroy all of his Princely fame. p. 29. <note>Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg (1487–1550), was a key but controversial figure who introduced the Reformation to his territory.</note>
->Answer:<-
(1) In the title, it was said that Arnold had written against the "Württemberg Rulers" <note>plural</note>; but here only one is specified. Before this matter itself is examined and answered, I first solemnly protest in a proper manner that I publish this forced defense of Arnold merely to rescue historical truth; and for the rest, I acknowledge myself bound to all most humble respect toward the High Princely House.

(2) Mr. Caroli complains that Arnold does not report on Duke Ulrich’s fame. I answer: what does not belong directly to the circumstances of Church History, Mr. Arnold neither could nor should report, because he did not have to write a history of princes, much less <term>panegyrics</term><note>original: "Encomia," speeches or writings in high praise of someone.</note> or laudatory orations for those princes. It is also well known what Luther testified of Ulrich as a "strange piece of game in heaven," <note>original: "seltsamen Wildpret im Himmel." Luther famously used this expression to suggest that Ulrich’s salvation was a surprising act of God's grace, given his turbulent and often violent life.</note> and thus how cautiously one must proceed in such histories.

(3) Thirdly, it is false that Mr. Arnold took a sought-after opportunity to smear the Duke. He appeals to the omniscient God that, while searching for historical documents, he happened upon this passage by chance; and because he viewed it as a not very common or well-known report, he included it, just as he had recorded it and found the ancient writings themselves.

(4) Mr. Caroli rages over this as if it were his sovereign's personal matter; and so far, one does not hold it against him. Now, the best historians of the 16th century do this—Sleidanus, Chytræus, Crusius, Leodius, Schardius, and others—as can be seen in Chapter 2 of Book XVI, § 5. And regarding what happened with Ulrich von Hutten, Mr. Arnold cites the oldest documents that can be had, Part IV, p. 97.

Around the year 1543, Duke Ulrich was indeed Lutheran and, as Mr. Caroli likes to say, enlightened. Nevertheless, the Lord von Seckendorff writes this of him without hesitation: *Book III, Section 25, on Lutheranism, § 105, p. 427:* <note>original: "Nocebat causæ communi Ulricus Wirtenbergicus, violenter cum Eslingensibus agens, & Cæsaris blandimentis mollitus. He refused the contribution of costs for the Brunswick war."** And afterwards, he relates how he incited others to war but managed himself [carefully], and how the Elector mocked him for it. If Mr. Arnold had written this, he would be threatened with harsh things. Something of these dealings is also to be found in Cranz’s *Vandalia & Saxonia continued*, which is not at hand right now. But what the famous historian Paulus Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> writes in *Book 32 of his Histories* sounds much harsher: <note>original: "Ulricus Dux Wirtenbergensis uxorem clarissimis natalibus ortam væcordi impetu diverberavit, agitavitque calcaribus, quum prostratæ jumenti more temulentus & insanus insideret:"</note> **"Duke Ulrich of Württemberg, in a senseless rage, beat his wife, who was of most noble birth, and spurred her with spurs while he, drunk and insane, sat upon her as she lay prostrate like a beast of burden."** This is also repeated from Jovius by Zwinger in the *Theater of Human Life, Volume XX, Book III, p. 3405*, and cited as an example of the cruelty that some husbands have inflicted upon their spouses.

(8) One therefore rightly leaves this regent his due glory, but also finds clearly in the histories, and especially in Seckendorff, that he harmed the common cause, and also proceeded violently against those in Esslingen, and previously against those in Reutlingen <note>Esslingen and Reutlingen were Free Imperial Cities that frequently had territorial and political disputes with the Dukes of Württemberg.</note>; which indeed indicates no such peaceful mind. The matter is clear;

## The 17th Accusation:

> He thinks he may prostitute the work of the Reformation, along with its tools and first defenders, however he wishes. p. 32.

### Answer:

(1) GOD has faithfully preserved the author from such a mind and intention; therefore he has written as much good about the work of the Reformation and its first tools as an impartial person ever can, as may be found in detail above in Part I, Number 9.

(2) The cause of this accusation is supposedly because Mr. Arnold says (*Part IV, p. 97*) that most who boasted of the Gospel were restless and raging heads. Now Mr. Caroli himself admits in § 6: there were indeed—which is not contradicted—such heads among them, just as there are always weeds among the wheat. He denies, however, that they were the "most." But oh, that Luther himself had not experienced this during his life among the high and low, and had not had to endure so much regarding the restless war-plots! Without doubt, the irreparable damage caused by the Schmalkaldic War <note>The war (1546–1547) between the forces of Emperor Charles V and the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League.</note> would not have occurred. Such obvious things cannot be covered up by those who know the sequence of events; but because they are **hateful** <note>original: "odiosa"</note>, they may be left to rest.

## The 18th Accusation.

> The Princely Württemberg Government did not do things right by Arnold. p. 33.

### Answer:

(1) Whether the Princely Government did right is not for any **private person** to judge. An historian only reports the **facts** as he finds them and writes modestly about them, as will also be seen here **in progress**.

(2) Mr. Caroli asserts: Arnold speaks ill of the fact that Anabaptist books were forbidden and confiscated. This "ill-speaking" consists in the fact that he wrote in Part II, p. 278: "They hoped to cleanse the land if they forbade their books."

(3) In this matter, one rightly distinguishes between the nature of the Anabaptists <note>The Anabaptists were a radical Reformation group that practiced adult baptism and often lived in separate communities; they were frequently persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> and our own position, in no way participating in their errors, but rather remaining within the bounds of a blameless defense <note>original: "in terminis inculpatæ defensionis"</note>. Much less is it intended to insult Your Princely Government in the slightest; rather, one speaks with Brenz <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), the primary reformer of the Duchy of Württemberg.</note>, who shall be cited below at the 28th Charge, §. 8, regarding the necessary leniency toward those in error.

(4) Mr. Caroli took the turn of phrase about "cleansing the land" from Chytraeus’s <note>David Chytraeus (1530–1600), a prominent Lutheran theologian and historian.</note> letter in Fecht, page 154, where he writes concerning the Anabaptists and Sacramentarians <note>A term for reformers, like the followers of Zwingli, who denied the physical presence of Christ in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper.</note> that the Augean stable <note>original: "Augiæ stabulum," a reference to the Greek myth of Hercules cleaning a filthy stable in a single day; here used as a metaphor for a city deemed full of "heretics."</note>—namely, Wismar—had been "cleansed" or "swept out" of them, after they had first been heard and instructed. Mr. Arnold used these words neither falsely nor perversely, as Mr. Caroli seems to think.

(5) Now, Mr. Caroli believes these people were nevertheless examined and refuted, and also given time to reconsider. But even setting aside that this "fact" is not proven at all, one knows well enough how such examining, refuting, and the like usually proceed once the spirits have become disordered with zeal against these poor erring souls—who are often stubborn, or at the very least, have fallen into deep mistrust of the clergy.

(6) Mr. Caroli asks in §. 4, page 34, what there is to criticize in such a method of proceeding <note>original: "modo procedendi"</note>? Certainly, a thorough and gentle examination, a proper correction, and a long-suffering wait for conversion is a blameless thing. But as blameless as it is, it is quite rare in history and practice <note>original: "Praxi"</note>; rarest of all is the "winning over" of people through forceful means, as will be seen as clear as day below in the 28th Charge.

(7) When Mr. Caroli further criticizes that Mr. Arnold wrote the Anabaptists were under much pressure in the 17th century (Part II, page 556), he does not rightly understand Mr. Arnold’s words. He calls them an unfair complaint or even a "lamentation," thus fighting against a shadow he has made for himself. For Arnold neither complained nor lamented here, but only presented the matter itself <note>original: "rem ipsam"</note>: how these people had to live in secret rather than openly.

(8) Mr. Arnold had found here and there in the cited Dr. Melchior Nicolaus’s refutation of the Anabaptists, especially on page 250, that they had complained about persecution. He briefly indicated this with that expression. A believer may certainly use such an expression even about sects from which he is quite distant. For example, nothing is more common than for historians to write of the Jews and Pagans under flourishing Christianity—

(9) When finally, on page 36, Mr. Caroli asks whether it matters to Mr. Arnold that the Anabaptists' books were banned: this question is impertinent and mocking. For what can it matter to Mr. Arnold, who was in Saxony, what happened in Swabia so many years ago? But it would matter even more to us preachers if we, through tireless diligence, could root out the devil's deceptions and errors from the hearts of our listeners and ground them firmly in the living faith of JESUS. On the other hand, if one only rages against the "heretic-wolves" but lets the sheep themselves wander into Epicureanism <note>A lifestyle focused on worldly pleasure and lack of religious fear.</note>, Libertinism <note>Living without regard for moral or divine law.</note>, and even practical Atheism <note>original: "Atheismo practico," or living as if God does not exist, regardless of one's stated beliefs.</note>, then the former will be of little use.

And the astonishment / expressed on page 40, §. 8 / was even less necessary / if one had not been overhasty in judging. Mr. Caroli cannot reconcile / that Mr. Arnold wrote the above concerning Württemberg / and yet elsewhere also disapproves of the severity against the Jews / namely that Justinian <note>Justinian I, the Byzantine Emperor known for his legal code which included restrictive laws against non-Christians.</note> tore down their synagogues: Likewise / that he writes / the Jews were tolerated more out of political maxims <note>term: "Staats-Maximen" (principles of statecraft or political pragmatism rather than religious conviction)</note> / than out of true Christian duty / etc.

(5) However, anyone who had a desire for a dispute over words / could ask here again: How should it finally be done / so that it is right? If one says / the Jews could well be tolerated / then it is called an un-Christian judgment. If one says / it happens by some for worldly reasons / then that is also said to be untrue. And yet it is more than certain on all sides / that sometimes in this matter multiple purposes <note>original: "plures fines"</note> are involved. Mr. Caroli must leave it as it stands in its place / and cannot contradict it. That Jews are to be tolerated / and indeed out of Christian abhorrence [of their error] for their improvement and the exercise of Christian patience toward Christ's enemies / is not contrary to the teaching of Christ / but in accordance with it. But experience teaches / that they have mostly been taken in for worldly intentions. And thus each point is irrefutable in its own kind <note>original: "in suo genere"</note> and in a certain respect <note>original: "certo respectu"</note> / regarding what Mr. Arnold writes about it / even if Mr. Caroli cannot or will not make it rhyme.

# Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence, Part IV, No. 22.
### Page 406
<header>Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence, Part IV, No. 22.</header>

Whoever reads of this will be able to judge the pain involved, but will also see an indifferent and free presentation of the matters.

(2) It has already been demonstrated above in Part I, in the 112th accusation, from Mr. A.'s <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the historian whose work is being defended.</note> own words, that he did not intend to defend this matter of Keil <note>Hans Keil of Geradstetten, a vine-dresser who in 1700 claimed that his vines were miraculously bleeding as a sign of divine judgment.</note>, much less to hold it as divine, as the Anonymous writer <note>Likely referring to the author of the "Innocent News" (Unschuldige Nachrichten), a contemporary journal.</note> had attributed to him there. For this reason, one does not take up the cause itself here, but remains within the bounds of a fair response to the accusations. Here it is first to be noted in general that Mr. A. took his account from contemporary writers <note>original: "Scriptoribus coævis"</note>, especially from Dr. Wagner's sermon, from a warning sermon by M. Hiemer (a preacher from Heilbronn), from Eckard, and from J. V. Andreae <note>Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), a famous theologian and social reformer.</note>. These he could and must have followed safely and with good reason.

(3) Now, Mr. Arnold nevertheless found this "bleeding" confirmed not only in Hiemer’s writing (which, as far as is known, he did not recant), but also encountered these circumstances in Dr. Wagner’s sermon on page 760: that the pastor, together with the Princely Commissioners, truly found upon inspection how 6 pruned vines were bloody and 280 vines dripped with blood. These were wretched enough circumstances. The aforementioned Anonymous writer in the so-called *Innocent News* <note>original: "Unſchuldigen Nachrichten"</note> of the year 1703, page 259, says that Keil had forced the blood from his nose. Whether a quantity of almost 300 vines could drip from so little nosebleed is left to its own place. At the very least, no sensible person will blame Mr. A. for presenting this history according to the documents he had before him. Added to this is the fact that Eckard, also cited by him, describes Keil as simple-minded, while Mr. Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism."</note> describes him as pious in *Theological Reflections* <note>original: "Theol. Bedencken"</note> Volume I, Part II, page 237. And the aforementioned Anonymous writer reports that he [Keil] intended for people to become pious through it. Indeed, Mr. Caroli <note>Andreas David Caroli (1662–1712), Arnold's critic.</note> himself does not dare to entirely deny on page 46 that he [Keil] had a good intention.

(4) What Mr. Caroli now thinks to find lacking in A.'s account consists of the following: a) it is said to be false that the preachers brought it to the point that Keil was thrown into prison and the reports confiscated. Regarding the first point—namely, that the preachers brought it about—Dr. Wagner's report is questionable, as he complains on page 740 that most of the city and congregation were so stuck in devotion toward this presumed prophet that they could soon hardly be greater toward Moses and the Prophets. This must certainly have been very much against him. Mr. Caroli himself also admits as much,

<meta>catchword: much,</meta>

<column-break/>

### Page 407
<header>Part IV, No. 22. Mr. Andreas David Caroli etc. 407</header>

much: that the Duke had the man examined <note>original: "examiniren"</note> by the court preachers and church counselors, who then only rendered a report, etc. However, above on page 33, he himself had assured us that in religious and ecclesiastical matters, the opinion of the theologians was always obtained. And that the religious and other such edicts <note>original: "Edicta"</note> are actually to be attributed to the theologians, not the great lords themselves, as the theologians at Tübingen themselves showed in the year 1624 in their *Friendly Admonition* <note>original: "Amica Admonitione"</note>. There, regarding the Electoral Saxon Mandate <note>original: "Mandato"</note> which was placed before the *Solid Decision* <note>original: "Solidæ Deciſioni"</note>, they wrote on page 14: "We desire what the authors of that same mandate of the Most Serene [Prince] say to the reader" <note>original: "Deſideramus, quod in eodem mandato Sereniſſimi lectoris Autores illius dicunt"</note>, where they contradicted the same, despite it being published under the Elector's name.

(5) Now, whoever knows how such mandates, opinions, and the like commonly also attach the nature of punishments for certain offenses <note>original: "Delicta"</note> cannot doubt that Keil’s deed would not only have been exaggerated <note>original: "exaggerirt"</note>, but also declared worthy of certain punishment. For although the Duke himself heard Keil first and noticed the fraud, as Mr. Caroli writes, one knows well how great lords decree nothing in such obscure things without the advice of the theologians <note>original: "Theologorum"</note>; which is also fair on his part, if the theologians are impartial and Christian.

(6) Secondly <note>original: "Vors ß"</note>, it is said to be an audacious assumption that Keil did not always answer with the same words during the inquiry <note>original: "Inquiſition"</note> out of fear. But who can doubt that such a simple vine-dresser would stand before a court <note>original: "Judicio"</note> with fear and be well confused in his statement? Especially after this Keil also saw the court preachers and church counselors before him, and yet had spoken very harshly against the greed of the clergy—saying that their minds were in the wine cellar, on the granary floor, in the field, and with their purses? Indeed, since many people had spoken thus against the preachers because of this Keil, among other things: they, as Pharisaical envious creatures <note>original: "Phariſeiſche Neidhämel" - a derogatory term for the clergy implying they were jealous and stubborn.</note>, were making it very difficult for themselves to suppress the Hosanna sung by the disciples and children in honor of the Lord Christ; as Dr. Wagner himself cites these and other words in the place cited <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> on page 742 and later on page 756. He calls this Keil a "scandal-prophet" whose words against the greed of the preachers were a "real and verbal desecration" of the preaching office, and further calls him a "crude fellow" on page 765, etc. Since he now saw himself in the hands of his adversaries and under their inquiry, he would certainly not have been without fear and confusion. Therefore, this is not a mere assumption, but an infallible consequence.

On the contrary, one might ask why they omitted producing the full records <term>Acta: Official legal or administrative documents.</term> that were issued in this matter—which must surely still be in the country—especially the formal opinions of the preachers. ### The 25th Accusation:

### He reproaches the Württemberg theologians for certain things. p. 54.

### Response:

(1) What a **historian** relates of certain undeniable facts from clear documents / no impartial person takes as a reproach. — Thus Mr. Caroli has displayed his passions here / through which / out of partiality / he has not been able to judge the history well.

(2) He says: α) Arnold views the matter quite contemptuously / namely the correspondence with the Greek Patriarch <note>This refers to the 16th-century attempt by Lutheran theologians at Tübingen to establish a union with Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople.</note>. But if such a relation is to be considered contempt / what would one say to the words of other **historians** / when, for example, Dr. Kortholt <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian.</note> writes of it: **no fruit redounded to the Church from that labor of our theologians.** <note>original: "nullum ex illo Theologorum nostrorum labore fructum in Ecclesiam redundavisse."</note> *Ecclesiastical History of the 16th Century, p. 833.* However, it is not actually contempt when one says / that sensible people judge / that it would not have been worth the effort for the Greeks to learn the Lutheran doctrine. For Mr. Arnold / as a **historian** / looks at the fruitless / indeed entirely contrary outcome of the whole matter / which he could not exactly praise / as it obviously ran against the wish and will of the theologians; since they themselves afterwards confessed in the report on page 3 / that the Patriarch agreed with the Pope in Rome on several articles / and had defended them poorly / consequently they could not win him over through their disputing. Indeed, Dr. Kortholt confesses **in the place cited** <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> that the theologians' zeal **for disputing so much about that controversy** <note>original: "tantopere de controversia illa disputandi"</note> displeased the Patriarch. This is what Mr. Arnold means / that the outcome was not worth the great effort. But whoever says only this much about the futile outcome / does not immediately despise the matter or the attempt itself. Rather, Mr. Arnold himself noted this benefit in Part II, Section 31, Chapter XVI / that through this, the doctrine of the Greeks became better known. That is certainly not calling it contemptible. But when Dannhauer <note>Johann Conrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> approves of such effort in his *Theology of Conscience, Vol I, p. 390* / he indeed calls it a **most praiseworthy attempt** <note>original: "laudatissimum conatum"</note> / but he still calls it an **attempt** <note>original: "conatum"</note> / a trial and undertaking / likewise a **plan** <note>original: "Consilium"</note> / an intention that did not achieve its effect.

(3) Regarding β) Mr. Arnold is said to accuse the theologians of an acting in a very un-theological manner / in that they sought to make their opinions pleasing to the Greeks. This is said to be incorrectly stated / but Mr. Caroli substitutes this instead: Their purpose was / to the Greeks

regarding the points which are still disputed between them and us / to provide the doctrine founded in **God’s** Word. Now, regarding the <term>Subjectum</term> <note>original: "Subjectum" — the subject matter or underlying topic being discussed.</note> and the matter in these propositions / Mr. Carolus calls it the doctrine founded in **God’s** Word / according to his own concept; Mr. Arnold, however, calls them "opinions" in the common sense / as one also says of certain truths: "That is my opinion"; therefore the word <term>Orthodoxia</term> <note>original: "Orthodoxia" from the Greek δόξαις (doxais) — "right opinion" or "correct belief."</note> takes its name from "opinions." Mr. Carolus seeks to "provide" the <term>Prædicatum</term> <note>original: "Prædicatum" — the predicate, or that which is asserted about the subject.</note> / Mr. Arnold joins together "making it agreeable" and "providing" it. Now, what one wishes to provide to another / he also likes to make it agreeable to him / and <term>vice versa</term> <note>original: "vice versa" — and the other way around.</note>. With this, he has neither accused the theologians in an untheological manner / nor done them wrong / as anyone can see. Carolus Senior even says in his *Memorabilia* <note>A work of historical or biographical recollections.</note> on page 282 that the Patriarch finally broke out in harsh words / and yet the Tübingen theologians had answered for the third time / and they were not given thorough satisfaction. It is a pity for the time / that it should be spent with such a battle of words.

(4 To the Greek letter $\gamma$ <note>Referring to a specific point or section in the original critique labeled with the Greek letter gamma.</note>) Mr. Arnold believes that "to flatter and fawn" upon the theologians is: The grand titles are obvious in the writings / and Mr. Arnold looks primarily toward this, and not at the doctrines themselves / as Mr. Carolus thinks. It depends / on how the reality of the matter stood. Paul's example does not fit here. For in the cited place of Acts 17:28 / he quoted well-known truths / and if he perhaps called Festus <term>kratiston</term> <note>original: κράτιστον — "most excellent," a formal title for a high-ranking official.</note> / he could well do so because of his eminence based on his office and conduct / Acts 26:25. But when theologians title foreign priests and those of other religions as "most wise," "most holy," "most godly," and "faithful shepherds" / that cannot well be excused before Christian ears with common <term>Civilité</term> <note>original: "Civilité" — social courtesy or politeness.</note> / based on the Divine ground / because these <term>Prædicata</term> <note>original: "Prædicata" — descriptive titles or attributes.</note> are not worldly or indifferent titles / but contain within themselves the most important <term>Realia</term> <note>original: "Realia" — actual, substantial realities or truths.</note> / as testimonies / that such a titled person actually possesses such Divine qualities / namely wisdom, holiness, godliness, and pastoral faithfulness. Now, the theologians knew something quite different about those Greek priests (for the ignorance and misery of those poor people is well known from all travel descriptions) / they also rejected the Pope's title of "Most Holy" / thus it was very dangerous / to attribute such a testimony and predicate to unknown people. This is / what Mr. Arnold means / when he writes in section 8: that there was nothing of the kind (namely of the most wise, holy, and most godly virtues) present in truth in either party. ### The 26th Accusation.

->Arnold sharply attacks the Württemberg theologians over the Work of Concord. p. 60.<-

### Answer:

(1) The specifics of how this allegedly happened are stated as follows: Arnold claimed that things were meant to go according to their [the theologians'] own wishes. Mr. Carolus interprets this for him as follows: It is as good as saying that they were seeking something for themselves and desired to dictate to other churches and theologians. But if one wishes to handle an author’s words in this way, and invent interpretations that never entered his mind, then one can accuse him of heaven knows what.

(2) Let a conscientious reader judge for himself whether a single iota of this meaning <note>original: "Sensu"</note> attributed to him is hidden in Mr. Arnold’s words. It seems people think they have the liberty to treat the book however they wish and substitute one thing for another <note>original: "quid pro quo"</note> within it. Mr. Arnold’s words suggest nothing more than this: that they sought to reach their purpose <note>original: "Propos"</note>; and that purpose was primarily that their doctrine might be maintained. Nothing more can ever be forced out of these words.

(3) If one were to complain here of reversal and distortion in the same way it was done against Mr. Arnold, there would certainly be the highest cause for it. However, we prefer to stick to the matter itself and abstain from such personal attacks. We are happy to leave it as Dr. Jakob Andreæ <note>A primary author of the Formula of Concord (1577), a document intended to unify Lutheran doctrine.</note> himself expressed his wish, explaining what it consisted of, when he says in the dedication of the 5th Sermon on the Work of Concord that it was his "ceaseless wish that the separation would be abolished," etc.

(4) And because one rightly judges an author's meaning from his own context: Mr. Arnold points these words regarding the theologians' wish toward the discovery of the Crypto-Calvinists in Saxony <note>Lutherans who were secretly sympathetic to the teachings of John Calvin, particularly regarding the Lord's Supper.</note>, as he mentions immediately before how the Württemberg writing was sent to the Elector so that he might see how far his theologians had strayed from the

(5) Since Mr. Carolus further doubts the citation of Hutter <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a staunch Lutheran defender of the Formula of Concord.</note>, questioning whether page 87 and following <note>original: "p. 87. sqq."</note> were correctly cited by Mr. Arnold: it is clearly found there how the Württemberg theologians had already contradicted the others from the year 1564 and even earlier, and sent their concerns against them to Elector August. This page contrasts Caroli's "blood-thirsty" arguments with those of the Catholic Inquisition and the Scholastic philosopher Thomas Aquinas.</meta>
