<header>Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence Part IV, No. 29.</header>

(10) Mr. Caroli <note>Andreas David Caroli (1646–1713), a Lutheran theologian known for his strict orthodoxy.</note> indeed admits that no truly Lutheran theologian ever considered it justifiable to imprison <term>Anabaptists</term><note>A radical reform movement that rejected infant baptism; they were widely persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> in and of themselves simply for their errors. However, he still maintains that they could rightfully be put to death by the sword for sedition or blasphemy. Yet he does not prove whether these people—of whom the gentlemen from Tübingen spoke—actually committed such <term>crimina</term><note>Latin: "crimes."</note> or merely led others into them. Above, in Part II, Number 103, the distinction between them and the <term>Münster rebels</term><note>A radical group of Anabaptists who took over the city of Münster in 1534, leading to a violent siege; the author argues peaceful Anabaptists should not be confused with these extremists.</note> was clearly demonstrated. Instead, he merely asserts they were "seducers" and asks again, in a very <term>Papist</term><note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics, used here to suggest Caroli is acting like the very Inquisition he should oppose.</note> manner: Why should a Christian authority not use the sword to remedy the seduction to such great horrors as blasphemy and sedition, if they cannot be controlled in any other way? And why should honest theologians not boldly present this to an authority? The Inquisitors in the Papacy cite exactly the same reasons; in particular, they pretend they do not slaughter and persecute heretics because they are mistaken, but because they are "seducers, wolves, blasphemers, and rebels," as can be seen in their books <term>contra haereticos</term><note>Latin: "against heretics."</note>. If one reads Limborch's *History of the Inquisition* <note>Philipp van Limborch’s "Historia Inquisitionis" (1692), a famous work documenting the practices of the Catholic Inquisition.</note>, the parallel will become obvious.

(11) Christians know how to steer others away from seduction through much more healing and improving means for the poor people than through hasty bloodshed and execution—neither of which helps the poor, straying souls nor the conscience of the judges. It is even more concerning when Mr. Caroli asks: How can they say it is good to improve the lives of those who live for nothing else but the danger and destruction of an entire people? One should consider whether this does not come close to <term>Caiaphas's blood-council</term><note>A reference to the High Priest Caiaphas in the New Testament, who argued it was better for one man (Jesus) to die than for the whole nation to perish.</note>. At the very least, it is sad enough when a Lutheran preacher, as Mr. Caroli was, lacks Evangelical support and instead appeals in such matters of blood to the judgment of the Papist Thomas Aquinas, who says generally of evildoers, not of those merely in error: <note>original: "Si sit vivens in periculum multitudinis sic bonum est eum occidi."</note> "If a living person poses a danger to the multitude, it is thus good for him to be killed." Thus, the Papist "spirit of persecution" is, alas, tangible even while one is trying to prove their "innocence"! One might rightly say to this, following the Lutheran jurist D. G. C. Walther in his *Post. Harm.* Part II, page 260: <note>original: "Vide quantum miseris Lutheranis apud Scholasticos barbaries nocuerit"</note> "See how much the barbarity among the Scholastics has harmed the wretched Lutherans," where he had observed: <note>original: "Haereticum non quidem de vita tollendum, ut NB. Thomas Aquinas verbum de vita exposuit."</note> "A heretic is certainly not to be deprived of life, as Thomas Aquinas (note well!) interpreted the phrase 'from life.'"

<meta>catchword: Scholastics</meta>

---

<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>Part IV, No. 29. Mr. Andreas David Caroli &c. 423</header>

For certainly, such principles are drawn from many schools, and through them, people become so barbaric and bloodthirsty.

(12) Furthermore, Mr. Caroli has become so heated here that he calls Mr. A.’s well-intentioned sentiment of modesty, gentleness, and mildness—which is unquestionably in accordance with the teaching of Christ—a "poisonous, offensive, and utterly disgusting rebuke." Oh God! When it comes to this among Christians, and indeed among Evangelicals, that the best suggestions for Christian mildness (as it should be known to all men) are interpreted so poorly, where will it end? Does it not point all too clearly to a falling away from the true Gospel of Jesus Christ? For in such procedures, has one been any better than the Papists? He cannot prove any sedition or such things against these people, and it was shown above in Part II, Number 103, how far the subsequent Anabaptists were removed from those of Münster; yet he still blames them for evildoings and all too insolent mischief, saying they could not have been thwarted by any other means. Thus, the right divine means to bring back lost and straying souls are entirely unknown!

(13) On page 69, Mr. Caroli refers here to Christ’s words in Matthew 26:52: *He who takes the sword, etc.*, and asks: Did Christ pronounce a mild and modest judgment, or was His decision Antichristian? But I will not remind him that the Savior showed true Christians entirely different means to convert straying, or even seductive or guilty sinners. Also, the question here is not about public evildoers, and especially not about rebels and murderers, to whom the judgment from Genesis 9:6 applies. In the present matter, however, the question is only whether theologians, in their opinions or responses, can refer to these words of Christ when they declare heretics worthy of death under the name of "blasphemers" or those who "cause unrest." Most interpreters have rendered Christ’s words not as a command, but in the future tense: <note>original Greek: "απολούνται" (apolountai)</note> "they shall perish"; which Jerome also indicates when he paraphrases these words in Book II on Proverbs, chapter 22: <note>original: "Gladio peribunt, h. e. qui injuste in alios sæviunt, ipsa sævitia sibimetipsis interitum consciscunt."</note> "They shall perish by the sword, i.e., those who act cruelly and unjustly toward others bring destruction upon themselves through that very cruelty." On this point, however, it is not necessary to say more here.

### The 30th Accusation:

<margin>page 70.</margin>
**That Arnold seeks to bring the Tübingen theologians into contempt.**

### Response:

(1) This is supposedly done through a certain *Oportebat* <note>Latin: "It was necessary."</note> regarding Dr. Schegk <note>Jakob Schegk (1511–1587), a famous physician and philosopher at Tübingen who often clashed with theologians.</note> mentioned in Part II, page 374. There he says: *Schegk* later explained himself in such a way that they (the *theologians*) "had to be" satisfied with him.

(2) Here, Mr. Arnold is wronged in several ways: α) It is claimed that the philosophical sciences are worth nothing to him. Because Mr. Caroli is speaking of Aristotelian philosophy, it is true that Arnold practiced it sufficiently at the academy and taught it publicly; however, along with all modern, upright philosophers, he certainly considers it of no value, and he has unshakeable reasons for this.

(3) For β) Mr. Caroli again interprets Arnold's words against their clear meaning, namely that he intended to say *Schegk* had given the *theologians* such a "mouthful" <note>An idiom suggesting he overwhelmed them or shut them up aggressively.</note> that they could not get at him but had to back down. This is not Mr. Arnold’s opinion, as is evident from the clear words; rather, the word "must" or "had to" here has a completely innocent and tolerable sense of sufficient conviction, reassurance, and satisfaction. It describes a situation where someone under suspicion explains himself so that the other person is convinced and thus has nothing more to object to, but must necessarily be satisfied with it. Such an *expression* is often used in this way even regarding persons of higher rank. Accordingly, he has by no means brought the *theologians* into contempt. One sees from this, however, how quickly self-love may interpret even a small word as contempt, and from whence this great indignation springs. Mr. Caroli himself uses this word "must" in somewhat the same way on the following page 79, where he says of these very Tübingen *theologians*: "One had to recognize afterward that *Huber* had hidden his opinion within the disputation."

(4) For γ) it is claimed that this was not an "internal conflict" among the Lutherans. But we do not wish to start an internal conflict over that here either. However, the types of such disputes are varied, and Mr. Arnold previously noted in Chapter 30 of Book XVI, § 10, that he only wished to briefly touch upon some peculiar disputes which—NB <note>Latin "Nota Bene": Mark well.</note>—did not exactly result in a public schism, but nevertheless concerned one or two questionable points. He then recounts these,

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

<header>Part IV, No. 30, 31. Mr. Andreas David Caroli etc.</header>
<page-num>425</page-num>

and indeed does so using the chronology of *Fechtius* <note>Johannes Fecht (1636–1716), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, whose words indicate nothing other than an internal conflict. On page 950: *J. Schegk assailed the doctrine of the Tübingen theologians regarding the personal union in private writings, eventually doing penance.* <note>Original Latin: "J. Schekius privatis scriptis doctrinam Theologorum Tubingenšium de unione personali lacešit, tandem poenitentiam agens." The "personal union" refers to the theological doctrine of how Christ’s divine and human natures are joined.</note> And the fact that the *theologians* also rejoiced over the settlement shows that there had been a dispute beforehand, as history also demonstrates.

### The 31st Accusation:

**That he makes a mockery of Dr. Huber’s controversial case, p. 77.**

### Response:

(1) The "mockery" is said to consist in what he writes in Part II, Book XVI, Chapter 30, § 1: "Huber showed himself very zealous against the Reformed in Tübingen." Here, Mr. Arnold is allegedly mocking this zeal, and it is claimed he pays little attention to whether such zeal was right or wrong. However, Mr. Arnold spoke here expressly with three Lutheran *theologians* (and thus did not mock at all), namely with *Osiander* from his *Centuries* XV, *Eccl. Hist.* Book IV, chap. 45, page 1091, and *Sagittarius*, *Intro. to H.E.* page 982, both of whom say of *Huber*: *He "fiercely and vigorously" opposed the theses of the Reformed.* <note>Original Latin/German: "er habe der Reformirten Theses acriter und strenue oppugniret."</note> How can one now blame Mr. Arnold for this *expression* or interpret it poorly? Since Dr. Kortholt writes even more, saying *he assailed the Calvinists "with great fervor,"* *H.E. Cent. XVI, p. 136.* <note>Original Latin: "magno ardore impugniret."</note>

(2) Mr. Caroli generally has a false *concept* of Mr. Arnold, as if he held no zeal whatsoever to be legitimate. The contrary was demonstrated above from Arnold's own words in the 20th Accusation. And in particular, Mr. Arnold himself thoroughly investigated the doctrine of absolute <term>election by grace</term> <note>Also known as predestination; the theological debate over whether God chooses who will be saved regardless of their actions.</note> in *True Christianity* <note>Arnold's "Wahres Christenthum," a core text of the Pietist movement.</note> A.T. p. 417ff, such that the *authors* of the so-called *Innocent News* <note>Unschuldige Nachrichten, the first German theological journal, which was often critical of Arnold but here is cited as agreeing with him.</note> themselves approved of this point in him in the year 1707, page 499. From this it is obvious that Mr. Arnold does not mock a divine and blameless zeal against such doctrine.

(3) But in this very matter, he has indeed paid attention to where such zeal was right or wrong. For whoever reads the polemical writings of those times will, alas, find with misery how such zeal was cloaked in bitterness and hostility—how they fell from the matter itself into personalities and insults, and thereby edified or improved no one. There is no need for reminders or special attention here: any reasonable reader can grasp the misery with their own hands and distinguish right zeal from the wrong kind.

(4) Furthermore, when Mr. Caroli seeks to *paraphrase* Arnold’s presentation: then he...

On the previous page, Arnold addressed the charge that he sought to bring the Tübingen faculty into contempt. Here, he specifically addresses the controversy surrounding Samuel Huber (a theologian who argued that all people are chosen for salvation) and why the Tübingen theologians initially remained silent about Huber’s unconventional views.</meta>

<header>Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence, Part IV, Nos. 31 and 32 / Part IV, No. 32. Mr. Andreas David Caroli, etc.</header>
<sig>Hhh 2</sig>

...finally, on page 78, he himself doubts whether this is the true meaning, even though he states: "Without doubt, this is how it is." Yet, be that as it may, he lets his accusation on this point drop. Thereupon, he turns to Mr. Arnold’s own words, and although he would dearly like to contradict them, he admits on page 79 that the disputed academic debate <note>original: "quæstionirte Disputation"</note> was prepared by Huber, and that the 748th thesis therein expressly says: **that all people are elected,** and that the 78th thesis mentions a general election <note>original: "Electionis communis"</note>. Likewise, he admits that Huber hid his opinion within the said debate, and that it could only be recognized after the fact.

(5) Indeed, from the report of the Wittenberg theologians, he cites these words: "It is clear as day that Dr. Huber was already occupied with this erroneous opinion even before he came to these lands and to the University of Wittenberg, as can be sufficiently seen from the theses debated at Tübingen." If this is "sufficiently seen," then it was not "hidden" therein, and Mr. Caroli is arguing against the obvious facts when he says that this latter point was proven by the Wittenberg report and nothing else. For what this report adds regarding the subsequent outbreak of the matter does not negate the prior evidence in the Tübingen debate; rather, it only shows certain stages <note>original: "gradus"</note> of the emerging opinion, the last of which resulted in public contradiction.

(6) Furthermore, Mr. Caroli blames Mr. Arnold for stating that the Tübingen theologians remained silent at that time. However, he himself confesses that it is true they did not wish to cause an uproar; he only tries to prove that they held proper conferences about it, even before the debate. Mr. Arnold does not deny this—namely, the private conference—for he saw it clearly in the *Anti-Huberiana* <note>A collection of writings against Samuel Huber’s universalist views.</note>. He is speaking, however, of a **public contradiction**, which was omitted against these publicly proposed theses. For when one says of a publicly proposed matter that it was met with silence, one is speaking, as is well known, by the nature of the subject matter <note>original: "à qualitate objecti"</note> of a public silence, even if something was moved against it in secret. Thus, they initially remained silent publicly, even if doubts were raised privately, as anyone can sufficiently judge from what has been cited. Indeed, Mr. Caroli himself admits on page 81, § 6, that the theologians did not desire to make much of a fuss about it.

### The 32nd Accusation.

That he draws poison from everything, however good and right it may be; this is a grave disregard for conscience. <margin>pages 81, 82.</margin>

<column-break/>

## Response:

(1) This "poison" is said to consist in Mr. Arnold writing: "The reason for their (the Tübingen theologians') silence was that Huber had shown himself very zealous against the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Calvinist branch of Protestantism.</note> on this point, and had thus made himself favorable to them in this regard." Now, Mr. Arnold has proven in the previous response how highly he esteems true divine or Christian zeal, even regarding the point of the Election of Grace. He considers this not a poison, but a **divine medicine**.

(2) Whether the theologians of that time showed such a blameless zeal in all respects is not the time to argue now; the writings still before our eyes can provide information to a reader with practiced senses. Mr. Arnold has in no way disregarded his conscience, much less accused the Tübingen theologians of fighting against the Calvinists (as he calls them) out of a fleshly zeal. For he speaks merely of "zeal," but does not determine with a single word whether it was fleshly or not.

(3) Indeed, the entire argument as Mr. Arnold set it forth could actually be used for a good cause. For example <note>original: "par Exemple"</note>: I will suppose a case where someone had argued well and thoroughly against the Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note>, but had mixed in several impure things which a Protestant might still have allowed to pass. One could then say, using Arnold's very words: "The latter remained silent because the former had shown himself very zealous against the Papists and had thus made himself favorable to them in this regard." Who would then rightly denounce this statement as unconscionable, or say out of evil suspicion that all Protestants fought against the Papacy out of fleshly zeal, or that they were being treated with such presumptuous violence and injustice? Now, Mr. Arnold is in agreement with our theologians on the point of the Election of Grace just as much as on the points against the Papacy, as has just been proven in the 31st Accusation, § 2.

(4) Therefore, he cannot be accused without unchristian suspicion of doing our Lutherans an injustice here. His words are weighed carefully and set down blamelessly; they do not determine what kind of zeal it was, whether good or evil. The forced interpretation of Mr. Caroli, however, arises from a mind preoccupied with suspicion. And if a member of the Reformed church reads the name "Calvinist" so often here, he will hardly be inclined to believe that such zeal was spiritual or divine...

He also rebuts the charge that he views Lutheran zeal against Calvinism as "poison," clarifying that he distinguishes between healthy theological passion and fleshly conflict.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gottfried Arnold’s defense against Andreas David Caroli regarding the "Huberian Controversy." ...it is [unjust] when one labels an entire religion with such a name, against which it has constantly protested.

(5) Regarding the 4th point—that Huberus greatly legitimized himself through the disputation at Tübingen—Mr. Caroli (page 81) has nothing significant to remind us. He only denies (page 82) that Huberus spoke and wrote much about the universal <term>election of grace</term> <note>original: "Gnaden-Wahl"; the theological concept that God chooses who will be saved</note> at Tübingen, and he wishes to confirm the opposite from the report of the Tübingen theologians. They merely said that he had "somewhat" let himself out regarding this controversy—namely, as he adds, against one pastor and several students. But he has forgotten that he himself already admitted as much in the preceding Number 31, Sections 4 and 5, where it is noted how Huberus had certain <term>theses</term> printed about it, over which he had disputed. How can a disputation take place without much speaking and writing? And how could the discourse—in which he alleged that <term>Gerlachius’s</term> <note>Stephan Gerlach, a prominent Lutheran theologian at Tübingen</note> theses were Reformed—have occurred without much speaking? Not to mention that Huberus, while still at Tübingen, had written various things about this in his *Thorough Proof that Jesus Christ Died for the Sins of the Whole World*. All of this was surely enough speaking and writing, so much so that Huberus himself stated in the preface to his refutation: that he had written thus in his books. That the Tübingen theologians later softened all of this and made it out to be only "something minor" had its reasons, as can easily be seen.

### The 33rd Accusation.

->He can finely mix, confuse, pervert, and twist according to his will, p. 84.<-

### Answer.

(1) If the good Mr. Caroli had known more expressions for this wicked accusation, they would have been written down. But what does Mr. Arnold mix up here that causes such a complaint? He writes: they nevertheless allowed Huber’s speaking and writing on universal <term>election by grace</term> to pass at Tübingen because he appealed to the passages 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9. Mr. Caroli cannot deny even the slightest part of this report. He admits himself: the Tübingen theologians had no cause at that time to suspect Dr. Huber of anything evil; therefore, they thought: <note>original: "eum in Phrasi duntaxat, non in rebus aliquid habere novi"</note> *that he had something new only in his phrasing, not in the matters themselves.* Mr. Arnold expresses all of this briefly thus: they had allowed Huber's speaking and writing to pass.

<column-break/>

<page-num>429</page-num>
<header>Part IV, No. 33 / 34 N. In. Andreas David Caroli, etc.</header>

In doing so, he certainly does not confuse or twist the slightest thing, as the reader can judge.

(2) Afterwards, Mr. Caroli says that because Huber appealed to the aforementioned passages regarding his doctrine, they allowed him his manner of speaking in that sense. Mr. Arnold says exactly the same thing: that he had appealed to those passages. The difference might be placed in the fact that Huber claimed he sought to maintain nothing other than what the passages themselves contained. However, even this Mr. Arnold has not denied—namely, that Huber made such a claim. Because these passages speak quite clearly of God's universal purpose to have all people saved, the theologians naturally had to be, and could be, satisfied with him and his explanation.

---

### The 34th Accusation.

According to Arnold’s narrative, the theologians then at Tübingen must have been dumb, simple, and thoughtless.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Arnold does not consider the theologians of Tübingen, then or now, to be dumb or simple at all, but respects them in their proper measure. However, he must endure it as an unprovable charge that the opposite is attributed to him, without proving that a theologian is immediately "dumb" if he does not instantly think that a certain ambiguous proposition is contrary to a <term>Symbolic Book</term> <note>original: "Libro Symbolico"; a formal statement of faith or confession of a church</note>. For this can certainly have other causes and not necessarily a "dumbness" or <note>original: "stuporem mentis"</note> *numbness of mind*. Here again, he has spoken quite innocently with the aforementioned cited theologians, <term>Osiander</term> and <term>Sagittarius</term>, the latter of whom writes in the cited place: <note>original: "nequaquam suspicantes, hominem aliquid moliri Symbolico Concordiæ libro adversum"</note> *never suspecting that the man was attempting anything against the Symbolic Book of Concord.* Mr. Arnold said this and nothing else along with them.

(2) Mr. Caroli again rushes far too much in this judgment of his, as he has not weighed Mr. Arnold's words very carefully. For Mr. Arnold does not say of the Tübingen theologians that they had thought Huber’s expression or way of speaking was contrary to the <term>Formula of Concord</term> <note>original: "Form. Concordiæ"; the definitive 1577 Lutheran confession</note>; for this expression was indeed ambiguous, and thus they had to judge it according to his explanation, as Mr. Caroli himself reminds us in Section 10. Rather, Mr. Arnold speaks deliberately of Huber’s universal election, and thus of the whole matter as it consisted in both its sense and meaning as well as in its expression.

Moreover, one sees <margin>γ)</margin> that *Mr. Arnold* clearly understands this "searching through" as a more precise <term>inquiry; a formal investigation</term> into the connection and meaning of those matters, the likes of which had not happened before, as they had not wanted to make much fuss about it, as *Mr. Caroli* himself admits in §. 6.

(5) Thus, *Mr. Caroli* contradicts the theologians in this and once again misunderstands *Mr. Arnold’s* words when he says: **He did not need much opening of books and searching through.** By "searching through," *Mr. Arnold* understands, firstly, the <term>quantity</term> of *Huber’s* books, because he had written many other books on the subject, as *Osiander* and *Sagittarius* specifically name as "private writings"; and secondly, the <term>quality</term> or nature of how *Huber* had presented his opinion in Tübingen, from which *Osiander* specified <note>original: "specificiret"</note> many other incorrect propositions on page 1093. Both of these certainly required searching or investigating, especially since *Mr. Caroli* himself says in §. 4 that *Huber* had hidden his opinion in a **devious manner**. Now, what one hides—and indeed so deviously and craftily—the other must certainly search through or <term>scrutinize; examine closely</term>.

## The 36th Accusation.

**That he [Arnold] maintained his usual manner in the Greek Controversy.**
<margin>page 91.</margin>

### Answer:

(1) This "manner" is alleged to be partisan, as will be explained hereafter. However, it was immediately apparent that Mr. Caroli reported in a partisan way himself. For right at the beginning of his counter-report, he wants to claim that the Tübingen theologians proved their opinion on the **state of Christ’s humiliation** <note>The "State of Humiliation" refers to the theological debate over how much of his divine power Christ "emptied" or set aside during his life on Earth</note> against the Giessen and later Saxon theologians not only from Scripture but also from so many Fathers and theologians. And at the end, on page 99 and following, he seeks to legitimize them in every way through the consensus of other theologians. By doing so, he immediately implies that the latter group—the Giessen and Saxon theologians—departed from Scripture, the Fathers, and the theologians in this matter. This is clearly a partisan account with which the other theologians cannot be satisfied.

(2) But as for his attempt to cite Mr. Arnold’s account as partisan, it consists of the following points: First, Mr. Arnold calls such things **useless school-questions.** <note>Arnold frequently criticized theological disputes that he felt were more about academic ego than spiritual growth</note> By this, Mr. Arnold proved that he approved of the conduct of neither one side nor the other, and thus remained impartial. As he reasoned quite Christianly in § 31, Chapter 6, Book XVII, most of it amounted to the "word-wars and disputes" forbidden by Paul <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:4</note>, which were without edification toward God. This is to say nothing of the philosophical propositions and logical syllogisms mixed into theology and this very question. And what must the dear Savior have judged of such bickering? Even Mr. Caroli himself must grant him this much on page 92: that it would have been more useful had both sides remained in agreement; he only wishes to argue that the questions were not "useless" for the sake of the subject matter itself.

(3) Furthermore, in § 3, he [Caroli] asserts out of love for the Tübingen party: that **Mentzer** <note>Balthasar Mentzer the Elder (1565–1627), a prominent theologian from Giessen</note> at Giessen began to write publicly against them. He cites Mr. Arnold’s *Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (Church and Heretic History) itself for this, thereby giving public and clear testimony to the history that it reports on the Tübingen side impartially—and thus does not maintain itself in a partisan manner, as his own accusation claims. That Mr. Arnold’s account is entirely consistent with the truth shall be made palpable by the following answer.

These things would never have been pointed out if Mr. **Caroli** had not all too carelessly intended to hold the gentlemen from Tübingen as entirely innocent in this matter. One can also find **Menzer’s** complaints about the Tübingen scholars’ insults—where they call him an *Innovator* and the like—in his *Disputation on the Four Questions*, section 184, and elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold (referred to as "Mr. U.") against the attacks of Andreas David Caroli (referred to as "Mr. Car."). **Life-Description / as Mr. Car. captiously interprets it.** <note>original: "Lebens=Beschreibung / wie es Hr. Car. captiosè deutet." Caroli is being accused of using deceptive or "captious" logic to twist the definition of a biography.</note> For who would say that the entire, extensive life story of such an ancient theologian and privy councilor is restricted to only three lines? Therefore, the good man—whose emotions were to blame for his misunderstanding—should not have been so offended by it.

(6) Fifthly, he wants to prove that **theologians should also be consulted in worldly matters, specifically citing Dannhauer, and that such a person has not overstepped into a foreign office.** <note>This refers to the Lutheran idea of "vocation" or "office," arguing that a preacher's "office" is strictly spiritual.</note> He cites from his *Theology of Conscience, Volume 1, page 252* <note>original: "Theol. Confc. To. I. p. 252." by Johann Conrad Dannhauer</note> certain words which show that Dannhauer recognized the **vices of most theologians** <note>original: "Vitia plerorumque Theologorum"</note> in this regard, which might well be worthy of blame, and indeed **especially** <note>original: "maximè"</note> in the **Papacy**, <note>the Roman Catholic Church</note> and thus perhaps also later in our own churches. The vices or excesses might be criticized, but not the thing itself. Thus, he readily admitted that overstepping into worldly affairs—**meddling in the business of others** <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοτριοεπισκοπία" (allotrioepiskopia)</note>, or interfering in state matters—which are purely **vices**, should be scolded; and **consequently**, Mr. U. was not wrong to note such things from history. Indeed, this same Dr. Dannhauer observes in his *Christeide, page 385*, the **incompatibility** <note>original Greek: "συναδυναμίαν" (synadynamian)</note> **of the Episcopacy and secular care**, and cites the words of **Cyprian** <note>An early Church Father, bishop of Carthage</note> from *Book 1, Letter 9*, which we shall soon hear. Thus, this theologian is not against Mr. U.

(7) Regarding the matter itself, however, we preachers have the precise command in *2 Timothy 2:4*, that no one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life. Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard, a leading 17th-century Lutheran scholastic</note> notes very well regarding this passage in *Loci Theologici, section 299*: **"Specifically this prohibition applies properly and primarily to the ministers of the Church, that they should not involve themselves in secular business, but keep themselves within the ministry of the Word."** <note>original: "In specie ad Ministros Ecclesiæ hanc prohibitionem propriè & primò spectare, ne involvant se negotiis secularibus, sed in Ministerio Verbi se contineant."</note> (Compare also his *Commentary on 1 Peter 4:15, question 9, page 674*.) And Luther also glosses neatly on the words of Christ in *Luke 12:13, Volume 6, Altenburg edition, folio 194*: "Leave me unentangled with such things; go to those to whom such things are commanded; I am a preacher, to whom something else is commanded." For it is just as much a matter of high wisdom to push away the affairs of others as it is to perform one's own commanded duties wisely and without pride.

(8) Among the ancients, Cyprian judged thus in the place cited:
> **"Since this has been said of all [soldiers] (2 Timothy 2:4), how much more should those who are occupied with divine and spiritual matters not be bound by secular troubles and snares, so that they cannot depart from the Church and be free for earthly and secular acts."** <note>original Latin: "Cum de omnibus dictum sit (2. Tim. II, 4.) quanto magis molestiis & laqueis secularibus obligari non debent, qui divinis rebus & spiritualibus occupati ab Ecclesia recedere, & ad terrenos & seculares actus vacare non possunt."</note>

He also will not permit a preacher to be a legal guardian; from which Dannhauer concludes that Cyprian **detested the joining and preoccupation of clerics with temporal things.** <note>original: "copulationem & occupationes Clericorum circa temporalia detestiret."</note> Compare Bebel, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities, page 565*; Quenstedt, *Pastoral Ethics, page 302*; Großgebauer, *The Watchman’s Voice, page 280*.

XVI. B. § 13. Regarding the remark about the "all-too-wide extension" of the dispute over **Ubiquity** <note>The Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s human nature is omnipresent because of its union with his divine nature</note>, this clearly refers to the abuse of the term by many—especially those who completely denied the doctrine. For this reason, H. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold</note>, in his *Sermons on the Epistles and Gospels*, in *True Christianity of the Old Testament*, and in other such devotional writings, constantly emphasizes the **Omnipresence** of the Lord Jesus. He seeks to apply this doctrine to truth-based edification and personal improvement, as anyone can see.

(3) Since H. A. is thus in total agreement with **Brenz** and **Luther** himself on this matter, one must interpret his historical citations of external passages not according to their literal expressions, but with all fairness according to his own Evangelical sense. Regarding the accusation of "imputation" <note>Attributing a scandalous view to someone</note>, H. Car. himself reminds us on page 119, § 1, that H. A. mentions the questioned words from **Peucer’s** *History of Prisons* <note>original: "Peuceri Historia Carcerum"</note>, and thus they are not his own expression. The words themselves are these, found in Chapter 32 of Book XVI, § 7: "Peucer attributed the origin of this legal process solely to Dr. **Andreae** <note>Jakob Andreae, a primary author of the Formula of Concord</note>, who, having found no support for the **Brenzian doctrine of Ubiquity** at the University of Wittenberg, had supposedly shown hostility toward the professors there for that reason." Here one clearly sees that these are only "foreign and narrative words" <note>original: "verba aliena und narrativa"</note>—things that Peucer had written. And in § 8, it further states: "The prisoners had alleged..." (among whom Peucer was the most prominent), whose words H. A. expressly labels as a "pretext."

(4) In this, H. A. proves himself to be impartial. In the matter itself, he is at one with H. Car., particularly because he disapproves of all the abuse and mockery regarding the name **Ubiquity** that was once used against this precious doctrine itself. Thus, H. A. in no way agrees with the opponents, nor does he give this doctrine a "foreign name." Rather, H. Car. improperly treats Peucer’s words as if they were H. A.’s own, which violates the "laws of a good interpreter" <note>original: "leges boni interpretis"</note>. On the contrary, H. Car. violates his own rule by mocking and joking with the word **Ubiquitist** below on page 244, as will be seen in Number 79, § 3.

(5) When, however, H. A. notes in Chapter 31 of Book XVI, § 14, how Brenz and Andreae revived this dispute after the death of Luther, and later Melanchthon in the year 1560: he indeed cited the public writings of Brenz, *On the Personal Union of the Two Natures* and *On the Majesty of Christ*, as well as the *Recognition of the Doctrine of the Majesty of Christ*. Indeed, **Hutter** <note>Leonhard Hutter, a strict Lutheran theologian</note> himself proves in his *Concordia Concors* <note>The Harmonious Harmony, a defense of the Book of Concord</note>, page 35, that Brenz had already asserted this doctrine against **Pedro de Soto** <note>A Spanish Dominican theologian</note> in the year 1555.

<column-break/>

(6) H. A. could also have cited the opposing party, whose works also appeared in that same year. However, had he done so, he might have been accused once again of only quoting "adversaries." When he writes about the "arousing of the dispute," he is primarily looking at the misery and scandal that arose from it between the **Württemberg** and **Brunswick** theologians, which he recounts immediately afterward and ultimately laments in earnest: "That through such quarreling, nothing less than Christ’s glory and majesty was promoted." No true Christian who loves Jesus Christ **sincerely** <note>original Greek: "εἰλικρινῶς" (purely or sincerely)</note> will deny this.

(7) For this reason, Brenz is by no means being "put through the mocking-comb" <note>A metaphor for harsh, mocking criticism</note> because of his zeal, as H. Car. believes. For "it is good to be zealous, provided it is always for a good cause," as is rightly quoted here from Galatians 4:18. The fact that human weakness was mixed in with him does not make him an object of mockery; H. Car. interprets everything H. A. writes about "zeal" as mockery without basis, as was shown above in Numbers 20 and 21. Whether the following theologians always showed divine zeal in this matter is not for us to say here; the histories and writings reveal it. Let whoever has an honest and Christian heart be the judge here!

->Answer:<-

(1) Truth is bitter and hated. Yet one does not want to entirely deny to Mr. Caroli that he was driven to armor and anger by the clear presentation of the intended history, since he viewed it at first glance <note>original: "primò intuitu"</note> with partisan eyes. This harsh accusation is also repeated very often; however, it was already refuted above in Part I, under the 113th Accusation, according to most of the circumstances. And although one could refer back to that and touch upon nothing further, the most prominent points raised by Mr. Caroli shall be briefly observed: yet with this protestation, that one does not wish to dispute here about the doctrine itself or what occurred because of it, but remains constantly devoted to the **Gospel**, especially since many Lutheran teachers themselves were not satisfied with Dr. Jakob Andreae’s <note>A primary author of the Formula of Concord</note> person and affairs in all things, and yet remained good Lutherans, as is well known. Regarding what concerns the general <note>original: "Præsupposita" — presuppositions</note> upon which Mr. Caroli refers on page 131 in the cited Letter (h), these were investigated above and refuted as found.

(2) Here Mr. Caroli says first: Arnold had the intention of not putting even the slightest bit of the good done by Dr. Andreae into writing. Regarding "intention" as an internal state of the human mind, a man’s judgment is not sufficient; rather, this remains reserved for the All-Knowing God alone. Mr. Caroli wants to prove this intention through an example from the results <note>original: "à posteriori"</note>, namely, that H. A. should have inserted the story of the Jew converted at the gallows into the *Church History*. This would have had to happen either in the life story of Dr. Andreae or in the chapter regarding the Jews.

(3) H. A. had no need or desire to describe the former in such detail anywhere, as he was not writing <note>original: "Vitas Theologorum" — Lives of the Theologians</note>, but rather a general *Church History* <note>original: "K. Indeed, one would certainly have to be quite blinded by partiality if one wanted to demand <note>original: "prætendiren"</note> of today's *Historians* that they should reject the more recent, abundant, and obvious historical sources and documents <note>original: "Fontes historiarum und Documenta"</note> just as one rightly rejects the many ancient counterfeit and false things. In the current light of history, this claim will not hold. Furthermore, whatever doubts <note>original: "Dubia"</note> can be raised against the histories of *Vanini, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, or Simon*, they have been sufficiently investigated partly in the history itself, partly in the defenses, and here in Parts I and II. ### The 50th Accusation:

->Answer:<-

(1) Because Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus, the critic Arnold is answering.</note> cannot deny the matter itself, as the clear testimonies shine too brightly in his eyes, he seeks to excuse it; in which one might gladly defer to him, as far as the truth itself allows. To that end, he first raises the question: **Whether all intensity in a teacher of the Church is to be scolded?**

(2) To this end, he very poorly misuses the example of our gentle Savior and his Apostle Paul. These are indeed blameless in the divine, pure sense of the Gospel—both in themselves and in these incomparable persons, Christ and Paul. However, how poorly and very dangerously they are applied to the subject at hand—without discretion or limitation regarding the manner, the goal, and the like—shall soon follow.

(3) Meanwhile, it has been noted so often that many gladly appeal to the zeal of Christ and his Apostles, but not to the patience, peaceability, self-denial, and deepest suffering that accompanied it. And when we soon hear of Dr. Andreæ’s damning of his brothers to all the devils—especially Flacius <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus, a strict Lutheran who clashed with Andreæ.</note>—the comparison between him and the Lord Jesus or Paul may be easily decided: seeing as the latter judged and condemned for the purpose of improvement, winning over, or conviction, while the former did so for destruction.

(4) But where are the clear Scriptural commands regarding a **servant of the Lord** (2 Timothy 2:24 and 4:2; 1 Corinthians 4:21) and regarding all **Christians**, how they should be gentle and compassionate toward strangers (Galatians 6:1, Matthew 11:29)? Had these teachings and examples been followed, how well it would sound in the histories! But who can help it if one must testify otherwise when the facts lie before one's eyes?

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold's "History of the Church and Heretics" (K.H.) against the criticisms of Andreas David Carolus. The debate focuses on the character and temper of the Lutheran theologian Jakob Andreæ (often referred to as Dr. A. or D.A.). ...exactly that and nothing less is what Mr. A. <note>Gottfried Arnold, the author of the history being defended</note> has written. Why then is he accused so vehemently because of it?

(8) Regarding point $\beta$) Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus, the critic</note> wants to show from the aforementioned panegyrics <note>original: "Panegyricis," formal speeches of high praise</note> (p. 140) that Dr. A. was also gentle, specifically in academic disputations. However, anyone who knows how things go at universities—how the most seemingly violent oppositions finally end with a submission under the pronouncements of the Presiding Professor as patron and teacher <note>original: "Præsidis als Patroni und Præceptoris effata"</note>—will well recognize the reason for such "gentleness." From other controversies, Mr. Carolus brings forward only a single instance involving Dr. Paul von Eizen (p. 140). On the other hand, anyone who looks at the catalog of Andreæ’s polemical writings (which runs to eight pages in his nephew's list) and compares various parts of it, will find the exact opposite to be true. Yet, Mr. Carolus has admitted it both above and here: that he [Andreæ] was violent and zealous when it concerned "God’s honor."

(9) How heartily would a Christian not wish that everything had truly concerned God’s honor! However, one is forced—because Mr. Carolus portrays the writing against Paul von Eizen as being so mild—to cite several passages from it as they appear in Hutter <note>Leonhard Hutter, a prominent Lutheran theologian</note> (in the cited place). Except for this necessity, one would certainly have reported nothing further of this hateful matter, were it not necessary for the reader to test how much trust can be placed in the assurances of the opponents. Dr. Andreæ nevertheless calls the aforementioned Dr. Paul von Eizen—who was also a Lutheran theologian—a "presumptuous man" in Hutter (p. 387), one who puts forward "public and shameless untruths." On page 389, he threatens that God will not leave such people unpunished. Item <note>Also</note>, on page 394, he says that Geneva is a "Calvinist wasp’s nest," etc. On page 396, he says he offers "defiance to Dr. Paul von Eizen and all devils." Item, he says everything the man puts forward is nothing but "shameful, shameless Zwinglian, Calvinist, and Sacramentarian <note>A term for those who denied the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist, often used as an insult</note> baselessness and wanton devilish calumnies," etc. Further down in Number 58, § 4, more of the same will appear. Let the reader judge for himself what kind of "embittered spirit" is visible here, and how these truthful reports can be interpreted as "bitterness" on the part of the author of the *History of the Church and Heretics*? For he could not have reported it otherwise than as he found it.

### The 51st Accusation.
Arnold attributes vengefulness to him [Andreæ]. p. 141.

->Antwort:<-

(1) The undeniable words against Strigelius <note>Victorinus Strigelius, a theologian who disagreed with Andreæ</note> from Fecht's *Theological Letters* <note>original: "Fechtii Epist. Theol."</note>

<column-break/>

page 250, wherein he [Andreæ] wishes for the man's destruction from God, and thereafter writes: "When the opportunity arises, I will treat him in such a way that he realizes I am not foolish" <note>original: "Occasione oblata ita tractabo eum, ut intelligat, me non desipere"</note>. Mr. Carolus seeks to rescue this in the following way: $\alpha$) he claims Mr. Arnold interpreted "the theologians" as what Dr. A. wrote about "the Church." But back then, who else did certain theologians call "the Church" but themselves? For the politicians and laypeople knew or understood little to nothing of their technical terms <note>original: "terminis"</note> and disputes. Thus, this is not a "gloss" <note>interpretive note</note> stemming from an evil mind, as Mr. Carolus has partially judged.

(2) Regarding $\beta$) Mr. Arnold is accused of having "craftily deceived with the word *malum* [evil/harm] by using the word *Dampff* [vapor/fumes]," even though it means "damage" here. But who does not see this wretched excuse? Arnold’s words are these: "May God now destroy him who has given the greatest evil to His church and will continue to do so" <note>original: "Deus illum modò perdat, qui Ecclesiae suæ maximum malum dedit, & porrò dabit."</note> Mr. Arnold translates this even too mildly; he uses the word "vapor" <note>The German text uses "Dampff," suggesting Arnold may have used it to downplay the harshness or as a specific idiom</note>, whereas it actually should have said: "he has done the Church the greatest evil or misfortune, and will continue to do so." This is indeed an even more terrible judgment of Strigelius’s stubbornness than Mr. Arnold expressed. He truly had no "craftiness" here, much less did he leave out the following words out of "unfaithfulness," since they did not strictly belong to the matter—indeed, they further prove Dr. A.’s harsh pronouncements. For how harshly do these words not sound coming from a Professor: "He was born for disturbances, a plainly inflammatory <note>original: "tribunitius," like a Roman tribune inciting the commoners</note> character, who breathes nothing arrogantly except his own praise"? Mr. Carolus translated them, but what did they help him in reaching his goal?

(3) Regarding $\gamma$) he excuses Dr. A. on page 142 by saying: "Strigelius treated his father-in-law shamefully." Had Mr. Arnold written this, it would be called incorrect. Furthermore, he wants to justify the horrific wish Dr. A. made against Strigelius—"May God destroy him!"—claiming it was not blameworthy, nor was "fleshly vengefulness" to be concluded from it. Certainly, every Gospel-minded Christian must be terrified by such things, especially when they are excused by using Paul’s exceptional example from Galatians 5:12 <note>"I wish those who unsettle you would castrate themselves!"</note>. Here one might say with better reason what the authors of the *Unschuldige Nachrichten* <note>"Innocent News," a contemporary Lutheran journal</note> wrote in 1705, page 740: "We would never hope that a man in the teaching office should be equal to Paul." Praise God! That the evangelical spirit of Christ, which also ruled in Paul, is now better known and more beloved than in those harsh times, when Christianity was placed in fighting and condemning!

(4) Furthermore, Mr. Carolus seeks to cloak it thus: To a "seducer" <note>deceiver or heretic</note>, as long as he only does harm to the Church and will not desist from it, one cannot wish happiness and success.

462 Response to the so-called Wurtemberg Innocence, Part IV, Section 1, 52nd Complaint.

If another person had concluded from this: "Therefore, Dr. Andreæ <note>Jacob Andreæ, a key author of the Formula of Concord</note> was probably allowed or even obligated to wish for Strigelius’s <note>Victorinus Strigelius, a theologian often at odds with the strict Lutherans</note> ruin," how much would people have exaggerated such a claim? However, first: the question was whether Strigelius was truly such a "seducer" as Andreæ viewed him, even if he had indeed erred. Second: one should surely bless even the worst enemy and wish for their conversion when they curse, rather than not only cursing them back, but even wishing for their ruin or final downfall. This is contrary to the clear Scriptures and should rightly require no proof among Christians.

(5) And how distressing it is when Mr. Carolus <note>Andreas David Carolus, the critic of Arnold's history</note> compares these horrifying expressions of Dr. Andreæ with the most innocent words of Paul from 2 Corinthians 10:11. Likewise, it is troubling when he tries to interpret the threatened treatment so forcedly, saying: Dr. Andreæ would have shown Strigelius through forceful conviction that he was no fool! How gladly one would believe this explanation, if the ruin he once wished upon him did not show the opposite! To be sure, Mr. Carolus wants to prove this from other words in Fecht <note>original: "bey Fechtio," referring to the theologian Johann Fecht</note> (cited location, page 289), but in that very same place, Andreæ also speaks of his enemies' journey to hell: "for whom I fear hell is prepared" <note>original: "quibus metuo infernum paratum esse"</note>. As much as one would like to excuse the man in this matter, one is forced by the truth to hesitate and confess that neither Dr. Andreæ nor this defender of his truly knew or had dwelling within them the gentle spirit of Christ in its power; and thus, that the former was poorly equipped for a truly divine Work of Concord <note>referring to the Formula of Concord, a document intended to unify Lutheranism</note>.

### The 52nd Complaint:
He says that Dr. Andreæ was of a restless mind (page 143).

### Answer:
(1) This was proven in that very place from the clear letters of his own friends, about which Mr. Carolus intends to speak further down, where the matter may remain deferred. Regarding his reputation as a "brave warrior of Jesus Christ," a scriptural reminder has already been given above in Number 40.

(2) Regarding the words that Mr. Arnold <note>The author, Gottfried Arnold</note> cites in the 16th Book, Chapter 19, Section 5, concerning the "Münzerite spirit" <note>referring to the radical reformer Thomas Münzer; to be called a "Münzerite" was a serious accusation of being a violent fanatic</note> from a Flacian <note>followers of Matthias Flacius Illyricus, known for their rigid Lutheranism</note> writing, Mr. Carolus (page 145) had no reason at all to threaten that things would not go so mildly if this reference were addressed as it deserves. Considering that in that same place, M. Spangenberg <note>Cyriacus Spangenberg, a Gnesio-Lutheran theologian</note> and others complain that Dr. Andreæ called them "Münzerite spirits" (which they call a devilish slander), and they then retorted this title back upon him.

retort. Mr. Arnold reported this merely to show, by virtue of his clear words there, how the followers of the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wiedertäuffer," a radical Reformation group</note> accused one another of these things. Thus, Mr. Arnold was not responsible for the fact that Dr. Andreæ labeled Spangenberg this way, or that the latter labeled the former in return. As for the charge of "frivolity," Mr. Carolus postpones the answer until further down.

### The 53rd Complaint:
Also: Dr. Andreæ possessed much outward boldness and the <term>gift of impudence</term> <note>original: "donum impudentiæ," meaning a natural talent for being shameless or brazen</note> (page 147).

### Answer:
(1) Here Mr. Carolus first asks whether this is a Christian way to speak—of a "gift of impudence"—since one should not make sport of divine gifts of grace. I answer: We do not wish to defend the phrasing, nor do we know whether it might have been introduced during copying or printing. However, it is also obvious that Mr. Arnold does not mean a divine gift of grace here, but a mere natural gift or a quality of the corrupted nature of man. This <term>boldness</term> <note>original: "Hardiesse," from the French for audacity or daring</note> is certainly not to be counted among divine gifts of grace, which is gladly conceded to Mr. Carolus.

(2) The only question is regarding the person in question, for whom Mr. Carolus demands proof, while he himself attributes these things to an undaunted heart and a joyful spirit that would not have relied on any Mammon <note>worldly wealth or greed</note>, etc. And he deduces this, among other things, from Andreæ's writing to the Prince of Anhalt, to whom Dr. Andreæ wrote as follows: "If Your Princely Grace should uphold your blasphemous writing, then Your Princely Grace, together with your theologians, will be held before God as a blasphemer of the majesty of Christ, and will certainly not remain unpunished." Mr. Carolus considers this a magnificent, singular, and—at that time—especially necessary and useful gift of God for the church. However, one gladly leaves the decision to an enlightened reader as to which belongs to nature and which to grace, and how to distinguish divine boldness from other natural characteristics.

Dr. Andreæ could play the part of a statesman <note>original: "Staats-Mann"</note> not poorly at all.

Mr. Arnold wanted to say nothing more than this: for he speaks, as mentioned, only of the <term>capacity</term>, not of the <term>act</term>, and thus so many words were not needed.

(4) What Mr. Carolus says regarding Anabaptists and Quakers <note>Groups often accused by mainstream Lutherans of overemphasizing internal "spirit" over formal scripture and church order</note> arises from resentment and other emotions, for which he may be excused. Mr. Arnold does not at all attribute the sermons of such people directly to the Holy Spirit. Nor does he say that God’s grace did nothing in other sermons; he is well aware of the passage cited for this from 2 Corinthians 3:5-6 <note>"Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think of anything as being from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God..."</note> and knows that it was often repeated before sermons more out of earnestness than habit! (5) Mr. Carolus answers this on page 156: "Cannot nature and grace exist together? Do these two struggle so much and so badly with each other that one drives out and nullifies the other? Must one think, when natural gifts are mentioned, that the gifts of grace are thereby excluded?" However, the question was not about any of these things, but rather whether grace should not be mentioned most of all alongside nature. If a theologian, in writing the <term>encomium <gloss>a speech or piece of writing that highly praises someone</gloss></term> of another, mentions all his natural gifts—and especially in praising his sermons—without mentioning grace or the Holy Spirit by a single word, what else should one think but that the latter and best part was forgotten? And must it not be that either the author or the praised person relied upon nature and its gifts? Now, look at the short biography of Dr. Andreæ in Osiander [page 1084] and see if a single word about God and His grace or the Holy Spirit stands there, despite so much being boasted regarding his **languages, philosophy, theology, dexterity of mind, the arts of speaking, disputations, natural eloquence, learned and vigorous sermons, serious rebukes, the praise and admiration of many, his title of Doctor, his abhorrence of heresies and sects, his pious zeal, and his honest and irreproachable life** <note>original: "linguis, Philosophia, Theologia, dexteritate ingenii, artibus dicendi, disputationibus, naturali facundia, concionibus doctis & nervosis, gravibus invectionibus, laude & admiratione multorum, Doctoratus titulo, abhorrere ab hæresibus & sectis, pio zelo, vita honesta & irreprehensibili"</note> and so forth. All of these things can undeniably exist in a merely natural man, so that such a person may be called respectable and blameless, yet still allows neither true grace nor the Holy Spirit to become powerful within him.

(6) One is in complete agreement here with Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the "Father of Pietism," whose work "Nature and Grace" is cited here</note> from his *Nature and Grace*, pages 3, 6, 7: for he only wishes it not to be denied that nature exists alongside grace. But he does not say—as Mr. Carolus would like—that grace is always present with nature, as that would be <term>Pelagian <gloss>the heretical belief that human nature is basically good and can take the first steps toward salvation without divine aid</gloss></term>. He admits that teachers are also useful according to their natural gifts, which everyone admits; but he denies in countless places in his

writings, and especially in this one, that nature without grace is sufficient in divine matters. And through the little word "also," he requires grace alongside nature. Thus, when he further says on page 7 that natural gifts are governed by grace, he is clearly speaking of converted and enlightened persons who have received grace, not of those who remain in mere nature and whose fruits show that they have never yet become good trees. Anyone can make the application to this or 그 subject themselves according to the rule of God’s Word.

### The 56th Accusation:

->He claims that the Lord Landgrave William complained about his [Andreæ's] sophistical way of debating and other tricks.<-

### Answer:

(1) Whether this is true or not, Mr. Carolus does not wish to linger upon it; he denies, however, that the complaint was justified, because Ahab also complained about Elijah <note>Referring to 1 Kings 18:17, where the wicked King Ahab calls the prophet Elijah the "troubler of Israel"</note>. How this comparison of the Lord Landgrave with the godless Ahab is founded, I will not ask just now; much less whether the <term>Sacramentarians <gloss>a derogatory term used by Lutherans for those who disagreed with Luther's view of the Lord's Supper, primarily Calvinists and Zwinglians</gloss></term> of that time, as he calls them, were "arch-sophists" and dealt in vain sophistry. For this does not belong here, and it has been debated enough *pro and contra* for many long years.

(2) We shall stick solely to the question at hand: namely, what others wrote rather than Mr. Arnold himself, and for which he did not take the specific burden of proof upon himself. We gladly allow Mr. Carolus to cite the testimonies of Dr. Leonhard Hutter and others—even his own—about how he [Dr. Andreæ] defeated and scattered all the arguments of the Sacramentarians in **disputations**. One could produce even more such praises from his friends, if only they carried any weight, especially with outsiders. As for what Dr. Andreæ himself boasts in his *Admonition* (found in Hutter’s *Concordia Concors*, page 960) regarding his disputation held at Wittenberg against the <term>Crypto-Calvinists <gloss>Lutherans suspected of secretly holding Calvinist views on the Eucharist</gloss></term>—that he challenged them all and many confessed their error—many would likely attribute this to fear of the Court, which Dr. Andreæ had on his side, rather than to the disputation itself. This is especially true since it occurred in the year 1580, the circumstances of which year could reveal much. However, we will not enter into this dispute, much less whether and to what extent the insults against Christ belong here or not, because time and space do not permit such long-windedness.

### The 57th Accusation.

->Some wrote that Dr. Andreæ was a drunkard.<-

### Response.

(1) This is found in Chapter 18 of the 16th Book, Section 21. Generally, one author writes publicly that Andreæ was a drunkard <note>original: "ebriosus"</note>; such a thing is also alleged by Irenzo Agnosto <note>A pseudonym for an unknown author</note>. Mr. Carolus rejects this latter author as anonymous, even though he refers to a specific incident. However, what Melchior Leydecker has written, Mr. Carolus considers to be slanderous words, and he wishes to prove that Calvin was also accused of such things by Jerome Bolsec—indeed, that Christ himself was scolded as a wine-bibber.

(2) One gladly grants all these excuses to anyone and merely asserts that Mr. Arnold did not occupy himself with trifles or create an excerpt from this, as Mr. Carolus thinks. Rather, as is evident, he came upon these circumstances while researching the Formula of Concord <note>The definitive statement of Lutheran faith produced in 1577, of which Jakob Andreæ was a primary author</note>, during which even Lutheran authors could not easily forget the magnificent feasts and even a farewell banquet <note>original: "Valet-Schmauss"</note> held by Crusius himself in Tübingen. Since he found these passages, which were nearly parallel to those others, he added them—yet in such a way that he did not approve of them, but simply reminded the reader that they had been publicly written. Thus, he does not make this dispute his own. For Hornius writes in his *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "H. E."</note> on page 353 of Brentius: "seduced by the drunkard Schmidlin" <note>original: "à Schmidlino ebrioso seductus"</note>; and Leydecker in Note 144 says of Andreæ: "He was an angry man and devoted to wine" <note>original: "Homo fuit iracundus & vino deditus"</note>. Whether these authors concluded such things from the *Fama Andreæ* <note>A collection of reports or rumors about Andreæ</note>, where something is told on page 128 about the "Lord God's wine," one cannot know.

(3) Mr. Carolus suspects that this was done because Dr. Andreæ was a Lutheran; whereas he claims Paracelsus's drunkenness was dismissed by Arnold because he was not a Lutheran. To this, let the reader be reminded how Mr. Arnold has nonetheless refuted many slanders here and there in his *Church History* against upright, godly, and peaceable Lutheran teachers—indeed, against Luther himself—wherever he found a certain basis to do so. However, he could not possibly reconcile Paracelsus's drunkenness with his manifest gifts of grace, uncommon cures, and other good testimonies of his Christian conduct, especially since sorcery and other horrors were also attributed to him, which so many learned men <note>original: "Eruditi"</note> clear him of.

(4) But Mr. Carolus does well to finally cast doubt on his own suspicion and declares: where he might be wrong, he would

<meta>catchword: he</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>469</page-num>
<header>Part IV, Section 57, 58. Mr. Andreas David Carolus etc.</header>

gladly be informed. I also believe that, had he lived longer, he would have liberated Mr. Arnold from this wicked suspicion, though it does not depend on human judgment. In the meantime, one gladly grants him the proof that Dr. Andreæ lived soberly, if only it were sufficient in all respects. His own words against drunkenness, which Mr. Carolus cites, are good; and if his practice agreed with them, it is even better—indeed, only then are the words truly good and a sign that they came from the heart.

(5) Nevertheless, many doubts regarding the practice of such teachings might remain for some when they read, for example, in the <term>eulogy <gloss>a speech of high praise, original: "encomio"</gloss></term> for Dr. Barenbüler cited by Mr. Carolus himself on page 169: "He showed himself cheerful and sober at banquets" <note>original: "Præbuit se in conviviis hilarem, sobrium"</note>; likewise in Crusius, a colleague of Dr. Andreæ, in his *Swabian Annals* on page 757, that the University arranged a magnificent farewell banquet for Dr. Andreæ. At the very least, it serves as no praise or recommendation for a truly blameless theologian among those who understand Christianity when he shows himself merry and joyful at feasts, allows magnificent banquets to be arranged for his sake, or at least permits them, etc. A Christian, impartial reader remains free to form their own sentiment on this according to the teaching of Christ.

(6) Mr. Carolus concludes here on page 168 that Arnold dragged Dr. Andreæ through the ten <term>Categories <gloss>the ten classifications of reality in Aristotelian logic, original: "Prædicamenta"</gloss></term> with all his might, but not lawfully or sincerely. However, just as the ten Categories in common logic are a fiction of Aristotelian philosophy, so too has this accusation—expressed with a mere Aristotelian jest—been found incorrect until now. Mr. Carolus, being partisan, could not form a capable judgment on it, but had to leave the cited passages of the authors standing alongside the facts, except for those he wished to reject as enemies according to his own mind, but could not entirely do so.

### The 61st Accusation:

->That Dr. Andreæ [D. A.] allegedly praised Cassander’s intention toward Emperor Maximilian II.<-

### Response:

(1) Here, Mr. Arnold [H. A.] cites Jakob Heerbrand’s funeral oration for Andreæ; however, because the specific page or passage is not listed, and that book may not have been paginated, Mr. Carolus [H. Car.] cannot find the passage. He simply asks: what does Arnold intend by this? The answer is this: the Protestants did not flatly condemn all of <term>Cassander’s</term> <note>George Cassander (1513–1566) was a Flemish theologian who sought to find a middle ground between Catholics and Protestants, often accused of "Syncretism"</note> proposals, though this does not mean Cassander gained greater authority through them. For the <term>grievances</term> <note>original: "Gravamina"</note> against him are also well known.

(2) When Mr. Carolus adds, in the heat of contradiction, that Arnold treated no one as shamefully as he did Jakob Andreæ—namely, that in Arnold’s view, Andreæ was a "sophistical, executioner-like man"—he is judged too severely by his own emotion and bias, which causes him to view historical accounts as mere insults. For where has Mr. Arnold described this man as "executioner-like"? Or by what means does one judge Mr. Arnold’s private thoughts or inner sense regarding him? These expressions are excessive and set against the truth.

(3) Finally, on page 180, he admits it may well be that Arnold allowed Cassander’s intention itself to be considered good, especially considering that Cassander was very modest and gave many a remarkable testimony to the Evangelical truth—both of which have always been praised by our own side. Regarding this, he cites Seckendorff, Hulsemann, Dorfcheus, and A. Osiander. He only wishes to prevent this from making Arnold suspect of <term>Cassandrian Syncretism</term> <note>The attempt to unify different religious denominations by overlooking fundamental dogmatic differences; a highly controversial "dirty word" in 17th-century theology</note>. However, Mr. Arnold does not claim this either, and thus there is no dispute over it.

### Response:

(1) Regarding this matter, it should be known that Selnecker had written in his *Recitation* that the Electoral Councillors had drafted this preface. But because there were so many scholastic terms within it, and the entire style showed something else, the response of <term>Hospinian</term> <note>Rudolf Hospinian (1547–1626), a Reformed theologian from Zurich known for his polemics against Lutheran and Catholic rituals</note> and the author who wrote the *Examination of Selnecker’s Recitation* is cited here, and indeed without the slightest addition of Arnold's own.

(2) Since Mr. Arnold merely refers to the words, he cannot have used them as a mocking taunt, nor in league with the "poisonous slanderer" Hospinian, as Mr. Carolus calls him. Indeed, from the very fact that Hospinian is so enormously scolded, learned people will eventually judge the opposite and, with Mr. <term>Thomasius</term> <note>Christian Thomasius, a famous jurist and philosopher who championed Enlightenment ideas and defended Arnold's work</note>, call him a writer who has served Church History most highly, as the *Reports* of 1707, page 35, note from his preface to the German Grotius. The matter here is all too clear: namely, that the Councillors did not write such scholastic abstractions; the contrary has not been thoroughly verified. Mr. Arnold did not take it upon himself to defend Hospinian’s expressions, but merely recounted them as he found them. And anyone can be convinced by Mr. Arnold’s other writings that he never used such speech himself.

(3) Therefore, Mr. Carolus’s harsh accusations do not apply to him, as he mocks Mr. Arnold’s enlightenment and love just as Hospinian mocks the "scholastic puddles." The former—namely, enlightenment and love—cannot be stolen by any man but remain for all eternity, because God’s gift and calling are without repentance. But the latter—namely, the terms fetched from the scholastic puddles—are, alas! often tangible in the writings of that time, and it were to be wished that Hospinian had not needed or been able to write of them. Luther himself (and thus not only Hospinian) calls such scholastic things "the bilgewater of the most tasteless specter of the Thomists" <note>original Latin: "sentinas insulsissimæ larvæ Thomistarum"</note> in his *Book Against the King of England*, folio 522, Volume V, Jena Latin Edition. The matter, alas, is all too clear; and Mr. Carolus himself repeats the terms on page 182: *essentially, habitually, formally, subjectively*, etc., which even the authors of the Preface to the Formula of Concord themselves call "words that are not Latin enough" <note>original Latin: "vocabula non satis Latina"</note>.

(4) However, in writing that the enemies of the Book of Concord made much of this at the time, and yet later attributing it to Mr. Arnold, he does him an injustice, as Arnold only reports it based on so many other writings. He says Arnold dare not give his name, yet Arnold cites two authors: the author of the *Examination* and Hospinian...

also almost word for word that of **Dr. Himmelins** <note>Johann Himmel (1581–1642), a Lutheran theologian and professor at Jena</note> in his treatise *on Scholastic Theology, p. 696.* <note>original: "de Theologia Scholastica"</note> Now, everyone knows that these *technical terms* <note>original: "Termini"</note> under discussion were taken from nowhere else but from School Theology <note>Scholasticism: a method of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities based on Aristotelian logic</note>. IV. Part 63. N. Mr. Andreas David Carolus, etc. 481

We wish that the word **divinely inspired** <note>original: "θεόπνευστος" (theopneustos)</note> be omitted in this case for many reasons of sacred prudence. **Mamphrasius** <note>A contemporary theologian</note>, however, praised it as a **Canon** or "rule and measuring line"; others, such as **Müller** and **Olearius**, have said that the authors were driven by no one but the Holy Spirit, etc., as is proven in that place. The words "without shame" actually belong to this proof, for they also appear first in that context.

(2) Now, if one further compares the words of **Mr. Arnold** <note>The author of the book being defended</note> with those that **Mr. Carolus** brings against them, the matter will become all the clearer. Mr. Arnold says in the cited place (p. 223) that the theologians had established that the Formula of Concord should—Note Well—alongside the other Creeds, be held as the **Norm of Doctrine** and **Rule of Judgment**. Mr. Carolus denies this and counters: the Formula of Concord itself calls God’s Word the "Only Rule." However, it is well known and requires no elaborate explanation what distinctions are made between the **primary and secondary norm**, between the **norm that norms** <note>original: "norma normante," the Bible</note> and the **norm that is normed** <note>original: "norma normata," the Creeds</note>, between the **essential and instrumental norm**, between the **applied norm**, and so forth. Therefore, it ultimately amounts to this: that the Confessional Books, and specifically the Formula of Concord, are to be and remain a norm and rule *next to* the Holy Scripture. This has been demonstrated by **Dr. Johann Michael Lange** in his answer to Mr. Storren’s letter, among others; and long before him by **Dr. Spener** <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the founder of Pietism</note> in his dismissal of Dr. Pfeiffer, in his *Theological Reflections*, and in other writings here and there, as well as in Mr. Lange's *Reports*, Vol II, p. 33, etc.

(3) As for these specific words of **Jakob Andreae** found in **Fecht's** *Theological Letters* <note>original: "Epist. Theol.," p. 346</note>, Mr. Carolus raises many complaints, as if they were interpreted wickedly and against conscience, or mutilated, etc. This is because Jakob Andreae there, and in the Formula of Concord, so often cites Scripture as the norm. However, Mr. Arnold knew this well; but he also knew no less, and proved it from the consequences (as mentioned above), how the very book in which Scripture was declared the norm was nevertheless afterward established as a norm—indeed, an **absolute norm** next to Scripture—and that consciences were bound to it. Regarding such **coercion of conscience**, he is so fully assured in his own conscience by undeniable foundations that he has written nothing against his conscience.

(4) It is also explicitly stated in the words of **Dr. Andreae** that the Creeds were to be held as the Norm next to the Holy Bible, and that the theologians in the Empire should declare and commit their consensus to these Creeds. That the Formula of Concord was also primarily made into a Norm or Canon is proven by the clear words of Mamphrasius...

### The 66th Accusation:

That Dr. Andreae threatened Strigelius <note>Victorinus Strigel, a theologian who disagreed with Andreae on the nature of free will</note> that he would *treat* <note>original: *tractiren*</note> him so that he should see he was no fool, etc. p. 193.

### Answer:

This matter has already been fully discussed above in the 51st Accusation. Mr. Carolus brings nothing new here, except that he proves Strigelius was also not pious and blameless. Mr. Arnold himself *observed* <note>original: *observiret*</note> this on p. 362, and no one will deny it. However, he should not have been threatened so harshly for that reason, much less have destruction from God wished upon him; rather, improvement should have been wished for him. In those days, people were accustomed to condemning and cursing all who would not agree; therefore, one heard more cursing than blessing. No matter how much one tries to excuse this, the vice, alas, still shines through! and one wastes one's time with such *excuses* <note>original: *Excusen*</note> not without harm. For it is one thing to restrain someone, and indeed properly so, and another to wish them destruction from God and threaten them with such *treatment* <note>original: *Tractament*</note>.

### The 67th Accusation:

If Mr. Arnold had made such a completely unjust conclusion, how he would have been *harassed* <note>original Latin: *exagitirt*</note> for it!
