(2) It is indeed forbidden for Christians not even to scold in return, let alone to be the first to scold—especially against those who were not entirely un-Christian in every respect, even if Mr. Carolus, following Dr. Andreae <note>Jacob Andreae (1528–1590), a prominent Lutheran theologian and primary author of the Formula of Concord.</note>, again calls them untruthful, devious, malicious, and seductive Sacramentarians <note>A term used, often derisively, for those who denied the physical presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, such as the followers of Zwingli or Calvin.</note>, who were supposedly not a hair better than the most lying rascals. Previously, Mr. Carolus wanted to excuse Dr. Andreae because he mocked in a *private* letter; but here, Mr. Carolus scolds even worse in a *public* writing than the other did secretly. However, before GOD, it does not justify an un-Christian act whether it is done secretly or publicly. While there is neither time nor desire here to investigate the actions of such people, this at least should be settled among Christians: that when one presents the reality of a person’s wrongdoing to convince them of their error, it should be done thoroughly but without scolding and wicked epithets. Such names greatly hinder improvement and destroy whatever good remains in them—no matter how small—making it useless along with the evil. Dr. Andreae scolded not only the Reformed, but also Flacius <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a strict Lutheran whose views on original sin led to fierce controversy.</note> in this manner, as seen *in Fecht’s work, page 508* <note>original Latin: *apud Fechtium p. 508.* Justus Fecht was a Lutheran theologian.</note>: "They are the most lying rascals the earth has ever carried, as are Illyricus and his followers."

(3) Now, compare this against the confessions of other theologians; for example, when Quenstedt of Wittenberg <note>Johann Andreas Quenstedt (1617–1688), a standard-bearer of Lutheran Scholasticism.</note> writes in his *Pastoral Ethics*, page 407, concerning such perverted zeal even against the Reformed: *Therefore, the untimely zeal of those who, in acting against sectarians—whether Papists or (take note) Calvinists or any others—burn with such anger and vehemence of passions that they tear down their adversaries with insults, overwhelm them with accusations, and pursue them with bitter invectives, etc., can and should by no means be approved.* <note>original: "Minime itaque probari potest aut debet eorum intempestivus Zelus, qui agendo contra Sectarios sive Pontificios sive NB. Calvinianos sive alios quoscunque ita ira & affectuum vehementia exardescunt --- adversarios convitiis proscindunt, criminationibus premunt, & acerbis invectivis persequuntur &c."</note> Likewise, Eilhardus Lubinus asks in his *Apologetic Response to Grauer*: When has it ever been heard that heretics were converted by scolding, quarreling, slandering, and name-calling? And who can blame our secular officials if they have long recognized: *That there is an extreme lack of restraint of the tongue even in sacred persons?* Also: *That even writings considered sacred are filled with so many injuries and insults,* as Brunnemann says in *Ecclesiastical Law*, page 5 <note>original: "Summam linguae intemperiem esse etiam in personis sacris? Item: Tot injuriis & convitiis scripta etiam sacra, ut putantur, referta esse, wie Brunnemannus redet Jure Eccles. p. 5."</note>.

(4) Regarding what Mr. Carolus cites from the letter of Elector Augustus <note>Augustus, Elector of Saxony (1526–1586), a staunch supporter of Lutheranism.</note>, in which he also scolded them almost as much: it is easy to think that the good gentleman followed the example of the theologians and thought it was not wrong because they were doing it. Thus, the great spiritual damage caused by Dr. Andreae’s scolding is highlighted even more by Mr. Carolus’s evidence, rather than being excused by it. And because Mr. Carolus refers to the

**Insult:** In the *Fama Andreana* <note>A biographical work about Jacob Andreae.</note>, the story of the hanged Jew is repeated twice; therefore, it is done out of a thirst for glory. Mr. Carolus would not have allowed this conclusion to stand.

(3) Equally suspicious is the following **question**. For he asks further: Why did Andreae translate the word *Coenare* <note>Latin: "to dine" or "to eat."</note> as "gorging like beasts" <note>German: *Fressen*, a term usually reserved for animals, used here as a derogatory term for eating.</note>? He further opines that in a *private letter* <note>original: *Privat-Schreiben*</note>, and one written in haste at that, one cannot take everything so precisely. Compare here Professor Röhrensee's *Dissertation on Speech as the Index of the Soul* <note>original Latin: *Diss. de Oratione Animi Indice*</note>. However, it has already been answered in the preceding number that before GOD, this makes no difference. To which should be added here that even before men, nothing better *expresses* <note>original: *exprimire*</note> the state of the human mind than such private letters, which are written securely and without pretense. Mr. Carolus also specifically praised these *Fechtianas* <note>Refers to a collection of letters edited by the theologian Johann Fecht.</note> as epistles published with remarkably laudable diligence on page 204.

(4) He rightly praises Flacius <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer known for his strict views on original sin.</note> on page 203 as a man of excellent gifts who earned great merit in the Evangelical Church. (But why should such a meritorious man be sent to all the devils?) But he supposedly went astray in the doctrine of Original Sin and remained stuck in it, having a stubborn, restless, and harmful mind. Of Cyriacus Spangenberg <note>A theologian and historian (1528–1604) who followed Flacius's controversial teachings.</note>, Mr. Carolus also admits on page 204 that he was an edifying preacher, but did not know how to navigate theological controversies very well and allowed himself to be drawn into Flacius’s net, bringing the error into the German language, and so forth.

(5) All of this is willingly admitted to a certain extent, as has been sufficiently shown in the *Church History*; but the question is whether a Lutheran can say of such deceased Lutherans—who erred in only one point—that they "gorged with all the devils"? Especially since other Lutherans believed that such a person would eventually be reconciled with God, as is proven regarding Flacius in the 29th Chapter of the 16th Book, paragraph 17. these questioned words come from a true zeal for pure doctrine and the welfare of the church? This is what Mr. Carolus claims on page 205, saying: It ultimately depends on whether Dr. Andreae was zealous there out of ignorance or rightfully? Truly, whoever refuses to recognize Jacob Andreae’s state of soul otherwise—what he was like or how he was minded—can finally see from these horrific and entirely irrational expressions what was truly behind him and his actions. He asks how Paul could have wished such a thing, as a disciple of Him who said: "Bless those who curse you"? And he answers: Paul committed a human weakness here, and one could say he did not so much curse them as pray for them, that they might lose their sinful members. And the Greek Fathers also take this wish as referring to such a "cutting off" <note>Referring to the literal meaning of Galatians 5:12, where Paul suggests his opponents might as well emasculate themselves.</note>, as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> summarizes it briefly on this passage and paraphrases the 12th verse: *If they wish, let them not only be circumcised, but also cut themselves off entirely.* <note>original Greek: εἰ βούλονται, μὴ περιτεμνέσθωσαν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀποκοπτέσθωσαν.</note> Augustine, Ambrose, Theodoret, and others agree with this.

(7) Even if this *literal meaning* <note>original: *propria significatio*</note> might not quite apply, one sees nonetheless in the new interpreters that they have interpreted it more as a temporal ban <note>Excommunication from the church for a period of time.</note> than an eternal damnation, as almost all the Reformed <note>Calvinist/Zwinglian theologians.</note> do. And those among our own people <note>The Lutherans.</note> who take it to mean damnation nonetheless attribute it to the prophetic spirit and utterance of Paul. But was that spirit in Jacob Andreae? And how does such a prophecy rhyme with a judgment passed after death? Tertullian <note>Early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD).</note> even calls Paul's words a *pleasantly rational indignation* <note>original: *artig rationalem indignationem*</note>, a sensible and well-founded displeasure that came from the *effect of discipline* <note>original: *effectu disciplinæ*</note> (Book *On the Soul*, chapter 6). But was this wish of Jacob Andreae against Flacius also so sensible? Certainly, if one did not otherwise know Jacob Andreae’s genius and mind, or might think Mr. Arnold had been too hard on him, one could recognize from these his own words (which are indeed *indicators of the soul* <note>original: *animi indices*</note>, according to the agreement of all moralists) how unbroken and miserable his state was.

(8) When Paul writes of bearing judgment and rooting out, he is heaven-wide distant from such quarrelsome, ungodly zeal.

He includes among the careless, untheological, and unchristian speeches of Dr. Andreae this one from Fecht <note>Johann Fecht (1636–1716), a Lutheran theologian and historian.</note>, page 580: "I have more barking dogs in my beard than gray hairs." Page 211.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Carolus first reminds us that this word <term>gray hairs</term> <note>original: *canos*</note> on page 211 does not appear in the cited passage; he suggests it must have been in Mr. A.'s mind because

Dr. Andreae wrote something similar elsewhere, namely in Fecht, page 540. This may well be the case, and it signifies nothing; the word in Mr. A.'s copy is also so obscured by pale printer's ink that he could easily have read "o" for "e," reading <term>gray hairs</term> <note>original: *canos*</note> instead of <term>dogs</term> <note>original: *canes*</note>. However, Mr. Carolus in vain draws this false accusation from it: that Mr. A. is not to be trusted even in small things, let alone weighty ones.

(2) For above in number 65, we observed a much more extensive error <term>in factual matters</term> <note>original: *in realibus*</note> from Mr. Carolus, and yet we did not make the unchristian conclusion: <term>Therefore</term> <note>original: *Ergo*</note> Mr. Carolus is not to be trusted even in small things—despite the fact that he had attributed strange errors to Mr. A. based on his own mistake. But that was the goal of everything: to make Mr. A. look suspicious. Yet the issue here does not actually concern the word "gray hairs," but rather the other part about barking dogs.

(3) Now, Mr. Carolus opines that it is not "untheological" when Dr. Andreae writes that he has barking dogs in his beard. However, it is at the very least also not "theological," as the application in section 4 shall soon show. For what does "theological" mean? It does not mean that which is generally held to be good or decent in a theologian, if it is merely human and helps itself along with pure weakness. Rather, it means that which befits such a <term>subject</term> <note>original: *subjecto*</note> who has <term>a spiritual eye of the mind, pure from malice, pious, enlightenable or teachable,</term> and <term>devoted</term> <note>original Latin: *oculum mentis spiritualem, purum à nequitia, pium, illuminabilem seu docilem et devotum*</note>—to speak with Dannhauer <note>Johann Conrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a prominent Lutheran theologian in Strasbourg.</note> from his *Hodosophia*, Preface page 10. Or as Dr. Johannes Olearius <note>Johann Olearius (1611–1684), author of *Theologia Universa*.</note> describes it in *Theologia Universa*, page 3: Theological is that which arises from <term>written revelation</term> <note>original: *revelation scripta*</note>, from which we grasp and hold the mind of Christ. And as Arndt <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), influential theologian and author of *True Christianity*.</note> states in his *Postils*: <term>Theology is the knowledge of God and the practice of the life of Christ</term> <note>original Latin: *Theologia est agnitio Dei & praxis vitæ Christi*</note>. Anyone can make the application for themselves.

(4) Mr. Carolus says himself that Dr. Andreae was no "silent dog" <note>A reference to Isaiah 56:10, often used to describe preachers who fail to speak out against sin.</note>; and there is no question about that, much less whether preachers are allowed to be such, which Mr. Carolus laboriously proves without necessity. Rather, the question is only: what kind of speech is it to "have barking dogs," and specifically "in one's beard," and what sense do such words indicate? The reader is free to form their own sentiment on this: I will not dwell on it, but only mention that Dr. Andreae wrote even more clearly elsewhere (page 540): "The preacher should earnestly show his gray hairs to the City Council, transform them into dogs, and bark bravely at the Council," which Mr. A. cites in Chapter 15 of Book 16, section 8. Because Mr. A. shows from this how some preachers have incited [the people] against the authorities in their disputes...

### Answer:

(1) Here Mr. Carolus asks: in what way? He claims he can find nothing of the sort in the following pages, except for the report by Hospinian <note>Rudolf Hospinian (1547–1626), a Reformed theologian and historian often critical of the Formula of Concord.</note>. (loco citato)</note>, which was significant enough to consider: 
> "In the year 1577, he (Dr. Andreae) began in Saxony to

> "several country pastors then asked how they could save

> "were now absolved *ipso facto* <note>by the fact itself</note> from the obligation of the
> "previous oath, because Melanchthon was suspect. With
> "this, the poor people had to be satisfied, etc." 
In this context, Hospinian's *Concordia Discors* <note>A famous history of the Lutheran-Reformed controversies.</note> is cited, p. 117.

(2) Against this, Mr. Carolus says nothing, other than that it is a "wanton mockery" regarding the "playing with oaths" and "assumed papal power," such that it is not worth an answer. The gravity of the terrifying misuse of oaths—the absolution from previous ones and the burdening with new ones—was certainly no joke or mockery to Mr. Andreae’s critic, but a matter of pure earnestness arising from a deep insight into the misery of that time. It is not good that such testimonies are viewed as mere mockery and thus dismissed without any sought-after improvement.

(3) The account from Hospinian is grounded in the entire historical course of events at that time. It could not have been otherwise; the preachers had to be absolved from their previous oath to Philipp Melanchthon's *Corpus*, and indeed *ipso facto* <note>by the act itself</note> through the new oath to the Formula of Concord. This may have weighed heavily on many a conscience. This "game" is then proven from section 23 to 26, which Mr. Andreae mostly looked toward, and which Mr. Carolus could well have found if he had wanted to. Regarding Hospinian's above account, he cites Hutter <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a prominent defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> on page 340 of *Concordia Concors*. However, in that place not a word is seen

concerning the oaths to the *Corpus Philippi*, much less a refutation of Hospinian on this point <note>original: "in hoc puncto"</note>. Rather, it only says that the same did not apply among all Lutherans. The reader can look up the passage himself.

(4) It is a "pure fraud," Mr. Carolus writes further, even though he did not once deem the presentation worthy of an answer or refute it. It seems so grievous to him that Dr. Andreae should be accused of mishandling oaths. And yet, Mr. Andreae does not speak generally or indefinitely <note>original: "generaliter oder indefinite"</note>, as Mr. Carolus interprets and complains about; rather, he points only to the following dealings in section 21 and thereafter, and to the compulsion of so many poor consciences, even including secular officials <note>original: "Politicorum"</note>, to the oath on the Formula of Concord. Bedenck."</note> p. 381, he explicitly confesses there that one goes too far if the oath implies that one intends to believe what is in the Symbolic Books <note>The Lutheran Confessions, such as the Augsburg Confession and the Formula of Concord.</note> based on their own authority. With this, he does not absolutely approve of all religious oaths, as Mr. Carolus would like. On the contrary, it is notorious what this blessed man constantly declared regarding the compulsion of conscience and the subscription of the Symbolic Books *per formulam Quia* <note>through the "Because" formula; subscribing to the confessions *because* they agree with Scripture, rather than *insofar as* they do.</note>, not to mention the forced oaths regarding them, and how much he suffered because of it. Gerhard argues (in the section on Magistrates, § 210, and following him S. Schmidt in *Obligation to the Formula of Concord*, p. 10) against the Reformed, who consider religious oaths to be wrong. This, however: α) does not go directly against Lutherans, who may well agree with the truth without an oath; β) the reasons given are in part of such a nature that they cannot always quiet a scrupulous conscience, as could easily be shown if there were time. One need only observe impartially how a religious oath is proven: a) because Moses had the people promise obedience, as did Joshua and the kings; b) because all causes of such an oath were good and legitimate, as the efficient cause <note>original: "cauſa efficiens"</note>—that the Magistrate has the power to demand the oath (which, however, is precisely the question regarding internal and purely spiritual matters <note>original: "de objectis internis & merè ſpiritualibus"</note>); and so forth; c) because Paul adjured the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians 5:27 <note>The text cites 5:17, likely a printer's error for 5:27: "I adjure you by the Lord that this letter be read to all..."</note>; d) because such an oath is useful. Who does not see the state of such reasons?

He recounts how Dr. Andreae gladly allowed himself to be corrected even by his disciples, citing Dr. Barenbüler’s Panegyric <note>a formal speech of high praise</note> and several examples. All this is gladly left as it is, and one grants the good man many more such testimonies. However, one remains with the citations [proving] that he must sometimes have been quite stubborn, which his previously shown fiery temperament demonstrates anyway.

### The 74th Accusation:

(2) <margin>a)</margin> However, **Mr. Arnold** explicitly calls them only **accusations**, as he writes in the 18th Chapter of the 16th Book, section 18: "the Reformed brought forward accusations," and so forth, regarding such **accusations**. However, how a secret lordship over consciences, the **suppression** of dissenters, and the like are nevertheless possible in all such actions requires no **logical demonstration** <note>original: "Deduction"</note> for sensible minds. Nothing of this is to be found in **Hutter’s** answer, much less regarding the **grievances** <note>original: "Gravamina"</note> alleged by **Pierius** <note>Urban Pierius (1546–1616), a "Philippist" or moderate Lutheran who was persecuted by Andreae's faction.</note> and others. Thus, it was and still is not enough to simply call something lies and blasphemies;

### The 75th Accusation:

According to **Timothy Kirchner’s** complaint (in Fecht, p. 638), **Dr. Andreae** condemned people without a hearing <note>original: "unverhörter Sache"</note>. p. 228.

### Answer:

(1) The words in Latin are these: "The reconciliation (of Dr. Jacob <note>Jacob Andreae</note> and Chemnitz <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a fellow author of the Formula of Concord who often moderated Andreae’s zeal.</note>) will be firm if Dr. Jacob keeps what he promised; that is, if he abstains from prejudices and does not condemn those who have not been heard." <note>original: "Firmia futura est conciliatio (D. Jacobi & Chemnitii) si D. J. servabit ea, quæ promisit, h. e. si abstinuerit a præjudiciis, & non condemnet non auditos."</note> **Mr. Caroli** opines that it only follows from this that **Andreae** was under such suspicion, but it cannot be concluded from it that he actually condemned them; he says one should let the teachers of **Logic** judge this, etc.

(2) Depending on who such teachers are, they can also judge whether this conclusion does not have its full correctness. Whoever must promise, upon his reconciliation with a sensible man (as **Chemnitz** was), that he will henceforth abstain from prejudices and not condemn others unheard—he must surely have done such things previously. For why else would his promise be necessary or useful if he had already demonstrated the opposite through modesty and gentleness? **Dr. Andreae** would surely have contradicted such an evil suspicion if he had not been convicted of the act. He was not one to let things sit on him easily. This conclusion is further strengthened because **Kirchner**, as the third theologian, reports this promise not from **Chemnitz**, but only from **Dr. Andreae** alone; indeed, in these very words, he still *tacitly* and to some extent doubts its fulfillment—which would have been impossible if **Dr. Andreae** had not already proven himself capable of such behavior.

One sees how he, out of necessity, brings an even more miserable counter-proof against the clear words, namely this: **Chemnitz** and **Dr. J. Andreae** simultaneously condemned false doctrine and its followers; therefore, **Jacob** could not have condemned anyone alone without a hearing. Whoever looks at **Kirchner’s** words and knows the first disputes of **Dr. Andreae** with him and **Chytraeus** <note>David Chytraeus (1530–1600), another influential Lutheran reformer.</note>, as well as other theologians (which **Mr. Caroli** himself mentioned several times above), can well see that **Kirchner** is speaking here of the condemning that occurred not so much against the enemies of the Formula of Concord, but against others—specifically fellow Lutherans—with whom he sometimes differed...

(6) Against this he argues on page 557 with the words of **1 Corinthians 2**: "the spiritual man judges all things." (3) Mr. Caroli says on page 231 that the words on page 217—claiming that he (**Jacob Andreae**) performed the work on the <term>Formula of Concord</term> <note>The "Formula of Concord" (1577) is a definitive doctrinal statement of the Lutheran Church.</note> alone—were a fraud, and he suspects they were patched in. The latter simply reports what he finds in the <term>authors</term> <note>original: "Autoribus."</note>; the former openly scolds and rages. Moreover, it is impossible that Mr. Arnold intended to say that Dr. Andreae created the <term>Formula of Concord</term> entirely alone without any help from others, especially since Arnold himself provides a detailed account elsewhere in section 16 of how first twelve and then six theologians worked on it, until finally three of them revised the work—see section 17, where he also explicitly names these three as the originators. In section 19, he calls Dr. Andreae the "chief <term>author</term>," and thus could not possibly have believed or meant that no one but Dr. Andreae created the <term>Formula of Concord</term>.

(5) Rather, the meaning is that he performed the most and greatest part of the labor and carried out the work as the primary task (of which Mr. Arnold is only speaking) by himself, even though others assisted him in secondary matters. Whatever else Mr. Caroli reminds us of on page 232 against the cited words of the <term>Neustadt theologians</term> <note>original: "Neostadiensium," referring to the Reformed/Calvinist theologians of Neustadt who were vocal critics of the Formula of Concord.</note> does not concern Mr. Arnold; likewise regarding his claim that God Himself is the author of the Book of Concord, the circumstances that occurred therein, etc. As for the doubts regarding whether everything proceeded in such a divine and blameless manner, the following answers will partially demonstrate further.

### The 77. Accusation:

It is stated on page 215, citing <term>Pierius</term> <note>Urban Pierius (1546–1616), a German theologian who was caught in the middle of the Lutheran-Reformed conflicts.</note>, that Dr. Andreae was never called to such a <term>General Work</term> of unification by the Reformed. p. 237.

### Answer:

(1) This is merely cited by Mr. Arnold from <term>Pierius</term>; however, <term>Pierius</term> was first a Saxon <term>theologian</term> and <term>Superintendent</term> <note>A high-ranking ecclesiastical official in the Lutheran church.</note> at Wittenberg, who surely knew whether his party had called Dr. Andreae or not.

not. Mr. Caroli, on the other hand, wants to prove that Andreae was outwardly called to it by Lutheran lords, which has not been contradicted here. For the words speak only of the Reformed alone, and Mr. Caroli himself finally admits on page 340 that Andreae was never called to such a <term>General Work</term> of unification. Why then the contradiction? He believes Dr. Andreae would have had to wait a long time before they called him to it. However, the discussion concerns a <term>General Work</term>, and specifically a unification, for which a call from both parties would indeed have been necessary. Yet there is no reason to get involved in such disputes here, as they do not belong to the matter. The reader sees from this that the proof promised by Mr. Caroli above in No. 73, section 2, and postponed to this section, has not followed at all regarding the connection.

### The 78. Accusation.

He says on page 216 b. that <term>Flacius</term> <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a strict Lutheran leader known for his rigid stance on doctrine.</note> wrote: Dr. Schmiedlein <note>A mocking nickname for Jacob Andreae, derived from his father's profession as a blacksmith (Schmied).</note> wanted to establish, plaster over, and whitewash a godless, devilish amnesty and compromise, and thus introduce nothing but a "Samaritan religion" <note>A term used by polemicists to describe a hybrid or "impure" religious compromise.</note> into the church. p. 241.

### Answer:

(1) This is cited from the refutation of the <term>Dialogues</term> <note>original: "Dialogi," likely referring to Flacius’s writings on Original Sin.</note> on Original Sin, which Mr. Caroli indeed did not possess, but nevertheless believes to be not entirely incorrect because he finds similar <term>expressions</term> <note>original: "Expressiones."</note> elsewhere, which he himself cites on page 242 and further deduces from the testimonies of his friends: (whereby also what Mr. Caroli posits concerning <term>Sulcer</term> <note>Simon Sulcer (1508–1585), a Swiss theologian who attempted to mediate between Lutheran and Reformed views.</note> was found to be false above in No. 65.)

(2) He notes from <term>Hutter</term> <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a prominent defender of Lutheran orthodoxy.</note>, page 109 and following, that Dr. Andreae first composed such <term>Articles</term> in the hope of unification; these were also drawn into conflicting interpretations by "pure" <term>theologians</term> out of misunderstanding, but were used by enemies as the basis for this accusation. And these <term>Articles</term> are what <term>Flacius</term> (who was likely not otherwise convinced) rages against here, albeit with all-too-vehement <term>expressions</term>, which Mr. Arnold certainly did not approve of, but merely <term>recounted</term> <note>original: "recensiret."</note>.

(3) Mr. Caroli became so indignant about this that he begins to speak of Mr. Arnold’s religion, saying how evil it is, and thus judges blindly as his prejudices drive him. However, so much was laid out concerning this at the beginning of Part II that no further dispute is necessary. For the attached slanders are willingly excused as coming from such a <term>preoccupied</term> <note>original: "præoccupirten," meaning biased or prejudiced.</note> mind.

504 Answer to the so-called Wirtemberg Innocence Part IV. No. 79. 80.
Part IV. No. 80. 81. In Joh. Andr. David Caroli etc. 505

### The 79th Accusation:

He notes on page 217: Dr. Jacob Andreae <note>original: "D. A." refers to Jakob Andreae (1528–1590), a primary architect of Lutheran orthodoxy.</note> traveled around the Lutheran courts for over a year and a half for that purpose, and meanwhile suspended his ordinary and very important offices at Tübingen; at which many were not a little offended. p. 244.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Caroli does not deny this neglect of ordinary duties; he only opines that it does not follow that people were offended by it, because many were also offended by Christ. He claims it was primarily the enemies of Dr. Andreae. However, setting aside the fact that a great difference remains between Christ and His actions and such persons—because Christ forced no one into faith, or into signing or swearing to certain points—Mr. Caroli herewith tacitly <note>original: "tacite"</note> admits that even friends were offended by Dr. Andreae’s excesses.

(2) That he neglected his ordinary and important offices in the process is also certain. And although Mr. Caroli pretends that no one should have been concerned about it, one well knows what the received and common teaching regarding an "ordinary calling" <note>The concept of "ordentlicher Beruf" or "orderly calling" was central to Lutheran ethics, emphasizing that one must faithfully serve in the specific role and location where God placed them.</note> and its neglect entails, and how, conversely, extraordinary things are usually viewed.

(3) It is also notable that Mr. Caroli himself mocks <term>Ubiquity</term> <note>The doctrine of "Ubiquity" holds that Christ's human body is present everywhere. It was a major point of contention between Lutherans and Calvinists.</note> here, which he previously considered a great sin in number 44, section 4. For here he writes: Dr. Andreae was not able to act the part of the "Ubiquitist" who could be at Tübingen and other places at the same time.

### The 80th Accusation:

It is stated on page 223 as if Dr. Andreae had established only quarrels and confusion instead of peace, for which verses by Johann Major are cited. p. 246.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Caroli reminds us that Andreae would call the poet unchristian who, in a poem written about a fanatic, would come out with "Vulcan" <note>Vulcan, the Roman god of fire, is used here as a metaphor for stirring up the "fire" of strife and discord.</note>. To this it must be known: first, that the Impartial Historian <note>original: "H. U." stands for "Historicus Unpartheyischer," referring to the author, Gottfried Arnold.</note> showed there in the 18th chapter of the 6th book, section 30, from the own confessions and complaints of Lutheran theologians—especially Chytraeus—how even more strife arose following the <term>Formula of Concord</term> <note>The "Formula of Concord" (1577) was intended to unite Lutherans but was seen by some as causing further division.</note>.

(2) For this Chytraeus wrote expressly in the year 1577: *The Formula of Concord in the Torgau assembly was a seedbed of discord among us,* <note>original: "Formula Concordiæ in conventu Torgensi - - seminarium discordiæ apud nos fuit"</note>

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<column-break/>

which was established through the dismissal of several preachers (*recorded in Fecht’s Theological Epistles, Part IV, p. 547*). And in the year 1580, he wrote of his colleagues, whom they called the "Bergen Fathers" <note>The "Patres Bergenses" were the group of theologians who finalized the Formula of Concord at the monastery of Bergen near Magdeburg.</note>; they were *also poorly cohesive among themselves* <note>original: "inter se quoque male cohærentes"</note>; likewise: the *actions of recent years regarding peace* <note>original: "actiones proximorum annorum de pace"</note> had increased the *disturbances* <note>original: "turbas"</note>. Indeed, he complains there that such great disagreement was blamed on the authors of the Formula of Concord that not a single one finally remained in agreement with the others, and he wishes: *Would that we could heal these most sorrowful wounds by some means!* <note>original: "Utinam mederi his tristissimis vulneribus aliqua ratione possimus!"</note>

(3) To these obvious marks, as well as to Duke Julius of Brunswick's ungracious words about the quarreling of Dr. Andreae and Heshusius (noting that there was no end to the bickering, contention, reviling, and incessant ambition), the Impartial Historian now adds, in the place cited, the two verses by Major from Scultetus's *Life*. He does this not so much for condemnation as for *illustration*, solely because of the matter contained therein and previously proven; in doing so, he left the words about Vulcan to the author. Similarly, he *disapproved* <note>original: "improbiret"</note> of the other verses against the "Flacian Asses" <note>A derogatory term for followers of Matthias Flacius, a strict Lutheran who had intense doctrinal conflicts with other reformers.</note> on page 367 solely because of the factual realities.

(4) Mr. Caroli confesses on page 247 that Chytraeus's thoughts on the quarrel following the Book of Concord were not superfluous, but he opines they were mixed with too much fear. Yet the outcome already displayed the misery, and it was not a case where only fear of the future was present. He only insists that Dr. Andreae was not to blame; which would be quite valid and lawful to demonstrate, if it is not to be a wanton calumny.

(5) But how valid and lawful Chytraeus's above confession is, rests on an impartial judgment, as nothing can be more evident than that. Therefore, there is no calumny to be thought of here, unless someone wishes to let himself be overcome by anger and dragged into reviling.

(6) Regarding the attached boast of unity following the Formula of Concord, there would be all too much to remind one of than the narrow space and time would allow: thus it is passed over here, but not conceded.

## The 82. Accusation:

On page 166, this occurs: A preacher wrote at that time that one sets all his value <note>original: "Datum," here meaning aim or focus.</note> on great treasures and wealth; and deals with God's Word and the controversies, engaging in huckstering <note>original: "Krämerey," a derogatory term for making a business out of spiritual matters.</note>, etc. The like we shall hear of Dr. J. ## Answer:

(1) Here Mr. Caroli answers on p. 255: If his (Dr. Andreae’s) efforts against the Reformed and others brought something about for him, how does it follow that he set his value on great treasures? --- Where is that written? Or what kind of revelation does the Impartial Historian <note>original: "A." or "H. U." refers to Gottfried Arnold, the author of the *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics*.</note> have of this? However, the Impartial Historian refers to the documents following on p. 217 or Chapter 18, § 21, namely, how Dr. Andreae himself admitted that he was honorably <note>original: "honorifice"</note> gifted by the Elector, as stated in the *Fama Andreana* <note>A biographical work praising Jakob Andreae.</note> p. 214—namely, with 900 gold guilders and a golden cup.

(2) Accordingly, the Impartial Historian needed no "revelation" of this, a term with which Mr. Caroli so mocks; indeed, Mr. Caroli himself does not deny it on p. 256 and likewise needed none, for the clear testimonies convicted him. He merely opines that Dr. Andreae did not necessarily have to turn it down, and that it is merely an eyesore to the Impartial Historian; which is a strange conjecture that surely no one will believe: that a gift after 100 or more years should first become an eyesore or make someone else envious.

(3) The Impartial Historian sought or intended to represent nothing else here than the impurity of such actions; therefore, according to the Scripture, he first reminded:

<meta>catchword: minded;</meta>

<column-break/>

minded: Dr. Andreae also did not avoid the appearance of evil against apostolic teaching and practice, in that he not only took gifts but also boasted of them. Mr. Caroli opines that he had to boast of it against Peucer, otherwise Peucer would have said the Elector had dismissed him in disgrace. But true Christians see well that a theologian <note>original: "Theologus"</note> in such a case must rather let the latter be said of him than cause the appearance of evil and an offense to the weak: especially since Dr. Andreae had also constantly retained his respectable income <note>original: "Reditus"</note> at home, and thus suffered no loss.

(4) One does not blame Mr. Caroli for fighting so vehemently for the cause; his partiality allows for nothing else but to claim a thorough innocence. He opines that Dr. Andreae had not received his reward there; how gladly one wishes that for him, as for all people? But the words of Christ are clear. One does not take up the words of the others whom he seeks to refute. This one thing Mr. Caroli urges most: that Dr. Andreae did not set his value on great treasures and wealth and did not deal with God's Word and the controversies.

(5) The Impartial Historian also did not say all of this about Andreae, but indicated with the word "the like" (which indeed does not mean each and every thing) how something similar would be seen of Dr. Andreae, namely the wealth, and how he was outwardly gifted with money for his controversies. The like is indeed clear from the cited testimonies, and Mr. Caroli has once again indulged his passions all too much when he extends the words beyond what the sense by the force of the connection and the word itself <note>original: "Sensus vi connexionis und vocis ipsius"</note> dictates. And if he thus gives this out as unchristian and dishonorable, the judgment remains to an impartial person: for Mr. Caroli goes so far in his accusations that he thinks he has shamed the Impartial Historian: though the matter of taking gifts cannot be denied, however much one might wish to excuse it.

(6) Finally, since Mr. Caroli expostulates with the Impartial Historian: whether he does not know what is recounted in the *Fama Andreana*, and why he does not mention it? It has already been reminded above that the Impartial Historian did not write *Lives of the Theologians* <note>original: "Vitas Theologorum"</note> or praising speeches <note>original: "Encomia"</note> (which he should have taken from such panegyrics <note>original: "Panegyricis," formal speeches of high praise</note>); but general observations of the Church History <note>original: "K. 508 Response to the so-called Wittenberg Innocence Part IV. No. 83. 84.

### The 83. Accusation:

->He writes on p. 179 (in the 15th Chap. § 7) that **Dr. A.** [Jakob Andreae] intended to introduce at the Saxon universities the rule that a theologian should always be Chancellor: from which he concludes that the clergy were seeking the upper hand, etc.<-

### Answer:

**Mr. Caroli** <note>Andreas David Caroli (1646–1713), a critic of Arnold's work.</note> does not deny the fact that **A.** proposed it; rather, he indicates that it aimed to maintain pure doctrine, namely through such a Chancellorship. However, he considers it a reckless use of power that **A.** supposedly intended to give the theologians command through this. Anyone familiar with what can arise at many academies through the Chancellorship of such theologians who do not love the peace and humility of Christ—even under the name of pure doctrine itself—will surely recognize that **Mr. Arnold's** observation is not without merit.

### The 84. Accusation:

->He brings forward on p. 140 and elsewhere this complaint: that **Dr. A.** abolished church penance. p. 264.<-

### Answer:

(1) The words of **Dr. Timotheus Kirchner** <note>Kirchner (1533–1587) was a Lutheran theologian who initially supported Andreae but later became a critic.</note> are these in his letter in **Fecht** p. 638: <note>original: "Abolet D. Jacobus in illis terris (D. Julii) publicam disciplinam seu pœnitentiam, ut vocant, & propterea male audit. Saxon. quam conscripsit, & Elector nunc publicavit."</note> "Dr. Jakob [Andreae] is abolishing public discipline or penance, as they call it, in those lands (of Duke Julius), and for this reason, he is poorly spoken of. Nor can I approve of this abolition, which nonetheless occurs to the scandal of many and confirms the ungodly in their security in no small measure. He inserted this into the Saxon Church Reformation which he drafted, and which the Elector has now published."

(2) The first evasion that Mr. **Caroli** seeks here is taken from the words *male audit* <note>Latin: "is poorly spoken of" or "has a bad reputation."</note>, as if they were not well translated: that **Dr. A.** was ill-reputed among the people. However, these words clearly stand in the **Church History** in smaller type just like **Arnold’s** other words; they are thus not a literal or word-for-word translation, but an expression of the sense. And fundamentally, or in the matter itself, it is the same thing: for **Kirchner** does not specify among whom **Dr. A.** is notorious, but says it generally. And how could this abolition of a public matter not also have become known to the people? And so it is with the remaining doubts.

(3) But he finally leaves it at that, concerning what matters in the main point of this change: he can thus find nothing here, because **Mr. Arnold** only presents it relatively according to the sense, and indeed several times so. And

gradually, and now remains in Saxony only in a few places, is shown by experience; for even those preachers who attempted something of the kind have occasionally been punished.

How often has **Mr. Caroli** cited only a single witness against **Mr. Arnold**, and often from *panegyrics* <note>original: "panegyricos" - speeches of high praise</note> and other laudatory sayings? The matter is all too clear, and **Mr. Caroli** in vain considers it an unlearned accusation by **Kirchner**. This theologian was nonetheless expelled several times for the sake of Lutheran doctrine, zealously opposed the Reformed <note>Calvinists</note>, and finally died as the General Superintendent of the Principality of Weimar. Therefore, **Mr. Caroli** should have, according to his own *principles* <note>original: "Principiis"</note>, judged him differently. Indeed, the Württemberg **Dr. Thummius** himself praises **Kirchner's** book against those from Anhalt, noting it was recommended by three universities in his *Examination of Menzer’s Defense* <note>original: "Examine Defens. Menzeri"</note> page 58; and yet **Mr. Caroli** rejects him here.

(10) He wishes to prove the *opposite* <note>original: "Contrarium"</note>—namely, that church penance was not abolished everywhere in Saxony—through examples from **Carpzov** and **Spener**. But this only proves that it was reintroduced in a few

<meta>catchword: places</meta>

<column-break/>

places, either during the times of **Crypto-Calvinism** <note>A movement where Calvinist ideas were secretly held within Lutheran territories.</note> or during the German Thirty Years' War. The discrepancy in such church customs is especially great in Saxony, as is well enough known, and thus also in this matter. Therefore, all these conclusions are in vain, and **Mr. Caroli** can report nothing certain about the churches in Brunswick (p. 268) without later citing the ordinance on page 269. And what should one say about the general complaint found in the preface to the Epistle to the Corinthians (No. 3 B) in the new Stuttgart Bible? There it says of the Württemberg and other Lutheran churches: "That nothing more of the earnestness and the form of **church excommunication** <note>term: "Kirchen-Bannes" - the practice of excluding unrepentant sinners from the community</note> is to be found among us Protestants." Is it not clear enough from this that **church discipline** <note>term: "Kirchen-Zucht"</note> is absent? If someone says, "Yes, but the harlots must still do church penance," then I answer with **Dr. J. Ad. Osiander** in his *Theological Cases* <note>original: "Theol. Cas. P. Adulterio, scandalizatur Ecclesia, sed aliis etiam extantioribus, nec æqvum videtur, ut in unum animadvertat Ecclesia, &c."</note>: "The Church is scandalized not only by one type of sin, for example adultery, but also by other even more prominent ones; nor does it seem fair that the Church should punish only one, etc." It is another matter entirely that in some places a better arrangement is now being made: here we are speaking only of past times, as times of ignorance.

(11) For the rest, one gladly accepts the distinction added there between church discipline itself and its *method* <note>original: "Modo"</note>. It may also be that **Dr. A.** <note>Jakob Andreae</note> in his first years as a preacher elsewhere approved of a Christian church discipline, as his *Centenary Reflection* suggests, along with the *Noah's Ark* <note>original: "Arca Noæ"</note> edited by **J. V. Andreae** <note>Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), grandson of Jakob Andreae and a famous theologian and social reformer.</note>. Concord." - the 1577 authoritative statement of Lutheran faith</note>, speaking as a Lutheran theologian, for which no man can blame him.

In doing so, he has not placed anyone on the **stool of shame** <note>term: "Schanden-Stuhl" - a reference to the pillory or public humiliation</note>, as **Mr. Caroli** thinks, but is ready to yield willingly if the *opposite* <note>original: "Contrarium"</note> could be rightly verified by **Dr. A.** In every way, he is concerned with the truth alone, as God knows him.

(13) In conclusion, one should remember here what such reformations must have been like: they insisted only on the outward form, while the righteous essence in Christ was either observed lukewarmly or not at all—indeed, what little discipline remained in the church was even done away with. ## The 85th Accusation:

It cannot be right / p. 209. what **Dr. A.** <note>Dr. Jakob Andreae (1528–1590), a primary author of the Formula of Concord.</note> did at Tübingen by virtue of his office regarding the Religious Oath. p. 275.

## Response:

(1) Regarding the Religious Oath, a reminder was already given above under the 70th accusation / whether the same is Christian and justifiable / when consciences are pressured and strained toward it. Regarding this specific one / which **Dr. A.** changed; before that time it was arranged, among other points, with these formal words: <term>That he wishes to cultivate religion piously and purely.</term> <note>original Latin: "Quod religionem piè & castè colere velit."</note> Afterward, even this was changed and more strictly limited.

(2) Concerning this, **Mr. A.** <note>Gottfried Arnold, the author of the "Church and Heretic History."</note> writes very modestly in the 18th Chapter of the 16th Book, § 8: That such an old oath might have been arranged that way out of good intentions: and he does not reject religious oaths entirely without any distinction. (3) He <note>Caroli</note> further desires to know / why it is said so simply that **Dr. A.** made a different oath / since it was done with the consent of the Academic Senate / and ratified by the Duke? However, **Dr. A.** was indeed 1) <note>original: "α)"</note> Chancellor at the University, 2) <note>original: "β)"</note> held in the highest esteem by everyone, and 3) <note>original: "γ)"</note> especially in religious matters: Therefore, in his undertaking, he could easily obtain the consent of the College and the Princely ratification. Thus, the cited manuscript regarding the actions of Siderocrates <note>original: "MSptum de Siderocratis actionibus"</note> also speaks of this. Therefore, no injustice has been done to him in this matter either.

### The 87th Accusation:

He recalls on p. 324 a dispute that J. A. <note>Jakob Andreae (1528–1590), the influential Lutheran theologian and Chancellor of the University of Tübingen.</note> is said to have had with Pietro Paolo Vergerio. <note>Pietro Paolo Vergerio (1498–1565) was a former Catholic bishop and papal legate who converted to Protestantism and served the Duke of Württemberg.</note> p. 279.

### Response:

(1) Most of the circumstances reported here from Book XVI, Chapter 22, § 26, are admitted by Mr. Caroli, except for the following: he claims the account regarding Vergerio’s accusation concerning the **Religious Union** is not sincere. For Mr. Seckendorff <note>Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff (1626–1692), a famous Lutheran historian whose "Commentarius Historicus de Lutheranismo" is a primary source here.</note> reports only: "he was not without suspicion" <note>original Latin: "non suspicione caruisse"</note> (which is nevertheless false, as shall be shown in § 4), and Pallavicini <note>Pietro Sforza Pallavicino (1607–1667), a Jesuit historian who wrote a history of the Council of Trent.</note> relates one thing and another that seems to be able to confirm such suspicion, namely his conversation with the Papal Nuncio in the year 1561 and his letter to Cardinal Gonzaga (*Commentary on Lutheranism, Book III, p. 601*). Therefore, he was not accused of this in Tübingen, but only held in suspicion.

(2.) At the same time, however, he is also held as suspicious in the cited authors, and Mr. Caroli himself admits from Vergerio's own writings on page 283: **that he was of the opinion that the Zwinglians could well join the Lutherans through the path of the Waldensian Confession.** Thus, he indeed wanted to unite the religions, or at least desired such a union.

(3) Indeed, what need is there for long accusations, as if Mr. Arnold had not reported sincerely here as well? Since the very Mr. von Seckendorff cited by Mr. Caroli says all of this expressly in the *Gotha Church History, Book II, Chapter 5, Section I, p. 165*, just as Mr. Arnold set it down, namely that Vergerio: "committed himself to no confession, although he usefully sharpened his pen against Papal errors and the Pope's rule." <note>original Latin: "nulli se confessioni addixit, quamvis adversus Pontificios errores atque dominatam Papæ stylum utiliter acueret."</note> Mr. Caroli undoubtedly looked this up as well as the other passages, but silently passed over it, only so it would seem that Arnold had not reported sincerely. Who here can speak of very wicked malice and deceit, that is for everyone to judge. Mr. Caroli says it of Mr. Arnold, but the contrary is clear and shall become even clearer.

<column-break/>

(4) Moreover, it is also false when Mr. Caroli says Seckendorff reports only this much: "nor was he without suspicion." <note>original Latin: "nec suspicione caruit"</note> For he passes over and keeps silent about the words immediately preceding and following, where Seckendorff says: "A versatile [or fickle] character is attributed to Vergerio." <note>original Latin: "Versatile ingenium Vergerio tribuitur"</note> After that it says: "nor was he without suspicion that he was attempting a religious conciliation by any means" <note>original Latin: "nec suspicione caruit, quod conciliationem religionis quovis modo moliretur"</note> (this is exactly what Mr. Arnold says: that he wanted to unite the religion, and this is set down as something certain, namely the *attempting of conciliation*, from which the suspicion arose, namely inconstancy) "and finally was thinking of returning to the old rites," <note>original Latin: "tandem ad vetera sacra redire cogitaret"</note> which Mr. Arnold renders as: "and even wanted to go over to the Papists again." If Mr. Caroli had added all of this without mutilating it, he could not have said that Seckendorff reports only "this much" and consequently that Mr. Arnold does not report sincerely. But it was decided to bring guilt upon Mr. Arnold and to maintain an "innocence" for oneself; therefore, these two passages from Seckendorff had to be treated in this way.

(5) Furthermore, Mr. Arnold's following account is no less entirely sincere and Christian, where he says in the cited place § 26: **God granted that Vergerio was moved by the reading of Lutheran books and taught the Gospel.** --- Afterward, he was moved even more by the terrible example of Spira. <note>Francesco Spiera (died 1548) was an Italian lawyer who recanted his Protestant faith to avoid the Inquisition and subsequently died in a state of profound spiritual despair. Concerning this, Dr. Andreae (D. A.) spoke to him upon his return, but was not angry with him, etc.

Therefore, much remains in doubt, especially since each party sought to maintain its own position, as one also sees from the letter by Dr. Andreae cited by Mr. Caroli (from Fecht, p. 415, *Epistles of the Theologians*). <note>original: "e Fechtio p. 415. Epist. Thol."; likely referring to a collection edited by Joannes Fecht.</note> For there, Dr. Andreae boasts of his letter as being **most friendly and brotherly**, <note>original: "amicissimam und fraternam"</note> while Flacius, in contrast, reproached him for his **heat**. <note>original: "fervorem"</note>

### The 90th Accusation.

->Answer:<-

Among theologians, Quenstedt explicitly states that one should withdraw from banquets where no spiritual fruit can be hoped for; he cites the words of Jerome, who says in the cited place: "You must avoid the banquets of worldly people" <note>original Latin: "Convivia tibi vitanda sunt secularium"</note>, etc. See *Pastoral Ethics* [Ethic. Pastor.] page 295.

(5) The reasons why Mr. Arnold [H. A.] considered this <term>supper</term> <note>original: "Cœnam," referring here to a formal evening meal</note> to be an academic feast [Schmauß] were recounted above. And anyone who knows those <term>suppers</term> <note>original: "Cœnas"</note> that are held at most Lutheran universities during <term>graduations</term> <note>original: "Promotionibus"</note> and other occasions will have even less doubt as to whether Mr. Arnold correctly rendered this word as "feast" [Schmauß]. Likewise, one might doubt whether Mr. Caroli’s argument is sufficient when he opines that there were nevertheless so many respected, famous public teachers present, and no dissolute students.

(6) For it is enough that this is the usual academic term [Terminus], which does not always bring with it dissolute boozing and similar excesses, but at the very least an abundance and misuse of God’s gifts. Now, this occurred at a university; therefore, Mr. Arnold described it with the most common expression. Thus, the absurd objection does not apply at all when it says: one would then also have to translate the biblical words into German as "There was a man who prepared a great feast [Schmauß]"; likewise: John 12, "they prepared a great feast [Schmauß] for Jesus." Who would speak of the most gracious Savior in such a way? But was that at a university? And must Mr. Caroli himself not recognize this as <term>blasphemous</term>?

(7) From where does one wish to prove that a "feast" [Schmauß] means only a <term>disorderly drinking session</term> <note>original Latin: "Compotatio inordinata"</note>? Are not all "Doctor-feasts"—even when theologians graduate—likewise called "Rectorate-feasts"? And yet one will not admit that these are merely <term>drinking sessions</term> <note>original Latin: "Compotationes"</note>, and <term>disorderly</term> <note>original Latin: "inordinatæ"</note> ones at that. Thus, one sees that Mr. Arnold has no more insulted the Academic Senate or committed a great, wicked injustice than such a word is currently considered insulting or wicked at universities. For Mr. Caroli has merely chosen to exaggerate these words so that he might produce a claim of innocence.

(8) But so that even less doubt remains as to how such banquets or <term>suppers</term> <note>original Latin: "Cœnis"</note> did not always proceed quite moderately and orderly, but rather that corrupt flesh sought its heaven therein, one should look below at Number 124 at what the very same Professor Crusius writes in the same book of *Annals* for the year 1562, page 713—not far from the above passage—concerning a certain banquet.

->The 98th Accusation:<-

He brings forward on page 218 that Doctor Andreae [D. A.] fell into the disfavor of Elector August. p. 302.

->Answer:<-

(1) Mr. Caroli says to this: alpha) it would be no wonder if it had happened. That Mr. Arnold is not the least bit hostile—let alone hostile to everything that is truly Lutheran—we have proven above in Numbers 3 and 6.

(2) Mr. Caroli denies all the cited <term>passages from authors</term> <note>original Latin: "loca autorum"</note> and says they were already refuted by Hutter. A.] unexpectedly received his dismissal from the Lords of the Chamber Council on December 26, 1580, as more specific details are provided there one after another in the 22nd paragraph of the 18th chapter. Thus, this account remains unshaken.

(3) Mr. Caroli cannot possibly reject or cast doubt on this account from Schneider’s *Leipzig Chronicle*; this chronicle is also popular and well-known enough in Saxony. From this, Mr. Caroli concludes: perhaps this is also a fable; yet while that was obviously cited as a fable, this account of the Elector's disfavor is cited as a true history. With such false conclusions, one could destroy entire chronicles if the rule were: "This or that author refutes a fable, therefore his whole book is a fable or full of fables," or "Therefore this or that true history is also a fable."

(5) Against this, Mr. Caroli objects on page 305: a) that Doctor Andreae [D. A.] himself boasted of the opposite in a speech. He might well have done so to maintain his **reputation**; he could hardly do otherwise. Yet even there, he could not deny the truth, but lamented in the speech (page 212 of *The Fame of Andreae* <note>original title: "Famæ Andreanæ"</note>) that *the efforts of his enemies shortly before his departure from Meissen had been most violent.* <note>original Latin: "hostium suorum conatum paulo ante suum è Misnia discessum fuisse vehementissimum."</note> Indeed, earlier on page 211, he complained that those who stood in authority had conspired unanimously against him, etc. Especially, however, he complained that rumors were spread that he would yet be dismissed with the greatest shame. Against such rumors, Doctor Andreae should rightly have taken a <term>contrary testimony<note>original Latin: "testimonium contrarium"; a formal document or letter of recommendation to refute the rumors of disgrace.</note></term> from the Elector (especially since it also concerned the matter of the <term>Formula of Concord<note>The Formula of Concord (1577) was a major Lutheran doctrinal document which Andreae helped author; his reputation was tied to its success.</note></term>), if he had truly left in favor. That this did not happen, and that no such documents are to be found, is very suspicious.

(6) Mr. Caroli says β) that Melchior Adam also reports—specifically—that Doctor Andreae was dismissed in favor on December 21st; therefore, it could not have happened on the 26th and in disgrace. However, the people of Leipzig could report the timing better than Adam, who was a stranger; and it is certain that the latter was more likely to be mistaken about the circumstances than the former. γ) It is said to be "unbelievable" that Doctor Andreae received his dismissal on the day after Christmas. But it is actually quite believable for that very reason: they simply told him beforehand and spared him on the first day of the feast, so that he could travel away immediately after the holiday. It might seem even more unbelievable to many that he should have had to begin such a long journey just 3 or 4 days before the feast if he had departed in favor.

(7) Mr. Caroli himself does not speak with much certainty on the matter: "Even if such a thing had happened to Doctor Jacob," etc. Yet he would rather hold it, with Dannhauer, to be a "fat lie," and considers it a fabricated fable. Nevertheless, Mr. Thomasius vindicated the account immediately thereafter, and the elder Jacob Thomasius acknowledged it even more. It is as if it were enough simply to cry "fable" at the accounts of public chronicles if they do not please someone. Furthermore, Mr. Arnold draws nothing more from it than what he found there: namely, that Doctor Andreae came to a disagreement with the Elector, which Hutter does not deny.

(8) Regarding these last words of Mr. Arnold, Mr. Caroli now judges very harshly, claiming he did not observe his conscience, despite the fact that Mr. Arnold did not add a single word or change anything from what is written in the cited author. A conscience is demanded of Mr. Arnold here, yet they do not heed it themselves. Jacobo nonnihil infensiorem redditum"</note> which he calls a "supposition" (*Formula of Concord*, Chapter 48, page 1231, 2nd Edition). The subsequent alleged reconciliation, however, is made uncertain by the reasons mentioned above; therefore, it was impossible to cite it as unproven, no matter how indignant someone else might be about it.

(10) Thus, Mr. Caroli’s partisan judgment again makes a "conscienceless" matter out of this, even though Mr. Arnold was sufficiently assured of the truth in his conscience from the aforementioned <term>historical records<note>original Latin: "monumentis"</note></term>. The account, however, was so unpleasant to Mr. Caroli that he resorted to such accusations against Mr. Arnold; for nature gladly falls upon personal attacks when <term>factual matters<note>original Latin: "realibus"</note></term> are lacking. (15) That he [Arnold] intended to make the reader believe it is a suspicion Mr. Caroli holds without ground or proof. For one can report much *from the mouths of others* <note>original Latin: "ex ore aliorum"</note> and yet not seek to make it specifically believable, but rather leave it for illustration or further investigation. Since Mr. Arnold was assured in his conscience by the history that Doctor Andreae had departed in disgrace, he could well append this passage for the sake of illustration, and thus did not act against his conscience. Mr. Arnold also reported nothing further on the matter. Therefore, it is not necessary to deal with it at greater length here, as Mr. Caroli himself is of the same opinion.

# The 100th Accusation:
He says on page 216 that the Duke of Würtemberg was himself not satisfied with Doctor Andreae’s <note>Jacob Andreae (1528–1590), a prominent Lutheran theologian and primary author of the Formula of Concord.</note> constant traveling and had often called him home with the sharpest commands.

## Answer:
(1) Mr. Caroli does not deny this account either, but rather excuses it as best he can. Johann Pappus <note>A Lutheran theologian (1549–1610) who was a contemporary of Andreae.</note> also calls such mandates "sharpest" <note>original Latin: *acerrima*</note> in Fecht, page 32 f. Mr. Caroli’s only objection here is why Arnold stated that Doctor Andreae was "often" called home, given that Pappus mentions only two instances.

(2) Here again, Mr. Caroli has focused on the bare words but failed to attend to the circumstances of the history, which Mr. Arnold was obliged to do. Had the Duke demanded Doctor Andreae back for the second time around the year 1579 or 1580, one could say with Mr. Caroli that Arnold had not acted uprightly. However, Pappus wrote this as early as the year 1570, and Doctor Andreae continued to travel for another nine years after that, hardly ever coming home during that time; indeed, in 1575, he even brought his wife and child with him into Saxony. He himself mentions in his oration (see *Fame of Andreae*, <note>original Latin: *vid. Fama Andreana*</note> p. 212) that later, in the year 1580, Duke Ludwig wrote twice more to the Elector on his behalf to call him back. How often might the Duke have demanded him home within so many years? How then can one deny that it happened "often"? And how can Mr. Caroli accuse Mr. Arnold of a breach of trust when he himself denies what the course of history over more than nine years clearly implies?

(3) Whether Doctor Andreae was permitted to leave and neglect his regular calling for the sake of foreign affairs was touched upon earlier in Number 79. Therefore, Mr. Caroli’s remaining reproaches on that point fall away, as he presupposes that all such actions were right and well done.

# The 101st Accusation:
It is stated on page 219 that Doctor Andreae wrote as late as the year 1578 that he faced great enmity in Leipzig and was in great danger. p. 317.

## Answer.
Mr. Caroli also agrees with this and proves it further from Doctor Andreae’s report to the Elector in Hutter’s *Harmony of the Concord*, <note>original Latin: *apud Hutterum Concord. Conc.* referring to Leonhard Hutter's work on the Formula of Concord.</note> p. 994.

# The 102nd Accusation.
He says in the same place that Doctor Andreae’s enemies had to sign everything (namely the *Formula of Concord*). <note>The 1577 Lutheran confession intended to settle doctrinal disputes.</note> p. 318.

## Answer:
(1) One can clearly see, Mr. Caroli adds, upon whom he wishes to place the blame—namely, on Doctor Andreae. In the cited passage (in the 18th Chapter of the 16th Book, § 23 and following), it was deduced in detail how consciences were forced into this subscription <note>term: subscription <gloss>the formal act of signing a document to indicate religious agreement</gloss></note>. Even Mr. Caroli cannot entirely deny it; he only says the guilt remains with those who signed with a bad conscience, because they had enough instruction and time for reflection, etc.

(2) It is not necessary to investigate this extensively here. The coercion of conscience is evident in the manner mentioned, as even political figures were removed from their governing bodies <note>original: *Collegiis*</note> and all officials had to sign the *Formula of Concord*. As Mr. Caroli himself confesses on page 318, those who admitted that their conscience did not allow them to sign could not remain in their positions. Now, we have seen above in Number 76 how Doctor Andreae was the principal author <note>original Latin: *Auctor*</note> of this book, and was also praised as a restorer <note>original Latin: *Instaurator*</note> of heavenly doctrine; therefore, it cannot be denied that this coercion originated, in part, from him.

(3) Whether such coercion of conscience is consistent with Protestant and Evangelical doctrine and the confession against the Papacy has been settled long ago. The question here is not whether those who signed against their conscience did right, but rather whether he did right who advised that such a signature be demanded from them, especially when he held them in suspicion and thus had to fear perjury <note>term: perjury <gloss>the act of lying under a religious oath, in this case by signing a confession one does not believe</gloss></note> from them? One should see, among others, the most recent reminders of Mr. Counselor Brenneysen on this matter in his *Vindication* <note>original: *Ehren-Rettung*</note>, page 30 and following.

(4) Finally, that Doctor Andreae regarded the hatred of these people who were forced to sign as unjust is not to be doubted and requires no proof, for he considered them his enemies. Mr. Arnold, however, reported Doctor Andreae's complaint only indirectly and not word-for-word <note>original Latin: *verbotenus*</note>, otherwise he would have had to provide it as follows:
> I suffer here the most unjust enmities and hover in the greatest dangers.

It is enough that the matter itself is uprightly expressed, as was appropriate here. A sincere Christian judges instead how uprightly such coercion of conscience is still defended!

### The 103rd Accusation:

He wrote on page 216: Even the most orthodox theologians could not get along with Doctor Andreae, nor be satisfied with him, and so on, page 319.

#### Answer:

(1) Mr. Arnold took this from Lucas Osiander’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, page 863, where it says regarding the <term>Articles</term> <note>Referring to the theological points being debated for the Formula of Concord.</note> of Doctor Andreae: "This endeavor of Dr. Jacob was not approved by all, even the most sincere theologians" <note>original Latin: *Is conatus D. Jacobi non omnibus, etiam maxime sinceris Theologis probabatur*</note>, and so on. Mr. Caroli even admits that among some legal scholars it did not pass without suspicion and misinterpretation, though this gradually faded away.

(2) At the same time, he says that Arnold acted against his conscience by simply alleging this, as if there were nothing but confusion and disunity between Doctor Andreae and others. However, it will immediately become clear who has acted against their conscience. Mr. Arnold's words appear in their proper <term>Connection</term> <note>The surrounding context of the argument.</note> in the 20th paragraph of the 18th chapter. "Because of these and other circumstances, even the most orthodox theologians could not get along with him." Had Mr. Arnold’s words been repeated by Mr. Caroli without change—namely, how they <term>connect</term> with the entire preceding history—then the reader would have seen Mr. Arnold’s upright report. But because Arnold was meant to be accused, Mr. Caroli had to change his words and place them *outside of their connection* <note>original Latin: *extra connexionem*</note> so that the accusation might have an appearance of truth.

(3) But what were those circumstances? These are listed one after another in the preceding paragraph: what Doctor Kirchner <term>found lacking</term> <note>original Latin: *desideriret*</note> in him, what Sulcer wished from him, and what his own words themselves indicate there. These were the circumstances, along with others, why many were not satisfied with him. How does Mr. Caroli now <term>report</term> Arnold's words? He sets them down *absolutely*: "because of many circumstances," without <term>Restriction</term> to those previously mentioned. Thus, he turns a *restrictive proposition* into an *absolute one*, and alleges that Mr. Arnold had simply made a general claim, even though Mr. Arnold binds and limits his presentation to the circumstances previously recounted. From this, anyone may judge who is acting uprightly.

(4) From this distortion, Mr. Caroli further falsely concludes that Mr. Arnold had written of nothing but confusion and disunity between Doctor Andreae and other theologians; yet Arnold speaks openly only of the <term>differences</term> which he had <term>specified</term>, and in no way deceives the reader with a cunning extraction of Osiander’s words. For one should see from the cited words of Osiander whether that which Mr. Arnold repeats from them is not clearly stated there: namely, that even the very purest
<meta>catchword: Theolo-</meta>

### The 104th Accusation:

(2) Mr. Caroli seeks here to <term>excuse</term> Doctor Andreae at great length, which shall be left in its place. That Doctor Andreae acted incautiously in this matter are not Mr. Arnold's words, but those of the zealous theologians who at that time <term>disapproved</term> <note>original Latin: *improbirten*</note> of this in him, as Mr. Caroli himself mentions on page 324. That they were angry with him, Mr. Caroli must also admit from Osiander's words; but he wants to shift the blame onto those of Jena. As he often prefers to despise other Lutheran theologians just to <term>save</term> <note>Preserve the reputation of.</note> Doctor Andreae, as has already been <term>observed</term> above and will occur again immediately.

### The 105th Accusation:

He recounts on page 216 what Dr. Bidenbach wrote of Dr. Andreae in the year 1570: how strangely and unsuccessfully he had dealt with the *Work of Concord* <note>The collaborative effort to resolve Lutheran theological disputes, resulting in the Formula of Concord (1577).</note> up to that point, and so on.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Caroli indicates the causes and then says: Dr. Bidenbach believed those "old wives' tales" <note>original: *Sag-Mähren*</note>, but the outcome showed otherwise. He claims they judged before the time; that Arnold brings forth what belongs to the "mist" which the sun had long since driven away. To this latter point, it serves to note that Mr. Arnold only wanted to show from Bidenbach's words how many theologians were not satisfied with him in all things, for which he also sets the year for better understanding, and thus intended to throw no "mist" or "blue haze" <note>A German idiom for a deception or distraction.</note> before anyone's eyes.

(2) Meanwhile, the words of Bidenbach, a Würtemberg theologian, sound quite thoughtful and <term>general</term>, concerning not only the *Work of Concord* but Dr. Andreae's <term>conduct</term> <note>original: *Conduite*</note> and mind in general: "He follows only himself, he listens to no one else—If only, if he ever returns to us,"

"he will cause no troubles even among us. For there will be those who will not approve of all his counsels, sayings, writings, deeds, commissions, and omissions, etc." <note>original Latin: *bit, nullas etiam apud nos (turbas) det. ### The 106th Accusation:

It is stated in the same place: The same circumstances had caused Dr. Andreae to fall out with Chemnitz <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a leading Lutheran theologian known as the "Second Martin."</note>. Page 330.

### Answer:

(1) First, Mr. Caroli says these two theologians were always at one in doctrine; however, he also admits on page 331 that it did not pass without disagreement at one time. Regarding the letter, the matter is uncertain; yet Chytræus wrote <term>expressly</term> about it in the year 1580: (in Fecht, page 628) "The letter of Chemnitz to Dr. Jacob, dated April 8th, flies through all the courts and cities in these regions, providing wonderful amusement everywhere." <note>original Latin: *Pervolat omnes aulas & urbes in his regionibus epistola Chemnitii ad D. Jacobum VIII. Aprilis data, quæ mirificos lusus passim præbet.*</note> And before this, he mentions the "miserable colleagues who also do not hold well together," <note>original Latin: *miserorum ac inter se quoque male cohærentium collegarum*</note> whom they called the *Bergen Fathers* <note>The group of theologians who met at the Bergen Abbey to finalize the Formula of Concord.</note>.

(2) It is certain, however, Mr. Caroli continues, that these theologians fell out after the *Work of Concord*, yet not over any point of doctrine, but over other things, and they were reconciled again: and this is excused with the example of Paul and Barnabas <note>A biblical reference to the sharp disagreement and eventual reconciliation between the two apostles in Acts 15.</note>. But because the matter itself over which they fell out is not <term>specified</term>, one cannot immediately assume that it did not happen over doctrine, or even during and not only after the *Work of Concord*: especially since Chytræus still calls them colleagues or co-workers, namely on the said work. Dr. Kirchner indeed mentions their reconciliation in the same place, page 637, but very <term>doubtingly</term> as to whether it would be lasting on Andreae's side, as shown above in number 75. Hutter, however, admits in general in the *Introduction to the Explanation of the Formula of Concord*, page 19: "that some in the course of time defected from the Formula of Concord." <note>original Latin: *nonnullos progressu temporis à Form. Conc. defecisse.*</note>
