### Response:

(1) This was already mentioned above in No. 104. Regarding **Chytræus** <note>David Chytræus (1530–1600), a prominent Lutheran theologian and co-author of the Formula of Concord.</note>, Mr. Caroli admits on page 333 that he did not always get along well with **Dr. Jacob Andreae**; however, he claims one cannot say exactly why. He suggests considering whether Chytræus perhaps disliked that Dr. Andreae discovered how **Philipp Melanchthon** <note>Luthers's successor, often accused by stricter Lutherans of compromising on doctrine.</note> had departed from Luther in important articles, or whether Chytræus was hindered by certain prejudices from a proper understanding of the declaration entered into the **Formula of Concord** <note>The authoritative Lutheran statement of faith completed in 1577.</note>. He suggests that Chytræus therefore occasionally formed unfavorable thoughts about Dr. Andreae and found his actions suspicious for a time, etc. With such suspicion, they would rather burden other Lutheran theologians before they would concede the slightest thing regarding Dr. Andreae that others might have found lacking in him.

(2) What is written on page 334 regarding **Huberus’s** <note>Samuel Huber, a controversial theologian who argued for universal election.</note> claims was also answered above in No. 31 and 33.

### The 108th Accusation:

It stands on page 215 regarding the Work of Concord that Dr. Andreae is called by his admirers a "highly enlightened, spiritual, and gifted theologian, an **Elijah**," etc., to which Arnold adds: "excessive praise," page 336.

### Response:

(1) Nothing is such a "thorn in the eye" to Arnold as the Work of Concord, says Mr. Caroli in response. But how can he conclude this from the quoted words? Mr. Arnold has, with the foundation of truth and according to God's Word, called these speeches of praise—that Dr. Andreae was an "Elijah" or a "divine man"—excessive; especially since they were linked with the reviling of others. What impartial person could think otherwise? Does it then follow that this Work itself is a thorn in the eye to an impartial person?

(2) It has also been mentioned several times how primarily the **coercion of conscience** <term>Gewissens-Zwang</term> <note>The practice of forcing individuals to subscribe to specific religious creeds under threat of legal or social penalty.</note> that occurred during such work is concerning to impartial Christians according to the Gospel. There is also no need to wish that Arnold would stop writing about it. Indeed, he would never have engaged in such controversial questions, and perhaps not another word would have been mentioned about the matter, if Mr. Caroli’s contradiction had not forced it.

(3) Here, Mr. Caroli claims Mr. Arnold has shown himself biased by recounting the praise of **Jacob Böhme** <note>A famous German Christian mystic (1575–1624) whose works were controversial among the orthodox.</note> and other such people from various authors, but

<column-break/>

IV. Part 108. 109. N. Mr. Andr. David Caroli &c. 539
539

cannot tolerate the praise of Dr. Andreae. However, who does not see how unequal these things are? In the history of Dr. Andreae, Mr. Arnold is not speaking of moderate praise, but of an **excessive** one that was coupled with the reviling of others, where they called him an "Elijah against the **Calvinist priests of Baal**" <note>A biblical reference used here as a harsh insult against Reformed/Calvinist theologians.</note> and the like. But the accolades from various authors concerning Jacob Böhme and others, repeated by Mr. Caroli from the *Church History*, are clearly not excessive, even if they may not please some.

(4) For example, if someone is noted for "uncommon gifts of grace, knowledge," or called "a raised light" and the like; or when **Paracelsus** <note>A famous physician and occultist.</note> is called by Morhof (a Lutheran professor) "a man of the highest genius and greatest merits" <note>original Latin: *vir summi ingenii & maximorum meritorum*</note> in Book 1 of his *Polyhistor*, chapter 10; or when Crollius says of **Weigel** <note>Valentin Weigel, another mystical writer often criticized by the orthodox.</note> that he was "enlightened in the school of Pentecost," etc.—these accolades from other writers are not at all the same as those written about Dr. Andreae. For there, no "Elijah" is imagined who drove out the "priests of Baal," no "divine head" <note>original Latin: *divinum caput*</note>, etc.; rather, only the matter itself is expressed as it was recognized by such authors.

(5) When Mr. Caroli calls Mr. Arnold a "closet admirer" or an **Anabaptist** <note>Used here as a derogatory term for anyone dissenting from the state church.</note> in this context, such mockery has already been answered above in Part I, No. 24, 50, 99, and 101, and in Part II, No. 60, as well as in this Part IV, No. 18. And if he further calls it a "reputation-robbing undertaking" that one cannot approve of such enormous accolades, then nothing is achieved by scolding. For this indicates a passionate foundation that is not capable of truth. Whether and to what extent Dr. Andreae had the Holy Spirit dwelling and ruling within him may be weighed by one who truly knows his characteristics from the investigations thus far, and especially from the judgment over the deceased **Flacius** <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus, a strict Lutheran who fell into controversy over his views on original sin.</note> above.

(1) Mr. Caroli makes a distinction between "theological" and "political" sharpness. He claims the theologians could not have abandoned the former, for Schwenkfeld had been a deceiver, and Dr. Andreae had especially—

### The 110th Accusation:

He writes on page 394, from **Peucer’s** <note>Caspar Peucer (1525–1602), a scholar and physician who was imprisoned for ten years for his "Philippist" or "Crypto-Calvinist" leanings.</note> *History*, that after the theologians Dr. Andreae and Selneccer had disputed in vain with Peucer, he was kept in even harsher imprisonment. Page 347.

### Response:

(1) Mr. Caroli says this was set down to persuade the reader that the theologians had argued themselves weary with Peucer but could gain no advantage over him, and therefore they became angry with him, making him pay for it with increasingly harsh treatment. But where is there a single word of all these consequences that one draws from Mr. Arnold’s words? And how would one think of such things if he drew similar conclusions from others? He merely reports, plainly, what is in the book; and Mr. Caroli also does not deny that the theologians disputed in vain.

<meta>catchword: (2) That</meta>

(2) However, that Peucer was thereafter kept more harshly was not the fault of the theologians, and Mr. Arnold did not say so either, but spoke only simply of the harsh treatment. Mr. Caroli refers to **Freherus** <note>Paul Freher (1611–1682), author of a famous biographical dictionary.</note>, who supposedly says: that Peucer came out of custody healthier than he went in. But the question is whether this is exactly what is in Freherus? This indeed stands there on page 1312 of the *Theater of Illustrious Men*: "From then on at Zerbst with the Princes of Anhalt, he lived for sixteen years with much firmer health than before." <note>original: "Abinde Servesta apud Principes Anhaltinor. XVI. Annos valetudine multò quam antea firmiore vixit."</note> But there is not a word there saying that he came out of prison with such "firmer health," only that he lived more healthily afterward. Thus Mr. Caroli himself does not report honestly, the very thing he so often seeks to accuse Mr. Arnold of doing.

(3) Conversely, this also stands in Freherus, which Mr. Caroli nevertheless denies: namely, that Peucer's illness could not be attributed—either not at all, or at least not solely—to the harsh treatment and poor food. For it says there: "condemned to prison, he led a life in squalor and sorrow." <note>original: "ad carcerem damnatum in squalore & mœrore vitam duxiffe."</note> and anyone who were to experience such treatment would likely no longer doubt with Mr. Caroli whether illness and consumption resulted from it.

(4) Mr. Caroli thinks it has not yet been proven that Dr. Andreae was the cause of Dr. Peucer's harsh treatment. Now, one does not enter further into this dispute: But **Hutten’s** <note>Referring to Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a staunch Lutheran defender of the Formula of Concord.</note> words could give one quite different thoughts when he writes in the margin on page 244: "Peucer deserved much more atrocious punishments" <note>original: "P. multo atrociores pœnas promeritus"</note>; indeed, when he wants to prove that people such as Peucer was should have been **beheaded** <note>original: "decolliret"</note>, mutilated in hands and feet, and so forth. He also does not deny that they wanted to put Peucer to the **torture** <note>The "rack" or judicial torture to extract confessions.</note>, and that his "perfidy and perjury" would have well deserved it, and so forth.

(5) Finally, Mr. Caroli complains on page 349 about Mr. Arnold, that he brought nothing of Peucer's "evil things" into the large book, but instead, for his sake, insulted and criticized the servants of God and theologians, especially Dr. Andreae, and so forth. But let an impartial person consider whether it would have been honorable for these theologians, or suited them as servants of God, if one had repeated from their writings what can be read, for example, in Hutter’s *Concord of Concord*: such as, that Peucer treats controversies like a physician who concerns himself with dung; that he should inspect the **urine-glass** <note>A derogatory reference to Peucer’s profession as a physician, implying his theological work was as lowly as examining medical waste.</note> for it; that he was worthy of a **donkey's burial** <note>original: "Esels-Begräbniß" — a term for being buried without Christian rites, like an animal.</note>, and so forth. But this does not belong here, and one sees well that Mr. Arnold would have been called a "good historian" if he had mimicked such speeches after the theologians and rejected all others in a partisan manner.

### The 112th Accusation:

It follows on p. 215: In the history itself, the authors (of the Formula of Concord) are called <gloss>theologians of the highest authority and constancy</gloss> <note>original Latin: "summa autoritatis & constantiæ Theologi"</note>. p. 356.

(2) That Mr. Arnold, regarding such words about "highest authority," noted it was a form of pride—Mr. Caroli twists this to find an excuse, applying it to "constancy," and vainly concludes: Therefore they were not proud. Therefore, it is not a "poisonous gloss," but the clear truth before all impartial eyes: For he who allows himself to be praised in words as a theologian of the highest authority, and also compels others through his actions in matters of conscience and faith, is certainly not humble. No further commentary is needed here; and in this view, which is in accordance with the word of the humble Jesus and his disciples, there is no poison, but life and peace for all who wish to be of the same mind as Christ.

Mr. Caroli [Hr. Car.] unauthorizedly alleges. Rather, it is a mere report of an outside objection, which was the most important and concerning one; thus, it is no formal complaint or denunciation by Mr. Arnold [H. A.] against these theologians. Since he leaves everything to its own merits and does not involve himself in the dispute against the <term>Formula of Concord</term> <note>The definitive 1577 Lutheran confession intended to settle internal disputes.</note>; here, however, he only reported what happened <note>original Latin: "pro & contra"</note> <gloss>for and against</gloss> at that time.

(2) Concerning the objection itself, Mr. Caroli sets forth the following against it: α) It is beyond dispute that the <term>Sacramentarians</term> <note>A term used, often pejoratively, for those who disagreed with the Lutheran view of the Real Presence in the Lord’s Supper, primarily followers of Zwingli or Calvin.</note> publicly and incessantly pressed for such a <term>synod</term> <note>A formal meeting or council of church leaders to decide on doctrine.</note>. β) But why does Arnold call these an "oppressed party"? he asks, and answers himself: Truly, those of the <term>Augsburg Confession</term> <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, 1530.</note> had not oppressed them; rather, the former were nearly oppressed by the latter, and had finally taken action, adopting orderly means for their preservation, and so forth. Every impartial person can see how far this argument goes. At one point, these were indeed overpowered by those, specifically through means that the weaker could not resist; therefore, Mr. Arnold rightly calls them such.

(3) Furthermore, γ) regarding the desired synod, it has long been answered that it was not necessary: they had already been heard enough, and so forth. All of these are <note>original Latin: "quæstiones factorum"</note> <gloss>questions of fact</gloss>, about which much could be reported if one loved conflict. However, everything at that time was aired in writings <note>original Latin: "pro & contra"</note> <gloss>for and against</gloss>, and whoever views the matter impartially can well recognize each side.

(4) He answers, δ) that he does not know how the theologians could have sought to play the master: and asks: What kind of masters did they then become afterward? However, it is better to let that old misery remain buried, insofar as it might spill over <note>original Latin: "extra historiæ fines ad personalia"</note> <gloss>beyond the boundaries of history into personal matters</gloss>, which in this case would be unavoidable.

(5) It is claimed that Mr. Arnold ε) wrote "wickedly" that some feared the matter might not be carried out as intended, or might even be thwarted. This is no wickedness, but a report founded in the matter itself, as the theologians most earnestly advised against the synod, even though the <term>Electors and Princes</term> <note>The high-ranking secular rulers of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> and other estates also wished for and advised it in the year 1577; moreover, the old Lutheran theologians had always recognized such synods as good. Whether and how the other parties were heard is shown by the entire history of those times regarding the doctrines and teachers condemned in the Formula of Concord.

(6) That ζ) the theologians here appealed to the authorities, who

<column-break/>

<page-num>545</page-num>

would not allow the synod, is not denied by Mr. Caroli; but he does deny that his own side followed this, which he wishes to prove from <term>Hutter</term> <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a strict Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note>. However, it is known to sensible men that great lords rarely undertook anything in church matters without the advice of theologians, and thus where this protest also originated. See above Num. 109. §. 2.

(7) Mr. Arnold cites here the <term>Apology of the Formula of Concord</term> <note>A defensive text written to justify the Formula of Concord against its critics.</note> chapter 15, where the authors write of their opponents: *They were also not the kind of people with whom one should involve oneself in such a manner (in a synod).* However, Mr. Caroli accuses him of a notable <note>original Latin: "criminis falsi"</note> <gloss>crime of falsehood</gloss>, claiming he interpreted these words to apply to the Calvinists, whereas the Apology made a distinction between <term>Sturmius’s</term> <note>Johannes Sturm (1507–1589), an influential educator and theologian whose views were caught between Lutheranism and Calvinism.</note> followers and the other Calvinists. But how easy it is to accuse an author of the "crime of falsehood"! One should consider the whole sequence of events. a) Had they not previously completely refused a synod to the so-called Calvinists before and after the Work of Concord?

(8) Yes, b) in this very Apology and in the words cited by Mr. Caroli, while offering a <term>colloquy</term> <note>A formal theological discussion.</note>, they nevertheless added conditions that were considered impossible by the theologians: *Provided it pleases their noble sovereigns and lordships; Item: if such a convention is deemed advisable.* Now, they had already thwarted all synods through these conditions and the reference to the authorities and the consideration of "advisability"; how then can one conclude otherwise than that they did not want to involve themselves with the so-called Calvinists altogether? c) Furthermore, what did they call Sturmius and his friends? Certainly Calvinists. Has Mr. Arnold then not truthfully stated that the Apology wrote this of the Calvinists: *They were not the people?* etc. Who, without extreme partiality, can fabricate such a crime from this? Certainly, the report is <note>original Latin: "in ipso facto"</note> <gloss>in the fact itself</gloss> only too well founded.

(9) He also in no way confuses the times before and after the Formula of Concord, but speaks very clearly of the *excuse of the theologians, namely why they had not admitted any synod*; and because this reproach was still repeated even after the Formula of Concord, even by other Lutheran theologians, the answer was also the same as that which they had given before the Formula of Concord. It would have been good if Mr. Arnold had written more <note>original Latin: "distinctius"</note> <gloss>distinctly</gloss> in this passage, which he also would have done if he had suspected such coarse accusations. But who can remain innocent when one wishes to treat a writer so, who presents the bitter truth?

### The 117th Accusation:

thinks. Thus, according to Osiander’s report, such sermons must necessarily have arisen from nature and art, because Osiander mentions nothing other than natural eloquence.

forbidden. Regardless of the excess involved, it caused him to wonder how the fathers of this Council <note>likely referring to a specific provincial synod or early church council</note> presumed to create a sin, and to punish an imagined sin where no sin actually existed.

(2) Regarding this observation, Mr. Arnold (H. A.) reminds us in the 14th Chapter of the 16th Book, §. 24, of the following: that such gruesome blindness only arose because people clung to the bare letter of the law, thinking that if the Bible said nothing of board games, cards, or dice, then everything was fine—no matter how much the game in general might incite the lusts of the flesh and lead to the wasting of time. Anyone who contradicts this reminder must deny all the words in Scripture that testify so earnestly against these specified sins.

(3) Mr. Caroli asks here: What then is to be blamed in Osiander's words? I answer: Osiander himself blames the Council for forbidding gambling. Mr. Arnold considers this prohibition to be in accordance with Scripture, and Osiander’s <term>Glosse: interpretive commentary</term> to be unfounded. Why should one wish to punish what is written according to one's best knowledge and conscience? Any theologian who has no desire for, nor secret pleasure in, these vanities will find it impossible to contradict the Council on this point.

(4) And what need is there for the long disputation that Mr. Caroli seeks here? He admits himself that he never plays, even when he is <term>Sauer-Brunnen trincke: drinking mineral waters at a spa</term> <note>a common social setting for games in the period</note>. If he does not consider it useful for himself, he cannot take it amiss if others state their opinion on it—especially since they appeal to clear passages of Scripture dealing with the lusts of the flesh, the wasting of time, and the like.

(5) But as for the claim that Mr. Arnold wasted his time with such testimonies, which he presented against common complacency—Mr. Caroli will convince no one who still loves true Christianity of that. One may read the entire 6th chapter of the 4th book of his *Abbildung* <note>Arnold’s *Abbildung der ersten Christen* or "Portrayal of the Early Christians"</note>, as well as what Mr. [August Hermann] Francke, Mr. Vockerodt, Mr. Beerensprung, Mr. Seidel, and others have published on the matter. There, one will recognize the truth that some wish to obscure, and will no longer be able to doubt or contradict it. Indeed, Mr. Caroli here contradicts the very [Philipp Jakob] Spener whom he himself so dearly praised.

## The 119th Accusation:

It is stated on page 219: Lucas Osiander sought it in another manner, and 
<meta>catchword: wrote</meta>

---

<page-num>555</page-num>
<header>IV. TH. 119. 120. N. Mr. Andr. David Caroli etc. 555</header>

wrote to the effect of how pleasing it would be to the Duke if the Council [of Strasbourg] would sign—namely, the *Formula of Concord* <note>The 1577 Lutheran confession of faith</note>, p. 390.

### Answer:

(1) Thus Osiander wrote as Court Preacher to Marbach in Strasbourg, according to Fecht, p. 565: "That renowned Council would do a very pleasing thing for my most illustrious Prince if it would hasten the subscription. For in this way, copies could be sent to the Electors more quickly. In this matter, I ask that Your Reverence work as much as will be permitted. And I believe the business can also be greatly advanced through the most famous man, Grempius." <note>Original Latin: "Valde gratam rem faceret Illustrissimo meo Principi Senatus ille inclytus, si subscriptionem maturaret... per Clarissimum Virum Grempium promoveri plurimum posse."</note>

(2) From this, the author who wrote the <term>Marginalia: notes in the margin</term> of the *K. H.* <note>Arnold’s *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie*</note> wrote: "Deceit, persuasion, and haste used." This refers not only to these words, but also to the preceding words of Dr. Andreae <note>Jakob Andreae, a primary author of the Formula of Concord</note>, who wrote to the same Marbach: that he should show his gray hairs in earnest to the Council, turn into a dog, and bark bravely at the Council. All of this together could certainly be called deceit, persuasion, and haste.

(3) Why then does Mr. Caroli complain so much about it? He says that Osiander was a famous man who had honestly earned a commendable name in the Church. Therefore, he claims it is pure untruth. However, the words of both theologians stand clearly there, and there has been no dishonorable mutilation or unchristian <term>Detorsion: twisting/distortion</term> of them. One only seeks such excuses when one has no other way out.

## The 120th Accusation:

It is reported on page 318 that Osiander's account of [Francesco] Pucci's burning in Rome is false. P. 392.

### Answer:

Mr. Arnold has shown this from Kipping's *Supplements to Pappus’s Church History*, which states on p. 56: "Having departed for Bohemia and having again professed the Roman religion of his homeland, he died in Prague." <note>Original Latin: "In Bohemiam digressus & pattiam religionem Romanensem denuo professus Pragae obiit."</note> Since Osiander reports the opposite and refers to common rumor, which Mr. Arnold refutes as false, Mr. Caroli cannot use this against Osiander as an insult, as if Mr. Arnold had accused him of a <term>Falsum: intentional falsehood</term>. For a historical error is not immediately an intentional falsehood, as Mr. Caroli interprets it in the worst way; rather, such things can happen to even the most practiced historian. And as for the falsehoods he accuses our author of, that depends on an investigation; in that case, sensible and impartial people will judge differently than Mr. Caroli has done in his bias toward the person.

### The 121st Accusation:

->He rebukes Osiander on page 319 for calling Puccius a gallows-bird and his book satanic. p. 395.<-

### Answer:

(1) Here Mr. Caroli asks first: what kind of sin is that supposed to be? Is one really doing an <term>enthusiast: a "Schwärmer," a derogatory term for radical religious reformers who claimed direct inspiration</term> too much harm by calling him a gallows-bird? and so forth. He wishes to prove this with the metaphor of one who poisons the pasture and the water; for Puccius has led souls astray, regarding which he cites several theologians. Indeed, he says that Puccius was insulted by Osiander with that same "theological gentleness" with which Christ called all false teachers wolves, thieves, and murderers, and Paul called the deceiver a child of the Devil. For thieves, wolves, and the like are no better than gallows-birds, and so forth.

(2) The good man has not known, or considered, <note>original: *non esse idem, cum duo faciunt idem*</note> that it is not the same thing when two people do the same thing. That Christ and Paul, with gentleness, called certain people thieves and murderers is true; but whether others can boast of that same gentleness in their own insulting is a higher question, which is easily answered "yes," but slowly proven. Mr. Caroli has remained stuck in the "respect of persons" and therein in a zeal that is not according to knowledge; therefore, he immediately equated the affairs of theologians with those of Christ. And whoever would not believe this, he became angry with and insulted; and Mr. Arnold has had to pay for this as well. For this reason, he [Caroli] accused him from the index of the Church History of things that one finds quite differently in the book itself, as was shown above in Part I, Numbers 2, 17, and 46, regarding the atheism of many Lutherans.

(3) Mr. Caroli burdens Arnold once again with evil accusations and the suspicion of a brazen deed—as if he had wanted to hide Puccius’s poisonous errors and had therefore miserably mutilated and twisted Osiander’s words. Now see again the man's over-hastiness (for I will still call it that out of compassion), how he wants to force such gruesome things upon Mr. Arnold! For Mr. Arnold begins right there (in Chapter 22, § 16): "Most of all, those propositions have been considered blasphemy which were **NB.** <note>Latin: *nota bene*, or "take special note"</note> drawn from his books," whereupon he lists one after another the points repeated by Mr. Caroli.

(4) Now the question is: Did Mr. Arnold take these only from Osiander, or also from others? Osiander is not cited there at all, but only
<meta>catchword: after</meta>

---

<page-num>557</page-num>
<header>IV. Part 121. 122. 123. N. Mr. Andr. David Caroli &c.</header>

after ten lines, during which other matters of Puccius's harmony with other sects are reported, and only then is Osiander cited. Regarding Puccius's teachings, however, Mr. Arnold had previously cited many other authors, such as Kipping, Boeckler, Kortholt, Benzelius, Colberg, Böttger, Kromayer, etc. How then can Mr. Caroli say that Arnold took it from Osiander alone, and mutilated him, indeed, miserably twisted him?

(5) Does one not see the obvious compulsions? Were there no other authors besides Osiander? Or is Puccius not refuted in almost all <term>systematic: works of systematic theology</term> and thus his teaching also reviewed? But it was firmly decided to make Mr. Arnold into a <term>falsario: a forger or deceiver</term> after the example of other opponents and to accuse him of presumptuous deception. But who has now deceived or acted presumptuously? And what is the conclusion worth when Mr. Caroli says: it is easy to judge what the doctrine of faith in Christ and the honor of Christ are worth to Arnold. God be thanked that another testimony exists before Him who does not judge by outward appearance!

### The 122nd Accusation:

->He amuses himself on page 337 with the name of Osiander. p. 397.<-

### Answer:

It is a poor amusement when a historian reports from old authors what a very notorious man, as Andreas Osiander was, was called in his youth. Mr. Arnold had done this from Joachim Camerarius, Seckendorff, Melchior Adam, Freher, Hartknoch, and others. If these many serious men did not amuse themselves with it, then it cannot be attributed to Mr. Arnold either. Yet these are trifles that Mr. Caroli seeks out only for the sake of excess.

### The 123rd Accusation:

->He mentions Dr. Gerlach in no other way than to write on page 369 that Huberus appealed to his testimony in his dispute.<-

### Answer:

This was spoken of above in Number 31 and following, in the matter of Huberus; and Mr. Caroli himself mentions here that Sarcerius, Chytraeus, Selneccer, and others also spoke of a universal election. Whether these theologians were not at one with him, however, is not to be disputed here.

### The 124th Accusation:

->Arnold accuses Crusius twice (p. 163 and 186) of having been an Epicurean.<-
<note>An "Epicurean" in this 18th-century religious context refers to someone who prioritizes worldly pleasure and physical comfort over spiritual devotion.</note>

### Answer:

(1) First, Mr. Caroli defends the **baptismal feasts** here, and distinguishes between their proper use and their abuse. However, well-informed Christians rightly recognize no proper use for such baptismal banqueting, and consider them a great hindrance to earnest prayer for the child; as can be read in *Arnold Mengering* in his *Scrutiny of Catechetical Concords p. 1260*, *Brunnemann’s Ecclesiastical Law Book I, Chapter VI. m. 3. §. 19. p. 176.* and Privy Councilor *Stryck* in his *Notes p. 312.*, where he expressly advises that a godfather should and can absent himself after the baptism if someone wishes to pressure him into a baptismal feast, etc. Thus, Mr. Caroli’s apology for these things—which in themselves are nothing but abuse—does not stand at all alongside the teachings of Christian jurists and theologians; for this reason, baptismal meals are also forbidden in the Royal Prussian lands: *Constitutional Order Article IX. p. m. 24.* and in the *Special Mandate page 111*, which every Christian preacher rejoices in and strictly upholds.

(2) Yet this does not actually belong here, insofar as it is being dragged in by Mr. Caroli. Concerning Crusius <note>Martin Crusius (1526–1607) was a famous German humanist and historian.</note> and his *passages*, the first is from his *Swabian Annals for the Year 1562, p. 713*, regarding the Imperial Banquet at Frankfurt: **"Oh, how magnificent and merry it was! It pains me far too much that one could not, or ever can, extend the time spent at such festivities."** In this passage, he particularly praises the excellent invitations, pleasant *discourse*, beautiful *music*, and lovely dances; and finally exclaims: **"Everything has its time: O Mother Eve, how you have ruined us!"**

(3) Regarding these words, Mr. Arnold then set down his thoughts there: namely, how such people, amidst all their feasting, nevertheless comforted themselves with the merit of Christ, since Crusius had written alongside this: **"He did not wish to rely on his own piety, for it was but like a stained garment."** Now, let anyone who knows and loves the teaching of Christ judge whether Mr. Arnold, with this *judgment*, acted against God, His word, or truth and fairness? The confession of Crusius is so clear for all to see that even a child can grasp how far it is from the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

(4) How does Mr. Caroli now seek to make him innocent? If he had

<meta>continuity: catchword "Lust" (desire/pleasure) connects to the next page.</meta>

---

<page-num>559</page-num>

the desire to agree with the pure truth, then no one would have blamed him if he had admitted that sometimes such persons lived even at the *universities* who loved pleasure more than God. But no: he first endeavors to prove that the same banquet was not a "feast," simply because the Emperor and King were present. Now, one may leave the affairs of great lords untouched; no one will call them Epicureans. However, where then are the countless complaints from the *16th Century* regarding the drinking and carousing of the Germans?

(5) And whom will Mr. Caroli persuade that everything at such a large banquet proceeded soberly and moderately? Do not so many Germans from those same times testify otherwise? Does not, among others, *Joachim Camerarius* write in the *Life of Eobanus Hessus*: **"Contests of the cups [drinking bouts] were then most vigorously fought in the courts and frequented by the nobility"**? <note>original Latin: "Poculorum certamina maxime tunc in aulis certabantur & à nobilitate frequentabantur"</note> Is Germany not a mockery to all nations for this very reason? Indeed, why then does Crusius so insistently praise the great merriment, *music*, dances, etc.? Why did he wish so longingly to be there forever, and for that reason complain about Mother Eve? Had Mr. Arnold sought to defend such manifest sins, what outrages and abominations would Mr. Caroli not have made of it, and rightly so? But still, it remains that people call bitter sweet and sweet bitter! *Isaiah 5:20.*

(6) Nevertheless, Mr. Arnold is alleged to have deceived the reader here because he called this banquet simply a banquet, and not a coronation banquet. But even if it were the highest banquet possible, the question remains whether Crusius did not indicate his fleshly mind through the above words? Mr. Caroli further asserts that Arnold mutilated Crusius’s words. However:

For what does this indicate: **"How was it (the banquet) worth seeing and hearing? How the old Romans would marvel that such great glory has come to the Germans?"** This cannot be excused by Mr. Caroli as the "thoughts of a German patriot" according to the rules of Christianity and the Gospel. For Romans and Christians should be heaven-wide apart—

(8) Furthermore, Mr. Caroli calls these the "thoughts of a proper subject" where Crusius writes: *Certainly such a (banquet) must also take place in its own time,* etc. And the words cited by Mr. Arnold regarding "exquisite meals, music, and lovely dances," he calls "natural ideas." In this way, everything can eventually be excused. However, Crusius’s own conscience dictated something else to him, which is why he finally begins to write about faith.

(9) For truly, he who cherishes living faith in his heart—not merely in imagination, but in power—will certainly not highlight such worldly luxuries so appetizingly, much less wish for their permanence or mourn over Eve <note>A reference to the Fall of Man and the loss of earthly paradise.</note> because of them. One necessarily cancels out the other, and faith cannot stand alongside friendship with and joy in the world; therefore, faith is so rare despite all the boastful claims of faith that hypocrites are accustomed to making.

(10) Now, because this testimony did not please Mr. Caroli, he had to become indignant and therefore sought to accuse Mr. Arnold of a falsification, even though it is fundamentally the same whether <term>tantum dolet mihi</term> <note>original: "tantum dolet mihi" — Latin for "it grieves me so much" or "it only grieves me."</note> means: "it only grieves me," or "it grieves me far too much." For it is enough that it grieved him—namely, the passing of his lusts. Mr. Caroli, on the other hand, seeks to make Crusius’s words blameless, which is certainly sad enough coming from a <term>Superintendent</term>! <note>A high-ranking administrative official in the Lutheran church, similar to a bishop.</note> He tries to prove it through other words of Crusius; but how far are these words from the actual deed? One gladly leaves the good Crusius his praise in his profession and hopes for the best for him according to Christian love; but one must not seek to completely annihilate such clear testimonies. One pays no mind to the mocking speeches regarding Mr. Arnold's faith, humility, and enlightenment, for there are other testimonies of those; and if Mr. Caroli had understood Arnold’s meaning, he would surely have refrained from such un-Christian judgments. Furthermore, one does not blame Mr. Caroli for taking Crusius's side because he had a good opinion of him; but he should not have misinterpreted the opposite view of another who has a closer insight into the matter according to the rule of the Gospel.

### The 125th Accusation.

Regarding Dr. Lucas Osiander the Son, <note>Lucas Osiander the Younger (1571–1638), a staunch Lutheran orthodox theologian known for his fierce polemics.</note> Arnold writes on page 479 that he was the chief among the blasphemers of Johann Arndt. p. 410.

### Answer:

(1) It would be desirable that such contradictions against the blessed Arndt <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), whose work *True Christianity* was foundational to Pietism but controversial among strict Lutherans.</note> and such defenses by Mr. Caroli had never been published and thus would no longer need to be mentioned; one is also reluctant to even begin the investigation of these objections. Mr. Caroli first acknowledges much good about Arndt, but he blames several of his ways of speaking, even though he admits again that these have been explained by Arndt himself and others. However, he also brings up various points that do not belong here, and afterwards he falls into very miserable excuses to maintain a claim of "innocence."

(2) Concerning Lucas Osiander, however, he writes on p. 412 against the truth: $\alpha$) that Osiander had excerpted Arndt’s offensive phrases and subjected them to a sharp examination. In fact, he did not just excerpt the book, but rejected and branded it as heretical altogether, as is evident to everyone, and as Mr. H. Varenius in his defense, along with Egardus and others, has thoroughly proven. (See below § 5, 6, 7, and 11, and the *Apologies for Arndt* newly edited in Leipzig, 1706, in octavo.)

(3) For point $\beta$), Mr. Caroli falsely asserts that Osiander had merely inspected Arndt’s speeches, and that this was not "blaspheming." He cites the passage from Acts 15:6 <note>A biblical reference to the Council of Jerusalem, where the Apostles gathered to consider a dispute.</note> and thus compares Osiander’s atrocious insults against Arndt to the holy Apostles' gentle conduct toward those in error. If Mr. Arnold had done this, he would no longer be a Christian. It would also be, at the very least, a great imprudence to call such a perversion "Apostolic." A theologian from Württemberg, Dr. M. Nicolai, does indeed excuse Osiander somewhat, but nevertheless confesses that he pursued the dispute more vehemently than necessity required. (See *Umbell. Somp. Jes. Forer. p. 161.*) Indeed, and this is well worth noting, Mr. Caroli’s own biological father reports on this more honestly in Book III of his *Memorabilia*, chapter 26, page 594, where he writes: <note>original: "Osiander adversus Arndium insurgit eosque impugnat stylo perquam acri. Etenim in præfatione statim dicit: Eos esse veneno hæretico imbutos, pestilentes, puro Evangelio contrarios, Papismo, Calvinismo, Flacianismo, Svenckfeldianismo, VVigelianismo &c. turgidos, qui sine periculo salutis à simplicioribus --- haut legi possint."</note> *Osiander rises up against Arndt and attacks his works with an exceedingly sharp style. For in the preface he immediately says: These are imbued with heretical poison, pestilential, contrary to the pure Gospel, swollen with Papism, Calvinism, Flacianism, Schwenkfeldianism, Weigelianism, etc., which cannot be read by the simple-minded without danger to their salvation.* Following this, he mentions that Varenius and Egardus had strenuously defended him, and also reports Dannhauer’s opinion. Thus, Mr. Caroli has departed from his own father in this matter, who found no "innocence" in Osiander here and spoke the truth of it.

His defenders have indeed shown how wretchedly **Osiander** <note>The text uses "Oliander," a common variant spelling for Lucas Osiander the Younger (1571–1638), a staunch Lutheran habitual polemicist.</note> was grounded in **God's** Word. It is also claimed that he did not blaspheme; however, **Mr. Director Lange** <note>Joachim Lange (1670–1744), a leading Pietist theologian at Halle.</note> in his *Sincere Report* against the so-called *Innocent Report* has quite clearly proven recently that even the most famous theologians at Wittenberg and other opponents of **Arnd** viewed and described him as a blasphemer. See **Volume VI, page 59 and following.** <note>original: "To. VI. p. 59. seqq."</note>

(5) Eighthly, it is claimed that **Osiander** did not personally portray **Arnd** as a **Calvinist**, **Papist**, **Flacian**, **Schwenkfelder**, **Weigelian**, <note>These were various theological groups and movements—such as the followers of Caspar Schwenckfeld and Valentin Weigel—that the Lutheran establishment often labeled as heretical.</note> or the like. However, the aforementioned defenders have shown how **Osiander**, contrary to his own profession, grievously sinned against Arnd's person himself. For example, **Varenius** <note>August Varenius (1620–1684), a Lutheran theologian who, despite his orthodoxy, defended Arnd’s piety.</note> writes in the preface of his *Vindication*, **page b. 3.**, that the entire work testifies all too much to how **Osiander** maintained such a **declaration** <note>original: "Protestation"</note>; especially in the 5th chapter, where the blessed man <note>Johann Arnd.</note> must truly suffer and be held to account. There, he must be regarded as equal not only to **NB. the Enthusiasts**, **Schwenkfelders**, and **Weigelians**, but even to false prophets and apostles, and must even be counted among the **SERVANTS OF THE DEVIL** <note>original: "Diaboli Ministros"</note>—and indeed in **CAPITAL LETTERS on page 1413** <note>original: "literis majusculis"</note> so that everyone might see it. All of these are strong **signs** <note>original: "Indicia"</note> of an embittered spirit. See also **page 37** and following, as well as the **Admonition, page 15.** <note>original: "Admonit."</note> I bypass the disputes of others for the sake of brevity; one can find a short extract in the mentioned **Arndian Apologetics** <note>original: "Apologeticis Arndianis"</note> in the preliminary report against **Osiander**.

(6) **Mr. Caroli** says on **page 413** that because **Arnd** mockingly calls **Osiander** a great **Doctor** <note>A title for a teacher or scholar of the church.</note>, he acts as a great transgressor. Until now, **Mr. Caroli** has not easily thrown around insulting titles and nicknames; but here, **Mr. Arnold** must be called a transgressor, and a great one at that, because he calls **Osiander** a great **Doctor**. The aforementioned **Lutheran** preacher **Varenius** addresses this same **Osiander** in the **II. Part** of his *Vindication*, **page 174**, in this way: *If one were to **judge** <note>original: "judiciren"</note> by the fruits, you could much sooner be accused of these vices (pride and arrogance) from this high-flown, presumptuous **style** <note>original: "Stylo"</note> and judgment of yours, in which you accuse him of leidig, devilish pride from your high provost's chair.* But was **Varenius** also a great transgressor for often calling **Osiander** a great Provost or a great **Doctor** elsewhere? It was surely not good for such a man to offend so greatly against **Arnd**.

(7) Seventhly, **Mr. Caroli** is not ashamed to write: that the worthy **Theologian** (**Osiander**) intended to prove himself an upright,

vigilant, and sincere **Doctor** through his *Reflection*. But now, let one consider the entire *Vindication* by **Varenius**, and especially the following words therein, and see whether they can be **reconciled** <note>original: "conciliiren"</note> in the slightest with **Mr. Caroli's praise** <note>original: "Encomio"</note>.

(8) He proves throughout what he promises on **page 48**: how completely untheologically **Dr. Osiander** dealt with **Arnd**, often twisting his words and pulling them into a foreign meaning, and attaching such fanaticism <note>The term "Schwärmerey" refers to religious enthusiasm or radicalism often viewed as irrational by the mainstream church.</note> to them that cannot be concluded through any correct reasoning. In many places, and among others on **page 680**, he shows what great **calumnies** <note>original: "Calumnien" — false and malicious statements.</note> and blasphemies **Osiander** allows to slip in. Further, on **page 685**, he states that everything (in **Osiander's** *Reflection*) aims at making him a heretic; there, everything must be vain **Enthusiastic**, **Schwenkfeldian**, and **Weigelian** fanaticism—so much so that if one were to give his book its own name, it could not be named better or more fittingly than *A Heretic-Making of the Four Books of True Christianity*.

(9) In the preface to the **II. Part**, he complains that **Osiander** counted **Arnd** among the coarsest heretics without significant cause and branded his Christian, highly useful work as heretical and rejected it. And in the conclusion on **page 430**, he says: **Osiander's** accusations regarding immediate revelation are vain, gross, fabricated **calumnies** (to speak as mildly as possible) which **Osiander** will never in eternity be able to force or prove from **Arnd** with all his might. Indeed, he convicts **Osiander** himself of great errors, as in **Part I, page 387, page 451**, and elsewhere, as well as in the **Brief Consideration** <note>original: "brevi Consideratione"</note> against **Rostius**, **page 2 and following, 14**, etc.

(10) Compare this detailed proof with **Mr. Caroli's** unproven pretension, and the outcome will be clear. **Mr. Caroli** appeals to the Day of Judgment, saying it will then be revealed whether he was a great or small **Doctor**; he claims it is not for **Arnd** to judge this. This latter thing **Mr. Arnold** has not done; he only **historically reported** <note>original: "historice referiret"</note> what **Arnd’s** defenders had proven long ago. Meanwhile, it is distressing when someone appeals to the Day of Judgment while still entangled in the aforementioned sins! And when **Mr. Caroli** leaves it to the recognition of all honorable **theologians** whether **Osiander** was blind, such a thing is now superfluous, as it has long since become a **settled matter** <note>original: "res judicata"</note>. The **retort** <note>original: "Retorsion"</note> used by **Mr. Caroli** against **Mr. Arnold** reveals the grounds from which the **retorting** <note>original: "retorquiret"</note> was done.

(11) The conclusion—that either the entire *Reflection* of **Osiander** or certain parts of it were made in blindness—was reached long ago by

Varenius and others have fully resolved this, as we saw above in § 9, where he called the entire critique a "hereticization" and deduced this point by point. In this matter, no one will be able to make the seeing blind, nor produce a true innocence where none exists. No further proof is necessary, as this has been perfectly accomplished in entire books for more than 80 years.

(12) Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the author of this work and a significant historian of radical pietism.</note> has invented nothing for himself, but found everything as clear as day in *Arnd's Defenders*, as it still lies before everyone's eyes. Mr. Caroli, however, writes off this mere repetition as a "vile spirit's" boldness (page 415); indeed, he wishes to declare Mr. Arnold once again much more dishonest than many naturally honest people—which is miserable enough to hear from a preacher. But how many have judged Osiander’s <note>Lucas Osiander the Younger (1571–1638), a staunch Lutheran polemicist known for his sharp attacks on Arnd.</note> critique in this way over so many years? And what did the Theological Faculty at Jena generally judge regarding all of Arnd's detractors? They call such people unteachable and frivolous, as **Varenius** (page 41) cites; and the latter counts Osiander among Arnd's *rigid censors, Aristarchuses, and perverters* <note>original: "rigidos Censores, Aristarchos und Perversores." Aristarchus was an ancient scholar whose name became a synonym for a severe critic.</note> (*Consider. Admonit. Rost.* page 11). Indeed, Franzius there calls such judgments against Arnd *scattered by the instinct of Satan* <note>original: "Judicia... Satanæ instinctu sparsa"</note> and complains that Satan cannot bear for people to be driven toward good works as the fruits of faith. Why then does Mr. Caroli only now ask whether it can be called "frivolous" that Osiander wrote of "spiritualized Arndian Christians"? All his sought-after excuses are not enough to cover the misery.

(13) The living GOD knows that Mr. Arnold did not compose this account with an evil mind, let alone an exceedingly evil one, but according to his conscience, which was convinced of Arnd's purity and Osiander's impurity through long examination. However, he now gladly lets these things rest, having moved on from historical matters. And had he been required to repeat everything from Varenius and others that they brought forward against Osiander regarding *factual matters* <note>original: "in realibus"</note>, Mr. Caroli would be even more indignant. For he has hardly read Varenius's book; otherwise, he would not have so thoughtlessly stated: "Arnold found no more horrors regarding Osiander, otherwise he would have brought more to market," whereas every page in Varenius testifies to them. This is no "merchandise" of Arnold's, but truth, against which Mr. Caroli's mocking helps nothing—a mocking he otherwise blames in Mr. Arnold.

(14) He further wishes to compare and equate Osiander with the late Arnd, and persuade the reader that the former did not take issue with certain expressions out of a bad intention, just as the latter did not use them out of a bad intention.

But the partiality and the resulting blindness are, alas, all too great, when one tries to reconcile Osiander's demonstrated terrible judgments against Arnd with Arnd's innocent expressions. The famous Witte, in the *Biographical Diary* <note>original: "Diar. Biograph." (Diarium Biographicum), a reference work by Henning Witte.</note> *Vol. 1, 1604, Sept. 17*, and others describe Osiander as Arnd's enemy. How can such a person agree with the one he treats as an enemy? Everyone can see it without further *deduction* <note>interpretation or formal argument</note>, and will find no "horror" in Mr. Arnold's short account—which is not nearly as harsh as Varenius's proof—if they love the truth. It pleases Mr. Caroli to further burden Mr. Arnold with great arrogance and similar sins, because he described certain persons, who were held too highly by other men, in a different light.

(15) But because Mr. Caroli repeats here once more that **Gerhardus** <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), one of the most important Lutheran orthodox theologians.</note> did not approve of Arnd's questionable *phrases*; let one hold against this what he, along with the entire Theological Faculty at Jena, testified about Arnd's books *in general* <note>original: "in genere"</note> (found in Varenius, page 13): "We have found that the author of such books was not devoted to any erroneous religion, false opinion, or any fanaticism <note>term: "Schwermerey" (Schwärmerei). A derogatory term used by orthodox Lutherans to label those they considered overly emotional or mystical, often implying heresy.</note>; and is not to be considered or scolded as a Weigelian, nor a Schwenkfelder, nor a Rosicrucian, or whatever names such enthusiasts and flighty spirits may have: but is in harmony and unanimous in all articles of faith with us and other pure Lutheran churches." The *encomiums* <note>formal expressions of high praise</note> of Arnd by other theologians such as **Hülsemann, Walther, Quenstedt**, and the Württemberg scholar **J. V. Andreae** are to be found in the *Church History* <note>original: "K. H." (Kirchen-Historie), likely referring to Arnold's own massive history of the church and heretics.</note> in the 6th Chapter of the 17th Book, § 5 and following. Andreae's** *Inaugural Oration* as *worthy of note*: "It happened that after the more inconvenient phrases were explained, Gerhardus thought excellently of him." More is to be found in the mentioned *Arndian Apologetics* of **Mr. M. Günther**. The said Württemberg theologian J. V. Andreae also says without exception of Arnd's adversaries that they had *stained him with much NB. calumny and envy* <note>original: "multâ NB. calumniâ & invidiâ maculiret"</note>, in his *Seleniana*, page 332.

### The 126th Accusation.

Mr. Arnold <note>Referred to as "H." or "H.A." in the text.</note> adds on page 480 / that it is remarkable / that a soldier ran up to the pulpit with a drawn sword during Osiander’s <note>Lucas Osiander the Younger (1571–1638), a prominent and polemical Lutheran theologian.</note> sermon / and said: Why do you not teach God’s Word? For which the soldier was indeed punished / but Osiander was undoubtedly reminded of his useless chatter / which he was accustomed to carry on outwardly and without God’s Word. p. 420.

->Antwort:<-

(1) The reader sees from Mr. Arnold’s words / that he does not excuse the soldier at all / or approve of his excess / but that he only wishes / Osiander might have allowed himself to be reminded by it / of what he was preaching. Mr. Caroli <note>Andreas David Caroli (1662–1713), the author of the "Württemberg Innocence" attacking Arnold.</note> on the other hand makes many unnecessary words / claiming Mr. Arnold "tickled himself" with it (which certainly cannot be seen from any of his words.) He calls Osiander a "righteous servant of God" / the reason for which was recognized in the previous number.

(2) He calls the observation "vile" / which nevertheless every true Christian can examine / to see if it be not Christian. For a Christian / much more a teacher / should indeed let the smallest occurrences serve him for the best / and thus for improvement / let alone such a strange event. He even accuses Mr. Arnold / on page 421 / of having held this deed to be a *heroic impulse* <note>original: "Motum heroicum"</note> and a proof of divine zeal ; but falsely and without the slightest true proof.

(3) This proof is supposed to be / because Mr. Arnold praises this man / namely Gifftheil / later in Part III, pages 98 and 100 / also in Part IV, page 76. If one looks it up there / one finds on page 100 / that Mr. Arnold explicitly attributes to this man a very fiery and sharp temperament / and such actions linked with much heavy zeal / of which he names this Tübingen action as an example. How then could Mr. Arnold have *approved* of this deed in the slightest? He considers it ungodly / to attack one’s neighbor with words in a private place / let alone in a public place with the sword. How should he have held this for a divine zeal / when he expressly ascribed it to the most violent zeal of nature? Thus one sees here also Mr. Caroli’s false accusations.

(4) Furthermore, it is said to be pure untruth and the malicious heart’s insolent fiction / that Osiander carried on useless chatter without God’s Word. However, whoever reads Osiander’s reflections against the late Arnd <note>Johann Arnd (1555–1621), author of "True Christianity," whom Osiander fiercely attacked.</note> / and his other German writings / in which he also wished to teach something of Christianity / he will

However, Mr. Arnold cited Dietericus <note>Conrad Dietericus (1575–1639), a Lutheran theologian.</note> alongside Carolus / where both are stated. Finally, he rails <note>original: "invehiret"</note> again in his usual manner against Mr. Arnold / because he did not approve of all the zeal of the theologians / which one may pass over in that well-known character.

<meta>catchword: above</meta>

...ter <note>original: "Polemosephus," a Greek-derived title meaning "Wise in War" or "Master of Polemics," used here as a nickname for Lucas Osiander.</note> who, out of great zeal, perfectly hated the enemies of GOD, and so forth.

### Response:

(1) Mr. Caroli seeks to excuse the name "Arndtians" <note>Followers of the mystical theologian Johann Arndt (1555–1621).</note> which is placed here alongside the Anabaptists and so-called Calvinists, and counted among the enemies of GOD; meanwhile, Osiander is praised as a "Master of Polemics" as if he deserved it. What help is there in such an excuse?

(2) For, he asks, why should "Polemosephus" be called a "pen-fighter"? Thus he himself admits that the conflict was led and fought with the pen, and so he himself reveals the basis of the word. He asks further: whether one should fight there with a sword, as Gifftheil <note>Ludwig Friedrich Gifftheil (1595–1661), a radical visionary known for his aggressive denunciations of the church.</note> did, against whose devilish undertaking Arnold does not say a single word? However, fighting with the sword against heretics is certainly something no Evangelical Christian would approve of; and against Gifftheil’s actions, Mr. Arnold has said not just one, but many words, as can be seen above in Number 126, paragraph 3.

(3) Finally, Mr. Caroli says that in Dr. Nicolai’s oration nothing is to be found regarding the Arndtians or the "Master of Polemics," based on which he accuses Mr. Arnold of a forgery. However, it should be known that Mr. Arnold actually took these words from the *Memorabilia*, Book V, page 920, by Carolus Senior <note>The elder Caroli, a previous historian.</note> and had cited him at the same time in the margin, as his draft still shows. The copyist, and subsequently the printer, had forgotten to insert this, which is why only the one citation stands. Mr. Caroli Junior himself cited these words of Carolus Senior on page 524 and set them in large letters, which he surely could have remembered. Here, from Dr. Nicolai’s oration, with a citation of page 103, not only are the Arndtians clearly mentioned, but the words "The master of polemics is worthy of no less praise" <note>original: "Polemosephus non minori laude dignus"</note> are read, alongside those other words: "wishing to see the destroyers of the Lord's flock exterminated" <note>original: "exterminatos cupiens videre gregis Dominici vastatores"</note>. Thus, everyone sees that this accusation does not hold up, because only the second author was omitted "among so many and so various objects of concern" <note>original: "inter tot & tam varia rerum objecta"</note>; a reader should not interpret this poorly, nor attribute it to the author himself as a forgery, if he wishes to allow for fairness.

## The 130th Accusation:

The intention with which Dr. Johann Valentin Andreae <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian and social reformer (1586–1654), often associated with the Rosicrucian fervor.</note> is praised by Arnold makes this honor quite poor. p. 432.

(1) Firstly, Mr. Caroli must admit on page 431 that Mr. Arnold records things from him that sound somewhat favorable, in Part II, page 465. From this, he could have clearly seen that Mr. Arnold has written impartially and according to the truth. However, even this was not allowed to count.

(2) For, so that he might have something to punish, he pretends that Arnold did not praise V. Andreae because he deserved it (this is a very wicked delusion for which there is no excuse: for Mr. Arnold is conscious before GOD of all faithfulness and truth in this matter, that he praised Andreae out of an honest mind and intention because he deserved it); but rather because Arnold wrote what occasionally seemed convenient to <term>confused fanatical heads</term> <note>The German term "Schwärmer" (fanatics/enthusiasts) was a common slur for those whose religious fervor was seen as disorderly or mystical.</note>.

(3) Thus, nothing is right to such minds who like to consider others confused and fanatical. The attached suspicion—that Mr. Arnold would have treated Dr. V. Andreae poorly or kept silent about him were it not for his own purpose—is wicked enough and unbecoming of a Christian, and even more so is this poor conclusion: that Dr. V. Andreae has no other honor from Arnold’s recommendation than this: that he should be in the draft according to that intention, as if he had been a friend of fanatics. What "fanatics" actually are, even among the Orthodox, can be read in the *Church History* in Book XVI, Chapter 9, Paragraph 2, and following. Mr. Caroli refers to the following investigations, in which we will now follow him and examine the specific details one after another.

Dr. V. Andreae is said to have been a patron of fanatics, according to Arnold’s delusion and claim. p. 433.

...out of his false conception and judgment of Mr. Arnold’s intention, which was sincerely attested to in Number 130. This and nothing else is what Mr. Arnold intended to say with the above words, and thus he in no way deserves the false consequences that Mr. Carolus attributes to him, as if he wanted to count Andreae entirely among the fanatics.

(5) That his writings were **suppressed**, Mr. Arnold understands according to the most common manner of speaking regarding their resulting rarity, in that he adds: "unknown"—which all scholars well know, how rare and pleasing these books are. But where has Mr. Arnold said or intended to say that they were confiscated or banned? It never happened anywhere, and Mr. Arnold knew it well. Mr. Carolus himself finally admits on page 436 that little more is seen of some of them now, and in a short time one could no longer obtain a copy of many, nor has he had any of them reprinted. Mr. Arnold intended to say nothing else, and thus Mr. Carolus rages and complains against him without ground or cause; one might conclude with more justice, if one wished to be argumentative: it is clear as day how Mr. Carolus gains nothing here for his purpose.

## The 132nd Accusation:

In the III. Part, page 117, he reports that Rathmann says Dr. Johann Valentin Andreae was also called a **Schwenckfelder** <note>A follower of the mystic Caspar Schwenckfeld; here used as a general sectarian slur.</note> by Corvinus because he praised Arndt.

### Response:

This stands in clear words in Rathmann’s "Necessary Response" on page D. 3., and Mr. Carolus should not doubt it at all, just as he doubts many such citations due to a lack of such books. Mr. Arnold’s intention in this citation is only this: it is clear that other upright people were also innocently called Schwenckfelders or otherwise generally termed heretics. He does not deny thereby that Andreae would have defended himself had he learned of it; and he himself sufficiently described Corvinus’s poor conduct in Book XVII, Chapter 6, Section 9, and in Part III, Chapter 12, page 113. Thus, there is no dispute here, and Mr. Carolus has worried in vain that Mr. Arnold wanted to count Andreae among the Schwenckfelders, whose judgments against Schwenckfeld he had certainly read in his *Theophilus*.

## The 133rd Accusation:

Arnold presents the following from Johann Valentin Andreae for the supposed reinforcement of his *prejudices* <note>original: "præjudiciorum"</note> and the sought-after benefit of his undertaking. p. 440.

In short: the good man, in his state of mind, was not fit to recognize Mr. Arnold’s intention, and has here continued to burden Mr. Arnold with false suspicion, and thus has not been zealous **according to true knowledge** <note>original: "κατ᾿ ἐπίγνωσιν" (kat' epignōsin). ### The 134th Accusation:

In Part II, page 548, Arnold reports that Johann Valentin Andreae wrote in *Menippus* <note>A satirical work by Andreae criticizing the state of the church</note> No. 24, page 57: that the improvement of the government has made the **Anabaptists** <note>original: "Wiedertäuffer," a radical Reformation group often persecuted by both Catholics and Lutherans</note> more tractable, more experienced in divine matters, and more blameless in life. page 449.

### The 135th Accusation:

It is stated on page 312 that Johann Valentin Andreae calls **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century physician, alchemist, and lay theologian</note> a **"tamer of monsters,"** <note>original: "monstrorum domitorem"</note> and counts him among the wonders of the 16th century, holding him also to be irrefutable. page 450.

### Response:

(1) To this Mr. Carolus adds that he can find nothing of Paracelsus in his copy of the *Menippus* from which these words are taken. But it should be noted a) that Johann Valentin Andreae first published two *Menippus* volumes in duodecimo format, one in the year 1617, namely the **former** <note>original: "priorem"</note>, and the other or **latter** <note>original: "posteriorem"</note> in 1618. Mr. Arnold’s edition is the Cologne one from the year 1673 in octavo, and thus a reprint: but these Latin terms clearly stand there in the cited place, where it says: **"Now Erasmus, a sea of learning—Paracelsus, tamer of monsters—besides many others they have; who would dare compare himself, who would not rather admire their divine geniuses?"** <note>original: "Jam Erasmus eruditionis mare, - - Paracelsus monstrorum domitor, præter complurimos alios quem habent, qui ſe conferre auſit, qui non potius divina eorum ingenia admiretur?"</note> Thus no one has cause to doubt the citation. Regarding β) Mr. Arnold cites not only *Menippus*, but also the **Sacred Mythology** <note>original: "Mythologiam Sacram"</note>, which came out in Strasbourg in 1619 in duodecimo, where the remaining words are to be found, which Mr. Carolus himself **acknowledges** <note>original: "agnosciret"</note>. Therefore, one should not doubt the citations.

(2) He further **objects** <note>original: "excipiret"</note> that the words were to be understood as referring to medical and physical studies. But even if one allows this (although Paracelsus mixed his **theological physics** into everything), it is at least recognizable from this that not all theologians and scholars had such an extreme hatred and loathing of Paracelsus, or **burdened** <note>original: "graviret"</note> him with such fables as Mr. Carolus does here anew, speaking of the pommel of his sword, in which he was said to have had a **familiar spirit**. <note>original: "Spiritum familiarem." Legend claimed Paracelsus kept a demon or "Azoth" in the hilt of his sword.</note>

(3) Mr. Carolus must confess that Johann Valentin Andreae states in the *Mythology*: **"Paracelsus built a new fortress of philosophy and medicine,"** <note>original: "Paracelsus habe novam Philosophiæ Medicinæque arcem"</note> which has not been torn down to this day. There, Andreae also calls it an injury of envy that Paracelsus is supposed to be a **sorcerer** <note>original: "Magus"</note> (which Mr. Carolus should have noted against his own accusation), and that he counts him among the **"greatest geniuses who were wise both above and against the common crowd."** <note>original: "maxima ingenia... quæ supra ſimul ac contra vulgus ſapuerint."</note>

Despite such claims, he remains a friend of the pure, wholesome truth, and through God's grace, he constantly enjoys it in his soul.

(6) Regarding δ) Mr. Carolus wishes to refute Arnold’s claim that V.A. <note>Andreae</note> was not the author of the Rosicrucian fiction. He rejects a) Breckling's report,

which Mr. Arnold cites, and refuses to grant him any experience in such matters, regardless of the fact that the man has concerned himself very seriously with such things for almost half a century <note>Latin: *Seculum*</note>. Therefore, one cannot immediately and completely abandon his report until the remaining foundations <note>Latin: *Fundamenta*</note> are examined, which we have already noted in Part II, No. 97.

(7) He also rejects b) Mr. Arnd’s missive, and does so merely by citing examples of other forged letters; yet regarding this specific one, he does not bring forward the slightest probable doubt <note>Latin: *Dubium*</note>. This is how one finally denies the documents <note>Latin: *Documenta*</note> when one can go no further.

(8) He wishes, however, to immediately prove a false narrative because Mr. Arnold states: J.V.A. wrote in his *Menippus* that the Rosicrucian Brothers organize everything according to Christ's rules; and yet J.V.A. only wrote: *if* they were to do it; which is not the same thing as Arnold reports <note>Latin: *referi*-re</note>. Andreae's words are these, as Mr. Carolus himself repeats them:

> If they (the Rosicrucians) direct their order toward a Christian life, it will truly consist of nothing else but the rules of Christ, which are revealed to us in the Holy Gospel.

Here Mr. Carolus leaves out the following words, which actually belong to the quote:

> for they will not make another Christ, nor make Christians into friends of the world.

(9) Now one should consider Mr. Arnold's sense and intention <note>Latin: *Intention*</note> in this. He believed, just as J.V.A. did, that the Brotherhood was a fiction, and he says immediately <note>Latin: *immediatè*</note> before these words: "Andreae writes of these fictitious brothers thus," and immediately thereafter he adds: "it was only a mockery <note>Latin: *Ludibrium*</note>." Since he held it to be a non-entity <note>Latin: *non ens*</note> (over which Mr. Carolus struggles against him unnecessarily), he could not have believed in any actions <note>Latin: *Affectionen*</note> by these people, and thus no Christian life; for they did not exist in reality <note>Latin: *in rerum natura*</note>. Consequently, he necessarily and obviously spoke only hypothetically <note>Latin: *ex hypothesi*</note>, and specifically from the mouth of Andreae, who presented this only conditionally <note>Latin: *conditionatè*</note>, not absolutely <note>Latin: *absolutè*</note>, as if such people were real or as if they truly organized their lives so Christianly.

Ernst relates that such people existed, and had he then turned this "if" into a "that," or a conditional statement into an absolute one <note>original Latin: "conditionatum in absolutum"</note>, then Mr. Carolus could accuse him of a false report; however, given the aforementioned circumstances, he can never do so, for the subject <note>Latin: "Subjectum"</note> was just as much a fiction as the predicate <note>Latin: "Praedicatum"</note>.

(11) In summary: H. Arnold did not intend to relate anything as if it were a true history, but only to report a fiction <note>original: "Gedichte," here meaning a literary invention or myth</note> and to briefly and summarily repeat the fictional attributes <note>Latin: "Praedicata"</note> of this fiction—namely, that of the Rosicrucians. Mr. Carolus, on the other hand, has viewed this as a historical report, and therefore took Mr. Arnold’s proposition regarding the Christian life of the Rosicrucians as an absolute one <note>Latin: "absolutam simpliciter"</note>, in which he erred and has once again fruitlessly pressured Mr. Arnold. Thus, Carolus himself does not remain with the truth when he accuses H. Arnold of a falsehood, and moreover burdens him with such unchristian suspicion, as if he had twisted the words, which is indeed unjustifiable.

(12) However, he does not achieve his purpose, which is to make the cited manuscripts <note>abbreviated "MSPta"</note> suspicious and useless. Indeed, he can even less answer before God or the world when he writes: Arnold perhaps did not see the manuscripts himself that he cites. This is certainly a truly conscienceless slander, which moreover rests on mere conjectures and nothing else. For if one is finally to deal so godlessly and shamelessly with writers, where will one find any further trust <note>Latin: "fidem"</note>? Are not all printed books first published from manuscripts <note>Latin: "e MSPtis ediret"</note>? Should one therefore resort to such a desperate presumption and say, perhaps the editors had not seen them? Is that theological? Where does the conscience remain? And what Holy Scriptures could such godless suspicion not eventually affect? Why then does one believe the so-called "Innocent News" <note>A contemporary theological journal</note>, which publishes so many letters even against the presumed fanatics? What should one say to that? Yet more is reminded of this in the preface here. One only sees how far desperation drives minds when the testimonies become unbearable to them.

### The 139th Accusation.

That he <note>Arnold</note> refuses to recognize anything good even in Dr. Tobias Wagner. Page 469.

### Response:

Because Mr. Arnold, as noted above, wrote a Universal Church History <note>original Latin: "universal-Kirchen-Historie"</note> and not the *Lives of Theologians* <note>original Latin: "Vitas Theologorum"</note>, it was impossible for him to name each and every theologian, let alone praise the teachers, relatives, or ancestors of everyone who desires it. He writes on page 598 that Dr. Wagner, in his *Refutatory Examination of Speculative Atheism* <note>original Latin: "Examine Elenctico Atheismi Speculativi"</note>, took much from Müller's *Atheism* and sinned against various people through public condemnation. p. 483.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Carolus admits that Dr. Wagner took one thing or another from Müller, but "not very much," and indeed with citation of the author. Therefore, Mr. Arnold’s report remains certain and is not a "scornful jab," as Mr. Carolus perceived it. The reader will not recognize the innocent report as such themselves.

(2) He wants proof of which innocent people Dr. Wagner condemned there? But the proof is easy. Mr. Carolus remains completely silent here regarding the specification of the atheists from **Brecklingen** <note>Referring to Friedrich Breckling (1629–1711), a radical Pietist and critic of the established church</note> condemned by Dr. Wagner. Yet, one should consider whether the old, honest **Breckling** is truly an **atheist**, or could even be called one with any appearance of truth? Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the father of Lutheran Pietism</note>, whom Mr. Carolus praises as a precious theologian, confesses in his *Theological Reflections* <note>original: "Theol. Bedencken P. III. c. 6. p. 189."</note> that he loves him heartily and respects most of his writings—as he does those of Baki and Hochburg—even if not all of them. Nevertheless, Dr. Wagner explicitly places him among the atheists in his *Examination of Atheism* <note>original: "Exam. Ath. pag. 74."</note>, and Colberg repeats this further in his *Platonic Christianity* <note>original: "Platonischen Christenthum I. Th. 5. Cap. p. 250."</note>.

(3) If one says that **Breckling** nevertheless wrote a book titled *The Bible, or the Word of the Devil* <note>original: "Biblia seu Verbum Diaboli"</note>, one should first read Director Lange’s **deduction** <note>A legal or logical presentation of facts</note> on this in his *Sincere Reports* <note>original: "Aufrichtigen Nachrichten I. Th. p. 35. and following"</note>; there, one will find Breckling’s innocence clearly proven in this matter as well, regarding which more will be said below in **Number 147**.

(4) I will not mention how poorly other authors, such as Browne, Angelus Marianus, and the like, are called atheists by Dr. Wagner; who,
