->The 145th Accusation:<-

He claims on page 83 of Part III that Dr. Wagner also scolded Campanella <note>Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), a Dominican friar and philosopher who spent years in prison for his radical ideas</note> as an atheist. p. 487.

->Answer:<-

(1) Dr. Wagner writes in his *Examination of Atheism* page 19 regarding Campanella: <note>original Latin: "Non mirum esse, Viros doctos, qui tantum non ὑπελκόν τι atheisticum his primalitatibus subesse suspicantur."</note> “It is no wonder that learned men suspect something subtly atheistic <note>original Greek: "ὑπελκόν τι" - something underlying or subtly present</note> lies beneath these 'primalities' <note>A technical term in Campanella’s philosophy referring to Power, Wisdom, and Love</note>.” Mr. Arnold now calls this an "evil suspicion" in Chapter 8 of Part III, page 83, § 39, and sets against it the more modest judgments of others, even among theologians, especially the famous Spizelius.

(2) From the latter’s *Letter on Eradicating Atheism* page 42, he first repeats in § 40 the words regarding Campanella’s intention from his preface to *Atheism Triumphed Over* <note>original: "Atheismum triumphatum"</note> (this is what it should be called, though it was changed by a printing error into "triumphalam," for which Mr. Carolus offers a reminder). Afterward, in § 41, Mr. Arnold confesses that Spizelius is not satisfied with Campanella because he based the proof of religion on the following: namely, on the three primalities or pre-eminences, etc. Thus, Mr. Arnold readily admits that Spizelius is not satisfied with Campanella in all things.

(3) In particular, Mr. Arnold cites Reiser's judgment from Spizelius page 43 in § 40: <note>original Latin: "non adeò erraturum, quod libro huic gloriam Atheismi Triumphanti adscriberet."</note> “that one would not err much in ascribing to this book the glory of a **Triumphing Atheism**.” Mr. Arnold had given this in his manuscript expressly and sincerely as "of a triumphing atheism" <note>meaning the book inadvertently promoted atheism</note>. But that the printers made the words **Triumph over Atheism** <note>meaning the book successfully defeated atheism</note> out of it by error—the author cannot be blamed for that, as he was more than 30 miles away from the printing press at the time.

(4) Mr. Carolus has indeed taken the opportunity here to turn this into a "falsehood" and to triumph greatly over it. However, Mr. Arnold has a joyful conscience in this matter, which is not aware of such malice. And how could he

<column-break/>

591 Part IV. 145. N. Mr. Andreas David Carolus etc.
<meta>catchword: accusation</meta>

even have dared to so grossly invert the words of a book? The other words of Reiser regarding Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a major figure in natural law and theology</note> are not softened, but well-expressed; for they read: <note>original Latin: "addita Grotii nota de Campanellæ ad Atheismum propinquitate."</note> “with Grotius's note added regarding Campanella’s proximity to atheism.” This "proximity" is explained in the following words of Spizelius: <note>original Latin: "Neque vero Grotio tantùm & aliis quibusdam nata est hæc suspicio, ipsummet scil. Campanellam Atheismi veneno infectum."</note> “Nor was this suspicion born only to Grotius and certain others, namely that Campanella himself was infected with the poison of atheism.”

(5) Mr. Carolus ponders this and calls it a "deceptively softening review" when Mr. Arnold writes: "of Grotius's concern that Campanella perhaps steps somewhat close to atheism." But does not Spizelius himself call Grotius's opinion a "suspicion" regarding Campanella's approach to atheism? Where then has Mr. Arnold deceived or softened here, without and against Spizelius's meaning and expression? Mr. Carolus simply wanted to have something to accuse him of once again.

(6) It is the same with the verdict of Spizelius, which Mr. Arnold cites from these words on page 44: <note>original Latin: "Etsi de sensu & intentione Campanellæ temerè judicare autem Vaniniani criminis reum peragere haud velim: præsertim cum ex libro ejus colligere nequiverim, eum volentem & scientem tale quid intendisse."</note> “Although I would not wish to judge rashly regarding the sense and intention of Campanella, nor to find him guilty of the crime of Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini, an Italian philosopher executed for atheism in 1619</note>: especially since I could not gather from his book that he intended such a thing willingly and knowingly.” These words, translated into German by Mr. Arnold, Mr. Carolus calls a "falsely alleged verdict." Why? Because Spizelius adds: <note>original Latin: "Attamen in ipso fortalitii istius antiatheistici vestibulo, scil. præfatione, verba notavi, quæ forsan pluribus Autorem suspectum reddidere,"</note> “Yet in the very entrance to that anti-atheistic fortress, namely the preface, I noted words which perhaps made the author suspect to many,” and concludes thereupon: <note>original Latin: "à vero neutiquam aberaffe videntur ii, qui libri ejus parum atheismo noceri, quin potius nonnihil eum promoveri judicarunt."</note> “those who judged that his book harmed atheism little, but rather promoted it somewhat, seem not to have wandered from the truth at all.”

(7) In these words, Spizelius says exactly that, and not the slightest bit more than what he said previously regarding the suspicion; for he says expressly that it seems those had not erred who judged Campanella's book as not harming atheism, but helping it in some way. There he clearly remains by his previous verdict, that Campanella had intended nothing of the sort with knowledge (and thus this promotion of atheism happened from his book without and against his intention); likewise: that he did not want to accuse him of the crime of Vanini.

(8) Why then should Mr. Arnold have withheld such things in a cunning way, or set aside his conscience, since Spizelius consistently remained with his first verdict? and has Mr. Arnold not sufficiently proven thereby that this judgment of Spizelius is more modest than that of Wagner? This was not pleasing to him, and thus such an accusation had to be made.

(3) Thereupon he also repeats from <term>Dr. Wagner’s Occasional Sermons</term> <note>original: "Casual-Predigten." (4) Given these and similar circumstances, an impartial reader cannot be blamed / if he does not flatly trust Dr. Wagner’s counter-arguments and adverse reports / especially since the aforementioned Pastor of Heilbronn also confirmed the above publicly and / as far as is known / has not revoked it / whereas in the legal process against Keilen, his opponent afterwards prevailed. As for what else is held among us Lutherans regarding <term>blood-signs</term> <note>These were "prodigies" or natural omens, like red sap in vines, which contemporaries interpreted as divine warnings of coming war or bloodshed.</note> / and how not everything is simply rejected / that is well known from the recent dispute over the <term>Leipzig Blood-Sign</term> / which was also sufficiently confirmed by the bloody defeat that followed.

### The 151st Accusation:

He criticized on page 544 of Part II, <term>Dr. Johann Adam Osiander</term> <note>A prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian from Tübingen (1622–1697).</note> because he had written to Mr. Wolfgang Förstner: <term>Dury</term> <note>John Dury (1596–1680), a Scottish theologian who traveled Europe trying to unite the Protestant churches.</note> was only a field preacher / had no authority / and was not instructed by the Church for such a great work / etc. page 501.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Carolus brings forward his oft-repeated prejudice / that the manuscripts at Mr. U.'s [Arnold's] house are not to be believed: but one repeats the foundations already often indicated. Yet he finally concedes it / but wishes that no "respect of persons" be concluded from it / despite the fact that Osiander's words undeniably demonstrate it. And because he sees this well / he says further from Meisner and Dannhauer / that not all respect of persons is reprehensible.

(2) This is now admitted in a certain harmless sense / but not in such a case / as this one was with Dury. For there, what <term>James</term> says in Chapter 2:1 applies expressly: <note>original: "Haltet es nicht dafür / daß der Glaube an JEsum Christum Ansehung der person leyde."</note> Do not hold the faith of Jesus Christ with respect of persons. For such <term>partiality</term> <note>original Greek: "προσωποληψία" (prosōpolēpsia), meaning showing favoritism based on status.</note> is ruinous among preachers / because it suppresses others due to their lesser gifts, even though for all faithful ministers there is

one office, one preaching <note>original Latin: "unum officium, una prædicatio"</note>, as <term>Gerhard</term> <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran theologian.</note> well reminds us in his *Homilies on the Gospel for the 4th Sunday of Advent*, homily 3, page 79. (3) Regarding Dury’s person, it is not necessary to dispute here. Here it only concerns us / that Mr. Carolus denies / that "the Church" in common style is understood to mean "the Clergy." And so it always sounds in such writings.

Whereby he [Campanella] suspects / it may be an angel or a <term>spirit</term> <note>original Latin: "dæmon"</note>, such as was with Socrates.

The conclusion is indeed obvious / that Campanella had more to do with the Devil than with God / and that Osiander uses this / to make Campanella suspicious / against his clear words / since he [Campanella] indeed mentions an angel first / by which he, as is well known, understands a middle-spirit / which the philosophers called a <term>daemon</term> <note>original Greek: "δαίμονα," referring to a guiding spirit or supernatural power, not necessarily an evil one in the classical sense.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold (Mr. A.) against Andreas David Carolus (Mr. Car.). The previous page discussed accusations regarding Arnold's honesty in citations and his treatment of theologians who labeled others as "companions of the devil." This page moves into a philological debate over the Latin word "laudare" and the nature of academic disputation.</meta>

<page-num>600</page-num>
<header>600 Answer to the so-called Württemberg Innocence, Part IV. [Accusations] 155. 156. N.</header>

The grammarian Nonius Marcellus, in *On the Propriety of Speech*, chapter IV, Number 276, writes: *To praise [laudare] is to extol with words; likewise, "to praise" also signifies "to name."* This grammarian, however, is praised by Jacob Gothofredus as one to be highly esteemed <note>original: "magnificiendum"</note>, in his notes on the *Theodosian Code*, Vol. I, p. 207. Pure Latinity also entails this; for example, when Cicero writes in Book III of *On the Orator*, chapter 18: *I can cite <note>original: "laudare"</note> most certain authors,* and other classical authors do the same.

(4) Mr. Carolus creates a false rule against the consensus of all ancient Latinity and against common usage, claiming that one uses the word **only when citing an author for a second time.** But who told him that? One clearly sees that he does not want it to appear as if his father [Carolus Senior] praised Scultetus, a Reformed theologian. But what is: α) blameworthy in the aforementioned counsel against polemical writings? β) Have not other Lutherans praised his books, especially the *Marrow of the Fathers* <note>original: "Medullam Patrum"</note>, the *Annals*, and the like? Indeed, did not Carolus Senior himself praise him as "most skilled in the knowledge of antiquity and ecclesiastical history, beyond theological science"? <note>original: "præter Theologicam Scientiam Antiquitatis & Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ peritissimum"</note> (Book III, *Memorabilia*, ch. 31, p. 613). How Seckendorf, Tribbechov, and other Lutherans praise him can be seen in Sagittarius’s *Introduction to Church History*, pp. 315 and 344. What more is it then, if he is also called "praised by Carolus" <note>original: "à Carolo laudatus"</note>? Must one therefore extend the praise from the person to his polemical writings? How suspicious <note>original: "supçonneux"</note> one is being there!

### The 156. Accusation:

He reports on p. 490, Part II, that Carolus, in his *Memorabilia* p. 618, placed an epigram by [John] Owen concerning the dispute between the Giessen and Tübingen [theologians]: *The elders strive,* etc. p. 524.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Carolus says his father placed this out of compassion and sadness; but regarding Mr. A., he thinks he "tickled himself" with it, expressed his embittered thoughts, rejected all disputation, etc., which he intends to prove with several citations.

(2) On the contrary, Mr. A.’s conscience bears witness to the misery and pain with which he viewed the great disunity at the universities and elsewhere for many years, and subsequently wrote about it. He does not deny that, given the great absurdities, he sometimes broke out into certain expressions that could have been more compassionate and earnest. But in the matter itself, he saw himself more than firmly grounded. And when Mr. Carolus, from

<page-num>601</page-num>
<header>Part IV. [Accusations] 156. 157. N. Citation of Andreas David Carolus, etc. 601</header>

Owen presents other epigrams to him, one could have presented many others in return that would have been useful to him, had he lived to see it. For example, the following from Book III, epigram 120:

> Theologians strive, and the lawsuit is still before the judge:
> O would that the whole lawsuit were before the judge!
> Would that there were as much strife of Love within us,
> As there is love of Strife in these torn times!
> <note>original: "Theologi certant, & adhuc sub judice lis est: / O utinam lis sub judice tota foret! / Tanta vel in nobis utinam lis esset Amoris, / Quantus in hoc lacero tempore Litis amor!"</note>

All of Owen is full of such necessary warnings to the Lords Disputants. See also Mr. Calvör’s *Pipes of Zion* <note>original: "Fistulas Sionis"</note> p. 616, where even this same Mr. Carolus Senior is attributed with "rather harsh bits" regarding <term>syncretism</term> <note>syncretism: the attempt to reconcile different Christian denominations, often viewed negatively by 17th-century orthodox theologians as a dangerous compromise of truth</note>, which could easily stir up strife.

### The 157. Accusation:

He says on p. 490 that Carolus admits on p. 619 that in this controversy, people disputed more "scholastically than ecclesiastically" (or more pedantically than edifyingly). p. 526.

### Answer:

(1) If Mr. Carolus did not have such an idolatrous concept of these same disputants, he would not have been so opposed to these added words (which are not actually an explanation, but only incidental thoughts of the reporter). The term "pedantic" is now quite common for useless school matters that do not serve improvement, and it requires no application of the definition by Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret was a mystic and philosopher whose definitions of "pedantry" were often debated in these circles</note>—of which Mr. A. never thought—but only of the useless Aristotelian disputes. The writings in this matter indeed show that people appealed to and based themselves on Aristotelian philosophy. Menzer repeats the words of a Württemberg theologian in the *Disputation on the 4 Questions* and appeals in § 182 to the Aristotelian <term>power</term> <note>original Greek: "δυναμιν" (dynamin). In Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to potentiality or the inherent force of a thing.</note>. That is certainly "scholastic" enough.

(2) Mr. A. does not say that those theologians were "vain, puffed-up fools," as Mr. Carolus accuses him; rather, he only indicates the misery of such disputes, which raise more questions than [they lead to] improvement toward God in faith. Mr. Carolus could well have spared himself the indignation. He also cannot prove that Mr. A. did not deal conscientiously and honestly with Carolus's words; for he left Carolus's words as they are, and only added his own thoughts, which Mr. Carolus cannot forbid anyone to do.

(3) And it is most distressing that he wants to persuade us that this conflict between those of Giessen <note>theologians from the University of Giessen</note> and those of Tübingen <note>theologians from the University of Tübingen</note> was edifying, when he himself admits that things occurred therein which were not edifying; just as he above in Number 40, § 2, called the Tübingen theologians "good soldiers of *JESUS Christ*." The *Solid Decision* <note>original: "Solida Decisio," a core Lutheran theological document</note> of the Saxon theologians, in the prefaced Electoral Mandate, explicitly acknowledged on page A. 3. that the **disagreeing parties** <note>original: "partes diffidentes"</note> accumulated **new, subtle questions** <note>original: "quæstiones novas subtiles"</note>, called the **genuine sense** <note>original: "genuinum sensum"</note> of the **Formula of Concord** <note>original: "Form. Concord."</note> into doubt, and each party cited it for their own side. It was also noted that the **amicable settlement** <note>original: "amicabilis compositio"</note> was not equally pleasing to all, and that no small offense was given through the **polemical writings** <note>original: "scripta polemica"</note>; indeed, a **stumbling block** was laid for posterity. That is certainly not edification. Thus, Mr. Carolus Junior, against all evidence and experience, wants to present common disputation as edifying for the knowledge of *Jesus Christ*, even though **Carolus Senior in this case** <note>original: "Carolus Sen. in hoc casu," referring to the elder Carolus</note> himself lamented so many **excesses**.

### The 158th Accusation:

> He [Arnold] writes on page 501, Part II, concerning the **Berlin Tumult**, stating that even Lutheran writers recount it and do not deny that it arose from the scolding of the preachers; among these, he also cites **Carolus** on page 529.

### Answer:

(1) Mr. Carolus forms three questions from this: 1) Whether the undertaking of the mob was a rebellion? This he wishes to deny, and yet he himself writes: that the mob gathered together, stormed houses, and did so with full fury; that the heat was great, that an **"Unmerciful" Sunday** <note>original: "Immisericordiæ," a pun on "Misericordia," the Sunday of Mercy</note> was made of it, and a very wicked Vespers service was held with gruesome **excesses**. He admits it was an unchristian revenge. But he claims it was not directed against the sovereign authority, even though the Margrave himself, as Governor (and thus the commanding authority), had to **retreat** <note>original: "retiriren"</note> from the street into the palace, and ten of the Elector's servants were murdered. Finally, he concludes it was a riot and not a rebellion, regardless of the fact that his own father in his **Memorable Deeds** <note>original: "Memorab."</note> and Clüver in his **Historical Letters** <note>original: "Epist. Hist."</note> call it a **sedition** <note>original: "Seditionem"</note>; the former on page 377, the latter on page 772. Had the Reformed <note>Calvinists</note> done this in **Stuttgart**, it would surely have been called something much worse.

(2) The 2nd question is: Whether it arose from the scolding of the Lutheran preachers? Mr. Arnold recounts this because it happened **immediately** <note>original: "immediatè"</note> on that Sunday evening, right after the preachers had **zealously spoken out** early that morning against the Reformed. Mr. Carolus says that not all scolding by preachers is blameworthy,

<column-break/>

and neither was the scolding back then. He **expostulates** <note>demands an explanation</note> with Mr. Arnold as if he [Arnold] wanted to make himself popular with the Reformed—to whom Arnold attributed the "storming" of altars, baptismal fonts, and images—and sing the **"I shall please"** <note>original: "Placebo," meaning to act as a sycophant</note> to them. However, his [Arnold's] conscience gave him a different testimony. And Mr. Carolus himself admits that Mr. Arnold also attributes the causes to the removal of altars and the like. He [Arnold] found these proceedings of the mob to be wrong; therefore, he wrote the course of events as they were, and Mr. Carolus contradicts him in vain.

(3) The 3rd question of Mr. Carolus is: What did **Carolus Senior** admit regarding this? He admits in **Book II, chapter 24, page 377** that in **Berlin** it had nearly reached a **grim insurrection** <note>original: "truculenta seditione"</note>; and in the **Summaries**: "the Berlin Tumult" <note>original: "tumultum Berolinensem"</note>. The son, however, does not want to admit that he [his father] called it a rebellion by that name, because "sedition" <note>original: "Seditio"</note> is not yet equivalent to a "faction," let alone a "rebellion," for which he cites **Ausonius Popma** <note>a 16th-century Dutch grammarian</note>. But I would like to know how else he would translate the word *Seditio* into German other than "uprising" [Aufruhr], as all **lexicographers** <note>dictionary writers</note> give it. Uprising and rebellion are surely the same thing. And why even ask, since in this **case** <note>original: "casu"</note> the Governor himself, according to **Carolus's** report, is said to have been **received with countless insults and pelted with stones and musket balls** <note>original: "innumeris contumeliis exceptus, lapidibus & globulis jaculatoriis petitus"</note>?

(4) Mr. Carolus exerts himself very fiercely here to **legitimize** his father's report and **criticizes** a great deal without necessity. He argues that when the father reports on the sharp preaching against one another, it is not meant to imply a **causal connection and influence** <note>original: "nexum & influxum causalem"</note>. But what is the need for such **abstract hair-splitting** <note>original: "abstraktiven Scrupulirens"</note>? It is enough that the **connection and influence are clear from the effect**, and the main issue itself lies plainly there in these and other writers. Mr. Arnold did not use **Carolus** as a false witness or distort him, as the hateful accusation claims; Mr. Carolus can prove nothing of the sort. He also remains silent regarding what his father reports there about a letter of protection from the **Elector of Brandenburg**.

### The 159th Accusation:

> He [Arnold] takes the side of the **Socinians** <note>a non-trinitarian Christian group considered heretical by both Lutherans and Catholics</note> on page 558, Part II, and says that **Carolus** calls the **Work of the Library of the Unitarians worthy of hell, not the press** <note>original: "Opus Bibliothecæ Unitariorum orco dignum, non prelo," p. 533</note>.

### Answer:

(1) Here Mr. Carolus **thunders** <note>original: "detoniret"</note> once again against Mr. Arnold, claiming he [Arnold] considers all poison, lies, disgrace, and blasphemy to be good and right, etc. But what purpose do such incessant accusations serve without grounded proof? They only give their inventors something to answer for, and they do not harm Mr. Arnold, who knows himself to be better than that. Against the gruesome...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold (referred to as "Mr. A.") against the attacks of Andreas David Carolus ("Mr. Car."). The previous page discussed the theological tensions between the universities of Giessen and Tübingen, specifically critiquing Carolus’s view that these bitter disputes were "edifying." Here, the text shifts to accusations regarding Arnold’s supposed sympathy for Socinians and his critique of Carolus's harsh rhetoric.</meta>

604 Answer to the so-called Württemberg Innocence Part IV. Num. 159.

Regarding the horrible blasphemies of <term>Socinianism</term> <note>A non-trinitarian movement following the teachings of Socinus, which denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, the necessary observations have already been made in Part I, Numbers 41 and 71, and in Part II, Numbers 6, 20, 25, 26, and 27.

(2) Mr. Carolus says on page 534 that Mr. Arnold misses the truth by saying that salvation is absolutely denied to the <term>Socinians</term> in polemical writings. But is this not to be seen in all books written against the <term>Socinians</term>? Mr. Carolus wants to help himself out with a limitation—namely, that they are denied salvation only insofar as they do not repent. However, is this same limitation not also understood in the condemnation of Pagans, Jews, and Turks, and yet salvation is still denied to them in general terms?

(3) Regarding the words of Carolus, Mr. Arnold cites them as an example of dubious and untheological formulas; specifically, because it is said of a book that it is worthy of hell and not of the printing press. That is indeed dubious, and not spoken so wisely or accurately and theologically, to say that a book, as a lifeless thing, belongs to hell. Mr. Arnold has himself recognized the errors found therein as highly dangerous, and he made his confession most recently in the preface to the <term>Twelve Pronouncements of the Jewish Church</term> <note>original: "All-XII Ausspruch der Jüdischen Kirche," a work by Arnold</note> against the <term>Unitarians</term> <note>Another term for those who rejected the Trinity</note>. But who would actually wish to consign a book itself to hell?

(4) Mr. Carolus would not have needed such an extensive proof against this <term>Library</term> <note>Likely referring to the *Bibliotheca Antitrinitariorum*, a bibliography of anti-trinitarian works</note>; for who that acknowledges the deity of JESUS Christ would deny that such errors are contained within it? It is only that saying the book itself is "worthy of hell" was spoken more out of **hasty zeal** <note>original: "precipitantem Eyffer"</note> than with proper theological accuracy. Christ indeed called the Pharisees, as persons, children of hell, but not their books. Therefore, this **passage** <note>original: "Locus"</note> proves nothing either. But what is the need to quarrel much over this?

(5) The good man <note>Carolus</note> is so incensed by his affection for his father that he finally breaks out on page 538: saying that Arnold has attacked Christ himself more than he attacked Carolus. Indeed, he calls upon Christ against Arnold, that He should publicly judge one day what was done by Carolus and what was done by Arnold, whom he calls a "lover of Christ's enemies" in this matter!

(6) Regarding this **appeal to God's judgment** <note>original: "Provocation auf GOttes Gericht"</note>, I remember what I once read in **Hilary of Poitiers** <note>An influential 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> in his *Commentary on Psalm 119, page 463*, where a very serious warning is given: <note>original: "Arduum esse & naturæ humanæ periculosissimum, Dei desiderare judicia. Quum enim nemo vivens in conspectu ipsius mundus sit, quomodo desiderabile ejus potest esse judicium? An quum ex omni otioso verbo rationem sumus præstituri, diem judicii concupiscimus, in quo nobis est ille indefessus ignis obeundus?"</note> "It is a difficult thing and most dangerous to human nature to desire the judgments of God. Since no living person is pure in His sight, how can His judgment be desirable? Or since we must give an account for every idle word, do we long for the day of judgment, in which we must undergo that unwearied fire?" etc.

---

605 Part IV. 159. 160. N. Mr. Andr. David Carolus etc. 605

(7) Even our own theologians have considered such a manner to be unchristian and have thoroughly **vindicated** the misused scriptural passages. **Dr. Johann Ernst Gerhard** has explained this well in his *Disputation on the Appeal to Jesus Christ as Judge*, and finally concluded on page 51: <note>original: "Intueamur atque imitemur ipsius dulcissimi Salvatoris nostri mansuetudinem, qui non maledicebat, nec ad severum ac vindex Dei judicium eos provocabat, sed pro illis ardenter orabat."</note> "Let us look upon and imitate the gentleness of our sweetest Savior himself, who did not speak evil, nor did he provoke them to the severe and vengeful judgment of God, but prayed ardently for them." And **Dr. Quenstedt**, in his work *On the Provocation of an Enemy to the Supreme Judge Jesus Christ*, proves very well in § 5 and following that <note>original: "non licere Christiano homini ad judicium divinum appellare"</note> "it is not permitted for a Christian man to appeal to divine judgment." The elder **Dr. Vincentius Schmuck** of Leipzig also warns well in his *Commentary on Genesis, Chapter 15, page 154*: We should rightly have a great fear of treating God's judgment lightly or being quick to appeal to it. Had Mr. Carolus first taken this to heart, he would not have broken out into such parting words, which may God not count against him!

(8) Here we see a sad example of **natural zeal** <note>Passionate emotion not governed by divine grace</note> that is not truly and divinely tempered according to knowledge. Dear Mr. Carolus likely meant well and thought how righteous his zeal against Mr. Arnold was. However, it is to be feared that this anger may have greatly harmed his health and hastened his death, which is a lamentable fruit of such zeal—one in which others might see their own reflection! May the LORD also graciously forgive him this **excess** and misuse of the name of JESUS! Meanwhile, Mr. Arnold, with all the joy of his conscience in the Holy Spirit, can now and one day testify before God that he wishes to honor, love, and praise Jesus as his only Lord and God above all things, even amidst all the shame heaped upon him by his detractors. Furthermore, he is a "lover of Jesus' enemies" no further than according to Christ's own word and example: insofar as they are fellow creatures, and according to that universal love with which he is obligated to love all poor, erring people, and is willing to do so according to the Spirit.

### The 160th Accusation.

He claims on page 606 of Part II that Mr. Arnold speaks in favor of the <term>Religion of the Prudent</term> <note>original: "Religioni Prudentum"; a term often used for a minimalist or rationalist approach to faith that avoids dogmatic conflict</note> and complains that in the 17th century it became almost common to attribute such a "Theology of the Prudent" to many people (page 539).

The discussion focuses on whether Arnold supported the "Religion of the Prudent" and his treatment of the scholar Thomas Reinesius, whom Carolus's father had harshly criticized.</meta>

<header>606 Response to the so-called Württemberg Innocence Part IV. 160. 161. N.</header>

### Answer:

(1) The first point is clearly false—namely, that Mr. Arnold is said to speak in favor of this so-called religion. For a) Mr. Carolus refutes himself by admitting that Arnold complains that many people have been accused of such things. Now, whatever an author complains about—specifically that it is attributed to honorable people—he cannot possibly regard as good or laudable; otherwise, he would not complain about it but rather praise it. For example, if someone complains that Mr. Carolus has accused Arnold of <term>Socinianism</term> <note>A non-trinitarian doctrine that denied the full divinity of Christ, viewed as a major heresy at the time.</note>, he would certainly not consider this erroneous teaching to be good or speak in its favor.

(2) Secondly, b) Mr. Arnold's own words in the cited passage (Chapter 16, Book XVII, § 21) also refute him. In the preceding § 20, Mr. Arnold had concluded: unfortunately, all lands were full of <term>Naturalists</term> <note>In the 17th century, this referred to those who prioritized natural reason over divine revelation.</note>. Then, in § 21, he begins: To this category (the <term>Naturalists</term>), one also reckons the <term>Religion of the Prudent</term> <note>original: "Religionem Prudentum"</note>, by virtue of which some are said to select for themselves at their own pleasure what they wish to believe or not (according to Kromayer’s definition). And he further observes: this name has also likely been innocently applied to many, as is common in this wicked world, etc.

(3) Thus, Mr. Arnold clearly considers this title of the <term>Religion of the Prudent</term> to be a term of abuse that is applied to many innocent people in this wicked world. How, then, can he be speaking in favor of this religion? He did indeed describe several persons there, but quite impartially noted their vices, even their <term>monstrous opinions</term> <note>original: "monstra opinionum"</note>: of which we shall immediately hear an example that will further clarify the matter. Meanwhile, one may consult Mr. Dr. Rechenberg's little book <term>On the Religion of Prudentius</term> <note>original: "de Religione Prudentii"</note>, where much of note will be found.

## The 161st Accusation.

He presents an example of this from Thomas Reinesius and cites Carolus's *Memorabilia*, Book VI, p. 97, who complains about him and calls him a <term>sycophant</term> <note>original: "Sycophantam"; here meaning a malicious informer or deceiver.</note>. p. 539.

### Answer:

(1) Regarding this Reinesius, Mr. Arnold later writes quite impartially in § 23 that he was stubborn and proud, and had wasted noble time with much useless criticism of pagan and idolatrous things. Indeed, he generally estimated that many a man may have

surely harbored countless <term>monstrous opinions</term> <note>original: "monstra opinionum"</note> in his heart, etc.

(2) Nevertheless, Mr. Carolus says that Mr. Arnold was annoyed by what Carolus wrote about Reinesius. But why should it annoy him, since he himself did not approve of this man’s affairs? One cannot find a single syllable in Mr. Arnold’s text from which any annoyance can be detected. Rather, it was Mr. Carolus who was annoyed that his father’s harsh insults against this learned man were noted.

(3) He claims that Mr. Arnold acted just like Reinesius and spoke of Lutheran preachers and professors in an even more <gloss>scabious</gloss> <note>Meaning scurrilous, offensive, or "itchy" with insults.</note> manner, etc. This is simply piling complaint upon complaint without proving anything; indeed, it is an open injustice toward the accused. For when Mr. Arnold speaks in § 21 of human books that cite Scripture in a perverted way but actually teach human decrees above and alongside it, he refers—as the whole context shows—to the private writings of those people who arrogate to themselves the right to make decisions in divine matters.

(4) Mr. Carolus, however, turns these into <term>Symbolic Books</term> <note>The official confessional documents of the Lutheran Church, such as the Augsburg Confession.</note> and claims that Mr. Arnold scolded them as the decrees of a single faction, or as the "sores" of the ancients. But where does a word about <term>Symbolic Books</term> appear there? Or where are they scolded? Is it enough to simply accuse in this way? Is that "innocence"? Or what author can remain innocent in the face of such procedures and forced interpretations?

(5) Mr. Carolus himself calls Reinesius a very learned <term>physician</term> <note>original: "Medicum"</note>; he was also the court <term>physician</term> to the Prince of Saxony and an Electoral Councilor, as well as Mayor of Altenburg. Furthermore, this man otherwise led a secluded life, wronged or deceived no one, but rather helped others gladly. The gentlemen of Leipzig also mention his <term>peaceful death</term> <note>original: "placidi obitus"</note> and other things quite honorably in the *Acts of the Learned* <note>original: "Act. Erud."</note> for the year 1682, page 92. I also recall that he made a significant foundation for poor students at a gymnasium established near Altenburg. He also enjoys the reputation among the learned of having been <term>most learned both in his art and in all literature</term> <note>original: "tam in sua arte, quam in omni literatura doctissimus"</note>, as Morhofius writes in Book I of his *Polyhistory*, chapter 23, page 287. Professor Schurzfleisch used to call him simply <term>a man of the highest erudition</term> <note>original: "summae eruditionis virum"</note>, and Professor Feller of Leipzig called him <term>the most accurate oracle of all antiquity</term> <note>original: "accuratissimum omnis antiquitatis oraculum"</note>, and likewise <term>multifaceted</term> <note>original: "multifcium"</note>.

(6) Now, Mr. Carolus Senior called this man a <term>sycophant</term> and a deceiver of people, a word of which Mr. Carolus Junior himself confesses

that it means, according to the most common definition, a backbiter or slanderer; he even proves this himself from Plutarch, and adds that his father had used the word here in such a most famous sense <note>original: "famosissimi"</note>; but he could not, in good conscience, present it otherwise, in order to rescue our teachers and doctrine. However, it was nevertheless settled with just a single word, etc.

(7) Scholars know that this abusive word means nothing better than the word "rogue" <note>German: "Schelm," a term for a dishonest or villainous person</note>. In Aristophanes' *Plutus*, Drama 1, Scene 1, line 30, **sycophants** <note>original: "συκοφάνται"</note> are counted among **temple-robbers**, **the wicked** <note>original: "ἱεροσύλους, πονηροὺς"</note>, and similar rascals. Suidas, in his entry on this word, which describes its origin, finally concludes that the Devil is such a one: **The Devil is a sycophant, for he slandered God.** <note>original: "Συκοφάντης ὁ διάβολος, τὸν γὰρ θεὸν ἐσυκοφάντησε"</note> Among the jurists, Alciatus (Book X, *Parerga*, chapter 4, page 560, Volume IV of his Works) and others interpret it as **wicked litigants** and **calumniators** <note>original: "improbos litigatores und calumniatores"</note>. Thus, it is certain that Reinesius is here as good as scolded as a rogue, deceiver, and slanderer.

(8) However, one might well ask whether it excuses a person before men if they call someone a "deceiver of land and people" and then say it was done "with a good conscience"? Whether and how much the doctrine has been "rescued" by this abusive word, and whether one cannot, with a single word, represent an honorable man so dishonorably that nothing more is needed? This is how miserably they excuse unchristian treatment, of which Mr. Arnold <note>H. A.</note> has also experienced enough. What Mr. Carolus <note>H. Car.</note> attaches there against Mr. Arnold applies to himself regarding such maintained abusive words—and indeed all the more so, because he insults one to whom he has not proven the insult applies.

### The 162nd Accusation:

->On page 615 of the second part, he counts Carolus among the writers who have given a completely false account of the entire life of Weigel <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and mystic whose writings were controversial for their spiritualist leanings.</note> throughout, etc.<-

### Answer.

(1) Mr. Carolus, following Erasmus, calls this an **atrocious insult** <note>original: "atrox convitium"</note>, and thus takes Mr. Arnold's observation of the false description of Weigel’s life as absolute and unconditional. This is despite the fact that Arnold excused these authors, including Carolus, on the grounds that they were deceived by the false report of the Senior Minister of Hamburg. Now, since Carolus Senior, in his report (Book I, *Memorabilia*, chapter 1, page 40), also added the word **it is reported** <note>original: "ferunt"</note> or "it is said," this observation cannot apply to him absolutely, and Mr. Carolus Junior complains about it unfairly.

<meta>catchword: (2) Because</meta>

<column-break/>

<header>IV. TH. 162. N. Mr. Andreas David Carolus etc. 609</header>
<page-num>609</page-num>

(2) Because Carolus Senior followed Schelhammer in his report, Mr. Carolus Junior wishes to defend him. He first presses the word "deceive," as if it were injurious, though **constantly** <note>original: "toto die"</note> this term is used for reports that are not grounded in themselves, yet are not brought forward out of malicious intent. Mr. Doctor Diecmann writes in the Preface to Arnd's *True Christianity*, page 45, regarding Carolus Senior: **Therefore, Mr. Carolus was mistaken** <note>original: "Falſius itaque eſt Dn. Carolus"</note>—namely, regarding a historical circumstance. For that reason, it is not immediately an **insult** <note>original: "Injuriæ"</note>. Schelhammer certainly reported it as he held it to be true; therefore, he could not have had any malice or evil purpose here.

(3) As for the matter itself—that Valentin Weigel is not to be confused with Vigelius of Mansfeld—this was very clearly proven in Saxony by Magister Rotthe in his *Instruction on Prophetic Predictions* (which Mr. Arnold also cites) from clear documents in Chapter 17 of Book XVII, § 2 and following. In this, one must believe those from Meissen more, because Weigel was raised, lived, and died in Meissen. Mr. Carolus has only wasted his noble time with such unnecessary hair-splitting and did not consider how short his remaining time in the world might be! He finally gives the deciding factor himself: whether this Weigel was from Mansfeld or Meissen did not matter. And yet he starts disputing all over again on page 543 about whether Weigel was born in Meissen, etc.

(4) He also disputes further: Whether Weigel died in the ministry and was buried in the church? He denies this against the testimony of so many learned people in Meissen, who long ago demonstrated this in public writings from the church records and from the tombstone still lying in the church at Zschopau, which Mr. Arnold describes from Magister Rotthe's *Instruction*. He questions and plagues himself over the gravestone—one has to wonder how it happened, who made it, when, why, what the inscription says, etc. And yet everything is clear before one's eyes; Mr. Doctor Geyer and others have shown it long ago. Why then is so much disputing and waste of time necessary?

(5) Even more superfluous words are made about Weigel's ministry, whether he remained in it until death, etc. The matter is once again settled among scholars, however many conjectures Mr. Carolus may make about it on page 545 to rescue his father, who explicitly writes on page 40: **that he was removed from the pastoral office in Zschopau** <note>original: "Ab officio Paſtoratus Tſchiopenſis remotum eſſe"</note>, and therefore calls him an **erroneous vagabond** <note>original: "vagabundum erroneum"</note>—all contrary to clear history.

That he <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and philosopher whose mystical writings were published posthumously and became controversial.</note> was rejected after his death, and that many writings were published as his own which he did not actually write, is no less well known. The circumstances regarding the signing of the **Formula of Concord** <note>The definitive doctrinal standard of the Lutheran Church, completed in 1577.</note> and similar matters have already appeared in the *Church and Heretic History*.

(6) That Weigel was supposedly truly under suspicion during his lifetime is something Mr. Carolus cannot possibly claim from Weigel's *Conversation on True Christianity*, p. 40: for he understands clearly enough the suspicion that would follow from a refusal to sign the **Formula of Concord**, but not that he had already been under suspicion beforehand.

(7) Mr. Carolus continues—regardless of the fact that these things do not concern the people of Württemberg—to reason about the "obscurity" of Weigel reported by Mr. Arnold, and wants to prove from other passages that his teachings could indeed be understood. However, Mr. Arnold speaks there in section 7 specifically about Weigel’s true meaning—particularly in his **alchemical** <note>original: "Chymischen"</note> and other modes of speech—and not about what others took from his words. He has not denied, however, that much of it should be popular and intelligible. The other alchemical and similar formulas were certainly so dark that those who refuted them likely erred regarding their true meaning. Just as the preface to Schelhammer's book expressly says: his matters were "too high," p. C. 4. But the matters themselves are left unexamined here.

(8) Mr. Carolus impresses once again on page 549 his often-repeated accusation, and particularly contradicts this presentation by Arnold from the last section of Chapter 17:
> "In every way, alas! constant practice and experience teach that most of what those—who praise themselves as orthodox and pure among all parties—have rejected as **Enthusiastic**, **Weigelian**, and the like, has come from the true Spirit of Jesus Christ himself, and that the Spirit has thereby been shamelessly blasphemed by them."

(9) Mr. Arnold had previously proven this a) from the mourning verses of **Gerhard** <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note>:
> **Whoever in this age zealously pursues the study of piety, he is considered a Rosicrucian or a Weigelian. Poisonous calumny has not feared to spread the same about me, etc.** <note>original: "Qui studium hoc ævo pietatis gnaviter urget, Ille Rosæcrucius vel Weigelianus habetur. De me non verita est virosa calumnia id ipsum Spargere &c."</note>

b) from Dr. **J. V. Andreae's** <note>Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), a theologian and social reformer often associated with the Rosicrucian manifestos.</note> *Inaugural Oration*, p. 86, where he complains that not only was **Arnd** <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), author of "True Christianity."</note> called a Weigelian (which we, alas! have seen above from **Osiander** <note>Lucas Osiander the Younger, a fierce critic of Arndt.</note> No. 125), but that also **Satan** wants to defile **all those** with such an infamous name who showed sincerity in

godliness and church discipline, so that it almost does not help anymore, and so on.

(10) Here these two Lutheran theologians clearly confess (along with Dr. B. Meisner in his *Preface to the Evangelical Festival Meditations*) that what the Holy Spirit has worked has been rejected as "Weigelian"; indeed, that Satan has so named all those who were earnestly godly. Other Lutheran theologians have also raised similar complaints, such as **Lassenius** in his *Political Atheist Secrets* <note>original: "Arcanis Ath. Even Mr. Carolus himself admits this elsewhere on page 453, where he cites J. V. Andreae’s complaint about this from Mr. Arnold’s *Church and Heretic History*. Mr. Arnold observes this here as well, yet still limits it by saying he does not speak of everyone, but of most. By this, he admits there is also much that is called Weigelian that does not come from the Holy Spirit.

(11) What does Mr. Carolus judge of this? He says on page 549: the Lord Jesus should open Arnold's eyes so that he recognizes what he has written here: for it is "horrible," and so on. An impartial reader, however, will have already recognized that Mr. Arnold has written the clear truth here, with and from Gerhard and others. Whoever finds such things horrible or highly presumptuous should have searched for the cause within himself. And how ready and willing Mr. Arnold would be to retract if he were truly convicted of error.

(12) The good Mr. Carolus rages here once again without true understanding, and thinks Mr. Arnold is speaking in the aforementioned words about Weigel’s actual teachings or speeches; whereas he is only speaking of what has come from the Holy Spirit itself; and of that, he says with Gerhard and Andreae that it has often been called "Weigelian." And oh, if only it were not true of those above-mentioned contradictions by Osiander, which Mr. Carolus still wants to justify! (One may see more concerning "Weigelian" abusive words above in Part II, No. 19.)

(13) Furthermore, Mr. Carolus wants to prove that nothing was added or lied about in the **Schelhammer** report concerning Weigel. Mr. Arnold had proven it with two examples. The first is: Schelhammer only conjectures that Weigel might have read **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note>, **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, and the like; others presented this as a certain historical fact, in which context he cites Hornbeek, Kromayer, and others, whose passages were examined above in Part II, No. 19.

(14) Carolus Senior <note>Andreas Carolus (1649–1715), a Lutheran theologian who was a critic of Arnold.</note> also states this as a certain matter and adds even more such books to it in the cited location, page 40: <note>original: "non nisi Hermetis, T. Paracelsi scripta nocturna diurnaque manu volvens & revolvens"</note> "turning over day and night in his hands the writings of none but Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note>, the Sibyls, Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous 16th-century occultist.</note>, and especially Paracelsus <note>The Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>." He also cites no one but Hornbeck and Kromayer; however, these men lived long after Weigel and refer to no one else from whom they might have obtained this information.

(15) Thus, Mr. Carolus must finally help himself on page 550 with this excuse: that whoever knows how to report something with truth about Weigel may do so with good reason, even if Schelhammer <note>Gunther Christoph Schelhammer, a contemporary scholar.</note> had only mere conjectures about it—indeed, even if nothing at all were to be found in his work. But where is this truth, and from where did these authors, upon whom Carolus Senior relies, obtain it?

(16) However, this was already discussed in the aforementioned place, and Mr. Arnold has never denied that Paracelsus was read by Weigel, about which there is no need for dispute. But Carolus Senior added Agrippa and Cardanus <note>Gerolamo Cardano, an Italian polymath.</note> without any foundation, and thus against the truth. Now, if Mr. Carolus calls upon everyone to judge this matter, one can allow it all the more confidently, because the matter has now become even clearer: that Mr. Arnold wrote correctly.

(17) The other example—wherein the authors added more than they found in Schelhammer—concerns Weigel’s citation before the Consistory <note>A church administrative council or court.</note>, his examination, and his removal from office. Schelhammer had written of this only quite conjecturally and uncertainly: that "the universities would doubtless have finally become aware of his heresy," etc. Others, however, and among them Carolus Senior, state this absolutely as a certain fact, and call him "removed from office" and a "wandering vagabond," as is written above in section 5. Mr. Arnold demonstrated the contrary irreffutably in section 3, chapter 17.

(18) Notwithstanding this, Mr. Carolus demands on page 552 more witnesses, proper documents, and the like, even though he could have encountered them all "as clear as day" in the cited author, Master Rothe. Only his partiality toward his father did not allow him to acknowledge his father’s error (which could have been done without a violation of love); instead, he preferred to reject the irreffutable documents of Dr. Geyer, Wecken, Rothe, and other men of Meissen <note>A region in Saxony.</note>. Nevertheless, he continually accuses Mr. Arnold of being biased. How many digressions would he have made if he could have presented such evidence against Mr. Arnold?

(19) Nevertheless, he seeks impertinent instances against the undeniable

### The 163rd Accusation:

He <note>Arnold</note> writes on page 41 of the 3rd Part that it is not in accordance with the truth what is written in Carolus's *Memorabilia*, page 354, concerning the death of Meth <note>Ezekiel Meth, a follower of the mystic Esaias Stiefel.</note> in prison, because his first imprisonment in Dresden is being confused with it.

### Answer:

(1) The matter is evident in itself; Mr. Carolus excuses his father by saying that he found in Kromayer that some of Meth’s companions were led away as prisoners to Königstein <note>A famous fortress and prison in Saxony.</note>, and he had "rationally concluded" from this that the same would have happened to Meth.

(2) When Mr. Arnold, by a good and ready consequence, concludes one thing from another in history, and it concerns one party or another that does not like it, then it must be nothing but falsification and malice. Here, however, Mr. Carolus admits that his father did not find the report in any author, but that he only concluded it "rationally."

(3) Yet he still thinks that Mr. Arnold himself is at fault regarding Carolus Senior with a false report, and thus wishes to extort the point. Indeed, he seeks to maintain his report from Mr. Arnold’s own narrative, regardless of the fact that he doubts whether he understands Arnold correctly. Since indeed Mr. Arnold speaks clearly of Meth’s first imprisonment in the year 1613 in Chapter 4, sections 20 and 23, he afterwards shows in section 30 that in the year 1615, Meth still defended his "swarm" <note>A derogatory term for a sect or group of enthusiasts.</note> at Weissenfels. Indeed, one still has a writing by Meth that was published in quarto in the year 1621, under the title: *Reasons why he withdrew from the Christian community of the A.C. <note>Augsburg Confession, the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church.</note> and now again...*

### The 164th Accusation:

It is read on page 80 of Part III, what a modest judgment was passed on Browne; they were happy to admit that many excellent reminders are to be found in this book, even if they do not accept some other points as so well-known. Carolus, Volume II, page 55 (p. 556.)

### Response:

(1) Mr. Carolus Junior first accepts this testimony of Carolus Senior’s modesty in Part III, Chapter 8, Section 30 with thanks; afterwards, he brings forward his previous complaints again and keeps adding new ones, but without proving them with a single word.

(2) Finally, he claims it was not faithfully reported. Now, Mr. Arnold had not only placed Carolus's words about the excellent reminders found in Browne’s *Religio Medici* <note>A famous work by the English polymath Sir Thomas Browne, exploring the relationship between his medical profession and his Christian faith.</note>, but also reported that these authors do not accept some points as so well-known and thus also find much to criticize in Browne. For it says there: "on the other hand, there were not a few paradoxes in it." Since Mr. Arnold reported all of this, he has indeed reported it faithfully.

(3) And when he wrote "very many," he found it in the *Acta Eruditorum* <note>The first scientific journal of the German-speaking lands, published in Latin from 1682.</note> and in Carolus, who call the book "filled with many excellent warnings" <note>original: "multis præclarè monitis refertum"</note> and, conversely, recognize "not a few paradoxes" <note>original: "non pauca paradoxa"</note> in comparison. However, the judgment of Doctor Rechenberg <note>Adam Rechenberg (1642–1721), a prominent Lutheran theologian at Leipzig.</note> against the book is not in the *Acta Eruditorum*, upon which Mr. Arnold mainly reflected, but only in Carolus.

(4) However, Mr. Arnold had already reported enough such judgments of theologians in the preceding Section 29, such as those of Micraelius, Pfeiffer, and the new editor; likewise, Doctor Müller and Wagner (of whom we treated above in No. 144). Thus, it was not necessary to dwell on more such judgments. Whether Mr. Carolus wants to dismiss it as "putting on glasses" <note>An idiomatic way of saying someone is being overly pedantic or searching for faults where none exist.</note> or not, Mr. Arnold's truthful account is sufficiently proven by this answer.

### The 165th Accusation:

He reports on page 206 of Part III concerning Ussher's <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, known for his biblical chronology and purported prophetic gifts.</note> prophecy regarding the Irish Bloodbath <note>Referring to the Irish Rebellion of 1641, which involved large-scale massacres of Protestant settlers.</note>, how Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian.</note> cites it as an extraordinary thing, and A. Carolus approves of it from him in *Memorabilia*, Book V, Chapter 23, page 990. Page 558.

### Response:

(1) Carolus Senior writes of it from Heidegger in the place cited: "The outcome corresponded to the words." <note>original: "Eventus verbis respondit"</note> Mr. Carolus Junior criticizes that Mr. Arnold adds: "the success occurred correctly and exactly with the words of Ussher." But is it not more than true that it occurred so exactly? Mr. Arnold looked at the wonderful prophecy of the number of years, where Ussher determined forty years from the words of Ezekiel 4:6, which afterwards occurred correctly and exactly in that many years.

(2) Is this then wrong or forbidden? May a historian, in such a remarkable matter which the authors admit, not speak of correctness and accuracy and thus add his judgment? Who has ever forbidden this to a writer "in such a serious and admirable matter"? <note>original: "in re tam seria & admiranda"</note>

(3) And why has Mr. Carolus interpreted this from his own biases as an insertion for the purpose of exaggeration? Is it exaggerated when one notes the correctness regarding a clear fact concerning the exact occurring of the time? Who does not see the unjustified imposition of this good man, who has completely spent his very short lifetime with such useless scrupulosity, which he could and should have applied much more blessedly to his office of pastor and superintendent?

(4) He is not satisfied with Mr. Arnold for placing Ussher among the number of divine prophets: but he should first have thoroughly refuted the other examples of his prophecies that Mr. Arnold cited there in Chapter 21 of Part III, page 206, alongside those above; then Mr. Arnold's statement would have been found false.

(5) He himself calls it a "fore-announcement" <term>fore-announcement: "Vorverkündigung," a prediction or pre-announcement of events</term> on page 559 and recounts even more examples from Jan Hus, Luther, and Dannhauer <note>Johann Konrad Dannhauer (1603–1666), a leading orthodox Lutheran theologian.</note>. However, a "fore-announcement" is in Latin and Greek a "prophetia" or "prophecy." Since it must be admitted that this Ussherian one was not demonic or merely natural, then it must be divine.

(6) And because Mr. Carolus himself mentions that our theologians did not reject or despise such things, but rather valued them as remarkable and recognized that the Holy Spirit with notable, although not imme-

### The 166th Accusation:

Finally, on page 475 of Part IV, it occurs that A. Carolus in *Memorab.* Vol. II, page 212, makes the Pomeranian city of Stargard out of a village in Lusatia <note>Laußniz/Lusatia is a region in eastern Germany.</note> named Stargard. p. 561.

### Response:

(1) Mr. Arnold pointed out this historical error of Carolus Senior in the most lenient manner, as can be seen; and if Mr. Carolus [Junior] had also dealt with Mr. Arnold in such a way alongside others, there would be less of a dispute. However, even here, Mr. Carolus [Junior] doubts without the slightest cause (p. 562) whether Mr. Arnold gave this reminder out of a good heart and what his intention was in doing so. He views everything so wrongly!

(2) He assures us of his father [Carolus Senior] that he well recognized that nothing can happen to a person so easily as to err; he also previously asked the reader for forgiveness with due diligence: therefore, nothing was more pleasant to him than when he was taught the truth of a matter.

(3) Mr. Arnold did the very same in the preface to the edition of his *Church History*, previously recognizing and asking forgiveness for his occasional historical errors and assuring that he would accept instruction. He also amended everything that came to his attention in the supplements. But how has he been treated in return? The responses so far to such detestable denunciations <note>The legal or formal accusations made by the Carolus family.</note> show how the gentlemen accusers practiced none of what they demanded from others. But we proceed with Mr. Carolus [Junior] to the conclusion.

## Response to the Conclusion.

(1) Here, Mr. Carolus [Junior] now fully repeats and accumulates the ugliest accusations anew, and on the contrary, thinks that his "innocence" is now as clear as day after the cited pieces. I hope, however, that this response of mine will have both thoroughly destroyed those denunciations and examined these even more closely to see how they can stand in the court <note>original: "Foro," a Latin legalism for forum or court.</note> of truth or not. As much as one wishes to leave every person, let alone a community or congregation, their innocence, one is also bound to keep the truth alone as a friend without respect of persons.

(2) It is not worth responding anew to the unchristian accusations of Mr. Carolus and the triumph he leads over them, or to delay the intelligent reader with them: Thanks be to God that they have all specifically <note>original: "in specie."</note> been found until now to be either entirely false or such that they do not affect the integrity of the *Church History*. One could still remind and repeat much regarding what violence Mr. Carolus often did to Arnold's words in order to accuse him of a failure: how miserably he defends his Lucas Osiander (the son) and other persons, even his own father; how he would rather reject other Lutherans than admit the mistakes of his own; how he denies things out of hand without reason; how obviously he has set aside the truth and shown partiality; how he makes many out of one ruler; how violently he let himself be carried away by his passions and also scolded the Reformed <note>The Calvinist branch of the Reformation.</note>, whose head in Germany he nevertheless wants to flatter here; especially how he absolutely did not practice what he promised on the title page. For there it was said it should be done not only thoroughly but also modestly, and thus an "innocence" would be shown in deed: instead, here he labels Mr. Arnold in §. 2. p. 564. with three slurs at once, and elsewhere calls him an enemy of pure doctrine, and even a great sinner <note>original: "Frevler."</note> regarding the history of his Osiander. (See above No. 125.) Whether this belongs to modesty or innocence, others may judge.

(3) But who wants to waste precious time with such back-and-forth exchanges <note>original: "Reciprocationibus."</note> when one has examples before them of how soon one might be called away into eternity? Only this must still be contradicted as a wicked slander: where Carolus accuses Mr. Arnold of having conceived a hatred against our entire Church for the sake of the doctrine contained in the Symbolic Books <note>The *Libri Symbolici*, the formal confessions of the Lutheran Church, such as the Augsburg Confession.</note>. This, I say, is too obvious a blasphemy, since it is now clear from Mr. Arnold's teaching and life...

# Part V.
## Concerning other contradictions regarding various writings and matters.
### Chapter 1.
#### Concerning another tract that appeared under the name of "The Innocence."

After considering these indicated objections, it should now be an easy thing to answer the rest, which have appeared here and there against Gottfried Arnold’s books, partly in their own tracts and partly in other writings. However, a truth-loving reader can undoubtedly judge the nature of the remaining objections by the quality of those addressed so far. In the future, if it pleases God and necessity requires, they may be further shown in detail <note>original: "in specie"</note>, though time and opportunity do not allow for it at this moment.

(2) Meanwhile, it will likely not be entirely unpleasant to provide a brief taste <note>original: "speciminis loco"</note> of the nature of the other objections: An author calling himself M. Schultetus has written a tract against the *Church History* <note>Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (Church and Heretic History).</note> under the same title of "The Innocence" (a title which is currently being much abused). He dedicated it to a very well-known theologian, whom he titles "Most Invincible, Most Religious, Most Benign, etc." <note>original: "Invictissimum, Religiosissimum, Benignissimum &c."</note>. But right at the threshold of the preface <note>original: "in limine Præfationis"</note>, he rails against the *Church History* as a book written through the immediate inspiration of the Devil. He calls the author a sworn and eternal enemy of the pure and divine flock, a "Chief Slanderer" <note>original: "Archi-Sycophantam"</note>, and whatever else he continues to rant <note>original: "peroriret"</note> about. This desperate behavior immediately reminds me of what I once read in Dr. Lassinius’s <note>Johannes Lassinius (1636–1684), a Lutheran theologian known for his polemics.</note> *Secrets* <note>original: "Arcanis"</note> on page 206: "At certain times, even the Devil must help in a pinch; if one says that so-and-so has a 'familiar spirit' <note>original: "Spiritum familiarem," a supernatural entity or demon thought to assist a person.</note>, everyone will soon be terrified. For who would not have a loathing for the Devil? And if someone objects that the man prays diligently, leads a good life, and writes spiritual books, then (a politician <note>original: "Statist"</note>) answers: the Devil can disguise himself as an angel of light, and so forth."

(3) Who could expect anything healthy from such contradictions? He insults the blessed Dr. Spener so crudely and wickedly—

(5) Indeed, what wonder is it that living, upright people are so attacked by a young man, since he does not even spare those men who for many years have retained the testimony of truth and godliness even after death? The dear Dr. Henrich Müller <note>A widely respected Lutheran devotional writer (1631–1675).</note> has the echoing reputation of an upright and simultaneously godly theologian throughout our entire church. Yet this author calls Müller's words regarding the "three silent church-idols" <note>Müller famously criticized the Pulpit, the Font, and the Altar when they were treated as dead idols without true living faith.</note>—which so many theologians approved of at the time—"a supreme injury to our church and very closely related to fanaticism" <note>original: "ſumme in Eccleſiam noſtram injuria & fanaticiſmo oppido cognata"</note> on page 160. What could possibly be written more poorly or perversely to prove the "innocence" of certain theologians?

(6) Despite this most immodest and slanderous conduct, he nevertheless pretends in the Preface to desire "modesty" <note>original: "modeſtiam"</note> from those who would refute him, and protests against "insults" <note>original: "convicia"</note> and a "Cyclopean style of writing" <note>original: "cyclopicum ſcribendi genus"; referring to a crude, monstrous, or uncivilized way of writing.</note>. Yet this very style of writing of his is plain to see for every sensible reader and makes one hesitate to engage with him.

(7) The entire work is filled with "irrelevant matters" <note>original: "allotriis"</note> and "digressions" <note>original: "evagationibus"</note> according to the habit of such people. But what is directed against the *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics* (K.H.)—which makes up the very smallest part of the treatise—often defends things that conflict directly and diametrically <note>original: "è diametro"</note> with the consensus of the learned. For example: he wants to thoroughly maintain Scheelhammer’s account of Weigel <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and mystic whose works were often attacked as heretical.</note> on page 133 and following, which was found to be fundamentally false here in Volume IV, Number 162. And when he can go no further, he must finally admit himself that it is a "literary error" <note>original: "Error literarius"</note>, yet he challenges Arnold to prove that it was a fraud; regarding this, one may look at the indicated place in Volume IV.

(8) At the same time, however, he seeks to take revenge for this and wants to convict Arnold of "literary errors" as well, but only in useless minutiae and without reason. He charges on page 136 that Arnold calls Adjutum an Italian, though he was born in Nineveh—notwithstanding that no one really knows if Nineveh is still in the world, and it was known in Wittenberg years ago that this man was quite variable and incorrect in his accounts. Not to mention that in the *Impartial History* (Book 17, Chapter 3, Section 16), he was only actually called an "Italian professor" because he had arrived from Italy, not because he was a born Italian.

(9) It is claimed to be an error that Speratus <note>Paul Speratus (1484–1551), an early Lutheran reformer and hymn writer.</note> wrote the hymn:
> Salvation has come to us here,
or that Ringwald <note>Bartholomäus Ringwaldt (1532–1599), a Lutheran pastor and poet.</note> wrote the other:
> Come here to me, says the Son of God.
Indeed, this latter hymn (as a truly earnest testimony against hypocrisy) is even preferred to be attributed to an Anabaptist <note>original: "Widertäuffer"; a radical wing of the Reformation often persecuted by both Catholics and Lutherans.</note>. All this is done out of bad intentions and against the consensus of all hymnals, indeed, against so many historians and certain documents. Thus, the other alleged errors are of no greater substance, which he himself finally calls "trifles" <note>original: "leviora"</note> on page 140.

(10) Although the "character" <note>original: "Ingenium"</note> of this author can be recognized from these few specimens, I must nevertheless present one more specimen from his first judgment against the *Impartial History* itself. Right at the beginning, on page 2, he accuses the author of the *History* of insulting the first Hamburg reformers, "seizing an opportunity rather than being given one" <note>original: "arreptâ potius quàm datâ occaſione"</note>, and says he does not tell the truth but lies, and is not a "historian" <note>original: "Hiſtoricus"</note> but a "slanderer" <note>original: "Conviciator"</note>. There he cites Volume II of the *History*, Book 16, Chapter 7, Section 13.

(11) The words in that very place read as follows: "In Hamburg, in the year 1523, came M. Stephan Kempe, a Franciscan, who, alongside M. Ordone St. Felio, taught there under many adversities until three years later, when Joh. Ziegenhagen from Magdeburg and Joh. Fritz from Lübeck joined them. However, because both the Papist <note>A common historical term for Roman Catholics, referring to their loyalty to the Pope.</note> and Lutheran preachers scolded one another from the pulpits more than they taught anything good, the Council—for the sake of peace—ordered both sides to conduct everything with gentleness. And yet, when no peace was to be hoped for, a disputation <note>A formal public debate used during the Reformation to settle theological differences.</note> was arranged, in which the Papist shouters were forced to give way. Thus, Dr. Bugenhagen arrived and established the church system in the year 1528, at which time a Church Order was published and Joh. Aepinus was appointed as Inspector." Accompanying this, citations are made from Dresser’s *Saxon Chronicle* p. 519; Chytraeus’s *Saxon Book* page 215; Scultetus’s *Evangelical Annals* Book I, p. 260 and Book II, p. 151; Seckendorf’s *History of Lutheranism* Book I, p. 244, Book II, p. 110, Book III, p. 88, etc.; as well as the authors of the *Annals*.

(12) Let a modest reader now judge for himself, without partiality, where in these words there is any insult, slander, or untruth spoken. Does it not say there that Kempe taught under many adversities, and that the Papist shouters had to give way? This is certainly neither an untruth, nor a slander, nor an insult against the Lutherans. And even if the author says that scolding is attributed to the Lutherans as much as to the Papists, he himself admits on page 5 that the former had cut away the incurable wound with the sword of the Word and publicly refuted the error, but without insults. However, he maliciously conceals the fact that the Council also had to forbid the Lutherans from scolding, just as they did the Papists, because one party exceeded the limits as much as the other.

(13) Such a fact, I say, the opponent denies and rejects against the clear letter of those authors cited in the *K.H.* <note>Abbreviation for Gottfried Arnold's "Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (History of the Church and Heretics).</note> at that very place. For thus writes Scultetus in his *Evangelical Annals* for the year 1528, p. 151: <note>original: "Senatus, ut Reip. paci consuleret, ante biennium omnibus Pontificiis & NB. Evangelicis Concionatoribus in Curiam convocatis mandarat, ut Verbum DEI piè & sincerè juxta interpretationem Scripturæ ab Eccl’esiâ receptam docerent, nec NB. mutuis convitiis inter se publicè ex suggestu certarent."</note> "The Senate, in order to provide for the peace of the Republic, had two years earlier summoned to the City Hall all the Papist and—note well—Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to the Lutheran preachers.</note> preachers, and commanded them to teach the Word of God piously and sincerely according to the interpretation of Scripture received by the Church, and—note well—not to contend among themselves publicly from the pulpit with mutual insults." Here, insults are indeed attributed to both parties, which the Honorable Council had to forbid them from using.

(14) But so that one might not think Scultetus, being a Reformed <note>Calvinist.</note> writer, says such things about the Lutherans out of hatred, let one hear what Seckendorf—in his *History of Lutheranism*, Book I, Section 55, § 139, p. 244—reports from this very Kempe's

<column-break/>

manuscript: <note>original: "Cum vero rixarum & NB. mutuæ inculpationis inter concionatores nullus finis esset, Senatum decretum edidisse, ut prædicatores se invicem publicè & ad offensionem plebis convitiis non proscinderent."</note> "When, however, there was no end to the bickering and—note well—mutual blame among the preachers, the Senate issued a decree that the preachers should not publicly tear each other apart with insults to the offense of the common people." These and other passages are all cited in the *K.H.* at that place and could therefore have easily been found; they also state unanimously that not only the Papists but also our own people used insults. Nonetheless, the author of *Innocence* <note>The critic's treatise titled "Unschuld" (Innocence).</note> contradicts them to their face and writes of our own: "having set aside all insults, they reproved and confuted." This is indeed a manifest falsehood, according to these undeniable testimonies. But at the same time, it is a sign that the author considers insults to be ungodly, yet he himself pours out so many insults in this *Innocence*. And why will one not rather candidly admit such failings of our own people along with the historians, than deny them to the offense of our enemies?

(15) I do not think that a reasonable reader will demand more examples of how things stand with this opponent. Yet, should it be desired by anyone, it can be done at any time. For I am certain that if the rhetorical and sophistical arts, together with the coarse insults, were removed from his writing, nothing truthful or solid would remain. Whoever has eyes will agree with me in this, since this author was caught right at the threshold <note>original: "in limine"; a Latin expression meaning at the very beginning.</note> in such a perverse contradiction.

### Chapter II

->On the Contradictions in Mr. Dr. Löscher’s *Praenotiones*<- <note>Valentin Ernst Löscher (1673–1749) was a prominent leader of Lutheran Orthodoxy and a fierce opponent of Arnold and the Pietists. "Praenotiones" refers to his introductory work "Praenotiones theologicae contra fanaticos."</note>

One can therefore easily calculate that nothing remains of it which has not already been fully settled above. Nevertheless, for the sake of completeness, the passages shall be summarily indicated and illuminated here, to spare the reader much searching.
