# Concerning the Contradictions, Part V, Vol. 2, Ch.

(17) He [Dr. Löscher] first accuses Mr. A. on page 23 of being, in general, a *patron of atheists*. However, anyone who Christianly considers the thorough refutation of such slanders here in Part I, No. 2, 17, and 46; in Part III, No. 17; and in Part IV, No. 143, will be immediately astonished at the ill intent of the accuser and will recognize Mr. A. as free from this cruel crime.

(18) Specifically, Dr. Löscher (1) claims it is stated in the *K. H.* <note>Arnold’s *Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (History of the Church and Heretics).</note> Book 17, Ch. 16, § 1, that Diagoras was falsely called an atheist. To this, it serves to note (a) that not only Diagoras, but also Socrates and others were numbered among the atheists by the pagan priests, even though, according to the testimony of so many ancient writers, they were not. For so that it may be recognized from a single and indeed Christian author, Justin Martyr expressly testifies (*Apol. II. p. 56*): "Socrates sought to discover this (the deception of the pagan gods) through true cause and investigation, and to lead men away from the demons: there, those same demons, through men who delight in malice, brought it about that he was murdered as an atheist and a godless man <note>original Greek: ὡς ἄθεον καὶ ἀσεβῆ</note>." Here, the ancient Christian teacher confesses that evil spirits incite unbelievers to scold innocent people as atheists (or even patrons of atheists).

(19) Antiquity reports almost the same of Diagoras: namely, that he revealed the Orphic rites to the people, betrayed the secrets and horrors of the idols, broke the statue of Hercules, and used the wood for cooking. The former was expressed by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> under this entry as follows: "he told the mysteries to everyone, making them common and small, and turning away those who wished to be initiated <note>original Greek: τὰ μυστήリア πᾶσι διηγεῖτο, κοινοποιῶν αὐτὰ καὶ μικρὰ ποιῶν, καὶ τοὺς βουλομένους μυεῖσθαι ἀποτρέπων</note>"; where he simultaneously reports from Aristophanes that it was proclaimed in Athens that he should be delivered up dead or alive. Now, it is well known that the pagan priests could by no means suffer it when their alleged mysteries were made public, because their entire livelihood depended upon them. Indeed, for this reason, they called such things <term>mysteries</term> <note>original: μυστήρια; hidden or sacred rites.</note> and <term>secret things</term> <note>original: ἀπόῤῥητα; things not to be spoken.</note>, as is clear from the *Etymologico Magno*, Varinus, Suidas, and others. Thus, since Diagoras ventured such a thing, one can easily imagine that he was proclaimed an atheist for that reason.

(20) It is true that Dr. L. (2) says it is written in Sextus Empiricus <note>A physician and philosopher of the Skeptic school.</note> specifically of him that he said: there is no GOD. However, Athenagoras (*Apol. pro Christ. pag. 5*) says the same. Nevertheless, G. Voetius observes from him that "the charge of impiety was *maliciously* pinned on Diagoras" (*Dispp. Select. P. I. p. 197*); others also do not agree with him, but rather state in the plural that he only denied many gods. Minutius

We have already heard the same from Suidas and others.

(21) One sees from this how Dr. L.'s first contradiction does not hold. The following one goes against the 2nd section of the cited chapter in the *K. H.*, namely against these words: "I will only cite those who became so infamous merely out of envy and other evil affects of the clergy." Such cases are then specified one after another in the following sections, first from the Papacy, then from other religions: Browne, Hobbes, Breeckling, Angelus Marianus Wahlmund, and the like.

(22) Thereupon, in section 6 and following, the actual and rightly so-called atheists in Italy, Holland, England, France, etc., are reported with distinction. Furthermore, in section 18, such people are mentioned who, either through hard temptations or through wanton contempt for GOD, fell into despair, or even died while denying and blaspheming Him; for which the then-latest booklet, *The Desperate Atheist* by Dr. Burnet, is recommended. Still further, the <term>Deists</term> <note>Those who believe in God based on reason but reject revelation.</note>, <term>Naturalists</term> <note>Those who believe only in natural laws and forces.</note>, <term>Latitudinarians</term> <note>Protestants who prioritized reason and tolerance over strict adherence to dogma.</note>, etc., are described, and in section 20, everything is attributed to corrupted nature and the mixing of pagan things with Christian ones.

(23) After all these reports, the author first comes to Spinoza in section 36 and following, and begins with this judgment concerning him: Because such men did not know the true way to GOD, and also hindered the light—which would gladly enlighten all men—through disobedience and their own will, or even through shame and sin, they further fell into doubt...

Let everyone judge whether Mr. Dr. Weber and Arnold deserved such a harsh judgment. The injustice of the Mr. Censor lies as clear as the bright sun.

(30) As for what is further cited on pages 88, 91, and 104 in the *Preliminary Notions* <note>original: *Prænotionibus*</note> concerning the **Transfiguration of Jesus** and the **Rightest Way to God**, namely that everything is from God and returns to God: the same has been explained and defended against *The Old and the New* in Part I, numbers 81, 85, 119, and 157, although here Dr. Spener, Prof. F. C. Lange, Mr. Freylinghausen, and others are also accused on that account.

(31) On the 94th leaf, he calls the highly-comforting Evangelical doctrine—that after sadness comes joy, and after darkness light arises in the heart—a **mystery fetched from the depths of Satan**, and cites the *Theological Counsels* <note>original: *Consilia Theol.*</note>, page 310. But that the above is the true meaning of these words in the *Counsels* alone, and indeed quite innocent and according to Scripture, is clearly proven above in the 2nd Appendix of the 1st Part, § 24. May God have mercy on those who blaspheme such precious truths as devilish mysteries! I fear they will be struck with even greater blindness because they so shamelessly and thoughtlessly scold the Divine as devilish.

(32) On page 96, he says Arnold so often recommends the **Divine Magic** <note>original: *Magiam DEI*</note> along with <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>A Swiss physician and alchemist who integrated spiritual and physical sciences.</note> and Felgenhauer. But this imputation has also already been brought forward by him in *The Old and the New*, and here in Part 1, numbers 45 and 72, it has been fully refuted.

(33) It is also handled quite un-Christianly when he incriminates [Arnold] on page 99, as if Mr. Arnold teaches there is no sin, and thus imitates <term>Sebastian Franck</term> <note>A 16th-century radical reformer and spiritualist often criticized by the orthodox.</note> as a wicked man, in the *Theological Counsels*, pages 284 and 360.

For it was shown above in the 2nd Appendix of Part I, § 26, how wickedly Mr. Dr. Löscher perverts the words from the *Counsels* and interprets them poorly. But then his accusation would have been in vain. (b) Arnold also immediately reminded [the reader] there that such things must be taken in a healthy sense, and cited Dr. Spener. Mr. Dr. Löscher remains silent about all of this so that it might only sound truly gruesome. (c) The author has elsewhere explained himself so scripturally and inoffensively regarding this that Mr. Dr. Löscher could well have recognized his blameless intent, had he any desire for truth and love, as is indicated with more detail above in number 43 of Part I.

But he certainly does not understand what this wish encompasses. Should He then not form them according to this, His knowledge and love, or renew them in the image of <term>God</term>? Or do we no longer sing correctly in the well-known <term>Doxology</term> <note>original: *Δοξολογία*—the "Glory Be" prayer.</note>:
> **As it was in the beginning, is now and ever shall be, world without end?** <note>original: *Wie es war von Anfang itzt und immerdar / und von Ewigkeit zu Ewigkeit?*</note>

Did <term>Clement of Rome, the disciple of Paul,</term> perhaps write incorrectly that the end should find the beginning again? <term>Arnold</term> has said no more and no less in this wish than what the <term>Apostles</term> and their <term>disciples</term> teach with clear words.

(39) To be sure, he wants to explain this wish from the <term>Transfiguration of Christ, page 481,</term> where it says:

This is the great mystery of the revealed Godhead. But what does he find here other than a testimony that he too must return to <term>God</term> and give an account for this and all his other perversions and tramplings of the truth? The misunderstanding has also been shown in Part I, numbers 81 and 85: namely, that one must not take such and similar words to mean an outflow and return according to the *essence*, but only according to the *power*. Indeed, in number 86, this entire contradiction is removed from its very foundation. Now, if <term>Mr. Dr. Löscher</term> calls this wish or foundation a <term>Satan</term>, or calls the one who brings it forward such, he must see to it whom he thus persecutes or rails against. I have only had to show the truth, how blameless it is, and how it can be wounded through misunderstanding,

(44) In all these and the following words, there is not a single little word about hatred against heretics, as if such hatred were not right, but merely about the coercion of conscience, persecution, and hostility. A Christian can indeed hate erroneous and flighty spirits, and do so with right earnestness; nevertheless, he can at the same time refrain from persecuting them or acting with real hostility. Instead, according to the mind and teaching of Christ, he should rebuke, convince, and finally avoid them, as all <term>Evangelical</term> <note>Meaning Lutheran or Protestant</note> teachers confess, concerning which more was mentioned above in Part III, No. 32, and in Part IV, Nos. 29 and 121. (45) Had Mr. Dr. Löscher <note>H. D. L.</note> also looked further and more deliberately into the same book, he would have clearly found that the author in every way abhors actual heresies. For there he proves in Chapter 21 of Book VIII, § 7, that heretics teach against the Holy Scripture; in § 9, that they set human inventions against it; in § 16, 17, and 18, that they struggle against godliness; in § 21, that they persist in a perverse sense; in § 19, that they are godless and hypocrites, and so forth. Likewise, in Book VI, Chapter 5, § 29, he shows how most heresies arose from pagan philosophy. Who would not hate and avoid all these things?

(Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie), Arnold's most famous work.</note> Part I, p. 49, are presented in a mangled way, so that the presentation should sound very harsh. For following the words cited by Mr. Dr. Löscher regarding some "concerning things" in Holy Scripture—which might not be accepted by everyone—it is shown immediately and after a mere comma where these words aim, and they are restricted by A. specifically to the passage of Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:4 and following. Now, in that place, Paul speaks of praying and says: "A man who has something on his head while doing so dishonors his head, but a woman dishonors hers if she is not covered," and the like.

(47) Regarding this passage, our own theologians confess that it is not necessarily to be observed by reason of the customs of our country. <term>Balduinus</term> <note>Friedrich Balduin (1575–1627), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> writes in his Commentary:

Commentary on this passage, p. 547: These are the kind of precepts that must be adapted to the custom of each people. This is certainly affirmed by me **Note Well** and is maintained according to the sense of the **Note Well** Holy Spirit **Note Well** **in** the Scripture."

(50) These last words regarding the sense of the Holy Spirit *in* the Scripture are left out by Mr. Dr. Löscher, and he twists them into a completely different meaning—namely, as if A. were positing that he holds the Bible to be a rule according to the "sense of the spirit," meaning his own spirit. He acts as if these words were the same as the others from the letter to Mr. Pfanner, where it says: "in a healthy sense" <note>original: *in sano sensu*</note>; but he claims this sense is the worst possible <note>original: *pessimus*</note>, namely the one contained in the words cited here in § 46 and presented so poorly <note>original: *pessimè*</note> and in a mangled way by Mr. Dr. Löscher. The Christian reader, however, should protect himself against this dangerous error by using Mr. Dr. Spener’s *General Theology*, as well as the later writings of Mr. Dr. Breithaupt, Mr. Dr. Zierold, and Mr. Director Langen, <note>These men were leading figures in the Pietist movement, which emphasized personal holiness over rigid dogma.</note> and pray to God that He might provide help so that one may teach with confidence.

(70) Therefore, the **Anonymous** gentleman follows without any basis the reasoning from **Irenaeus**, as if all Christians were bound to follow this so-called **Creed** <note>original: "Symbolo"</note> not only in matters of substance and opinion, but also in the very words and turns of phrase, lest they be deemed heretics and condemned. (72) It remains undisputed by all who truly possess the Spirit of Christ that the dear **Irenaeus** wrote down his words according to the circumstances of that time in Christian freedom and love, in order to voluntarily bear witness to his faith and that of his brothers; by no means, however, did he intend to bind a single conscience to all the words and phrases. "his and our faith is one and the same" <note>original: "una & eadem illius & nostra est fides"</note>. Finally, in Chapter 41: "Christ the supreme cornerstone sustaining all things and gathering into the one faith of Abraham those who..." etc. Just as the faith of Abraham and the first Christians did not consist precisely in words and turns of phrase, but rather in "power and substance" <term>virtue & argumento; the inner strength and core meaning of the message</term>—as Irenaeus himself expresses it—so too does Irenaeus mean the power and the sense, understanding, or content by "one faith" <term>unam fidem</term> in the passage cited by the **Anonymous** author. Otherwise, he would have had to deviate from his own supposed "Creed" <term>Symbolo; a formal statement of faith</term> as often as he used a different word or "expression" <term>Locution; a way of speaking</term> regarding the points of faith (as such things appear throughout his writings) than what he himself was supposed to have prescribed for himself and others in the **Creed**.

(77) Just as certainly as the Honorable **Anonymous** has proven nothing with the above "passage" <term>loco</term>, he accomplishes even less with the following on page 10 from Book III, Chapter 4. For, 1) Irenaeus indeed praises "the preaching that is everywhere constant and equally persevering" <note>original: "prædicationem undique constantem & æqualiter perseverantem"</note>, but nowhere does he say in a single word that this was maintained through a connection to the exact same words and turns of phrase. Rather, 2) he explicitly confesses that this happens through the Holy Spirit, as the pledge of "incorruptibility" <note>original: "Incorruptelæ"</note>, who makes all true members alive through his—take note—"inspiration" <term>Adspiration; literally a 'breathing into'</term>. Paul calls this the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), which binds a thousand times more firmly through a voluntary harmony of hearts and minds than all outward words and mere turns of phrase, as experience testifies.

(78) Yes, what is more, Irenaeus actually disapproves in this very "passage" <term>loco</term> of the heretics, stating that they would rather be "sophists of words" <term>Sophistæ verborum; people who use clever but misleading language</term> than students of the truth, and therefore always intended different things. Had he wanted to write according to the **Anonymous** author’s sense, it would have had to say: they did not speak with the words and turns of phrase of his **Creed** or the confession which he had presented above. But now he merely complains that they "intended differently," and were sophists of words—that is, they deceived through words by using the same "expressions" <term>Expressiones</term> while meaning something else. For the complaints of the ancients about the heretics are common: that they seemed to teach the same things in words and spoke from the Scriptures, but hid other opinions in their hearts. The word "sophist" <note>original: σοφιςὴς</note> also brings this "sense" <term>Sensum</term> here, as the commentator on Lucian explains in the notes to *The Cock*, page 18 (Graevius edition): "In general they called those 'sophists' who deceived through words" <note>original: καθόλου σοφιςὰς ἐκάλουν τὀς ἀπατῶντας διὰ τῶν λόγων</note>, and thus made themselves appear equal to the orthodox in that regard.

They did not, however, fill their theology with empty technical terms and **vocabulary** <note>original: "Terminis"</note>, but rather spoke earnestly against the follies of Aristotelian **logic** and **metaphysics**."

It does not please him; instead, he accuses the author of wanting to **banish** <note>original: "relegiren"</note> the **use** of philosophy from theology. But the author speaks only 1) of empty technical terms and thus of the **abuse** which the Honorable Anonymous himself **detects** on page 17; and 2) of Aristotle's **logic** and **metaphysics**. Regarding this **philosopher**, however, Justin explicitly says in his *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: "Cohort. ad Gr."</note>, page 6, that his ignorance (<term>ἀγνωσία; agnosia</term>) is clearly to be recognized. He also earnestly **refutes** him here and there, especially in *Questions and Answers to the Greeks* <note>original: "Quæst. & Resp. ad Gr."</note>, page 197. Is it then no longer permitted among Christians to **think** <note>original: "sentire"</note> thus of Aristotle? I am reminded here of the courageous testimony that the learned Barhius sets down in his *Soliloquies*, Book X, Chapter 7, page 827, even so many hundreds of years after pagan **logic** and philosophy were introduced into theology:
> "Why (O man) do you involve yourself in the dreams of pagan fictions? Why do you force yourself to learn the rules of sophists and the entanglements of syllogisms, so that the conclusion might seem fearsome to foolish listeners, and catch adversaries, make books, discourse, debate, and dispute, so that you are often named by fools, held in glory, and judged learned by triflers? Why do you cloud the eyes of the soul with the ravings of human wisdom, which has been purified by the most precious blood of Christ, God and man, so that it may believe purely in God, and not mix human rot with purifying faith? Can your wretched speculations uncover any other foundation of truth in the world besides this? Do your speculations lead there? Are not all other doctrines and wisdoms merely straw and dust, filth and dregs? etc."

<gloss>In particular, he writes on page 829 exactly what the Anonymous criticizes in the author here:</gloss>
> "Among these (the practices of Christianity), what use is philosophical learning? What place is there among these for the glory of sophisticated debates, which the cunning of Satan long ago thrust into the churches and schools? Who heard of such things while the Greek and Latin Church was thriving through tortures and flourishing through persecutions? Who learned by hearsay or experienced by use—**note this**—or inserted into sacred matters the conclusions of syllogisms, so many engines of complication, so many traps of altercation, as pertaining to the instruction or strengthening of faith?"

<meta>This page continues the defense of Gottfried Arnold’s *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics* (often abbreviated as *K.H.*) against a critic referred to as "the Anonymous." The discussion centers on the definition of heresy in the early church. # 652 Concerning the Records of the Fathers. Vol. 5, Ch. 3.

The description of a scandalous teacher of heresy stands quite deliberately expressed in the *History of the Church and Heretics*, Book II, Section 2, Chapter 8, Paragraph 7: **"They (the teachers) do not place the distinction between the orthodox and the erroneous—Note—in mere theoretical opinions, or even in certain words and** *symbols*, **but—Note—primarily in a perverse nature that runs contrary to Christianity—Note—as it manifests itself in practice."** From this, one sees that it is not entirely denied that heresy consists in doctrine as well; rather, it is denied that it consists *primarily* and *solely* or *merely* therein. No one can truthfully find fault with this <note>original: "improbiren"</note>; instead, one would rather agree with Dr. B. Meisner <note>Balthasar Meisner (1587–1626), a Lutheran theologian</note>, as this theologian confesses in the Preface to Part I of *Sober Philosophy*, page b. 2: "Turn through the catalog of heretics and the histories of all centuries, and you will see clearly how—Note—every heresy was born from previous impiety and perversity of life." <note>original Latin: "Evolve Catalogum hæreticorum, omnivm seculorum historias, & videbis luculenter, quomodo NB. omnis hærefis ex prænuate impietate & vitæ perverfitate enata sit."</note> No less will one agree with the late Arndt <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), author of "True Christianity"</note>, who demonstrated such a truth through an entire chapter, namely Chapter 36 in the First Book of *True Christianity* <note>original: "W. C." for *Wahres Christenthum*</note>.

(100) Mr. Anonymous exerts himself (1) to prove that the Fathers described the heretics as being erroneous in doctrine. This **truth**, according to the style of Christ and John—indeed, of the entire Scripture—includes not only theory but also practice. On the contrary, there are also such obvious passages from Irenaeus cited in the *History of the Church and Heretics* which can never be understood otherwise than that heresy consists both in false doctrine and a wicked life, and that the latter is inseparable from the former. One rightly pays no mind to the reviling of a loveless pen, which also contradicts the otherwise beloved Colbergius <note>Ehrenegott Daniel Colberg, a critic of mysticism</note> on page 45, and knows that God and His lovers judge with a completely different and better judgment. Such words of abuse not only do no harm, but they also bring a blessing to those who suffer injustice with Christ, until the Lord Himself looks into the matter.

Concerning the first, namely <term>Priscillian</term> <note>A 4th-century Spanish bishop executed for heresy</note>, Bishop of Avila, the judgment of <term>Jerome</term> <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 347–420 AD)</note> is cited in Section 11 from his *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Volume 1, page 194, which reads: <note>original: "Priscillianus Abilæ Episcopus, qui NB. factione Hilarii & Ithacii Treveris à Maximo NB. tyranno, cæsus est, edidit multa opuscula, de quibus ad nos aliqua pervenerunt : Hic usque adeò à nonnullis Gnosticæ i. e. Basilidis & Marcionis, de quibus Irenæus scripsit, hæreseos accusatur, defendentibus aliis, non ita eum sensisse, ut arguitur."</note> "Priscillian, Bishop of Avila, who <insert>note:</insert> by the faction of Hilarius and Ithacius was killed at Trier by the <insert>note:</insert> tyrant Maximus, published many short works, some of which have reached us: He is accused by some of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the heresy of Basilides and Marcion, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, saying he did not believe as is alleged." Likewise, passages from Sulpitius Severus are cited one after another—works which are in everyone’s hands—who recounts a great deal against Priscillian's enemies. At the same time, the words of the famous <term>Spanheim</term> <note>Friedrich Spanheim, a 17th-century theologian</note> from his *Oration on Christian Decay*, page 560, are cited: <note>original: "Quiniplum Priscillianum Abilæ Episcopum, NB. aequior a fortè sentientem audisse tam domum impiæ familiæ in Hispanis patrem, postquam Coëpiscoporum quorundam factione opprimendus fuit, ex Hieron. haud obscurè colligimus."</note> "Regarding Priscillian, Bishop of Avila, <insert>note:</insert> who perhaps held more favorable views, we gather quite clearly from Jerome that he was called the father of a godless family in Spain only after he was to be oppressed by a faction of certain fellow bishops." If these proven men could not approve of such a trial against Priscillian, whom the tyrant Maximus had beheaded, but instead testify that many among the ancients defended him: why then should Arnold be considered in the wrong for it?

(127) So it is also with the second, namely <term>Montanus</term> <note>A 2nd-century Christian who claimed to receive new prophecies</note>; concerning his circumstances, the testimonies of Jerome and others are cited in Section 13, and also

The late Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation</note> writes significantly in the 8th Wittenberg German Part, f. 91, regarding the 128th Psalm: Jovinian (against whom Jerome <note>Hieronymus/Jerome, a 4th-century Church Father known for his Latin translation of the Bible</note> wrote poisonous books *for celibacy and against marriage* <note>original: "pro coelibatu contra conjugium"</note>) had, as it appears, more skill and understanding in one finger than Jerome had in his entire body. Whoever does not wish to agree with this may take it up with the cited theologians, whom Arnold was safely able to follow in this matter.

(130) Finally, it is all too miserable when page 461 is also cited, as if old heretics were defended there. It is proven there in §. 25 that sometimes such sects were devised that hardly existed *in reality* <note>original: "in rerum natura"</note>, such as the Ascites (or Flask-bearers) and the Pattalorhynchites (or Tascodrugites), who were mostly invented by the Greeks long after the decline. What stout-hearted and sensible man would still uphold such fables today, or look askance when they are exposed? The good testimonies of their lives are presented only *comparatively* <note>original: "comparativè"</note> and in comparison with others: that is indeed an impartial report, and no exculpation of the heretics, much less of their heresies.

(134) Finally, A. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), the author being defended, known for his radical church history.</note> is said to have disparaged the *Council of Nicaea* <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the Nicene Creed and addressed the Arian controversy.</note> on page 396. But how can he disparage it, when right at the beginning of Section 21 (Chapter 19 of the 8th Book), he produces our own theologians, Chemnitz <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a leading Lutheran theologian known as the "Second Martin."</note> and Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note>, who do not value this Council as equal to the first Synods <note>Referring to the earliest gatherings of the Apostolic era.</note> or approve of all its conclusions? Do these theologians also disparage it when they select excerpts against the Papists <note>A common early modern term for Roman Catholics.</note> regarding the citations of this Synod? *The age of the Nicene Synod is not the most ancient time of Christ's Church* <note>original: "Seculum Nicenae Synodi non est vetuſtiſſimum tempus Ecclesiae Christi"</note>, as they say; the former in the *Examination of the Council of Trent, Part II, Book on the Supper, page 473* <note>original: "Exam. Conc. Trid. Part. II. L. de Coena pag. 473."</note>; the latter in the *Theological Commonplaces on the Supper, Number 297, Volume V, page 165* <note>original: "Loc. Theol. de Coena Num. 297. To. V. p. 165."</note>? What was further observed about this Council in the *Portrayal* <note>Referring to Arnold's book *Die Abbildung der ersten Christen* (The Portrayal of the First Christians).</note> is not only sufficiently proven there with the *authority* of certain *writers*, but is also more thoroughly deduced in the *Church History* <note>Referring to Arnold's *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* (Impartial History of the Church and Heretics).</note>, and vindicated and explained here in Part III, Number 14.

(135) Whatever has been brought forth against the *Form of an Evangelical Teacher* <note>Another of Arnold's works, likely *Die Gestalt eines Evangelischen Lehrers* (1698).</note> is not specified there. There is also enough time in the future to investigate such accusations, as they will likely be no better or more accurate than those we have examined thus far and found to be too light.

(136) Various other counter-arguments against the *Church History* are also said to have been published here and there. However, in our region, these were not particularly well-known or obtainable; except for some academic *disputations* <note>Formal academic debates or theses common in 17th-century universities.</note>, which are of just as little weight and Christian moderation or sincerity as to actually infringe upon the truth itself. The nature of the very first disputation against the *Church History* can be seen at the end of Part IV of the same; of others, very clear *examples* <note>original: "Specimina"</note> are found right here in Part V, Sections 16 to 57. Many things are also hidden here and there in all sorts of little tracts, prefaces, *dedications*, and the like, and very little of it has come to our sight. Who would want to spend time or effort seeking out all such trifles, unless one were to consider it necessary at some later time to gather them all together and answer them once and for all. One person always copies his *contradictions* from another, and it is found that they repeat many untruths three times or more, as is evident right here in the aforementioned Part V at the cited location.

(138) Everyone can easily see that this is not a *refutation* at all, but a mere unproven *imputation* <note>An accusation or attribution of a fault to someone.</note>. For if it were to be the former, then it would have to be thoroughly and extensively proven and confirmed that the Papal *distinction between Clerics and Laity* <note>original: "diſtinction inter Clericos & Laicos"</note> is good and Evangelical, since the *contrary* is shown from our theologians right here in Section 93 and following. Likewise, it must be proven that A. *censures* <note>original: "perstringire"</note> the affected *episcopacy* of *Constantine the Great* <note>The Roman Emperor who legalized Christianity. These may indeed be important capital complaints, but they are not touched upon by a single syllable, let alone *demonstrated*. And yet it is boasted that A. has been *confuted*. But what could not be *confuted* in such a manner, and what honest man would finally be safe from such a *refutation*?

(18) If it should seem questionable to a reader that Vanini's <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher executed in 1619 for atheism and blasphemy; Arnold's work was controversial for suggesting such executions were unchristian.</note> burning is disapproved of, let one consider what Dr. Titius <note>Gottlieb Gerhard Titius (1661–1714), a prominent legal scholar and professor at Leipzig.</note> of Leipzig recently deduced generally regarding the slaying of atheists in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical Law* <note>original: "Geiſtl. Rechts"</note>, Chapter 5, § 61. There, he writes against Grotius, Pufendorf <note>Hugo Grotius and Samuel von Pufendorf, two of the most influential legal philosophers of the 17th century, who generally supported the state's right to punish atheists.</note>, and others as follows: "When one reflects that atheism, in regard to human society, is no crime, and a known atheist is not only no worse than a godless, superstitious, or sanctimonious hypocrite, but is also better in many respects; and after this considers that, in regard to God, it is indeed a great crime, but (Note well!) one not to be remedied by human punishments; and finally considers the cruelty by which a human being is executed without knowledge of God, who might perhaps have come to such knowledge if one had had patience with him; such a person will easily be able to judge what in this matter is rational or foolish, lawful or Papist. <note>In this context, "Papist" is used as a pejorative for what the author considers irrational or authoritarian religious practices.</note> All of this is thus left to the judgment of the wise. And with this, we may rightly let the matter rest."

C."</note> himself will no doubt admit that even in common life, and outside the so-called Mystical Way, enough **hypocrisy**, **spiritual pride**, **contempt for Holy Scripture**, and the like occurs. Yet he lists these here as mere faults of the *Mystics* <note>original: "Mysticorum"</note> in order to portray them in such a bad light.

(2) Furthermore (c) he says: "It might well seem to many reflective minds that such things are intended for the excuse of some *Fanatics* <note>original: "Fanaticorum" — a term used by critics to describe radical religious dissenters.</note> and of that which the *Author* has done and written before all the world; so that, despite all this, and with ongoing *excesses*, one should still consider such people to be well-meaning and pious men. There would be much to *reply* to this; but to stay with the *Author* for now, Mr. C. betrays his suspicious heart very powerfully, and yet excuses it as a 'reflective mind.' For he speaks merely of what 'seems' to be, and does not prove his evil suspicion even with a semblance of a reason; he thus *merits* no *specific rebuttal* <note>original: "special-Refutation"</note>. Nevertheless, he writes down such evil slanders as if they were true; however, regarding this, the second chapter of the second book in this very same *Treatise* <note>original: "Tractat"</note> should be read. The *Author* has presented his honest Christian *intention* in the preface and throughout to all upright readers, to which his conscience also gives testimony before GOD—indeed, it will give testimony on that Day—how faithfully he meant it toward both friend and foe. What he has written and done before all the world is sufficiently defended here against these evil judgments. But let Mr. C. also examine his heart, how he meant it with these suspicious judgments, in which he bases himself only on appearances; then he will surely be terrified by it. He confesses immediately thereafter: A. <note>Referring to Arnold himself</note> makes many good reminders against 'splinter-judging' <note>A reference to Matthew 7:3, judging the small faults of others while ignoring one's own.</note>. But how poorly does the Mr. *Censor* attend to them?

(3) He also confesses (d) that A. makes many good reminders on page 168 against the contempt of Holy Scripture; but instead of Mr. C. *limiting* or withdrawing his previous accusations—as if A. despised the Scripture—he heaps up such sins even further. For he presents as very offensive what A. writes on page 171. Now the words there in §. 10 read thus: "And it cannot be sufficiently described how easily and imperceptibly a **Preacher**, even now, can fall into a mere literal scholarship, while he—**NB.** <note>Latin: "Nota Bene" or "Note Well"</note>—according to custom, must constantly explain the Bible and preach something about it. In doing so, the **Spirit** is so easily **quenched**—**NB.**—and abandoned; while on the other hand—**NB.**—nothing but rationally devised propositions and doctrines arise in the brain without power and

<meta>catchword: Life</meta>

(677)

**life**: So that nothing is more necessary here than **NB.** the discipline and power of the Holy Spirit, etc." This is proven there from the clear words of **Paul in Titus 3:9; 2 Timothy 2:23; 1 Timothy 6:4; 1:4;** and thereafter from **Jerome, Didymus, Mark the Ascetic, Maximus, Ephrem the Syrian, etc.**, who say exactly the same thing in their own terms. But so that this foundation (which is recognized by all true Christians and which has convicted Mr. C.'s conscience) might seem offensive, he leaves out the most necessary parts and presents the words entirely *mutilated* <note>original: "mutilirt"</note> like this: "It cannot be described how easily a preacher, who must constantly preach on the Bible, can fall into mere literal scholarship and quench the Spirit." This makes it sound as if the author considered all preaching on the Bible to be dangerous or seductive—even though it is explicitly stated there that it is only meant for the case when one, in explaining and preaching, falls into **NB.** nothing but rational propositions and doctrines, namely those that arise in the brain without power and life. But this is indeed exactly what all true **Theologians** have unanimously taught against false scribes in order to maintain the true ones. Why then is it offensive to Mr. C., unless he perhaps finds himself in that which has been warned against here? And why did he not clearly show the offense, so that his neighbor could guard against it?

(4) He further accuses (e) on page 148 that on page 174 the **Anointing** <note>The "Anointing" (Salbung) refers to the inner guidance of the Holy Spirit as mentioned in 1 John 2:27.</note> is set in opposition to the **Scripture**, as the sole ground of faith. Now, in §. 14, the words of **Didymus of Alexandria** <note>original: "Didymi Alexandrini"</note> regarding **1 John 2** are cited, where he says: "Even if someone preached the Scripture, one should still not look to him if he has departed from the will of the same and turned to godless opinions, and thus—**NB.**—had abandoned the **Anointing** which he received from the Holy Spirit." To this, A. adds this *observation*: "By which, then, the Anointing of the Holy Spirit (who teaches all things according to **1 John 2:22**) was pointed to as the ground of faith, without which—**NB.**—even with the external words of Scripture, one can nonetheless be an Antichrist and a heretic." Here he certainly does not set the Anointing against the Scripture (as Mr. C. claims), insofar as both letter and Spirit are understood together; but rather only against the **external words of Scripture**, insofar as they are, as it were, separated from the Spirit by erroneous and worldly scholars, or used without the Holy Spirit, whom they admittedly needed on their side for that purpose. What, then, can be spoken more innocently, but also what can be more evilly twisted? Mr. C. should have remembered the testimony which he himself gave to Mr. A.

<summary>In this passage, Gottfried Arnold defends his work against a critic ("Mr. C.") who accuses him of encouraging "fanaticism" and despising the Bible. Arnold argues that "literal scholarship" without the Holy Spirit's guidance leads to empty preaching, a point he supports with citations from the Apostle Paul and several Church Fathers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gottfried Arnold's point-by-point rebuttal of Mr. C.'s (Ernst Salomon Cyprian's) critiques. Arnold is defending his views on the relationship between the written Word of God and the inner experience of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

<header>* ( 678 ) *</header>

Published publicly in the year 1704, p. 484: He points specifically (in the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ) to the Holy Scripture, and connects the Divine Power with the same; he also insists that God reveals nothing in the soul other than what already stands in the Scripture. And on p. 480 he writes: "We praise once again that the Holy Author <note>Arnold is likely referring to himself in the third person or quoting a supportive review of his work.</note> writes: 'Do not separate the outward Word from the inward, for both are one.'" Following such personal testimonies, they nevertheless wish to accuse him here of the exact opposite, but certainly against all fairness and love.

(5) It is also (f) contrary to him that on p. 181, Christ's words in John 5:39 are understood in the **imperative** <note>original: "Imperativo." This refers to the command "Search the Scriptures!" rather than the statement "You search the Scriptures."</note>, yet he brings nothing against it. Regarding the doctrine of the **letter** <note>The "letter" refers to a purely literal or academic reading of the Bible without spiritual life.</note>, however, he says on p. 188ff. that it is pushed to the no small **prejudice** <note>original: "Præjudiz"</note> of the Scripture. But whoever's conscience tells him that he faithfully gives space to the Holy Spirit when dealing with the Scripture will not view the doctrine of the letter as a prejudice—as did the ancient scribes and Pharisees—but as a salutary warning, which is indeed necessary even for the most experienced. And if Mr. A. <note>The Author, Gottfried Arnold.</note> had spun such a doctrine out of his own brain, one might call it a preconceived notion. But as it is, he presents nothing but undeniable **Passages from the Fathers** <note>original: "Loca Patrum" — writings of early Christian leaders.</note> and primarily from our own theologians, such as on p. 184 Irenæus, Tertullian, Ambrose, Jerome, etc.; on p. 186 Theodoret, Chrysostom, Caesarius, Prosper of Reggio, and from our most prominent teachers on p. 188ff. Luther, Melanchthon, Arnd, Selnecker, Musculus, Brentius, Avenarius, Varenius, etc. How then can one say that all these teachers have created a prejudice against the Holy Scripture? Can one really not tolerate the ancient, unanimous truth?

(6) Regarding the misunderstanding of the doctrine of **Christ's Indwelling**, Arnold begins to speak very well on p. 250, where it says: (g) However, he still wants to consider those as truly pious for whom the **history of Christ outside of us** <note>The "history of Christ outside of us" refers to the historical facts of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, as opposed to the internal "mystical" experience of Christ.</note> is "disgusting" and "too simple," and that these should only be temptations for them, even though many remained in that state until their end. Mr. C. could have seen from the title and the entire context that Mr. A. does not consider such erring people to be truly pious at all; in that he explicitly calls such a title before the History of Christ on p. 258, §. 3, such a **difficulty** <note>original: "Schwürigkeit"</note> that does not pass without harm and danger to the true, only way to life. Now, whoever describes such people as those who suffer harm and danger to their salvation cannot possibly hold them to be truly pious, but perhaps to some extent well-meaning or zealous souls, as they are also described in §. 4.

<page-num>679</page-num>
<header>* ( 679 ) *</header>

Thus, Mr. C. sees how his allegation is once again in vain, as he so eagerly seeks to snatch at something where he finds nothing.

(7) Mr. A. is also said (h) to excuse those who want to **be Christ** (p. 259), though with many good reminders. But let one see whether this is called "excusing" when Arnold writes on p. 257, §. 17: "From this, that particular **imagination** is to be properly judged and prevented, when some people, on the occasion of the doctrine of union with Christ, have wanted to conclude <note>Note: "NB." (nota bene) — mark of importance.</note> in a perverted way as if they were now **Christ himself essentially**..." — which they wanted to derive from such sayings of the teachers — though these teachers understood it quite differently than human reason thinks. Where then, further on p. 258 and 259, nothing else is proven than that the **Fathers** <note>original: "Patres"</note> sometimes used some such expressions, but not like those who want to be Christ, according to the speech of the Mr. Censor. For of these latter, Arnold says quite clearly on p. 264 §. 28, it is an **abuse and dangerous application**, item §. 29, a **false conclusion**, and §. 30, such people (who namely want to be Christ and God) apply and use the innocent meaning of the teachers very badly through their reason; further, p. 267, the Fathers had criticized and rejected such abuse in certain people and parties; it is a great concept of the **participation in the Divine nature**, yes, a **dangerous error**, where some, out of a false delusion, have held and presented themselves as God or Christ, who then further on p. 268 are called **errant spirits**, even **godless and devilish people** in Ruusbroec <note>original: "Rusbrochio" — Jan van Ruusbroec, a 14th-century Flemish mystic.</note>. And finally, p. 269 §. 39 concludes: That for no error or false concept and statement on such matters <note>Note: "NB." (nota bene) — mark of importance.</note> has the word been spoken, but rather it has been contradicted throughout: with the exhortation that such people should reconsider and be more modest. The reader can see from this whether that is called excusing or not, and whether these good reminders do not also suffice for the manner of speaking about **deification** <note>original: "Vergöttern" — the mystical concept of becoming "god-like" through union with the divine.</note>, which Mr. C. calls into question. If one takes the trouble to read the passages of Macarius <note>original: "Macarii" — likely Macarius of Egypt.</note> and other Fathers themselves, and compares them with the clear distinction that Mr. A. cites, then one will gladly acquiesce and not, like Mr. C., commit a fault through unfounded accusations.

(8) This further alleges (i) that Arnold teaches very poorly regarding **external worship** <note>original: "äusserlicher Gottesdienst" — traditional church rituals, liturgy, and formal services.</note> on p. 174: namely, that a Christian can indeed endure it and participate, but it is not true worship. But where does that stand in the cited passage? There, Mr. A. proves from the Scripture and the theologians that worship must primarily be spiritual and internal. Following that, it says of the external in §. 4, that a true Christian, alongside his internal worship, also **endures** the external...

...and out of love for the weak, may and can keep them. How this is to be understood, the Author explains thus: **It is certain that external worship in certain assemblies, because of human misery, cannot be entirely without some order and manner, and consequently, that certain types and orders, which are in themselves innocent, may well be retained in public worship. Indeed, he specifically sees regarding truly edifying orders that they cannot be rejected by the Gentile Christians, but rather that God Himself has always loved and blessed such things. And in Section 6, it says that in the first Church, there were sensible orders at the gatherings.** From these and the following passages, Mr. Censor's poor interpretation refutes itself—namely, his claim that Arnold does not consider external worship to be the right kind. Yet this imputation has already been expressly <note>original: "ex professo"</note> rejected above in numbers 6, 35, 52, 99, and 143, and in Part II, number 5.

(9) Regarding **Henry More** <note>A famous English philosopher and "Cambridge Platonist" known for his mystical leanings.</note>, whom Mr. C. calls very disreputable, more can be seen in Part II, number 94; I do not believe, however, that Mr. C. is capable of judging whether More is Evangelical <note>meaning "Lutheran" in this context</note> or not, as the previous investigation has shown. And this following un-Evangelical judgment shows it even more, where he judges on page 249: **"Mr. Arnold's teaching on theology does not sit well with Mr. Spener." On page 150, Arnold refers there to the late Dr. Spener's <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism."</note> general divinity regarding the question of the difference between external and literal knowledge from internal and living knowledge—which Dr. Spener proved irrefutably from ancient and modern teachers. Who, then, teaches poorly or un-Evangelically: the one who, with all true Evangelical teachers and the Scripture itself, does not consider the literal and external knowledge to be sufficient and soul-saving, or the one who says the opposite but does not prove it? May God have mercy on the misery that the precious Evangelical truth must no longer be called good doctrine!**

(10) Finally, it also does not sit right with him when Mr. Arnold gives a Christian account and explanation for his behavior thus far: but he does not state clearly what is wrong with it, so the matter rests there; it has also already been discussed above. And so far, these reports have come to our hands.

(5) Finally, Arnold has said much less than Dr. Ittig <note>Thomas Ittig (1643–1710), a prominent Lutheran theologian and professor at Leipzig.</note> in Leipzig; for he reasons about it thus in his *Spiritual Law*, published there in the Lanckian bookstore, Book II, Chapter 2, Section 59:

> "As far as the duty of the parishioners is concerned, they are (1) bound according to **Papal principles** to hear God’s Word nowhere else than in their own parish. Therefore, in the past, foreign parishioners were cast out if they were caught in another church. See Ziegler on *The Rights of the Royal Majesty* <note>original: "ad F. Roy J J C"</note> 1. 2. 7. 14 § 9.
> For the Papal clergy makes a **closed guild** out of divine service; therefore, they had to prevent even the slightest opportunity by which the 'customers' might be lured away from 'buying' there. However, this is a **godless coercion of conscience**, and thus in no way to be approved. Dr. Falckner, *On Parishes*, chapter 3, section 2. According to these same doctrines, the parishioners must also make use of confession and the Lord’s Supper at certain times and specifically in their own parish, otherwise they are compelled to do so by force—which is also approved by Carpzov and not rejected by Siegler. But that this too is Papal and wrong, I will show in the proper place," etc.

<meta>The previous page concluded the alphabetical index of subjects and names. This page begins a bibliographic appendix, listing the various works by Gottfried Arnold that were cited or defended within the preceding text.</meta>

# Dear Reader /

The writings, which have been partly cited and defended in these considerations, are titled and available as follows:

## In Folio <note>A "folio" is a large book format where the paper is folded only once, resulting in large, prestigious volumes.</note>

*Portrait of the First Christians*, 1697. <note>original: "Abbildung der ersten Christen"</note> Halberstadt, published by C. Genschen.
*Impartial History of the Church and Heretics*. <note>original: "Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie"; this is Arnold's most famous and controversial work, which argued that "heretics" were often truer Christians than the established church hierarchy.</note> Leipzig, published by Thomas Fritsch.
*Universal Chronological History Table*. <note>original: "Tabula Hist. Chronol. Universalis"</note> ibid. <note>short for "ibidem," meaning the same place/publisher as above.</note> 1698.

## In Quarto <note>A medium-sized book format where the paper is folded twice.</note>

*The Lives of the Ancient Fathers*, Halle, at the Orphanage, 1700. <note>The Halle Orphanage (Waysenhauß) was the center of Pietist activity under August Hermann Francke.</note>
*Lives of the Believers from the Year 1500 to 1700*. ibid. 1701.
*The Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, or Epistle Sermons*. <note>original: "Epistel-Postill"</note> Leipzig 1704, published by Thomas Fritsch.
*Gospel Message of the Glory of God in Christ, or Gospel Sermons*. ibid. 1706.
*True Christianity of the Old Testament from the Proverbs of the Holy Father Moses*. ibid. 1707.
*Supplements, Illustrations, and Corrections to the Church History*. <note>original: "Supplementa, Illustrationes und Emendationes der K. Hist."</note> ibid. 1703.
*True Portrait of Interior Christianity*. ibid. 1709.
*Preface to Dr. Allix's Remarks on the Holy Trinity*. <note>original: "Vorrede über D. Alix Aussprüche von der H. Dreyeinigkeit"</note> ibid. 1709.
*Preface to Ruysbroeck’s Spiritual Writings*, <note>Jan van Ruysbroeck (1293–1381) was an influential Flemish mystic.</note> Frankfurt, published by B. de Launoy 1706.
*Deviations, Errors, and Temptations of Well-Intentioned People*, Leipzig, published by Thomas Fritsch. 1708.
*Confession regarding the Resignation of Profession*, <note>Arnold famously resigned his professorship at Gießen after only a few months, feeling that academic life was incompatible with true Christian humility.</note> Frankfurt 1698, and other editions.
*Explanation and Renewal*, Leipzig 1700, published by Thomas Fritsch.
*Clarification*. ibid. 1701.
*Representation*. ibid.
*Historical-Theological Observations*. Ibid. 1709.

## In Octavo <note>A standard-sized book format, roughly the size of a modern hardcover.</note>

*History of Christian Kinship and Brotherhood*. <note>original: "Historia Cognationis & Fraternitatis Christianæ"</note>
*History of Christians Condemned to the Mines*, <note>original: "Historia Christianorum ad Metalla damnatorum"</note> Goslar 1697, published by J. C. König.
*History and Description of Mystical Theology*. <note>original: "Historia & Descriptio Theologiæ Mysticæ"</note> Leipzig 1702.
The same work in German. ibid.
*Writings of Macarius and other Ancients, or Memorial of Ancient Christianity*. <note>Macarius of Egypt was a 4th-century monk whose spiritual homilies were highly prized by Pietists.</note>
Also: *Use and Abuse of Evil Examples*, Goslar, published by J. C. König 1700.
*Concise Church History of the Old and New Testaments*, Leipzig 1698 and 1706.
*Mystery of Divine Wisdom*. <note>original: "Geheimniß der Göttlichen Weißheit"</note> ibid. 1700.
*The Surest Way through Christ to God* 1700. ibid.

<column-break/>

*Married and Unbound Life*. ibid.
*The Love-Confessions of J. More* 1704. <note>likely referring to Gertrude More, an English nun and mystic.</note>
*Theological Counsels and Answers* ibid. 1704.
*The Garden-Plants of Wisdom*. ibid.
*Epistles of the Ancients*, Quedlinburg, published by P. T. Calvisius 1700.
*Signs of These Times* ibid. 1698.
*Letters of Cardinal Petrucci with a Preface on Primary Devotion*. <note>Pier Matteo Petrucci was a leader of the Quietist movement in Italy.</note> Halle, at the Orphanage 1705.
*The Book of Wisdom and Sirach translated and explained*, ibid. <note>original: "Das Buch der Weißheit und Sprachs"</note>
*Spiritual Form of a Teacher* ibid. 1704.
*Travels of the Apostle Peter*, Berlin, published by J. M. Rüdiger 1702.
*The Caused and Moderated Flood, along with an Historical Account of the Signs of such Floods and Great Cold*, ibid. 1709.
*Preface to Spiritual Sermons on P. Schröder’s Reminders to his Congregation*. Hamburg, published by G. Liebezeit 1707.
*Gospel Speeches on the Gospels with a Preface on the Heroic Method*. <note>original: "de Methodo Heroica"</note> Leipzig, published by Thomas Fritsch 1709.

## In Duodecimo <note>A small, portable pocket-book format.</note>

*The Epistles of St. Clement and Barnabas*, Halle, at the Orphanage 1689.
*First Martyrdom*. ibid.
*Divine Sparks of Love*, Frankfurt, published by J. D. Zunner 1701.
*Jesus in the Soul*, ibid.
*The Cherubic Wanderer by Johannes Angelus*, ibid. <note>Johannes Scheffler, known as Angelus Silesius, was a famous mystic poet.</note>
*Candid Confessions* 1698, 1700. ibid.
*Perception of the Current Times*, Magdeburg 1699.
*Dr. Molinos' Spiritual Guide*. <note>Miguel de Molinos was the founder of Quietism, a movement emphasizing inner stillness.</note> Goslar, published by J. C. König 1700 and 1707.
*Spiritual Writings of Guyon*. <note>Madame Guyon was a prominent French mystic often persecuted for her views on "disinterested love" for God.</note> ibid.
*Paradise Garden of Delight*. Stendal, published by J. H. Campen 1709.

->**TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY**<-
<note>original: "SOLI DEO GLORIA"</note>
